Second, regarding the teaching of the miracle of gathering the retinue: then, through the previous signs, he exhorted the bodhisattvas of the world systems of the ten directions, such as the Bodhisattva Samantaraśmi, the principal of the retinue of the Tathāgata Ratnākara in the eastern world system Ratnavatī, and the Bodhisattva Aśoka, the principal of the retinue of the Tathāgata Aśokaśrī in the southern world system Aśokā. In order to make it understood that it is improper to listen to the Dharma from others without having asked one's own guru, those bodhisattvas paid homage to their respective Jinas and asked for the reason. Also, having heard those Jinas speak the praises of the Teacher, they requested permission to go to this field and obtained it accordingly. In order for those Jinas to make offerings to this Teacher, they bestowed upon them gifts of lotuses made of various jewels, words inquiring about his health, and instructions saying, "Be heedful in that impure field." Having received these, they worshipped the Jinas along the way, arrived in this field, and with paying homage to the Teacher preceding it, they blessed the collections of offerings. Having taken their respective seats, they offered the earlier words inquiring about his health and the lotuses; this is the second miracle of illumination. Then, when the Teacher scattered those lotuses in their respective directions in order to make offerings to the sublime Dharma, emanations sat upon them, and having realized that the disciples endowed with the fortune to be taught the Mother had gathered, he spoke this precious sutra of the perfection of wisdom that is virtuous in the beginning, middle, and end. Because I have not seen the introductory setting explained extensively in the manuals of our own tradition, with the thought of hoping to benefit slightly myself and others of equal fortune, I have explained it by gathering from various texts and slightly elaborating.

From among these ten, as for the initial teaching of the generation of the mind here: for example, just as a painter of deities strikes a plumb line so that faults such as crookedness do not occur in the deity's body, this is in order to know that whatever dharmic activity is done, so that it does not go astray but becomes solely the cause for Buddhahood, one must initially clearly invoke at least an artificial generation of the mind as a motivation. translation: Incidental topic. Secondly, demonstrating through an example the incidental point that the śrāvakas' teaching of the perfection of wisdom is due to the power of the Buddha: The meaning taught by the three verses beginning with 'Here in Jambudvīpa' is as follows. By way of example, it is called Jambu because it is located to the south of Mount Meru and when the fruit of the Jambu tree falls into the lake it makes the sound 'jambu'; and it is called Jambudvīpa because it is a continent surrounded by water at its borders. Since its shape resembles a chariot, three of its sides are two thousand yojanas each, and one is three and a half yojanas, as the Abhidharmakośa states: 'Jambudvīpa has three sides / of two thousand, the shape of a chariot; / one has three and a half yojanas.' Here in this central southern continent, however many rivers flow, such as the Gaṅgā, the Pakṣu, the Sindhu, and the Sītā, and whatever flowers there are such as lotuses and kumudas, and whatever fruit-bearing trees there are such as mango trees, and whatever medicines and forests are produced and flourish—they all rely and depend upon that great lord, whoever is the chief or lord of the nāgas dwelling in the great lake Anavatapta—Anavatapta meaning that which overcomes heat because it is filled with water possessing the eight qualities—and upon the nāga Vāsuki and so forth. All of that arises from the power and majesty of that great lord of the nāgas, who is preeminent among those nāgas, who is free from the fears of hot sand and so forth, and who has attained independence.

translation: Likewise, similar to the example, whenever the Jina's śrāvakas, Subhūti and so forth, teach whatever dharmas there are—such as the twelve branches of scripture—saying 'This is the meaning of this' in order to generate the wisdom arisen from hearing through the three valid cognitions and authentic reasoning; and when they explain the words and meanings extensively in order to generate the wisdom arisen from reflection; and when they express them verbally along with the four categories of reasoning—such as the reasoning of performing a function—and the methods for clearing away hindrances and enhancing practice, in order to generate the wisdom arisen from meditation; and when the ultimate fruition of teaching those dharmas brings about the attainment of the supremely noble bliss of a Buddha, non-abiding nirvāṇa; and furthermore, when the temporary fruition of teaching those dharmas brings about the attainment of the four fruitions of stream-enterer, once-returner, non-returner, and śrāvaka arhat: all of these arise from the power—that is, the blessing—of the person of the Tathāgata, who has realized dharmatā, suchness, and teaches it just as he has seen it.

translation: If one asks, for what reason are all those the power of the Buddha? As an answer: Since [the Buddha] has been victorious over all four māras without exception, whatever dharma system of the selflessness of persons and phenomena is taught, Subhūti and the others who have become disciples of the supreme human, the Buddha Bhagavat, actualize their training in it through the stages of hearing, reflecting, and meditating, and having realized it directly, they also teach it to other trainees exactly as they themselves have trained in it. They do all of that through the power of the Buddha, and not through the power of the śrāvakas' own strength. Furthermore, having come to know the inconceivable enlightened activities and qualities—such as how, by the power of the Buddha's blessing, the sound of dharma emerges even from trees swaying in the wind and from the sky, thereby establishing trainees in ripening and liberation—one should take refuge from the depths of one's heart. Regarding how this text serves as an incidental topic of the generation of the awakening mind (bodhicitta): Tri Gungtangpa states, 'Śrāvakas [are born from] the Buddha, and he too is born from the generation of the awakening mind, which is like the summary of the perfection of wisdom; therefore, wishing to become a Buddha who independently teaches the perfection of wisdom, one should train in it.' Thus, it is established from the perspective of the result.

translation: Instructions. Secondly, regarding instructions: The Mahāyāna utterance that teaches the methods for attaining the objective sought for the sake of the Mahāyāna generation of the awakening mind is the definition of a Mahāyāna instruction. Regarding that, if divided by way of essence, there are two: instructions given so that qualities already attained do not degenerate, and ensuing instructions given so that qualities not yet attained may be attained. If divided by way of the expressed meaning, as stated in the Ornament: 'Practice and the truths / ... / should be known,' there are ten instructions: instructions given on the essence of practice itself, on the four truths as objects of observation, on the Three Jewels as the basis of practice, on the three types of diligence as the companions of practice, on the five eyes that make practice independent of others, on the six superknowledges as the causes for fully perfecting the practice, on the path of seeing that newly sees the truths, and on the path of meditation that habituates what has already been seen—making ten instructions. From among these, the principal instruction—the instruction given so that practice does not transgress the stages of the two truths in its own essence—is taught by one verse beginning with 'For whomever wisdom'. The meaning is as follows: For whatever bodhisattva who is thus instructed, regarding the object of instruction: when one searches for the designated meaning of the conventional designation of the supreme perfection of wisdom—which realizes the selflessness of phenomena and persons with respect to the six perfections, giving and so forth, which are the objects to be practiced—and analyzes it, one does not observe it as established in its own essence or established by its own nature, and, through realizing this, it abides merely as a designation. Furthermore, if one searches with reasoning for whether the practitioner, the bodhisattva, is established as identical to or different from the aggregates that are their basis of designation, and whether they are established by their own nature, one does not find the essence of the person in the slightest, and not observing it, they are like an illusion merely posited by names and symbols. The essence of the awakening mind, which is to be practiced, is also not observed in the slightest as truly established.

Incidental topic. Secondly, demonstrating through an example the incidental point that the śrāvakas' teaching of the perfection of wisdom is due to the power of the Buddha: The meaning taught by the three verses beginning with 'Here in Jambudvīpa' is as follows. By way of example, it is called Jambu because it is located to the south of Mount Meru and when the fruit of the Jambu tree falls into the lake it makes the sound 'jambu'; and it is called Jambudvīpa because it is a continent surrounded by water at its borders. Since its shape resembles a chariot, three of its sides are two thousand yojanas each, and one is three and a half yojanas, as the Abhidharmakośa states: 'Jambudvīpa has three sides / of two thousand, the shape of a chariot; / one has three and a half yojanas.' Here in this central southern continent, however many rivers flow, such as the Gaṅgā, the Pakṣu, the Sindhu, and the Sītā, and whatever flowers there are such as lotuses and kumudas, and whatever fruit-bearing trees there are such as mango trees, and whatever medicines and forests are produced and flourish—they all rely and depend upon that great lord, whoever is the chief or lord of the nāgas dwelling in the great lake Anavatapta—Anavatapta meaning that which overcomes heat because it is filled with water possessing the eight qualities—and upon the nāga Vāsuki and so forth. All of that arises from the power and majesty of that great lord of the nāgas, who is preeminent among those nāgas, who is free from the fears of hot sand and so forth, and who has attained independence.

If one asks, for what reason are all those the power of the Buddha? As an answer: Since [the Buddha] has been victorious over all four māras without exception, whatever dharma system of the selflessness of persons and phenomena is taught, Subhūti and the others who have become disciples of the supreme human, the Buddha Bhagavat, actualize their training in it through the stages of hearing, reflecting, and meditating, and having realized it directly, they also teach it to other trainees exactly as they themselves have trained in it. They do all of that through the power of the Buddha, and not through the power of the śrāvakas' own strength. Furthermore, having come to know the inconceivable enlightened activities and qualities—such as how, by the power of the Buddha's blessing, the sound of dharma emerges even from trees swaying in the wind and from the sky, thereby establishing trainees in ripening and liberation—one should take refuge from the depths of one's heart. Regarding how this text serves as an incidental topic of the generation of the awakening mind (bodhicitta): Tri Gungtangpa states, 'Śrāvakas [are born from] the Buddha, and he too is born from the generation of the awakening mind, which is like the summary of the perfection of wisdom; therefore, wishing to become a Buddha who independently teaches the perfection of wisdom, one should train in it.' Thus, it is established from the perspective of the result.

heading: **གདམས་ངག**
translation: Having heard this speech that teaches that the agent, the object, and the action are not truly existent, the bodhisattva who—while there is no ultimate existence of the bodhisattva and so forth—is unconfused about practicing the perfection of wisdom merely conventionally, and who is 'not frightened'—meaning without the slightest fear—at the teaching that they are empty of inherent nature or true establishment, but practices the two truths in union; that bodhisattva possesses the fortune to practice the profound path of the perfection of wisdom taught by the Sugata. Thus it is instructed that when practicing Mahāyāna practice, one does not transgress the practice of the union of the two truths: the stages of the path based on conventional truth, which is to practice the practitioner, the objects to be practiced, and the results in an illusion-like manner conventionally; and the stages of the path based on ultimate truth, which is to practice having realized those to be empty of true existence. As for the instruction on practice, having explicitly taught the basis of qualities or the general isolate, the others—being its qualities or particulars—are implicitly indicated. Likewise, as stated in the Sixty Stanzas on Reasoning: 'By this virtue, may all beings / accumulate the provisions of merit and wisdom, / and attain the two supreme kāyas / arising from merit and wisdom.' Accordingly, one should know that the supreme vital point of practice is to practice without transgressing the union of the two truths as the basis, the union of method and wisdom as the path, and the union of the two kāyas as the result.

Secondly, demonstrating through an example the incidental point that the śrāvakas' teaching of the perfection of wisdom is due to the power of the Buddha: The meaning taught by the three verses beginning with 'Here in Jambudvīpa' is as follows. By way of example, it is called Jambu because it is located to the south of Mount Meru and when the fruit of the Jambu tree falls into the lake it makes the sound 'jambu'; and it is called Jambudvīpa because it is a continent surrounded by water at its borders. Since its shape resembles a chariot, three of its sides are two thousand yojanas each, and one is three and a half yojanas, as the Abhidharmakośa states: 'Jambudvīpa has three sides / of two thousand, the shape of a chariot; / one has three and a half yojanas.' Here in this central southern continent, however many rivers flow, such as the Gaṅgā, the Pakṣu, the Sindhu, and the Sītā, and whatever flowers there are such as lotuses and kumudas, and whatever fruit-bearing trees there are such as mango trees, and whatever medicines and forests are produced and flourish—they all rely and depend upon that great lord, whoever is the chief or lord of the nāgas dwelling in the great lake Anavatapta—Anavatapta meaning that which overcomes heat because it is filled with water possessing the eight qualities—and upon the nāga Vāsuki and so forth. All of that arises from the power and majesty of that great lord of the nāgas, who is preeminent among those nāgas, who is free from the fears of hot sand and so forth, and who has attained independence.

Likewise, similar to the example, whenever the Jina's śrāvakas, Subhūti and so forth, teach whatever dharmas there are—such as the twelve branches of scripture—saying 'This is the meaning of this' in order to generate the wisdom arisen from hearing through the three valid cognitions and authentic reasoning; and when they explain the words and meanings extensively in order to generate the wisdom arisen from reflection; and when they express them verbally along with the four categories of reasoning—such as the reasoning of performing a function—and the methods for clearing away hindrances and enhancing practice, in order to generate the wisdom arisen from meditation; and when the ultimate fruition of teaching those dharmas brings about the attainment of the supremely noble bliss of a Buddha, non-abiding nirvāṇa; and furthermore, when the temporary fruition of teaching those dharmas brings about the attainment of the four fruitions of stream-enterer, once-returner, non-returner, and śrāvaka arhat: all of these arise from the power—that is, the blessing—of the person of the Tathāgata, who has realized dharmatā, suchness, and teaches it just as he has seen it.

If one asks, for what reason are all those the power of the Buddha? As an answer: Since [the Buddha] has been victorious over all four māras without exception, whatever dharma system of the selflessness of persons and phenomena is taught, Subhūti and the others who have become disciples of the supreme human, the Buddha Bhagavat, actualize their training in it through the stages of hearing, reflecting, and meditating, and having realized it directly, they also teach it to other trainees exactly as they themselves have trained in it. They do all of that through the power of the Buddha, and not through the power of the śrāvakas' own strength. Furthermore, having come to know the inconceivable enlightened activities and qualities—such as how, by the power of the Buddha's blessing, the sound of dharma emerges even from trees swaying in the wind and from the sky, thereby establishing trainees in ripening and liberation—one should take refuge from the depths of one's heart. Regarding how this text serves as an incidental topic of the generation of the awakening mind (bodhicitta): Tri Gungtangpa states, 'Śrāvakas [are born from] the Buddha, and he too is born from the generation of the awakening mind, which is like the summary of the perfection of wisdom; therefore, wishing to become a Buddha who independently teaches the perfection of wisdom, one should train in it.' Thus, it is established from the perspective of the result.

translation: Path of preparation. Thirdly, regarding the explanation of the path of preparation, which is the beginning of what arises from meditation on the meaning of the instruction: the definition of the Mahāyāna path of preparation is that Mahāyāna mundane path that accords with the clear realization of the truths, which abides in the class of clear realizations that arise after the completion of its cause, the Mahāyāna aids to liberation. Such a Mahāyāna path of preparation is exceptionally superior to the Hīnayāna path of preparation by way of five or six qualities. This is because it is exceptionally superior by way of its object of observation, its aspect, its manner of acting as a cause, its manner of being completely held, its manner of possessing the conceptualization of true apprehension as the principal object to be abandoned, and its division into small, medium, and great, as stated in the Ornament: 'Object of observation and aspect,' and so forth. Regarding it, by way of its essence, there are four—heat and so forth; and by way of occasions, there are twelve, as each has three—small, medium, and great. In the Eight Thousand Line and the Twenty Thousand Line and so forth, there is a sūtra section on the objects of observation, aspects, and causes of preparation for each of all [the stages of] the paths of preparation, whereas here, since there is only one sūtra section for each of the four—heat, peak, patience, and supreme phenomenon:

Instructions. Secondly, regarding instructions: The Mahāyāna utterance that teaches the methods for attaining the objective sought for the sake of the Mahāyāna generation of the awakening mind is the definition of a Mahāyāna instruction. Regarding that, if divided by way of essence, there are two: instructions given so that qualities already attained do not degenerate, and ensuing instructions given so that qualities not yet attained may be attained. If divided by way of the expressed meaning, as stated in the Ornament: 'Practice and the truths / ... / should be known,' there are ten instructions: instructions given on the essence of practice itself, on the four truths as objects of observation, on the Three Jewels as the basis of practice, on the three types of diligence as the companions of practice, on the five eyes that make practice independent of others, on the six superknowledges as the causes for fully perfecting the practice, on the path of seeing that newly sees the truths, and on the path of meditation that habituates what has already been seen—making ten instructions. From among these, the principal instruction—the instruction given so that practice does not transgress the stages of the two truths in its own essence—is taught by one verse beginning with 'For whomever wisdom'. The meaning is as follows: For whatever bodhisattva who is thus instructed, regarding the object of instruction: when one searches for the designated meaning of the conventional designation of the supreme perfection of wisdom—which realizes the selflessness of phenomena and persons with respect to the six perfections, giving and so forth, which are the objects to be practiced—and analyzes it, one does not observe it as established in its own essence or established by its own nature, and, through realizing this, it abides merely as a designation. Furthermore, if one searches with reasoning for whether the practitioner, the bodhisattva, is established as identical to or different from the aggregates that are their basis of designation, and whether they are established by their own nature, one does not find the essence of the person in the slightest, and not observing it, they are like an illusion merely posited by names and symbols. The essence of the awakening mind, which is to be practiced, is also not observed in the slightest as truly established.

Having heard this speech that teaches that the agent, the object, and the action are not truly existent, the bodhisattva who—while there is no ultimate existence of the bodhisattva and so forth—is unconfused about practicing the perfection of wisdom merely conventionally, and who is 'not frightened'—meaning without the slightest fear—at the teaching that they are empty of inherent nature or true establishment, but practices the two truths in union; that bodhisattva possesses the fortune to practice the profound path of the perfection of wisdom taught by the Sugata. Thus it is instructed that when practicing Mahāyāna practice, one does not transgress the practice of the union of the two truths: the stages of the path based on conventional truth, which is to practice the practitioner, the objects to be practiced, and the results in an illusion-like manner conventionally; and the stages of the path based on ultimate truth, which is to practice having realized those to be empty of true existence. As for the instruction on practice, having explicitly taught the basis of qualities or the general isolate, the others—being its qualities or particulars—are implicitly indicated. Likewise, as stated in the Sixty Stanzas on Reasoning: 'By this virtue, may all beings / accumulate the provisions of merit and wisdom, / and attain the two supreme kāyas / arising from merit and wisdom.' Accordingly, one should know that the supreme vital point of practice is to practice without transgressing the union of the two truths as the basis, the union of method and wisdom as the path, and the union of the two kāyas as the result.

Instructions. Secondly, regarding instructions: The Mahāyāna utterance that teaches the methods for attaining the objective sought for the sake of the Mahāyāna generation of the awakening mind is the definition of a Mahāyāna instruction. Regarding that, if divided by way of essence, there are two: instructions given so that qualities already attained do not degenerate, and ensuing instructions given so that qualities not yet attained may be attained. If divided by way of the expressed meaning, as stated in the Ornament: 'Practice and the truths / ... / should be known,' there are ten instructions: instructions given on the essence of practice itself, on the four truths as objects of observation, on the Three Jewels as the basis of practice, on the three types of diligence as the companions of practice, on the five eyes that make practice independent of others, on the six superknowledges as the causes for fully perfecting the practice, on the path of seeing that newly sees the truths, and on the path of meditation that habituates what has already been seen—making ten instructions. From among these, the principal instruction—the instruction given so that practice does not transgress the stages of the two truths in its own essence—is taught by one verse beginning with 'For whomever wisdom'. The meaning is as follows: For whatever bodhisattva who is thus instructed, regarding the object of instruction: when one searches for the designated meaning of the conventional designation of the supreme perfection of wisdom—which realizes the selflessness of phenomena and persons with respect to the six perfections, giving and so forth, which are the objects to be practiced—and analyzes it, one does not observe it as established in its own essence or established by its own nature, and, through realizing this, it abides merely as a designation. Furthermore, if one searches with reasoning for whether the practitioner, the bodhisattva, is established as identical to or different from the aggregates that are their basis of designation, and whether they are established by their own nature, one does not find the essence of the person in the slightest, and not observing it, they are like an illusion merely posited by names and symbols. The essence of the awakening mind, which is to be practiced, is also not observed in the slightest as truly established.

Having heard this speech that teaches that the agent, the object, and the action are not truly existent, the bodhisattva who—while there is no ultimate existence of the bodhisattva and so forth—is unconfused about practicing the perfection of wisdom merely conventionally, and who is 'not frightened'—meaning without the slightest fear—at the teaching that they are empty of inherent nature or true establishment, but practices the two truths in union; that bodhisattva possesses the fortune to practice the profound path of the perfection of wisdom taught by the Sugata. Thus it is instructed that when practicing Mahāyāna practice, one does not transgress the practice of the union of the two truths: the stages of the path based on conventional truth, which is to practice the practitioner, the objects to be practiced, and the results in an illusion-like manner conventionally; and the stages of the path based on ultimate truth, which is to practice having realized those to be empty of true existence. As for the instruction on practice, having explicitly taught the basis of qualities or the general isolate, the others—being its qualities or particulars—are implicitly indicated. Likewise, as stated in the Sixty Stanzas on Reasoning: 'By this virtue, may all beings / accumulate the provisions of merit and wisdom, / and attain the two supreme kāyas / arising from merit and wisdom.' Accordingly, one should know that the supreme vital point of practice is to practice without transgressing the union of the two truths as the basis, the union of method and wisdom as the path, and the union of the two kāyas as the result.

གདམས་ངག གཉིས་པ་གདམས་ངག་ནི། ཐེག་ཆེན་སེམས་བསྐྱེད་ཀྱི་ཆེད་དུ་གཉེར་བྱ་ཐོབ་པའི་ཐབས་སྟོན་པའི་ཐེག་ཆེན་གྱི་ངག་དེ། ཐེག་ཆེན་གྱི་གདམས་ངག་གི་མཚན་ཉིད། དེ་ལ་ངོ་བོའི་སྒོ་ནས་སྔར་ཐོབ་ཟིན་གྱི་ཡོན་ཏན་མི་ཉམས་པའི་ཕྱིར་འདོམས་པའི་གདམས་ངག་དང༌། ཡོན་ཏན་མ་ཐོབ་པ་ཐོབ་པའི་ཕྱིར་འདོམས་པ་རྗེས་བསྟན་གྱི་གདམས་ངག་གཉིས་ཡོད། བརྗོད་བྱའི་སྒོ་ནས་དབྱེ་ན། རྒྱན་ལས། སྒྲུབ་དང་བདེན་པ་རྣམས་དང་ནི། །ནས། ཤེས་པར་བྱ། ཞེས་གསུངས་པ་ལྟར།སྒྲུབ་པ་རང་གི་ངོ་བོ་ལ་འདོམས་པ། དམིགས་ཡུལ་བདེན་པ་བཞི། སྒྲུབ་པའི་རྟེན་དཀོན་མཆོག་གསུམ། སྒྲུབ་པའི་གྲོགས་བརྩོན་འགྲུས་གསུམ། སྒྲུབ་ལ་གཞན་དྲིང་མི་འཇོག་པའི་སྤྱན་ལྔ། སྒྲུབ་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་རྫོགས་པའི་རྒྱུ་མངོན་ཤེས་དྲུག །བདེན་པ་གསར་དུ་མཐོང་བའི་མཐོང་ལམ། མཐོང་ཟིན་གོམས་པར་བྱེད་པའི་སྒོམ་ལམ་ལ་འདོམས་པའི་གདམས་ངག་དང་བཅུ་ཡོད་པ་ལས། གདམས་ངག་གི་གཙོ་བོ་སྒྲུབ་པར་རང་གི་ངོ་བོ་བདེན་པ་གཉིས་ཀྱི་རིམ་པ་ལས་མི་འདའ་བར་བདོམས་པའི་གདམས་ངག་ནི། གང་ལ་ཤེས་རབ་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གཅིག་གིས་བསྟན། དོན་ནི། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གང་ལ་འདི་སྐད་དུ། གདམས་པར་བྱ་པའི་ཡུལ་ལ་ཉམས་སུ་བླང་བྱ་སྦྱིན་སོགས་ཕར་ཕྱིན་དྲུག་ལ་ཆོས་དང་གང་ཟག་གི་བདག་མེད་པར་རྟོགས་པའི་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་མཆོག་དེའང་ཐ་སྙད་བཏགས་པའི་བཏགས་དོན་བཙལ་ནས་དཔྱད་པའི་ཚེ་རང་གི་ངོ་བོའི་གྲུབ་པའམ་རང་བཞིན་གྱིས་གྲུབ་པར་མི་དམིགས་ཤིང་རྟོགས་པས་བཏགས་པ་ཙམ་དུ་གནས་པ་དང་། ཉམས་སུ་ལེན་པ་པོ་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཡང་རང་གི་གདགས་གཞིའི་ཕུང་པོ་དང་རང་བཞིན་གྱིས་གྲུབ་པའི་གཅིག་དང་ཐ་དད་གང་དུ་གྲུབ་རིགས་པས་པཙལ་ན། གང་ཟག་གི་ངོ་བོ་ཅུང་ཟད་ཀྱང་མ་རྙེད་ཅིང་མི་དམིགས་པར་མིང་བརྡས་བཞག་ཙམ་གྱི་སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟ་བུ། ཉམས་སུ་བླང་བྱའི་ངོ་བོ་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཀྱི་སེམས་ཀྱང་བདེན་པར་གྲུབ་པ་ཅུང་ཟད་མི་དམིགས་སོ། །
[3-22] translation already produced for this document:
Instructions. Secondly, regarding instructions: The Mahāyāna utterance that teaches the methods for attaining the objective sought for the sake of the Mahāyāna generation of the awakening mind is the definition of a Mahāyāna instruction. Regarding that, if divided by way of essence, there are two: instructions given so that qualities already attained do not degenerate, and ensuing instructions given so that qualities not yet attained may be attained. If divided by way of the expressed meaning, as stated in the Ornament: 'Practice and the truths / ... / should be known,' there are ten instructions: instructions given on the essence of practice itself, on the four truths as objects of observation, on the Three Jewels as the basis of practice, on the three types of diligence as the companions of practice, on the five eyes that make practice independent of others, on the six superknowledges as the causes for fully perfecting the practice, on the path of seeing that newly sees the truths, and on the path of meditation that habituates what has already been seen—making ten instructions. From among these, the principal instruction—the instruction given so that practice does not transgress the stages of the two truths in its own essence—is taught by one verse beginning with 'For whomever wisdom'. The meaning is as follows: For whatever bodhisattva who is thus instructed, regarding the object of instruction: when one searches for the designated meaning of the conventional designation of the supreme perfection of wisdom—which realizes the selflessness of phenomena and persons with respect to the six perfections, giving and so forth, which are the objects to be practiced—and analyzes it, one does not observe it as established in its own essence or established by its own nature, and, through realizing this, it abides merely as a designation. Furthermore, if one searches with reasoning for whether the practitioner, the bodhisattva, is established as identical to or different from the aggregates that are their basis of designation, and whether they are established by their own nature, one does not find the essence of the person in the slightest, and not observing it, they are like an illusion merely posited by names and symbols. The essence of the awakening mind, which is to be practiced, is also not observed in the slightest as truly established.

བྱེད་པ་པོ་དང་ལས་དང་བྱ་བ་བདེན་པར་མེད་པར་སྟོན་པའི་གཏམ་དེ་སྐད་བསྟན་པ་ཐོས་ནས་བྱང་སེམས་སོགས་དོན་དམ་པར་མེད་ཀྱང་ཐ་སྙད་ཙམ་དུ་ཤེར་ཕྱིན་ཉམས་སུ་ལེན་པ་ལ་རྨོངས་པ་མེད་ཅིང་། རང་བཞིན་གྱིས་སམ་བདེན་གྲུབ་ཀྱིས་སྟོང་པར་བསྟན་པ་ལ་མི་སྐྲག་པ་སྟེ་སྐྲག་པ་ཅུང་ཟད་ཀྱང་མེད་པར་བདེན་གཉིས་བཟུང་འབྲེལ་དུ་ཉམས་སུ་ལེན་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་དེ་ནི་བདེ་བར་གཤེགས་པས་བསྟན་པའི་ལམ་ཟབ་མོ་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལ་སྤྱོད་པའི་སྐལ་བ་དང་ལྡན་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །ཞེས་པ་སྟེ། ཐེག་ཆེན་སྒྲུབ་པ་ཉམས་སུ་ལེན་པའི་ཚེ་ཉམས་སུ་ལེན་པ་པོ་དང་བླང་བྱ་དང་འབྲས་བུ་རྣམས་ཐ་སྙད་དུ་སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟ་བའི་ཚུལ་གྱིས་ཉམས་སུ་ལེན་པ་ཀུན་རྫོབ་བདེན་པ་ལ་བརྟེན་པའི་ལམ་གྱི་རིམ་པ་དང༌། དེ་རྣམས་བདེན་སྟོང་དུ་རྟོགས་ནས་ཉམས་སུ་ལེན་པ་དོན་དམ་བདེན་པ་ལ་བརྟེན་པའི་ལམ་གྱི་རིམ་པ་སྟེ་བདེན་གཉིས་ཟུང་འབྲེལ་གྱི་ཉམས་ལེན་ལས་མི་འདའ་བར་གདམས་པ་སྟེ། སྒྲུབ་པ་གདམས་པ་ནི་ཁྱད་གཞིའམ་སྤྱི་ལྡོག་དངོས་སུ་བསྟན་ནས་གཞན་དེའི་ཁྱད་ཆོས་སམ་བྱེ་བྲག་ཡིན་པས་དོན་གྱིས་འཕངས་སོ། །དེ་ལྟར་དུ་རིགས་པ་དྲུག་ཅུ་པ་ལས། དགེ་བ་འདི་ཡིས་སྐྱེ་བོ་ཀུན། །བསོད་ནམས་ཡེ་ཤེས་ཚོགས་བསགས་ཤིང༌། །བསོད་ནམས་ཡེ་ཤེས་ལས་བྱུང་བའི། །དམ་པ་སྐུ་གཉིས་ཐོབ་བར་ཤོག །ཅེས་གསུངས་པ་ལྟར། གཞི་བདེན་གཉིས་བཟུང་འཇུག །ལམ་ཐབས་ཤེས་ཟུང་འཇུག །འབྲས་བུ་སྐུ་གཉིས་ཟུང་འཇུག་ལས་མི་འདའ་བར་ཉམས་སུ་ལེན་པ་ནི་ཉམས་ལེན་གྱི་གནད་དམ་པར་ཤེས་པར་བྱའོ། །
[3-23] translation already produced for this document:
Having heard this speech that teaches that the agent, the object, and the action are not truly existent, the bodhisattva who—while there is no ultimate existence of the bodhisattva and so forth—is unconfused about practicing the perfection of wisdom merely conventionally, and who is 'not frightened'—meaning without the slightest fear—at the teaching that they are empty of inherent nature or true establishment, but practices the two truths in union; that bodhisattva possesses the fortune to practice the profound path of the perfection of wisdom taught by the Sugata. Thus it is instructed that when practicing Mahāyāna practice, one does not transgress the practice of the union of the two truths: the stages of the path based on conventional truth, which is to practice the practitioner, the objects to be practiced, and the results in an illusion-like manner conventionally; and the stages of the path based on ultimate truth, which is to practice having realized those to be empty of true existence. As for the instruction on practice, having explicitly taught the basis of qualities or the general isolate, the others—being its qualities or particulars—are implicitly indicated. Likewise, as stated in the Sixty Stanzas on Reasoning: 'By this virtue, may all beings / accumulate the provisions of merit and wisdom, / and attain the two supreme kāyas / arising from merit and wisdom.' Accordingly, one should know that the supreme vital point of practice is to practice without transgressing the union of the two truths as the basis, the union of method and wisdom as the path, and the union of the two kāyas as the result.

source: དྲོད་ཀྱི་དམིགས་པ། དྲོད་ཀྱི་དམིགས་པ་ནི། གཟུགས་མེད་ཚོར་བ་མེད། ཅེས་པ་ནས། རྣམ་ཤེས་ཞེས་པའི་བར་གྱིས་བསྟན། དོན་ནི། འདིར་གཟུགས་ཀྱི་ཕུང་པོས་བསྡུས་པ་དབང་པོ་ལྔ་དོན་ལྔ་ལ་སོགས་པ་ནི། རྡུལ་དུ་མ་འདུས་ཤིང་བསགས་པ་ཡིན་པས་ཆ་དུ་མ་དང་བཅས་ལ། དེ་ཡང་རང་གི་ཆ་ཤས་རྣམས་དང་རང་བཞིན་གྱིས་གཅིག་དང་དུ་མ་གང་དུ་གྲུབ་ཅེས་དོན་དམ་དཔྱོད་བྱེད་ཀྱི་རིགས་པས་དཔྱད་ན་རང་གི་ངོ་བོས་གྲུབ་པ་ཅུང་ཟད་ཀྱང་མེད་ལ། ཆ་ཤས་རྡུལ་ཕྲན་རྣམས་ཀྱང་ཕྱོགས་ཆ་དང་བཅས་པས་སྔར་ལྟར་དཔྱད་ན་བདེན་པར་གྲུབ་པ་ཅུང་ཟད་ཀྱང་མེདཔའི་ཕྱིར། གཟུགས་འདི་ནི་སྣང་ཡང་བདེན་པར་མེད་པ་ཡིན་ལ། དེ་བཞིན་དུ་རང་གཞན་གྱི་རྒྱུད་ཀྱིས་བསྡུས་པའི་བདེ་སྡུག་བཏང་སྙོམས་ཀྱི་ཚོར་བ་འདི་དག་ལའང་གཅིག་ཏུ་དྲལ་གྱི་རིགས་པས་དཔྱད་ན་བདེན་པར་གྲུབ་མེད་ཅིང་དེ་དང་འདྲ་བར་འདུ་ཤེས་ཕུང་བོ་དང་སེམས་ཡུལ་ལ་གཡོ་བར་བྱེད་པའི་སེམས་བྱུང་སེམས་པ་སོགས་འདུ་བྱེད་ཀྱི་ཕུང་པོ་རྣམས་ཀྱང་བདེན་པར་མེད་ལ། ཚུལ་དེ་ལྟ་བུ་ལ་རྣམ་པར་ཤེས་པའམ་བདེན་པར་གྲུབ་པ་ཅུང་ཟད་ཀྱང་མེད་དོ། །ཅེས་པ་འདིས་སྡུག་བདེན་གྱི་གཙོ་བོ་གཟུགས་ལ་སོགས་པའི་ཕུང་ལྔ་དྲོད་ཀྱི་ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་དམིགས་པར་བསྟན་ཏོ། །རྣམ་པ་ནི། གནས་ནི་རྡུལ་ཙམ་ན། ཞེས་པས་བསྟན་ཏེ། དེ་ལ་བདེན་པར་གནས་པ་སྡེ་མངོན་པར་ཞེན་པ་ནི་རྡུལ་ཙམ་ཡང་ཡོད་པ་མིན་ཞེས་པ་འདིས་སྟེ། འདིས་བདེན་པར་རྣམ་པར་མི་རྟོག་པའི་དྲོད་ཀྱི་ཡེ་ཤེས་དེ་རྣམ་པ་ཡིན་པར་བསྟུན་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །
translation: The object of observation of heat. The object of observation of heat is taught by [the verse] from 'There is no form, no feeling,' up to 'consciousness.' The meaning is as follows: Here, the five faculties, five objects, and so forth, subsumed by the aggregate of form, are a collection and accumulation of many particles, and so they possess many parts. Furthermore, if one analyzes with the reasoning that analyzes the ultimate—asking whether they are established as identical to or different from their parts by their own nature—they are not established by their own essence in the slightest. And because the parts, the subtle particles, also possess directional parts, if one analyzes them as before, they are not truly established in the slightest; therefore, although this form appears, it does not truly exist. Likewise, regarding these feelings of pleasure, pain, and neutrality subsumed by one's own and others' continuums, if one analyzes them with the reasoning of neither one nor many, they are not truly established. And similarly, the aggregate of discrimination, and the aggregates of compositional factors such as the mental factor of intention that makes the mind move toward objects, do not truly exist either. Towards such a manner, consciousness or true establishment does not exist in the slightest. This teaches that the five aggregates, form and so forth, which are the principal aspects of the truth of suffering, are the object of observation of the wisdom of heat. As for the aspect, it is taught by 'if abides even as a mere particle': this means that abiding truly in that—that is, true clinging—does not exist even as a mere particle. By this, it is taught that this wisdom of heat that is non-conceptual regarding true existence is the aspect.

གདམས་ངག གཉིས་པ་གདམས་ངག་ནི། ཐེག་ཆེན་སེམས་བསྐྱེད་ཀྱི་ཆེད་དུ་གཉེར་བྱ་ཐོབ་པའི་ཐབས་སྟོན་པའི་ཐེག་ཆེན་གྱི་ངག་དེ། ཐེག་ཆེན་གྱི་གདམས་ངག་གི་མཚན་ཉིད། དེ་ལ་ངོ་བོའི་སྒོ་ནས་སྔར་ཐོབ་ཟིན་གྱི་ཡོན་ཏན་མི་ཉམས་པའི་ཕྱིར་འདོམས་པའི་གདམས་ངག་དང༌། ཡོན་ཏན་མ་ཐོབ་པ་ཐོབ་པའི་ཕྱིར་འདོམས་པ་རྗེས་བསྟན་གྱི་གདམས་ངག་གཉིས་ཡོད། བརྗོད་བྱའི་སྒོ་ནས་དབྱེ་ན། རྒྱན་ལས། སྒྲུབ་དང་བདེན་པ་རྣམས་དང་ནི། །ནས། ཤེས་པར་བྱ། ཞེས་གསུངས་པ་ལྟར།སྒྲུབ་པ་རང་གི་ངོ་བོ་ལ་འདོམས་པ། དམིགས་ཡུལ་བདེན་པ་བཞི། སྒྲུབ་པའི་རྟེན་དཀོན་མཆོག་གསུམ། སྒྲུབ་པའི་གྲོགས་བརྩོན་འགྲུས་གསུམ། སྒྲུབ་ལ་གཞན་དྲིང་མི་འཇོག་པའི་སྤྱན་ལྔ། སྒྲུབ་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་རྫོགས་པའི་རྒྱུ་མངོན་ཤེས་དྲུག །བདེན་པ་གསར་དུ་མཐོང་བའི་མཐོང་ལམ། མཐོང་ཟིན་གོམས་པར་བྱེད་པའི་སྒོམ་ལམ་ལ་འདོམས་པའི་གདམས་ངག་དང་བཅུ་ཡོད་པ་ལས། གདམས་ངག་གི་གཙོ་བོ་སྒྲུབ་པར་རང་གི་ངོ་བོ་བདེན་པ་གཉིས་ཀྱི་རིམ་པ་ལས་མི་འདའ་བར་བདོམས་པའི་གདམས་ངག་ནི། གང་ལ་ཤེས་རབ་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གཅིག་གིས་བསྟན། དོན་ནི། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གང་ལ་འདི་སྐད་དུ། གདམས་པར་བྱ་པའི་ཡུལ་ལ་ཉམས་སུ་བླང་བྱ་སྦྱིན་སོགས་ཕར་ཕྱིན་དྲུག་ལ་ཆོས་དང་གང་ཟག་གི་བདག་མེད་པར་རྟོགས་པའི་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་མཆོག་དེའང་ཐ་སྙད་བཏགས་པའི་བཏགས་དོན་བཙལ་ནས་དཔྱད་པའི་ཚེ་རང་གི་ངོ་བོའི་གྲུབ་པའམ་རང་བཞིན་གྱིས་གྲུབ་པར་མི་དམིགས་ཤིང་རྟོགས་པས་བཏགས་པ་ཙམ་དུ་གནས་པ་དང་། ཉམས་སུ་ལེན་པ་པོ་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཡང་རང་གི་གདགས་གཞིའི་ཕུང་པོ་དང་རང་བཞིན་གྱིས་གྲུབ་པའི་གཅིག་དང་ཐ་དད་གང་དུ་གྲུབ་རིགས་པས་པཙལ་ན། གང་ཟག་གི་ངོ་བོ་ཅུང་ཟད་ཀྱང་མ་རྙེད་ཅིང་མི་དམིགས་པར་མིང་བརྡས་བཞག་ཙམ་གྱི་སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟ་བུ། ཉམས་སུ་བླང་བྱའི་ངོ་བོ་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཀྱི་སེམས་ཀྱང་བདེན་པར་གྲུབ་པ་ཅུང་ཟད་མི་དམིགས་སོ། །

Instructions. Secondly, regarding instructions: The Mahāyāna utterance that teaches the methods for attaining the objective sought for the sake of the Mahāyāna generation of the awakening mind is the definition of a Mahāyāna instruction. Regarding that, if divided by way of essence, there are two: instructions given so that qualities already attained do not degenerate, and ensuing instructions given so that qualities not yet attained may be attained. If divided by way of the expressed meaning, as stated in the Ornament: 'Practice and the truths / ... / should be known,' there are ten instructions: instructions given on the essence of practice itself, on the four truths as objects of observation, on the Three Jewels as the basis of practice, on the three types of diligence as the companions of practice, on the five eyes that make practice independent of others, on the six superknowledges as the causes for fully perfecting the practice, on the path of seeing that newly sees the truths, and on the path of meditation that habituates what has already been seen—making ten instructions. From among these, the principal instruction—the instruction given so that practice does not transgress the stages of the two truths in its own essence—is taught by one verse beginning with 'For whomever wisdom'. The meaning is as follows: For whatever bodhisattva who is thus instructed, regarding the object of instruction: when one searches for the designated meaning of the conventional designation of the supreme perfection of wisdom—which realizes the selflessness of phenomena and persons with respect to the six perfections, giving and so forth, which are the objects to be practiced—and analyzes it, one does not observe it as established in its own essence or established by its own nature, and, through realizing this, it abides merely as a designation. Furthermore, if one searches with reasoning for whether the practitioner, the bodhisattva, is established as identical to or different from the aggregates that are their basis of designation, and whether they are established by their own nature, one does not find the essence of the person in the slightest, and not observing it, they are like an illusion merely posited by names and symbols. The essence of the awakening mind, which is to be practiced, is also not observed in the slightest as truly established.

Having heard this speech that teaches that the agent, the object, and the action are not truly existent, the bodhisattva who—while there is no ultimate existence of the bodhisattva and so forth—is unconfused about practicing the perfection of wisdom merely conventionally, and who is 'not frightened'—meaning without the slightest fear—at the teaching that they are empty of inherent nature or true establishment, but practices the two truths in union; that bodhisattva possesses the fortune to practice the profound path of the perfection of wisdom taught by the Sugata. Thus it is instructed that when practicing Mahāyāna practice, one does not transgress the practice of the union of the two truths: the stages of the path based on conventional truth, which is to practice the practitioner, the objects to be practiced, and the results in an illusion-like manner conventionally; and the stages of the path based on ultimate truth, which is to practice having realized those to be empty of true existence. As for the instruction on practice, having explicitly taught the basis of qualities or the general isolate, the others—being its qualities or particulars—are implicitly indicated. Likewise, as stated in the Sixty Stanzas on Reasoning: 'By this virtue, may all beings / accumulate the provisions of merit and wisdom, / and attain the two supreme kāyas / arising from merit and wisdom.' Accordingly, one should know that the supreme vital point of practice is to practice without transgressing the union of the two truths as the basis, the union of method and wisdom as the path, and the union of the two kāyas as the result.

heading: **དྲོད་ཀྱི་དམིགས་པ།**
translation: The distinction of the cause is taught by the two lines, 'He does not abide in all phenomena' and so forth. The meaning is as follows: In that way, these phenomena, the five aggregates and so forth, are established conventionally, pleasant when unexamined; but when examined and analyzed, a special ascertainment arises seeing them as like dreams and illusions, without even a mere particle of establishment by their own essence. At that time, that bodhisattva who abides on the Mahāyāna paths of preparation—heat and so forth—practices, that is, experiences, the perfection of wisdom without abiding in all phenomena from form up to omniscience in the manner of true clinging, and without abiding in any extreme of permanence or annihilation. Thus, by relying on the very expansion and increase, higher and higher, of that wisdom realizing the emptiness endowed with all supreme aspects, without the meditatively poised wisdom that is single-pointedly poised in meditative equipoise on reality completely holding any conventional phenomena, form and so forth, the great unexcelled awakening in the mental continuums of the Sugatas will be attained.

Path of preparation. Thirdly, regarding the explanation of the path of preparation, which is the beginning of what arises from meditation on the meaning of the instruction: the definition of the Mahāyāna path of preparation is that Mahāyāna mundane path that accords with the clear realization of the truths, which abides in the class of clear realizations that arise after the completion of its cause, the Mahāyāna aids to liberation. The object of observation of heat. The object of observation of heat is taught by [the verse] from 'There is no form, no feeling,' up to 'consciousness.' The meaning is as follows: Here, the five faculties, five objects, and so forth, subsumed by the aggregate of form, are a collection and accumulation of many particles, and so they possess many parts. Furthermore, if one analyzes with the reasoning that analyzes the ultimate—asking whether they are established as identical to or different from their parts by their own nature—they are not established by their own essence in the slightest. And because the parts, the subtle particles, also possess directional parts, if one analyzes them as before, they are not truly established in the slightest; therefore, although this form appears, it does not truly exist. Likewise, regarding these feelings of pleasure, pain, and neutrality subsumed by one's own and others' continuums, if one analyzes them with the reasoning of neither one nor many, they are not truly established. And similarly, the aggregate of discrimination, and the aggregates of compositional factors such as the mental factor of intention that makes the mind move toward objects, do not truly exist either. Towards such a manner, consciousness or true establishment does not exist in the slightest. This teaches that the five aggregates, form and so forth, which are the principal aspects of the truth of suffering, are the object of observation of the wisdom of heat. As for the aspect, it is taught by 'if abides even as a mere particle': this means that abiding truly in that—that is, true clinging—does not exist even as a mere particle. By this, it is taught that this wisdom of heat that is non-conceptual regarding true existence is the aspect.

heading: **རྩེ་མོའི་དམིགས་པ།**
translation: The object of observation of peak. The object of observation of peak is taught by one stanza, 'Just as' and so forth. The meaning is as follows: For example, just as the wandering ascetic Śreṇika, or the one known as the Garland-bearer, knowing through the power of his own wisdom that he could not attain liberation freeing him from all the sufferings of saṃsāra by relying merely on the view of his own tradition asserting the existence of a personal self and the meditative absorptions of the actual states of the concentrations and the formless [realms] he had attained, came into the presence of the teacher Buddha and asked what the path for attaining liberation was; and when the teacher taught the subtle selflessness of persons and phenomena, he had exceptional inclination and belief in it, and by relying on the path of the perfection of wisdom that realizes the absence of even the slightest focal target of true apprehension, there arose a nirvāṇa in which the appropriated aggregates propelled by karma and afflictions are completely destroyed, or the continuum of cycling again in saṃsāra is severed—likewise, any bodhisattva who thus knows all phenomena, form and so forth, to not truly exist, because he is embraced by special methods such as great compassion, does not touch the extreme of peace, the nirvāṇa without remainder of aggregates, and he will abide in the wisdom that realizes existence and peace as equal in being empty of true existence. This teaches that form and so forth, devoid of marks, are the object of observation.

Path of preparation. Thirdly, regarding the explanation of the path of preparation, which is the beginning of what arises from meditation on the meaning of the instruction: the definition of the Mahāyāna path of preparation is that Mahāyāna mundane path that accords with the clear realization of the truths, which abides in the class of clear realizations that arise after the completion of its cause, the Mahāyāna aids to liberation. Such a Mahāyāna path of preparation is exceptionally superior to the Hīnayāna path of preparation by way of five or six qualities. This is because it is exceptionally superior by way of its object of observation, its aspect, its manner of acting as a cause, its manner of being completely held, its manner of possessing the conceptualization of true apprehension as the principal object to be abandoned, and its division into small, medium, and great, as stated in the Ornament: 'Object of observation and aspect,' and so forth. Regarding it, by way of its essence, there are four—heat and so forth; and by way of occasions, there are twelve, as each has three—small, medium, and great. The object of observation of heat. The object of observation of heat is taught by [the verse] from 'There is no form, no feeling,' up to 'consciousness.' The meaning is as follows: Here, the five faculties, five objects, and so forth, subsumed by the aggregate of form, are a collection and accumulation of many particles, and so they possess many parts. Furthermore, if one analyzes with the reasoning that analyzes the ultimate—asking whether they are established as identical to or different from their parts by their own nature—they are not established by their own essence in the slightest. And because the parts, the subtle particles, also possess directional parts, if one analyzes them as before, they are not truly established in the slightest; therefore, although this form appears, it does not truly exist. Likewise, regarding these feelings of pleasure, pain, and neutrality subsumed by one's own and others' continuums, if one analyzes them with the reasoning of neither one nor many, they are not truly established. And similarly, the aggregate of discrimination, and the aggregates of compositional factors such as the mental factor of intention that makes the mind move toward objects, do not truly exist either. Towards such a manner, consciousness or true establishment does not exist in the slightest. This teaches that the five aggregates, form and so forth, which are the principal aspects of the truth of suffering, are the object of observation of the wisdom of heat. As for the aspect, it is taught by 'if abides even as a mere particle': this means that abiding truly in that—that is, true clinging—does not exist even as a mere particle. By this, it is taught that this wisdom of heat that is non-conceptual regarding true existence is the aspect.

heading: **རྩེ་མོའི་དམིགས་པ།**
source: རྣམ་པ་ནི། ཡང་འདི་ཤེས་རབ་ཅེས་སོགས་ཆིགས་བཅད་གཅིག་གིས་བསྟན། དོན་ནི། ཡང་འདི་མཉམ་དུ་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་རང་བཞིན་གྱིས་མེད་པར་རྟོགས་པའི་ཤེས་རབ་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ཐར་བར་བསྒྲོད་པའི་ལམ་གཅིག་པུ་འདི་ནི། གཟུགས་ལ་སོགས་པའི་ཕུང་པོའམ་རྫས་སམ་ཡོན་ཏན་ནམ། ལས་སམ། སྤྱིའམ། ཁྱད་པར་རམ། འདུ་བ་གང་ཡིན། གང་ཟག་སུ་ཡི་ཡིན། མཐའ་བཞི་གང་ལས་སྐྱེ་བ་ཡིན་ཞེས་བརྟགས་ཤིང་དཔྱད་ན་གང་ཡང་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། དོན་དམ་པར་སྐྱེ་བ་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར། རིགས་པ་དེ་ཉིད་ཀྱིས་གཟུགས་ནས་རྣམ་མཁྱེན་གྱི་བར་གྱི་ཆོས་འདི་ཐམསཅད་རང་གི་ངོ་བོས་སྟོང་པར་རྟོག་ཅིང་དཔྱོད་པར་བྱེད་དོ། །དེ་ལྟར་གཅིག་དུ་བྲལ་དང་རྡོ་རྗེ་ཟེགས་མའིགཏན་ཚིགས་ལ་སོགས་པ་རིག་པ་ཡང་དག་གིས་ཉེ་བར་བཏགས་ནས་རང་བཞིན་གྱིས་སྟོང་པར་མཐོང་བ་ན་ཞུམ་པ་མེད་ཅིང་གནས་ལུགས་ཀྱི་ཀྱི་དོན་ལ་སྐྲག་པ་མེད་པ་ཡི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་དེ་ནི་རྫོགས་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་ལ་ཉེ་བ་ཡིན་ནོ། །ཞེས་རྒྱུའི་ཁྱད་པརདང་། རྣམ་པར་དཔྱད་ན་ཆོས་རྣམས་རང་བཞིན་མེད་པར་མཐོང་བ་ནི་རྣམ་པ་ཡིན་པར་བསྟན་ཏོ། །
translation: As for the aspect, it is taught by one stanza, 'Moreover this wisdom' and so forth. The meaning is as follows: Moreover, if one examines and analyzes, thinking thus: 'As to this sole path for traveling to liberation called the wisdom that realizes all phenomena to not exist by their own nature, what is it—whether it is the aggregates of form and so forth, or a substance, or a quality, or an action, or a universal, or a particular, or an inherence? Whose, which person's, is it? From which of the four extremes is it produced?'—it is none of these, because it is ultimately unproduced. By this very reasoning, it examines and analyzes all these phenomena from form up to omniscience as being empty of their own essence. Thus, that bodhisattva who, when closely investigating with authentic reasonings such as [the reasoning of] neither one nor many and the diamond slivers and so forth, sees them as empty of nature, and is undaunted and unafraid of the meaning of the abiding nature, is near to perfect awakening. This teaches the distinction of the cause; and that seeing phenomena as lacking nature when thoroughly analyzed is the aspect.

Path of preparation. Thirdly, regarding the explanation of the path of preparation, which is the beginning of what arises from meditation on the meaning of the instruction: the definition of the Mahāyāna path of preparation is that Mahāyāna mundane path that accords with the clear realization of the truths, which abides in the class of clear realizations that arise after the completion of its cause, the Mahāyāna aids to liberation. Such a Mahāyāna path of preparation is exceptionally superior to the Hīnayāna path of preparation by way of five or six qualities. This is because it is exceptionally superior by way of its object of observation, its aspect, its manner of acting as a cause, its manner of being completely held, its manner of possessing the conceptualization of true apprehension as the principal object to be abandoned, and its division into small, medium, and great, as stated in the Ornament: 'Object of observation and aspect,' and so forth. Regarding it, by way of its essence, there are four—heat and so forth; and by way of occasions, there are twelve, as each has three—small, medium, and great. In the Eight Thousand Line and the Twenty Thousand Line and so forth, there is a sūtra section on the objects of observation, aspects, and causes of preparation for each of all [the stages of] the paths of preparation, whereas here, since there is only one sūtra section for each of the four—heat, peak, patience, and supreme phenomenon:

[3-25] source:
ངོ་བོ་དམིགས་རྣམ་རྒྱུ་གསུམ་གྱི་ཁྱད་པར་འབྲས་བུ་མཚུངས་ལྡན་སྤངས་རྟོགས་ཁྱད་པར། ཡོངས་འཛིན་བཤེས་གཉེན་གྱི་ཁྱད་པར་དང་གསུམ།
[3-25] translation already produced for this document:
[There are] three [parts]: the distinction of the three—essence, object of observation and aspect, and cause; the distinction of abandonment and realization associated with the result; and the distinction of the spiritual friend who completely holds [one].

[3-26] source:
ངོ་བོ་དམིགས་རྣམ་རྒྱུ་གསུམ་གྱི་ཁྱད་པར།དང་པོ་ལ་དྲོད་རྩེ་མོ་བཟོད་པ་ཆོས་མཆོག་དང་བཞི་ལས།
[3-26] translation already produced for this document:
The distinction of the three—essence, object of observation and aspect, and cause. Regarding the first, from among the four: heat, peak, patience, and supreme phenomenon:

[3-27] source:
དྲོད་ཀྱི་དམིགས་པ། དྲོད་ཀྱི་དམིགས་པ་ནི། གཟུགས་མེད་ཚོར་བ་མེད། ཅེས་པ་ནས། རྣམ་ཤེས་ཞེས་པའི་བར་གྱིས་བསྟན། དོན་ནི། འདིར་གཟུགས་ཀྱི་ཕུང་པོས་བསྡུས་པ་དབང་པོ་ལྔ་དོན་ལྔ་ལ་སོགས་པ་ནི། རྡུལ་དུ་མ་འདུས་ཤིང་བསགས་པ་ཡིན་པས་ཆ་དུ་མ་དང་བཅས་ལ། དེ་ཡང་རང་གི་ཆ་ཤས་རྣམས་དང་རང་བཞིན་གྱིས་གཅིག་དང་དུ་མ་གང་དུ་གྲུབ་ཅེས་དོན་དམ་དཔྱོད་བྱེད་ཀྱི་རིགས་པས་དཔྱད་ན་རང་གི་ངོ་བོས་གྲུབ་པ་ཅུང་ཟད་ཀྱང་མེད་ལ། ཆ་ཤས་རྡུལ་ཕྲན་རྣམས་ཀྱང་ཕྱོགས་ཆ་དང་བཅས་པས་སྔར་ལྟར་དཔྱད་ན་བདེན་པར་གྲུབ་པ་ཅུང་ཟད་ཀྱང་མེདཔའི་ཕྱིར། གཟུགས་འདི་ནི་སྣང་ཡང་བདེན་པར་མེད་པ་ཡིན་ལ། དེ་བཞིན་དུ་རང་གཞན་གྱི་རྒྱུད་ཀྱིས་བསྡུས་པའི་བདེ་སྡུག་བཏང་སྙོམས་ཀྱི་ཚོར་བ་འདི་དག་ལའང་གཅིག་ཏུ་དྲལ་གྱི་རིགས་པས་དཔྱད་ན་བདེན་པར་གྲུབ་མེད་ཅིང་དེ་དང་འདྲ་བར་འདུ་ཤེས་ཕུང་བོ་དང་སེམས་ཡུལ་ལ་གཡོ་བར་བྱེད་པའི་སེམས་བྱུང་སེམས་པ་སོགས་འདུ་བྱེད་ཀྱི་ཕུང་པོ་རྣམས་ཀྱང་བདེན་པར་མེད་ལ། ཚུལ་དེ་ལྟ་བུ་ལ་རྣམ་པར་ཤེས་པའམ་བདེན་པར་གྲུབ་པ་ཅུང་ཟད་ཀྱང་མེད་དོ། །ཅེས་པ་འདིས་སྡུག་བདེན་གྱི་གཙོ་བོ་གཟུགས་ལ་སོགས་པའི་ཕུང་ལྔ་དྲོད་ཀྱི་ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་དམིགས་པར་བསྟན་ཏོ། །རྣམ་པ་ནི། གནས་ནི་རྡུལ་ཙམ་ན། ཞེས་པས་བསྟན་ཏེ། དེ་ལ་བདེན་པར་གནས་པ་སྡེ་མངོན་པར་ཞེན་པ་ནི་རྡུལ་ཙམ་ཡང་ཡོད་པ་མིན་ཞེས་པ་འདིས་སྟེ། འདིས་བདེན་པར་རྣམ་པར་མི་རྟོག་པའི་དྲོད་ཀྱི་ཡེ་ཤེས་དེ་རྣམ་པ་ཡིན་པར་བསྟུན་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །
[3-27] translation already produced for this document:
The object of observation of heat. The object of observation of heat is taught by [the verse] from 'There is no form, no feeling,' up to 'consciousness.' The meaning is as follows: Here, the five faculties, five objects, and so forth, subsumed by the aggregate of form, are a collection and accumulation of many particles, and so they possess many parts. Furthermore, if one analyzes with the reasoning that analyzes the ultimate—asking whether they are established as identical to or different from their parts by their own nature—they are not established by their own essence in the slightest. And because the parts, the subtle particles, also possess directional parts, if one analyzes them as before, they are not truly established in the slightest; therefore, although this form appears, it does not truly exist. Likewise, regarding these feelings of pleasure, pain, and neutrality subsumed by one's own and others' continuums, if one analyzes them with the reasoning of neither one nor many, they are not truly established. And similarly, the aggregate of discrimination, and the aggregates of compositional factors such as the mental factor of intention that makes the mind move toward objects, do not truly exist either. Towards such a manner, consciousness or true establishment does not exist in the slightest. This teaches that the five aggregates, form and so forth, which are the principal aspects of the truth of suffering, are the object of observation of the wisdom of heat. As for the aspect, it is taught by 'if abides even as a mere particle': this means that abiding truly in that—that is, true clinging—does not exist even as a mere particle. By this, it is taught that this wisdom of heat that is non-conceptual regarding true existence is the aspect.

heading: **བཟོད་པའི་དམིགས་པ།**
source: བཟོད་པའི་དམིགས་པ།བཟོད་པའི་དམིགས་པ་ནི། གལ་ཏེ་མི་ཤེས་ཞེས་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གཅིག་གིས་བསྟན། དོན་ནི། གལ་ཏེ་གཟུགས་ལ་སོགས་པའི་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་གདོང་མ་ནས་རང་བཞིན་གྱིས་སྟོང་པའི་དོན་མི་ཤེས་བཞིན་དུ་གཟུགས་ལ་རང་གི་ངོ་བ་ཉིད་ཀྱིས་གྲུབ་པའི་གཟུགས་སུ་མངོན་པར་འདུ་ཤེས་ཤིང་། དེ་བཞིན་དུ་ཚོར་བ་དང༌། སེམས་པ་སྟེ་འདུ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་ཕུང་བ་དང་རྣམ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་ཕུང་པོར་བདེན་པར་མངོན་པར་ཞེན་པའི་འདུ་ཤེས་ཀྱིས་སྤྱོད་པར་བྱེད་ན་མཚན་མ་ལ་སྤྱོད་པར་མ་ཟད་སྟོང་ཉིད་ལ་གཅིག་ཏུ་མཉམ་པར་བཞག་པའི་ཚེ་གཟུགས་ཕུང་པོ་འདི་ནི་རང་བཞིན་གྱིས་སྟོང་པའོ་ཞེས་རྣམ་པར་རྟོག་ནའང་མངོན་པར་འདུ་བྱེད་པའི་སེམས་པ་ལ་སྤྱོད་ཅིང་ཕུང་པོ་ལྔའི་སྣང་བ་མ་ཁེགས་པས།  དེ་ལྟར་བསྒོམ་ཀྱང་དེ་འདྲའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་དེ་ནི་མཚན་མ་ལ་སྤྱོད་པ་ཡིན་གྱི། རང་བཞིན་གྱིས་སྐྱེ་བ་མེད་པའི་གནས་ལ་ཡིད་ཆེས་པའི་དད་པ་ཐོབ་སྟེ་ཤེར་ཕྱིན་རྣལ་མ་གནས་པ་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །འདིས་དོན་དམ་པར་ངོ་བ་ཉིད་མེད་པའི་ཁྱད་པར་དུ་བྱས་པའི་གཟུགས་སོགས་དམིགས་པར་བསྟན་ཏོ། །ཁ་ཅིག །མདོ་འདིས་དོན་དུ་བསམ་ནས་དགག་བྱ་བདེན་གྲུབ་བཀག་པའི་མེད་དགག་སྟོང་པ་ཉིད་དེ་ཙམ་གནས་ལུགས་མཐར་ཐུག་མ་ཡིན་པར་འདོད་པ་དང་། གཟུགས་སོགས་བདེན་པས་སྟོང་ངོ་སྙམ་དུ་འཛིན་མི་རུང་བར་འདོད་པ་སོགས་ནི་འཐད་པ་མ་ཏེ། རིགས་པ་དང་ལུང་ཚད་མས་གནོད་པའི་ཕྱིར།  རྩ་ཤེས་ཊིཀ་ཆེན་ལས། དེ་བཞིན་དུ་དངོས་པོ་རྣམས་ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་ཀྱིས་ཡོད་པ་མིན་ནོ་ཞེས་སྟོན་པ་ན་འདི་རྣམས་བདེན་པས་སྟོང་ངོ་སྙམ་དུ་བཟུང་དུ་མི་རུང་བ་མིན་གྱི་དངོས་པོ་བདེན་པས་སྟོང་པ་འདི་བདེན་ནོ་སྙམ་དུ་བཟུང་མི་རུང་བ་ཡིན་ནོ། །དེས་ན་ཆོས་རྣམས་སྟོང་པའོ་སྙམ་དུ་བཟུང་ན་ཡང་གསོར་མི་རུང་བར་གཞུང་འདིས་བསྟན་པར་འདོད་པ་ནི་མ་བརྟགས་པར་སྨྲ་བ་ཆེན་པའོ། ། སློབ་དཔོན་གཉིས་ཀས་སྟོང་པ་ཉིད་དུ་ལྟ་བ་ཞེས་པའི་དོན་སྟོང་པ་ཉིད་ལ་དངོས་པོར་ཞེན་པ་ལ་གསུངས་ལ་དེ་ནི་སྟོང་ཉིད་བདེན་པར་བཟུང་བའམ་སྟོང་ཉིད་ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་ཀྱིས་ཡོད་པར་འཛིན་པ་ཡིན་གྱི་རང་བཞིན་མེད་དོ་སྙམ་དུ་འཛིན་པ་ཙམ་ག་ལ་ཡིན། ཞེས་དང་། དེ་ལྟར་གཞུང་གི་དོན་ལོག་པར་བཟུང་ན་ནི་དོན་དམ་པའི་བདེན་པ་མི་སྲིད་ཅེས་སྐུར་བ་འདེབས་པ་དང་། སྲིད་ཀྱང་དེ་ངེས་པའིངེས་ཤེས་བསྐྱངས་ན་མཚན་འཛིན་དུ་འགྲོ་བར་བཟུང་ནས་ཡང་དག་པའི་དོན་ཚུལ་བཞིན་དུ་ངེས་པའི་ལྟ་བ་སྐྱོང་བའི་གེགས་ཆེན་པོ་བྱེད་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །ཞེས་གསུངས།  ཤེས་རབ་སྙིང་པོ་ལས་ཀྱང་། translation: The object of observation of patience. The object of observation of patience is taught by one stanza, 'If one does not know' and so forth. The meaning is as follows: If, while not knowing the meaning of all phenomena, form and so forth, being empty of nature from the very beginning, one manifestly conceptualizes form as form established by its own essence, and likewise practices with the perception of true clinging to feeling, and volition, that is, the aggregate of perception and the aggregate of consciousness; not only is one practicing on marks, but even if, when single-pointedly poised in meditative equipoise on emptiness, one conceptualizes, 'This aggregate of form is empty of nature', one is practicing on volitions that manifestly condition, and because the appearance of the five aggregates is not blocked, even if one meditates in that way, such a bodhisattva is practicing on marks, but has not attained the faith of believing in the state of being unproduced by nature, and does not abide in the genuine perfection of wisdom. This teaches that form and so forth, distinguished by being ultimately without essence, are the object of observation. Some think of the meaning of this sūtra and assert that the emptiness that is merely a non-affirming negation negating the object of negation, true establishment, is not the ultimate abiding nature, and assert that it is inappropriate to apprehend, 'Form and so forth are empty of true existence', and so forth—these are incorrect, because they are invalidated by valid reasonings and scriptures. From the Great Commentary on the Root of Wisdom: 'Likewise, when it is taught, "Things do not exist by their essence", it is not that it is inappropriate to apprehend, "These are empty of true existence", but rather it is inappropriate to apprehend, "This emptiness of things of true existence is true". Therefore, asserting that this text teaches that even apprehending "Phenomena are empty" is incurable, is greatly unexamined speech. Both masters stated that the meaning of "view of emptiness" is clinging to emptiness as a thing, and that is apprehending emptiness as true, or apprehending emptiness as existing by its essence; how could it be merely apprehending, "It lacks nature"?' And it states: 'If one wrongly apprehends the meaning of the text in that way, one deprecates ultimate truth by saying it is impossible, and even if it is possible, by apprehending that maintaining the ascertainment ascertaining it leads to apprehending marks, one creates a great obstacle to maintaining the view that properly ascertains the authentic meaning.' Also from the Heart of Wisdom: In answer to the question of how to practice the profound perfection of wisdom, it is stated, 'He rightly sees those five aggregates also as empty of nature'—stating that one must see them as empty of nature; and also from this very sūtra: 'Whenever, analyzing conditioned and unconditioned and white and black phenomena with wisdom, not even a mere particle is observed; at that time it counts as the perfection of wisdom in the world'—because it states that if, by analyzing phenomena with wisdom, one sees that not even a mere particle is observed, it counts as the perfection of wisdom. There are certainly many other scriptures and reasonings, but fearing too many words, I have not expanded upon them.

The distinction of the cause is taught by the two lines, 'He does not abide in all phenomena' and so forth. The meaning is as follows: In that way, these phenomena, the five aggregates and so forth, are established conventionally, pleasant when unexamined; but when examined and analyzed, a special ascertainment arises seeing them as like dreams and illusions, without even a mere particle of establishment by their own essence. At that time, that bodhisattva who abides on the Mahāyāna paths of preparation—heat and so forth—practices, that is, experiences, the perfection of wisdom without abiding in all phenomena from form up to omniscience in the manner of true clinging, and without abiding in any extreme of permanence or annihilation. Thus, by relying on the very expansion and increase, higher and higher, of that wisdom realizing the emptiness endowed with all supreme aspects, without the meditatively poised wisdom that is single-pointedly poised in meditative equipoise on reality completely holding any conventional phenomena, form and so forth, the great unexcelled awakening in the mental continuums of the Sugatas will be attained.

The meaning is as follows: For example, just as the wandering ascetic Śreṇika, or the one known as the Garland-bearer, knowing through the power of his own wisdom that he could not attain liberation freeing him from all the sufferings of saṃsāra by relying merely on the view of his own tradition asserting the existence of a personal self and the meditative absorptions of the actual states of the concentrations and the formless [realms] he had attained, came into the presence of the teacher Buddha and asked what the path for attaining liberation was; and when the teacher taught the subtle selflessness of persons and phenomena, he had exceptional inclination and belief in it, and by relying on the path of the perfection of wisdom that realizes the absence of even the slightest focal target of true apprehension, there arose a nirvāṇa in which the appropriated aggregates propelled by karma and afflictions are completely destroyed, or the continuum of cycling again in saṃsāra is severed—likewise, any bodhisattva who thus knows all phenomena, form and so forth, to not truly exist, because he is embraced by special methods such as great compassion, does not touch the extreme of peace, the nirvāṇa without remainder of aggregates, and he will abide in the wisdom that realizes existence and peace as equal in being empty of true existence. This teaches that form and so forth, devoid of marks, are the object of observation.

As for the aspect, it is taught by one stanza, 'Moreover this wisdom' and so forth. The meaning is as follows: Moreover, if one examines and analyzes, thinking thus: 'As to this sole path for traveling to liberation called the wisdom that realizes all phenomena to not exist by their own nature, what is it—whether it is the aggregates of form and so forth, or a substance, or a quality, or an action, or a universal, or a particular, or an inherence? Whose, which person's, is it? From which of the four extremes is it produced?'—it is none of these, because it is ultimately unproduced. By this very reasoning, it examines and analyzes all these phenomena from form up to omniscience as being empty of their own essence. Thus, that bodhisattva who, when closely investigating with authentic reasonings such as [the reasoning of] neither one nor many and the diamond slivers and so forth, sees them as empty of nature, and is undaunted and unafraid of the meaning of the abiding nature, is near to perfect awakening. This teaches the distinction of the cause; and that seeing phenomena as lacking nature when thoroughly analyzed is the aspect.

heading: **བཟོད་པའི་དམིགས་པ།**
translation: As for the aspect, it is taught by one stanza, 'Whoever [apprehends] not form' and so forth. The meaning is as follows: Whoever does not apprehend form as form established by its own essence, and likewise does not apprehend feeling as established by nature, and does not apprehend perception, volition, and so forth themselves as established from their own side, and also does not practice or abide by way of apprehending consciousness as established by its own mode of abiding or essence; in short, that meditative equipoise, which, having blocked the appearance of the five aggregates from the perspective of meditative equipoise poised in emptiness, practices without abiding with true clinging to any object whatsoever, is not observed as [thinking], 'I practice on emptiness', because the wisdom that is free from all conceit of the three spheres being true has become stable. Having taught the aspect thus, the manner in which it acts as a cause is: Endowed with the mind that realizes the three—agent, action, and object—as truly unproduced in that way, one attains the supreme utter pacification of distraction and so forth in the samādhis named 'heroic stride' and so forth, which is to say one touches the Mahāyāna path of seeing that completely obtains the classes of realization of the three vehicles. This teaches that realizing that what is ultimately without essence is conventionally the essence of form and so forth is the aspect. The term 'patience' is because one is free from manifest fear regarding the profound unproduced phenomena.

དེ་བཞིན་དུ་དངོས་པོ་རྣམས་ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་ཀྱིས་ཡོད་པ་མིན་ནོ་ཞེས་སྟོན་པ་ན་འདི་རྣམས་བདེན་པས་སྟོང་ངོ་སྙམ་དུ་བཟུང་དུ་མི་རུང་བ་མིན་གྱི་དངོས་པོ་བདེན་པས་སྟོང་པ་འདི་བདེན་ནོ་སྙམ་དུ་བཟུང་མི་རུང་བ་ཡིན་ནོ། །དེས་ན་ཆོས་རྣམས་སྟོང་པའོ་སྙམ་དུ་བཟུང་ན་ཡང་གསོར་མི་རུང་བར་གཞུང་འདིས་བསྟན་པར་འདོད་པ་ནི་མ་བརྟགས་པར་སྨྲ་བ་ཆེན་པའོ། སྲིད་ཀྱང་དེ་ངེས་པའིངེས་ཤེས་བསྐྱངས་ན་མཚན་འཛིན་དུ་འགྲོ་བར་བཟུང་ནས་ཡང་དག་པའི་དོན་ཚུལ་བཞིན་དུ་ངེས་པའི་ལྟ་བ་སྐྱོང་བའི་གེགས་ཆེན་པོ་བྱེད་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །ཞེས་གསུངས།  ཤེས་རབ་སྙིང་པོ་ལས་ཀྱང་། ཤེར་ཕྱིན་ཟབ་མོ་ལ་ཇི་ལྟར་སྤྱད་པ་དྲིས་པའི་ལན་དུ། ཕུང་པོ་ལྔ་པོ་དེ་དག་ཀྱང་རང་བཞིན་གྱི་སྟོང་པ་རྣམ་བར་ཡང་དག་བར་རྗེས་སུ་ལྟའོ། །ཞེས་རང་བཞིན་གྱིས་སྟོང་པ་ལྟ་དགོས་པར་གསུངས་པ་དང་། མདོ་འདི་ཉིད་ལས་ཀྱང་། གང་ཚེ་འདུས་བྱས་འདུས་མ་བྱས་དང་དཀར་ནག་ཆོས། ཤེས་རབ་རྣམ་པར་བཤིག་ནས་བརྔུལ་ཙམ་མི་དམིགས་ཚེ། །འཇིག་རྟེན་དྲག་ན་ཤེས་རབ་ཕ་རོལ་ཕྱིན་གྲངས་འགྲོ། The object of observation of patience. The object of observation of patience is taught by one stanza, 'If one does not know' and so forth. The meaning is as follows: If, while not knowing the meaning of all phenomena, form and so forth, being empty of nature from the very beginning, one manifestly conceptualizes form as form established by its own essence, and likewise practices with the perception of true clinging to feeling, and volition, that is, the aggregate of perception and the aggregate of consciousness; not only is one practicing on marks, but even if, when single-pointedly poised in meditative equipoise on emptiness, one conceptualizes, 'This aggregate of form is empty of nature', one is practicing on volitions that manifestly condition, and because the appearance of the five aggregates is not blocked, even if one meditates in that way, such a bodhisattva is practicing on marks, but has not attained the faith of believing in the state of being unproduced by nature, and does not abide in the genuine perfection of wisdom. This teaches that form and so forth, distinguished by being ultimately without essence, are the object of observation. Some think of the meaning of this sūtra and assert that the emptiness that is merely a non-affirming negation negating the object of negation, true establishment, is not the ultimate abiding nature, and assert that it is inappropriate to apprehend, 'Form and so forth are empty of true existence', and so forth—these are incorrect, because they are invalidated by valid reasonings and scriptures. From the Great Commentary on the Root of Wisdom: 'Likewise, when it is taught, "Things do not exist by their essence", it is not that it is inappropriate to apprehend, "These are empty of true existence", but rather it is inappropriate to apprehend, "This emptiness of things of true existence is true". Therefore, asserting that this text teaches that even apprehending "Phenomena are empty" is incurable, is greatly unexamined speech. Both masters stated that the meaning of "view of emptiness" is clinging to emptiness as a thing, and that is apprehending emptiness as true, or apprehending emptiness as existing by its essence; how could it be merely apprehending, "It lacks nature"?' And it states: 'If one wrongly apprehends the meaning of the text in that way, one deprecates ultimate truth by saying it is impossible, and even if it is possible, by apprehending that maintaining the ascertainment ascertaining it leads to apprehending marks, one creates a great obstacle to maintaining the view that properly ascertains the authentic meaning.' Also from the Heart of Wisdom: In answer to the question of how to practice the profound perfection of wisdom, it is stated, 'He rightly sees those five aggregates also as empty of nature'—stating that one must see them as empty of nature; and also from this very sūtra: 'Whenever, analyzing conditioned and unconditioned and white and black phenomena with wisdom, not even a mere particle is observed; at that time it counts as the perfection of wisdom in the world'—because it states that if, by analyzing phenomena with wisdom, one sees that not even a mere particle is observed, it counts as the perfection of wisdom. There are certainly many other scriptures and reasonings, but fearing too many words, I have not expanded upon them.

heading: **ཆོས་མཆོག་གི་དམིགས་པ།**
translation: The object of observation of supreme dharma. The object of observation of supreme dharma is taught by one stanza, 'Whatever bodhisattva' and so forth. The meaning is as follows: Whatever bodhisattva, when meditating on the perfection of wisdom that has become the essence of the path of preparation in the manner explained previously, at this time when the manifest apprehension of self of phenomena and persons in their own continuum is appeased, abides in the samādhi of supreme dharma of the path—they are prophesied by the former Tathāgatas to not turn back from unexcelled perfect awakening; at that time, for that bodhisattva, there arises no conceit thinking, 'I am poised in meditative equipoise on emptiness' or 'I have arisen from it', or 'I am prophesied'. If one asks for what reason, it is because they completely know the nature of all phenomena to be the equality of emptiness of true existence. By this, it is taught that form and so forth, indivisible in essence from the special cause by which one is prophesied by the Buddhas when one realizes its nature, are the object of observation.

As for the aspect, it is taught by one stanza, 'Moreover this wisdom' and so forth. The meaning is as follows: Moreover, if one examines and analyzes, thinking thus: 'As to this sole path for traveling to liberation called the wisdom that realizes all phenomena to not exist by their own nature, what is it—whether it is the aggregates of form and so forth, or a substance, or a quality, or an action, or a universal, or a particular, or an inherence? Whose, which person's, is it? From which of the four extremes is it produced?'—it is none of these, because it is ultimately unproduced. By this very reasoning, it examines and analyzes all these phenomena from form up to omniscience as being empty of their own essence. Thus, that bodhisattva who, when closely investigating with authentic reasonings such as [the reasoning of] neither one nor many and the diamond slivers and so forth, sees them as empty of nature, and is undaunted and unafraid of the meaning of the abiding nature, is near to perfect awakening. This teaches the distinction of the cause; and that seeing phenomena as lacking nature when thoroughly analyzed is the aspect.

སེམས་པ་སྟེ་འདུ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་ཕུང་བ་དང་རྣམ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་ཕུང་པོར་བདེན་པར་མངོན་པར་ཞེན་པའི་འདུ་ཤེས་ཀྱིས་སྤྱོད་པར་བྱེད་ན་མཚན་མ་ལ་སྤྱོད་པར་མ་ཟད་སྟོང་ཉིད་ལ་གཅིག་ཏུ་མཉམ་པར་བཞག་པའི་ཚེ་གཟུགས་ཕུང་པོ་འདི་ནི་རང་བཞིན་གྱིས་སྟོང་པའོ་ཞེས་རྣམ་པར་རྟོག་ནའང་མངོན་པར་འདུ་བྱེད་པའི་སེམས་པ་ལ་སྤྱོད་ཅིང་ཕུང་པོ་ལྔའི་སྣང་བ་མ་ཁེགས་པས།  དེ་ལྟར་བསྒོམ་ཀྱང་དེ་འདྲའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་དེ་ནི་མཚན་མ་ལ་སྤྱོད་པ་ཡིན་གྱི། རང་བཞིན་གྱིས་སྐྱེ་བ་མེད་པའི་གནས་ལ་ཡིད་ཆེས་པའི་དད་པ་ཐོབ་སྟེ་ཤེར་ཕྱིན་རྣལ་མ་གནས་པ་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །འདིས་དོན་དམ་པར་ངོ་བ་ཉིད་མེད་པའི་ཁྱད་པར་དུ་བྱས་པའི་གཟུགས་སོགས་དམིགས་པར་བསྟན་ཏོ། །ཁ་ཅིག །མདོ་འདིས་དོན་དུ་བསམ་ནས་དགག་བྱ་བདེན་གྲུབ་བཀག་པའི་མེད་དགག་སྟོང་པ་ཉིད་དེ་ཙམ་གནས་ལུགས་མཐར་ཐུག་མ་ཡིན་པར་འདོད་པ་དང་། གཟུགས་སོགས་བདེན་པས་སྟོང་ངོ་སྙམ་དུ་འཛིན་མི་རུང་བར་འདོད་པ་སོགས་ནི་འཐད་པ་མ་ཏེ། རིགས་པ་དང་ལུང་ཚད་མས་གནོད་པའི་ཕྱིར།  རྩ་ཤེས་ཊིཀ་ཆེན་ལས། དེ་བཞིན་དུ་དངོས་པོ་རྣམས་ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་ཀྱིས་ཡོད་པ་མིན་ནོ་ཞེས་སྟོན་པ་ན་འདི་རྣམས་བདེན་པས་སྟོང་ངོ་སྙམ་དུ་བཟུང་དུ་མི་རུང་བ་མིན་གྱི་དངོས་པོ་བདེན་པས་སྟོང་པ་འདི་བདེན་ནོ་སྙམ་དུ་བཟུང་མི་རུང་བ་ཡིན་ནོ། །དེས་ན་ཆོས་རྣམས་སྟོང་པའོ་སྙམ་དུ་བཟུང་ན་ཡང་གསོར་མི་རུང་བར་གཞུང་འདིས་བསྟན་པར་འདོད་པ་ནི་མ་བརྟགས་པར་སྨྲ་བ་ཆེན་པའོ། ། སློབ་དཔོན་གཉིས་ཀས་སྟོང་པ་ཉིད་དུ་ལྟ་བ་ཞེས་པའི་དོན་སྟོང་པ་ཉིད་ལ་དངོས་པོར་ཞེན་པ་ལ་གསུངས་ལ་དེ་ནི་སྟོང་ཉིད་བདེན་པར་བཟུང་བའམ་སྟོང་ཉིད་ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་ཀྱིས་ཡོད་པར་འཛིན་པ་ཡིན་གྱི་རང་བཞིན་མེད་དོ་སྙམ་དུ་འཛིན་པ་ཙམ་ག་ལ་ཡིན། ཞེས་དང་། དེ་ལྟར་གཞུང་གི་དོན་ལོག་པར་བཟུང་ན་ནི་དོན་དམ་པའི་བདེན་པ་མི་སྲིད་ཅེས་སྐུར་བ་འདེབས་པ་དང་། སྲིད་ཀྱང་དེ་ངེས་པའིངེས་ཤེས་བསྐྱངས་ན་མཚན་འཛིན་དུ་འགྲོ་བར་བཟུང་ནས་ཡང་དག་པའི་དོན་ཚུལ་བཞིན་དུ་ངེས་པའི་ལྟ་བ་སྐྱོང་བའི་གེགས་ཆེན་པོ་བྱེད་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །ཞེས་གསུངས།  ཤེས་རབ་སྙིང་པོ་ལས་ཀྱང་། ཤེར་ཕྱིན་ཟབ་མོ་ལ་ཇི་ལྟར་སྤྱད་པ་དྲིས་པའི་ལན་དུ། ཕུང་པོ་ལྔ་པོ་དེ་དག་ཀྱང་རང་བཞིན་གྱི་སྟོང་པ་རྣམ་བར་ཡང་དག་བར་རྗེས་སུ་ལྟའོ། །ཞེས་རང་བཞིན་གྱིས་སྟོང་པ་ལྟ་དགོས་པར་གསུངས་པ་དང་། མདོ་འདི་ཉིད་ལས་ཀྱང་། གང་ཚེ་འདུས་བྱས་འདུས་མ་བྱས་དང་དཀར་ནག་ཆོས། ཤེས་རབ་རྣམ་པར་བཤིག་ནས་བརྔུལ་ཙམ་མི་དམིགས་ཚེ། །འཇིག་རྟེན་དྲག་ན་ཤེས་རབ་ཕ་རོལ་ཕྱིན་གྲངས་འགྲོ། །ཞེས་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱིས་ཆོས་རྣམས་ལ་དཔྱད་པས་རྡུལ་ཙམ་ཡང་མི་དམིགས་པར་མཐོང་ན་ཤེར་ཕྱིན་དུ་འགྲོ་བར་གསུངས་པའི་ཕྱིར། ལུང་རིགས་གཞན་ཡང་མང་མོད་ཀྱང་ཡི་གེས་འཇིགས་ནས་མ་སྤྲས་སོ། །
