The object of observation of patience. The object of observation of patience is taught by one stanza, 'If one does not know' and so forth. The meaning is as follows: If, while not knowing the meaning of all phenomena, form and so forth, being empty of nature from the very beginning, one manifestly conceptualizes form as form established by its own essence, and likewise practices with the perception of true clinging to feeling, and volition, that is, the aggregate of perception and the aggregate of consciousness; not only is one practicing on marks, but even if, when single-pointedly poised in meditative equipoise on emptiness, one conceptualizes, 'This aggregate of form is empty of nature', one is practicing on volitions that manifestly condition, and because the appearance of the five aggregates is not blocked, even if one meditates in that way, such a bodhisattva is practicing on marks, but has not attained the faith of believing in the state of being unproduced by nature, and does not abide in the genuine perfection of wisdom. This teaches that form and so forth, distinguished by being ultimately without essence, are the object of observation. Some think of the meaning of this sūtra and assert that the emptiness that is merely a non-affirming negation negating the object of negation, true establishment, is not the ultimate abiding nature, and assert that it is inappropriate to apprehend, 'Form and so forth are empty of true existence', and so forth—these are incorrect, because they are invalidated by valid reasonings and scriptures. From the Great Commentary on the Root of Wisdom: 'Likewise, when it is taught, "Things do not exist by their essence", it is not that it is inappropriate to apprehend, "These are empty of true existence", but rather it is inappropriate to apprehend, "This emptiness of things of true existence is true". Therefore, asserting that this text teaches that even apprehending "Phenomena are empty" is incurable, is greatly unexamined speech. Both masters stated that the meaning of "view of emptiness" is clinging to emptiness as a thing, and that is apprehending emptiness as true, or apprehending emptiness as existing by its essence; how could it be merely apprehending, "It lacks nature"?' And it states: 'If one wrongly apprehends the meaning of the text in that way, one deprecates ultimate truth by saying it is impossible, and even if it is possible, by apprehending that maintaining the ascertainment ascertaining it leads to apprehending marks, one creates a great obstacle to maintaining the view that properly ascertains the authentic meaning.' Also from the Heart of Wisdom: In answer to the question of how to practice the profound perfection of wisdom, it is stated, 'He rightly sees those five aggregates also as empty of nature'—stating that one must see them as empty of nature; and also from this very sūtra: 'Whenever, analyzing conditioned and unconditioned and white and black phenomena with wisdom, not even a mere particle is observed; at that time it counts as the perfection of wisdom in the world'—because it states that if, by analyzing phenomena with wisdom, one sees that not even a mere particle is observed, it counts as the perfection of wisdom. There are certainly many other scriptures and reasonings, but fearing too many words, I have not expanded upon them.

heading: **ཆོས་མཆོག་གི་དམིགས་པ།**
translation: As for the aspect, it is taught by one stanza, 'If one practices in that way' and so forth. The meaning is as follows: If one practices in that way without conceit of truth regarding any phenomenon whatsoever, one is practicing the wisdom of the Sugatas, because that bodhisattva thoroughly knows that the very fact that there is ultimately no practicing regarding any phenomenon is the holy practice of a conqueror's child. Regarding any phenomenon of the path of preparation and so forth, one does not observe as true the object of practice which is the perfection of wisdom, the practitioner which is the bodhisattva, or the action of practicing which is the practice; this practice without observing the three spheres is practicing the supreme perfection of wisdom. Thus, this teaches the aspect as being without conceit, and also teaches the distinction of the cause. Each of the path of preparation's [levels of] heat and so forth has three—small, middling, and great—making twelve; and although there are distinctions of dissimilar objects of observation and aspects of these to be correlated with the extensive and middling sūtras and so forth, here, owing to the abbreviated words of the sūtra, they cannot be explicitly correlated, but they should be known to be taught implicitly.

As for the aspect, it is taught by one stanza, 'Moreover this wisdom' and so forth. The meaning is as follows: Moreover, if one examines and analyzes, thinking thus: 'As to this sole path for traveling to liberation called the wisdom that realizes all phenomena to not exist by their own nature, what is it—whether it is the aggregates of form and so forth, or a substance, or a quality, or an action, or a universal, or a particular, or an inherence? Whose, which person's, is it? From which of the four extremes is it produced?'—it is none of these, because it is ultimately unproduced. By this very reasoning, it examines and analyzes all these phenomena from form up to omniscience as being empty of their own essence. Thus, that bodhisattva who, when closely investigating with authentic reasonings such as [the reasoning of] neither one nor many and the diamond slivers and so forth, sees them as empty of nature, and is undaunted and unafraid of the meaning of the abiding nature, is near to perfect awakening. This teaches the distinction of the cause; and that seeing phenomena as lacking nature when thoroughly analyzed is the aspect.

གཟུགས་སོགས་བདེན་པས་སྟོང་ངོ་སྙམ་དུ་འཛིན་མི་རུང་བར་འདོད་པ་སོགས་ནི་འཐད་པ་མ་ཏེ། རིགས་པ་དང་ལུང་ཚད་མས་གནོད་པའི་ཕྱིར།  རྩ་ཤེས་ཊིཀ་ཆེན་ལས། །དེས་ན་ཆོས་རྣམས་སྟོང་པའོ་སྙམ་དུ་བཟུང་ན་ཡང་གསོར་མི་རུང་བར་གཞུང་འདིས་བསྟན་པར་འདོད་པ་ནི་མ་བརྟགས་པར་སྨྲ་བ་ཆེན་པའོ། གང་ཚེ་འདུས་བྱས་འདུས་མ་བྱས་དང་དཀར་ནག་ཆོས། ཤེས་རབ་རྣམ་པར་བཤིག་ནས་བརྔུལ་ཙམ་མི་དམིགས་ཚེ། །འཇིག་རྟེན་དྲག་ན་ཤེས་རབ་ཕ་རོལ་ཕྱིན་གྲངས་འགྲོ། །ཞེས་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱིས་ཆོས་རྣམས་ལ་དཔྱད་པས་རྡུལ་ཙམ་ཡང་མི་དམིགས་པར་མཐོང་ན་ཤེར་ཕྱིན་དུ་འགྲོ་བར་གསུངས་པའི་ཕྱིར། ལུང་རིགས་གཞན་ཡང་མང་མོད་ཀྱང་ཡི་གེས་འཇིགས་ནས་མ་སྤྲས་སོ། །

The object of observation of patience. The object of observation of patience is taught by one stanza, 'If one does not know' and so forth. The meaning is as follows: If, while not knowing the meaning of all phenomena, form and so forth, being empty of nature from the very beginning, one manifestly conceptualizes form as form established by its own essence, and likewise practices with the perception of true clinging to feeling, and volition, that is, the aggregate of perception and the aggregate of consciousness; not only is one practicing on marks, but even if, when single-pointedly poised in meditative equipoise on emptiness, one conceptualizes, 'This aggregate of form is empty of nature', one is practicing on volitions that manifestly condition, and because the appearance of the five aggregates is not blocked, even if one meditates in that way, such a bodhisattva is practicing on marks, but has not attained the faith of believing in the state of being unproduced by nature, and does not abide in the genuine perfection of wisdom. This teaches that form and so forth, distinguished by being ultimately without essence, are the object of observation. Some think of the meaning of this sūtra and assert that the emptiness that is merely a non-affirming negation negating the object of negation, true establishment, is not the ultimate abiding nature, and assert that it is inappropriate to apprehend, 'Form and so forth are empty of true existence', and so forth—these are incorrect, because they are invalidated by valid reasonings and scriptures. From the Great Commentary on the Root of Wisdom: 'Likewise, when it is taught, "Things do not exist by their essence", it is not that it is inappropriate to apprehend, "These are empty of true existence", but rather it is inappropriate to apprehend, "This emptiness of things of true existence is true". Therefore, asserting that this text teaches that even apprehending "Phenomena are empty" is incurable, is greatly unexamined speech. Both masters stated that the meaning of "view of emptiness" is clinging to emptiness as a thing, and that is apprehending emptiness as true, or apprehending emptiness as existing by its essence; how could it be merely apprehending, "It lacks nature"?' And it states: 'If one wrongly apprehends the meaning of the text in that way, one deprecates ultimate truth by saying it is impossible, and even if it is possible, by apprehending that maintaining the ascertainment ascertaining it leads to apprehending marks, one creates a great obstacle to maintaining the view that properly ascertains the authentic meaning.' Also from the Heart of Wisdom: In answer to the question of how to practice the profound perfection of wisdom, it is stated, 'He rightly sees those five aggregates also as empty of nature'—stating that one must see them as empty of nature; and also from this very sūtra: 'Whenever, analyzing conditioned and unconditioned and white and black phenomena with wisdom, not even a mere particle is observed; at that time it counts as the perfection of wisdom in the world'—because it states that if, by analyzing phenomena with wisdom, one sees that not even a mere particle is observed, it counts as the perfection of wisdom. There are certainly many other scriptures and reasonings, but fearing too many words, I have not expanded upon them.

As for the aspect, it is taught by one stanza, 'Moreover this wisdom' and so forth. The meaning is as follows: Moreover, if one examines and analyzes, thinking thus: 'As to this sole path for traveling to liberation called the wisdom that realizes all phenomena to not exist by their own nature, what is it—whether it is the aggregates of form and so forth, or a substance, or a quality, or an action, or a universal, or a particular, or an inherence? Whose, which person's, is it? From which of the four extremes is it produced?'—it is none of these, because it is ultimately unproduced. By this very reasoning, it examines and analyzes all these phenomena from form up to omniscience as being empty of their own essence. Thus, that bodhisattva who, when closely investigating with authentic reasonings such as [the reasoning of] neither one nor many and the diamond slivers and so forth, sees them as empty of nature, and is undaunted and unafraid of the meaning of the abiding nature, is near to perfect awakening. This teaches the distinction of the cause; and that seeing phenomena as lacking nature when thoroughly analyzed is the aspect.

།དེས་ན་ཆོས་རྣམས་སྟོང་པའོ་སྙམ་དུ་བཟུང་ན་ཡང་གསོར་མི་རུང་བར་གཞུང་འདིས་བསྟན་པར་འདོད་པ་ནི་མ་བརྟགས་པར་སྨྲ་བ་ཆེན་པའོ། ཞེས་དང་། དེ་ལྟར་གཞུང་གི་དོན་ལོག་པར་བཟུང་ན་ནི་དོན་དམ་པའི་བདེན་པ་མི་སྲིད་ཅེས་སྐུར་བ་འདེབས་པ་དང་། The object of observation of patience. The object of observation of patience is taught by one stanza, 'If one does not know' and so forth. The meaning is as follows: If, while not knowing the meaning of all phenomena, form and so forth, being empty of nature from the very beginning, one manifestly conceptualizes form as form established by its own essence, and likewise practices with the perception of true clinging to feeling, and volition, that is, the aggregate of perception and the aggregate of consciousness; not only is one practicing on marks, but even if, when single-pointedly poised in meditative equipoise on emptiness, one conceptualizes, 'This aggregate of form is empty of nature', one is practicing on volitions that manifestly condition, and because the appearance of the five aggregates is not blocked, even if one meditates in that way, such a bodhisattva is practicing on marks, but has not attained the faith of believing in the state of being unproduced by nature, and does not abide in the genuine perfection of wisdom. This teaches that form and so forth, distinguished by being ultimately without essence, are the object of observation. Some think of the meaning of this sūtra and assert that the emptiness that is merely a non-affirming negation negating the object of negation, true establishment, is not the ultimate abiding nature, and assert that it is inappropriate to apprehend, 'Form and so forth are empty of true existence', and so forth—these are incorrect, because they are invalidated by valid reasonings and scriptures. From the Great Commentary on the Root of Wisdom: 'Likewise, when it is taught, "Things do not exist by their essence", it is not that it is inappropriate to apprehend, "These are empty of true existence", but rather it is inappropriate to apprehend, "This emptiness of things of true existence is true". Therefore, asserting that this text teaches that even apprehending "Phenomena are empty" is incurable, is greatly unexamined speech. Both masters stated that the meaning of "view of emptiness" is clinging to emptiness as a thing, and that is apprehending emptiness as true, or apprehending emptiness as existing by its essence; how could it be merely apprehending, "It lacks nature"?' And it states: 'If one wrongly apprehends the meaning of the text in that way, one deprecates ultimate truth by saying it is impossible, and even if it is possible, by apprehending that maintaining the ascertainment ascertaining it leads to apprehending marks, one creates a great obstacle to maintaining the view that properly ascertains the authentic meaning.' Also from the Heart of Wisdom: In answer to the question of how to practice the profound perfection of wisdom, it is stated, 'He rightly sees those five aggregates also as empty of nature'—stating that one must see them as empty of nature; and also from this very sūtra: 'Whenever, analyzing conditioned and unconditioned and white and black phenomena with wisdom, not even a mere particle is observed; at that time it counts as the perfection of wisdom in the world'—because it states that if, by analyzing phenomena with wisdom, one sees that not even a mere particle is observed, it counts as the perfection of wisdom. There are certainly many other scriptures and reasonings, but fearing too many words, I have not expanded upon them.

heading: **ཤེས་སྒྲིབ་བཟུང་རྟོག**
translation: The conceptualization of the apprehended, a cognitive obscuration. If the first is also divided by way of its root, there are two: the conceptualization of the apprehended regarding the thoroughly afflicted and the conceptualization of the apprehended regarding the completely purified. If divided by way of its branches: for the conceptualization of the apprehended regarding the thoroughly afflicted which is a cognitive obscuration, there are nine, such as the clinging awareness that, observing afflicted ignorance, clings to it as truly being an object to be enjoyed. For the conceptualization of the apprehended regarding the completely purified which is a cognitive obscuration, there are also nine, such as the clinging awareness that, observing the completely purified aggregates, clings to them as truly being objects to be enjoyed. As for these two conceptualizations of the apprehended, by one stanza, 'Whatever does not exist' and so forth, from the opposite side of explicitly teaching the object of observation of the conceptualization of the apprehended regarding the completely purified, it teaches ignorance that is deluded regarding the mode of existence of the two truths as the object of observation of the conceptualization of the apprehended regarding the thoroughly afflicted. Moreover, whatever apprehended object of the thoroughly afflicted or completely purified, when analyzed by reasonings such as the refutation of production from the four extremes and so forth, is unable to withstand analysis and so is not truly existent; this is called 'not established by nature', because it is established by scripture and reasoning. Childish ordinary beings, having properly analyzed those phenomena, posit them as existing merely conventionally and not existing ultimately, and these two—existing conventionally and not existing ultimately—are also phenomena that are not truly existent, because both are merely posited by the power of conceptuality and cannot withstand analysis by reasoning. Therefore, if whatever bodhisattva knows this manner in which, just as pebbles and sticks in an illusion appearing as horses and elephants does not contradict their being empty of that, phenomena existing conventionally and not existing ultimately not only do not contradict one another but act as mutually helpful companions, they will definitely emerge from the extremes of existence and peace and will obtain non-abiding nirvāṇa.

As for the aspect, it is taught by one stanza, 'Whoever [apprehends] not form' and so forth. The meaning is as follows: Whoever does not apprehend form as form established by its own essence, and likewise does not apprehend feeling as established by nature, and does not apprehend perception, volition, and so forth themselves as established from their own side, and also does not practice or abide by way of apprehending consciousness as established by its own mode of abiding or essence; in short, that meditative equipoise, which, having blocked the appearance of the five aggregates from the perspective of meditative equipoise poised in emptiness, practices without abiding with true clinging to any object whatsoever, is not observed as [thinking], 'I practice on emptiness', because the wisdom that is free from all conceit of the three spheres being true has become stable. Having taught the aspect thus, the manner in which it acts as a cause is: Endowed with the mind that realizes the three—agent, action, and object—as truly unproduced in that way, one attains the supreme utter pacification of distraction and so forth in the samādhis named 'heroic stride' and so forth, which is to say one touches the Mahāyāna path of seeing that completely obtains the classes of realization of the three vehicles. This teaches that realizing that what is ultimately without essence is conventionally the essence of form and so forth is the aspect. The term 'patience' is because one is free from manifest fear regarding the profound unproduced phenomena.

The meaning is as follows: Whatever bodhisattva, when meditating on the perfection of wisdom that has become the essence of the path of preparation in the manner explained previously, at this time when the manifest apprehension of self of phenomena and persons in their own continuum is appeased, abides in the samādhi of supreme dharma of the path—they are prophesied by the former Tathāgatas to not turn back from unexcelled perfect awakening; at that time, for that bodhisattva, there arises no conceit thinking, 'I am poised in meditative equipoise on emptiness' or 'I have arisen from it', or 'I am prophesied'. If one asks for what reason, it is because they completely know the nature of all phenomena to be the equality of emptiness of true existence. By this, it is taught that form and so forth, indivisible in essence from the special cause by which one is prophesied by the Buddhas when one realizes its nature, are the object of observation.

As for the aspect, it is taught by one stanza, 'If one practices in that way' and so forth. The meaning is as follows: If one practices in that way without conceit of truth regarding any phenomenon whatsoever, one is practicing the wisdom of the Sugatas, because that bodhisattva thoroughly knows that the very fact that there is ultimately no practicing regarding any phenomenon is the holy practice of a conqueror's child. Regarding any phenomenon of the path of preparation and so forth, one does not observe as true the object of practice which is the perfection of wisdom, the practitioner which is the bodhisattva, or the action of practicing which is the practice; this practice without observing the three spheres is practicing the supreme perfection of wisdom. Thus, this teaches the aspect as being without conceit, and also teaches the distinction of the cause. Each of the path of preparation's [levels of] heat and so forth has three—small, middling, and great—making twelve; and although there are distinctions of dissimilar objects of observation and aspects of these to be correlated with the extensive and middling sūtras and so forth, here, owing to the abbreviated words of the sūtra, they cannot be explicitly correlated, but they should be known to be taught implicitly.

heading: **ཤེས་སྒྲིབ་འཛིན་རྟོག**
translation: The conceptualization of the apprehender, a cognitive obscuration. Second, for the conceptualization of the apprehender which is a cognitive obscuration, if divided by way of its root, there are two: the conceptualization of the apprehender of the substantial and the conceptualization of the apprehender of the imputed. If divided by way of its branches: for the conceptualization of the apprehender of the substantial which is a cognitive obscuration, there are nine, such as the true apprehension of an enjoyer observing the apprehension of a self as independent. For the conceptualization of the apprehender of the imputed which is a cognitive obscuration, there are also nine, such as the true apprehension of an enjoyer observing the apprehension of a person as imputed. These two conceptualizations of the apprehender are taught by one stanza, 'Whoever here [apprehends] the five aggregates' and so forth. Furthermore, from the opposite side of explicitly teaching the 'I' imputed upon the five aggregates—the first of the nine objects of observation—as the object of observation of the apprehension of the imputed, it teaches the self independent of the aggregates as the object of observation of the apprehension of the substantial. Whoever, here during the time of training on the path, knows all phenomena such as the five aggregates to be like an illusion, for example, appearing yet not truly existent, and regarding that also, does not make a distinction of true and untrue between those two by treating the illusion as one thing that is false and the aggregates as another thing that is true, but knowing the five aggregates themselves to be like an illusion, a dream, a mirage, and so forth, is free from the perception of the various conceptualizations of the apprehender and practices the thorough pacification of all fabrications; this is practicing the supreme perfection of wisdom. In this context, being free from the conceptualizations of the apprehended and apprehender is not abandoning their seeds, but being free from their manifestation.

As for the aspect, it is taught by one stanza, 'Whoever [apprehends] not form' and so forth. The meaning is as follows: Whoever does not apprehend form as form established by its own essence, and likewise does not apprehend feeling as established by nature, and does not apprehend perception, volition, and so forth themselves as established from their own side, and also does not practice or abide by way of apprehending consciousness as established by its own mode of abiding or essence; in short, that meditative equipoise, which, having blocked the appearance of the five aggregates from the perspective of meditative equipoise poised in emptiness, practices without abiding with true clinging to any object whatsoever, is not observed as [thinking], 'I practice on emptiness', because the wisdom that is free from all conceit of the three spheres being true has become stable. Having taught the aspect thus, the manner in which it acts as a cause is: Endowed with the mind that realizes the three—agent, action, and object—as truly unproduced in that way, one attains the supreme utter pacification of distraction and so forth in the samādhis named 'heroic stride' and so forth, which is to say one touches the Mahāyāna path of seeing that completely obtains the classes of realization of the three vehicles. This teaches that realizing that what is ultimately without essence is conventionally the essence of form and so forth is the aspect. The term 'patience' is because one is free from manifest fear regarding the profound unproduced phenomena.

The object of observation of supreme dharma. The object of observation of supreme dharma is taught by one stanza, 'Whatever bodhisattva' and so forth. The meaning is as follows: Whatever bodhisattva, when meditating on the perfection of wisdom that has become the essence of the path of preparation in the manner explained previously, at this time when the manifest apprehension of self of phenomena and persons in their own continuum is appeased, abides in the samādhi of supreme dharma of the path—they are prophesied by the former Tathāgatas to not turn back from unexcelled perfect awakening; at that time, for that bodhisattva, there arises no conceit thinking, 'I am poised in meditative equipoise on emptiness' or 'I have arisen from it', or 'I am prophesied'. If one asks for what reason, it is because they completely know the nature of all phenomena to be the equality of emptiness of true existence. By this, it is taught that form and so forth, indivisible in essence from the special cause by which one is prophesied by the Buddhas when one realizes its nature, are the object of observation.

As for the aspect, it is taught by one stanza, 'If one practices in that way' and so forth. The meaning is as follows: If one practices in that way without conceit of truth regarding any phenomenon whatsoever, one is practicing the wisdom of the Sugatas, because that bodhisattva thoroughly knows that the very fact that there is ultimately no practicing regarding any phenomenon is the holy practice of a conqueror's child. Regarding any phenomenon of the path of preparation and so forth, one does not observe as true the object of practice which is the perfection of wisdom, the practitioner which is the bodhisattva, or the action of practicing which is the practice; this practice without observing the three spheres is practicing the supreme perfection of wisdom. Thus, this teaches the aspect as being without conceit, and also teaches the distinction of the cause. Each of the path of preparation's [levels of] heat and so forth has three—small, middling, and great—making twelve; and although there are distinctions of dissimilar objects of observation and aspects of these to be correlated with the extensive and middling sūtras and so forth, here, owing to the abbreviated words of the sūtra, they cannot be explicitly correlated, but they should be known to be taught implicitly.

heading: **ཤེས་སྒྲིབ་འཛིན་རྟོག**
translation: Third, teaching the distinction of the spiritual friend who is a spiritual mentor is taught by one stanza, 'Endowed with a spiritual friend' and so forth. Regarding this, from the two spiritual mentors, outer and inner: the outer spiritual mentor, being skillful in means, teaches, 'There are faults of the māras and actions such as this,' and turns [one] away from them, and then, in accordance with the mind of the disciple, gradually guides them on the paths of the lesser and middling persons, such as impermanence, suffering, and so forth, and when their continuum is well-ripened, acts as a spiritual mentor by way of teaching the meaning of the perfection of wisdom, such as emptiness and so forth. The inner spiritual mentor, being endowed with distinguished means and wisdom, holds [one] back from the two: attention of the lower vehicles and clinging to true existence.

[3-36] translation already produced for this document:
The conceptualization of the apprehended, a cognitive obscuration. If the first is also divided by way of its root, there are two: the conceptualization of the apprehended regarding the thoroughly afflicted and the conceptualization of the apprehended regarding the completely purified. If divided by way of its branches: for the conceptualization of the apprehended regarding the thoroughly afflicted which is a cognitive obscuration, there are nine, such as the clinging awareness that, observing afflicted ignorance, clings to it as truly being an object to be enjoyed. For the conceptualization of the apprehended regarding the completely purified which is a cognitive obscuration, there are also nine, such as the clinging awareness that, observing the completely purified aggregates, clings to them as truly being objects to be enjoyed. As for these two conceptualizations of the apprehended, by one stanza, 'Whatever does not exist' and so forth, from the opposite side of explicitly teaching the object of observation of the conceptualization of the apprehended regarding the completely purified, it teaches ignorance that is deluded regarding the mode of existence of the two truths as the object of observation of the conceptualization of the apprehended regarding the thoroughly afflicted. Moreover, whatever apprehended object of the thoroughly afflicted or completely purified, when analyzed by reasonings such as the refutation of production from the four extremes and so forth, is unable to withstand analysis and so is not truly existent; this is called 'not established by nature', because it is established by scripture and reasoning. Childish ordinary beings, having properly analyzed those phenomena, posit them as existing merely conventionally and not existing ultimately, and these two—existing conventionally and not existing ultimately—are also phenomena that are not truly existent, because both are merely posited by the power of conceptuality and cannot withstand analysis by reasoning. Therefore, if whatever bodhisattva knows this manner in which, just as pebbles and sticks in an illusion appearing as horses and elephants does not contradict their being empty of that, phenomena existing conventionally and not existing ultimately not only do not contradict one another but act as mutually helpful companions, they will definitely emerge from the extremes of existence and peace and will obtain non-abiding nirvāṇa.

The conceptualization of the apprehender, a cognitive obscuration. Second, for the conceptualization of the apprehender which is a cognitive obscuration, if divided by way of its root, there are two: the conceptualization of the apprehender of the substantial and the conceptualization of the apprehender of the imputed. If divided by way of its branches: for the conceptualization of the apprehender of the substantial which is a cognitive obscuration, there are nine, such as the true apprehension of an enjoyer observing the apprehension of a self as independent. For the conceptualization of the apprehender of the imputed which is a cognitive obscuration, there are also nine, such as the true apprehension of an enjoyer observing the apprehension of a person as imputed. These two conceptualizations of the apprehender are taught by one stanza, 'Whoever here [apprehends] the five aggregates' and so forth. Furthermore, from the opposite side of explicitly teaching the 'I' imputed upon the five aggregates—the first of the nine objects of observation—as the object of observation of the apprehension of the imputed, it teaches the self independent of the aggregates as the object of observation of the apprehension of the substantial. Whoever, here during the time of training on the path, knows all phenomena such as the five aggregates to be like an illusion, for example, appearing yet not truly existent, and regarding that also, does not make a distinction of true and untrue between those two by treating the illusion as one thing that is false and the aggregates as another thing that is true, but knowing the five aggregates themselves to be like an illusion, a dream, a mirage, and so forth, is free from the perception of the various conceptualizations of the apprehender and practices the thorough pacification of all fabrications; this is practicing the supreme perfection of wisdom. In this context, being free from the conceptualizations of the apprehended and apprehender is not abandoning their seeds, but being free from their manifestation.

heading: **ཤེས་སྒྲིབ་འཛིན་རྟོག**
translation: The meaning of the words: Bodhisattvas are endowed with a spiritual friend who guides them on the virtuous path by way of completely teaching phenomena of means and wisdom, such as the profound mode of existence, emptiness, and mind generation, dedication, aspiration prayers, and so forth; and being endowed with the two spiritual mentors, outer and inner, such as special insight that is the nature of the wisdom realizing emptiness embraced by distinguished means, by having heard the perfection of wisdom, the generating mother of the Victors, they will absolutely never become frightened, will comprehend the meaning of the mode of existence, and will not degenerate from the Mahāyāna. Having thus taught the distinction of the spiritual mentor by way of forward sequence, furthermore teaching it by way of reverse sequence: Whichever beginner who, not being inclined toward the Mahāyāna, is endowed with a non-virtuous friend who turns them away from it, and is devoid of the inner spiritual mentor of realizing the meaning of the perfection of wisdom by their own power, is left to the kindness of others, that is, dependent on others—for example, just as an unbaked vessel falls apart when touched by water, like water being poured into a clay pot not fired in a fire, causing it to spill and the clay pot to be destroyed, because they too, being frightened by emptiness, will discard the perfection of wisdom, and like the destroyed clay pot, all their previously existing conduct and practice will be destroyed.

The conceptualization of the apprehended, a cognitive obscuration. If the first is also divided by way of its root, there are two: the conceptualization of the apprehended regarding the thoroughly afflicted and the conceptualization of the apprehended regarding the completely purified. If divided by way of its branches: for the conceptualization of the apprehended regarding the thoroughly afflicted which is a cognitive obscuration, there are nine, such as the clinging awareness that, observing afflicted ignorance, clings to it as truly being an object to be enjoyed. For the conceptualization of the apprehended regarding the completely purified which is a cognitive obscuration, there are also nine, such as the clinging awareness that, observing the completely purified aggregates, clings to them as truly being objects to be enjoyed. As for these two conceptualizations of the apprehended, by one stanza, 'Whatever does not exist' and so forth, from the opposite side of explicitly teaching the object of observation of the conceptualization of the apprehended regarding the completely purified, it teaches ignorance that is deluded regarding the mode of existence of the two truths as the object of observation of the conceptualization of the apprehended regarding the thoroughly afflicted. Moreover, whatever apprehended object of the thoroughly afflicted or completely purified, when analyzed by reasonings such as the refutation of production from the four extremes and so forth, is unable to withstand analysis and so is not truly existent; this is called 'not established by nature', because it is established by scripture and reasoning. Childish ordinary beings, having properly analyzed those phenomena, posit them as existing merely conventionally and not existing ultimately, and these two—existing conventionally and not existing ultimately—are also phenomena that are not truly existent, because both are merely posited by the power of conceptuality and cannot withstand analysis by reasoning. Therefore, if whatever bodhisattva knows this manner in which, just as pebbles and sticks in an illusion appearing as horses and elephants does not contradict their being empty of that, phenomena existing conventionally and not existing ultimately not only do not contradict one another but act as mutually helpful companions, they will definitely emerge from the extremes of existence and peace and will obtain non-abiding nirvāṇa.

The conceptualization of the apprehender, a cognitive obscuration. Second, for the conceptualization of the apprehender which is a cognitive obscuration, if divided by way of its root, there are two: the conceptualization of the apprehender of the substantial and the conceptualization of the apprehender of the imputed. If divided by way of its branches: for the conceptualization of the apprehender of the substantial which is a cognitive obscuration, there are nine, such as the true apprehension of an enjoyer observing the apprehension of a self as independent. For the conceptualization of the apprehender of the imputed which is a cognitive obscuration, there are also nine, such as the true apprehension of an enjoyer observing the apprehension of a person as imputed. These two conceptualizations of the apprehender are taught by one stanza, 'Whoever here [apprehends] the five aggregates' and so forth. Furthermore, from the opposite side of explicitly teaching the 'I' imputed upon the five aggregates—the first of the nine objects of observation—as the object of observation of the apprehension of the imputed, it teaches the self independent of the aggregates as the object of observation of the apprehension of the substantial. Whoever, here during the time of training on the path, knows all phenomena such as the five aggregates to be like an illusion, for example, appearing yet not truly existent, and regarding that also, does not make a distinction of true and untrue between those two by treating the illusion as one thing that is false and the aggregates as another thing that is true, but knowing the five aggregates themselves to be like an illusion, a dream, a mirage, and so forth, is free from the perception of the various conceptualizations of the apprehender and practices the thorough pacification of all fabrications; this is practicing the supreme perfection of wisdom. In this context, being free from the conceptualizations of the apprehended and apprehender is not abandoning their seeds, but being free from their manifestation.

source: ཐེག་ཆེན་སྒྲུབ་པ།བཞི་པ་ཐེག་ཆེན་སྒྲུབ་པའི་རྟེན་རང་བཞིན་གནས་རིགས་ནི། རྒྱན་ལས། རྟོགས་པ་ཡིན་ནི། ཆོས་དྲུག་དང་། ནས། རིགས་ཞེས་བྱ། ཞེས་གསུངས། འདི་ལ་མཚན་ཉིད། དབྱེ་བ། ས་མཚམས་གསུམ་ལས། དང་པོ་ནི། རང་གི་རྟེན་ཆོས་སུ་གྱུར་བའི་དྲི་མ་དང་བཅས་པའི་སེམས་ཀྱི་ཆོས་ཉིད་གང་ཞིག །ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་སྐུ་འགྱུར་དུ་རུང་བ། རང་བཞིན་གནས་རིགས་ཀྱི་མཚན་ཉིད། བྱང་སེམས་ཀྱི་རྒྱུད་ཀྱི་ཆོས་ཉིད་ཀྱང་ཡིན། ཐེག་ཆེན་སྒྲུབ་པའི་དངོས་ཀྱི་རྟེན་གཞི་ཡང་ཡིན་པའི་གཞི་མཐུན་པ་དེ། ཐེག་ཆེན་སྒྲུབ་པའི་རྟེན་རང་བཞིན་གནས་རིགས་ཀྱི་མཚན་ཉིད། རིགས་ལ་སྒྲས་བརྗོད་རིགས་ཀྱི་སྒོ་ནས་དབྱེ་ན། རང་བཞིན་གནས་རིགས་དང་། རྗེས་འགྱུར་གྱི་རིགས་གཉིས་ཡོད། ཐེག་ཆེན་སྒྲུབ་པའི་རྟེན་རང་བཞིན་གནས་རིགས་ལ་དབྱེ་ན། དྲོད་སོགས་བཞི་དང་མཐོང་སྒོམ་གཉིས་ཏེ་རྟོགས་པའི་ཆོས་དྲུག་དང་། གཉེན་པོའི་སྒྲུབ་པ། སྤོང་བའི་སྒྲུབ་པ། སྤངས་བྱ་དེ་དག་ཏུ་གཏུགས་པའི་སྒྲུབ་པ། ཤེས་རབ་སྙིང་བརྩེར་བཅས་པའི་སྒྲུབ་པ། སློབ་མ་ཉན་ཐོས་སོགས་དང་ཐུན་མོང་མ་ཡིན་པའི་སྒྲུབ་པ། གཞན་དོན་གོ་རིམ་དུ་བྱེད་པའི་སྒྲུབ་པ། ཡེ་ཤེས་རྩོལ་བ་མི་མངའ་བར་འཇུག་པའི་སྒྲུབ་པའི་རྟེན་རང་བཞིན་གནས་རིགས་དང་བཅུ་གསུམ་ཡོད། ས་མཚམས་ཐེག་ཆེན་གྱི་ཚོགས་ལམ་ནས་རྒྱུན་མཐའི་བར་ན་ཡོད།
translation: Mahāyāna practice. Fourth, the naturally abiding affinity which is the support for Mahāyāna practice: The Ornament says, 'Realization is / the six phenomena,' down to, 'is called the affinity.' Regarding this, there are three: the definition, the divisions, and the boundaries. The first: the true nature of the mind with stains that has become its own support phenomenon, which is suitable to transform into the nature body, is the definition of the naturally abiding affinity. The common locus of being the true nature of the continuum of a bodhisattva and being the actual support basis for Mahāyāna practice is the definition of the naturally abiding affinity which is the support for Mahāyāna practice. If the affinity is divided by way of explicitly expressed affinities, there are two: the naturally abiding affinity and the developing affinity. If the naturally abiding affinity which is the support for Mahāyāna practice is divided, there are thirteen naturally abiding affinities which are the supports for: the six phenomena of realization, which are the four such as heat and so forth, and the two, seeing and meditation; the practice of antidotes; the practice of abandonment; the practice reaching the end of those objects of abandonment; the practice endowed with wisdom and compassion; the practice uncommon with disciples such as śrāvakas and so forth; the practice accomplishing the welfare of others in sequence; and the practice of engaging in pristine wisdom without effort. The boundaries are from the Mahāyāna path of accumulation up to the end of the continuum.

The conceptualization of the apprehended, a cognitive obscuration. If the first is also divided by way of its root, there are two: the conceptualization of the apprehended regarding the thoroughly afflicted and the conceptualization of the apprehended regarding the completely purified. If divided by way of its branches: for the conceptualization of the apprehended regarding the thoroughly afflicted which is a cognitive obscuration, there are nine, such as the clinging awareness that, observing afflicted ignorance, clings to it as truly being an object to be enjoyed. For the conceptualization of the apprehended regarding the completely purified which is a cognitive obscuration, there are also nine, such as the clinging awareness that, observing the completely purified aggregates, clings to them as truly being objects to be enjoyed. As for these two conceptualizations of the apprehended, by one stanza, 'Whatever does not exist' and so forth, from the opposite side of explicitly teaching the object of observation of the conceptualization of the apprehended regarding the completely purified, it teaches ignorance that is deluded regarding the mode of existence of the two truths as the object of observation of the conceptualization of the apprehended regarding the thoroughly afflicted. Moreover, whatever apprehended object of the thoroughly afflicted or completely purified, when analyzed by reasonings such as the refutation of production from the four extremes and so forth, is unable to withstand analysis and so is not truly existent; this is called 'not established by nature', because it is established by scripture and reasoning. Childish ordinary beings, having properly analyzed those phenomena, posit them as existing merely conventionally and not existing ultimately, and these two—existing conventionally and not existing ultimately—are also phenomena that are not truly existent, because both are merely posited by the power of conceptuality and cannot withstand analysis by reasoning. Therefore, if whatever bodhisattva knows this manner in which, just as pebbles and sticks in an illusion appearing as horses and elephants does not contradict their being empty of that, phenomena existing conventionally and not existing ultimately not only do not contradict one another but act as mutually helpful companions, they will definitely emerge from the extremes of existence and peace and will obtain non-abiding nirvāṇa.

The conceptualization of the apprehender, a cognitive obscuration. Second, for the conceptualization of the apprehender which is a cognitive obscuration, if divided by way of its root, there are two: the conceptualization of the apprehender of the substantial and the conceptualization of the apprehender of the imputed. If divided by way of its branches: for the conceptualization of the apprehender of the substantial which is a cognitive obscuration, there are nine, such as the true apprehension of an enjoyer observing the apprehension of a self as independent. For the conceptualization of the apprehender of the imputed which is a cognitive obscuration, there are also nine, such as the true apprehension of an enjoyer observing the apprehension of a person as imputed. These two conceptualizations of the apprehender are taught by one stanza, 'Whoever here [apprehends] the five aggregates' and so forth. Furthermore, from the opposite side of explicitly teaching the 'I' imputed upon the five aggregates—the first of the nine objects of observation—as the object of observation of the apprehension of the imputed, it teaches the self independent of the aggregates as the object of observation of the apprehension of the substantial. Whoever, here during the time of training on the path, knows all phenomena such as the five aggregates to be like an illusion, for example, appearing yet not truly existent, and regarding that also, does not make a distinction of true and untrue between those two by treating the illusion as one thing that is false and the aggregates as another thing that is true, but knowing the five aggregates themselves to be like an illusion, a dream, a mirage, and so forth, is free from the perception of the various conceptualizations of the apprehender and practices the thorough pacification of all fabrications; this is practicing the supreme perfection of wisdom. In this context, being free from the conceptualizations of the apprehended and apprehender is not abandoning their seeds, but being free from their manifestation.

heading: **ཐེག་ཆེན་སྒྲུབ་པ།**
translation: Although the thirteen are taught individually in the extensive sutras, here, since the words are summarized, teaching just the general naturally abiding affinity is taught by the two lines 'For what reason is this' and so forth. Furthermore, if one asks, 'For what reason is this person to be designated as a bodhisattva?' The answer is: if the mind were truly established, it would not provide the space for the arising of qualities, so one would not obtain the name 'bodhisattva'; however, since the naturally luminous mind, the basis from which all the qualities of a Buddha arise, is suitable for the abandonment of faults and suitable for the arising of qualities, by means of the wisdom of hearing, thinking, and meditating that realizes the true nature of the mind, one cuts off without remainder clinging to true existence or attachment to all phenomena such as forms and so forth; and having completely abandoned the conceptualizations of attachment through clinging to true existence toward all phenomena of objects of knowledge along with their seeds, by desiring their exhaustion, and because one will gradually obtain great awakening, one obtains the name 'bodhisattva'. For example, just as space provides room for other things with form, on the occasion when the sun gradually rises in space, it obtains the names of 'morning', 'noon', and so forth. From the Uttaratantra: 'Impure, both impure and pure, / and completely pure, in sequence, / are expressed as sentient beings, bodhisattvas, / and tathāgatas.' Thus, on the occasion of being impure with stains, they are designated as ordinary beings; when partially pure, as bodhisattvas; and when completely pure, they are designated with the name 'tathāgata'. Here too, all the thirteen bodhisattvas designated based on the different occasions of practice should be known to be designated based on the occasions of the gradual purification of the stains of that naturally abiding affinity—the true nature of the mind that provides the space or acts as the basis for the arising of qualities—and the occasions when qualities have gone on to increase.

Mahāyāna practice. Fourth, the naturally abiding affinity which is the support for Mahāyāna practice: The Ornament says, 'Realization is / the six phenomena,' down to, 'is called the affinity.' Regarding this, there are three: the definition, the divisions, and the boundaries. The first: the true nature of the mind with stains that has become its own support phenomenon, which is suitable to transform into the nature body, is the definition of the naturally abiding affinity. The common locus of being the true nature of the continuum of a bodhisattva and being the actual support basis for Mahāyāna practice is the definition of the naturally abiding affinity which is the support for Mahāyāna practice. If the affinity is divided by way of explicitly expressed affinities, there are two: the naturally abiding affinity and the developing affinity. If the naturally abiding affinity which is the support for Mahāyāna practice is divided, there are thirteen naturally abiding affinities which are the supports for: the six phenomena of realization, which are the four such as heat and so forth, and the two, seeing and meditation; the practice of antidotes; the practice of abandonment; the practice reaching the end of those objects of abandonment; the practice endowed with wisdom and compassion; the practice uncommon with disciples such as śrāvakas and so forth; the practice accomplishing the welfare of others in sequence; and the practice of engaging in pristine wisdom without effort. The boundaries are from the Mahāyāna path of accumulation up to the end of the continuum.

Mahāyāna practice. Fourth, the naturally abiding affinity which is the support for Mahāyāna practice: The Ornament says, 'Realization is / the six phenomena,' down to, 'is called the affinity.' Regarding this, there are three: the definition, the divisions, and the boundaries. The first: the true nature of the mind with stains that has become its own support phenomenon, which is suitable to transform into the nature body, is the definition of the naturally abiding affinity. The common locus of being the true nature of the continuum of a bodhisattva and being the actual support basis for Mahāyāna practice is the definition of the naturally abiding affinity which is the support for Mahāyāna practice. If the affinity is divided by way of explicitly expressed affinities, there are two: the naturally abiding affinity and the developing affinity. If the naturally abiding affinity which is the support for Mahāyāna practice is divided, there are thirteen naturally abiding affinities which are the supports for: the six phenomena of realization, which are the four such as heat and so forth, and the two, seeing and meditation; the practice of antidotes; the practice of abandonment; the practice reaching the end of those objects of abandonment; the practice endowed with wisdom and compassion; the practice uncommon with disciples such as śrāvakas and so forth; the practice accomplishing the welfare of others in sequence; and the practice of engaging in pristine wisdom without effort. The boundaries are from the Mahāyāna path of accumulation up to the end of the continuum.

Mahāyāna practice. Fourth, the naturally abiding affinity which is the support for Mahāyāna practice: The Ornament says, 'Realization is / the six phenomena,' down to, 'is called the affinity.' Regarding this, there are three: the definition, the divisions, and the boundaries. The first: the true nature of the mind with stains that has become its own support phenomenon, which is suitable to transform into the nature body, is the definition of the naturally abiding affinity. The common locus of being the true nature of the continuum of a bodhisattva and being the actual support basis for Mahāyāna practice is the definition of the naturally abiding affinity which is the support for Mahāyāna practice. If the affinity is divided by way of explicitly expressed affinities, there are two: the naturally abiding affinity and the developing affinity. If the naturally abiding affinity which is the support for Mahāyāna practice is divided, there are thirteen naturally abiding affinities which are the supports for: the six phenomena of realization, which are the four such as heat and so forth, and the two, seeing and meditation; the practice of antidotes; the practice of abandonment; the practice reaching the end of those objects of abandonment; the practice endowed with wisdom and compassion; the practice uncommon with disciples such as śrāvakas and so forth; the practice accomplishing the welfare of others in sequence; and the practice of engaging in pristine wisdom without effort. The boundaries are from the Mahāyāna path of accumulation up to the end of the continuum.

heading: **ཐེག་ཆེན་སྒྲུབ་པའི་དམིགས་པ།**
source: གཉིསཔ་དེ་ལ་དབྱེ་ན། དགེ་མི་དགེ་ལུང་མ་བསྟན་གསུམ། འཇིག་རྟེན་སོར་སྐྱས་ཀྱི་ཕུང་པོ། འཇིག་རྟེན་ལས་འདས་པའི་འཕགས་རྒྱུད་ཀྱི་བསམ་གཏན། ཟག་བཅས་ཉེར་ལེན་གྱི་ཕུང་པོ། དྲན་སོགས་ཟག་མེད། འདུ་བྱས་ལམ་བདེན། འདུས་མ་བྱས་འགོག་བདེན། ཐེག་གསུམ་མཐུན་མོང་གི་ཡོན་ཏན་བསམ་གཏན། ཐུན་མོང་མ་ཡིན་པ་སྟོབས་བཅུ་སྟེ་བཅུ་གཅིག་ཡོད། ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་ཐོག་ཆེན་སྒྲུབ་པའི་དམིགས་པ་ཡིན་ཀྱང་གཙོ་བོ་རྣམ་དག་ལམ་གྱི་དམིགས་པ་མཐར་ཐུག་ལ་བྱེད་དགོས་ཏེ། སེམས་བདེན་སྟོང་ལ་དམིགས་ནས་བསྒོམས་ན་སྤྲིན་ནམ་མཁའ་ལ་ཟད་པ་དང། ཆུ་བུར་ཆུ་ལ་ཐིམ་པ་ལྟར་འགོག་པ་རང་སྟེང་དུ་མཐོང་བ་དང་དྲི་མ་ཆོས་དབྱིངས་སུ་ཟད་པ་དང་འགོག་བདེན་དོན་དམ་བདེན་པར་འཇོག་པ་སོགས་འོངས་ཤིང་གནད་གཅིག་པའི་ཕྱིར་དང༌། འདིར་སྟོང་ཉིད་གཙོ་བོར་དངོས་སུ་བསྟན་ན་རིགས་སྟོན་པའི་གཞུང་དང་ཟློས་སྐྱོན་མེད་ཚུལ་ཇི་ལྟར་ཞེ་ན། རང་བཞིན་གཙོ་བོར་གྱུར་པ་རིགས་དང་རྣམ་འགྱུར་གཙོ་བོར་གྱུར་པ་དམིགས་པ་ཞེས་བཤད་བས་རིགས་ཀྱི་སྐབས་སུ་བདེན་སྟོང་ཁྱད་གཞི་དང་གཞན་ཐམས་ཅད་དེའི་ཁྱད་ཆོས་སུ་སྒྲུབ་པས་ཆོས་ཅན་གྱི་ཚུལ་གྱིས་བརྗོད་ལ།དམིགས་པའི་སྐབས་སུ་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་ཁྱད་གཞི་དང་བདེན་མེད་ཁྱད་ཆོས་ལྟ་བུར་བརྗོད་པས་སྐྱོན་མེད་ཅེས་གུང་ཐང་འཇམ་པའི་དབྱངས་ཀྱིས་གསུངས།
translation: Second, if that is divided, there are eleven: the three, virtuous, non-virtuous, and unspecified; the aggregates of worldly ordinary beings; the concentrations of the continuums of supramundane noble ones; the contaminated appropriated aggregates; the uncontaminated ones such as mindfulness and so forth; the conditioned path truth; the unconditioned cessation truth; the qualities common to the three vehicles, the concentrations; and the uncommon ones, the ten powers. Although all phenomena are focal objects of Mahāyāna practice, one must primarily treat the ultimate focal object of the completely pure path [as the focal object], because if one meditates by focusing on the mind as empty of true existence, just as clouds exhaust in the sky and a water bubble dissolves into water, such things as seeing cessation upon itself, stains exhausting into the dharmadhātu, and positing the cessation truth as the ultimate truth come about, and because they have the same vital point; and if one asks, 'If emptiness is primarily explicitly taught here, how is there no fault of repetition with the text teaching the affinity?' Gungthang Jamyang said there is no fault, because it is explained that the affinity is primarily the nature and the focal object is primarily the manifestation, so on the occasion of the affinity, by establishing emptiness of true existence as the basis of attributes and all other things as its attributes, it is expressed in the manner of the subject, whereas on the occasion of the focal object, all phenomena are expressed as the basis of attributes and the lack of true existence as like the attribute.

Mahāyāna practice. Fourth, the naturally abiding affinity which is the support for Mahāyāna practice: The Ornament says, 'Realization is / the six phenomena,' down to, 'is called the affinity.' Regarding this, there are three: the definition, the divisions, and the boundaries. The first: the true nature of the mind with stains that has become its own support phenomenon, which is suitable to transform into the nature body, is the definition of the naturally abiding affinity. The common locus of being the true nature of the continuum of a bodhisattva and being the actual support basis for Mahāyāna practice is the definition of the naturally abiding affinity which is the support for Mahāyāna practice. If the affinity is divided by way of explicitly expressed affinities, there are two: the naturally abiding affinity and the developing affinity. If the naturally abiding affinity which is the support for Mahāyāna practice is divided, there are thirteen naturally abiding affinities which are the supports for: the six phenomena of realization, which are the four such as heat and so forth, and the two, seeing and meditation; the practice of antidotes; the practice of abandonment; the practice reaching the end of those objects of abandonment; the practice endowed with wisdom and compassion; the practice uncommon with disciples such as śrāvakas and so forth; the practice accomplishing the welfare of others in sequence; and the practice of engaging in pristine wisdom without effort. The boundaries are from the Mahāyāna path of accumulation up to the end of the continuum.

heading: **ཐེག་ཆེན་སྒྲུབ་པའི་དམིགས་པ།**
translation: Having taught the affinity, to teach the focal object of practice, the two lines 'of the Victors' and so forth were spoken. The meaning is: By realizing and habituating to all phenomena as empty of true existence, one abandons the grasping at true existence along with its seeds and attains contact with 'the great awakening of the Victors,' which has become free from attachment through clinging to true existence; therefore, this person obtains the name 'bodhisattva'. Thus, on this occasion, since the two bodies are taught as the result, it is established that at the time of the cause one focuses on both the mode of being and the multiplicity; and if so, it is established that all phenomena are posited as the focal object of practice.

Although the thirteen are taught individually in the extensive sutras, here, since the words are summarized, teaching just the general naturally abiding affinity is taught by the two lines 'For what reason is this' and so forth. Furthermore, if one asks, 'For what reason is this person to be designated as a bodhisattva?' The answer is: if the mind were truly established, it would not provide the space for the arising of qualities, so one would not obtain the name 'bodhisattva'; however, since the naturally luminous mind, the basis from which all the qualities of a Buddha arise, is suitable for the abandonment of faults and suitable for the arising of qualities, by means of the wisdom of hearing, thinking, and meditating that realizes the true nature of the mind, one cuts off without remainder clinging to true existence or attachment to all phenomena such as forms and so forth; and having completely abandoned the conceptualizations of attachment through clinging to true existence toward all phenomena of objects of knowledge along with their seeds, by desiring their exhaustion, and because one will gradually obtain great awakening, one obtains the name 'bodhisattva'. For example, just as space provides room for other things with form, on the occasion when the sun gradually rises in space, it obtains the names of 'morning', 'noon', and so forth. From the Uttaratantra: 'Impure, both impure and pure, / and completely pure, in sequence, / are expressed as sentient beings, bodhisattvas, / and tathāgatas.' Thus, on the occasion of being impure with stains, they are designated as ordinary beings; when partially pure, as bodhisattvas; and when completely pure, they are designated with the name 'tathāgata'. Here too, all the thirteen bodhisattvas designated based on the different occasions of practice should be known to be designated based on the occasions of the gradual purification of the stains of that naturally abiding affinity—the true nature of the mind that provides the space or acts as the basis for the arising of qualities—and the occasions when qualities have gone on to increase.

གཉིསཔ་དེ་ལ་དབྱེ་ན། དགེ་མི་དགེ་ལུང་མ་བསྟན་གསུམ། འཇིག་རྟེན་སོར་སྐྱས་ཀྱི་ཕུང་པོ། འཇིག་རྟེན་ལས་འདས་པའི་འཕགས་རྒྱུད་ཀྱི་བསམ་གཏན། ཟག་བཅས་ཉེར་ལེན་གྱི་ཕུང་པོ། དྲན་སོགས་ཟག་མེད། འདུ་བྱས་ལམ་བདེན། འདུས་མ་བྱས་འགོག་བདེན། ཐེག་གསུམ་མཐུན་མོང་གི་ཡོན་ཏན་བསམ་གཏན། ཐུན་མོང་མ་ཡིན་པ་སྟོབས་བཅུ་སྟེ་བཅུ་གཅིག་ཡོད། ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་ཐོག་ཆེན་སྒྲུབ་པའི་དམིགས་པ་ཡིན་ཀྱང་གཙོ་བོ་རྣམ་དག་ལམ་གྱི་དམིགས་པ་མཐར་ཐུག་ལ་བྱེད་དགོས་ཏེ། སེམས་བདེན་སྟོང་ལ་དམིགས་ནས་བསྒོམས་ན་སྤྲིན་ནམ་མཁའ་ལ་ཟད་པ་དང། ཆུ་བུར་ཆུ་ལ་ཐིམ་པ་ལྟར་འགོག་པ་རང་སྟེང་དུ་མཐོང་བ་དང་དྲི་མ་ཆོས་དབྱིངས་སུ་ཟད་པ་དང་འགོག་བདེན་དོན་དམ་བདེན་པར་འཇོག་པ་སོགས་འོངས་ཤིང་གནད་གཅིག་པའི་ཕྱིར་དང༌། འདིར་སྟོང་ཉིད་གཙོ་བོར་དངོས་སུ་བསྟན་ན་རིགས་སྟོན་པའི་གཞུང་དང་ཟློས་སྐྱོན་མེད་ཚུལ་ཇི་ལྟར་ཞེ་ན། རང་བཞིན་གཙོ་བོར་གྱུར་པ་རིགས་དང་རྣམ་འགྱུར་གཙོ་བོར་གྱུར་པ་དམིགས་པ་ཞེས་བཤད་བས་རིགས་ཀྱི་སྐབས་སུ་བདེན་སྟོང་ཁྱད་གཞི་དང་གཞན་ཐམས་ཅད་དེའི་ཁྱད་ཆོས་སུ་སྒྲུབ་པས་ཆོས་ཅན་གྱི་ཚུལ་གྱིས་བརྗོད་ལ།དམིགས་པའི་སྐབས་སུ་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་ཁྱད་གཞི་དང་བདེན་མེད་ཁྱད་ཆོས་ལྟ་བུར་བརྗོད་པས་སྐྱོན་མེད་ཅེས་གུང་ཐང་འཇམ་པའི་དབྱངས་ཀྱིས་གསུངས།

Second, if that is divided, there are eleven: the three, virtuous, non-virtuous, and unspecified; the aggregates of worldly ordinary beings; the concentrations of the continuums of supramundane noble ones; the contaminated appropriated aggregates; the uncontaminated ones such as mindfulness and so forth; the conditioned path truth; the unconditioned cessation truth; the qualities common to the three vehicles, the concentrations; and the uncommon ones, the ten powers. Although all phenomena are focal objects of Mahāyāna practice, one must primarily treat the ultimate focal object of the completely pure path [as the focal object], because if one meditates by focusing on the mind as empty of true existence, just as clouds exhaust in the sky and a water bubble dissolves into water, such things as seeing cessation upon itself, stains exhausting into the dharmadhātu, and positing the cessation truth as the ultimate truth come about, and because they have the same vital point; and if one asks, 'If emptiness is primarily explicitly taught here, how is there no fault of repetition with the text teaching the affinity?' Gungthang Jamyang said there is no fault, because it is explained that the affinity is primarily the nature and the focal object is primarily the manifestation, so on the occasion of the affinity, by establishing emptiness of true existence as the basis of attributes and all other things as its attributes, it is expressed in the manner of the subject, whereas on the occasion of the focal object, all phenomena are expressed as the basis of attributes and the lack of true existence as like the attribute.

མདོ་རྒྱས་པ་རྣམས་སུ་བཅུ་གསུམ་པོ་སོ་སོར་བསྟན་ཀྱང་འདིར་ཚིག་བསྡུས་པས་རང་བཞིན་གནས་རིགས་སྤྱི་ཙམ་སྟོན་པར། ཅི་ཕྱིར་འདི་ནི་ཞེས་སོགས་རྐང་པ་གཉིས་ཀྱི་བསྟན། དེ་ཡང་ཅི་ཡི་ཕྱིར་གང་ཟག་འདི་ནི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཞེས་གདགས་པར་བྱ་ཞེ་ན། ལན་ནི་སེམས་བདེན་པར་གྲུབ་ན་ཡོན་ཏན་མར་སྐྱེ་བའི་གོ་མི་འབྱེད་པས་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའི་མིང་མི་ཐོབ་ཀྱང༌། སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་ཡོན་ཏན་ཐམས་ཅད་འབྱུང་བའི་གཞི་སེམས་ཀྱི་རང་བཞིན་འོད་གསལ་བ་ལ་སྐྱོན་སྤངས་རུང་དང་ཡོན་ཏན་སྐྱེ་རུང་ཡིན་པས་སེམས་ཀྱི་ཆོས་ཉིད་རྟོགས་པའི་ཐོས་བསམ་སྒོམ་གསུམ་གྱི་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱིས་གཟུགས་ལ་སོགས་པའི་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་ལ་བདེན་པར་ཞེན་པའམ་ཆགས་པ་མ་ལུས་པར་གཅོད་པར་བྱེད་ཅིང་། ཤེས་བྱའི་ཆོས་ཀུན་ལ་བདེན་ཞེན་གྱིས་ཆགས་པའི་རྣམ་པར་རྟོག་པ་ས་བོན་དང་བཅས་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་སྤངས་ཏེ་ཟད་པར་འདོད་པ་དང་། མཐར་གྱིས་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཆེན་པོ་ཐོབ་པར་འགྱུར་བས་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམའ་དཔའ་ཞེས་པའི་མིང་ཐོབ་སྟེ་། དཔེར་ན་ནམ་མཁས་གཟུགས་ཅན་གཞན་གྱི་གོ་འབྱེད་པས་ནམ་མཁའ་ལ་ཉི་མ་རིམ་གྱིས་ཤར་བའི་གནས་སྐབས་ལ་སྔ་དྲོ་དང་གོང་སོགས་ཀྱི་མིང་ཐོབ་པ་བཞིན་ནོ། །རྒྱུད་བླ་མ་ལས། མ་དག་མ་དག་དག་པ་དང་། །ཤིན་ཏུ་རྣམ་དག་གོ་རིམ་བཞིན། །སེམས་ཅན་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་དང་། །དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ཞེས་བརྗོད་དོ། །ཅེས་དྲི་མས་མ་དག་པའི་གནས་སྐབས་ན་སོར་སྐྱེས་དང་། ཆ་གཅིག་དག་པ་ལ་བྱང་སེམས་དང༌། ཐམསཅད་དག་པ་ལ་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ཞེས་པའི་མིང་བཏགས་པ་དང་། འདིར་ཡང་སྒྲུབ་པའི་གནས་སྐབས་ཐ་དད་པ་ལ་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་བཅུ་གསུམ་དུ་བཏགས་པ་ཐམས་ཅད་ཡོན་ཏན་སྐྱེ་བའི་གོ་འབྱེད་པའམ་གཞིར་གྱུར་བའི་སེམས་ཀྱི་ཆོས་ཉིད་རང་བཞིན་གནས་རིགས་དེའི་དྲི་མ་རིམ་གྱིས་དག་པ་དང་། ཡོན་ཏན་གོང་འཕེལ་དུ་སོང་བའི་གནས་སྐབས་ལ་བཏགས་པ་ཡིན་པར་ཤེས་པར་བྱའོ། །
[3-41] translation already produced for this document:
Although the thirteen are taught individually in the extensive sutras, here, since the words are summarized, teaching just the general naturally abiding affinity is taught by the two lines 'For what reason is this' and so forth. Furthermore, if one asks, 'For what reason is this person to be designated as a bodhisattva?' The answer is: if the mind were truly established, it would not provide the space for the arising of qualities, so one would not obtain the name 'bodhisattva'; however, since the naturally luminous mind, the basis from which all the qualities of a Buddha arise, is suitable for the abandonment of faults and suitable for the arising of qualities, by means of the wisdom of hearing, thinking, and meditating that realizes the true nature of the mind, one cuts off without remainder clinging to true existence or attachment to all phenomena such as forms and so forth; and having completely abandoned the conceptualizations of attachment through clinging to true existence toward all phenomena of objects of knowledge along with their seeds, by desiring their exhaustion, and because one will gradually obtain great awakening, one obtains the name 'bodhisattva'. For example, just as space provides room for other things with form, on the occasion when the sun gradually rises in space, it obtains the names of 'morning', 'noon', and so forth. From the Uttaratantra: 'Impure, both impure and pure, / and completely pure, in sequence, / are expressed as sentient beings, bodhisattvas, / and tathāgatas.' Thus, on the occasion of being impure with stains, they are designated as ordinary beings; when partially pure, as bodhisattvas; and when completely pure, they are designated with the name 'tathāgata'. Here too, all the thirteen bodhisattvas designated based on the different occasions of practice should be known to be designated based on the occasions of the gradual purification of the stains of that naturally abiding affinity—the true nature of the mind that provides the space or acts as the basis for the arising of qualities—and the occasions when qualities have gone on to increase.

Regarding this, there are two: the definition and the divisions. The first: the basis upon which superimpositions are to be cut off by Mahāyāna practice is the definition of the focal object of Mahāyāna practice.

[3-44] source:
གཉིསཔ་དེ་ལ་དབྱེ་ན། དགེ་མི་དགེ་ལུང་མ་བསྟན་གསུམ། འཇིག་རྟེན་སོར་སྐྱས་ཀྱི་ཕུང་པོ། འཇིག་རྟེན་ལས་འདས་པའི་འཕགས་རྒྱུད་ཀྱི་བསམ་གཏན། ཟག་བཅས་ཉེར་ལེན་གྱི་ཕུང་པོ། དྲན་སོགས་ཟག་མེད། འདུ་བྱས་ལམ་བདེན། འདུས་མ་བྱས་འགོག་བདེན། ཐེག་གསུམ་མཐུན་མོང་གི་ཡོན་ཏན་བསམ་གཏན། ཐུན་མོང་མ་ཡིན་པ་སྟོབས་བཅུ་སྟེ་བཅུ་གཅིག་ཡོད། ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་ཐོག་ཆེན་སྒྲུབ་པའི་དམིགས་པ་ཡིན་ཀྱང་གཙོ་བོ་རྣམ་དག་ལམ་གྱི་དམིགས་པ་མཐར་ཐུག་ལ་བྱེད་དགོས་ཏེ། སེམས་བདེན་སྟོང་ལ་དམིགས་ནས་བསྒོམས་ན་སྤྲིན་ནམ་མཁའ་ལ་ཟད་པ་དང། ཆུ་བུར་ཆུ་ལ་ཐིམ་པ་ལྟར་འགོག་པ་རང་སྟེང་དུ་མཐོང་བ་དང་དྲི་མ་ཆོས་དབྱིངས་སུ་ཟད་པ་དང་འགོག་བདེན་དོན་དམ་བདེན་པར་འཇོག་པ་སོགས་འོངས་ཤིང་གནད་གཅིག་པའི་ཕྱིར་དང༌། འདིར་སྟོང་ཉིད་གཙོ་བོར་དངོས་སུ་བསྟན་ན་རིགས་སྟོན་པའི་གཞུང་དང་ཟློས་སྐྱོན་མེད་ཚུལ་ཇི་ལྟར་ཞེ་ན། རང་བཞིན་གཙོ་བོར་གྱུར་པ་རིགས་དང་རྣམ་འགྱུར་གཙོ་བོར་གྱུར་པ་དམིགས་པ་ཞེས་བཤད་བས་རིགས་ཀྱི་སྐབས་སུ་བདེན་སྟོང་ཁྱད་གཞི་དང་གཞན་ཐམས་ཅད་དེའི་ཁྱད་ཆོས་སུ་སྒྲུབ་པས་ཆོས་ཅན་གྱི་ཚུལ་གྱིས་བརྗོད་ལ།དམིགས་པའི་སྐབས་སུ་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་ཁྱད་གཞི་དང་བདེན་མེད་ཁྱད་ཆོས་ལྟ་བུར་བརྗོད་པས་སྐྱོན་མེད་ཅེས་གུང་ཐང་འཇམ་པའི་དབྱངས་ཀྱིས་གསུངས།

Second, if that is divided, there are eleven: the three, virtuous, non-virtuous, and unspecified; the aggregates of worldly ordinary beings; the concentrations of the continuums of supramundane noble ones; the contaminated appropriated aggregates; the uncontaminated ones such as mindfulness and so forth; the conditioned path truth; the unconditioned cessation truth; the qualities common to the three vehicles, the concentrations; and the uncommon ones, the ten powers. Although all phenomena are focal objects of Mahāyāna practice, one must primarily treat the ultimate focal object of the completely pure path [as the focal object], because if one meditates by focusing on the mind as empty of true existence, just as clouds exhaust in the sky and a water bubble dissolves into water, such things as seeing cessation upon itself, stains exhausting into the dharmadhātu, and positing the cessation truth as the ultimate truth come about, and because they have the same vital point; and if one asks, 'If emptiness is primarily explicitly taught here, how is there no fault of repetition with the text teaching the affinity?' Gungthang Jamyang said there is no fault, because it is explained that the affinity is primarily the nature and the focal object is primarily the manifestation, so on the occasion of the affinity, by establishing emptiness of true existence as the basis of attributes and all other things as its attributes, it is expressed in the manner of the subject, whereas on the occasion of the focal object, all phenomena are expressed as the basis of attributes and the lack of true existence as like the attribute.

source: འདི་ལ་མཚན་ཉིད། དབྱེ་བ། ས་མཚམས་དང་གསུམ། དང་པོ་ནི། གང་གི་ཆེད་དུ་བྱ་བ་ལ་འཇུག་པའི་འབྲས་བུ་མཐར་ཐུག་དེ། ཐེག་ཆེན་སྒྲུབ་པའི་ཆེད་དུ་བྱ་བའི་མཚན་ཉིད། དབྱེ་ན། སེམས་དཔའ་ཆེན་པོ། སྤངས་པ་ཆེན་པོ།རྟོགས་པ་ཆེན་པོ་དང་གསུམ་ཡོད། ས་མཚམས་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱིས་ཁོ་ནར་ཡོད། དེ་ལྟ་བུའི་ཆེད་དུ་བྱ་བ་ཆེན་པ་ོགསུམ་ནི། ཅི་ཕྱིར་དེ་ནི་ཞེས་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གཅིག་གིས་བསྟན་པའི་དོན། ཡང་ཅི་ཡི་ཕྱིར་གང་ཟག་དེ་ལ་ནི་སེམས་དཔའ་ཆེ་ཞེས་མིང་དུ་གདགས་པར་བྱ་ཞེ་ན། འདི་ནི་སེམས་ཅན་གྱི་སྡེ་ཆེན་པོ་དང་ཚོགས་རྣམས་མང་པོའི་མགོན་དང་དཔུང་གཉེན་དུ་གྱུར་པས་མཆོག་ཏུ་གྱུར་པ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་ཕྱིར་དང་ཆེན་པོར་གྱུར་པས་སེམས་ཆེན་པོ་དང། སེམས་ཅན་ཁམས་དང་མོས་པ་མི་འདྲ་བ་རྣམས་ཀྱི་རང་རང་གི་མོས་པའི་དབང་གིས་འཇིག་ལྟའི་རྩ་བ་ཅན་གྱི་སྔོན་གྱི་མཐའ་ལ་བརྟེན་པ་ཞེ་བརྒྱད། ཕྱིར་མཐའ་ལ་བརྟེན་པ་བཅུ་བཞི་སྟེ་ལྟ་ངན་རེ་གཉིས་དང་། ལྟ་ངན་སུམ་བརྒྱ་སོགསས་ལྟ་ངན་མཐའ་ཡས་པ་རྣམས་ཐོག་མེད་ནས་གོམས་པས་གཞིག་དཀའ་ཞིང་མང་བས་ཕྱིར་ཆེན་པོ་སྟེ། དེ་དག་རྒྱུན་གཅོད་པའི་ཕྱིར་སྟོང་པ་ཉིད་ལ་སོགས་པའི་ཆོས་བསྟན་པས་སེལ་བར་བྱེད་པ་སྟེ་སེལ་བར་བྱེད་ལ། དེའང་ཐོག་མར་རང་ཉིད་ཀྱིས་སྤངས་དགོས་པས། སྤངས་པ་ཆེན་པོ་སྟེ་དེ་གཉིས་དངོས་སུ་བསྟན་ནས། སྒྲིབ་བྱེད་དང་བྲལ་བ་ན་གཟུགས་མཐོང་བ་ལྟར་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་རྟོགས་པ་ལ་གེགས་བྱེད་ཀྱི་སྒྲིབ་པ་སྤངས་པར་དངོས་སུ་བསྟན་པས་དེ་རྟོགས་པའི་ཡེ་ཤེས་རྣམ་པ་ཐམས་ཅད་མཁྱེན་པའི་རྟོགས་པ་ཆེན་པོའང་དོན་གྱིས་གོ་པའི་ཕྱིར། དེ་བས་ན་འབྲས་བུ་སྐུ་གསུམ་ཐོབ་པའི་ཕྱིར་དུ་ལམ་ཉམས་སུ་ལེན་པ་ཞུགས་པ་དེ་ཡི་ཕྱིར་ན་སེམས་དཔའ་ཆེན་པོ་ཞེས་པར་ནི་རབ་ཏུ་བརྗོད་དོ། །ཞེས་སོ། །
translation: Regarding this, there are three: the definition, the divisions, and the boundaries. The first: the ultimate result for the sake of which one engages in practice is the definition of the objective of Mahāyāna practice. If divided, there are three: great being, great abandonment, and great realization. The boundaries exist only at the Buddha stage. The meaning taught by the one verse 'For what reason is that' and so forth concerning such three great objectives is this: Furthermore, if one asks, 'For what reason is that person to be designated with the name "great being"?' Because this one has become the protector and ally of a great host and many assemblies of sentient beings, and thus has become supreme and has become great, it is the great mind; and due to the respective inclinations of sentient beings with different elements and inclinations, there are sixty-two bad views rooted in the view of the transitory collection—forty-eight relying on the past limit and fourteen relying on the future limit—and limitless bad views such as the three hundred bad views and so forth; because they have been habituated since beginningless time, they are difficult to destroy, and because they are many, therefore they are great; in order to sever their continuum, by teaching phenomena such as emptiness and so forth, one clears them away; and since one must first abandon them oneself, it is the great abandonment. Having explicitly taught those two, just as one sees forms when freed from things that obscure, by explicitly teaching the abandonment of the obscurations that hinder the realization of all phenomena, the great realization of the exalted wisdom of omniscience that realizes them is also implicitly understood. Therefore, because one has entered into practicing the path for the sake of obtaining the three bodies as the result, 'for that reason it is fully expressed as "great being".'

Although the thirteen are taught individually in the extensive sutras, here, since the words are summarized, teaching just the general naturally abiding affinity is taught by the two lines 'For what reason is this' and so forth. Furthermore, if one asks, 'For what reason is this person to be designated as a bodhisattva?' The answer is: if the mind were truly established, it would not provide the space for the arising of qualities, so one would not obtain the name 'bodhisattva'; however, since the naturally luminous mind, the basis from which all the qualities of a Buddha arise, is suitable for the abandonment of faults and suitable for the arising of qualities, by means of the wisdom of hearing, thinking, and meditating that realizes the true nature of the mind, one cuts off without remainder clinging to true existence or attachment to all phenomena such as forms and so forth; and having completely abandoned the conceptualizations of attachment through clinging to true existence toward all phenomena of objects of knowledge along with their seeds, by desiring their exhaustion, and because one will gradually obtain great awakening, one obtains the name 'bodhisattva'. For example, just as space provides room for other things with form, on the occasion when the sun gradually rises in space, it obtains the names of 'morning', 'noon', and so forth. From the Uttaratantra: 'Impure, both impure and pure, / and completely pure, in sequence, / are expressed as sentient beings, bodhisattvas, / and tathāgatas.' Thus, on the occasion of being impure with stains, they are designated as ordinary beings; when partially pure, as bodhisattvas; and when completely pure, they are designated with the name 'tathāgata'. Here too, all the thirteen bodhisattvas designated based on the different occasions of practice should be known to be designated based on the occasions of the gradual purification of the stains of that naturally abiding affinity—the true nature of the mind that provides the space or acts as the basis for the arising of qualities—and the occasions when qualities have gone on to increase.

Second, if that is divided, there are eleven: the three, virtuous, non-virtuous, and unspecified; the aggregates of worldly ordinary beings; the concentrations of the continuums of supramundane noble ones; the contaminated appropriated aggregates; the uncontaminated ones such as mindfulness and so forth; the conditioned path truth; the unconditioned cessation truth; the qualities common to the three vehicles, the concentrations; and the uncommon ones, the ten powers. Although all phenomena are focal objects of Mahāyāna practice, one must primarily treat the ultimate focal object of the completely pure path [as the focal object], because if one meditates by focusing on the mind as empty of true existence, just as clouds exhaust in the sky and a water bubble dissolves into water, such things as seeing cessation upon itself, stains exhausting into the dharmadhātu, and positing the cessation truth as the ultimate truth come about, and because they have the same vital point; and if one asks, 'If emptiness is primarily explicitly taught here, how is there no fault of repetition with the text teaching the affinity?' Gungthang Jamyang said there is no fault, because it is explained that the affinity is primarily the nature and the focal object is primarily the manifestation, so on the occasion of the affinity, by establishing emptiness of true existence as the basis of attributes and all other things as its attributes, it is expressed in the manner of the subject, whereas on the occasion of the focal object, all phenomena are expressed as the basis of attributes and the lack of true existence as like the attribute.

heading: **གོ་སྒྲུབ།**
source: གོ་སྒྲུབ།བདུན་པ་གོ་སྒྲུབ་ནི། རྒྱུན་ལས། དེ་དག་སོ་སོར་སྦྱིན་ལ་སོགས། །ནས། དྲུག་གིས་ཇི་བཞིན་བཤད། །ཅེས་གསུངས། ཐེག་ཆེན་སེམས་བསྐྱེད་ལ་བརྟེན་ནས་དོན་གཉིས་ཕུན་ཚོགས་སུ་སྒྲུབ་པར་བྱེད་པའི་ཆེན་པོ་དྲུག་ལྡན་གྱི་སེམས་དཔའི་རྣལ་འབྱོར། ཐེག་ཆེན་སྒྲུབ་པའི་མཚན་ཉིད། དབྱེ་ན་དཔེར་ན། གཡུལ་འགྱེད་པ་ལ་གོ་གྱོན་པ་དང༌། གཡུལ་དུ་ཞུགས་པ་དང་། དགྲ་ལས་རྒྱལ་བྱེད་ཀྱི་གྲོགས་དང་མཚོན་ཆ་དང་། དགྲ་ལས་རྒྱལ་བ་དང་འདྲ་བར་གོ་སྒྲུབ། འཇུག་སྒྲུབ། ཚོགས་སྒྲུབ། ངེས་འབྱུང་སྒྲུབ་པ་དང་བཞི་ཡོད། དང་པོ་གོ་སྒྲུབ་ལ་མཚན་ཉིད། དབྱེ་བ་ས་མཚམས་གསུམ་ལས། དང་པོ་ནི། སྦྱིན་སོགས་ཕར་ཕྱིན་རེ་རེའི་ནང་དུ་ཕར་ཕྱིན་དྲུག་དང་ཚང་བར་བསྡུས་ནས་ཉམས་སུ་ལེན་པར་འདོད་པའི་བསམ་པའི་བྱ་བ་རྒྱ་ཆེན་པོས་ཟིན་པའི་སེམས་དཔའི་རྣལ་འབྱོར། གོ་སྒྲུབ་ཀྱི་མཚན་ཉིད། དེ་དང་བྱང་སེམས་ཀྱི་མཁྱེན་པ་དོན་ཅིག །གཉིས་པ་དེ་ལ་དབྱེ་ན།  སྦྱིན་པ་ནས་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་གོ་སྒྲུབ་ཀྱི་བར་དྲུག་ཡོད། རྒྱས་པོར་ཕྱེ་ན། སྦྱིན་སོགས་རེ་རེ་ལ་དྲུག་དྲུག་སྟེ་སོ་དྲུག་ཡོད།  གསུམ་པ་ས་མཚམས་ཐེག་ཆེན་གྱི་ཚོགས་ལམ་ནས་རྒྱུན་མཐའི་བར་དུ་ཡོད། གོ་སྒྲུབ་དེ་ནི་གཏོང་བ་ཆེ་དང་ཞེས་སོགས་རྐང་པ་གཉིས་ཀྱིས་བསྟན། དོན་ནི། བཤད་མ་ཐག་པ་དེ་ཙམ་མ་ཟད་གཞན་ཡང་གོ་ཆ་ཆེན་པ་ོབགོས་པའི་ཕྱིར་ན་ཡང་སེམས་དཔའ་ཆེན་པ་ོཞེས་བྱ་ལ། གོ་ཆ་དེ་གང་ཞེ་ན། སྤྱོད་འཇུག་ལས། བདོག་པ་ཐམས་ཅད་འབྲས་བཅས་ཏེ། །སྐྱེ་བོ་ཀུན་ལ་གཏོང་སེམས་ཀྱིས། །ཞེས་གསུངས་པ་ལྟར།  ལུས་ལོངས་སྤྱོད་དུས་གསུམ་གྱི་དགེ་རྩ་ཐམས་ཅད་གཏོང་པ་ནི་གཏོང་བ་ཆེ་བ་དང་ལྡན་པ་སྦྱིན་པའི་གོ་ཆའི་སྒྲུབ་པ་དང་། ཉེས་སྤྱོད་སྡོམ་པ་དང༌། དགེ་བ་ཆོས་སྡུད་པ་དང༌། སེམས་ཅན་དོན་བྱེད་ཀྱི་ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་སོགས་འཆལ་ཚུལ་སྤོང་བའི་སེམས་དཔའ་འམ་བློ་ཆུང་བ་ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་ཀྱི་གོ་སྒྲུབ་དང༌། མཐུ་ཆེ་བ་ནི་ཕར་ཕྱིན་ཕྱི་མ་བཞི་སྟེ། དེ་ཡང་ཕར་ཕན་གཏགས་པའི་ལན་དུ་ཚུར་གནོད་པ་བྱེད་པ་དང་དྲིན་ལན་ལོག་པར་འཇལ་བ་སོགས་ནི་བཟོད་དཀའ་ནའང་དེས་ཀྱང་མི་རྫི་བའི་བཟོད་པ་དང་། རྐང་ལག་སྦྱིན་པ་གཏོང་བ་སོགས་བྱ་དཀའ་བའི་རྒྱལ་སྲས་ཀྱི་སྤྱོད་པ་ལ་སྐྱོ་ངལ་མེད་པའི་བརྩོན་འགྲུས་དང་། ཐེག་དམན་ཡིད་བྱེད་དང་མ་འདྲེས་པར་རྩེ་གཅིག་པའི་བསམ་གཏན་དང༌། བྱ་བྱེད་ལས་གསུམ་བདེན་མེད་དུ་རྟོགས་པའི་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་གོ་སྒྲུབ་སོགས་རང་རང་ག་ིམི་མཐུན་ཕྱོགས་འཇོམ་པའི་མཐུ་ཆེ་བ་དང་། རྒྱལ་བ་རྣམས་ཀྱི་ཐེག་པ་ཆེན་པོ་མཆོག་ལ་སེམས་བསྐྱེད་པ་ནས་རྣམ་མཁྱེན་གྱི་བར་ལམ་འབྲས་བུ་དང་བཅས་པ་ཉམས་སུ་ལེན་པ་ལ་ཞུགས་པ་དང་ལྡན་པའི་ཕྱིར་གོ་ཆ་ཆེན་པོ་བགོས་པ་ཡིན་ནོ།
