དེ་ཡང་དུས་ཀྱི་ཚེ་ཞེས་པས་གཟེགས་ཟན་ལ་སོགས་པས་དུས་རྟག་པར་འདོད་པ་འགོག་པར་གསུངས་པའི་དོན་ནི། དཔེར་ན་འཇིག་རྟེན་ན་སྔར་དེ་འདྲ་ཞིག་གི་ཐད་སོར་ཞེས་བརྗོད་པའི་ཚེ་ད་ལྟ་སྔར་གྱི་སྐབས་དེ་ལས་འགྱུར་སོང་བ་གོ་བ་བཞིན་དུ། དུས་ཀྱི་ཚེ་ཞེས་པས་དུས་འགྱུར་བར་གོ་བས་དུས་རྟག་པ་འགོག་ནུས་པ་ཡིན་ཞེས་ཕར་ཕྱིན་གཟབ་བཤད་ལས་གསུངས།  དེ་ཡང་ཇི་ལྟར་གནས་ཞེ་ན། འགྲོ་བ་ཀུན་སྡུག་བསྔལ་ལས་བྲལ་བར་འདོད་པའི་བརྩེ་བ་སྙིང་རྗེ་ཆེན་པོ་བསྐྱེད་ཀྱང་། བདག་དང་སེམས་ཅན་དུ་བདེན་པར་མངོན་པར་ཞེན་པའི་སྒོ་ནས་སེམས་ཅན་འདུ་ཤེས་པ་མེད་པ་འདི་ནི་དོན་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་ཆེད་དུ་བྱ་བའི་ངེས་པར་འབྱུང་བའི་ངོ་བོར་གྱུར་བའི་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་མཆོོག་ལ་སྤྱོད་པ་ཡིན་ནི། །སེམས་ཅན་དུ་དམིགས་ན་ཉེས་པ་ཅི་འགྱུར་ཞེ་ན། གལ་ཏེ་རང་དང་སེམས་ཅན་བདེན་པར་ཡོད་པར་འདུ་ཤེས་དང་། དེ་བཞིན་དུ་སྡུག་བསྔལ་ཡང་བདེན་པར་ཡོད་པར་འདུ་ཤེས་སྐྱེད་ནས་སྦྱིན་སོགས་ཕར་ཕྱིན་ལ་དཀའ་པས་སྤྱོད་ཅིང༌། བདག་གིས་འགྲོ་བ་རྣམས་དོན་བྱ་ཞིང་དེ་དག་གི་སྡུག་བསྔལ་སྤངས་པར་བྱའོ་སྙམ་སྟེ། བདག་དང་སེམས་ཅན་དུ་མངོན་པར་ཞེན་པའི་སྒོ་ནས་བདེན་བར་ཡོངས་སུ་རྟོགས་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་དེ་ནི་རྒྱུད་བདེན་འཛིན་གྱིས་བཅིངས་པ་ཡིན་ལ་དེ་བས་ན་བདག་དང་གཞན་དུ་འཛིན་པའི་ཉེས་པ་དེ་ལས་ཆགས་སྡང་སོགས་ཉེས་པ་ཐམས་ཅད་འབྱུང་སྟེ། རིགས་པའི་དབང་ཕྱུག་གིས། བདག་ཡོད་ན་ནི་གཞན་དུ་ཤེས། །བདག་གཞན་ཆ་ལས་འཛིན་དང་སྡང༌། །འདི་དག་དང་ནི་ཡོངས་འབྲེལ་ལས། །ཉེས་པ་ཐམས་ཅད་འབྱུང་བར་འགྱུར། །ཞེས་པ་ལྟར་རོ། །དེ་ལྟ་བས་ན་ཚུལ་འདི་ལྟར་སྤྱོད་པ་ནི་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཕྱིན་པ་མཆོག་ལ་ཡོངས་སུ་སྤྱོད་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །

Furthermore, the meaning of stating that the words "at the time" refute Kaṇāda and others' assertion of time as permanent is: "For example, when one says in the world, 'Previously, right around such-and-such,' it is understood that the present has changed from that previous occasion; likewise, by understanding from 'at the time' that time changes, it is able to refute time as permanent," as taught in the *Detailed Exegesis of the Perfection of Wisdom*. If one asks, "Furthermore, how do they abide?" Even though they generate great "love" and "compassion" wishing for "all beings" to be free from suffering, not conceptualizing them as sentient beings by way of manifestly adhering to self and sentient beings as truly existent, "this is practicing the supreme perfection of wisdom," which is in nature the progressing practice for the sake of "all" objectives. If one asks, "What fault is there in observing them as sentient beings?" "If", generating the concept that oneself and "sentient beings" truly exist, "and likewise" the concept that "suffering" also truly exists, they practice "with hardship" the perfections such as giving, and think, "'I shall' benefit beings and 'abandon their suffering'"; that bodhisattva who "thoroughly conceives" them "as true" by way of manifestly adhering to self and sentient beings is bound by true grasping in their continuum, and "because of that", from that fault of apprehending self and other, all faults such as attachment and hostility arise; as the Lord of Reasoning says: "If self exists, one cognizes other. / From the division of self and other, grasping and hostility. / In complete connection with these, / all faults will arise." "Therefore, practicing in this way is not thoroughly practicing the supreme perfection of wisdom."

heading: **ངེས་འབྱུང་སྒྲུབ་པ།**
translation: Thus, to completely know the phenomena of the basis, path, and fruit as the equality of lacking intrinsic nature, as the single taste of being empty of true existence, like this "is practicing the supreme perfection of wisdom" which is in nature the progressing practice. Thus it is said. Because this text summarizes the entire meaning of the One Hundred Thousand, it would be appropriate to align the chapters in accordance with it, but since those of lesser intellect would not understand, they were not aligned; and similarly, it was not made to accord with the Twenty-five Thousand. The Difficult Points Commentary states, "In order to make it easy to realize and to know the meaning as one, the chapters were aligned in accordance with the Eight Thousand." Thus, having finished teaching the ten phenomena characterizing omniscience, the teaching of the name of the chapter and the conclusion of the topic by correlating it with the Ornament of Clear Realization is: From the Commentary on the Verses of the Precious Qualities Collection: The Jewel Lamp That Illuminates the Suchness of Profound Dependent Arising, Fulfilling the Hopes of the Fortunate, the first chapter, Engaging in Omniscience, and the commentary on the first topic.

The practitioner of the path, "the bodhisattva", is "unobservable" in the "past limit"—that is, the phase of an ordinary being in the past time—and the "future limit"—that is, the phase of a Buddha in the future time—"and also" the "presently arisen" phase of a noble bodhisattva. This is because they have not arisen from their own side, nor will they arise later. Therefore, being free from a truly established one or many in the three times, they are "naturally pure", and there is no distinguishing them by any time.

Progressing practice. The tenth, progressing practice: The *Ornament* says, "Objective, equality," up to "is called progressing practice." Regarding this, there are three [topics]: definition, divisions, and limits. The first: the definition of progressing practice is a yoga of the pure grounds that infallibly causes progression to omniscience. The second, dividing it, there are eight: progressing practice for the sake of the three great objectives, that of equality, that of the welfare of sentient beings, that of spontaneous accomplishment, that of passing beyond extremes, progressing practice to omniscience, and progressing practice having the path as its object. The third, the limits: it is present on the three pure grounds. In the extensive sūtra, these eight are taught by way of being the bases of attributes, and emptiness by way of being the attribute; to know that this must also be practiced by way of unobservability from beginning to end, Gungtang Jamyang states, "It is progression by means of unobservability itself." Although Buddhaśrī applies [the text] from "whoever mounts" onwards to progressing practice, our own system follows the master [Haribhadra]. The meaning taught by the five verses starting with "A" bodhisattva "skilled..." is this: "Whatever bodhisattva" is "skilled" in the manner of positing conventionalities, and "at the time" of engaging in the conduct of a conqueror's son, such as the progressing practice for the objective, having investigated the abiding nature, suchness, with whatever reasoning, such as the refutation of arising from the four extremes, "reflects" upon the meaning of naturally non-arising, and having realized the meaning of non-arising, "practices in this way" and abides.

Furthermore, the meaning of stating that the words "at the time" refute Kaṇāda and others' assertion of time as permanent is: "For example, when one says in the world, 'Previously, right around such-and-such,' it is understood that the present has changed from that previous occasion; likewise, by understanding from 'at the time' that time changes, it is able to refute time as permanent," as taught in the *Detailed Exegesis of the Perfection of Wisdom*. If one asks, "Furthermore, how do they abide?" Even though they generate great "love" and "compassion" wishing for "all beings" to be free from suffering, not conceptualizing them as sentient beings by way of manifestly adhering to self and sentient beings as truly existent, "this is practicing the supreme perfection of wisdom," which is in nature the progressing practice for the sake of "all" objectives. If one asks, "What fault is there in observing them as sentient beings?" "If", generating the concept that oneself and "sentient beings" truly exist, "and likewise" the concept that "suffering" also truly exists, they practice "with hardship" the perfections such as giving, and think, "'I shall' benefit beings and 'abandon their suffering'"; that bodhisattva who "thoroughly conceives" them "as true" by way of manifestly adhering to self and sentient beings is bound by true grasping in their continuum, and "because of that", from that fault of apprehending self and other, all faults such as attachment and hostility arise; as the Lord of Reasoning says: "If self exists, one cognizes other. / From the division of self and other, grasping and hostility. / In complete connection with these, / all faults will arise." "Therefore, practicing in this way is not thoroughly practicing the supreme perfection of wisdom."

translation: Knowledge of the path. Since, in order to attain that omniscience, one must train in its uncommon cause, the knowledge of the path, regarding the second, the explanation of the knowledge of the path: As the Ornament states from "Making obscure and so forth" up to "The knowledge of the path itself is explained like that," the definition of the knowledge of the path is: a Mahāyāna noble one's knowledge embraced by the wisdom that directly realizes emptiness in the continuum of a person who possesses it in their own continuum. There are eleven phenomena characterizing the knowledge of the path, because they exist as: the branches of the knowledge of the path, the knowledge of the path that knows the path of the śrāvakas, the knowledge of the path that knows the path of the pratyekabuddhas, the Mahāyāna path of seeing, the function of the path of meditation, the path of meditation of aspiration, its benefits—praise, respect, and commendation, the path of meditation of dedication, the path of meditation of rejoicing, the path of meditation of progressing practice, and the perfectly pure path of meditation.

If one asks, "Then how should they practice?" Because sentient beings and suffering are not truly existent, it is reasonable to accomplish the welfare of others and liberate them from suffering; and furthermore, regarding that lack of true existence, between the two, phenomena and persons, examining persons, and between the two, self and other, looking initially at the manner in which this appears to one's own mind, the object of negation is easy to recognize. By that vital point, emptiness, the non-affirming negation that refutes that object of negation, is also easy to ascertain. Therefore, initially one "should know oneself," the bodhisattva, as "without intrinsic nature," and "then," just as self is not established by intrinsic nature, "in that manner" one "should know all sentient beings" also as not established by intrinsic nature; and just as all sentient beings are without intrinsic nature, "in that manner," having known "all phenomena" such as the generation of the mind as without intrinsic nature, one does "not conceptualize" either ultimate non-arising or conventional arising as truly existent. Having realized them as a unity, the indivisible essence of the two truths, and having known the abiding nature of the two truths just as it is, abiding in the meaning of the lack of true existence, "this is practicing the supreme" progressing practice, the topic of "the perfection of wisdom."

If one asks, "What is to be attained by that non-dual, non-conceptual pristine wisdom?" For all phenomena—whether the ten phenomena such as the generation of mind, or all phenomena from form up to omniscience, whatever names of phenomena are suitable to be fully expressed in the nine worlds—having abandoned the extreme of ultimate "arising and" perfect "passing away" or ceasing, whatever non-conceptual pristine wisdom of the Buddha's mind abides in the equality of being empty of true existence, without ultimate arising or ceasing, having abandoned all decline and harm without exception, and because it does not degenerate from that, it is "deathless," "and" there is no other that is "supreme" compared to that "holy pristine wisdom" of omniscience. Since it causes the attainment of that very excellent and unsurpassed phenomenon, "therefore" this path that realizes all phenomena as ultimately unobservable is called progressing practice for the objective, "the supreme" of "wisdom," the "perfection." "Holy deathless pristine wisdom" and so forth teach the two—abandonment and realization—for one's own welfare within progressing practice.

If one asks, "Then how should they practice?" Because sentient beings and suffering are not truly existent, it is reasonable to accomplish the welfare of others and liberate them from suffering; and furthermore, regarding that lack of true existence, between the two, phenomena and persons, examining persons, and between the two, self and other, looking initially at the manner in which this appears to one's own mind, the object of negation is easy to recognize. By that vital point, emptiness, the non-affirming negation that refutes that object of negation, is also easy to ascertain. Therefore, initially one "should know oneself," the bodhisattva, as "without intrinsic nature," and "then," just as self is not established by intrinsic nature, "in that manner" one "should know all sentient beings" also as not established by intrinsic nature; and just as all sentient beings are without intrinsic nature, "in that manner," having known "all phenomena" such as the generation of the mind as without intrinsic nature, one does "not conceptualize" either ultimate non-arising or conventional arising as truly existent. Having realized them as a unity, the indivisible essence of the two truths, and having known the abiding nature of the two truths just as it is, abiding in the meaning of the lack of true existence, "this is practicing the supreme" progressing practice, the topic of "the perfection of wisdom."

If one asks, "What is to be attained by that non-dual, non-conceptual pristine wisdom?" For all phenomena—whether the ten phenomena such as the generation of mind, or all phenomena from form up to omniscience, whatever names of phenomena are suitable to be fully expressed in the nine worlds—having abandoned the extreme of ultimate "arising and" perfect "passing away" or ceasing, whatever non-conceptual pristine wisdom of the Buddha's mind abides in the equality of being empty of true existence, without ultimate arising or ceasing, having abandoned all decline and harm without exception, and because it does not degenerate from that, it is "deathless," "and" there is no other that is "supreme" compared to that "holy pristine wisdom" of omniscience. Since it causes the attainment of that very excellent and unsurpassed phenomenon, "therefore" this path that realizes all phenomena as ultimately unobservable is called progressing practice for the objective, "the supreme" of "wisdom," the "perfection." If one asks, "Then how should they practice?" Because sentient beings and suffering are not truly existent, it is reasonable to accomplish the welfare of others and liberate them from suffering; and furthermore, regarding that lack of true existence, between the two, phenomena and persons, examining persons, and between the two, self and other, looking initially at the manner in which this appears to one's own mind, the object of negation is easy to recognize. By that vital point, emptiness, the non-affirming negation that refutes that object of negation, is also easy to ascertain. Therefore, initially one "should know oneself," the bodhisattva, as "without intrinsic nature," and "then," just as self is not established by intrinsic nature, "in that manner" one "should know all sentient beings" also as not established by intrinsic nature; and just as all sentient beings are without intrinsic nature, "in that manner," having known "all phenomena" such as the generation of the mind as without intrinsic nature, one does "not conceptualize" either ultimate non-arising or conventional arising as truly existent. Having realized them as a unity, the indivisible essence of the two truths, and having known the abiding nature of the two truths just as it is, abiding in the meaning of the lack of true existence, "this is practicing the supreme" progressing practice, the topic of "the perfection of wisdom."

If one asks, "What is to be attained by that non-dual, non-conceptual pristine wisdom?" For all phenomena—whether the ten phenomena such as the generation of mind, or all phenomena from form up to omniscience, whatever names of phenomena are suitable to be fully expressed in the nine worlds—having abandoned the extreme of ultimate "arising and" perfect "passing away" or ceasing, whatever non-conceptual pristine wisdom of the Buddha's mind abides in the equality of being empty of true existence, without ultimate arising or ceasing, having abandoned all decline and harm without exception, and because it does not degenerate from that, it is "deathless," "and" there is no other that is "supreme" compared to that "holy pristine wisdom" of omniscience. Since it causes the attainment of that very excellent and unsurpassed phenomenon, "therefore" this path that realizes all phenomena as ultimately unobservable is called progressing practice for the objective, "the supreme" of "wisdom," the "perfection." "Holy deathless pristine wisdom" and so forth teach the two—abandonment and realization—for one's own welfare within progressing practice.

If one asks, "Then how should they practice?" Because sentient beings and suffering are not truly existent, it is reasonable to accomplish the welfare of others and liberate them from suffering; and furthermore, regarding that lack of true existence, between the two, phenomena and persons, examining persons, and between the two, self and other, looking initially at the manner in which this appears to one's own mind, the object of negation is easy to recognize. By that vital point, emptiness, the non-affirming negation that refutes that object of negation, is also easy to ascertain. Therefore, initially one "should know oneself," the bodhisattva, as "without intrinsic nature," and "then," just as self is not established by intrinsic nature, "in that manner" one "should know all sentient beings" also as not established by intrinsic nature; and just as all sentient beings are without intrinsic nature, "in that manner," having known "all phenomena" such as the generation of the mind as without intrinsic nature, one does "not conceptualize" either ultimate non-arising or conventional arising as truly existent. Having realized them as a unity, the indivisible essence of the two truths, and having known the abiding nature of the two truths just as it is, abiding in the meaning of the lack of true existence, "this is practicing the supreme" progressing practice, the topic of "the perfection of wisdom."

heading: **ས་མཚམས།**
translation: The boundaries. Third, the boundaries: they exist from before entering the path up to the buddha ground. That branch of the knowledge of the path is taught by one stanza, "Whoever in form..." and so forth. According to Buddhapāda's Commentary on the Verse Summary, it appears appropriate to correlate this with the aids to penetration, which are the cause of the knowledge of the path. However, here, the master's Commentary on the Verse Summary is mainly taken as the basis, and the literal meaning of this is: "Whatever bodhisattva" does "not abide" in the manner of clinging as truly existent "to the aggregate of form," and "similarly" does "not abide in feeling," and "whoever" does "not abide" by manifestly clinging as truly existent "to perception," "and similarly" does "not abide in volition," and does "not abide" by way of clinging as truly existent to "consciousness" or any object whatsoever, having directly realized them as empty of true existence and free from proliferation, resting one-pointedly in equipoise is to "abide in the suchness," the dharmatā of those things; like this "is practicing the supreme perfection of wisdom" which is the nature of the knowledge of the path. Thus it is said.

If one asks, "Then how should they practice?" Because sentient beings and suffering are not truly existent, it is reasonable to accomplish the welfare of others and liberate them from suffering; and furthermore, regarding that lack of true existence, between the two, phenomena and persons, examining persons, and between the two, self and other, looking initially at the manner in which this appears to one's own mind, the object of negation is easy to recognize. By that vital point, emptiness, the non-affirming negation that refutes that object of negation, is also easy to ascertain. Therefore, initially one "should know oneself," the bodhisattva, as "without intrinsic nature," and "then," just as self is not established by intrinsic nature, "in that manner" one "should know all sentient beings" also as not established by intrinsic nature; and just as all sentient beings are without intrinsic nature, "in that manner," having known "all phenomena" such as the generation of the mind as without intrinsic nature, one does "not conceptualize" either ultimate non-arising or conventional arising as truly existent. Having realized them as a unity, the indivisible essence of the two truths, and having known the abiding nature of the two truths just as it is, abiding in the meaning of the lack of true existence, "this is practicing the supreme" progressing practice, the topic of "the perfection of wisdom."

If one asks, "What is to be attained by that non-dual, non-conceptual pristine wisdom?" For all phenomena—whether the ten phenomena such as the generation of mind, or all phenomena from form up to omniscience, whatever names of phenomena are suitable to be fully expressed in the nine worlds—having abandoned the extreme of ultimate "arising and" perfect "passing away" or ceasing, whatever non-conceptual pristine wisdom of the Buddha's mind abides in the equality of being empty of true existence, without ultimate arising or ceasing, having abandoned all decline and harm without exception, and because it does not degenerate from that, it is "deathless," "and" there is no other that is "supreme" compared to that "holy pristine wisdom" of omniscience. Since it causes the attainment of that very excellent and unsurpassed phenomenon, "therefore" this path that realizes all phenomena as ultimately unobservable is called progressing practice for the objective, "the supreme" of "wisdom," the "perfection." "Holy deathless pristine wisdom" and so forth teach the two—abandonment and realization—for one's own welfare within progressing practice.

Thus, to completely know the phenomena of the basis, path, and fruit as the equality of lacking intrinsic nature, as the single taste of being empty of true existence, like this "is practicing the supreme perfection of wisdom" which is in nature the progressing practice. Thus it is said. Because this text summarizes the entire meaning of the One Hundred Thousand, it would be appropriate to align the chapters in accordance with it, but since those of lesser intellect would not understand, they were not aligned; and similarly, it was not made to accord with the Twenty-five Thousand. The Difficult Points Commentary states, "In order to make it easy to realize and to know the meaning as one, the chapters were aligned in accordance with the Eight Thousand." Thus, having finished teaching the ten phenomena characterizing omniscience, the teaching of the name of the chapter and the conclusion of the topic by correlating it with the Ornament of Clear Realization is: From the Commentary on the Verses of the Precious Qualities Collection: The Jewel Lamp That Illuminates the Suchness of Profound Dependent Arising, Fulfilling the Hopes of the Fortunate, the first chapter, Engaging in Omniscience, and the commentary on the first topic.

heading: **ས་མཚམས།**
translation: Regarding how this teaches the branches of the knowledge of the path, in the Difficult Points Commentary, although there is no clarification other than merely saying "abiding, that is, five aspects," if one looks at the flow of the speech: Because it teaches that, abiding in the dharmatā of the five aggregates, one must train in higher paths without being satisfied or being proud merely by practicing the perfection of wisdom and attaining qualities, it teaches freedom from the hindrance to the basis. Because the word "abiding" implicitly teaches that merely abiding in the aspect of wisdom is not sufficient, but one must also add the aspect of method on top of that, it teaches that the knowledge of the path arises for one who practices complete method and wisdom, and does not arise for others; thus it teaches the certainty of individual occasions. Furthermore, although "abiding" certainly also applies to meditating by making dharmatā the object of the mode of apprehension, the Detailed Explanation of the Perfection of Wisdom states that it is applied to the naturally abiding disposition, and thus being pervaded by the causal disposition, as well as the nature and the function, are taught.

[3-57] translation already produced for this document:
If one asks, "Then how should they practice?" Because sentient beings and suffering are not truly existent, it is reasonable to accomplish the welfare of others and liberate them from suffering; and furthermore, regarding that lack of true existence, between the two, phenomena and persons, examining persons, and between the two, self and other, looking initially at the manner in which this appears to one's own mind, the object of negation is easy to recognize. By that vital point, emptiness, the non-affirming negation that refutes that object of negation, is also easy to ascertain. Therefore, initially one "should know oneself," the bodhisattva, as "without intrinsic nature," and "then," just as self is not established by intrinsic nature, "in that manner" one "should know all sentient beings" also as not established by intrinsic nature; and just as all sentient beings are without intrinsic nature, "in that manner," having known "all phenomena" such as the generation of the mind as without intrinsic nature, one does "not conceptualize" either ultimate non-arising or conventional arising as truly existent. Having realized them as a unity, the indivisible essence of the two truths, and having known the abiding nature of the two truths just as it is, abiding in the meaning of the lack of true existence, "this is practicing the supreme" progressing practice, the topic of "the perfection of wisdom."

[3-58] source:
གཉིས་སུ་མི་རྟོག་པའི་ཡེ་ཤེས་དེའི་ཐོབ་བྱ་ཇི་ལྟ་བུ་ཞེ་ན། འཇིག་རྟེན་དགུ་ན་ཆོས་ཀྱི་མིང་ཇི་སྙེད་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་བརྗོད་པར་རུང་བ་སེམས་བསྐྱེད་ལ་སོགས་པའི་ཆོས་བཅུ་འམ་གཟུགས་ནས་རྣམ་མཁྱེན་གྱི་བར་གྱི་ཆོས་ཀུན་ལ་དོན་དམ་པར་སྐྱེ་བ་དང་ནི་ཡང་དག་པར་འདས་པའམ་འགག་པའི་མཐའ་སྤངས་ནས་དོན་དམ་པར་སྐྱེ་འགག་མེད་པར་བདེན་སྟོང་མཉམ་པ་ཉིད་དུ་གནས་པའི་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་ཐུགས་རྣམ་པར་མི་རྟོག་པའི་ཡེ་ཤེས་གང་ཞིག་རྒུད་པ་དང་ཉེར་འཚེ་མ་ལུས་པ་སྤངས་ཤིང་དེ་ལས་ཉམས་པ་མེད་པས་འཆི་བ་མེད་པ་དང་རྣམ་པ་ཐམས་ཅད་མཁྱེན་པའི་ཡེ་ཤེས་དམ་པ་དེ་ལས་མཆོག་ཏུ་གྱུར་བ་གཞན་མེད་པ་སྟེ། ཆོས་ཕུལ་དུ་བྱུང་ཞིང་བླ་ན་མེད་པ་དེ་ཉིད་ཐོབ་པར་བྱེད་པ་དེ་ཡི་ཕྱིར་ན་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་དོན་དམ་པར་དམིགས་སུ་མེད་པར་རྟོག་པའི་ལམ་འདི་ནི་ཆེད་དུ་བྱ་བའི་ངེས་འབྱུང་སྒྲུབ་པའི་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ནི་མཆོག་སྟེ་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ཞེས་བྱའོ། །ཡེ་ཤེས་འཆི་མེད་དམ་པ་ཞེས་སོགས་ཀྱིས་ངེས་འབྱུང་སྒྲུབ་པའི་རང་དོན་སྤངས་རྟོགས་གཉིས་བསྟན་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །
[3-58] translation already produced for this document:
If one asks, "What is to be attained by that non-dual, non-conceptual pristine wisdom?" For all phenomena—whether the ten phenomena such as the generation of mind, or all phenomena from form up to omniscience, whatever names of phenomena are suitable to be fully expressed in the nine worlds—having abandoned the extreme of ultimate "arising and" perfect "passing away" or ceasing, whatever non-conceptual pristine wisdom of the Buddha's mind abides in the equality of being empty of true existence, without ultimate arising or ceasing, having abandoned all decline and harm without exception, and because it does not degenerate from that, it is "deathless," "and" there is no other that is "supreme" compared to that "holy pristine wisdom" of omniscience. Since it causes the attainment of that very excellent and unsurpassed phenomenon, "therefore" this path that realizes all phenomena as ultimately unobservable is called progressing practice for the objective, "the supreme" of "wisdom," the "perfection." "Holy deathless pristine wisdom" and so forth teach the two—abandonment and realization—for one's own welfare within progressing practice.

"Whatever bodhisattva," having found certain knowledge through valid cognition regarding their own grounds such as progressing practice, practices and experiences exactly as taught previously "without doubt" and hesitation, they are said to be "endowed with the supreme wisdom" embraced by extraordinary methods, and one should know that person as abiding in the equality of existence and peace being empty of true existence.

[3-60] source:
དེ་ལྟར་གཞི་ལམ་འབྲས་བུའི་ཆོས་རྣམས་རང་བཞིན་མེད་པ་མཉམ་པ་ཉིད་བདེན་སྟོང་རོ་གཅིག་པར་ཡོངས་སུ་ཤེས་པར་གྱུར་བ་འདི་ལྟ་བུ་ནི་ངེས་འབྱུང་སྒྲུབ་པའི་རང་བཞིན་གྱི་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་མཆོག་ལ་སྤྱོད་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །ཞེས་པའོ། །གཞུང་འདིའི་སྟོང་ཕྲག་བརྒྱ་བའི་དོན་ཐམས་ཅད་བསྡུས་པའི་ཕྱིར་དེ་དང་མཐུན་པར་ལེའུ་སྦྱར་རིགས་ཀྱང་བློ་དམན་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་མི་རྟོགས་པས་མ་སྦྱར་ལ། དེ་བཞིན་དུ་ཉི་ཁྲི་དང་མཐུན་པར་ཡང་མ་བྱས་སོ། །རྟོགས་སླ་ཞིང་དོན་གཅིག་པར་ཤེས་པར་བྱ་བའི་ཕྱིར་བརྒྱད་སྟོང་དང་མཐུན་པར་ལེའུ་སྦྱར་བ་ཡིན་ཞེས་དཀའ་འགྲེལ་ལས་གསུངས་སོ། །དེ་ལྟར་རྣམ་མཁྱེན་མཚོན་བྱེད་ཀྱི་ཆོས་བཅུ་བསྟན་ཟིན་ནས་ལེའུའི་མཚན་བསྟན་པ་དང༌། མངོན་རྟོགས་རྒྱན་དང་སྦྱར་ནས་སྐབས་བསྡུ་བ་ནི། ཡོན་ཏན་རིན་པོ་ཆེ་སྡུད་པ་ཚིགས་སུ་བཅད་པའི་འགྲེལ་བ་ཟབ་མོ་རྟེན་འབྱུང་གི་དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཉིད་གསལ་བར་བྱེད་པའི་ནོར་བུའི་སྒྲོན་མེ་སྐལ་བཟང་རེ་སྐོང་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལས་རྣམ་པ་ཐམས་ཅད་མཁྱེན་པ་ཉིད་ལ་འཇུག་པའི་ལེའུ་སྟེ་དང་པོ་དང་། །སྐབས་དང་པོའི་འགྲེལ་བའོ།
[3-60] translation already produced for this document:
Thus, to completely know the phenomena of the basis, path, and fruit as the equality of lacking intrinsic nature, as the single taste of being empty of true existence, like this "is practicing the supreme perfection of wisdom" which is in nature the progressing practice. Thus it is said. Because this text summarizes the entire meaning of the One Hundred Thousand, it would be appropriate to align the chapters in accordance with it, but since those of lesser intellect would not understand, they were not aligned; and similarly, it was not made to accord with the Twenty-five Thousand. The Difficult Points Commentary states, "In order to make it easy to realize and to know the meaning as one, the chapters were aligned in accordance with the Eight Thousand." Thus, having finished teaching the ten phenomena characterizing omniscience, the teaching of the name of the chapter and the conclusion of the topic by correlating it with the Ornament of Clear Realization is: From the Commentary on the Verses of the Precious Qualities Collection: The Jewel Lamp That Illuminates the Suchness of Profound Dependent Arising, Fulfilling the Hopes of the Fortunate, the first chapter, Engaging in Omniscience, and the commentary on the first topic.

heading: **ཉན་ཐོས་ཀྱི་ལམ་ཤེས།**
translation: The knowledge of the path of the śrāvakas. Second, regarding the knowledge of the path that knows the path of the śrāvakas, there are two: its actual essence and its cause, the aids to penetration.
style_instruction: Translate this passage of a Tibetan Buddhist commentary on the Verse Summary of the Perfection of Wisdom (Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā) into clear, accurate English prose. If one asks, "Then how should they practice?" Because sentient beings and suffering are not truly existent, it is reasonable to accomplish the welfare of others and liberate them from suffering; and furthermore, regarding that lack of true existence, between the two, phenomena and persons, examining persons, and between the two, self and other, looking initially at the manner in which this appears to one's own mind, the object of negation is easy to recognize. By that vital point, emptiness, the non-affirming negation that refutes that object of negation, is also easy to ascertain. Therefore, initially one "should know oneself," the bodhisattva, as "without intrinsic nature," and "then," just as self is not established by intrinsic nature, "in that manner" one "should know all sentient beings" also as not established by intrinsic nature; and just as all sentient beings are without intrinsic nature, "in that manner," having known "all phenomena" such as the generation of the mind as without intrinsic nature, one does "not conceptualize" either ultimate non-arising or conventional arising as truly existent. Having realized them as a unity, the indivisible essence of the two truths, and having known the abiding nature of the two truths just as it is, abiding in the meaning of the lack of true existence, "this is practicing the supreme" progressing practice, the topic of "the perfection of wisdom."

If one asks, "What is to be attained by that non-dual, non-conceptual pristine wisdom?" For all phenomena—whether the ten phenomena such as the generation of mind, or all phenomena from form up to omniscience, whatever names of phenomena are suitable to be fully expressed in the nine worlds—having abandoned the extreme of ultimate "arising and" perfect "passing away" or ceasing, whatever non-conceptual pristine wisdom of the Buddha's mind abides in the equality of being empty of true existence, without ultimate arising or ceasing, having abandoned all decline and harm without exception, and because it does not degenerate from that, it is "deathless," "and" there is no other that is "supreme" compared to that "holy pristine wisdom" of omniscience. Since it causes the attainment of that very excellent and unsurpassed phenomenon, "therefore" this path that realizes all phenomena as ultimately unobservable is called progressing practice for the objective, "the supreme" of "wisdom," the "perfection." "Holy deathless pristine wisdom" and so forth teach the two—abandonment and realization—for one's own welfare within progressing practice.

Thus, to completely know the phenomena of the basis, path, and fruit as the equality of lacking intrinsic nature, as the single taste of being empty of true existence, like this "is practicing the supreme perfection of wisdom" which is in nature the progressing practice. Thus it is said. Because this text summarizes the entire meaning of the One Hundred Thousand, it would be appropriate to align the chapters in accordance with it, but since those of lesser intellect would not understand, they were not aligned; and similarly, it was not made to accord with the Twenty-five Thousand. The Difficult Points Commentary states, "In order to make it easy to realize and to know the meaning as one, the chapters were aligned in accordance with the Eight Thousand." Thus, having finished teaching the ten phenomena characterizing omniscience, the teaching of the name of the chapter and the conclusion of the topic by correlating it with the Ornament of Clear Realization is: From the Commentary on the Verses of the Precious Qualities Collection: The Jewel Lamp That Illuminates the Suchness of Profound Dependent Arising, Fulfilling the Hopes of the Fortunate, the first chapter, Engaging in Omniscience, and the commentary on the first topic.

If one asks, "Then how should they practice?" Because sentient beings and suffering are not truly existent, it is reasonable to accomplish the welfare of others and liberate them from suffering; and furthermore, regarding that lack of true existence, between the two, phenomena and persons, examining persons, and between the two, self and other, looking initially at the manner in which this appears to one's own mind, the object of negation is easy to recognize. By that vital point, emptiness, the non-affirming negation that refutes that object of negation, is also easy to ascertain. Therefore, initially one "should know oneself," the bodhisattva, as "without intrinsic nature," and "then," just as self is not established by intrinsic nature, "in that manner" one "should know all sentient beings" also as not established by intrinsic nature; and just as all sentient beings are without intrinsic nature, "in that manner," having known "all phenomena" such as the generation of the mind as without intrinsic nature, one does "not conceptualize" either ultimate non-arising or conventional arising as truly existent. Having realized them as a unity, the indivisible essence of the two truths, and having known the abiding nature of the two truths just as it is, abiding in the meaning of the lack of true existence, "this is practicing the supreme" progressing practice, the topic of "the perfection of wisdom."

If one asks, "What is to be attained by that non-dual, non-conceptual pristine wisdom?" For all phenomena—whether the ten phenomena such as the generation of mind, or all phenomena from form up to omniscience, whatever names of phenomena are suitable to be fully expressed in the nine worlds—having abandoned the extreme of ultimate "arising and" perfect "passing away" or ceasing, whatever non-conceptual pristine wisdom of the Buddha's mind abides in the equality of being empty of true existence, without ultimate arising or ceasing, having abandoned all decline and harm without exception, and because it does not degenerate from that, it is "deathless," "and" there is no other that is "supreme" compared to that "holy pristine wisdom" of omniscience. Since it causes the attainment of that very excellent and unsurpassed phenomenon, "therefore" this path that realizes all phenomena as ultimately unobservable is called progressing practice for the objective, "the supreme" of "wisdom," the "perfection." "Holy deathless pristine wisdom" and so forth teach the two—abandonment and realization—for one's own welfare within progressing practice.

Regarding how this teaches the branches of the knowledge of the path, in the Difficult Points Commentary, although there is no clarification other than merely saying "abiding, that is, five aspects," if one looks at the flow of the speech: Because it teaches that, abiding in the dharmatā of the five aggregates, one must train in higher paths without being satisfied or being proud merely by practicing the perfection of wisdom and attaining qualities, it teaches freedom from the hindrance to the basis. Because the word "abiding" implicitly teaches that merely abiding in the aspect of wisdom is not sufficient, but one must also add the aspect of method on top of that, it teaches that the knowledge of the path arises for one who practices complete method and wisdom, and does not arise for others; thus it teaches the certainty of individual occasions. Furthermore, although "abiding" certainly also applies to meditating by making dharmatā the object of the mode of apprehension, the Detailed Explanation of the Perfection of Wisdom states that it is applied to the naturally abiding disposition, and thus being pervaded by the causal disposition, as well as the nature and the function, are taught.

Regarding how this teaches the branches of the knowledge of the path, in the Difficult Points Commentary, although there is no clarification other than merely saying "abiding, that is, five aspects," if one looks at the flow of the speech: Because it teaches that, abiding in the dharmatā of the five aggregates, one must train in higher paths without being satisfied or being proud merely by practicing the perfection of wisdom and attaining qualities, it teaches freedom from the hindrance to the basis. Because the word "abiding" implicitly teaches that merely abiding in the aspect of wisdom is not sufficient, but one must also add the aspect of method on top of that, it teaches that the knowledge of the path arises for one who practices complete method and wisdom, and does not arise for others; thus it teaches the certainty of individual occasions. Furthermore, although "abiding" certainly also applies to meditating by making dharmatā the object of the mode of apprehension, the Detailed Explanation of the Perfection of Wisdom states that it is applied to the naturally abiding disposition, and thus being pervaded by the causal disposition, as well as the nature and the function, are taught.

[3-68] translation already produced for this document:
Its actual essence. The first: as the Ornament states from "In the method of the knowledge of the path itself," up to "This śrāvaka path should be known." For this, among the three—the definition, the divisions, and the boundaries:

heading: **ས་མཚམས།**
translation: The boundaries. Third: they exist from the Mahāyāna path of seeing up to the buddha ground. That is taught by one stanza, "Permanent and impermanent" and so forth. Regarding that, although the Detailed Explanation of the Perfection of Wisdom says, "I wonder whether 'permanent,' 'impermanent,' 'happiness,' 'suffering' and so forth teach the aspects of the first two truths, and 'obtaining the fruit' and 'the ground of an arhat' and so forth teach the aspects of cessation and path?", if one examines the master's Commentary on the Verse Summary, I wonder whether the aspects of the truth of suffering are taught from "permanent" and "impermanent" up to "selfless," and the aspects of the latter three truths are taught by "suchness" and "empty of that." Those endowed with discernment should analyze this in detail. The literal meaning is: whoever does "not abide" in the manner of clinging as truly existent to "permanent" which does not disintegrate, "and impermanent" which is its opposite, "happiness" having the aspect of soothing feeling, "and" contaminated "suffering," "attractive" because of being agreeable to the mind, "and unattractive" because of being disagreeable to the mind, an existing "self" of a person that has become one's own essence, "and selfless," "and in suchness" meaning ultimately existent, "and" although appearing truly existent, "empty" of existing "like that" or being established like that, and so forth, regarding any dharma; "and" does "not abide" with manifest clinging to "obtaining the three fruits" of stream-enterer, once-returner, and non-returner, "and the ground of a śrāvaka arhat"; "and" does "not abide" with manifest clinging "to the ground of a pratyekabuddha, and similarly to the buddha ground"; in short, "does not abide" by manifestly clinging as truly existent to this and that, regarding any phenomena subsumed by the three—the basis, path, and fruit. Thus it is said. This means that that śrāvaka path of directly realizing the sixteen aspects such as impermanence is a path to be known by bodhisattvas, but they do not practice it by way of striving for the enlightenment of the inferior vehicle, and it teaches that they perform the three—generating, knowing, and completing—in order to care for trainees of the śrāvaka disposition by unifying method and wisdom, such as the generation of the mind, dedication, and wisdom realizing emptiness.

Work: ཡོན་ཏན་རིན་པོ་ཆེ་སྡུད་པ་ཚིགས་སུ་བཅད་པའི་འགྲེལ་པ་ཟབ་མོ་རྟེན་འབྱུང་གི་དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཉིད་གསལ་བར་བྱེད་པའི་ནོར་བུའི་སྒྲོན་མེ་སྐལ་བཟང་རེ་སྐོང་། (Khenrab Jamyang, Commentary on the Verses of the Precious Qualities Collection), author: མཁྱེན་རབ་འཇམ་དབྱངས་བློ་བཟང་འཕྲིན་ལས།. [3-63] source:
མཚན་ཉིད།དང་པོ་ནི། ལམ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་རྒྱུ་ངོ་བོ་འབྲས་བུ་གསུམ་པོ་གང་རུང་གིས་བསྡུས་པའི་སྙིང་རྗེ་ཆེན་པོས་ཟིན་པའི་ཡོན་ཏན་ཁྱད་པར་ཅན་དེ། ལམ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་ཡན་ལག་གི་མཚན་ཉིད།
[3-63] translation already produced for this document:
The definition. The first: the definition of the branches of the knowledge of the path is that extraordinary quality embraced by great compassion which is subsumed by any of the three—the cause, essence, or fruit of the knowledge of the path.

[3-64] source:
དབྱེ་བ།གཉིས་པ་དེ་ལ་དབྱེ་ན། རྟེན་གེགས་ང་རྒྱལ་མངོན་གྱུར་པ་དང་བྲལ་བ། ཉེར་ལེན་གྱི་རྒྱུ་སེམས་བསྐྱེད་པ་དང༌། རྒྱུ་རིགས་ཀྱིས་ཁྱབ་པ། འཁོར་བ་མི་འདོར་བའི་རང་བཞིན་དང༌། གཞན་འཁོར་དུ་སྡུད་པ་སོགས་ཀྱི་བྱེད་ལས་བྱེད་དང་ལྔ་ཡོད།
[3-64] translation already produced for this document:
The divisions. Second, if that is divided, there are five: freedom from the hindrance to the basis, manifest pride; the generating cause, the generation of the mind; being pervaded by the causal disposition; the nature of not abandoning cyclic existence; and the function of gathering others into one's retinue and so forth.

[3-65] source:
ས་མཚམས།གསུམ་པ་ས་མཚམས་ནི། ལམ་མ་ཞུགས་ནས་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་སའི་བར་དུ་ཡོད། ལམ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་ཡན་ལག་དེ་ནི། གང་ཞིག་གཟུགས་ལ་ཞེས་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གཅིག་གིས་བསྟན། སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་ཞབས་ཀྱི་སྡུད་འགྲེལ་ལྟར་ན། འདི་ལམ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་རྒྱུ་ངེས་འབྱེད་ཆ་མཐུན་ལ་སྦྱར་བ་འགྲིགས་པ་ལྟར་སྣང་ཡང༌། འདིར་གཅོ་བོར་སློབ་དཔོན་གྱི་སྡུད་འགྲེལ་གཞིར་བཞག་པ་ཡིན་ལ། འདིའི་ཚིག་དོན་ནི། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གང་ཞིག་གཟུགས་ཀྱི་ཕུང་པ་ལ་བདེན་པར་ཞེན་པའི་ཚུལ་གྱི་མི་གནས་ལ་དེ་བཞིན་དུ་ཚོར་བ་ལ་ཡང་མི་གནས་ཤིང་། གང་ཞིག་འདུས་ཤེས་ལ་བདེན་པར་མངོན་པར་ཞེན་ནས་མི་གནས་པ་དང༌།དེ་བཞིན་དུ་སེམས་པར་མི་གནས་ལ་རྣམ་པར་ཤེས་པ་སོགས་ཡུལ་གང་ལ་ཡང་བདེན་པར་ཞེན་པའི་སྒོ་ནས་མི་གནས་པ་དེ་དག་བདེན་སྟོང་སྤྲོས་བྲལ་དུ་མངོན་སུམ་དུ་རྟོགས་ནས་རྩེ་ཏུ་མཉམ་པར་བཞག་པ་ནི། དེ་དག་གི་ཆོས་ཉིད་དེ་བཞིན་ཉིད་ལ་གནས་པ་སྟེ་འདི་ལྟ་བུ་ནི་ལམ་ཤེས་པའི་རང་བཞིན་གྱི་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་མཆོག་ལ་སྤྱོད་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །ཞེས་སོ།
[3-65] translation already produced for this document:
The boundaries. Third, the boundaries: they exist from before entering the path up to the buddha ground. That branch of the knowledge of the path is taught by one stanza, "Whoever in form..." and so forth. According to Buddhapāda's Commentary on the Verse Summary, it appears appropriate to correlate this with the aids to penetration, which are the cause of the knowledge of the path. However, here, the master's Commentary on the Verse Summary is mainly taken as the basis, and the literal meaning of this is: "Whatever bodhisattva" does "not abide" in the manner of clinging as truly existent "to the aggregate of form," and "similarly" does "not abide in feeling," and "whoever" does "not abide" by manifestly clinging as truly existent "to perception," "and similarly" does "not abide in volition," and does "not abide" by way of clinging as truly existent to "consciousness" or any object whatsoever, having directly realized them as empty of true existence and free from proliferation, resting one-pointedly in equipoise is to "abide in the suchness," the dharmatā of those things; like this "is practicing the supreme perfection of wisdom" which is the nature of the knowledge of the path. Thus it is said.

[3-66] source:
འདིས་ལམ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་ཡན་ལག་བསྟན་ཚུལ་དཀའ་འགྲེལ་དུ། གནས་སྟེ་རྣམ་པ་ལྔ་ཞེས་པ་ཙམ་ལས་གསལ་ཁ་མེད་ཀྱང་གསུང་གི་བབ་ལ་བལྟས་ན། ཕུང་པོ་ལྔའི་ཆོས་ཉིད་ལ་གནས་ཏེ་ཤེར་ཕྱིན་ལ་སྤྱོད་པ་དང་ཡོན་ཏན་ཐོབ་པ་དེ་ཙམ་གྱིས་ཆོག་ཤེས་དང་རློམས་སེམས་མི་བྱེད་པར་ལམ་གོང་མར་སློབ་དགོས་པར་སྟོན་པས་རྟེན་གེགས་དང་བྲལ་བར་བསྟན། ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཆ་ལ་གནས་པ་དེ་ཙམ་གྱིས་མི་ཆོག་པར་ཐབས་ཀྱི་ཆའང་དེའི་སྟེང་དུ་བསྣན་དགོས་པར་གནས་ཏེ་ཞེས་པས་ཚིག་གི་ནུས་པས་སྟོན་པས་ན་ཐབས་ཤེས་ཆ་ཚང་ཞིག་ཉམས་སུ་ལེན་པ་དེ་ལ་ལམ་ཤེས་སྐྱེ་ཡི་གཞན་ལ་མི་སྐྱེ་བས་གནས་སྐབས་སོ་སོར་ངེས་པ་དེ་བསྟན། ཡང་གནས་ཞེས་ཆོས་ཉིད་འཛིན་སྟངས་ཀྱི་ཡུལ་དུ་བྱས་ནས་སྒོམ་པ་ལའང་བྱེད་མོད་དེ། རང་བཞིན་གནས་རིགས་ལ་བྱས་ཏེ་རྒྱུ་རིགས་ཀྱིས་ཁྱབ་པ་དང༌། རང་བཞིན་དང་བྱེད་ལས་རྣམས་བསྟན་པ་ཡིན་ཞེས་ཕར་ཕྱིན་གཟབ་བཤད་ལས་གསུངས།
[3-66] translation already produced for this document:
Regarding how this teaches the branches of the knowledge of the path, in the Difficult Points Commentary, although there is no clarification other than merely saying "abiding, that is, five aspects," if one looks at the flow of the speech: Because it teaches that, abiding in the dharmatā of the five aggregates, one must train in higher paths without being satisfied or being proud merely by practicing the perfection of wisdom and attaining qualities, it teaches freedom from the hindrance to the basis. Because the word "abiding" implicitly teaches that merely abiding in the aspect of wisdom is not sufficient, but one must also add the aspect of method on top of that, it teaches that the knowledge of the path arises for one who practices complete method and wisdom, and does not arise for others; thus it teaches the certainty of individual occasions. Furthermore, although "abiding" certainly also applies to meditating by making dharmatā the object of the mode of apprehension, the Detailed Explanation of the Perfection of Wisdom states that it is applied to the naturally abiding disposition, and thus being pervaded by the causal disposition, as well as the nature and the function, are taught.

[3-67] source:
ཉན་ཐོས་ཀྱི་ལམ་ཤེས།གཉིས་པ་ཉན་ཐོས་ཀྱི་ལམ་ཤེས་པའི་ལམ་ཤེས་ལ་གཉིས། དེའི་ངོ་བོ་དངོས་དང་། དེའི་རྒྱུ་ངེས་འབྱེད་ཆ་མཐུན་ནོ། །
[3-67] translation already produced for this document:
The knowledge of the path of the śrāvakas. Second, regarding the knowledge of the path that knows the path of the śrāvakas, there are two: its actual essence and its cause, the aids to penetration.

[3-68] source:
དེའི་ངོ་བོ་དངོས།དང་པ་ོནི་རྒྱན་ལས། ལམ་ཤེས་ཉིད་ཀྱི་ཚུལ་ལ་ནི། ནས། ཉན་ཐོས་ལམ་འདི་ཤེས་པར་བྱ། ཞེས་གསུངས་འདི་ལ་མཚན་ཉིད། དབྱེ་བ། ས་མཚམས་གསུམ་ལས།
[3-68] translation already produced for this document:
Its actual essence. The first: as the Ornament states from "In the method of the knowledge of the path itself," up to "This śrāvaka path should be known." For this, among the three—the definition, the divisions, and the boundaries:

heading: **དེའི་རྒྱུ་ངེས་འབྱེད་ཆ་མཐུན།**
translation: Its cause, the aids to penetration. Second, to teach its cause, the aids to penetration, the meaning of what is stated in the one stanza "Just as the Guide" and so forth is: for example of not abiding in any dharma, "just as" the mind of "the Guide," the Bhagavan Buddha, does "not abide in the unconditioned realm," the basic space of nirvāṇa wherein mere arising in cyclic existence is pacified, "and similarly" does "not abide" by way of clinging as truly existent "to the conditioned" side of "the three realms" of cyclic existence, "practicing" without abiding in any extreme of existence or peace; "likewise," "a bodhisattva" having realized all phenomena as lacking inherent existence, "abides" on paths such as the aids to penetration, but "abiding without" abiding by "clinging" as truly existent "even to that" means abiding without abiding ultimately in any dharma, but rather abiding in the suchness free from proliferation; "like this" manner, the King of Dharma, "the Victor, has stated" is to "abide in" the definitive "perfection of wisdom." Thus it is said.

Regarding how this teaches the branches of the knowledge of the path, in the Difficult Points Commentary, although there is no clarification other than merely saying "abiding, that is, five aspects," if one looks at the flow of the speech: Because it teaches that, abiding in the dharmatā of the five aggregates, one must train in higher paths without being satisfied or being proud merely by practicing the perfection of wisdom and attaining qualities, it teaches freedom from the hindrance to the basis. Because the word "abiding" implicitly teaches that merely abiding in the aspect of wisdom is not sufficient, but one must also add the aspect of method on top of that, it teaches that the knowledge of the path arises for one who practices complete method and wisdom, and does not arise for others; thus it teaches the certainty of individual occasions. Furthermore, although "abiding" certainly also applies to meditating by making dharmatā the object of the mode of apprehension, the Detailed Explanation of the Perfection of Wisdom states that it is applied to the naturally abiding disposition, and thus being pervaded by the causal disposition, as well as the nature and the function, are taught.

Regarding how this teaches the branches of the knowledge of the path, in the Difficult Points Commentary, although there is no clarification other than merely saying "abiding, that is, five aspects," if one looks at the flow of the speech: Because it teaches that, abiding in the dharmatā of the five aggregates, one must train in higher paths without being satisfied or being proud merely by practicing the perfection of wisdom and attaining qualities, it teaches freedom from the hindrance to the basis. Because the word "abiding" implicitly teaches that merely abiding in the aspect of wisdom is not sufficient, but one must also add the aspect of method on top of that, it teaches that the knowledge of the path arises for one who practices complete method and wisdom, and does not arise for others; thus it teaches the certainty of individual occasions. Furthermore, although "abiding" certainly also applies to meditating by making dharmatā the object of the mode of apprehension, the Detailed Explanation of the Perfection of Wisdom states that it is applied to the naturally abiding disposition, and thus being pervaded by the causal disposition, as well as the nature and the function, are taught.

The boundaries. Third: they exist from the Mahāyāna path of seeing up to the buddha ground. That is taught by one stanza, "Permanent and impermanent" and so forth. Regarding that, although the Detailed Explanation of the Perfection of Wisdom says, "I wonder whether 'permanent,' 'impermanent,' 'happiness,' 'suffering' and so forth teach the aspects of the first two truths, and 'obtaining the fruit' and 'the ground of an arhat' and so forth teach the aspects of cessation and path?", if one examines the master's Commentary on the Verse Summary, I wonder whether the aspects of the truth of suffering are taught from "permanent" and "impermanent" up to "selfless," and the aspects of the latter three truths are taught by "suchness" and "empty of that." Those endowed with discernment should analyze this in detail. The literal meaning is: whoever does "not abide" in the manner of clinging as truly existent to "permanent" which does not disintegrate, "and impermanent" which is its opposite, "happiness" having the aspect of soothing feeling, "and" contaminated "suffering," "attractive" because of being agreeable to the mind, "and unattractive" because of being disagreeable to the mind, an existing "self" of a person that has become one's own essence, "and selfless," "and in suchness" meaning ultimately existent, "and" although appearing truly existent, "empty" of existing "like that" or being established like that, and so forth, regarding any dharma; "and" does "not abide" with manifest clinging to "obtaining the three fruits" of stream-enterer, once-returner, and non-returner, "and the ground of a śrāvaka arhat"; "and" does "not abide" with manifest clinging "to the ground of a pratyekabuddha, and similarly to the buddha ground"; in short, "does not abide" by manifestly clinging as truly existent to this and that, regarding any phenomena subsumed by the three—the basis, path, and fruit. Thus it is said. This means that that śrāvaka path of directly realizing the sixteen aspects such as impermanence is a path to be known by bodhisattvas, but they do not practice it by way of striving for the enlightenment of the inferior vehicle, and it teaches that they perform the three—generating, knowing, and completing—in order to care for trainees of the śrāvaka disposition by unifying method and wisdom, such as the generation of the mind, dedication, and wisdom realizing emptiness.

The boundaries. Third: they exist from the Mahāyāna path of seeing up to the buddha ground. That is taught by one stanza, "Permanent and impermanent" and so forth. Regarding that, although the Detailed Explanation of the Perfection of Wisdom says, "I wonder whether 'permanent,' 'impermanent,' 'happiness,' 'suffering' and so forth teach the aspects of the first two truths, and 'obtaining the fruit' and 'the ground of an arhat' and so forth teach the aspects of cessation and path?", if one examines the master's Commentary on the Verse Summary, I wonder whether the aspects of the truth of suffering are taught from "permanent" and "impermanent" up to "selfless," and the aspects of the latter three truths are taught by "suchness" and "empty of that." Those endowed with discernment should analyze this in detail. The literal meaning is: whoever does "not abide" in the manner of clinging as truly existent to "permanent" which does not disintegrate, "and impermanent" which is its opposite, "happiness" having the aspect of soothing feeling, "and" contaminated "suffering," "attractive" because of being agreeable to the mind, "and unattractive" because of being disagreeable to the mind, an existing "self" of a person that has become one's own essence, "and selfless," "and in suchness" meaning ultimately existent, "and" although appearing truly existent, "empty" of existing "like that" or being established like that, and so forth, regarding any dharma; "and" does "not abide" with manifest clinging to "obtaining the three fruits" of stream-enterer, once-returner, and non-returner, "and the ground of a śrāvaka arhat"; "and" does "not abide" with manifest clinging "to the ground of a pratyekabuddha, and similarly to the buddha ground"; in short, "does not abide" by manifestly clinging as truly existent to this and that, regarding any phenomena subsumed by the three—the basis, path, and fruit. Thus it is said. This means that that śrāvaka path of directly realizing the sixteen aspects such as impermanence is a path to be known by bodhisattvas, but they do not practice it by way of striving for the enlightenment of the inferior vehicle, and it teaches that they perform the three—generating, knowing, and completing—in order to care for trainees of the śrāvaka disposition by unifying method and wisdom, such as the generation of the mind, dedication, and wisdom realizing emptiness.

Work: ཡོན་ཏན་རིན་པོ་ཆེ་སྡུད་པ་ཚིགས་སུ་བཅད་པའི་འགྲེལ་པ་ཟབ་མོ་རྟེན་འབྱུང་གི་དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཉིད་གསལ་བར་བྱེད་པའི་ནོར་བུའི་སྒྲོན་མེ་སྐལ་བཟང་རེ་སྐོང་། (Khenrab Jamyang, Commentary on the Verses of the Precious Qualities Collection), author: མཁྱེན་རབ་འཇམ་དབྱངས་བློ་བཟང་འཕྲིན་ལས།. Its actual essence. The first: as the Ornament states from "In the method of the knowledge of the path itself," up to "This śrāvaka path should be known." For this, among the three—the definition, the divisions, and the boundaries:

[3-69] source:
མཚན་ཉིད།དང་པོ་ནི། སེམས་བསྐྱེད་བསྔོ་བ་སྟོང་ཉིད་རྟོགས་པའི་ཤེས་རབ་གསུམ་གྱིས་ཟིན་པའི་སྒོ་ནས་གདུལ་བྱ་ཉན་ཐོས་ཀྱི་རིགས་ཅན་རྗེས་སུ་བཟུང་བའི་ཕྱིར་དུ་ཤེས་པར་བྱ་བའི་མངོན་རྟོགས་ཀྱི་རིགས་སུ་གནས་པའིི་ཐེག་ཆན་འཕགས་པའི་མཁྱེན་པ་དེ། ཉན་ཐོས་ཀྱི་ལམ་ཤེས་པའི་ལམ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་མཚན་ཉིད།
[3-69] translation already produced for this document:
The definition. The first: the definition of the knowledge of the path that knows the path of the śrāvakas is that exalted knowledge of a Mahāyāna noble one abiding in the category of clear realization to be known, for the sake of caring for trainees of the śrāvaka disposition by means of being embraced by the three—generation of the mind, dedication, and wisdom realizing emptiness.

[3-71] source:
ས་མཚམས།གསུམ་པ་ནི། ཐེག་ཆེན་གྱི་མཐོང་ལམ་ནས་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་སའི་བར་དུ་ཡོད། དེ་ནི། རྟག་དང་མི་རྟག་ཅེས་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གཅིག་གིས་བསྟན། དེ་ཡང་རྟག་མི་རྟག་བདེ་སྡུག་སོགས་ཀྱིས་བདེན་པ་དང་པོ་གཉིས་ཀྱི་རྣམ་པ་དང་། འབྲས་བུ་ཐོབ་པ་དང་དགྲ་བཅོམ་ས་ལ་སོགས་ཀྱིས་འགོག་ལམ་རྣམ་པ་བསྟན་ནམ་སྙམ་ཞེས་ཕར་ཕྱིན་གཟབ་བཤད་ལས་གསུངས་ཀྱང་སློབ་དཔོན་གྱི་སྡུད་འགྲེལ་ལ་བརྟགས་ན། རྟག་དང་མི་རྟག་ནས་བདག་མེད་ཅེས་པའི་བར་གྱིས་སྡུག་བདེན་གྱི་རྣམ་པ་དང༌། དེ་བཞིན་ཉིད་དང་དེ་བཞིན་སྟོང་ཞེས་པས་བདེན་པ་ཕྱི་མ་གསུམ་གྱི་རྣམ་པ་བསྟན་པར་བྱས་ཨེ་འདུག་སྙམ་སྟེ་རྣམ་དཔྱོད་དང་ལྡན་པ་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་ཞིབ་ཏུ་དཔྱད་པར་བྱའོ། །ཚིག་དོན་ནི། གཟུགས་ལ་སོགས་པའི་ཆོས་རྣམས་ལ་མི་འཇིག་པའི་རྟག་པ་དང་དེ་ལས་ལྡོག་པའི་མི་རྟག་པ་དང་ཚོར་བ་སིམ་པའི་རྣམ་པ་ཅན་གྱི་བདེ་བ་དང་ཟག་པ་དང་བཅས་པའི་སྔུག་བསྔལ་དང་ཡིད་དུ་འཐད་པས་སྡུག་པ་དང་ཡིད་དུ་མི་འོང་བས་མི་སྡུག་པ་དང་རང་གི་ངོ་བོར་གྱུར་བའི་གང་ཟག་གི་བདག་ཡོད་པ་དང་བདག་མེད་པ་དང་དེ་བཞིན་ཉིད་དུ་སྟེ་དོན་དམ་པར་ཡོད་པ་དང་བདེན་པར་སྣང་ཡང་དེབཞིན་དུའམ་དེ་ལྟར་གྲུབ་པས་སྟོང་པ་སོགས་ཆོས་གང་ལའང་བདེན་པར་ཞེན་པའི་ཚུལ་གྱིས་མི་གནས་པ་དང་། རྒྱུན་ཞུགས་དང་ཕྱིར་འོང་ཕྱིར་མི་འོང་སྟེ་འབྲས་བུ་གསུམ་ཐོབ་པ་དང་ཉན་ཐོས་དགྲ་བཅོམ་པའི་ས་ལའང་མངོན་ཞེན་གྱིས་མི་གནས་ཤིང་། རང་རྒྱལ་གྱིས་དང་དེ་བཞིན་དུ་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་སར་ཡང་མངོན་ཞེན་གྱིས་མི་གནས་ཏེ་མདོར་ན་གཞི་ལམ་འབྲས་གསུམ་གྱིས་བསྡུས་པའི་ཆོས་གང་ལ་ཡང་དེ་དང་དེར་བདེན་པར་མངོན་པར་ཞེན་ནས་གནས་པར་མི་བྱེད་དོ། །ཞེས་པ་སྟེ། མི་རྟག་སོགས་བཅུ་དྲུག་མངོན་སུམ་དུ་རྟོགས་པའི་ཉན་ཐོས་ཀྱི་ལམ་དེ་བྱང་སེམས་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་ཤེས་པར་བྱ་བའི་ལམ་ཡིན་གྱི་ཐེག་དམན་གྱི་བྱང་ཆུབ་དོན་དུ་གཉེར་བའི་སྒོ་ནས་ཉམས་སུ་མི་ལེན་པ་དང་སེམས་བསྐྱེད་བསྔོ་བ་སྟོང་ཉིད་རྟོགས་པའི་ཤེས་རབ་སོགས་ཐབས་ཤེས་ཟུང་དུ་འབྲེལ་པར་ཉན་ཐོས་ཀྱི་རིགས་ཅན་རྗེས་སུ་བཟུང་བའི་ཆེད་དུ་བསྐྱེད་ཤེས་རྫོགས་གསུམ་བྱེད་པར་བསྟན་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །
[3-71] translation already produced for this document:
The boundaries. Third: they exist from the Mahāyāna path of seeing up to the buddha ground. That is taught by one stanza, "Permanent and impermanent" and so forth. Regarding that, although the Detailed Explanation of the Perfection of Wisdom says, "I wonder whether 'permanent,' 'impermanent,' 'happiness,' 'suffering' and so forth teach the aspects of the first two truths, and 'obtaining the fruit' and 'the ground of an arhat' and so forth teach the aspects of cessation and path?", if one examines the master's Commentary on the Verse Summary, I wonder whether the aspects of the truth of suffering are taught from "permanent" and "impermanent" up to "selfless," and the aspects of the latter three truths are taught by "suchness" and "empty of that." Those endowed with discernment should analyze this in detail. The literal meaning is: whoever does "not abide" in the manner of clinging as truly existent to "permanent" which does not disintegrate, "and impermanent" which is its opposite, "happiness" having the aspect of soothing feeling, "and" contaminated "suffering," "attractive" because of being agreeable to the mind, "and unattractive" because of being disagreeable to the mind, an existing "self" of a person that has become one's own essence, "and selfless," "and in suchness" meaning ultimately existent, "and" although appearing truly existent, "empty" of existing "like that" or being established like that, and so forth, regarding any dharma; "and" does "not abide" with manifest clinging to "obtaining the three fruits" of stream-enterer, once-returner, and non-returner, "and the ground of a śrāvaka arhat"; "and" does "not abide" with manifest clinging "to the ground of a pratyekabuddha, and similarly to the buddha ground"; in short, "does not abide" by manifestly clinging as truly existent to this and that, regarding any phenomena subsumed by the three—the basis, path, and fruit. Thus it is said. This means that that śrāvaka path of directly realizing the sixteen aspects such as impermanence is a path to be known by bodhisattvas, but they do not practice it by way of striving for the enlightenment of the inferior vehicle, and it teaches that they perform the three—generating, knowing, and completing—in order to care for trainees of the śrāvaka disposition by unifying method and wisdom, such as the generation of the mind, dedication, and wisdom realizing emptiness.

[3-72] source:
དེའི་རྒྱུ་ངེས་འབྱེད་ཆ་མཐུན།གཉིས་པ་དེའི་རྒྱུ་ངེས་འབྱེད་ཆ་མཐུན་སྟོན་པར། ཇི་ལྟར་འདྲེན་པ་ཞེས་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གཅིག་གསུངས་པའི་དོན་ནི། ཆོས་གང་ལ་ཡང་མི་གནས་པའི་དཔེ་ཇི་ལྟར་ན་འདྲེན་པ་སངས་རྒྱས་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱི་ཐུགས་ནི་འདུས་མ་བྱས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཏེ་སྲིད་པ་སྐྱེ་བ་ཚད་ཙམ་གྱིས་ཞི་བ་མྱ་ངན་ལས་འདས་པའི་དབྱིངས་ལ་མི་གནས་ཤིང་། དེ་བཞིན་དུ་འདུས་བྱས་ཁམས་གསུམ་འཁོར་བའི་ཕྱོགས་ལ་ཡང་བདེན་ཞེན་གྱིས་མི་གནས་ལ། སྲིད་ཞིའི་མཐའ་གང་ལ་ཡང་གནས་པ་མེད་པར་སྤྱོད་པ་དེ་ལྟར་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་རང་བཞིན་མེད་པར་རྟོགས་ནས་ངེས་འབྱེད་ཆ་མཐུན་ལ་སོགས་པའི་ལམ་ལ་གནས་ཀྱང་དེ་ལའང་བདེན་པར་ཞེན་ནས་གནས་པ་མེད་པར་གནས་པ་དེ་ནི། ཆོས་གང་ལ་ཡང་དོན་དམ་པར་གནས་པ་མེད་པར་སྤྲོས་བྲལ་དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཉིད་ལ་གནས་པ་ཡིན་ཏེ་ཚུལ་འདི་ལྟ་བུ་ནི་ཆོས་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་པོ་རྒྱལ་བས་སྙིང་པོ་དོན་གྱི་ཤེར་ཕྱིན་ལ་གནས་པར་གསུངས་སོ། །ཞེས་པའོ། །

Its cause, the aids to penetration. Second, to teach its cause, the aids to penetration, the meaning of what is stated in the one stanza "Just as the Guide" and so forth is: for example of not abiding in any dharma, "just as" the mind of "the Guide," the Bhagavan Buddha, does "not abide in the unconditioned realm," the basic space of nirvāṇa wherein mere arising in cyclic existence is pacified, "and similarly" does "not abide" by way of clinging as truly existent "to the conditioned" side of "the three realms" of cyclic existence, "practicing" without abiding in any extreme of existence or peace; "likewise," "a bodhisattva" having realized all phenomena as lacking inherent existence, "abides" on paths such as the aids to penetration, but "abiding without" abiding by "clinging" as truly existent "even to that" means abiding without abiding ultimately in any dharma, but rather abiding in the suchness free from proliferation; "like this" manner, the King of Dharma, "the Victor, has stated" is to "abide in" the definitive "perfection of wisdom." Thus it is said.

heading: **དངོས།**
source: དངོས།དང་པོ་ནི། གང་དག་བདེ་གཤེགས་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གཅིག་གིས་བསྟན། དེའང་ཉན་རང་གཉིས་རང་ཁ་ོནའི་དོན་དུ་ཐར་པ་དོན་དུ་གཉེར་བ་སོགས་འདྲ་བས་ཉན་ཐོས་ལས་ལོགས་སུ་རང་རྒྱལ་གྱི་ལམ་སྟོན་པ་མི་རིགས་སོ་སྙམ་པའི་དོགས་པ་གསལ་བའི་ཕྱིར། རེ་ཞིག་རང་རྒྱལ་དེ་ཉན་ཐོས་ལས་ཁྱད་ཞུགས་པར་བསྟན་ན་དེའི་ཐེག་པའི་རྣམ་བཞག་དཔོག་ནུས་པས་དེ་གཉིས་ཀྱི་ཁྱདཔར་ནི། ཉན་ཐོས་རྣམས་སྲིད་པ་ཐ་མའི་ཚེ་གཞན་ལ་གདམས་ངག་ཉན་ནས་རང་གི་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཐོབ་པ་དང་། འབྲས་བུ་ཐོབ་ནས་གཞན་ལའང་སྒྲ་བཅས་སུ་ཆོས་སྟོན་པའི་ཁྱད་པར་གཉིས་དང་ལྡན་ལ། རང་རྒྱལ་ནི་སྲིད་པ་ཐ་མའི་ཚེ་སངས་རྒྱས་སོགས་ཀྱིས་ཆོས་སྟོན་པ་ལ་མི་ལྟོས་པར་རང་སྟོབས་ཀྱིས་བྱང་ཆུབ་མངོན་དུ་བྱེད་པས་རང་བྱུང་ཞེས་བརྗོད་པ་དང་། སྒྲ་མེད་ལུས་ཀྱི་རྫུ་འཕྲུལ་གྱིས་གཞན་ལ་ཆོས་སྟོན་པ་སྟེ་ཁྱད་ཆོས་གཉིས་ཀྱིས་ཁྱད་པར་དུ་འཕགས་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །དེ་ལྟར་ཁྱད་ཞུགས་པར་བརྗོད་ནས་རང་རྒྱལ་གྱི་ལམ་ཤེས་པ་ལ་དེའི་ངོ་བོ་སྟོན་དགོས་པས་དེའི་ངོ་བོ་སྟོན་པ་ནི། སྔར་བཤད་པ་ལྟར་གཞི་དང་ལམ་དང་རྣམ་པ་ཐམས་ཅད་བདེན་སྟོང་དུ་མ་རྟོགས་པར་བྱང་ཆུབ་གསུམ་པོ་གང་ཡང་ཐོབ་པར་མི་ནུས་པས་སྙིང་པོའི་དོན་གྱི་ཤེར་ཕྱིན་ལ་སློབ་དགོས་པ་ནི། སྐྱེ་བོ་གང་དག་བདེ་བར་གཤེགས་བའི་སློབ་མ་ཉན་ཐོས་སུ་འགྱུར་བར་བྱའོ་སྙམ་པ་དང་། གཟུང་བ་ཕྱི་རོལ་དོན་འཛིན་གྱི་རྟོག་པ་སྤངས་བྱའི་གཙོ་བོར་བྱེད་པའི་རང་སངས་རྒྱས་སུ་འགྱུར་བ་དང་དེ་བཞིན་དུ་ཆོས་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་པོ་སངས་རྒྱས་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་སུ་འགྱུར་བར་འདོད་པ་སྟེ་མདོར་ན་བྱང་ཆུབ་གསུམ་པོ་གང་འཐོབ་པར་འདོད་ན་ཡང། གནས་ལུགས་ཟབ་མོ་སྟོང་པ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་དོན་ལ་མི་སྐྲག་པའི་བཟོད་པ་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་རང་བཞིན་མེད་པར་རྟོགས་པའི་ལམ་འདི་ལ་མ་བརྟེན་པར་འབྲས་བུ་དེ་དག་གང་ཡང་ཐོབ་བར་མི་ནུས་ཏེ། དཔེར་ན་གྲུ་ལ་མ་བརྟེན་པར་རྒྱ་མཚོའི་ཕ་རོལ་དང་ཚུལ་རོལ་ཏུ་འགྲོ་བའི་འཇུག་ངོགས་མི་མཐོང་བ་བཞིན་ནོ། །ཞེས་སོ། །འདིས་ལམ་ཤེས་ཐེག་པ་གསུམ་གྱི་ལམ་གྱི་ཡུལ་ཅན་དུ་བསྟན་ཀྱང་གཙོ་བོ་རང་རྒྱལ་གྱིས་བཟུང་རྟོག་སྤང་བར་བསྟན་ཏོ། །ཁ་གཅིག །ཉན་རང་ལ་ཆོས་ཀྱི་བདག་མེད་ཕྲ་མོ་རྟོགས་པ་སོགས་མེད་བར་འདོད་པ་ནི། མདོ་འདི་དང་དངོས་སུ་འགལ་ཞིང་། བརྒྱད་སྟོང་པ་ལས། ལྷའི་བུ་དག་དེ་ལྟ་བས་ན་གང་རྒྱུན་དུ་ཞུགས་པའི་འབྲསབུ་ཐོབ་པར་འདོད་པ་དང་རྒྱུན་དུ་ཞུགས་པའི་འབྲས་བུ་ལ་གནས་པར་འདོད་པ་དེས་བཟོད་པ་འདི་ལ་མ་བརྟེན་པར་མི་འགྲུབ་བོ། །དེ་བཞིན་སྦྱར་ཏེ་གང་ལ་ལན་གཅིག་ཕྱིར་འོངས་པའི་འབྲས་བུ་ཐོབ་པར་འདོད་པ་དང་། ལེན་གཅིག་ཕྱིར་འོངས་པའི་འབྲས་བུ་ལ་གནས་པར་འདོད་པ་དང་། ནས། རང་བྱང་ཆུབ་ལ་གནས་པར་འདོད་པ་དེས་བཟོད་པ་འདི་ལ་མ་བརྟེན་པར་མ་འགྲུབ་བོ། །ཞེས་དང་། རྡོ་རྗེ་གཅོད་པ་ལས་ཀྱང་། རབ་འབྱོར་འདི་ཅི་སྙམ་དུ་སེམས་རྒྱུན་དུ་ཞུགས་པ་འདི་སྙམ་དུ་བདག་གིས་རྒྱུན་དུ་ཞུགས་པའི་འབྲས་བུ་ཐོབ་བོ་སྙམ་དུ་སེམས་སམ། རབ་འབྱོར་གྱིས་གསོལ་བ། བཅོམ་ལྡནའདས་དེ་ནི་མ་ལགས་སོ། །དེ་ཅིའི་སླད་དུ་ཞེ་ན། བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་དེ་ནི་གང་ལ་ཡང་ཞུགས་པ་མ་མཆིས་པའི་སླད་དུ་སྟེ། དེས་ན་རྒྱུན་དུ་ཞུགས་པ་ཞེས་བགྱིའོ། །ཞེས་དང་། འཕགས་པ་ཡུལ་འཁོར་སྐྱོང་གིས་ཞུས་པའི་མདོ་ལས། སྟོང་པ་ཞི་བ་སྐྱེ་བ་མེད་པའི་ཚུལ། །མི་ཤེས་པས་ན་འགྲོ་བ་འཁྱམས་གྱུར་པ། །དེ་དག་ཐུགས་རྗེ་མངའ་བས་ཐབས་ཚུལ་དང༌། །རིགས་པ་བརྒྱ་དག་གིས་ནི་འཛུད་པར་མཛད། །ཅེས་འཁོར་བ་ལས་གྲོལ་བ་ལ་སྟོང་ཉིད་རྟོགས་དགོས་པར་གསུངས་པ་སོགས་ངེས་དོན་གྱི་མདོ་དུ་མ་དང་འགལ་ཞིང་། འཕགས་པ་ཀླུ་སྒྲུབ་དང་ཟླ་བ་གྲགས་པ་སོགས་ཀྱི་ལུགས་ལས་ཕྱི་རོལ་ཏུ་གྱུར་པ་ཡིན་ཏེ། རྩ་ཤེས་ལས། ལས་དང་ཉོན་མོངས་ཟད་པས་ཐར། །ལས་དང་ཉོན་མོངས་རྣམ་རྟོག་ལས། །དེ་དག་སྤྲོས་ལས་སྤྲོས་པ་ནི། །སྟོང་པ་ཉིད་ཀྱིས་འགག་བར་འགྱུར། །ཞེས་དང་། དཔལ་ལྡན་ཟླ་བས། ཉན་རང་ལ་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་རང་བཞིན་མེད་པར་རྟོགས་པ་ཡོད་པར་རིགས་པ་གསུམ་དང་ལུང་དུ་མས་སྒྲུབ་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཏེ། འཇུག་པ་རང་འགྲེལ་ལས། ལུགས་འདི་ལས་ནི་ཉན་ཐོས་དང་རང་སངས་རྒྱས་རྣམས་ལ་ཡང་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་རང་བཞིན་མེད་པར་ཤེས་པ་ཡང་ཡོད་དོ། །ཞེས་བྱ་བ་གསལ་བར་ངེས་ཏེ། དེ་ལྟར་མ་ཡིན་ན་དངོས་པོ་རང་བཞིན་མེད་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་ཤེས་པ་དང་བྲལ་བའི་ཕྱིར། འཇིག་རྟེན་པའི་འདོད་ཆགས་དང་བྲལ་བ་ལྟར་དེ་དག་ཀྱང་སེམས་བསྐྱེད་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་རང་གི་བློས་རྣམ་པར་དཔྱད་པས་ཀྱང་ཟིལ་གྱིས་གནོན་པར་འགྱུར་ལ། ཕྱི་རོལ་པ་བཞིན་དུ་འདི་དག་གིས་ཁམས་གསུམ་ན་སྤྱོད་པའི་ཕྲ་རྒྱས་ཐམས་ཅད་སྤངས་པར་ཡང་མི་འགྱུར་རོ། །གཟུགས་ལ་སོགས་པའི་རང་གི་ངོ་བོ་ལ་དམིགས་པས་ཕྱིན་ཅི་ལོག་ཏུ་འགྱུར་བའི་ཕྱིར། གང་ཟག་གི་བདག་མེད་རྟོགས་པར་མ་འགྱུར་ཏེ། བདག་ཏུ་བཏགས་པའི་རྒྱུ་ཕོང་པོ་ལ་དམིགས་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །ཇི་སྐད་དུ་རིན་ཆེན་འཕྲེང་བ་ལས། ཇི་སྲིད་ཕུང་པོར་འཛིན་ཡོད་པ། །དེ་སྲིད་དེ་ལ་ངར་འཛིན་ཡོད། །ངར་འཛིན་ཡོད་ན་ཡང་ལས་ཏེ། །དེ་ལས་ཡང་ན་སྐྱེ་བ་ཡིན། །ལམ་གསུམ་ཐོག་མཐའ་དབུས་མེད་པ། །འཁོར་བའི་དཀྱིལ་འཁོར་འགལ་མེ་ཡི། །དཀྱིལ་འཁོར་ལྟ་བུར་ཕན་ཚུན་གྱི། །རྒྱུ་ཅན་འདི་ནི་འཁོར་བར་འགྱུར། །དེ་ནི་རང་བཞིན་གཉིས་ཀ་དང་། །དུས་གསུམ་ཉིད་དུ་མ་མཐོང་ཕྱིར། །ངར་འཛིན་པ་ནི་ཟད་པར་འགྱུར། །དེ་ལས་ལས་དང་སྐྱེ་བ་ཡང༌། །ཞེས་གསུངས་སོ། །ཞེས་གསུངས་ཤིང་། དེའི་ཤེས་བྱེད་དུ་བསམ་གཏན་དཔེ་འཁྱུད་ཀྱི་མདོ་སོགས་དྲངས་སོ། །ཐེག་པ་ཆེ་ཆུང་གི་ཁྱད་པར་ཡང་། ལྟ་བའི་སྒོ་ནས་མི་འཇོག་པར་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའི་སྨོན་ལམ་དང་རྒྱ་ཆེ་བའི་སྤྱོད་པ་དང་ཡོངས་སུ་བསྔོ་བའི་ཁྱད་པར་རྣམས་ཀྱི་སྒོ་ནས་འཇོག་པ་ཡིན་ཏེ། ཇི་སྐད་དུ་རིན་ཆེན་འཕྲེང་བ་ལས། ཉན་ཐོས་ཐེག་པ་དེ་ལས་ནི། །བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའི་སྨོན་ལམ་དང་། །སྤྱོད་པ་ཡོངས་བསྔོ་མ་བཤད་དེ། །བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔར་ག་ལ་འགྱུར། །བྱང་ཆུབ་སྤྱོད་ལ་གནས་པའི་དོན། །མདོ་སྡ་ེལས་ནི་བཀའ་མ་སྩལ། །ཐེག་པ་ཆེ་ལས་བཀའ་སྩལ་པ། །དེ་ཕྱིར་མཁས་པ་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་བཟུང༌། །ཞེས་གསུངས་པའི་ཕྱིར། འོན་ཀྱང་རིགས་པའི་རྣམ་གྲངས་མཐའ་ཡས་པའི་སྒོ་ནས་སྟོང་ཉིད་རྟོགས་མ་རྟོགས་དང་། སྟོང་ཉིད་རྫོགས་པར་སྒོམ་མི་བསྒོམ་གྱི་ཁྱད་པར་ཡོད་ཚུལ་སོགས་ནི་དབུ་མའི་གཞུང་ལ་ཞིབ་ཏུ་སྦྱངས་ཏེ་ཤེས་པར་བྱའོ། །
translation: The actual. First, it is taught by one stanza, "Whoever" "Sugata" and so forth. Moreover, because the two—śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas—are similar in striving for liberation only for their own sake and so forth, in order to clear away the doubt thinking it is inappropriate to teach the path of pratyekabuddhas separately from that of śrāvakas, if one first shows that the pratyekabuddha is distinguished from the śrāvaka, one is able to deduce the presentation of their vehicle; thus the difference between those two is: śrāvakas are endowed with the two distinctions of obtaining their own enlightenment by listening to instructions from others during their final existence, and having obtained the fruit, teaching Dharma to others vocally; whereas the pratyekabuddha is distinguished by the two special qualities of manifestly actualizing enlightenment by their own power without depending on others such as buddhas teaching Dharma to them during their final existence, and thus being called "self-arisen," and teaching Dharma to others non-vocally through physical miracles. Having thus stated how they are distinguished, because it is necessary to teach the essence of the knowledge of the path of the pratyekabuddhas, teaching its essence is as follows: as explained before, because one cannot obtain any of the three enlightenments without realizing all bases, paths, and aspects as empty of true existence, having to train in the perfection of wisdom of the definitive essence means: "whoever" among people thinks, "I shall become a śrāvaka" "disciple" "of the Sugata," "and" wants to become a "pratyekabuddha" who mainly abandons the conceptualization grasping at external apprehended objects, "and likewise" wants to become the King of Dharma, the Bhagavan "Buddha"—in short, whichever of the three enlightenments one desires to obtain, without relying on "this patience" unafraid of the definitive profound natural state of emptiness, the path realizing all phenomena as lacking inherent existence, one is unable to obtain any of those fruits; "just as" without depending on a "boat," one does "not see the landing" for going to "the further shore and the near shore" of the ocean. Thus it is said. Although this teaches the knowledge of the path as having the objects of the paths of the three vehicles, it mainly teaches that the pratyekabuddha abandons the conceptualization of the apprehended. As for the assertion by some that śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas lack the realization of subtle selflessness of phenomena and so forth, it directly contradicts this sūtra, and the Aṣṭasāhasrikā: "Sons of the gods, therefore, whoever wishes to obtain the fruit of a stream-enterer and wishes to abide in the fruit of a stream-enterer will not accomplish it without relying on this patience. Applying it similarly: whoever wishes to obtain the fruit of a once-returner and wishes to abide in the fruit of a once-returner, and ... up to ... wishes to abide in pratyeka-enlightenment, will not accomplish it without relying on this patience." And from the Vajracchedikā: "Subhūti, what do you think? Does a stream-enterer think, 'I have obtained the fruit of a stream-enterer'?" Subhūti replied, "Bhagavan, that is not so. Why is that? Bhagavan, it is because he has not entered into anything whatsoever, therefore he is called a stream-enterer." And from the Ārya-rāṣṭrapālaparipṛcchā-sūtra: "Because they do not know the way of being empty, peaceful, and non-arising, beings wander. To them, those endowed with compassion apply skillful methods and hundreds of reasonings," which states that realizing emptiness is necessary for liberation from cyclic existence. Thus, it contradicts many sūtras of definitive meaning, and it falls outside the system of the noble Nāgārjuna, Candrakīrti, and so forth, because the Mūlamadhyamakakārikā says: "Through the exhaustion of karma and afflictions, there is liberation. Karma and afflictions arise from conceptualization. Those arise from proliferations. Proliferations are stopped by emptiness." And because the glorious Candrakīrti establishes with three reasonings and many scriptures that śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas have the realization that all phenomena lack inherent existence. From his Madhyamakāvatārabhāṣya: "From this system, it is clearly ascertained that 'śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas also have the knowledge that all phenomena lack inherent existence.' If it were not so, because they would lack the complete knowledge that entities lack inherent existence, like worldly beings free from attachment, they would also be outshone by the intellectual analysis of bodhisattvas who have generated the mind. And like non-Buddhists, they would not abandon all latent tendencies operating in the three realms either. Because they apprehend the essence of form and so forth, it would become perverse, so they would not realize the selflessness of the person, because they apprehend the aggregates, which are the basis for imputing the self. As the Ratnāvalī states: 'As long as there is grasping at the aggregates, so long is there grasping at "I" regarding them. When there is grasping at "I", there is karma again, and from that there is birth again. With the three paths lacking beginning, middle, or end, this wheel of cyclic existence, like the wheel of a firebrand, having mutual causes, turns. Because of not seeing it in its nature, as both, or as the three times themselves, the grasping at "I" will be exhausted, and from that, karma and birth as well.' Thus it is stated." And to prove that, he cites the Dhyānānusmṛti-sūtra and so forth. Furthermore, the difference between the great and lesser vehicles is not posited by way of view, but is posited by way of the differences of the bodhisattva's aspiration prayers, extensive deeds, and complete dedication, because the Ratnāvalī states: "Since the bodhisattva's aspiration prayers, deeds, and complete dedications are not explained in that śrāvaka vehicle, how could one become a bodhisattva through it? The meaning of abiding in bodhisattva deeds was not spoken in the sūtras. It was spoken in the Mahāyāna, therefore the wise hold it." Nevertheless, how there are differences in realizing or not realizing emptiness through infinite modes of reasoning, and in meditating or not meditating on emptiness perfectly, and so forth, should be known by studying the Madhyamaka texts in detail.

[3-71] translation already produced for this document:
The boundaries. Third: they exist from the Mahāyāna path of seeing up to the buddha ground. That is taught by one stanza, "Permanent and impermanent" and so forth. Regarding that, although the Detailed Explanation of the Perfection of Wisdom says, "I wonder whether 'permanent,' 'impermanent,' 'happiness,' 'suffering' and so forth teach the aspects of the first two truths, and 'obtaining the fruit' and 'the ground of an arhat' and so forth teach the aspects of cessation and path?", if one examines the master's Commentary on the Verse Summary, I wonder whether the aspects of the truth of suffering are taught from "permanent" and "impermanent" up to "selfless," and the aspects of the latter three truths are taught by "suchness" and "empty of that." Those endowed with discernment should analyze this in detail. The literal meaning is: whoever does "not abide" in the manner of clinging as truly existent to "permanent" which does not disintegrate, "and impermanent" which is its opposite, "happiness" having the aspect of soothing feeling, "and" contaminated "suffering," "attractive" because of being agreeable to the mind, "and unattractive" because of being disagreeable to the mind, an existing "self" of a person that has become one's own essence, "and selfless," "and in suchness" meaning ultimately existent, "and" although appearing truly existent, "empty" of existing "like that" or being established like that, and so forth, regarding any dharma; "and" does "not abide" with manifest clinging to "obtaining the three fruits" of stream-enterer, once-returner, and non-returner, "and the ground of a śrāvaka arhat"; "and" does "not abide" with manifest clinging "to the ground of a pratyekabuddha, and similarly to the buddha ground"; in short, "does not abide" by manifestly clinging as truly existent to this and that, regarding any phenomena subsumed by the three—the basis, path, and fruit. Thus it is said. This means that that śrāvaka path of directly realizing the sixteen aspects such as impermanence is a path to be known by bodhisattvas, but they do not practice it by way of striving for the enlightenment of the inferior vehicle, and it teaches that they perform the three—generating, knowing, and completing—in order to care for trainees of the śrāvaka disposition by unifying method and wisdom, such as the generation of the mind, dedication, and wisdom realizing emptiness.

Its cause, the aids to penetration. Second, to teach its cause, the aids to penetration, the meaning of what is stated in the one stanza "Just as the Guide" and so forth is: for example of not abiding in any dharma, "just as" the mind of "the Guide," the Bhagavan Buddha, does "not abide in the unconditioned realm," the basic space of nirvāṇa wherein mere arising in cyclic existence is pacified, "and similarly" does "not abide" by way of clinging as truly existent "to the conditioned" side of "the three realms" of cyclic existence, "practicing" without abiding in any extreme of existence or peace; "likewise," "a bodhisattva" having realized all phenomena as lacking inherent existence, "abides" on paths such as the aids to penetration, but "abiding without" abiding by "clinging" as truly existent "even to that" means abiding without abiding ultimately in any dharma, but rather abiding in the suchness free from proliferation; "like this" manner, the King of Dharma, "the Victor, has stated" is to "abide in" the definitive "perfection of wisdom." Thus it is said.
