source: ཞར་བྱུང་།གཉིས་པ་དེའི་ཞར་བྱུང་དུ་ཆོས་འཆད་པ་དང་ཉན་པ་དང་། བསྒོམ་ནས་འབྲས་བུ་ཐོབ་པའི་བར་ཐམས་ཅད་བདེན་སྟོང་སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟ་བུར་བསྟན་པ་ནི། ཆོས་འཆད་པ་དང་ཞེས་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གསུམ་གྱིས་བསྟན་པའི་དོན་ནི། སློབ་དཔོན་གྱིས་ཆོས་འཆད་པ་དང་། སློབ་མས་ཚུལ་བཞིན་ཉན་པ་དང་། བཤད་པར་བྱ་བའི་ཆོས་གང་ཡིན་པ་དང་། ཐོས་པའི་དོན་ཚུལ་བཞིན་ཡིད་ལ་བྱས་ཏེ། ལམ་སྒོམ་པས་རྒྱུན་ཞུགས་ལ་སོགས་པའི་ཉན་ཐོས་ཀྱི་འབྲས་བུ་བཞི་ཐོབ་པ་དང༌། དེ་བཞིན་དུ་རྐྱེན་རྒྱལ་སྟེ་རང་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་མཐོང་སྒོམ་མི་སློབ་ལམ་སོགས་ཐོབ་པ་དང༌། དེ་བཞིན་དུ་འཇིག་རྟེན་གསུམ་གྱི་སྐྱབས་དང་དཔུང་གཉེན་མགོན་པ་ོསངས་རྒྱས་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱི་བྱང་ཆུབ་མངོན་དུ་མཛད་པ་དང་། རང་དང་གཞན་གྱི་དོན་སྒྲུབ་པ་ལ་མཁས་པ་ཕུལ་དུ་བྱུང་བའི་ཤེས་རབ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་དང་ལྡན་ཞིང་ལམ་གྱི་ཚུལ་ལ་བློ་གྲོས་གསལ་བས་ཐབས་ཤེས་ཟུང་དུ་འབྲེལ་བར་ཐེག་པ་ཆེན་པོའི་ལམ་བསྒོམས་པའི་སྟོབས་ཀྱིས་ཐོབ་པའི་མཐར་ཐུག་གི་འབྲས་བུ་མི་གནས་པའི་མྱང་ངན་ལས་འདས་པ་གང་ཡིན་པ་དེ་ཀུན་ཀྱང་རྟེན་འབྲེལ་གྱི་གཏན་ཚིགས་སོགས་ཀྱིས་བརྟགས་ཤིང་དཔྱད་ན་བདེན་པར་གྲུབ་པ་ཅུང་ཟད་ཀྱང་མེད་པར་བདེན་པས་སྟོང་པ་སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟ་བུར་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ཡང་དག་པར་རྫོགས་པའི་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱིས་བསྟན་ཏོ། ཡུམ་རྒྱས་པ་ལས། ལྷའི་བུ་དག་ཁོ་བོ་ལས་ཆོས་ཉན་པ་ནི་སྒྱུ་མ་དང་སྤྲུལ་པ་ལྟ་བུར་བལྟ་བར་བྱའོ། །ཞེས་པ་ནས། བདག་ནི་མྱ་ངན་འདས་པ་ལས་ལྷག་པའི་ཆོས་གཞན་ཞིག་ཡོད་ན་དེ་ཡང་སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟ་བུར་བླཏའོ། །ཞེས་དང་། བརྒྱད་སྟོང་པ་ལས་ཀྱང༌། དེ་ནས་ཡང་ལྷའི་བུ་དེ་དག་འདི་སྙམ་དུ་སེམས་ཏེ། འཕགས་པ་རབ་འབྱོར་འདི་ལ་ཆོས་ཉན་པ་རང་བཞིན་ཇི་ལྟ་བུ་ཞིག་བཙལ་བར་བྱ་སྙམ་པ་དང༌། དེ་ནས་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་མཐུས་ཚེ་དང་ལྡན་པ་རབ་འབྱོར་གྱིས་ལྷའི་བུ་དེ་དག་གི་སེམས་ཀྱི་རྟོག་པ་སེམས་ཀྱིས་ཤེས་ནས་ལྷའི་བུ་དེ་དག་ལ་སྨྲས་པ། ལྷའི་བུ་དག་ཁོ་བོ་ལ་ཆོས་ཉན་པ་ནི་སྒྱུ་མ་དང་སྤྲུལ་པ་ལྟ་བུ་དག་ལྟ་བར་བྱའོ། །ཞེས་པ་ནས། ལྷའི་བུ་དག་སེམས་ཅན་ད་ེདག་ནི་སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟ་བུ། ལྷའི་བུ་དག་སེམས་ཅནདེ་དག་ནི་རྨི་ལམ་ལྟ་སྟེ། ནས། ཡང་དག་པར་རྫོགས་པའི་སངས་རྒྱས་ཉིད་སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟ་བུ་དང་རྨི་ལམ་ལྟ་བུའོ། །ནས། མྱ་ངན་ལས་འདས་པ་ཡང་སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟ་བུ་རྨི་ལམ་ལྟ་བུར་ན་ཆོས་གཞན་ལྟ་ཅི་སྨོས། ཞེས་གསུངས། ཇི་སྐད་བཤད་པའི་དོན་དེ་ལ་གང་ཟག་སུ་ཞིག་གུས་ནས་སློབ་ནུས་ཤེ་ན། གང་ཟག་བཞི་པོ་དེ་འདི་དག་ནི་བཤད་མ་ཐག་པའི་གནས་ལུགས་ཀྱི་དོན་ཟབ་མོ་དེ་ལ་མི་སྐྲག་སྟེ་བཞི་པོ་དེ་གང་ཞེ་ན། རྒྱལ་སྲས་བདེན་དོན་ལ་མཁས་པ་རང་རྒྱལ་ཚོགས་སྤྱོད་ཙམ་དང༌། ཕྱིར་མི་ལྡོག་པ་སྦྱོར་ལམ་པ་དང། འཕགས་པ་དགྲ་བཅོམ་པ་ཉོན་སྒྲིབ་སོགས་བློ་ཡི་དྲི་མ་བསལ་ཞིང་ཟད་པར་བྱས་ནས་གནས་ལུགས་ཟབ་མོའི་དོན་ལ་སོམ་ཉི་སྤངས་པ་དེ་གསུམ་དང་། བཞི་པ་ནི་ལས་དང་པོ་པ་ཡིན་དུ་ཟིན་ཀྱང་སྔོན་གྱི་རྒྱལ་བ་ལ་ལྷག་པར་བྱ་བ་བྱས་པ་སོགས་ཀྱིས་ད་ལྟ་ཤེར་ཕྱིན་གྱི་དོན་ཕྱིན་ཅི་མ་ལོག་པར་སྟོན་པར་ནུས་པའི་དགེ་བའི་བཤེས་གཉེན་གྱིས་ཡོངས་སུ་ཟིན་པའོ། །འདིའི་རྒྱལ་སྲས་བདེན་ལ་མཁས་ཞེས་རང་རྒྱལ་དངོས་གནས་གོ་དགོས་པས་རྟེན་རང་རྒྱལ་དངོས་སུ་བསྟན་པ་ཡིན་ལ། བརྒྱད་སྟོང་སོགས་ལས་དེ་ལྟར་བསྟན་ཅིང་རང་རྒྱལ་ལ་རྒྱལ་སྲས་སམ་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཞེས་གསུངས་པ་ནི། རང་དོན་དུ་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཐོབ་པས་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་དང༌། སྒྲ་མེད་པར་ཆོས་སྟོན་པས་སེམས་དཔའ་ཆེན་པོ་ཞེས་བཤད་པ་ཡིན་ཞེས་ཕར་ཕྱིན་ཟབ་བཤད་ལས་གསུངས། འདིས་དངོས་བསྟན་ཕལ་བ་རང་རྒྱལ་དང་གཅོ་བོ་བྱང་སེམས་ལ་བྱས་ན་འགྲིགས་སམ་སྙམ་ཡང་དཔྱད་འཚལ།
translation: Incidental Topic. Second, incidentally demonstrating that all activities from teaching and listening to the Dharma up to attaining the fruit by meditating are empty of true existence, like an illusion: The meaning taught by the three verses starting with "Teaching the Dharma..." is that the teacher teaching the Dharma, the student properly listening, the Dharma to be taught, and having properly taken to mind the meaning heard, meditating on the path and thereby attaining the four fruits of a Hearer, such as Stream Enterer; and similarly, attaining the path of seeing, path of meditation, and path of no-more-learning, etc., of a pratyekabuddha, that is, a solitary realizer; and similarly, actualizing the awakening of a Buddha, a Bhagavan, the protector, refuge, and ally of the three worlds; and whatever is the ultimate fruit, the non-abiding nirvana, attained by the power of meditating on the Mahayana path with the union of method and wisdom by someone endowed with the excellent, supreme wisdom skilled in accomplishing their own and others' purpose and with clear intelligence regarding the methods of the path - all these, when examined and analyzed by means of the reasoning of dependent origination and so forth, do not have even the slightest true establishment and were taught by the Tathagata, the perfectly complete Buddha, to be empty of true existence, like an illusion. From the Extensive Mother [the Prajñāpāramitā in 100,000 lines]: "Sons of the gods, listening to the Dharma from me is to be seen as like an illusion and like an emanation." Up to: "If there were any other dharma superior to nirvana, I would see that too as like an illusion." And from the Eight Thousand Line [Prajñāpāramitā]: Then, those sons of the gods thought this: "What is the nature of those who seek to listen to the Dharma from the Noble Subhūti?" And then, by the Buddha's power, venerable Subhūti knew with his mind the thoughts in the minds of those sons of the gods, and said to those sons of the gods: "Sons of the gods, listening to the Dharma from me is to be seen as like an illusion and like an emanation." Up to: "Sons of the gods, those sentient beings are like an illusion. Sons of the gods, those sentient beings are like a dream." Up to: "The perfectly complete Buddha himself is like an illusion and like a dream." Up to: "If even nirvana is like an illusion and like a dream, what need is there to speak of other dharmas?" If one asks what kind of person can respectfully train in the meaning explained in that way: These four persons are not frightened of the profound meaning of the abiding nature that has just been explained. If one asks who these four are: A "Child of the Victor skilled in the truth"—merely a pratyekabuddha on the paths of accumulation and preparation; an "irreversible one"—one on the path of preparation; an arhat, a noble one who has dispelled and exhausted the stains of the mind such as the afflictive obscurations and has abandoned doubt regarding the profound meaning of the abiding nature; those three, and fourthly, one who, although a beginner, has rendered special service to the Victors of the past and so forth, and is now fully embraced by a spiritual friend capable of teaching the meaning of the perfection of wisdom unmistakably. Here, because "Child of the Victor skilled in the truth" must be understood as an actual pratyekabuddha, the support is taught as being an actual pratyekabuddha; and texts such as the Eight Thousand Line teach it in that way. The reason why a pratyekabuddha is called a "Child of the Victor" or a "bodhisattva" is explained in the Profound Explanation of the Perfection of Wisdom [by Haribhadra]: "Because they attain awakening for their own sake, they are a bodhisattva, and because they teach the Dharma without words, they are called a mahāsattva." I wonder if it would be suitable to take what is explicitly taught here as principally a bodhisattva and secondarily a pratyekabuddha; but this should be examined.

translation: Having thus taught the support, if one asks what the manner of a bodhisattva's training in the path-knowledge of a pratyekabuddha is like: A bodhisattva who is skilled in accomplishing the purpose of those of the three lineages and in practicing the paths of the three vehicles, and who, having realized all dharmas as empty of true existence and free from conceptual proliferation, understands the logic of how they are ultimately established as the single vehicle, and who thus practices the perfection of wisdom that realizes non-apprehension and is embraced by special methods such as great compassion, does not themselves train in the stage that attains the arhatship of a Hearer, nor do they train in the stage that attains the awakening of a solitary realizer who realizes conditions, but rather, in order to attain the exalted wisdom of the omniscient knowledge of all aspects that without omission contains the purposes of those of the three lineages, they train by following the Dharma through which the Buddhas have gone and will go.

ཞར་བྱུང་།གཉིས་པ་དེའི་ཞར་བྱུང་དུ་ཆོས་འཆད་པ་དང་ཉན་པ་དང་། བསྒོམ་ནས་འབྲས་བུ་ཐོབ་པའི་བར་ཐམས་ཅད་བདེན་སྟོང་སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟ་བུར་བསྟན་པ་ནི། ཆོས་འཆད་པ་དང་ཞེས་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གསུམ་གྱིས་བསྟན་པའི་དོན་ནི། སློབ་དཔོན་གྱིས་ཆོས་འཆད་པ་དང་། སློབ་མས་ཚུལ་བཞིན་ཉན་པ་དང་། བཤད་པར་བྱ་བའི་ཆོས་གང་ཡིན་པ་དང་། ཐོས་པའི་དོན་ཚུལ་བཞིན་ཡིད་ལ་བྱས་ཏེ། ལམ་སྒོམ་པས་རྒྱུན་ཞུགས་ལ་སོགས་པའི་ཉན་ཐོས་ཀྱི་འབྲས་བུ་བཞི་ཐོབ་པ་དང༌། དེ་བཞིན་དུ་རྐྱེན་རྒྱལ་སྟེ་རང་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་མཐོང་སྒོམ་མི་སློབ་ལམ་སོགས་ཐོབ་པ་དང༌། དེ་བཞིན་དུ་འཇིག་རྟེན་གསུམ་གྱི་སྐྱབས་དང་དཔུང་གཉེན་མགོན་པ་ོསངས་རྒྱས་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱི་བྱང་ཆུབ་མངོན་དུ་མཛད་པ་དང་། རང་དང་གཞན་གྱི་དོན་སྒྲུབ་པ་ལ་མཁས་པ་ཕུལ་དུ་བྱུང་བའི་ཤེས་རབ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་དང་ལྡན་ཞིང་ལམ་གྱི་ཚུལ་ལ་བློ་གྲོས་གསལ་བས་ཐབས་ཤེས་ཟུང་དུ་འབྲེལ་བར་ཐེག་པ་ཆེན་པོའི་ལམ་བསྒོམས་པའི་སྟོབས་ཀྱིས་ཐོབ་པའི་མཐར་ཐུག་གི་འབྲས་བུ་མི་གནས་པའི་མྱང་ངན་ལས་འདས་པ་གང་ཡིན་པ་དེ་ཀུན་ཀྱང་རྟེན་འབྲེལ་གྱི་གཏན་ཚིགས་སོགས་ཀྱིས་བརྟགས་ཤིང་དཔྱད་ན་བདེན་པར་གྲུབ་པ་ཅུང་ཟད་ཀྱང་མེད་པར་བདེན་པས་སྟོང་པ་སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟ་བུར་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ཡང་དག་པར་རྫོགས་པའི་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱིས་བསྟན་ཏོ། ཡུམ་རྒྱས་པ་ལས། ལྷའི་བུ་དག་ཁོ་བོ་ལས་ཆོས་ཉན་པ་ནི་སྒྱུ་མ་དང་སྤྲུལ་པ་ལྟ་བུར་བལྟ་བར་བྱའོ། །ཞེས་པ་ནས། བདག་ནི་མྱ་ངན་འདས་པ་ལས་ལྷག་པའི་ཆོས་གཞན་ཞིག་ཡོད་ན་དེ་ཡང་སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟ་བུར་བླཏའོ། །ཞེས་དང་། བརྒྱད་སྟོང་པ་ལས་ཀྱང༌། དེ་ནས་ཡང་ལྷའི་བུ་དེ་དག་འདི་སྙམ་དུ་སེམས་ཏེ། འཕགས་པ་རབ་འབྱོར་འདི་ལ་ཆོས་ཉན་པ་རང་བཞིན་ཇི་ལྟ་བུ་ཞིག་བཙལ་བར་བྱ་སྙམ་པ་དང༌། དེ་ནས་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་མཐུས་ཚེ་དང་ལྡན་པ་རབ་འབྱོར་གྱིས་ལྷའི་བུ་དེ་དག་གི་སེམས་ཀྱི་རྟོག་པ་སེམས་ཀྱིས་ཤེས་ནས་ལྷའི་བུ་དེ་དག་ལ་སྨྲས་པ། ལྷའི་བུ་དག་ཁོ་བོ་ལ་ཆོས་ཉན་པ་ནི་སྒྱུ་མ་དང་སྤྲུལ་པ་ལྟ་བུ་དག་ལྟ་བར་བྱའོ། །ཞེས་པ་ནས། ལྷའི་བུ་དག་སེམས་ཅན་ད་ེདག་ནི་སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟ་བུ། ལྷའི་བུ་དག་སེམས་ཅནདེ་དག་ནི་རྨི་ལམ་ལྟ་སྟེ། ནས། ཡང་དག་པར་རྫོགས་པའི་སངས་རྒྱས་ཉིད་སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟ་བུ་དང་རྨི་ལམ་ལྟ་བུའོ། །ནས། མྱ་ངན་ལས་འདས་པ་ཡང་སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟ་བུ་རྨི་ལམ་ལྟ་བུར་ན་ཆོས་གཞན་ལྟ་ཅི་སྨོས། ཞེས་གསུངས། ཇི་སྐད་བཤད་པའི་དོན་དེ་ལ་གང་ཟག་སུ་ཞིག་གུས་ནས་སློབ་ནུས་ཤེ་ན། གང་ཟག་བཞི་པོ་དེ་འདི་དག་ནི་བཤད་མ་ཐག་པའི་གནས་ལུགས་ཀྱི་དོན་ཟབ་མོ་དེ་ལ་མི་སྐྲག་སྟེ་བཞི་པོ་དེ་གང་ཞེ་ན། རྒྱལ་སྲས་བདེན་དོན་ལ་མཁས་པ་རང་རྒྱལ་ཚོགས་སྤྱོད་ཙམ་དང༌། ཕྱིར་མི་ལྡོག་པ་སྦྱོར་ལམ་པ་དང། འཕགས་པ་དགྲ་བཅོམ་པ་ཉོན་སྒྲིབ་སོགས་བློ་ཡི་དྲི་མ་བསལ་ཞིང་ཟད་པར་བྱས་ནས་གནས་ལུགས་ཟབ་མོའི་དོན་ལ་སོམ་ཉི་སྤངས་པ་དེ་གསུམ་དང་། བཞི་པ་ནི་ལས་དང་པོ་པ་ཡིན་དུ་ཟིན་ཀྱང་སྔོན་གྱི་རྒྱལ་བ་ལ་ལྷག་པར་བྱ་བ་བྱས་པ་སོགས་ཀྱིས་ད་ལྟ་ཤེར་ཕྱིན་གྱི་དོན་ཕྱིན་ཅི་མ་ལོག་པར་སྟོན་པར་ནུས་པའི་དགེ་བའི་བཤེས་གཉེན་གྱིས་ཡོངས་སུ་ཟིན་པའོ། །འདིའི་རྒྱལ་སྲས་བདེན་ལ་མཁས་ཞེས་རང་རྒྱལ་དངོས་གནས་གོ་དགོས་པས་རྟེན་རང་རྒྱལ་དངོས་སུ་བསྟན་པ་ཡིན་ལ། བརྒྱད་སྟོང་སོགས་ལས་དེ་ལྟར་བསྟན་ཅིང་རང་རྒྱལ་ལ་རྒྱལ་སྲས་སམ་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཞེས་གསུངས་པ་ནི། རང་དོན་དུ་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཐོབ་པས་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་དང༌། སྒྲ་མེད་པར་ཆོས་སྟོན་པས་སེམས་དཔའ་ཆེན་པོ་ཞེས་བཤད་པ་ཡིན་ཞེས་ཕར་ཕྱིན་ཟབ་བཤད་ལས་གསུངས། འདིས་དངོས་བསྟན་ཕལ་བ་རང་རྒྱལ་དང་གཅོ་བོ་བྱང་སེམས་ལ་བྱས་ན་འགྲིགས་སམ་སྙམ་ཡང་དཔྱད་འཚལ།

Incidental Topic. Second, incidentally demonstrating that all activities from teaching and listening to the Dharma up to attaining the fruit by meditating are empty of true existence, like an illusion: The meaning taught by the three verses starting with "Teaching the Dharma..." is that the teacher teaching the Dharma, the student properly listening, the Dharma to be taught, and having properly taken to mind the meaning heard, meditating on the path and thereby attaining the four fruits of a Hearer, such as Stream Enterer; and similarly, attaining the path of seeing, path of meditation, and path of no-more-learning, etc., of a pratyekabuddha, that is, a solitary realizer; and similarly, actualizing the awakening of a Buddha, a Bhagavan, the protector, refuge, and ally of the three worlds; and whatever is the ultimate fruit, the non-abiding nirvana, attained by the power of meditating on the Mahayana path with the union of method and wisdom by someone endowed with the excellent, supreme wisdom skilled in accomplishing their own and others' purpose and with clear intelligence regarding the methods of the path - all these, when examined and analyzed by means of the reasoning of dependent origination and so forth, do not have even the slightest true establishment and were taught by the Tathagata, the perfectly complete Buddha, to be empty of true existence, like an illusion. From the Extensive Mother [the Prajñāpāramitā in 100,000 lines]: "Sons of the gods, listening to the Dharma from me is to be seen as like an illusion and like an emanation." Up to: "If there were any other dharma superior to nirvana, I would see that too as like an illusion." And from the Eight Thousand Line [Prajñāpāramitā]: Then, those sons of the gods thought this: "What is the nature of those who seek to listen to the Dharma from the Noble Subhūti?" And then, by the Buddha's power, venerable Subhūti knew with his mind the thoughts in the minds of those sons of the gods, and said to those sons of the gods: "Sons of the gods, listening to the Dharma from me is to be seen as like an illusion and like an emanation." Up to: "Sons of the gods, those sentient beings are like an illusion. Sons of the gods, those sentient beings are like a dream." Up to: "The perfectly complete Buddha himself is like an illusion and like a dream." Up to: "If even nirvana is like an illusion and like a dream, what need is there to speak of other dharmas?" If one asks what kind of person can respectfully train in the meaning explained in that way: These four persons are not frightened of the profound meaning of the abiding nature that has just been explained. If one asks who these four are: A "Child of the Victor skilled in the truth"—merely a pratyekabuddha on the paths of accumulation and preparation; an "irreversible one"—one on the path of preparation; an arhat, a noble one who has dispelled and exhausted the stains of the mind such as the afflictive obscurations and has abandoned doubt regarding the profound meaning of the abiding nature; those three, and fourthly, one who, although a beginner, has rendered special service to the Victors of the past and so forth, and is now fully embraced by a spiritual friend capable of teaching the meaning of the perfection of wisdom unmistakably. Here, because "Child of the Victor skilled in the truth" must be understood as an actual pratyekabuddha, the support is taught as being an actual pratyekabuddha; and texts such as the Eight Thousand Line teach it in that way. The reason why a pratyekabuddha is called a "Child of the Victor" or a "bodhisattva" is explained in the Profound Explanation of the Perfection of Wisdom [by Haribhadra]: "Because they attain awakening for their own sake, they are a bodhisattva, and because they teach the Dharma without words, they are called a mahāsattva." I wonder if it would be suitable to take what is explicitly taught here as principally a bodhisattva and secondarily a pratyekabuddha; but this should be examined.

heading: **ཞར་བྱུང་།**
translation: Training in whatever path by way of taking to mind the knowledge of all aspects and not apprehending it as truly existent, and not training through mental engagement in the lower vehicles and clinging to true existence—having realized that both of these are not truly established, not training in any path with mental engagement in the lower vehicles and clinging to true existence is to train in the genuine path, the path-knowledge of a bodhisattva. So it is said.

རང་དོན་དུ་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཐོབ་པས་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་དང༌། སྒྲ་མེད་པར་ཆོས་སྟོན་པས་སེམས་དཔའ་ཆེན་པོ་ཞེས་བཤད་པ་ཡིན་ཞེས་ཕར་ཕྱིན་ཟབ་བཤད་ལས་གསུངས། Incidental Topic. Second, incidentally demonstrating that all activities from teaching and listening to the Dharma up to attaining the fruit by meditating are empty of true existence, like an illusion: The meaning taught by the three verses starting with "Teaching the Dharma..." is that the teacher teaching the Dharma, the student properly listening, the Dharma to be taught, and having properly taken to mind the meaning heard, meditating on the path and thereby attaining the four fruits of a Hearer, such as Stream Enterer; and similarly, attaining the path of seeing, path of meditation, and path of no-more-learning, etc., of a pratyekabuddha, that is, a solitary realizer; and similarly, actualizing the awakening of a Buddha, a Bhagavan, the protector, refuge, and ally of the three worlds; and whatever is the ultimate fruit, the non-abiding nirvana, attained by the power of meditating on the Mahayana path with the union of method and wisdom by someone endowed with the excellent, supreme wisdom skilled in accomplishing their own and others' purpose and with clear intelligence regarding the methods of the path - all these, when examined and analyzed by means of the reasoning of dependent origination and so forth, do not have even the slightest true establishment and were taught by the Tathagata, the perfectly complete Buddha, to be empty of true existence, like an illusion. From the Extensive Mother [the Prajñāpāramitā in 100,000 lines]: "Sons of the gods, listening to the Dharma from me is to be seen as like an illusion and like an emanation." Up to: "If there were any other dharma superior to nirvana, I would see that too as like an illusion." And from the Eight Thousand Line [Prajñāpāramitā]: Then, those sons of the gods thought this: "What is the nature of those who seek to listen to the Dharma from the Noble Subhūti?" And then, by the Buddha's power, venerable Subhūti knew with his mind the thoughts in the minds of those sons of the gods, and said to those sons of the gods: "Sons of the gods, listening to the Dharma from me is to be seen as like an illusion and like an emanation." Up to: "Sons of the gods, those sentient beings are like an illusion. Sons of the gods, those sentient beings are like a dream." Up to: "The perfectly complete Buddha himself is like an illusion and like a dream." Up to: "If even nirvana is like an illusion and like a dream, what need is there to speak of other dharmas?" If one asks what kind of person can respectfully train in the meaning explained in that way: These four persons are not frightened of the profound meaning of the abiding nature that has just been explained. If one asks who these four are: A "Child of the Victor skilled in the truth"—merely a pratyekabuddha on the paths of accumulation and preparation; an "irreversible one"—one on the path of preparation; an arhat, a noble one who has dispelled and exhausted the stains of the mind such as the afflictive obscurations and has abandoned doubt regarding the profound meaning of the abiding nature; those three, and fourthly, one who, although a beginner, has rendered special service to the Victors of the past and so forth, and is now fully embraced by a spiritual friend capable of teaching the meaning of the perfection of wisdom unmistakably. Here, because "Child of the Victor skilled in the truth" must be understood as an actual pratyekabuddha, the support is taught as being an actual pratyekabuddha; and texts such as the Eight Thousand Line teach it in that way. The reason why a pratyekabuddha is called a "Child of the Victor" or a "bodhisattva" is explained in the Profound Explanation of the Perfection of Wisdom [by Haribhadra]: "Because they attain awakening for their own sake, they are a bodhisattva, and because they teach the Dharma without words, they are called a mahāsattva." I wonder if it would be suitable to take what is explicitly taught here as principally a bodhisattva and secondarily a pratyekabuddha; but this should be examined.

heading: **ཞར་བྱུང་།**
translation: Since that path-knowledge of a pratyekabuddha also does not arise without causes and conditions, its cause, the aids to penetration: The meaning taught by the one verse starting with "[When] form increases..." is: Regarding what does a bodhisattva not train and instead discard? They do not train in order to fully apprehend by clinging to ultimate increasing or completely diminishing—that is, decreasing—and to true existence regarding all dharmas on the side of total affliction, such as form, and all dharmas of complete purification, such as the placements of mindfulness. This is because, since all these dharmas are naturally pure, ultimate increasing and decreasing, arising and ceasing, and so forth are not apprehended. They do not train through application in order to completely apprehend through manifest clinging to, or to generate within their own mindstream, any of the various aspects of dharmas from form up to the knowledge of all aspects, but rather they train by way of not apprehending the aids to penetration and so forth; and for the sake of others, by knowing that even the knowledge of all aspects itself lacks a nature, they conventionally fully apprehend it and attain it; and whatever definite emergence—that is, attainment—in that ultimate state of a Buddha there is in dependence upon having practiced the path through the union of method and wisdom, this is the manner in which bodhisattvas who delight in the qualities of the Mahayana train in the path.

གང་ཟག་བཞི་པོ་དེ་འདི་དག་ནི་བཤད་མ་ཐག་པའི་གནས་ལུགས་ཀྱི་དོན་ཟབ་མོ་དེ་ལ་མི་སྐྲག་སྟེ་བཞི་པོ་དེ་གང་ཞེ་ན། རྒྱལ་སྲས་བདེན་དོན་ལ་མཁས་པ་རང་རྒྱལ་ཚོགས་སྤྱོད་ཙམ་དང༌། ཕྱིར་མི་ལྡོག་པ་སྦྱོར་ལམ་པ་དང། །འདིའི་རྒྱལ་སྲས་བདེན་ལ་མཁས་ཞེས་རང་རྒྱལ་དངོས་གནས་གོ་དགོས་པས་རྟེན་རང་རྒྱལ་དངོས་སུ་བསྟན་པ་ཡིན་ལ། བརྒྱད་སྟོང་སོགས་ལས་དེ་ལྟར་བསྟན་ཅིང་རང་རྒྱལ་ལ་རྒྱལ་སྲས་སམ་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཞེས་གསུངས་པ་ནི། རང་དོན་དུ་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཐོབ་པས་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་དང༌། སྒྲ་མེད་པར་ཆོས་སྟོན་པས་སེམས་དཔའ་ཆེན་པོ་ཞེས་བཤད་པ་ཡིན་ཞེས་ཕར་ཕྱིན་ཟབ་བཤད་ལས་གསུངས། Incidental Topic. Second, incidentally demonstrating that all activities from teaching and listening to the Dharma up to attaining the fruit by meditating are empty of true existence, like an illusion: The meaning taught by the three verses starting with "Teaching the Dharma..." is that the teacher teaching the Dharma, the student properly listening, the Dharma to be taught, and having properly taken to mind the meaning heard, meditating on the path and thereby attaining the four fruits of a Hearer, such as Stream Enterer; and similarly, attaining the path of seeing, path of meditation, and path of no-more-learning, etc., of a pratyekabuddha, that is, a solitary realizer; and similarly, actualizing the awakening of a Buddha, a Bhagavan, the protector, refuge, and ally of the three worlds; and whatever is the ultimate fruit, the non-abiding nirvana, attained by the power of meditating on the Mahayana path with the union of method and wisdom by someone endowed with the excellent, supreme wisdom skilled in accomplishing their own and others' purpose and with clear intelligence regarding the methods of the path - all these, when examined and analyzed by means of the reasoning of dependent origination and so forth, do not have even the slightest true establishment and were taught by the Tathagata, the perfectly complete Buddha, to be empty of true existence, like an illusion. From the Extensive Mother [the Prajñāpāramitā in 100,000 lines]: "Sons of the gods, listening to the Dharma from me is to be seen as like an illusion and like an emanation." Up to: "If there were any other dharma superior to nirvana, I would see that too as like an illusion." And from the Eight Thousand Line [Prajñāpāramitā]: Then, those sons of the gods thought this: "What is the nature of those who seek to listen to the Dharma from the Noble Subhūti?" And then, by the Buddha's power, venerable Subhūti knew with his mind the thoughts in the minds of those sons of the gods, and said to those sons of the gods: "Sons of the gods, listening to the Dharma from me is to be seen as like an illusion and like an emanation." Up to: "Sons of the gods, those sentient beings are like an illusion. Sons of the gods, those sentient beings are like a dream." Up to: "The perfectly complete Buddha himself is like an illusion and like a dream." Up to: "If even nirvana is like an illusion and like a dream, what need is there to speak of other dharmas?" If one asks what kind of person can respectfully train in the meaning explained in that way: These four persons are not frightened of the profound meaning of the abiding nature that has just been explained. If one asks who these four are: A "Child of the Victor skilled in the truth"—merely a pratyekabuddha on the paths of accumulation and preparation; an "irreversible one"—one on the path of preparation; an arhat, a noble one who has dispelled and exhausted the stains of the mind such as the afflictive obscurations and has abandoned doubt regarding the profound meaning of the abiding nature; those three, and fourthly, one who, although a beginner, has rendered special service to the Victors of the past and so forth, and is now fully embraced by a spiritual friend capable of teaching the meaning of the perfection of wisdom unmistakably. Here, because "Child of the Victor skilled in the truth" must be understood as an actual pratyekabuddha, the support is taught as being an actual pratyekabuddha; and texts such as the Eight Thousand Line teach it in that way. The reason why a pratyekabuddha is called a "Child of the Victor" or a "bodhisattva" is explained in the Profound Explanation of the Perfection of Wisdom [by Haribhadra]: "Because they attain awakening for their own sake, they are a bodhisattva, and because they teach the Dharma without words, they are called a mahāsattva." I wonder if it would be suitable to take what is explicitly taught here as principally a bodhisattva and secondarily a pratyekabuddha; but this should be examined.

heading: **ཞར་བྱུང་།**
translation: Here, it is said that the statement "form increases [or] completely diminishes" corresponds to "no increasing or decreasing" from the Ornament; and the statement "not for the sake of apprehending" corresponds to "patience in order not to apprehend".

Incidental Topic. Second, incidentally demonstrating that all activities from teaching and listening to the Dharma up to attaining the fruit by meditating are empty of true existence, like an illusion: The meaning taught by the three verses starting with "Teaching the Dharma..." is that the teacher teaching the Dharma, the student properly listening, the Dharma to be taught, and having properly taken to mind the meaning heard, meditating on the path and thereby attaining the four fruits of a Hearer, such as Stream Enterer; and similarly, attaining the path of seeing, path of meditation, and path of no-more-learning, etc., of a pratyekabuddha, that is, a solitary realizer; and similarly, actualizing the awakening of a Buddha, a Bhagavan, the protector, refuge, and ally of the three worlds; and whatever is the ultimate fruit, the non-abiding nirvana, attained by the power of meditating on the Mahayana path with the union of method and wisdom by someone endowed with the excellent, supreme wisdom skilled in accomplishing their own and others' purpose and with clear intelligence regarding the methods of the path - all these, when examined and analyzed by means of the reasoning of dependent origination and so forth, do not have even the slightest true establishment and were taught by the Tathagata, the perfectly complete Buddha, to be empty of true existence, like an illusion. From the Extensive Mother [the Prajñāpāramitā in 100,000 lines]: "Sons of the gods, listening to the Dharma from me is to be seen as like an illusion and like an emanation." Up to: "If there were any other dharma superior to nirvana, I would see that too as like an illusion." And from the Eight Thousand Line [Prajñāpāramitā]: Then, those sons of the gods thought this: "What is the nature of those who seek to listen to the Dharma from the Noble Subhūti?" And then, by the Buddha's power, venerable Subhūti knew with his mind the thoughts in the minds of those sons of the gods, and said to those sons of the gods: "Sons of the gods, listening to the Dharma from me is to be seen as like an illusion and like an emanation." Up to: "Sons of the gods, those sentient beings are like an illusion. Sons of the gods, those sentient beings are like a dream." Up to: "The perfectly complete Buddha himself is like an illusion and like a dream." Up to: "If even nirvana is like an illusion and like a dream, what need is there to speak of other dharmas?" If one asks what kind of person can respectfully train in the meaning explained in that way: These four persons are not frightened of the profound meaning of the abiding nature that has just been explained. If one asks who these four are: A "Child of the Victor skilled in the truth"—merely a pratyekabuddha on the paths of accumulation and preparation; an "irreversible one"—one on the path of preparation; an arhat, a noble one who has dispelled and exhausted the stains of the mind such as the afflictive obscurations and has abandoned doubt regarding the profound meaning of the abiding nature; those three, and fourthly, one who, although a beginner, has rendered special service to the Victors of the past and so forth, and is now fully embraced by a spiritual friend capable of teaching the meaning of the perfection of wisdom unmistakably. Here, because "Child of the Victor skilled in the truth" must be understood as an actual pratyekabuddha, the support is taught as being an actual pratyekabuddha; and texts such as the Eight Thousand Line teach it in that way. The reason why a pratyekabuddha is called a "Child of the Victor" or a "bodhisattva" is explained in the Profound Explanation of the Perfection of Wisdom [by Haribhadra]: "Because they attain awakening for their own sake, they are a bodhisattva, and because they teach the Dharma without words, they are called a mahāsattva." I wonder if it would be suitable to take what is explicitly taught here as principally a bodhisattva and secondarily a pratyekabuddha; but this should be examined.

heading: **བྱང་སེམས་ཀྱི་མཐོང་ལམ།**
source: བྱང་སེམས་ཀྱི་མཐོང་ལམ།བཞི་པ་བྱང་སེམས་ཀྱི་མཐོང་ལམ་ནི། རྒྱན་ལས། བདེན་དང་བདེན་ལ་བཟོད་པ་དང༌། ནས། ལམ་ཤེས་ཉིད་ཀྱི་སྐད་ཅིག་མ། །ཞེས་གསུངས། །འདི་ལ་མཚན་ཉིད། དབྱེབ། ས་མཚམས་གསུམ།
translation: The Bodhisattva's Path of Seeing. Fourth, the bodhisattva's path of seeing: From the Ornament: "Truth and patience regarding truth," up to, "Moments of the path-knowledge itself." Regarding this, there are three [topics]: the definition, the divisions, and the boundaries.

ཞར་བྱུང་།གཉིས་པ་དེའི་ཞར་བྱུང་དུ་ཆོས་འཆད་པ་དང་ཉན་པ་དང་། བསྒོམ་ནས་འབྲས་བུ་ཐོབ་པའི་བར་ཐམས་ཅད་བདེན་སྟོང་སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟ་བུར་བསྟན་པ་ནི། ཆོས་འཆད་པ་དང་ཞེས་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གསུམ་གྱིས་བསྟན་པའི་དོན་ནི། སློབ་དཔོན་གྱིས་ཆོས་འཆད་པ་དང་། སློབ་མས་ཚུལ་བཞིན་ཉན་པ་དང་། བཤད་པར་བྱ་བའི་ཆོས་གང་ཡིན་པ་དང་། ཐོས་པའི་དོན་ཚུལ་བཞིན་ཡིད་ལ་བྱས་ཏེ། ལམ་སྒོམ་པས་རྒྱུན་ཞུགས་ལ་སོགས་པའི་ཉན་ཐོས་ཀྱི་འབྲས་བུ་བཞི་ཐོབ་པ་དང༌། དེ་བཞིན་དུ་རྐྱེན་རྒྱལ་སྟེ་རང་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་མཐོང་སྒོམ་མི་སློབ་ལམ་སོགས་ཐོབ་པ་དང༌། དེ་བཞིན་དུ་འཇིག་རྟེན་གསུམ་གྱི་སྐྱབས་དང་དཔུང་གཉེན་མགོན་པ་ོསངས་རྒྱས་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱི་བྱང་ཆུབ་མངོན་དུ་མཛད་པ་དང་། རང་དང་གཞན་གྱི་དོན་སྒྲུབ་པ་ལ་མཁས་པ་ཕུལ་དུ་བྱུང་བའི་ཤེས་རབ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་དང་ལྡན་ཞིང་ལམ་གྱི་ཚུལ་ལ་བློ་གྲོས་གསལ་བས་ཐབས་ཤེས་ཟུང་དུ་འབྲེལ་བར་ཐེག་པ་ཆེན་པོའི་ལམ་བསྒོམས་པའི་སྟོབས་ཀྱིས་ཐོབ་པའི་མཐར་ཐུག་གི་འབྲས་བུ་མི་གནས་པའི་མྱང་ངན་ལས་འདས་པ་གང་ཡིན་པ་དེ་ཀུན་ཀྱང་རྟེན་འབྲེལ་གྱི་གཏན་ཚིགས་སོགས་ཀྱིས་བརྟགས་ཤིང་དཔྱད་ན་བདེན་པར་གྲུབ་པ་ཅུང་ཟད་ཀྱང་མེད་པར་བདེན་པས་སྟོང་པ་སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟ་བུར་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ཡང་དག་པར་རྫོགས་པའི་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱིས་བསྟན་ཏོ། ཡུམ་རྒྱས་པ་ལས། ལྷའི་བུ་དག་ཁོ་བོ་ལས་ཆོས་ཉན་པ་ནི་སྒྱུ་མ་དང་སྤྲུལ་པ་ལྟ་བུར་བལྟ་བར་བྱའོ། །ཞེས་པ་ནས། བདག་ནི་མྱ་ངན་འདས་པ་ལས་ལྷག་པའི་ཆོས་གཞན་ཞིག་ཡོད་ན་དེ་ཡང་སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟ་བུར་བླཏའོ། །ཞེས་དང་། བརྒྱད་སྟོང་པ་ལས་ཀྱང༌། དེ་ནས་ཡང་ལྷའི་བུ་དེ་དག་འདི་སྙམ་དུ་སེམས་ཏེ། འཕགས་པ་རབ་འབྱོར་འདི་ལ་ཆོས་ཉན་པ་རང་བཞིན་ཇི་ལྟ་བུ་ཞིག་བཙལ་བར་བྱ་སྙམ་པ་དང༌། དེ་ནས་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་མཐུས་ཚེ་དང་ལྡན་པ་རབ་འབྱོར་གྱིས་ལྷའི་བུ་དེ་དག་གི་སེམས་ཀྱི་རྟོག་པ་སེམས་ཀྱིས་ཤེས་ནས་ལྷའི་བུ་དེ་དག་ལ་སྨྲས་པ། ལྷའི་བུ་དག་ཁོ་བོ་ལ་ཆོས་ཉན་པ་ནི་སྒྱུ་མ་དང་སྤྲུལ་པ་ལྟ་བུ་དག་ལྟ་བར་བྱའོ། །ཞེས་པ་ནས། ལྷའི་བུ་དག་སེམས་ཅན་ད་ེདག་ནི་སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟ་བུ། ལྷའི་བུ་དག་སེམས་ཅནདེ་དག་ནི་རྨི་ལམ་ལྟ་སྟེ། ནས། ཡང་དག་པར་རྫོགས་པའི་སངས་རྒྱས་ཉིད་སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟ་བུ་དང་རྨི་ལམ་ལྟ་བུའོ། །ནས། མྱ་ངན་ལས་འདས་པ་ཡང་སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟ་བུ་རྨི་ལམ་ལྟ་བུར་ན་ཆོས་གཞན་ལྟ་ཅི་སྨོས། ཞེས་གསུངས། ཇི་སྐད་བཤད་པའི་དོན་དེ་ལ་གང་ཟག་སུ་ཞིག་གུས་ནས་སློབ་ནུས་ཤེ་ན། གང་ཟག་བཞི་པོ་དེ་འདི་དག་ནི་བཤད་མ་ཐག་པའི་གནས་ལུགས་ཀྱི་དོན་ཟབ་མོ་དེ་ལ་མི་སྐྲག་སྟེ་བཞི་པོ་དེ་གང་ཞེ་ན། རྒྱལ་སྲས་བདེན་དོན་ལ་མཁས་པ་རང་རྒྱལ་ཚོགས་སྤྱོད་ཙམ་དང༌། ཕྱིར་མི་ལྡོག་པ་སྦྱོར་ལམ་པ་དང། འཕགས་པ་དགྲ་བཅོམ་པ་ཉོན་སྒྲིབ་སོགས་བློ་ཡི་དྲི་མ་བསལ་ཞིང་ཟད་པར་བྱས་ནས་གནས་ལུགས་ཟབ་མོའི་དོན་ལ་སོམ་ཉི་སྤངས་པ་དེ་གསུམ་དང་། བཞི་པ་ནི་ལས་དང་པོ་པ་ཡིན་དུ་ཟིན་ཀྱང་སྔོན་གྱི་རྒྱལ་བ་ལ་ལྷག་པར་བྱ་བ་བྱས་པ་སོགས་ཀྱིས་ད་ལྟ་ཤེར་ཕྱིན་གྱི་དོན་ཕྱིན་ཅི་མ་ལོག་པར་སྟོན་པར་ནུས་པའི་དགེ་བའི་བཤེས་གཉེན་གྱིས་ཡོངས་སུ་ཟིན་པའོ། །འདིའི་རྒྱལ་སྲས་བདེན་ལ་མཁས་ཞེས་རང་རྒྱལ་དངོས་གནས་གོ་དགོས་པས་རྟེན་རང་རྒྱལ་དངོས་སུ་བསྟན་པ་ཡིན་ལ། བརྒྱད་སྟོང་སོགས་ལས་དེ་ལྟར་བསྟན་ཅིང་རང་རྒྱལ་ལ་རྒྱལ་སྲས་སམ་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཞེས་གསུངས་པ་ནི། རང་དོན་དུ་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཐོབ་པས་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་དང༌། སྒྲ་མེད་པར་ཆོས་སྟོན་པས་སེམས་དཔའ་ཆེན་པོ་ཞེས་བཤད་པ་ཡིན་ཞེས་ཕར་ཕྱིན་ཟབ་བཤད་ལས་གསུངས། འདིས་དངོས་བསྟན་ཕལ་བ་རང་རྒྱལ་དང་གཅོ་བོ་བྱང་སེམས་ལ་བྱས་ན་འགྲིགས་སམ་སྙམ་ཡང་དཔྱད་འཚལ།

Incidental Topic. Second, incidentally demonstrating that all activities from teaching and listening to the Dharma up to attaining the fruit by meditating are empty of true existence, like an illusion: The meaning taught by the three verses starting with "Teaching the Dharma..." is that the teacher teaching the Dharma, the student properly listening, the Dharma to be taught, and having properly taken to mind the meaning heard, meditating on the path and thereby attaining the four fruits of a Hearer, such as Stream Enterer; and similarly, attaining the path of seeing, path of meditation, and path of no-more-learning, etc., of a pratyekabuddha, that is, a solitary realizer; and similarly, actualizing the awakening of a Buddha, a Bhagavan, the protector, refuge, and ally of the three worlds; and whatever is the ultimate fruit, the non-abiding nirvana, attained by the power of meditating on the Mahayana path with the union of method and wisdom by someone endowed with the excellent, supreme wisdom skilled in accomplishing their own and others' purpose and with clear intelligence regarding the methods of the path - all these, when examined and analyzed by means of the reasoning of dependent origination and so forth, do not have even the slightest true establishment and were taught by the Tathagata, the perfectly complete Buddha, to be empty of true existence, like an illusion. From the Extensive Mother [the Prajñāpāramitā in 100,000 lines]: "Sons of the gods, listening to the Dharma from me is to be seen as like an illusion and like an emanation." Up to: "If there were any other dharma superior to nirvana, I would see that too as like an illusion." And from the Eight Thousand Line [Prajñāpāramitā]: Then, those sons of the gods thought this: "What is the nature of those who seek to listen to the Dharma from the Noble Subhūti?" And then, by the Buddha's power, venerable Subhūti knew with his mind the thoughts in the minds of those sons of the gods, and said to those sons of the gods: "Sons of the gods, listening to the Dharma from me is to be seen as like an illusion and like an emanation." Up to: "Sons of the gods, those sentient beings are like an illusion. Sons of the gods, those sentient beings are like a dream." Up to: "The perfectly complete Buddha himself is like an illusion and like a dream." Up to: "If even nirvana is like an illusion and like a dream, what need is there to speak of other dharmas?" If one asks what kind of person can respectfully train in the meaning explained in that way: These four persons are not frightened of the profound meaning of the abiding nature that has just been explained. If one asks who these four are: A "Child of the Victor skilled in the truth"—merely a pratyekabuddha on the paths of accumulation and preparation; an "irreversible one"—one on the path of preparation; an arhat, a noble one who has dispelled and exhausted the stains of the mind such as the afflictive obscurations and has abandoned doubt regarding the profound meaning of the abiding nature; those three, and fourthly, one who, although a beginner, has rendered special service to the Victors of the past and so forth, and is now fully embraced by a spiritual friend capable of teaching the meaning of the perfection of wisdom unmistakably. Here, because "Child of the Victor skilled in the truth" must be understood as an actual pratyekabuddha, the support is taught as being an actual pratyekabuddha; and texts such as the Eight Thousand Line teach it in that way. The reason why a pratyekabuddha is called a "Child of the Victor" or a "bodhisattva" is explained in the Profound Explanation of the Perfection of Wisdom [by Haribhadra]: "Because they attain awakening for their own sake, they are a bodhisattva, and because they teach the Dharma without words, they are called a mahāsattva." I wonder if it would be suitable to take what is explicitly taught here as principally a bodhisattva and secondarily a pratyekabuddha; but this should be examined.

སློབ་དཔོན་གྱིས་ཆོས་འཆད་པ་དང་། སློབ་མས་ཚུལ་བཞིན་ཉན་པ་དང་། བཤད་པར་བྱ་བའི་ཆོས་གང་ཡིན་པ་དང་། ཐོས་པའི་དོན་ཚུལ་བཞིན་ཡིད་ལ་བྱས་ཏེ། ལམ་སྒོམ་པས་རྒྱུན་ཞུགས་ལ་སོགས་པའི་ཉན་ཐོས་ཀྱི་འབྲས་བུ་བཞི་ཐོབ་པ་དང༌། དེ་བཞིན་དུ་རྐྱེན་རྒྱལ་སྟེ་རང་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་མཐོང་སྒོམ་མི་སློབ་ལམ་སོགས་ཐོབ་པ་དང༌། དེ་བཞིན་དུ་འཇིག་རྟེན་གསུམ་གྱི་སྐྱབས་དང་དཔུང་གཉེན་མགོན་པ་ོསངས་རྒྱས་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱི་བྱང་ཆུབ་མངོན་དུ་མཛད་པ་དང་། རང་དང་གཞན་གྱི་དོན་སྒྲུབ་པ་ལ་མཁས་པ་ཕུལ་དུ་བྱུང་བའི་ཤེས་རབ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་དང་ལྡན་ཞིང་ལམ་གྱི་ཚུལ་ལ་བློ་གྲོས་གསལ་བས་ཐབས་ཤེས་ཟུང་དུ་འབྲེལ་བར་ཐེག་པ་ཆེན་པོའི་ལམ་བསྒོམས་པའི་སྟོབས་ཀྱིས་ཐོབ་པའི་མཐར་ཐུག་གི་འབྲས་བུ་མི་གནས་པའི་མྱང་ངན་ལས་འདས་པ་གང་ཡིན་པ་དེ་ཀུན་ཀྱང་རྟེན་འབྲེལ་གྱི་གཏན་ཚིགས་སོགས་ཀྱིས་བརྟགས་ཤིང་དཔྱད་ན་བདེན་པར་གྲུབ་པ་ཅུང་ཟད་ཀྱང་མེད་པར་བདེན་པས་སྟོང་པ་སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟ་བུར་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ཡང་དག་པར་རྫོགས་པའི་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱིས་བསྟན་ཏོ། ཡུམ་རྒྱས་པ་ལས། ལྷའི་བུ་དག་ཁོ་བོ་ལས་ཆོས་ཉན་པ་ནི་སྒྱུ་མ་དང་སྤྲུལ་པ་ལྟ་བུར་བལྟ་བར་བྱའོ། །ཞེས་པ་ནས། བདག་ནི་མྱ་ངན་འདས་པ་ལས་ལྷག་པའི་ཆོས་གཞན་ཞིག་ཡོད་ན་དེ་ཡང་སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟ་བུར་བླཏའོ། །ཞེས་དང་། བརྒྱད་སྟོང་པ་ལས་ཀྱང༌། དེ་ནས་ཡང་ལྷའི་བུ་དེ་དག་འདི་སྙམ་དུ་སེམས་ཏེ། འཕགས་པ་རབ་འབྱོར་འདི་ལ་ཆོས་ཉན་པ་རང་བཞིན་ཇི་ལྟ་བུ་ཞིག་བཙལ་བར་བྱ་སྙམ་པ་དང༌། དེ་ནས་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་མཐུས་ཚེ་དང་ལྡན་པ་རབ་འབྱོར་གྱིས་ལྷའི་བུ་དེ་དག་གི་སེམས་ཀྱི་རྟོག་པ་སེམས་ཀྱིས་ཤེས་ནས་ལྷའི་བུ་དེ་དག་ལ་སྨྲས་པ། ལྷའི་བུ་དག་ཁོ་བོ་ལ་ཆོས་ཉན་པ་ནི་སྒྱུ་མ་དང་སྤྲུལ་པ་ལྟ་བུ་དག་ལྟ་བར་བྱའོ། །ཞེས་པ་ནས། ལྷའི་བུ་དག་སེམས་ཅན་ད་ེདག་ནི་སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟ་བུ། ལྷའི་བུ་དག་སེམས་ཅནདེ་དག་ནི་རྨི་ལམ་ལྟ་སྟེ། ནས། ཡང་དག་པར་རྫོགས་པའི་སངས་རྒྱས་ཉིད་སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟ་བུ་དང་རྨི་ལམ་ལྟ་བུའོ། །ནས། མྱ་ངན་ལས་འདས་པ་ཡང་སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟ་བུ་རྨི་ལམ་ལྟ་བུར་ན་ཆོས་གཞན་ལྟ་ཅི་སྨོས། ཞེས་གསུངས། ཇི་སྐད་བཤད་པའི་དོན་དེ་ལ་གང་ཟག་སུ་ཞིག་གུས་ནས་སློབ་ནུས་ཤེ་ན། གང་ཟག་བཞི་པོ་དེ་འདི་དག་ནི་བཤད་མ་ཐག་པའི་གནས་ལུགས་ཀྱི་དོན་ཟབ་མོ་དེ་ལ་མི་སྐྲག་སྟེ་བཞི་པོ་དེ་གང་ཞེ་ན། རྒྱལ་སྲས་བདེན་དོན་ལ་མཁས་པ་རང་རྒྱལ་ཚོགས་སྤྱོད་ཙམ་དང༌། ཕྱིར་མི་ལྡོག་པ་སྦྱོར་ལམ་པ་དང། འཕགས་པ་དགྲ་བཅོམ་པ་ཉོན་སྒྲིབ་སོགས་བློ་ཡི་དྲི་མ་བསལ་ཞིང་ཟད་པར་བྱས་ནས་གནས་ལུགས་ཟབ་མོའི་དོན་ལ་སོམ་ཉི་སྤངས་པ་དེ་གསུམ་དང་། བཞི་པ་ནི་ལས་དང་པོ་པ་ཡིན་དུ་ཟིན་ཀྱང་སྔོན་གྱི་རྒྱལ་བ་ལ་ལྷག་པར་བྱ་བ་བྱས་པ་སོགས་ཀྱིས་ད་ལྟ་ཤེར་ཕྱིན་གྱི་དོན་ཕྱིན་ཅི་མ་ལོག་པར་སྟོན་པར་ནུས་པའི་དགེ་བའི་བཤེས་གཉེན་གྱིས་ཡོངས་སུ་ཟིན་པའོ། །འདིའི་རྒྱལ་སྲས་བདེན་ལ་མཁས་ཞེས་རང་རྒྱལ་དངོས་གནས་གོ་དགོས་པས་རྟེན་རང་རྒྱལ་དངོས་སུ་བསྟན་པ་ཡིན་ལ། བརྒྱད་སྟོང་སོགས་ལས་དེ་ལྟར་བསྟན་ཅིང་རང་རྒྱལ་ལ་རྒྱལ་སྲས་སམ་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཞེས་གསུངས་པ་ནི། རང་དོན་དུ་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཐོབ་པས་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་དང༌། སྒྲ་མེད་པར་ཆོས་སྟོན་པས་སེམས་དཔའ་ཆེན་པོ་ཞེས་བཤད་པ་ཡིན་ཞེས་ཕར་ཕྱིན་ཟབ་བཤད་ལས་གསུངས། Incidental Topic. Second, incidentally demonstrating that all activities from teaching and listening to the Dharma up to attaining the fruit by meditating are empty of true existence, like an illusion: The meaning taught by the three verses starting with "Teaching the Dharma..." is that the teacher teaching the Dharma, the student properly listening, the Dharma to be taught, and having properly taken to mind the meaning heard, meditating on the path and thereby attaining the four fruits of a Hearer, such as Stream Enterer; and similarly, attaining the path of seeing, path of meditation, and path of no-more-learning, etc., of a pratyekabuddha, that is, a solitary realizer; and similarly, actualizing the awakening of a Buddha, a Bhagavan, the protector, refuge, and ally of the three worlds; and whatever is the ultimate fruit, the non-abiding nirvana, attained by the power of meditating on the Mahayana path with the union of method and wisdom by someone endowed with the excellent, supreme wisdom skilled in accomplishing their own and others' purpose and with clear intelligence regarding the methods of the path - all these, when examined and analyzed by means of the reasoning of dependent origination and so forth, do not have even the slightest true establishment and were taught by the Tathagata, the perfectly complete Buddha, to be empty of true existence, like an illusion. From the Extensive Mother [the Prajñāpāramitā in 100,000 lines]: "Sons of the gods, listening to the Dharma from me is to be seen as like an illusion and like an emanation." Up to: "If there were any other dharma superior to nirvana, I would see that too as like an illusion." And from the Eight Thousand Line [Prajñāpāramitā]: Then, those sons of the gods thought this: "What is the nature of those who seek to listen to the Dharma from the Noble Subhūti?" And then, by the Buddha's power, venerable Subhūti knew with his mind the thoughts in the minds of those sons of the gods, and said to those sons of the gods: "Sons of the gods, listening to the Dharma from me is to be seen as like an illusion and like an emanation." Up to: "Sons of the gods, those sentient beings are like an illusion. Sons of the gods, those sentient beings are like a dream." Up to: "The perfectly complete Buddha himself is like an illusion and like a dream." Up to: "If even nirvana is like an illusion and like a dream, what need is there to speak of other dharmas?" If one asks what kind of person can respectfully train in the meaning explained in that way: These four persons are not frightened of the profound meaning of the abiding nature that has just been explained. If one asks who these four are: A "Child of the Victor skilled in the truth"—merely a pratyekabuddha on the paths of accumulation and preparation; an "irreversible one"—one on the path of preparation; an arhat, a noble one who has dispelled and exhausted the stains of the mind such as the afflictive obscurations and has abandoned doubt regarding the profound meaning of the abiding nature; those three, and fourthly, one who, although a beginner, has rendered special service to the Victors of the past and so forth, and is now fully embraced by a spiritual friend capable of teaching the meaning of the perfection of wisdom unmistakably. Here, because "Child of the Victor skilled in the truth" must be understood as an actual pratyekabuddha, the support is taught as being an actual pratyekabuddha; and texts such as the Eight Thousand Line teach it in that way. The reason why a pratyekabuddha is called a "Child of the Victor" or a "bodhisattva" is explained in the Profound Explanation of the Perfection of Wisdom [by Haribhadra]: "Because they attain awakening for their own sake, they are a bodhisattva, and because they teach the Dharma without words, they are called a mahāsattva." I wonder if it would be suitable to take what is explicitly taught here as principally a bodhisattva and secondarily a pratyekabuddha; but this should be examined.

སློབ་དཔོན་གྱིས་ཆོས་འཆད་པ་དང་། སློབ་མས་ཚུལ་བཞིན་ཉན་པ་དང་། བཤད་པར་བྱ་བའི་ཆོས་གང་ཡིན་པ་དང་། ཐོས་པའི་དོན་ཚུལ་བཞིན་ཡིད་ལ་བྱས་ཏེ། ལམ་སྒོམ་པས་རྒྱུན་ཞུགས་ལ་སོགས་པའི་ཉན་ཐོས་ཀྱི་འབྲས་བུ་བཞི་ཐོབ་པ་དང༌། དེ་བཞིན་དུ་རྐྱེན་རྒྱལ་སྟེ་རང་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་མཐོང་སྒོམ་མི་སློབ་ལམ་སོགས་ཐོབ་པ་དང༌། དེ་བཞིན་དུ་འཇིག་རྟེན་གསུམ་གྱི་སྐྱབས་དང་དཔུང་གཉེན་མགོན་པ་ོསངས་རྒྱས་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱི་བྱང་ཆུབ་མངོན་དུ་མཛད་པ་དང་། རང་དང་གཞན་གྱི་དོན་སྒྲུབ་པ་ལ་མཁས་པ་ཕུལ་དུ་བྱུང་བའི་ཤེས་རབ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་དང་ལྡན་ཞིང་ལམ་གྱི་ཚུལ་ལ་བློ་གྲོས་གསལ་བས་ཐབས་ཤེས་ཟུང་དུ་འབྲེལ་བར་ཐེག་པ་ཆེན་པོའི་ལམ་བསྒོམས་པའི་སྟོབས་ཀྱིས་ཐོབ་པའི་མཐར་ཐུག་གི་འབྲས་བུ་མི་གནས་པའི་མྱང་ངན་ལས་འདས་པ་གང་ཡིན་པ་དེ་ཀུན་ཀྱང་རྟེན་འབྲེལ་གྱི་གཏན་ཚིགས་སོགས་ཀྱིས་བརྟགས་ཤིང་དཔྱད་ན་བདེན་པར་གྲུབ་པ་ཅུང་ཟད་ཀྱང་མེད་པར་བདེན་པས་སྟོང་པ་སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟ་བུར་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ཡང་དག་པར་རྫོགས་པའི་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱིས་བསྟན་ཏོ། ཡུམ་རྒྱས་པ་ལས། ལྷའི་བུ་དག་ཁོ་བོ་ལས་ཆོས་ཉན་པ་ནི་སྒྱུ་མ་དང་སྤྲུལ་པ་ལྟ་བུར་བལྟ་བར་བྱའོ། །ཞེས་པ་ནས། བདག་ནི་མྱ་ངན་འདས་པ་ལས་ལྷག་པའི་ཆོས་གཞན་ཞིག་ཡོད་ན་དེ་ཡང་སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟ་བུར་བླཏའོ། །ཞེས་དང་། བརྒྱད་སྟོང་པ་ལས་ཀྱང༌། དེ་ནས་ཡང་ལྷའི་བུ་དེ་དག་འདི་སྙམ་དུ་སེམས་ཏེ། འཕགས་པ་རབ་འབྱོར་འདི་ལ་ཆོས་ཉན་པ་རང་བཞིན་ཇི་ལྟ་བུ་ཞིག་བཙལ་བར་བྱ་སྙམ་པ་དང༌། དེ་ནས་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་མཐུས་ཚེ་དང་ལྡན་པ་རབ་འབྱོར་གྱིས་ལྷའི་བུ་དེ་དག་གི་སེམས་ཀྱི་རྟོག་པ་སེམས་ཀྱིས་ཤེས་ནས་ལྷའི་བུ་དེ་དག་ལ་སྨྲས་པ། ལྷའི་བུ་དག་ཁོ་བོ་ལ་ཆོས་ཉན་པ་ནི་སྒྱུ་མ་དང་སྤྲུལ་པ་ལྟ་བུ་དག་ལྟ་བར་བྱའོ། །ཞེས་པ་ནས། ལྷའི་བུ་དག་སེམས་ཅན་ད་ེདག་ནི་སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟ་བུ། ལྷའི་བུ་དག་སེམས་ཅནདེ་དག་ནི་རྨི་ལམ་ལྟ་སྟེ། ནས། ཡང་དག་པར་རྫོགས་པའི་སངས་རྒྱས་ཉིད་སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟ་བུ་དང་རྨི་ལམ་ལྟ་བུའོ། །ནས། མྱ་ངན་ལས་འདས་པ་ཡང་སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟ་བུ་རྨི་ལམ་ལྟ་བུར་ན་ཆོས་གཞན་ལྟ་ཅི་སྨོས། ཞེས་གསུངས། ཇི་སྐད་བཤད་པའི་དོན་དེ་ལ་གང་ཟག་སུ་ཞིག་གུས་ནས་སློབ་ནུས་ཤེ་ན། གང་ཟག་བཞི་པོ་དེ་འདི་དག་ནི་བཤད་མ་ཐག་པའི་གནས་ལུགས་ཀྱི་དོན་ཟབ་མོ་དེ་ལ་མི་སྐྲག་སྟེ་བཞི་པོ་དེ་གང་ཞེ་ན། རྒྱལ་སྲས་བདེན་དོན་ལ་མཁས་པ་རང་རྒྱལ་ཚོགས་སྤྱོད་ཙམ་དང༌། ཕྱིར་མི་ལྡོག་པ་སྦྱོར་ལམ་པ་དང། འཕགས་པ་དགྲ་བཅོམ་པ་ཉོན་སྒྲིབ་སོགས་བློ་ཡི་དྲི་མ་བསལ་ཞིང་ཟད་པར་བྱས་ནས་གནས་ལུགས་ཟབ་མོའི་དོན་ལ་སོམ་ཉི་སྤངས་པ་དེ་གསུམ་དང་། བཞི་པ་ནི་ལས་དང་པོ་པ་ཡིན་དུ་ཟིན་ཀྱང་སྔོན་གྱི་རྒྱལ་བ་ལ་ལྷག་པར་བྱ་བ་བྱས་པ་སོགས་ཀྱིས་ད་ལྟ་ཤེར་ཕྱིན་གྱི་དོན་ཕྱིན་ཅི་མ་ལོག་པར་སྟོན་པར་ནུས་པའི་དགེ་བའི་བཤེས་གཉེན་གྱིས་ཡོངས་སུ་ཟིན་པའོ། །འདིའི་རྒྱལ་སྲས་བདེན་ལ་མཁས་ཞེས་རང་རྒྱལ་དངོས་གནས་གོ་དགོས་པས་རྟེན་རང་རྒྱལ་དངོས་སུ་བསྟན་པ་ཡིན་ལ། བརྒྱད་སྟོང་སོགས་ལས་དེ་ལྟར་བསྟན་ཅིང་རང་རྒྱལ་ལ་རྒྱལ་སྲས་སམ་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཞེས་གསུངས་པ་ནི། རང་དོན་དུ་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཐོབ་པས་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་དང༌། སྒྲ་མེད་པར་ཆོས་སྟོན་པས་སེམས་དཔའ་ཆེན་པོ་ཞེས་བཤད་པ་ཡིན་ཞེས་ཕར་ཕྱིན་ཟབ་བཤད་ལས་གསུངས། Incidental Topic. Second, incidentally demonstrating that all activities from teaching and listening to the Dharma up to attaining the fruit by meditating are empty of true existence, like an illusion: The meaning taught by the three verses starting with "Teaching the Dharma..." is that the teacher teaching the Dharma, the student properly listening, the Dharma to be taught, and having properly taken to mind the meaning heard, meditating on the path and thereby attaining the four fruits of a Hearer, such as Stream Enterer; and similarly, attaining the path of seeing, path of meditation, and path of no-more-learning, etc., of a pratyekabuddha, that is, a solitary realizer; and similarly, actualizing the awakening of a Buddha, a Bhagavan, the protector, refuge, and ally of the three worlds; and whatever is the ultimate fruit, the non-abiding nirvana, attained by the power of meditating on the Mahayana path with the union of method and wisdom by someone endowed with the excellent, supreme wisdom skilled in accomplishing their own and others' purpose and with clear intelligence regarding the methods of the path - all these, when examined and analyzed by means of the reasoning of dependent origination and so forth, do not have even the slightest true establishment and were taught by the Tathagata, the perfectly complete Buddha, to be empty of true existence, like an illusion. From the Extensive Mother [the Prajñāpāramitā in 100,000 lines]: "Sons of the gods, listening to the Dharma from me is to be seen as like an illusion and like an emanation." Up to: "If there were any other dharma superior to nirvana, I would see that too as like an illusion." And from the Eight Thousand Line [Prajñāpāramitā]: Then, those sons of the gods thought this: "What is the nature of those who seek to listen to the Dharma from the Noble Subhūti?" And then, by the Buddha's power, venerable Subhūti knew with his mind the thoughts in the minds of those sons of the gods, and said to those sons of the gods: "Sons of the gods, listening to the Dharma from me is to be seen as like an illusion and like an emanation." Up to: "Sons of the gods, those sentient beings are like an illusion. Sons of the gods, those sentient beings are like a dream." Up to: "The perfectly complete Buddha himself is like an illusion and like a dream." Up to: "If even nirvana is like an illusion and like a dream, what need is there to speak of other dharmas?" If one asks what kind of person can respectfully train in the meaning explained in that way: These four persons are not frightened of the profound meaning of the abiding nature that has just been explained. If one asks who these four are: A "Child of the Victor skilled in the truth"—merely a pratyekabuddha on the paths of accumulation and preparation; an "irreversible one"—one on the path of preparation; an arhat, a noble one who has dispelled and exhausted the stains of the mind such as the afflictive obscurations and has abandoned doubt regarding the profound meaning of the abiding nature; those three, and fourthly, one who, although a beginner, has rendered special service to the Victors of the past and so forth, and is now fully embraced by a spiritual friend capable of teaching the meaning of the perfection of wisdom unmistakably. Here, because "Child of the Victor skilled in the truth" must be understood as an actual pratyekabuddha, the support is taught as being an actual pratyekabuddha; and texts such as the Eight Thousand Line teach it in that way. The reason why a pratyekabuddha is called a "Child of the Victor" or a "bodhisattva" is explained in the Profound Explanation of the Perfection of Wisdom [by Haribhadra]: "Because they attain awakening for their own sake, they are a bodhisattva, and because they teach the Dharma without words, they are called a mahāsattva." I wonder if it would be suitable to take what is explicitly taught here as principally a bodhisattva and secondarily a pratyekabuddha; but this should be examined.

སློབ་དཔོན་གྱིས་ཆོས་འཆད་པ་དང་། སློབ་མས་ཚུལ་བཞིན་ཉན་པ་དང་། བཤད་པར་བྱ་བའི་ཆོས་གང་ཡིན་པ་དང་། ཐོས་པའི་དོན་ཚུལ་བཞིན་ཡིད་ལ་བྱས་ཏེ། ལམ་སྒོམ་པས་རྒྱུན་ཞུགས་ལ་སོགས་པའི་ཉན་ཐོས་ཀྱི་འབྲས་བུ་བཞི་ཐོབ་པ་དང༌། དེ་བཞིན་དུ་རྐྱེན་རྒྱལ་སྟེ་རང་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་མཐོང་སྒོམ་མི་སློབ་ལམ་སོགས་ཐོབ་པ་དང༌། དེ་བཞིན་དུ་འཇིག་རྟེན་གསུམ་གྱི་སྐྱབས་དང་དཔུང་གཉེན་མགོན་པ་ོསངས་རྒྱས་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱི་བྱང་ཆུབ་མངོན་དུ་མཛད་པ་དང་། རང་དང་གཞན་གྱི་དོན་སྒྲུབ་པ་ལ་མཁས་པ་ཕུལ་དུ་བྱུང་བའི་ཤེས་རབ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་དང་ལྡན་ཞིང་ལམ་གྱི་ཚུལ་ལ་བློ་གྲོས་གསལ་བས་ཐབས་ཤེས་ཟུང་དུ་འབྲེལ་བར་ཐེག་པ་ཆེན་པོའི་ལམ་བསྒོམས་པའི་སྟོབས་ཀྱིས་ཐོབ་པའི་མཐར་ཐུག་གི་འབྲས་བུ་མི་གནས་པའི་མྱང་ངན་ལས་འདས་པ་གང་ཡིན་པ་དེ་ཀུན་ཀྱང་རྟེན་འབྲེལ་གྱི་གཏན་ཚིགས་སོགས་ཀྱིས་བརྟགས་ཤིང་དཔྱད་ན་བདེན་པར་གྲུབ་པ་ཅུང་ཟད་ཀྱང་མེད་པར་བདེན་པས་སྟོང་པ་སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟ་བུར་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ཡང་དག་པར་རྫོགས་པའི་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱིས་བསྟན་ཏོ། ཡུམ་རྒྱས་པ་ལས། ལྷའི་བུ་དག་ཁོ་བོ་ལས་ཆོས་ཉན་པ་ནི་སྒྱུ་མ་དང་སྤྲུལ་པ་ལྟ་བུར་བལྟ་བར་བྱའོ། །ཞེས་པ་ནས། བདག་ནི་མྱ་ངན་འདས་པ་ལས་ལྷག་པའི་ཆོས་གཞན་ཞིག་ཡོད་ན་དེ་ཡང་སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟ་བུར་བླཏའོ། །ཞེས་དང་། བརྒྱད་སྟོང་པ་ལས་ཀྱང༌། དེ་ནས་ཡང་ལྷའི་བུ་དེ་དག་འདི་སྙམ་དུ་སེམས་ཏེ། འཕགས་པ་རབ་འབྱོར་འདི་ལ་ཆོས་ཉན་པ་རང་བཞིན་ཇི་ལྟ་བུ་ཞིག་བཙལ་བར་བྱ་སྙམ་པ་དང༌། དེ་ནས་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་མཐུས་ཚེ་དང་ལྡན་པ་རབ་འབྱོར་གྱིས་ལྷའི་བུ་དེ་དག་གི་སེམས་ཀྱི་རྟོག་པ་སེམས་ཀྱིས་ཤེས་ནས་ལྷའི་བུ་དེ་དག་ལ་སྨྲས་པ། ལྷའི་བུ་དག་ཁོ་བོ་ལ་ཆོས་ཉན་པ་ནི་སྒྱུ་མ་དང་སྤྲུལ་པ་ལྟ་བུ་དག་ལྟ་བར་བྱའོ། །ཞེས་པ་ནས། ལྷའི་བུ་དག་སེམས་ཅན་ད་ེདག་ནི་སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟ་བུ། ལྷའི་བུ་དག་སེམས་ཅནདེ་དག་ནི་རྨི་ལམ་ལྟ་སྟེ། ནས། ཡང་དག་པར་རྫོགས་པའི་སངས་རྒྱས་ཉིད་སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟ་བུ་དང་རྨི་ལམ་ལྟ་བུའོ། །ནས། མྱ་ངན་ལས་འདས་པ་ཡང་སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟ་བུ་རྨི་ལམ་ལྟ་བུར་ན་ཆོས་གཞན་ལྟ་ཅི་སྨོས། ཞེས་གསུངས། ཇི་སྐད་བཤད་པའི་དོན་དེ་ལ་གང་ཟག་སུ་ཞིག་གུས་ནས་སློབ་ནུས་ཤེ་ན། གང་ཟག་བཞི་པོ་དེ་འདི་དག་ནི་བཤད་མ་ཐག་པའི་གནས་ལུགས་ཀྱི་དོན་ཟབ་མོ་དེ་ལ་མི་སྐྲག་སྟེ་བཞི་པོ་དེ་གང་ཞེ་ན། རྒྱལ་སྲས་བདེན་དོན་ལ་མཁས་པ་རང་རྒྱལ་ཚོགས་སྤྱོད་ཙམ་དང༌། ཕྱིར་མི་ལྡོག་པ་སྦྱོར་ལམ་པ་དང། བཞི་པ་ནི་ལས་དང་པོ་པ་ཡིན་དུ་ཟིན་ཀྱང་སྔོན་གྱི་རྒྱལ་བ་ལ་ལྷག་པར་བྱ་བ་བྱས་པ་སོགས་ཀྱིས་ད་ལྟ་ཤེར་ཕྱིན་གྱི་དོན་ཕྱིན་ཅི་མ་ལོག་པར་སྟོན་པར་ནུས་པའི་དགེ་བའི་བཤེས་གཉེན་གྱིས་ཡོངས་སུ་ཟིན་པའོ། །འདིའི་རྒྱལ་སྲས་བདེན་ལ་མཁས་ཞེས་རང་རྒྱལ་དངོས་གནས་གོ་དགོས་པས་རྟེན་རང་རྒྱལ་དངོས་སུ་བསྟན་པ་ཡིན་ལ། བརྒྱད་སྟོང་སོགས་ལས་དེ་ལྟར་བསྟན་ཅིང་རང་རྒྱལ་ལ་རྒྱལ་སྲས་སམ་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཞེས་གསུངས་པ་ནི། རང་དོན་དུ་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཐོབ་པས་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་དང༌། སྒྲ་མེད་པར་ཆོས་སྟོན་པས་སེམས་དཔའ་ཆེན་པོ་ཞེས་བཤད་པ་ཡིན་ཞེས་ཕར་ཕྱིན་ཟབ་བཤད་ལས་གསུངས། Incidental Topic. Second, incidentally demonstrating that all activities from teaching and listening to the Dharma up to attaining the fruit by meditating are empty of true existence, like an illusion: The meaning taught by the three verses starting with "Teaching the Dharma..." is that the teacher teaching the Dharma, the student properly listening, the Dharma to be taught, and having properly taken to mind the meaning heard, meditating on the path and thereby attaining the four fruits of a Hearer, such as Stream Enterer; and similarly, attaining the path of seeing, path of meditation, and path of no-more-learning, etc., of a pratyekabuddha, that is, a solitary realizer; and similarly, actualizing the awakening of a Buddha, a Bhagavan, the protector, refuge, and ally of the three worlds; and whatever is the ultimate fruit, the non-abiding nirvana, attained by the power of meditating on the Mahayana path with the union of method and wisdom by someone endowed with the excellent, supreme wisdom skilled in accomplishing their own and others' purpose and with clear intelligence regarding the methods of the path - all these, when examined and analyzed by means of the reasoning of dependent origination and so forth, do not have even the slightest true establishment and were taught by the Tathagata, the perfectly complete Buddha, to be empty of true existence, like an illusion. From the Extensive Mother [the Prajñāpāramitā in 100,000 lines]: "Sons of the gods, listening to the Dharma from me is to be seen as like an illusion and like an emanation." Up to: "If there were any other dharma superior to nirvana, I would see that too as like an illusion." And from the Eight Thousand Line [Prajñāpāramitā]: Then, those sons of the gods thought this: "What is the nature of those who seek to listen to the Dharma from the Noble Subhūti?" And then, by the Buddha's power, venerable Subhūti knew with his mind the thoughts in the minds of those sons of the gods, and said to those sons of the gods: "Sons of the gods, listening to the Dharma from me is to be seen as like an illusion and like an emanation." Up to: "Sons of the gods, those sentient beings are like an illusion. Sons of the gods, those sentient beings are like a dream." Up to: "The perfectly complete Buddha himself is like an illusion and like a dream." Up to: "If even nirvana is like an illusion and like a dream, what need is there to speak of other dharmas?" If one asks what kind of person can respectfully train in the meaning explained in that way: These four persons are not frightened of the profound meaning of the abiding nature that has just been explained. If one asks who these four are: A "Child of the Victor skilled in the truth"—merely a pratyekabuddha on the paths of accumulation and preparation; an "irreversible one"—one on the path of preparation; an arhat, a noble one who has dispelled and exhausted the stains of the mind such as the afflictive obscurations and has abandoned doubt regarding the profound meaning of the abiding nature; those three, and fourthly, one who, although a beginner, has rendered special service to the Victors of the past and so forth, and is now fully embraced by a spiritual friend capable of teaching the meaning of the perfection of wisdom unmistakably. Here, because "Child of the Victor skilled in the truth" must be understood as an actual pratyekabuddha, the support is taught as being an actual pratyekabuddha; and texts such as the Eight Thousand Line teach it in that way. The reason why a pratyekabuddha is called a "Child of the Victor" or a "bodhisattva" is explained in the Profound Explanation of the Perfection of Wisdom [by Haribhadra]: "Because they attain awakening for their own sake, they are a bodhisattva, and because they teach the Dharma without words, they are called a mahāsattva." I wonder if it would be suitable to take what is explicitly taught here as principally a bodhisattva and secondarily a pratyekabuddha; but this should be examined.

heading: **དངོས།**
translation: Actual [meaning]. First: It is taught by the two verses starting with "Form is not wisdom..." The meaning: If one asks what that perfection of wisdom which is the nature of the path of seeing is like: Form is not one with the perfection of wisdom which is the subject that realizes its mode of existence, because they are different. Also, the perfection of wisdom which is its subject does not exist in form as a different entity or as abiding differently ultimately, because it is not apprehended as such. Similarly, the aggregate of consciousness, and these aggregates of discrimination, feeling, volition, and compositional factors are not one with wisdom, nor does the perfection of wisdom which is the subject exist in them in the manner of a different entity, because ultimately they are not established as one, different, or as object and subject. This dharmadhātu, which is the object of observation of the Mahayana path of seeing's exalted wisdom of meditative equipoise, is a non-affirming negation devoid of all conventional signs and elaborations of dualistic appearance before the perception of that non-conceptual exalted wisdom of meditative equipoise; such suchness is, for example, similar to how the spatial element is designated upon the mere aspect of negating obstruction and contact, because there is not even a particle of dualistic phenomena such as one and different.

Since that path-knowledge of a pratyekabuddha also does not arise without causes and conditions, its cause, the aids to penetration: The meaning taught by the one verse starting with "[When] form increases..." is: Regarding what does a bodhisattva not train and instead discard? They do not train in order to fully apprehend by clinging to ultimate increasing or completely diminishing—that is, decreasing—and to true existence regarding all dharmas on the side of total affliction, such as form, and all dharmas of complete purification, such as the placements of mindfulness. This is because, since all these dharmas are naturally pure, ultimate increasing and decreasing, arising and ceasing, and so forth are not apprehended. They do not train through application in order to completely apprehend through manifest clinging to, or to generate within their own mindstream, any of the various aspects of dharmas from form up to the knowledge of all aspects, but rather they train by way of not apprehending the aids to penetration and so forth; and for the sake of others, by knowing that even the knowledge of all aspects itself lacks a nature, they conventionally fully apprehend it and attain it; and whatever definite emergence—that is, attainment—in that ultimate state of a Buddha there is in dependence upon having practiced the path through the union of method and wisdom, this is the manner in which bodhisattvas who delight in the qualities of the Mahayana train in the path.

heading: **དངོས།**
translation: As it is also said regarding the statement in the Mother Sūtra, "The perfection of wisdom is to be sought from the chapter of Subhūti": "Kauśika, the perfection of wisdom is not to be sought from form; it is not to be sought elsewhere than form. This is because those dharmas have a single characteristic, which is to say, they have no characteristic," and so forth. This verse specifically highlights and teaches the aspect of the truth of suffering from among the four truths, and the general teaching of the aspects of the four truths is: Among the sixteen objects of observation of the Mahayana path of seeing, such as impermanence, the nature or essence of the truths of suffering is the dharmadhātu empty of being established as a self of phenomena and persons, which is boundless because it is devoid of a beginning and an end and is not divided into directions or categories; and whatever is the nature of the truth of origin—the causes that generate the aggregates and so forth of sentient beings—is also boundless because it is equal in being the dharmadhātu empty of true existence; and just as the spatial element is posited upon the mere negation of obstruction and contact, the nature of the truth of cessation, the dharmadhātu in which obscurations are exhausted, is also boundless.

Since that path-knowledge of a pratyekabuddha also does not arise without causes and conditions, its cause, the aids to penetration: The meaning taught by the one verse starting with "[When] form increases..." is: Regarding what does a bodhisattva not train and instead discard? They do not train in order to fully apprehend by clinging to ultimate increasing or completely diminishing—that is, decreasing—and to true existence regarding all dharmas on the side of total affliction, such as form, and all dharmas of complete purification, such as the placements of mindfulness. This is because, since all these dharmas are naturally pure, ultimate increasing and decreasing, arising and ceasing, and so forth are not apprehended. They do not train through application in order to completely apprehend through manifest clinging to, or to generate within their own mindstream, any of the various aspects of dharmas from form up to the knowledge of all aspects, but rather they train by way of not apprehending the aids to penetration and so forth; and for the sake of others, by knowing that even the knowledge of all aspects itself lacks a nature, they conventionally fully apprehend it and attain it; and whatever definite emergence—that is, attainment—in that ultimate state of a Buddha there is in dependence upon having practiced the path through the union of method and wisdom, this is the manner in which bodhisattvas who delight in the qualities of the Mahayana train in the path.

translation: Therefore, those bodhisattvas on the path of seeing who attain such a view devoid of all discriminative awarenesses that grasp at true existence abide in the word of the Teacher that teaches prophecies by Buddhas saying, "In this life they are irreversible and remember their future births, and having gone to the perfection of the grounds and paths, they will become perfectly awakened as a Buddha named such-and-such," and so forth. If one says, "Because meditating on the path and so forth exist, establishment by nature exists": Even if the Sugata, the Teacher who has become a valid cognition, were to reside for eons equal to the sand grains of the river Ganges and fully proclaim the sound, "Sentient beings exist," how could sentient beings ultimately exist or be born by nature? They would not, because from the very beginning they are unborn by nature and completely pure without defilements entering their nature. Therefore, directly realizing this meaning of not being born by nature is engaging in the supreme perfection of wisdom, which has become the essence of the path of seeing.

Actual [meaning]. First: It is taught by the two verses starting with "Form is not wisdom..." The meaning: If one asks what that perfection of wisdom which is the nature of the path of seeing is like: Form is not one with the perfection of wisdom which is the subject that realizes its mode of existence, because they are different. Also, the perfection of wisdom which is its subject does not exist in form as a different entity or as abiding differently ultimately, because it is not apprehended as such. Similarly, the aggregate of consciousness, and these aggregates of discrimination, feeling, volition, and compositional factors are not one with wisdom, nor does the perfection of wisdom which is the subject exist in them in the manner of a different entity, because ultimately they are not established as one, different, or as object and subject. This dharmadhātu, which is the object of observation of the Mahayana path of seeing's exalted wisdom of meditative equipoise, is a non-affirming negation devoid of all conventional signs and elaborations of dualistic appearance before the perception of that non-conceptual exalted wisdom of meditative equipoise; such suchness is, for example, similar to how the spatial element is designated upon the mere aspect of negating obstruction and contact, because there is not even a particle of dualistic phenomena such as one and different.

As it is also said regarding the statement in the Mother Sūtra, "The perfection of wisdom is to be sought from the chapter of Subhūti": "Kauśika, the perfection of wisdom is not to be sought from form; it is not to be sought elsewhere than form. This is because those dharmas have a single characteristic, which is to say, they have no characteristic," and so forth. This verse specifically highlights and teaches the aspect of the truth of suffering from among the four truths, and the general teaching of the aspects of the four truths is: Among the sixteen objects of observation of the Mahayana path of seeing, such as impermanence, the nature or essence of the truths of suffering is the dharmadhātu empty of being established as a self of phenomena and persons, which is boundless because it is devoid of a beginning and an end and is not divided into directions or categories; and whatever is the nature of the truth of origin—the causes that generate the aggregates and so forth of sentient beings—is also boundless because it is equal in being the dharmadhātu empty of true existence; and just as the spatial element is posited upon the mere negation of obstruction and contact, the nature of the truth of cessation, the dharmadhātu in which obscurations are exhausted, is also boundless.

heading: **འཕྲོས་དོན།**
translation: To teach by way of an example that meditating on the path of seeing will attain the prophecy by the Tathāgata: The Victorious One, the Lion of the Śākyas himself, who was victorious over the enemies of the four māras, spoke thus: "At whatever time I, the Teacher Śākyamuni, came to speak in accordance with this supreme perfection of wisdom which is the essence of the path of seeing, at that time the former supreme being Dīpaṃkara prophesied me, saying, 'You, brahmin boy, will become a Buddha in future times.'" Therefore, having understood that it is implicitly taught that the trainees of future generations will also abide in this perfection of wisdom, be prophesied by Buddhas, and become completely and perfectly awakened, one should rely on exertion in practicing the Mahayana path like the continuous flow of a river. This completes the commentary on the second chapter, the chapter of Śakra, from the Commentary on the Verses of the Precious Qualities Collection, Clarifying the Suchness of Profound Dependent Arising, the Jewel Lamp Fulfilling the Hopes of the Fortunate.

Actual [meaning]. First: It is taught by the two verses starting with "Form is not wisdom..." The meaning: If one asks what that perfection of wisdom which is the nature of the path of seeing is like: Form is not one with the perfection of wisdom which is the subject that realizes its mode of existence, because they are different. Also, the perfection of wisdom which is its subject does not exist in form as a different entity or as abiding differently ultimately, because it is not apprehended as such. Similarly, the aggregate of consciousness, and these aggregates of discrimination, feeling, volition, and compositional factors are not one with wisdom, nor does the perfection of wisdom which is the subject exist in them in the manner of a different entity, because ultimately they are not established as one, different, or as object and subject. This dharmadhātu, which is the object of observation of the Mahayana path of seeing's exalted wisdom of meditative equipoise, is a non-affirming negation devoid of all conventional signs and elaborations of dualistic appearance before the perception of that non-conceptual exalted wisdom of meditative equipoise; such suchness is, for example, similar to how the spatial element is designated upon the mere aspect of negating obstruction and contact, because there is not even a particle of dualistic phenomena such as one and different.

This verse specifically highlights and teaches the aspect of the truth of suffering from among the four truths, and the general teaching of the aspects of the four truths is: Among the sixteen objects of observation of the Mahayana path of seeing, such as impermanence, the nature or essence of the truths of suffering is the dharmadhātu empty of being established as a self of phenomena and persons, which is boundless because it is devoid of a beginning and an end and is not divided into directions or categories; and whatever is the nature of the truth of origin—the causes that generate the aggregates and so forth of sentient beings—is also boundless because it is equal in being the dharmadhātu empty of true existence; and just as the spatial element is posited upon the mere negation of obstruction and contact, the nature of the truth of cessation, the dharmadhātu in which obscurations are exhausted, is also boundless.

Actual [meaning]. First: It is taught by the two verses starting with "Form is not wisdom..." The meaning: If one asks what that perfection of wisdom which is the nature of the path of seeing is like: Form is not one with the perfection of wisdom which is the subject that realizes its mode of existence, because they are different. Also, the perfection of wisdom which is its subject does not exist in form as a different entity or as abiding differently ultimately, because it is not apprehended as such. Similarly, the aggregate of consciousness, and these aggregates of discrimination, feeling, volition, and compositional factors are not one with wisdom, nor does the perfection of wisdom which is the subject exist in them in the manner of a different entity, because ultimately they are not established as one, different, or as object and subject. Actual [meaning]. First: It is taught by the two verses starting with "Form is not wisdom..." The meaning: If one asks what that perfection of wisdom which is the nature of the path of seeing is like: Form is not one with the perfection of wisdom which is the subject that realizes its mode of existence, because they are different. Also, the perfection of wisdom which is its subject does not exist in form as a different entity or as abiding differently ultimately, because it is not apprehended as such. Similarly, the aggregate of consciousness, and these aggregates of discrimination, feeling, volition, and compositional factors are not one with wisdom, nor does the perfection of wisdom which is the subject exist in them in the manner of a different entity, because ultimately they are not established as one, different, or as object and subject. This dharmadhātu, which is the object of observation of the Mahayana path of seeing's exalted wisdom of meditative equipoise, is a non-affirming negation devoid of all conventional signs and elaborations of dualistic appearance before the perception of that non-conceptual exalted wisdom of meditative equipoise; such suchness is, for example, similar to how the spatial element is designated upon the mere aspect of negating obstruction and contact, because there is not even a particle of dualistic phenomena such as one and different.

As it is also said regarding the statement in the Mother Sūtra, "The perfection of wisdom is to be sought from the chapter of Subhūti": "Kauśika, the perfection of wisdom is not to be sought from form; it is not to be sought elsewhere than form. This is because those dharmas have a single characteristic, which is to say, they have no characteristic," and so forth. This verse specifically highlights and teaches the aspect of the truth of suffering from among the four truths, and the general teaching of the aspects of the four truths is: Among the sixteen objects of observation of the Mahayana path of seeing, such as impermanence, the nature or essence of the truths of suffering is the dharmadhātu empty of being established as a self of phenomena and persons, which is boundless because it is devoid of a beginning and an end and is not divided into directions or categories; and whatever is the nature of the truth of origin—the causes that generate the aggregates and so forth of sentient beings—is also boundless because it is equal in being the dharmadhātu empty of true existence; and just as the spatial element is posited upon the mere negation of obstruction and contact, the nature of the truth of cessation, the dharmadhātu in which obscurations are exhausted, is also boundless.

Second, the supplementary meaning: If one asks why all functional things are said to be empty of true existence: Because all dharmas are nothing but mere nominal designations, those who go to the perfection of excellent view must meditate by breaking apart the discriminative awareness that clings to true existence; in order to teach this, it is stated: "Because of perceiving all dharmas as a self, one is left behind here in this place of cyclic existence on the near shore"—thus it was fully proclaimed and spoken by the Guide, the perfectly and fully awakened Buddha; and by breaking apart the discriminative awareness of grasping at a self through individually analyzing wisdom, the uninterrupted path of the path of seeing that directly realizes the lack of true existence acts as the actual antidote to all those [afflictions] to be abandoned by seeing, without exception, and the path of liberation completely abandons them, thereby going to the perfection of excellent abandonment.

translation: Divisions. Second, if that is divided, there are six: the function of having mastered the mind and completely pacifying pride and so forth; the function of apprehending all sentient beings as spiritual friends and respecting and bowing to them; the function of being victorious over afflictions such as the three poisons; the function of not being subdued by the harm of humans and non-humans; the function of accomplishing perfectly complete awakening; and the function of the place where the support, the bodhisattva on the path of meditation, resides also becoming an object of homage and worship by all beings.

[3-87] translation already produced for this document:
Actual [meaning]. First: It is taught by the two verses starting with "Form is not wisdom..." The meaning: If one asks what that perfection of wisdom which is the nature of the path of seeing is like: Form is not one with the perfection of wisdom which is the subject that realizes its mode of existence, because they are different. Also, the perfection of wisdom which is its subject does not exist in form as a different entity or as abiding differently ultimately, because it is not apprehended as such. Similarly, the aggregate of consciousness, and these aggregates of discrimination, feeling, volition, and compositional factors are not one with wisdom, nor does the perfection of wisdom which is the subject exist in them in the manner of a different entity, because ultimately they are not established as one, different, or as object and subject. This dharmadhātu, which is the object of observation of the Mahayana path of seeing's exalted wisdom of meditative equipoise, is a non-affirming negation devoid of all conventional signs and elaborations of dualistic appearance before the perception of that non-conceptual exalted wisdom of meditative equipoise; such suchness is, for example, similar to how the spatial element is designated upon the mere aspect of negating obstruction and contact, because there is not even a particle of dualistic phenomena such as one and different.

[3-88] translation already produced for this document:
As it is also said regarding the statement in the Mother Sūtra, "The perfection of wisdom is to be sought from the chapter of Subhūti": "Kauśika, the perfection of wisdom is not to be sought from form; it is not to be sought elsewhere than form. This is because those dharmas have a single characteristic, which is to say, they have no characteristic," and so forth. This verse specifically highlights and teaches the aspect of the truth of suffering from among the four truths, and the general teaching of the aspects of the four truths is: Among the sixteen objects of observation of the Mahayana path of seeing, such as impermanence, the nature or essence of the truths of suffering is the dharmadhātu empty of being established as a self of phenomena and persons, which is boundless because it is devoid of a beginning and an end and is not divided into directions or categories; and whatever is the nature of the truth of origin—the causes that generate the aggregates and so forth of sentient beings—is also boundless because it is equal in being the dharmadhātu empty of true existence; and just as the spatial element is posited upon the mere negation of obstruction and contact, the nature of the truth of cessation, the dharmadhātu in which obscurations are exhausted, is also boundless.

Second, the supplementary meaning: If one asks why all functional things are said to be empty of true existence: Because all dharmas are nothing but mere nominal designations, those who go to the perfection of excellent view must meditate by breaking apart the discriminative awareness that clings to true existence; in order to teach this, it is stated: "Because of perceiving all dharmas as a self, one is left behind here in this place of cyclic existence on the near shore"—thus it was fully proclaimed and spoken by the Guide, the perfectly and fully awakened Buddha; and by breaking apart the discriminative awareness of grasping at a self through individually analyzing wisdom, the uninterrupted path of the path of seeing that directly realizes the lack of true existence acts as the actual antidote to all those [afflictions] to be abandoned by seeing, without exception, and the path of liberation completely abandons them, thereby going to the perfection of excellent abandonment.
