The qualities of the training. Third, regarding the qualities of the training, the Ornament states: "Crushing the power of maras and so forth, / Are the fourteen aspects of qualities." The definition of a quality of a Mahayana training is: the benefit obtained by the power of meditating on a Mahayana training that serves as the method to obtain it. When divided, there are fourteen: the quality of crushing the power of maras by the power of meditating on the training, the quality of the Buddhas considering and knowing one, the quality of the Buddhas actualising one, the quality of becoming close to perfect awakening, the quality of great benefit and so forth, the quality of experiencing the object, the quality of completing all uncontaminated qualities, the quality of becoming an eloquent being, the quality of not being divided by discordant sides, the quality of generating uncommon roots of virtue, the quality of accomplishing the meaning of what was promised, the quality of thoroughly holding a vast result, the quality of accomplishing the benefit of sentient beings, and the quality of definitely attaining the Mother. The boundary of its levels is from the Mahayana path of accumulation up to the level of a Buddha. In order to generally teach those qualities, the meaning of the verse spoken starting with "Whoever engages here..." is: Whatever bodhisattva meditating on the two selflessnesses properly practices and engages here in this Mahayana training does not conceptualise by adhering as truly existent to such and such Buddha dharmas, such as the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and so forth; similarly, they do not conceptually apprehend as truly existent the path, the five faculties, powers, bases of miraculous power, close placements of mindfulness, seven branches of awakening, and so forth, and the result, nirvana, supreme peaceful awakening, nor do they conceptually apprehend the dharmas of the aggregates, elements, and sense sources, but rather, engaging in this Mahayana training that generates qualities such as crushing the power of maras through the blessings of the Buddhas in suchness free from elaborations, which is devoid of all conceptions of dualistic appearance, is engaging in the non-conceptual exalted wisdom of the supreme perfection of wisdom that has become the essence of all aspects. The Eight Thousand Line [Perfection of Wisdom] states: "The venerable Subhūti said this to the Bhagavān: 'Bhagavān, holding the perfection of wisdom...' and so forth." This is the commentary on the tenth chapter, Thoroughly Expressing the Qualities of Holding, from the Commentary on the Verse Summary of the Precious Qualities: The Jewel Lamp Fulfilling the Hopes of the Fortunate, Illuminating the Suchness of Profound Dependent Arising.

heading: **ལན།**
translation: Moreover, out of the forty-six faults of the training, there are eight actually taught here. The first of these is the instability of being proud of overly swift eloquence and turning back midway. The meaning of the occurrence of one verse starting with "By the Victor..." is: When one writes, holds, reads, explains, and listens to this perfection of wisdom, the Mother of the Victors of the three times, various uncertain and different instances of eloquence conceptualising objects such as forms and sounds, and many aspects such as excitement, dullness, sleep, regret, attachment, and hostility will arise; and due to this, without having accomplished one's own benefit of realizing the meaning of the perfection of wisdom and so forth and the benefit of other beings, activities like writing, reading, explaining, and listening will swiftly vanish like a flash of lightning, interrupting one's effort, so that one thoroughly falls away from the training; this should be known as the action of a mara. To teach apprehending the reason for turning away from the Mahayana pitaka and abandoning it, that is, the actual cause of abandoning, one verse starting with "When this is explained..." is spoken. When this sutra is explained, some will have doubt and hesitation about it, and will think: "In this Mother sutra, the Guide has not thoroughly expressed and not taught even my name, and has not thoroughly expressed my family, the places where I abide, or my clan," and, because they have not been clearly prophesied, they will think, "Therefore, what is the use of listening to this? It is not the speech of the omniscient one." By apprehending the reason for turning away from the Mother, with that erroneous mind they will not listen to that profound dharma and will abandon it; this is the action of a mara.

To explain the training of not seeing dharma and non-dharma and so forth, the meaning of the occurrence of the two lines starting with "Whatever dharma..." is: "Even if whatever bodhisattva does not ultimately see virtuous dharmas, non-virtuous non-dharmas, and the way dharmas abide, suchness, the dharmadhatu, and abides in suchness free from elaborations in which all referents of apprehending signs are thoroughly pacified, they do not touch—that is, they do not abide in—the nirvana of mere one-sided peace, and that awakening is an abiding in supreme wisdom that has passed beyond the two extremes of existence and peace."

སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱིས་དགོངས་ཤིང་མཁྱེན་པའི་ཡོན་ཏན། སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱིས་མངོན་སུམ་དུ་མཛད་པའི་ཡོན་ཏན། རྫོགས་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་དང་ཉེ་བར་འགྱུར་བའི་ཡོན་ཏན། དོན་ཆེ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པའི་ཡོན་ཏན། ཡུལ་སྤྱད་པའི་ཡོན་ཏན། ཟག་མེད་ཀྱི་ཡོན་ཏན་ཐམས་ཅད་རྫོགས་པའི་ཡོན་ཏན། སྨྲ་བའི་སྐྱེས་བུ་ཉིད་དུ་འགྱུར་བའི་ཡོན་ཏན། མི་མཐུན་ཕྱོགས་ཀྱིས་མི་ཕྱེད་པའི་ཡོན་ཏན། དགེ་བའི་རྩ་བ་ཐུན་མོང་མ་ཡིན་པ་སྐྱེ་བའི་ཡོན་ཏན། དམ་བཅས་པའི་དོན་འགྲུབ་པའི་ཡོན་ཏན། འབྲས་བུ་རྒྱ་ཆེན་པོ་ཡོངས་སུ་འཛིན་པའི་ཡོན་ཏན། སེམས་ཅན་གྱི་དོན་གྲུབ་པའི་ཡོན་ཏན། ཡུམ་ངེས་པར་ཐོབ་པའི་ཡོན་ཏན་དང་བཅུ་བཞི་ཡོད། ས་མཚམས་ཐེག་ཆེན་གྱི་ཚོགས་ལམ་ནས་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱིས་སའི་བར་ན་ཡོད། ཡོན་ཏན་དེ་རྣམས་སྤྱིར་སྟོན་པར། གང་ཞིག་འདིར་སྤྱོད་ཅེས་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གསུངས་པའི་དོན་ནི། བདག་མེད་གཉིས་བསྒོམ་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གང་ཞིག་ཐེག་ཆེེན་གྱི་སྦྱོར་བ་འདིར་ཚུལ་བཞིན་ཉམས་སུ་ལེན་ཅིང་སྤྱོད་པ་དེ་ནི་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་ཆོས་སྟོབས་བཅུ་དང་མི་འཇིགས་པ་བཞི་ལ་སོགས་པ་རྣམས་ལ་དེ་དང་དེར་བདེན་པར་མངོན་པར་ཞེན་ནས་མི་རྟོག་སྟེ། དེ་བཞིན་དུ་ལམ་དང་སོགས་དབང་པོ་ལྔ་དང་སྟོབས་དང་རྫུ་འཕྲུལ་གྱི་རྐང་པ་དང་དྲན་པ་ཉེར་བཞག་དང་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཀྱི་ཡན་ལག་བདུན་པ་སོགས་དང་། འབྲས་བུ་མྱ་ངན་ལས་འདས་པ་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཞི་བ་མཆོག་ལ་ཡང་བདེན་པར་རྣམ་པར་མི་རྟོག་ལ། ཕུང་ཁམས་སྐྱེ་མཆེད་ཀྱི་ཆོས་ལའང་རྣམ་པར་མི་རྟོག་པར་གཉིས་སྣང་གི་རྟོག་པ་ཐམས་ཅད་དང་བྲལ་བའི་སྤྲོས་བྲལ་དེ་བཞིིན་ཉིད་ལ་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་བྱིན་གྱིས་རླབས་ཀྱིས་བདུད་ཀྱི་མཐུ་བཅོམ་པ་ལ་སོགས་པའི་ཡོན་ཏན་བསྐྱེད་པའི་ཐེག་ཆེན་གྱི་སྦྱོར་བ་ལ་སྤྱོད་པ་འདི་ནི་རྣམ་ཀུན་གྱི་ངོ་བོར་གྱུར་པའི་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་མཆོག་རྣམ་པར་མི་རྟོག་པའི་ཡེ་ཤེས་ལ་སྤྱོད་པ་ཡིན་ནོ་ཞེས་པའོ། The qualities of the training. Third, regarding the qualities of the training, the Ornament states: "Crushing the power of maras and so forth, / Are the fourteen aspects of qualities." The definition of a quality of a Mahayana training is: the benefit obtained by the power of meditating on a Mahayana training that serves as the method to obtain it. When divided, there are fourteen: the quality of crushing the power of maras by the power of meditating on the training, the quality of the Buddhas considering and knowing one, the quality of the Buddhas actualising one, the quality of becoming close to perfect awakening, the quality of great benefit and so forth, the quality of experiencing the object, the quality of completing all uncontaminated qualities, the quality of becoming an eloquent being, the quality of not being divided by discordant sides, the quality of generating uncommon roots of virtue, the quality of accomplishing the meaning of what was promised, the quality of thoroughly holding a vast result, the quality of accomplishing the benefit of sentient beings, and the quality of definitely attaining the Mother. The boundary of its levels is from the Mahayana path of accumulation up to the level of a Buddha. In order to generally teach those qualities, the meaning of the verse spoken starting with "Whoever engages here..." is: Whatever bodhisattva meditating on the two selflessnesses properly practices and engages here in this Mahayana training does not conceptualise by adhering as truly existent to such and such Buddha dharmas, such as the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and so forth; similarly, they do not conceptually apprehend as truly existent the path, the five faculties, powers, bases of miraculous power, close placements of mindfulness, seven branches of awakening, and so forth, and the result, nirvana, supreme peaceful awakening, nor do they conceptually apprehend the dharmas of the aggregates, elements, and sense sources, but rather, engaging in this Mahayana training that generates qualities such as crushing the power of maras through the blessings of the Buddhas in suchness free from elaborations, which is devoid of all conceptions of dualistic appearance, is engaging in the non-conceptual exalted wisdom of the supreme perfection of wisdom that has become the essence of all aspects. The Eight Thousand Line [Perfection of Wisdom] states: "The venerable Subhūti said this to the Bhagavān: 'Bhagavān, holding the perfection of wisdom...' and so forth." This is the commentary on the tenth chapter, Thoroughly Expressing the Qualities of Holding, from the Commentary on the Verse Summary of the Precious Qualities: The Jewel Lamp Fulfilling the Hopes of the Fortunate, Illuminating the Suchness of Profound Dependent Arising.

translation: Regarding the falling away of adhering to the reason, that is, the falling away of apprehending excessively, the meaning of the occurrence of the two lines starting with "Thus not knowing..." is: Thus, the perfection of wisdom is the root of the Mahayana path. Those ignorant, bewildered persons who are blessed by maras, having forsaken this precious sutra of the perfection of wisdom which is like the root of a Buddha, will seek out the śrāvaka piṭaka which is like branches and leaves, because they are obscured by bewilderment; this too is the action of a mara.

To explain the training of not seeing dharma and non-dharma and so forth, the meaning of the occurrence of the two lines starting with "Whatever dharma..." is: "Even if whatever bodhisattva does not ultimately see virtuous dharmas, non-virtuous non-dharmas, and the way dharmas abide, suchness, the dharmadhatu, and abides in suchness free from elaborations in which all referents of apprehending signs are thoroughly pacified, they do not touch—that is, they do not abide in—the nirvana of mere one-sided peace, and that awakening is an abiding in supreme wisdom that has passed beyond the two extremes of existence and peace."

The qualities of the training. Third, regarding the qualities of the training, the Ornament states: "Crushing the power of maras and so forth, / Are the fourteen aspects of qualities." The definition of a quality of a Mahayana training is: the benefit obtained by the power of meditating on a Mahayana training that serves as the method to obtain it. When divided, there are fourteen: the quality of crushing the power of maras by the power of meditating on the training, the quality of the Buddhas considering and knowing one, the quality of the Buddhas actualising one, the quality of becoming close to perfect awakening, the quality of great benefit and so forth, the quality of experiencing the object, the quality of completing all uncontaminated qualities, the quality of becoming an eloquent being, the quality of not being divided by discordant sides, the quality of generating uncommon roots of virtue, the quality of accomplishing the meaning of what was promised, the quality of thoroughly holding a vast result, the quality of accomplishing the benefit of sentient beings, and the quality of definitely attaining the Mother. The boundary of its levels is from the Mahayana path of accumulation up to the level of a Buddha. In order to generally teach those qualities, the meaning of the verse spoken starting with "Whoever engages here..." is: Whatever bodhisattva meditating on the two selflessnesses properly practices and engages here in this Mahayana training does not conceptualise by adhering as truly existent to such and such Buddha dharmas, such as the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and so forth; similarly, they do not conceptually apprehend as truly existent the path, the five faculties, powers, bases of miraculous power, close placements of mindfulness, seven branches of awakening, and so forth, and the result, nirvana, supreme peaceful awakening, nor do they conceptually apprehend the dharmas of the aggregates, elements, and sense sources, but rather, engaging in this Mahayana training that generates qualities such as crushing the power of maras through the blessings of the Buddhas in suchness free from elaborations, which is devoid of all conceptions of dualistic appearance, is engaging in the non-conceptual exalted wisdom of the supreme perfection of wisdom that has become the essence of all aspects. The Eight Thousand Line [Perfection of Wisdom] states: "The venerable Subhūti said this to the Bhagavān: 'Bhagavān, holding the perfection of wisdom...' and so forth." This is the commentary on the tenth chapter, Thoroughly Expressing the Qualities of Holding, from the Commentary on the Verse Summary of the Precious Qualities: The Jewel Lamp Fulfilling the Hopes of the Fortunate, Illuminating the Suchness of Profound Dependent Arising.

translation: Regarding the falling away from apprehending the supreme vehicle in all aspects, the meaning of the occurrence of the two lines starting with "Even finding an elephant..." is: How is it? Just as a person seeking an elephant, even though they find the actual elephant, leaves it and seeks the elephant's footprints, having heard the perfection of wisdom that teaches means and wisdom completely, one discards practicing it earnestly. Seeking the meaning of sutras of provisional meaning other than that should be known as being like what is taught by the example, so this too is the action of a mara.

The faults of the training. Fourth, to teach the faults of the training, the Ornament states: "The faults, forty-six in number, / Should be understood with certainty." The definition of a fault of the training is: that demonic action which causes an obstacle to either the generation, the abiding, or the completion of the training. When divided, there are forty-six, from "obtaining with great difficulty" up to "generating joy not in accordance with the object". This is because there are twenty-three discordant conditions for generating the ungenerated training and twenty-three incomplete concordant conditions. The boundary of its levels is from before entering the path up to the seventh level. Since they are taught extensively in the Eight Thousand Line and so forth, there are correlations with the sutra for each one, but in this Summary, they are correlated with only about seven or eight. In this there are also two parts: explaining the faults to be eliminated, and explaining the antidotes that eliminate them.

Moreover, out of the forty-six faults of the training, there are eight actually taught here. The first of these is the instability of being proud of overly swift eloquence and turning back midway. The meaning of the occurrence of one verse starting with "By the Victor..." is: When one writes, holds, reads, explains, and listens to this perfection of wisdom, the Mother of the Victors of the three times, various uncertain and different instances of eloquence conceptualising objects such as forms and sounds, and many aspects such as excitement, dullness, sleep, regret, attachment, and hostility will arise; and due to this, without having accomplished one's own benefit of realizing the meaning of the perfection of wisdom and so forth and the benefit of other beings, activities like writing, reading, explaining, and listening will swiftly vanish like a flash of lightning, interrupting one's effort, so that one thoroughly falls away from the training; this should be known as the action of a mara. To teach apprehending the reason for turning away from the Mahayana pitaka and abandoning it, that is, the actual cause of abandoning, one verse starting with "When this is explained..." is spoken. When this sutra is explained, some will have doubt and hesitation about it, and will think: "In this Mother sutra, the Guide has not thoroughly expressed and not taught even my name, and has not thoroughly expressed my family, the places where I abide, or my clan," and, because they have not been clearly prophesied, they will think, "Therefore, what is the use of listening to this? It is not the speech of the omniscient one." By apprehending the reason for turning away from the Mother, with that erroneous mind they will not listen to that profound dharma and will abandon it; this is the action of a mara.

Regarding the falling away of adhering to the reason, that is, the falling away of apprehending excessively, the meaning of the occurrence of the two lines starting with "Thus not knowing..." is: Thus, the perfection of wisdom is the root of the Mahayana path. Those ignorant, bewildered persons who are blessed by maras, having forsaken this precious sutra of the perfection of wisdom which is like the root of a Buddha, will seek out the śrāvaka piṭaka which is like branches and leaves, because they are obscured by bewilderment; this too is the action of a mara.

translation: Regarding the falling away from experiencing the joy of the supreme fruit, the excellent taste, the meaning of the occurrence of one verse starting with "For example, someone [finding food with] a hundred tastes..." is: For example, just as someone having found food possessing a hundred tastes does not experience its taste, but having found supreme food seeks out inferior food such as sixty-day rice, whichever beginner bodhisattva, having found this profound sutra of the perfection of wisdom, does not accomplish the enlightenment of a Buddha, but seeks unsurpassable enlightenment relying upon texts that teach the path that brings about the attainment of the level of śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha arhats is like that above example; this too is the action of a mara.

The faults of the training. Fourth, to teach the faults of the training, the Ornament states: "The faults, forty-six in number, / Should be understood with certainty." The definition of a fault of the training is: that demonic action which causes an obstacle to either the generation, the abiding, or the completion of the training. When divided, there are forty-six, from "obtaining with great difficulty" up to "generating joy not in accordance with the object". This is because there are twenty-three discordant conditions for generating the ungenerated training and twenty-three incomplete concordant conditions. The boundary of its levels is from before entering the path up to the seventh level. Since they are taught extensively in the Eight Thousand Line and so forth, there are correlations with the sutra for each one, but in this Summary, they are correlated with only about seven or eight. In this there are also two parts: explaining the faults to be eliminated, and explaining the antidotes that eliminate them.

[3-169] translation already produced for this document:
Moreover, out of the forty-six faults of the training, there are eight actually taught here. The first of these is the instability of being proud of overly swift eloquence and turning back midway. The meaning of the occurrence of one verse starting with "By the Victor..." is: When one writes, holds, reads, explains, and listens to this perfection of wisdom, the Mother of the Victors of the three times, various uncertain and different instances of eloquence conceptualising objects such as forms and sounds, and many aspects such as excitement, dullness, sleep, regret, attachment, and hostility will arise; and due to this, without having accomplished one's own benefit of realizing the meaning of the perfection of wisdom and so forth and the benefit of other beings, activities like writing, reading, explaining, and listening will swiftly vanish like a flash of lightning, interrupting one's effort, so that one thoroughly falls away from the training; this should be known as the action of a mara. To teach apprehending the reason for turning away from the Mahayana pitaka and abandoning it, that is, the actual cause of abandoning, one verse starting with "When this is explained..." is spoken. When this sutra is explained, some will have doubt and hesitation about it, and will think: "In this Mother sutra, the Guide has not thoroughly expressed and not taught even my name, and has not thoroughly expressed my family, the places where I abide, or my clan," and, because they have not been clearly prophesied, they will think, "Therefore, what is the use of listening to this? It is not the speech of the omniscient one." By apprehending the reason for turning away from the Mother, with that erroneous mind they will not listen to that profound dharma and will abandon it; this is the action of a mara.

Regarding the falling away of adhering to the reason, that is, the falling away of apprehending excessively, the meaning of the occurrence of the two lines starting with "Thus not knowing..." is: Thus, the perfection of wisdom is the root of the Mahayana path. Those ignorant, bewildered persons who are blessed by maras, having forsaken this precious sutra of the perfection of wisdom which is like the root of a Buddha, will seek out the śrāvaka piṭaka which is like branches and leaves, because they are obscured by bewilderment; this too is the action of a mara.

translation: Regarding tasting the flavor of gain, honor, and verses [of praise], and looking for that, the meaning of the occurrence of the two lines starting with "Desiring respect..." is: One will desire fame for oneself and desire to taste the flavor of respect and honor by others, and one will desire to obtain gain such as food and wealth; with a mind possessing the desire to look at forms and various arrangements of objects, one associates and becomes familiar with householders and so forth; and by being distracted by various activities, one falls away from listening to the perfection of wisdom and so forth; this is the action of a mara.

The faults of the training. Fourth, to teach the faults of the training, the Ornament states: "The faults, forty-six in number, / Should be understood with certainty." The definition of a fault of the training is: that demonic action which causes an obstacle to either the generation, the abiding, or the completion of the training. When divided, there are forty-six, from "obtaining with great difficulty" up to "generating joy not in accordance with the object". This is because there are twenty-three discordant conditions for generating the ungenerated training and twenty-three incomplete concordant conditions. The boundary of its levels is from before entering the path up to the seventh level. Since they are taught extensively in the Eight Thousand Line and so forth, there are correlations with the sutra for each one, but in this Summary, they are correlated with only about seven or eight. In this there are also two parts: explaining the faults to be eliminated, and explaining the antidotes that eliminate them.

དེ་ཡང་སྦྱོར་བའི་སྐྱོན་ཞེ་དྲུག་ཡོད་པ་ལས་འདིར་དངོས་སུ་བསྟན་པ་བརྒྱད་ཡོད་པའི་དང་པོ་སྤོབ་པ་ཧ་ཀྱང་མྱུར་པས་རློམ་ཞིང་བར་མདོར་ལྡོག་པའི་མི་བརྟན་པ་། རྒྱལ་བས་ཞེས་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གཅིག་གསུངས་པའི་དོན་ནི། དུས་གསུམ་གྱི་རྒྱལ་བའི་ཡུམ་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་འདི་ཡི་ག་འདི་བ་དང་། འཛིན་པ་དང་། ཀློག་པ་དང་། འཆད་ཉན་ལ་སོགས་པ་བྱེད་པའི་ཚེ་གཟུགས་སྒྲ་སོགས་ཡུལ་ལ་རྟོག་པའི་སྤོབས་པ་མ་ངེས་པ་ཐ་དད་པ་དུ་མ་རྒོད་རྨུགས་གཉིད་འགྱོད་ཆགས་སྡང་སོགས་རྣམ་པ་དུ་མ་འབྱུང་བརའགྱུར་ཞིང༌། དེའི་དབང་གིས་ཤེར་ཕྱིན་གྱི་དོན་རྟོགས་པ་སོགས་རང་དང་གཞན་འགྲོ་བའི་དོན་མ་བྱས་པར་འདྲི་ཀློག་འཆད་ཉན་བྱེད་པ་སོགས་གློག་འགྱུ་བ་བཞིན་དུ་མྱུར་དུ་ཡང་ཡལ་ནས་བརྩོན་པ་འཕྲོ་བཅད་དེ། སྦྱོར་བ་ལས་ཡོངས་སུ་ཉམས་པར་འགྱུར་བ་འདི་ནི་བདུད་ཀྱི་ལས་སུ་ཤེས་པར་བྱའོ། །ཞེས་སོ། །ཐེག་ཆེན་གྱི་སྡེ་སྣོད་ལས་ཕྱིར་ཕྱོགས་ཤིང་སྤོང་བའི་རྒྱུ་མཚན་འཛིན་པ་སྟེ་སྤང་བའི་རྒྱུ་དངོས་སྟོན་པར། འདི་བཤད་ཚེ་ན་ཞེས་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གཅིག་གསུངས། མདོ་འདི་བཤད་པའི་ཚེ་ན་ཁ་ཅིག་འདི་ལ་ཡིད་གཉིས་དང་ཉི་ཟ་བར་འགྱུར་ཏེ། འདྲེན་པས་ཡུམ་གྱི་མདོ་འདིར་ནི་བདག་གི་མིང་ཡང་ཡོངས་སུ་མ་བརྗོད་ཅིང་མ་བསྟན་ལ། བདག་གི་རིགས་དང་གང་དུ་གནས་པའི་ས་ཕྱོགས་ཕྱོགས་དང་རུས་ཀྱང་ཡོངས་སུ་མ་བརྗོད་ཅེས་བསམ་ནས་བདག་གསལ་བར་ལུང་མ་བསྟན་པས། དེས་ན་འདི་ཉན་པས་ཅི་ཞིག་བྱ་ཐམས་ཅད་མཁྱེན་པའི་གསུང་མ་ཡིན་ནོ་སྙམ་སྟེ་ཡུམ་ལས་ཕྱིར་ཕྱོགས་པའི་རྒྱུ་མཚན་བཟུང་ནས་ཕྱིན་ཅི་ལོག་གི་བློ་དེས། ཆོས་ཟབ་མོ་དེ་ནི་ཉན་པར་མི་འགྱུར་ཞིང་སྤོང་པར་འགྱུར་བ་འདི་ནི་བདུད་ཀྱི་ལས་ཡིན་ནོ། །ཞེས་སོ། །

Moreover, out of the forty-six faults of the training, there are eight actually taught here. The first of these is the instability of being proud of overly swift eloquence and turning back midway. The meaning of the occurrence of one verse starting with "By the Victor..." is: When one writes, holds, reads, explains, and listens to this perfection of wisdom, the Mother of the Victors of the three times, various uncertain and different instances of eloquence conceptualising objects such as forms and sounds, and many aspects such as excitement, dullness, sleep, regret, attachment, and hostility will arise; and due to this, without having accomplished one's own benefit of realizing the meaning of the perfection of wisdom and so forth and the benefit of other beings, activities like writing, reading, explaining, and listening will swiftly vanish like a flash of lightning, interrupting one's effort, so that one thoroughly falls away from the training; this should be known as the action of a mara. To teach apprehending the reason for turning away from the Mahayana pitaka and abandoning it, that is, the actual cause of abandoning, one verse starting with "When this is explained..." is spoken. When this sutra is explained, some will have doubt and hesitation about it, and will think: "In this Mother sutra, the Guide has not thoroughly expressed and not taught even my name, and has not thoroughly expressed my family, the places where I abide, or my clan," and, because they have not been clearly prophesied, they will think, "Therefore, what is the use of listening to this? It is not the speech of the omniscient one." By apprehending the reason for turning away from the Mother, with that erroneous mind they will not listen to that profound dharma and will abandon it; this is the action of a mara.

translation: Regarding seeking skillful means from the piṭaka taught by maras, which is a non-path, the meaning of the two lines starting with "Having discarded the dharma..." is: Having discarded practicing the dharma of the Mahayana, one engages in various worldly activities that are not dharma; and having forsaken the excellent path that brings about the attainment of Buddhahood, one deviates and goes onto the bad path taught by maras; this is the action of a mara.

The faults of the training. Fourth, to teach the faults of the training, the Ornament states: "The faults, forty-six in number, / Should be understood with certainty." The definition of a fault of the training is: that demonic action which causes an obstacle to either the generation, the abiding, or the completion of the training. When divided, there are forty-six, from "obtaining with great difficulty" up to "generating joy not in accordance with the object". This is because there are twenty-three discordant conditions for generating the ungenerated training and twenty-three incomplete concordant conditions. The boundary of its levels is from before entering the path up to the seventh level. Since they are taught extensively in the Eight Thousand Line and so forth, there are correlations with the sutra for each one, but in this Summary, they are correlated with only about seven or eight. In this there are also two parts: explaining the faults to be eliminated, and explaining the antidotes that eliminate them.

Moreover, out of the forty-six faults of the training, there are eight actually taught here. The first of these is the instability of being proud of overly swift eloquence and turning back midway. The meaning of the occurrence of one verse starting with "By the Victor..." is: When one writes, holds, reads, explains, and listens to this perfection of wisdom, the Mother of the Victors of the three times, various uncertain and different instances of eloquence conceptualising objects such as forms and sounds, and many aspects such as excitement, dullness, sleep, regret, attachment, and hostility will arise; and due to this, without having accomplished one's own benefit of realizing the meaning of the perfection of wisdom and so forth and the benefit of other beings, activities like writing, reading, explaining, and listening will swiftly vanish like a flash of lightning, interrupting one's effort, so that one thoroughly falls away from the training; this should be known as the action of a mara. To teach apprehending the reason for turning away from the Mahayana pitaka and abandoning it, that is, the actual cause of abandoning, one verse starting with "When this is explained..." is spoken. When this sutra is explained, some will have doubt and hesitation about it, and will think: "In this Mother sutra, the Guide has not thoroughly expressed and not taught even my name, and has not thoroughly expressed my family, the places where I abide, or my clan," and, because they have not been clearly prophesied, they will think, "Therefore, what is the use of listening to this? It is not the speech of the omniscient one." By apprehending the reason for turning away from the Mother, with that erroneous mind they will not listen to that profound dharma and will abandon it; this is the action of a mara.

Regarding the falling away of adhering to the reason, that is, the falling away of apprehending excessively, the meaning of the occurrence of the two lines starting with "Thus not knowing..." is: Thus, the perfection of wisdom is the root of the Mahayana path. Those ignorant, bewildered persons who are blessed by maras, having forsaken this precious sutra of the perfection of wisdom which is like the root of a Buddha, will seek out the śrāvaka piṭaka which is like branches and leaves, because they are obscured by bewilderment; this too is the action of a mara.

heading: **ལན།**
translation: Regarding the listener having great aspiration but the holder failing through laziness, causing the listener to also lose faith and turn away from listening to the dharma, the meaning of the occurrence of one verse starting with "Whoever at that time..." is: At that time when the explainer of the perfection of wisdom sutra has become distracted by gain, honor, and so forth, whichever listeners with great pursuit go to listen to this holy dharma, having aspiration and faith in the Mother, those listeners see that the speaker of the dharma possesses adherence and attachment to bad activities such as rejoicing in gain, honor, and fame; and from this, lacking joy in listening to the dharma and lacking faith, they become unhappy, thinking "Now I will not request dharma," and they turn back; this too is an action of a mara that acts as an obstacle to listening to the perfection of wisdom and so forth.

The faults of the training. Fourth, to teach the faults of the training, the Ornament states: "The faults, forty-six in number, / Should be understood with certainty." The definition of a fault of the training is: that demonic action which causes an obstacle to either the generation, the abiding, or the completion of the training. When divided, there are forty-six, from "obtaining with great difficulty" up to "generating joy not in accordance with the object". This is because there are twenty-three discordant conditions for generating the ungenerated training and twenty-three incomplete concordant conditions. The boundary of its levels is from before entering the path up to the seventh level. Since they are taught extensively in the Eight Thousand Line and so forth, there are correlations with the sutra for each one, but in this Summary, they are correlated with only about seven or eight. In this there are also two parts: explaining the faults to be eliminated, and explaining the antidotes that eliminate them.

Moreover, out of the forty-six faults of the training, there are eight actually taught here. The first of these is the instability of being proud of overly swift eloquence and turning back midway. The meaning of the occurrence of one verse starting with "By the Victor..." is: When one writes, holds, reads, explains, and listens to this perfection of wisdom, the Mother of the Victors of the three times, various uncertain and different instances of eloquence conceptualising objects such as forms and sounds, and many aspects such as excitement, dullness, sleep, regret, attachment, and hostility will arise; and due to this, without having accomplished one's own benefit of realizing the meaning of the perfection of wisdom and so forth and the benefit of other beings, activities like writing, reading, explaining, and listening will swiftly vanish like a flash of lightning, interrupting one's effort, so that one thoroughly falls away from the training; this should be known as the action of a mara. To teach apprehending the reason for turning away from the Mahayana pitaka and abandoning it, that is, the actual cause of abandoning, one verse starting with "When this is explained..." is spoken. When this sutra is explained, some will have doubt and hesitation about it, and will think: "In this Mother sutra, the Guide has not thoroughly expressed and not taught even my name, and has not thoroughly expressed my family, the places where I abide, or my clan," and, because they have not been clearly prophesied, they will think, "Therefore, what is the use of listening to this? It is not the speech of the omniscient one." By apprehending the reason for turning away from the Mother, with that erroneous mind they will not listen to that profound dharma and will abandon it; this is the action of a mara.

Those ignorant, bewildered persons who are blessed by maras, having forsaken this precious sutra of the perfection of wisdom which is like the root of a Buddha, will seek out the śrāvaka piṭaka which is like branches and leaves, because they are obscured by bewilderment; this too is the action of a mara.

heading: **ལན།**
translation: Regarding summarizing their meaning, the meaning of the occurrence of the four verses starting with "At that time..." is: At that time of listening to the sutra of the perfection of wisdom and so forth, these actions of a mara that act as obstacles to the application, such as not possessing the gathering for explaining and listening, will occur. If one asks what those are: At that time of listening to and reflecting upon this dharma and so forth, those sinful maras who are hostile to the dharma will become tormented by suffering and pain; and they, having disturbed the mind-streams of many bhikshus who hold this sutra, by means of various types of methods of making obstacles, many types of dharma that act as obstacles causing one not to hold and reflect upon the meaning of this perfection of wisdom and so forth, which are not explained here, as well as many others, will also occur; one should know all such obstacles to be from maras. Thus also, from the Gaganagañja Sutra: "Son of noble family, engaging in whatever non-virtuous dharmas and discarding whatever virtuous dharmas should all be known as the actions of a mara." Regarding establishing the reason for there being many obstacles by means of an example: Just as whoever has found invaluable things such as a jewel king, they are rare because they are very difficult to find; and at all times of having found and holding them, harms by enemies, thieves, and so forth are also always abundant; similarly, the supreme dharma of the Mother of the Conquerors, the perfection of wisdom, which is invaluable like a precious jewel, is also very rare, and because the dharma is profound, harms are also always abundant. In order to make obstacles for whichever sentient being of small intellect, a beginner newly entered into the Mahayana, who has not previously found such a very rare and profound dharma as this precious sutra of the perfection of wisdom—that is, who has not brought it into their experience—maras will become joyful and will initiate obstacles.

རྣམ་པ་ཐམས་ཅད་དུ་ཐེག་པ་མཆོག་ཏུ་འཛིན་པ་ལས་ཉམས་པ་ནི། གླང་པོ་རྙེད་ཀྱང་ཞེས་སོགས་རྐང་བ་གཉིས་གསུངས་པའི་དོན་ནི། ཇི་ལྟར་ན། གླང་བོ་ཚོལ་བའི་མིས་གླང་པོ་དངོས་རྙེད་ཀྱང་དེ་བཞག་ནས་གླང་པོའི་རྗེས་ནི་ཚོལ་བར་བྱེད་པ་ལྟར་ཐབས་ཤེས་ཆ་ཚང་བར་སྟོན་པའི་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ཐོས་ནས་ནན་ཏན་གྱིས་ཉམས་སུ་ལེན་པར་དོར་ནས། དེ་ལས་གཞན་པའི་དྲང་དོན་གྱི་མདོ་དོན་ཚོལ་བ་ནི། དཔེས་བསྟན་པ་དེ་བཞིན་དུ་ཤེས་པར་བྱ་སྟེ་འདི་ཡང་བདུད་ཀྱི་ལས་ཡིན་ནོ། །
[3-171] translation already produced for this document:
Regarding the falling away from apprehending the supreme vehicle in all aspects, the meaning of the occurrence of the two lines starting with "Even finding an elephant..." is: How is it? Just as a person seeking an elephant, even though they find the actual elephant, leaves it and seeks the elephant's footprints, having heard the perfection of wisdom that teaches means and wisdom completely, one discards practicing it earnestly. Seeking the meaning of sutras of provisional meaning other than that should be known as being like what is taught by the example, so this too is the action of a mara.

[3-172] source:
གྱ་ནོམ་པའི་རོ་འབྲས་བུ་མཆོག་གི་བདེ་བ་མྱོང་བ་ལས་ཉམས་པ་ནི། དཔེར་ན་ལ་ལས་རོ་བརྒྱ་ཞེས་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གཅིག་གསུངས་པའི་དོན། དཔེར་ན་ལ་ལས་རོ་བརྒྱ་དང་ལྡན་པའི་ཁ་ཟས་རྙེད་པ་དེའི་རོ་མི་མྱོང་བར་ཟས་མཆོག་རྙེད་ནས་ཞག་དྲུག་ཅུ་པའི་འབྲས་ཆེན་སོགས་ཟས་ངན་ཚོལ་བར་བྱེད་བ་ལྟར། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ལས་དང་པོ་པ་གང་གིས་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ཟབ་མོའི་མདོ་འདི་རྙེད་ནས་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སྒྲུབ་པར་མི་བྱེད་པར། ཉན་རང་དགྲ་བཅོམ་པའི་ས་ཐོབ་བྱེད་ཀྱི་ལམ་སྟོན་པ་ཡི་གཞུང་ལ་བརྟེན་ནས་བླ་མེད་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཚོལ་བར་བྱེད་པ་ནི་གོང་གི་དཔེ་དེ་བཞིིན་སྟེ་འདི་ཡང་བདུད་ཀྱི་ལས་ཡིན་ནོ། །ཞེས་སོ། །
[3-172] translation already produced for this document:
Regarding the falling away from experiencing the joy of the supreme fruit, the excellent taste, the meaning of the occurrence of one verse starting with "For example, someone [finding food with] a hundred tastes..." is: For example, just as someone having found food possessing a hundred tastes does not experience its taste, but having found supreme food seeks out inferior food such as sixty-day rice, whichever beginner bodhisattva, having found this profound sutra of the perfection of wisdom, does not accomplish the enlightenment of a Buddha, but seeks unsurpassable enlightenment relying upon texts that teach the path that brings about the attainment of the level of śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha arhats is like that above example; this too is the action of a mara.

[3-173] source:
རྙེད་པ་དང་བཀུར་སྟི་དང་ཚིགས་སུ་བཅད་པའི་རོ་མྱོང་ཞིང་དེ་ལ་བལྟ་བ་ནི། བསྟི་སྟངས་འདོད་པར་ཞེས་སོགས་རྐང་པ་གཉིས་གསུངས་པའི་དོན། རང་ཉིད་སྙན་པའི་གྲགས་པ་དང་གཞན་གྱིས་བསྟི་སྟངས་དང་བསྙེན་བཀུར་གྱི་རོ་མྱོང་བར་འདོད་པར་འགྱུར་ཞིང་། ཟས་ནོར་སོགས་རྙེད་པར་ཐོབ་པར་འདོད་པར་འགྱུར་བ་དང་གཟུགས་དང་ཡུལ་གྱི་བཀོད་པ་སྣ་ཚོགས་བ་ལྟ་བར་འདོད་པ་དང་བཅས་པའི་སེམས་ཀྱིས་ཁྱིམ་པ་སོགས་དང་འགྲོགས་འདྲིས་བྱེད་པ་དང་ལྡན་ཞིང་བྱ་བ་དུ་མས་གཡེངས་ནས་ཤེར་ཕྱིན་ཉན་པ་སོགས་ལས་ཉམས་པ་ནི་བདུད་ཀྱི་ལས་སོ། །ཞེས་སོ། །
[3-173] translation already produced for this document:
Regarding tasting the flavor of gain, honor, and verses [of praise], and looking for that, the meaning of the occurrence of the two lines starting with "Desiring respect..." is: One will desire fame for oneself and desire to taste the flavor of respect and honor by others, and one will desire to obtain gain such as food and wealth; with a mind possessing the desire to look at forms and various arrangements of objects, one associates and becomes familiar with householders and so forth; and by being distracted by various activities, one falls away from listening to the perfection of wisdom and so forth; this is the action of a mara.

[3-174] source:
ལམ་མ་ཡིན་པ་བདུད་ཀྱིས་བསྟན་པའི་སྡེ་སྣོད་ལས་ཐབས་མཁས་པ་འཚོལ་བ་ནི། ཆོས་བཏང་ནས་ནི་ཞེས་སོགས་རྐང་བ་གཉིས་ཀྱི་དོན། ཐེག་པ་ཆེན་པོའི་ཆོས་ཉམས་སུ་ལེན་པ་བཏང་ནས་ནི་ཆོས་མིན་པའི་འཇིག་རྟེན་གྱི་བྱ་བ་སྣ་ཚོགས་ལ་སྤྱོད་པར་འགྱུར་བ་དང་སངས་རྒྱས་ཐོབ་བྱེད་ཀྱི་ལམ་བཟང་པོ་བོར་ནས་བདུད་ཀྱིས་བསྟན་པའི་ལམ་ངན་དུ་གོལ་ཏེ་འགྲོ་བར་འགྱུར་བ་འདི་ནི་བདུད་ཀྱི་ལས་སོ། །ཞེས་སོ། །
[3-174] translation already produced for this document:
Regarding seeking skillful means from the piṭaka taught by maras, which is a non-path, the meaning of the two lines starting with "Having discarded the dharma..." is: Having discarded practicing the dharma of the Mahayana, one engages in various worldly activities that are not dharma; and having forsaken the excellent path that brings about the attainment of Buddhahood, one deviates and goes onto the bad path taught by maras; this is the action of a mara.

[3-175] source:
ཉན་པ་པོ་འདུན་པ་ཆེ་ཡང་འཆང་བ་པོ་སྙོམས་ལས་ཀྱིས་ཉམས་པས་ཉན་པ་པོ་ཡང་མ་དད་པར་གྱུར་ཏེ་ཆོས་ཉན་པ་ལས་བཟློག་པ་ནི། གང་དག་དེ་ཡི་ཚེ་ཞེས་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གཅིག་གསུངས་པའི་དོན། ཉན་པ་པོ་གང་དག་དོན་གཉེར་ཆེན་པོས་ཤེར་ཕྱིན་གྱི་མདོ་འཆད་པ་པོ་རྙེད་བཀུར་སོགས་ཀྱིས་གཡེང་བར་གྱུར་པ་དེ་ཡི་ཚེ་ན་ཡུམ་ལ་འདུན་ཅིང་དད་པར་གྱུར་ནས་ཆོས་ཀྱི་དམ་པ་འདི་ནི་ཉན་དུ་སོང་བ་ལས། ཉན་པ་པོ་དེ་དག་གིས་ནི་ཆོས་སྨྲ་བ་པོ་དེ་རྙེད་བཀུར་སྙན་གྲགས་ལ་དགའ་བ་སོགས་བྱ་བ་ངན་པ་ལ་ཞེན་ཅིང་ཆགས་པ་དང་ལྡན་པར་རིགས་ནས་ཆོས་ཉན་པ་ལ་དགའ་བ་མེད་ཅིང་མ་དད་པས་ད་ན་ཆོས་ཞུ་བར་མི་བྱའོ་སྙམ་དུ་ཡིད་མི་བདེ་བར་གྱུར་ནས་ཕྱིར་འགྲོ་བ་འདི་ཡང་ཤེར་ཕྱིན་ཉན་པ་སོགས་ཀྱི་བར་ཆད་དུ་འགྱུར་བའི་བདུད་ཀྱི་ལས་སོ། །ཞེས་པའོ། །
[3-175] translation already produced for this document:
Regarding the listener having great aspiration but the holder failing through laziness, causing the listener to also lose faith and turn away from listening to the dharma, the meaning of the occurrence of one verse starting with "Whoever at that time..." is: At that time when the explainer of the perfection of wisdom sutra has become distracted by gain, honor, and so forth, whichever listeners with great pursuit go to listen to this holy dharma, having aspiration and faith in the Mother, those listeners see that the speaker of the dharma possesses adherence and attachment to bad activities such as rejoicing in gain, honor, and fame; and from this, lacking joy in listening to the dharma and lacking faith, they become unhappy, thinking "Now I will not request dharma," and they turn back; this too is an action of a mara that acts as an obstacle to listening to the perfection of wisdom and so forth.

heading: **སེལ་བྱེད་ཀྱི་གཉེན་པོ།**
translation: The antidotes that eliminate. Second, regarding the antidotes that eliminate, the meaning of the occurrence of the five lines starting with "The Buddhas of the ten directions..." is: Even though there are many obstacles like that, they will not find an opportunity. If one asks why: Because the Buddhas of the ten directions, whose power that mara exerting himself like that in obstacles is unable to rival even by a fraction, perform the three—guarding, protecting, and hiding—from those obstacles, and thereby apply one to fully holding the perfection of wisdom. From the commentary on the Verses of the Precious Qualities Collection, Clarifying the Suchness of Profound Dependent Arising, Fulfilling the Hopes of the Fortunate, this is the commentary on the eleventh chapter, the chapter on Maras.

རྒྱུ་མཚན་མངོན་པར་ཞེན་པ་ཉམས་པ་སྟེ་ཆེད་ཆེར་འཛིན་པ་ཉམས་པ་ནི། དེ་ལྟར་མི་ཤེས་ཞེས་སོགས་རྐང་པ་གཉིས་གསུངས་པའི་དོན། ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ནི་ཐེག་ཆེན་ལམ་གྱི་རྩ་བ་ཡིན་པ་དེ་ལྟར། བདུད་ཀྱི་བྱིན་གྱིས་རླབས་པའི་གང་ཟག་མི་ཤེས་པ་རྨོངས་པ་དེ་དག་གིས་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་རྩ་བ་ལྟ་བུའི་ཤེར་ཕྱིན་གྱི་མདོ་སྡེ་རིན་པོ་ཆེ་འདི་བོར་ནས་ནི། རྨོངས་པས་སྒྲིབ་པས་ཡལ་ག་དག་དང་འདབ་མ་དང་འདྲ་བའི་ཉན་ཐོས་ཀྱི་སྡེ་སྣོད་ཚོལ་བར་འགྱུར་བ་འདི་ཡང་བདུད་ཀྱི་ལས་སོ། །ཞེས་པའོ། །
[3-170] translation already produced for this document:
Regarding the falling away of adhering to the reason, that is, the falling away of apprehending excessively, the meaning of the occurrence of the two lines starting with "Thus not knowing..." is: Thus, the perfection of wisdom is the root of the Mahayana path. Those ignorant, bewildered persons who are blessed by maras, having forsaken this precious sutra of the perfection of wisdom which is like the root of a Buddha, will seek out the śrāvaka piṭaka which is like branches and leaves, because they are obscured by bewilderment; this too is the action of a mara.

[3-171] source:
རྣམ་པ་ཐམས་ཅད་དུ་ཐེག་པ་མཆོག་ཏུ་འཛིན་པ་ལས་ཉམས་པ་ནི། གླང་པོ་རྙེད་ཀྱང་ཞེས་སོགས་རྐང་བ་གཉིས་གསུངས་པའི་དོན་ནི། ཇི་ལྟར་ན། གླང་བོ་ཚོལ་བའི་མིས་གླང་པོ་དངོས་རྙེད་ཀྱང་དེ་བཞག་ནས་གླང་པོའི་རྗེས་ནི་ཚོལ་བར་བྱེད་པ་ལྟར་ཐབས་ཤེས་ཆ་ཚང་བར་སྟོན་པའི་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ཐོས་ནས་ནན་ཏན་གྱིས་ཉམས་སུ་ལེན་པར་དོར་ནས། དེ་ལས་གཞན་པའི་དྲང་དོན་གྱི་མདོ་དོན་ཚོལ་བ་ནི། དཔེས་བསྟན་པ་དེ་བཞིན་དུ་ཤེས་པར་བྱ་སྟེ་འདི་ཡང་བདུད་ཀྱི་ལས་ཡིན་ནོ། །
[3-171] translation already produced for this document:
Regarding the falling away from apprehending the supreme vehicle in all aspects, the meaning of the occurrence of the two lines starting with "Even finding an elephant..." is: How is it? Just as a person seeking an elephant, even though they find the actual elephant, leaves it and seeks the elephant's footprints, having heard the perfection of wisdom that teaches means and wisdom completely, one discards practicing it earnestly. Seeking the meaning of sutras of provisional meaning other than that should be known as being like what is taught by the example, so this too is the action of a mara.

[3-172] source:
གྱ་ནོམ་པའི་རོ་འབྲས་བུ་མཆོག་གི་བདེ་བ་མྱོང་བ་ལས་ཉམས་པ་ནི། དཔེར་ན་ལ་ལས་རོ་བརྒྱ་ཞེས་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གཅིག་གསུངས་པའི་དོན། དཔེར་ན་ལ་ལས་རོ་བརྒྱ་དང་ལྡན་པའི་ཁ་ཟས་རྙེད་པ་དེའི་རོ་མི་མྱོང་བར་ཟས་མཆོག་རྙེད་ནས་ཞག་དྲུག་ཅུ་པའི་འབྲས་ཆེན་སོགས་ཟས་ངན་ཚོལ་བར་བྱེད་བ་ལྟར། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ལས་དང་པོ་པ་གང་གིས་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ཟབ་མོའི་མདོ་འདི་རྙེད་ནས་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སྒྲུབ་པར་མི་བྱེད་པར། ཉན་རང་དགྲ་བཅོམ་པའི་ས་ཐོབ་བྱེད་ཀྱི་ལམ་སྟོན་པ་ཡི་གཞུང་ལ་བརྟེན་ནས་བླ་མེད་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཚོལ་བར་བྱེད་པ་ནི་གོང་གི་དཔེ་དེ་བཞིིན་སྟེ་འདི་ཡང་བདུད་ཀྱི་ལས་ཡིན་ནོ། །ཞེས་སོ། །
[3-172] translation already produced for this document:
Regarding the falling away from experiencing the joy of the supreme fruit, the excellent taste, the meaning of the occurrence of one verse starting with "For example, someone [finding food with] a hundred tastes..." is: For example, just as someone having found food possessing a hundred tastes does not experience its taste, but having found supreme food seeks out inferior food such as sixty-day rice, whichever beginner bodhisattva, having found this profound sutra of the perfection of wisdom, does not accomplish the enlightenment of a Buddha, but seeks unsurpassable enlightenment relying upon texts that teach the path that brings about the attainment of the level of śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha arhats is like that above example; this too is the action of a mara.

[3-173] source:
རྙེད་པ་དང་བཀུར་སྟི་དང་ཚིགས་སུ་བཅད་པའི་རོ་མྱོང་ཞིང་དེ་ལ་བལྟ་བ་ནི། བསྟི་སྟངས་འདོད་པར་ཞེས་སོགས་རྐང་པ་གཉིས་གསུངས་པའི་དོན། རང་ཉིད་སྙན་པའི་གྲགས་པ་དང་གཞན་གྱིས་བསྟི་སྟངས་དང་བསྙེན་བཀུར་གྱི་རོ་མྱོང་བར་འདོད་པར་འགྱུར་ཞིང་། ཟས་ནོར་སོགས་རྙེད་པར་ཐོབ་པར་འདོད་པར་འགྱུར་བ་དང་གཟུགས་དང་ཡུལ་གྱི་བཀོད་པ་སྣ་ཚོགས་བ་ལྟ་བར་འདོད་པ་དང་བཅས་པའི་སེམས་ཀྱིས་ཁྱིམ་པ་སོགས་དང་འགྲོགས་འདྲིས་བྱེད་པ་དང་ལྡན་ཞིང་བྱ་བ་དུ་མས་གཡེངས་ནས་ཤེར་ཕྱིན་ཉན་པ་སོགས་ལས་ཉམས་པ་ནི་བདུད་ཀྱི་ལས་སོ། །ཞེས་སོ། །
[3-173] translation already produced for this document:
Regarding tasting the flavor of gain, honor, and verses [of praise], and looking for that, the meaning of the occurrence of the two lines starting with "Desiring respect..." is: One will desire fame for oneself and desire to taste the flavor of respect and honor by others, and one will desire to obtain gain such as food and wealth; with a mind possessing the desire to look at forms and various arrangements of objects, one associates and becomes familiar with householders and so forth; and by being distracted by various activities, one falls away from listening to the perfection of wisdom and so forth; this is the action of a mara.

[3-174] source:
ལམ་མ་ཡིན་པ་བདུད་ཀྱིས་བསྟན་པའི་སྡེ་སྣོད་ལས་ཐབས་མཁས་པ་འཚོལ་བ་ནི། ཆོས་བཏང་ནས་ནི་ཞེས་སོགས་རྐང་བ་གཉིས་ཀྱི་དོན། ཐེག་པ་ཆེན་པོའི་ཆོས་ཉམས་སུ་ལེན་པ་བཏང་ནས་ནི་ཆོས་མིན་པའི་འཇིག་རྟེན་གྱི་བྱ་བ་སྣ་ཚོགས་ལ་སྤྱོད་པར་འགྱུར་བ་དང་སངས་རྒྱས་ཐོབ་བྱེད་ཀྱི་ལམ་བཟང་པོ་བོར་ནས་བདུད་ཀྱིས་བསྟན་པའི་ལམ་ངན་དུ་གོལ་ཏེ་འགྲོ་བར་འགྱུར་བ་འདི་ནི་བདུད་ཀྱི་ལས་སོ། །ཞེས་སོ། །
[3-174] translation already produced for this document:
Regarding seeking skillful means from the piṭaka taught by maras, which is a non-path, the meaning of the two lines starting with "Having discarded the dharma..." is: Having discarded practicing the dharma of the Mahayana, one engages in various worldly activities that are not dharma; and having forsaken the excellent path that brings about the attainment of Buddhahood, one deviates and goes onto the bad path taught by maras; this is the action of a mara.

[3-175] source:
ཉན་པ་པོ་འདུན་པ་ཆེ་ཡང་འཆང་བ་པོ་སྙོམས་ལས་ཀྱིས་ཉམས་པས་ཉན་པ་པོ་ཡང་མ་དད་པར་གྱུར་ཏེ་ཆོས་ཉན་པ་ལས་བཟློག་པ་ནི། གང་དག་དེ་ཡི་ཚེ་ཞེས་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གཅིག་གསུངས་པའི་དོན། ཉན་པ་པོ་གང་དག་དོན་གཉེར་ཆེན་པོས་ཤེར་ཕྱིན་གྱི་མདོ་འཆད་པ་པོ་རྙེད་བཀུར་སོགས་ཀྱིས་གཡེང་བར་གྱུར་པ་དེ་ཡི་ཚེ་ན་ཡུམ་ལ་འདུན་ཅིང་དད་པར་གྱུར་ནས་ཆོས་ཀྱི་དམ་པ་འདི་ནི་ཉན་དུ་སོང་བ་ལས། ཉན་པ་པོ་དེ་དག་གིས་ནི་ཆོས་སྨྲ་བ་པོ་དེ་རྙེད་བཀུར་སྙན་གྲགས་ལ་དགའ་བ་སོགས་བྱ་བ་ངན་པ་ལ་ཞེན་ཅིང་ཆགས་པ་དང་ལྡན་པར་རིགས་ནས་ཆོས་ཉན་པ་ལ་དགའ་བ་མེད་ཅིང་མ་དད་པས་ད་ན་ཆོས་ཞུ་བར་མི་བྱའོ་སྙམ་དུ་ཡིད་མི་བདེ་བར་གྱུར་ནས་ཕྱིར་འགྲོ་བ་འདི་ཡང་ཤེར་ཕྱིན་ཉན་པ་སོགས་ཀྱི་བར་ཆད་དུ་འགྱུར་བའི་བདུད་ཀྱི་ལས་སོ། །ཞེས་པའོ། །
[3-175] translation already produced for this document:
Regarding the listener having great aspiration but the holder failing through laziness, causing the listener to also lose faith and turn away from listening to the dharma, the meaning of the occurrence of one verse starting with "Whoever at that time..." is: At that time when the explainer of the perfection of wisdom sutra has become distracted by gain, honor, and so forth, whichever listeners with great pursuit go to listen to this holy dharma, having aspiration and faith in the Mother, those listeners see that the speaker of the dharma possesses adherence and attachment to bad activities such as rejoicing in gain, honor, and fame; and from this, lacking joy in listening to the dharma and lacking faith, they become unhappy, thinking "Now I will not request dharma," and they turn back; this too is an action of a mara that acts as an obstacle to listening to the perfection of wisdom and so forth.

heading: **སེལ་བྱེད་ཀྱི་གཉེན་པོ།**
translation: If one asks why all the Buddhas keep them in mind and protect them, establishing that very thing by means of an example is: For example, if a mother becomes ill, all of her many sons will be unhappy, and they will perform services for that mother such as seeking a doctor who removes the illness; similarly, all those Bhagavan Buddhas of the world systems in the ten directions also exert themselves in order to remove the actions of maras and keep in mind this generation of bodhicitta and holy wisdom realizing emptiness which have become their own respective generating Mothers.

Work: ཡོན་ཏན་རིན་པོ་ཆེ་སྡུད་པ་ཚིགས་སུ་བཅད་པའི་འགྲེལ་པ་ཟབ་མོ་རྟེན་འབྱུང་གི་དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཉིད་གསལ་བར་བྱེད་པའི་ནོར་བུའི་སྒྲོན་མེ་སྐལ་བཟང་རེ་སྐོང་། (Khenrab Jamyang, Commentary on the Verses of the Precious Qualities Collection), author: མཁྱེན་རབ་འཇམ་དབྱངས་བློ་བཟང་འཕྲིན་ལས།. A canonical Tibetan text; the blocks below are being translated in order.

Preceding blocks of this same document and their translations — match this terminology, register and line shape:

[3-170] source:
རྒྱུ་མཚན་མངོན་པར་ཞེན་པ་ཉམས་པ་སྟེ་ཆེད་ཆེར་འཛིན་པ་ཉམས་པ་ནི། དེ་ལྟར་མི་ཤེས་ཞེས་སོགས་རྐང་པ་གཉིས་གསུངས་པའི་དོན། ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ནི་ཐེག་ཆེན་ལམ་གྱི་རྩ་བ་ཡིན་པ་དེ་ལྟར། བདུད་ཀྱི་བྱིན་གྱིས་རླབས་པའི་གང་ཟག་མི་ཤེས་པ་རྨོངས་པ་དེ་དག་གིས་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་རྩ་བ་ལྟ་བུའི་ཤེར་ཕྱིན་གྱི་མདོ་སྡེ་རིན་པོ་ཆེ་འདི་བོར་ནས་ནི། རྨོངས་པས་སྒྲིབ་པས་ཡལ་ག་དག་དང་འདབ་མ་དང་འདྲ་བའི་ཉན་ཐོས་ཀྱི་སྡེ་སྣོད་ཚོལ་བར་འགྱུར་བ་འདི་ཡང་བདུད་ཀྱི་ལས་སོ། །ཞེས་པའོ། །
[3-170] translation already produced for this document:
Regarding the falling away of adhering to the reason, that is, the falling away of apprehending excessively, the meaning of the occurrence of the two lines starting with "Thus not knowing..." is: Thus, the perfection of wisdom is the root of the Mahayana path. Those ignorant, bewildered persons who are blessed by maras, having forsaken this precious sutra of the perfection of wisdom which is like the root of a Buddha, will seek out the śrāvaka piṭaka which is like branches and leaves, because they are obscured by bewilderment; this too is the action of a mara.

[3-171] source:
རྣམ་པ་ཐམས་ཅད་དུ་ཐེག་པ་མཆོག་ཏུ་འཛིན་པ་ལས་ཉམས་པ་ནི། གླང་པོ་རྙེད་ཀྱང་ཞེས་སོགས་རྐང་བ་གཉིས་གསུངས་པའི་དོན་ནི། ཇི་ལྟར་ན། གླང་བོ་ཚོལ་བའི་མིས་གླང་པོ་དངོས་རྙེད་ཀྱང་དེ་བཞག་ནས་གླང་པོའི་རྗེས་ནི་ཚོལ་བར་བྱེད་པ་ལྟར་ཐབས་ཤེས་ཆ་ཚང་བར་སྟོན་པའི་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ཐོས་ནས་ནན་ཏན་གྱིས་ཉམས་སུ་ལེན་པར་དོར་ནས། དེ་ལས་གཞན་པའི་དྲང་དོན་གྱི་མདོ་དོན་ཚོལ་བ་ནི། དཔེས་བསྟན་པ་དེ་བཞིན་དུ་ཤེས་པར་བྱ་སྟེ་འདི་ཡང་བདུད་ཀྱི་ལས་ཡིན་ནོ། །
[3-171] translation already produced for this document:
Regarding the falling away from apprehending the supreme vehicle in all aspects, the meaning of the occurrence of the two lines starting with "Even finding an elephant..." is: How is it? Just as a person seeking an elephant, even though they find the actual elephant, leaves it and seeks the elephant's footprints, having heard the perfection of wisdom that teaches means and wisdom completely, one discards practicing it earnestly. Seeking the meaning of sutras of provisional meaning other than that should be known as being like what is taught by the example, so this too is the action of a mara.

[3-172] source:
གྱ་ནོམ་པའི་རོ་འབྲས་བུ་མཆོག་གི་བདེ་བ་མྱོང་བ་ལས་ཉམས་པ་ནི། དཔེར་ན་ལ་ལས་རོ་བརྒྱ་ཞེས་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གཅིག་གསུངས་པའི་དོན། དཔེར་ན་ལ་ལས་རོ་བརྒྱ་དང་ལྡན་པའི་ཁ་ཟས་རྙེད་པ་དེའི་རོ་མི་མྱོང་བར་ཟས་མཆོག་རྙེད་ནས་ཞག་དྲུག་ཅུ་པའི་འབྲས་ཆེན་སོགས་ཟས་ངན་ཚོལ་བར་བྱེད་བ་ལྟར། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ལས་དང་པོ་པ་གང་གིས་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ཟབ་མོའི་མདོ་འདི་རྙེད་ནས་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སྒྲུབ་པར་མི་བྱེད་པར། ཉན་རང་དགྲ་བཅོམ་པའི་ས་ཐོབ་བྱེད་ཀྱི་ལམ་སྟོན་པ་ཡི་གཞུང་ལ་བརྟེན་ནས་བླ་མེད་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཚོལ་བར་བྱེད་པ་ནི་གོང་གི་དཔེ་དེ་བཞིིན་སྟེ་འདི་ཡང་བདུད་ཀྱི་ལས་ཡིན་ནོ། །ཞེས་སོ། །
[3-172] translation already produced for this document:
Regarding the falling away from experiencing the joy of the supreme fruit, the excellent taste, the meaning of the occurrence of one verse starting with "For example, someone [finding food with] a hundred tastes..." is: For example, just as someone having found food possessing a hundred tastes does not experience its taste, but having found supreme food seeks out inferior food such as sixty-day rice, whichever beginner bodhisattva, having found this profound sutra of the perfection of wisdom, does not accomplish the enlightenment of a Buddha, but seeks unsurpassable enlightenment relying upon texts that teach the path that brings about the attainment of the level of śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha arhats is like that above example; this too is the action of a mara.

[3-173] source:
རྙེད་པ་དང་བཀུར་སྟི་དང་ཚིགས་སུ་བཅད་པའི་རོ་མྱོང་ཞིང་དེ་ལ་བལྟ་བ་ནི། བསྟི་སྟངས་འདོད་པར་ཞེས་སོགས་རྐང་པ་གཉིས་གསུངས་པའི་དོན། རང་ཉིད་སྙན་པའི་གྲགས་པ་དང་གཞན་གྱིས་བསྟི་སྟངས་དང་བསྙེན་བཀུར་གྱི་རོ་མྱོང་བར་འདོད་པར་འགྱུར་ཞིང་། ཟས་ནོར་སོགས་རྙེད་པར་ཐོབ་པར་འདོད་པར་འགྱུར་བ་དང་གཟུགས་དང་ཡུལ་གྱི་བཀོད་པ་སྣ་ཚོགས་བ་ལྟ་བར་འདོད་པ་དང་བཅས་པའི་སེམས་ཀྱིས་ཁྱིམ་པ་སོགས་དང་འགྲོགས་འདྲིས་བྱེད་པ་དང་ལྡན་ཞིང་བྱ་བ་དུ་མས་གཡེངས་ནས་ཤེར་ཕྱིན་ཉན་པ་སོགས་ལས་ཉམས་པ་ནི་བདུད་ཀྱི་ལས་སོ། །ཞེས་སོ། །
[3-173] translation already produced for this document:
Regarding tasting the flavor of gain, honor, and verses [of praise], and looking for that, the meaning of the occurrence of the two lines starting with "Desiring respect..." is: One will desire fame for oneself and desire to taste the flavor of respect and honor by others, and one will desire to obtain gain such as food and wealth; with a mind possessing the desire to look at forms and various arrangements of objects, one associates and becomes familiar with householders and so forth; and by being distracted by various activities, one falls away from listening to the perfection of wisdom and so forth; this is the action of a mara.

[3-174] source:
ལམ་མ་ཡིན་པ་བདུད་ཀྱིས་བསྟན་པའི་སྡེ་སྣོད་ལས་ཐབས་མཁས་པ་འཚོལ་བ་ནི། ཆོས་བཏང་ནས་ནི་ཞེས་སོགས་རྐང་བ་གཉིས་ཀྱི་དོན། ཐེག་པ་ཆེན་པོའི་ཆོས་ཉམས་སུ་ལེན་པ་བཏང་ནས་ནི་ཆོས་མིན་པའི་འཇིག་རྟེན་གྱི་བྱ་བ་སྣ་ཚོགས་ལ་སྤྱོད་པར་འགྱུར་བ་དང་སངས་རྒྱས་ཐོབ་བྱེད་ཀྱི་ལམ་བཟང་པོ་བོར་ནས་བདུད་ཀྱིས་བསྟན་པའི་ལམ་ངན་དུ་གོལ་ཏེ་འགྲོ་བར་འགྱུར་བ་འདི་ནི་བདུད་ཀྱི་ལས་སོ། །ཞེས་སོ། །
[3-174] translation already produced for this document:
Regarding seeking skillful means from the piṭaka taught by maras, which is a non-path, the meaning of the two lines starting with "Having discarded the dharma..." is: Having discarded practicing the dharma of the Mahayana, one engages in various worldly activities that are not dharma; and having forsaken the excellent path that brings about the attainment of Buddhahood, one deviates and goes onto the bad path taught by maras; this is the action of a mara.

[3-175] source:
ཉན་པ་པོ་འདུན་པ་ཆེ་ཡང་འཆང་བ་པོ་སྙོམས་ལས་ཀྱིས་ཉམས་པས་ཉན་པ་པོ་ཡང་མ་དད་པར་གྱུར་ཏེ་ཆོས་ཉན་པ་ལས་བཟློག་པ་ནི། གང་དག་དེ་ཡི་ཚེ་ཞེས་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གཅིག་གསུངས་པའི་དོན། ཉན་པ་པོ་གང་དག་དོན་གཉེར་ཆེན་པོས་ཤེར་ཕྱིན་གྱི་མདོ་འཆད་པ་པོ་རྙེད་བཀུར་སོགས་ཀྱིས་གཡེང་བར་གྱུར་པ་དེ་ཡི་ཚེ་ན་ཡུམ་ལ་འདུན་ཅིང་དད་པར་གྱུར་ནས་ཆོས་ཀྱི་དམ་པ་འདི་ནི་ཉན་དུ་སོང་བ་ལས། ཉན་པ་པོ་དེ་དག་གིས་ནི་ཆོས་སྨྲ་བ་པོ་དེ་རྙེད་བཀུར་སྙན་གྲགས་ལ་དགའ་བ་སོགས་བྱ་བ་ངན་པ་ལ་ཞེན་ཅིང་ཆགས་པ་དང་ལྡན་པར་རིགས་ནས་ཆོས་ཉན་པ་ལ་དགའ་བ་མེད་ཅིང་མ་དད་པས་ད་ན་ཆོས་ཞུ་བར་མི་བྱའོ་སྙམ་དུ་ཡིད་མི་བདེ་བར་གྱུར་ནས་ཕྱིར་འགྲོ་བ་འདི་ཡང་ཤེར་ཕྱིན་ཉན་པ་སོགས་ཀྱི་བར་ཆད་དུ་འགྱུར་བའི་བདུད་ཀྱི་ལས་སོ། །ཞེས་པའོ། །
[3-175] translation already produced for this document:
Regarding the listener having great aspiration but the holder failing through laziness, causing the listener to also lose faith and turn away from listening to the dharma, the meaning of the occurrence of one verse starting with "Whoever at that time..." is: At that time when the explainer of the perfection of wisdom sutra has become distracted by gain, honor, and so forth, whichever listeners with great pursuit go to listen to this holy dharma, having aspiration and faith in the Mother, those listeners see that the speaker of the dharma possesses adherence and attachment to bad activities such as rejoicing in gain, honor, and fame; and from this, lacking joy in listening to the dharma and lacking faith, they become unhappy, thinking "Now I will not request dharma," and they turn back; this too is an action of a mara that acts as an obstacle to listening to the perfection of wisdom and so forth.

heading: **མདོར་བསྟན་པ།**
translation: The defining characteristics of the application. Brief teaching. Fifth, regarding teaching the defining characteristics of the application, from the Ornament: "By what it is characterized, that is the defining characteristic," having briefly taught with one verse starting with that,
style_instruction: Translate this passage of a Tibetan Buddhist commentary on the Verse Summary of the Perfection of Wisdom (Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā) into clear, accurate English prose. Translate the whole passage completely and in the same order: do not summarise, shorten or omit anything, and keep the same number of lines as the source. Where the commentary quotes or glosses words of the root verses, keep those quoted words recognisable in the translation. Keep proper names in their standard Sanskrit forms (Subhūti, Śāriputra, Maitreya, Haribhadra) and technical terms recognisable (prajñāpāramitā = perfection of wisdom, bodhisattva). Do not add commentary, notes, or explanation of your own.
context:
A canonical Tibetan Buddhist text, translated block by block from the critical edition in this vault. The blocks below are being translated in order.

Work: ཡོན་ཏན་རིན་པོ་ཆེ་སྡུད་པ་ཚིགས་སུ་བཅད་པའི་འགྲེལ་པ་ཟབ་མོ་རྟེན་འབྱུང་གི་དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཉིད་གསལ་བར་བྱེད་པའི་ནོར་བུའི་སྒྲོན་མེ་སྐལ་བཟང་རེ་སྐོང་། (Khenrab Jamyang, Commentary on the Verses of the Precious Qualities Collection), author: མཁྱེན་རབ་འཇམ་དབྱངས་བློ་བཟང་འཕྲིན་ལས།. A canonical Tibetan text; the blocks below are being translated in order.

Preceding blocks of this same document and their translations — match this terminology, register and line shape:

[3-170] source:
རྒྱུ་མཚན་མངོན་པར་ཞེན་པ་ཉམས་པ་སྟེ་ཆེད་ཆེར་འཛིན་པ་ཉམས་པ་ནི། དེ་ལྟར་མི་ཤེས་ཞེས་སོགས་རྐང་པ་གཉིས་གསུངས་པའི་དོན། ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ནི་ཐེག་ཆེན་ལམ་གྱི་རྩ་བ་ཡིན་པ་དེ་ལྟར། བདུད་ཀྱི་བྱིན་གྱིས་རླབས་པའི་གང་ཟག་མི་ཤེས་པ་རྨོངས་པ་དེ་དག་གིས་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་རྩ་བ་ལྟ་བུའི་ཤེར་ཕྱིན་གྱི་མདོ་སྡེ་རིན་པོ་ཆེ་འདི་བོར་ནས་ནི། རྨོངས་པས་སྒྲིབ་པས་ཡལ་ག་དག་དང་འདབ་མ་དང་འདྲ་བའི་ཉན་ཐོས་ཀྱི་སྡེ་སྣོད་ཚོལ་བར་འགྱུར་བ་འདི་ཡང་བདུད་ཀྱི་ལས་སོ། །ཞེས་པའོ། །
[3-170] translation already produced for this document:
Regarding the falling away of adhering to the reason, that is, the falling away of apprehending excessively, the meaning of the occurrence of the two lines starting with "Thus not knowing..." is: Thus, the perfection of wisdom is the root of the Mahayana path. Those ignorant, bewildered persons who are blessed by maras, having forsaken this precious sutra of the perfection of wisdom which is like the root of a Buddha, will seek out the śrāvaka piṭaka which is like branches and leaves, because they are obscured by bewilderment; this too is the action of a mara.

[3-171] source:
རྣམ་པ་ཐམས་ཅད་དུ་ཐེག་པ་མཆོག་ཏུ་འཛིན་པ་ལས་ཉམས་པ་ནི། གླང་པོ་རྙེད་ཀྱང་ཞེས་སོགས་རྐང་བ་གཉིས་གསུངས་པའི་དོན་ནི། ཇི་ལྟར་ན། གླང་བོ་ཚོལ་བའི་མིས་གླང་པོ་དངོས་རྙེད་ཀྱང་དེ་བཞག་ནས་གླང་པོའི་རྗེས་ནི་ཚོལ་བར་བྱེད་པ་ལྟར་ཐབས་ཤེས་ཆ་ཚང་བར་སྟོན་པའི་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ཐོས་ནས་ནན་ཏན་གྱིས་ཉམས་སུ་ལེན་པར་དོར་ནས། དེ་ལས་གཞན་པའི་དྲང་དོན་གྱི་མདོ་དོན་ཚོལ་བ་ནི། དཔེས་བསྟན་པ་དེ་བཞིན་དུ་ཤེས་པར་བྱ་སྟེ་འདི་ཡང་བདུད་ཀྱི་ལས་ཡིན་ནོ། །
[3-171] translation already produced for this document:
Regarding the falling away from apprehending the supreme vehicle in all aspects, the meaning of the occurrence of the two lines starting with "Even finding an elephant..." is: How is it? Just as a person seeking an elephant, even though they find the actual elephant, leaves it and seeks the elephant's footprints, having heard the perfection of wisdom that teaches means and wisdom completely, one discards practicing it earnestly. Seeking the meaning of sutras of provisional meaning other than that should be known as being like what is taught by the example, so this too is the action of a mara.

[3-172] source:
གྱ་ནོམ་པའི་རོ་འབྲས་བུ་མཆོག་གི་བདེ་བ་མྱོང་བ་ལས་ཉམས་པ་ནི། དཔེར་ན་ལ་ལས་རོ་བརྒྱ་ཞེས་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གཅིག་གསུངས་པའི་དོན། དཔེར་ན་ལ་ལས་རོ་བརྒྱ་དང་ལྡན་པའི་ཁ་ཟས་རྙེད་པ་དེའི་རོ་མི་མྱོང་བར་ཟས་མཆོག་རྙེད་ནས་ཞག་དྲུག་ཅུ་པའི་འབྲས་ཆེན་སོགས་ཟས་ངན་ཚོལ་བར་བྱེད་བ་ལྟར། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ལས་དང་པོ་པ་གང་གིས་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ཟབ་མོའི་མདོ་འདི་རྙེད་ནས་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སྒྲུབ་པར་མི་བྱེད་པར། ཉན་རང་དགྲ་བཅོམ་པའི་ས་ཐོབ་བྱེད་ཀྱི་ལམ་སྟོན་པ་ཡི་གཞུང་ལ་བརྟེན་ནས་བླ་མེད་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཚོལ་བར་བྱེད་པ་ནི་གོང་གི་དཔེ་དེ་བཞིིན་སྟེ་འདི་ཡང་བདུད་ཀྱི་ལས་ཡིན་ནོ། །ཞེས་སོ། །
[3-172] translation already produced for this document:
Regarding the falling away from experiencing the joy of the supreme fruit, the excellent taste, the meaning of the occurrence of one verse starting with "For example, someone [finding food with] a hundred tastes..." is: For example, just as someone having found food possessing a hundred tastes does not experience its taste, but having found supreme food seeks out inferior food such as sixty-day rice, whichever beginner bodhisattva, having found this profound sutra of the perfection of wisdom, does not accomplish the enlightenment of a Buddha, but seeks unsurpassable enlightenment relying upon texts that teach the path that brings about the attainment of the level of śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha arhats is like that above example; this too is the action of a mara.

[3-173] source:
རྙེད་པ་དང་བཀུར་སྟི་དང་ཚིགས་སུ་བཅད་པའི་རོ་མྱོང་ཞིང་དེ་ལ་བལྟ་བ་ནི། བསྟི་སྟངས་འདོད་པར་ཞེས་སོགས་རྐང་པ་གཉིས་གསུངས་པའི་དོན། རང་ཉིད་སྙན་པའི་གྲགས་པ་དང་གཞན་གྱིས་བསྟི་སྟངས་དང་བསྙེན་བཀུར་གྱི་རོ་མྱོང་བར་འདོད་པར་འགྱུར་ཞིང་། ཟས་ནོར་སོགས་རྙེད་པར་ཐོབ་པར་འདོད་པར་འགྱུར་བ་དང་གཟུགས་དང་ཡུལ་གྱི་བཀོད་པ་སྣ་ཚོགས་བ་ལྟ་བར་འདོད་པ་དང་བཅས་པའི་སེམས་ཀྱིས་ཁྱིམ་པ་སོགས་དང་འགྲོགས་འདྲིས་བྱེད་པ་དང་ལྡན་ཞིང་བྱ་བ་དུ་མས་གཡེངས་ནས་ཤེར་ཕྱིན་ཉན་པ་སོགས་ལས་ཉམས་པ་ནི་བདུད་ཀྱི་ལས་སོ། །ཞེས་སོ། །
[3-173] translation already produced for this document:
Regarding tasting the flavor of gain, honor, and verses [of praise], and looking for that, the meaning of the occurrence of the two lines starting with "Desiring respect..." is: One will desire fame for oneself and desire to taste the flavor of respect and honor by others, and one will desire to obtain gain such as food and wealth; with a mind possessing the desire to look at forms and various arrangements of objects, one associates and becomes familiar with householders and so forth; and by being distracted by various activities, one falls away from listening to the perfection of wisdom and so forth; this is the action of a mara.

[3-174] source:
ལམ་མ་ཡིན་པ་བདུད་ཀྱིས་བསྟན་པའི་སྡེ་སྣོད་ལས་ཐབས་མཁས་པ་འཚོལ་བ་ནི། ཆོས་བཏང་ནས་ནི་ཞེས་སོགས་རྐང་བ་གཉིས་ཀྱི་དོན། ཐེག་པ་ཆེན་པོའི་ཆོས་ཉམས་སུ་ལེན་པ་བཏང་ནས་ནི་ཆོས་མིན་པའི་འཇིག་རྟེན་གྱི་བྱ་བ་སྣ་ཚོགས་ལ་སྤྱོད་པར་འགྱུར་བ་དང་སངས་རྒྱས་ཐོབ་བྱེད་ཀྱི་ལམ་བཟང་པོ་བོར་ནས་བདུད་ཀྱིས་བསྟན་པའི་ལམ་ངན་དུ་གོལ་ཏེ་འགྲོ་བར་འགྱུར་བ་འདི་ནི་བདུད་ཀྱི་ལས་སོ། །ཞེས་སོ། །
[3-174] translation already produced for this document:
Regarding seeking skillful means from the piṭaka taught by maras, which is a non-path, the meaning of the two lines starting with "Having discarded the dharma..." is: Having discarded practicing the dharma of the Mahayana, one engages in various worldly activities that are not dharma; and having forsaken the excellent path that brings about the attainment of Buddhahood, one deviates and goes onto the bad path taught by maras; this is the action of a mara.

[3-175] source:
ཉན་པ་པོ་འདུན་པ་ཆེ་ཡང་འཆང་བ་པོ་སྙོམས་ལས་ཀྱིས་ཉམས་པས་ཉན་པ་པོ་ཡང་མ་དད་པར་གྱུར་ཏེ་ཆོས་ཉན་པ་ལས་བཟློག་པ་ནི། གང་དག་དེ་ཡི་ཚེ་ཞེས་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གཅིག་གསུངས་པའི་དོན། ཉན་པ་པོ་གང་དག་དོན་གཉེར་ཆེན་པོས་ཤེར་ཕྱིན་གྱི་མདོ་འཆད་པ་པོ་རྙེད་བཀུར་སོགས་ཀྱིས་གཡེང་བར་གྱུར་པ་དེ་ཡི་ཚེ་ན་ཡུམ་ལ་འདུན་ཅིང་དད་པར་གྱུར་ནས་ཆོས་ཀྱི་དམ་པ་འདི་ནི་ཉན་དུ་སོང་བ་ལས། ཉན་པ་པོ་དེ་དག་གིས་ནི་ཆོས་སྨྲ་བ་པོ་དེ་རྙེད་བཀུར་སྙན་གྲགས་ལ་དགའ་བ་སོགས་བྱ་བ་ངན་པ་ལ་ཞེན་ཅིང་ཆགས་པ་དང་ལྡན་པར་རིགས་ནས་ཆོས་ཉན་པ་ལ་དགའ་བ་མེད་ཅིང་མ་དད་པས་ད་ན་ཆོས་ཞུ་བར་མི་བྱའོ་སྙམ་དུ་ཡིད་མི་བདེ་བར་གྱུར་ནས་ཕྱིར་འགྲོ་བ་འདི་ཡང་ཤེར་ཕྱིན་ཉན་པ་སོགས་ཀྱི་བར་ཆད་དུ་འགྱུར་བའི་བདུད་ཀྱི་ལས་སོ། །ཞེས་པའོ། །
[3-175] translation already produced for this document:
Regarding the listener having great aspiration but the holder failing through laziness, causing the listener to also lose faith and turn away from listening to the dharma, the meaning of the occurrence of one verse starting with "Whoever at that time..." is: At that time when the explainer of the perfection of wisdom sutra has become distracted by gain, honor, and so forth, whichever listeners with great pursuit go to listen to this holy dharma, having aspiration and faith in the Mother, those listeners see that the speaker of the dharma possesses adherence and attachment to bad activities such as rejoicing in gain, honor, and fame; and from this, lacking joy in listening to the dharma and lacking faith, they become unhappy, thinking "Now I will not request dharma," and they turn back; this too is an action of a mara that acts as an obstacle to listening to the perfection of wisdom and so forth.

heading: **རྒྱས་པར་བཤད་པ།**
translation: Extensive explanation. Regarding the extensive explanation, it is stated: "The occurrence of Tathāgatas..." up to "...is asserted as four defining characteristics." Regarding that, between the two, the defining characteristics and the divisions,
style_instruction: Translate this passage of a Tibetan Buddhist commentary on the Verse Summary of the Perfection of Wisdom (Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā) into clear, accurate English prose. Translate the whole passage completely and in the same order: do not summarise, shorten or omit anything, and keep the same number of lines as the source. Where the commentary quotes or glosses words of the root verses, keep those quoted words recognisable in the translation. Keep proper names in their standard Sanskrit forms (Subhūti, Śāriputra, Maitreya, Haribhadra) and technical terms recognisable (prajñāpāramitā = perfection of wisdom, bodhisattva). Do not add commentary, notes, or explanation of your own.
context:
A canonical Tibetan Buddhist text, translated block by block from the critical edition in this vault. The blocks below are being translated in order.

Work: ཡོན་ཏན་རིན་པོ་ཆེ་སྡུད་པ་ཚིགས་སུ་བཅད་པའི་འགྲེལ་པ་ཟབ་མོ་རྟེན་འབྱུང་གི་དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཉིད་གསལ་བར་བྱེད་པའི་ནོར་བུའི་སྒྲོན་མེ་སྐལ་བཟང་རེ་སྐོང་། (Khenrab Jamyang, Commentary on the Verses of the Precious Qualities Collection), author: མཁྱེན་རབ་འཇམ་དབྱངས་བློ་བཟང་འཕྲིན་ལས།. A canonical Tibetan text; the blocks below are being translated in order.

Preceding blocks of this same document and their translations — match this terminology, register and line shape:

[3-170] source:
རྒྱུ་མཚན་མངོན་པར་ཞེན་པ་ཉམས་པ་སྟེ་ཆེད་ཆེར་འཛིན་པ་ཉམས་པ་ནི། དེ་ལྟར་མི་ཤེས་ཞེས་སོགས་རྐང་པ་གཉིས་གསུངས་པའི་དོན། ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ནི་ཐེག་ཆེན་ལམ་གྱི་རྩ་བ་ཡིན་པ་དེ་ལྟར། བདུད་ཀྱི་བྱིན་གྱིས་རླབས་པའི་གང་ཟག་མི་ཤེས་པ་རྨོངས་པ་དེ་དག་གིས་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་རྩ་བ་ལྟ་བུའི་ཤེར་ཕྱིན་གྱི་མདོ་སྡེ་རིན་པོ་ཆེ་འདི་བོར་ནས་ནི། རྨོངས་པས་སྒྲིབ་པས་ཡལ་ག་དག་དང་འདབ་མ་དང་འདྲ་བའི་ཉན་ཐོས་ཀྱི་སྡེ་སྣོད་ཚོལ་བར་འགྱུར་བ་འདི་ཡང་བདུད་ཀྱི་ལས་སོ། །ཞེས་པའོ། །
[3-170] translation already produced for this document:
Regarding the falling away of adhering to the reason, that is, the falling away of apprehending excessively, the meaning of the occurrence of the two lines starting with "Thus not knowing..." is: Thus, the perfection of wisdom is the root of the Mahayana path. Those ignorant, bewildered persons who are blessed by maras, having forsaken this precious sutra of the perfection of wisdom which is like the root of a Buddha, will seek out the śrāvaka piṭaka which is like branches and leaves, because they are obscured by bewilderment; this too is the action of a mara.

[3-171] source:
རྣམ་པ་ཐམས་ཅད་དུ་ཐེག་པ་མཆོག་ཏུ་འཛིན་པ་ལས་ཉམས་པ་ནི། གླང་པོ་རྙེད་ཀྱང་ཞེས་སོགས་རྐང་བ་གཉིས་གསུངས་པའི་དོན་ནི། ཇི་ལྟར་ན། གླང་བོ་ཚོལ་བའི་མིས་གླང་པོ་དངོས་རྙེད་ཀྱང་དེ་བཞག་ནས་གླང་པོའི་རྗེས་ནི་ཚོལ་བར་བྱེད་པ་ལྟར་ཐབས་ཤེས་ཆ་ཚང་བར་སྟོན་པའི་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ཐོས་ནས་ནན་ཏན་གྱིས་ཉམས་སུ་ལེན་པར་དོར་ནས། དེ་ལས་གཞན་པའི་དྲང་དོན་གྱི་མདོ་དོན་ཚོལ་བ་ནི། དཔེས་བསྟན་པ་དེ་བཞིན་དུ་ཤེས་པར་བྱ་སྟེ་འདི་ཡང་བདུད་ཀྱི་ལས་ཡིན་ནོ། །
[3-171] translation already produced for this document:
Regarding the falling away from apprehending the supreme vehicle in all aspects, the meaning of the occurrence of the two lines starting with "Even finding an elephant..." is: How is it? Just as a person seeking an elephant, even though they find the actual elephant, leaves it and seeks the elephant's footprints, having heard the perfection of wisdom that teaches means and wisdom completely, one discards practicing it earnestly. Seeking the meaning of sutras of provisional meaning other than that should be known as being like what is taught by the example, so this too is the action of a mara.

[3-172] source:
གྱ་ནོམ་པའི་རོ་འབྲས་བུ་མཆོག་གི་བདེ་བ་མྱོང་བ་ལས་ཉམས་པ་ནི། དཔེར་ན་ལ་ལས་རོ་བརྒྱ་ཞེས་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གཅིག་གསུངས་པའི་དོན། དཔེར་ན་ལ་ལས་རོ་བརྒྱ་དང་ལྡན་པའི་ཁ་ཟས་རྙེད་པ་དེའི་རོ་མི་མྱོང་བར་ཟས་མཆོག་རྙེད་ནས་ཞག་དྲུག་ཅུ་པའི་འབྲས་ཆེན་སོགས་ཟས་ངན་ཚོལ་བར་བྱེད་བ་ལྟར། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ལས་དང་པོ་པ་གང་གིས་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ཟབ་མོའི་མདོ་འདི་རྙེད་ནས་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སྒྲུབ་པར་མི་བྱེད་པར། ཉན་རང་དགྲ་བཅོམ་པའི་ས་ཐོབ་བྱེད་ཀྱི་ལམ་སྟོན་པ་ཡི་གཞུང་ལ་བརྟེན་ནས་བླ་མེད་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཚོལ་བར་བྱེད་པ་ནི་གོང་གི་དཔེ་དེ་བཞིིན་སྟེ་འདི་ཡང་བདུད་ཀྱི་ལས་ཡིན་ནོ། །ཞེས་སོ། །
[3-172] translation already produced for this document:
Regarding the falling away from experiencing the joy of the supreme fruit, the excellent taste, the meaning of the occurrence of one verse starting with "For example, someone [finding food with] a hundred tastes..." is: For example, just as someone having found food possessing a hundred tastes does not experience its taste, but having found supreme food seeks out inferior food such as sixty-day rice, whichever beginner bodhisattva, having found this profound sutra of the perfection of wisdom, does not accomplish the enlightenment of a Buddha, but seeks unsurpassable enlightenment relying upon texts that teach the path that brings about the attainment of the level of śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha arhats is like that above example; this too is the action of a mara.

[3-173] source:
རྙེད་པ་དང་བཀུར་སྟི་དང་ཚིགས་སུ་བཅད་པའི་རོ་མྱོང་ཞིང་དེ་ལ་བལྟ་བ་ནི། བསྟི་སྟངས་འདོད་པར་ཞེས་སོགས་རྐང་པ་གཉིས་གསུངས་པའི་དོན། རང་ཉིད་སྙན་པའི་གྲགས་པ་དང་གཞན་གྱིས་བསྟི་སྟངས་དང་བསྙེན་བཀུར་གྱི་རོ་མྱོང་བར་འདོད་པར་འགྱུར་ཞིང་། ཟས་ནོར་སོགས་རྙེད་པར་ཐོབ་པར་འདོད་པར་འགྱུར་བ་དང་གཟུགས་དང་ཡུལ་གྱི་བཀོད་པ་སྣ་ཚོགས་བ་ལྟ་བར་འདོད་པ་དང་བཅས་པའི་སེམས་ཀྱིས་ཁྱིམ་པ་སོགས་དང་འགྲོགས་འདྲིས་བྱེད་པ་དང་ལྡན་ཞིང་བྱ་བ་དུ་མས་གཡེངས་ནས་ཤེར་ཕྱིན་ཉན་པ་སོགས་ལས་ཉམས་པ་ནི་བདུད་ཀྱི་ལས་སོ། །ཞེས་སོ། །
[3-173] translation already produced for this document:
Regarding tasting the flavor of gain, honor, and verses [of praise], and looking for that, the meaning of the occurrence of the two lines starting with "Desiring respect..." is: One will desire fame for oneself and desire to taste the flavor of respect and honor by others, and one will desire to obtain gain such as food and wealth; with a mind possessing the desire to look at forms and various arrangements of objects, one associates and becomes familiar with householders and so forth; and by being distracted by various activities, one falls away from listening to the perfection of wisdom and so forth; this is the action of a mara.

[3-174] source:
ལམ་མ་ཡིན་པ་བདུད་ཀྱིས་བསྟན་པའི་སྡེ་སྣོད་ལས་ཐབས་མཁས་པ་འཚོལ་བ་ནི། ཆོས་བཏང་ནས་ནི་ཞེས་སོགས་རྐང་བ་གཉིས་ཀྱི་དོན། ཐེག་པ་ཆེན་པོའི་ཆོས་ཉམས་སུ་ལེན་པ་བཏང་ནས་ནི་ཆོས་མིན་པའི་འཇིག་རྟེན་གྱི་བྱ་བ་སྣ་ཚོགས་ལ་སྤྱོད་པར་འགྱུར་བ་དང་སངས་རྒྱས་ཐོབ་བྱེད་ཀྱི་ལམ་བཟང་པོ་བོར་ནས་བདུད་ཀྱིས་བསྟན་པའི་ལམ་ངན་དུ་གོལ་ཏེ་འགྲོ་བར་འགྱུར་བ་འདི་ནི་བདུད་ཀྱི་ལས་སོ། །ཞེས་སོ། །
[3-174] translation already produced for this document:
Regarding seeking skillful means from the piṭaka taught by maras, which is a non-path, the meaning of the two lines starting with "Having discarded the dharma..." is: Having discarded practicing the dharma of the Mahayana, one engages in various worldly activities that are not dharma; and having forsaken the excellent path that brings about the attainment of Buddhahood, one deviates and goes onto the bad path taught by maras; this is the action of a mara.

[3-175] source:
ཉན་པ་པོ་འདུན་པ་ཆེ་ཡང་འཆང་བ་པོ་སྙོམས་ལས་ཀྱིས་ཉམས་པས་ཉན་པ་པོ་ཡང་མ་དད་པར་གྱུར་ཏེ་ཆོས་ཉན་པ་ལས་བཟློག་པ་ནི། གང་དག་དེ་ཡི་ཚེ་ཞེས་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གཅིག་གསུངས་པའི་དོན། ཉན་པ་པོ་གང་དག་དོན་གཉེར་ཆེན་པོས་ཤེར་ཕྱིན་གྱི་མདོ་འཆད་པ་པོ་རྙེད་བཀུར་སོགས་ཀྱིས་གཡེང་བར་གྱུར་པ་དེ་ཡི་ཚེ་ན་ཡུམ་ལ་འདུན་ཅིང་དད་པར་གྱུར་ནས་ཆོས་ཀྱི་དམ་པ་འདི་ནི་ཉན་དུ་སོང་བ་ལས། ཉན་པ་པོ་དེ་དག་གིས་ནི་ཆོས་སྨྲ་བ་པོ་དེ་རྙེད་བཀུར་སྙན་གྲགས་ལ་དགའ་བ་སོགས་བྱ་བ་ངན་པ་ལ་ཞེན་ཅིང་ཆགས་པ་དང་ལྡན་པར་རིགས་ནས་ཆོས་ཉན་པ་ལ་དགའ་བ་མེད་ཅིང་མ་དད་པས་ད་ན་ཆོས་ཞུ་བར་མི་བྱའོ་སྙམ་དུ་ཡིད་མི་བདེ་བར་གྱུར་ནས་ཕྱིར་འགྲོ་བ་འདི་ཡང་ཤེར་ཕྱིན་ཉན་པ་སོགས་ཀྱི་བར་ཆད་དུ་འགྱུར་བའི་བདུད་ཀྱི་ལས་སོ། །ཞེས་པའོ། །
[3-175] translation already produced for this document:
Regarding the listener having great aspiration but the holder failing through laziness, causing the listener to also lose faith and turn away from listening to the dharma, the meaning of the occurrence of one verse starting with "Whoever at that time..." is: At that time when the explainer of the perfection of wisdom sutra has become distracted by gain, honor, and so forth, whichever listeners with great pursuit go to listen to this holy dharma, having aspiration and faith in the Mother, those listeners see that the speaker of the dharma possesses adherence and attachment to bad activities such as rejoicing in gain, honor, and fame; and from this, lacking joy in listening to the dharma and lacking faith, they become unhappy, thinking "Now I will not request dharma," and they turn back; this too is an action of a mara that acts as an obstacle to listening to the perfection of wisdom and so forth.

heading: **མཚན་ཉིད།**
translation: Defining characteristics. First, a bodhisattva's yoga embraced by the union of calm abiding and special insight, which has become a method that acts to attain the perfection of wisdom which is the result to be accomplished by it, is the defining characteristic of the yoga of the path perfection of wisdom. This is the general defining characteristic of the application; as for the definiendum, in general terms it is the yoga of the path perfection of wisdom itself; and here, the "application" in "the defining characteristics of the application" is also the path perfection of wisdom itself, and its defining characteristics are called the defining characteristics of the application.
style_instruction: Translate this passage of a Tibetan Buddhist commentary on the Verse Summary of the Perfection of Wisdom (Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā) into clear, accurate English prose. Translate the whole passage completely and in the same order: do not summarise, shorten or omit anything, and keep the same number of lines as the source. [3-176] translation already produced for this document:
Regarding summarizing their meaning, the meaning of the occurrence of the four verses starting with "At that time..." is: At that time of listening to the sutra of the perfection of wisdom and so forth, these actions of a mara that act as obstacles to the application, such as not possessing the gathering for explaining and listening, will occur. If one asks what those are: At that time of listening to and reflecting upon this dharma and so forth, those sinful maras who are hostile to the dharma will become tormented by suffering and pain; and they, having disturbed the mind-streams of many bhikshus who hold this sutra, by means of various types of methods of making obstacles, many types of dharma that act as obstacles causing one not to hold and reflect upon the meaning of this perfection of wisdom and so forth, which are not explained here, as well as many others, will also occur; one should know all such obstacles to be from maras. Thus also, from the Gaganagañja Sutra: "Son of noble family, engaging in whatever non-virtuous dharmas and discarding whatever virtuous dharmas should all be known as the actions of a mara." Regarding establishing the reason for there being many obstacles by means of an example: Just as whoever has found invaluable things such as a jewel king, they are rare because they are very difficult to find; and at all times of having found and holding them, harms by enemies, thieves, and so forth are also always abundant; similarly, the supreme dharma of the Mother of the Conquerors, the perfection of wisdom, which is invaluable like a precious jewel, is also very rare, and because the dharma is profound, harms are also always abundant. In order to make obstacles for whichever sentient being of small intellect, a beginner newly entered into the Mahayana, who has not previously found such a very rare and profound dharma as this precious sutra of the perfection of wisdom—that is, who has not brought it into their experience—maras will become joyful and will initiate obstacles.

The antidotes that eliminate. Second, regarding the antidotes that eliminate, the meaning of the occurrence of the five lines starting with "The Buddhas of the ten directions..." is: Even though there are many obstacles like that, they will not find an opportunity. If one asks why: Because the Buddhas of the ten directions, whose power that mara exerting himself like that in obstacles is unable to rival even by a fraction, perform the three—guarding, protecting, and hiding—from those obstacles, and thereby apply one to fully holding the perfection of wisdom.
