translation: Divisions. Second, regarding dividing that, there are ninety-one, because there are forty-eight defining characteristics of knowledge that define the application of the three knowledges, sixteen distinguishing defining characteristics that define the application which is particularly superior to the application of sravakas and pratyekabuddhas, eleven defining characteristics of action that define the application possessing the special action of accomplishing the welfare of others, and sixteen defining characteristics of entity. Among the three even within the first, regarding teaching the first, the sixteen defining characteristics of knowledge of the knowledge of bases, such as the defining characteristic of knowledge of knowing the occurrence of Tathagatas, the meaning of the occurrence of the two verses starting with "Whichever past..." is: If one calls this perfection of wisdom the Mother of the Conquerors, if one asks what the manner of its being a mother is: just as in the world, because of giving birth to a son and establishing him in his activities, one is posited as a mother, similarly, whatever Buddhas are past because they have already appeared previously, whatever present Bhagavan Buddhas, protectors of the world, there are residing in the fields of the ten directions, and whatever Buddhas will occur in future times, because they all arise from this very perfection of wisdom, it has become the Mother of all the Conquerors of the three times. By this, the defining characteristic of knowledge of knowing the occurrence of Tathagatas is taught. That the Buddhas, having seen the reality of the world—that is, all dharmas subsumed by aggregates, constituents, and sense sources—just as it is, teach it to other disciples, also arose in dependence upon this very perfection of wisdom, the generating Mother of the Conquerors. The limitless infinite behaviors of the minds of others in the realms of sentient beings—withdrawn inward, distracted outward, associated with attachment, free from attachment, and so forth—this Mother entirely teaches to her sons, the noble Buddhas; and since the suchness of the five aggregates of the world, the suchness of sravaka arhats, the suchness of pratyekabuddhas, and the suchness of bodhisattvas, the sons of the Conquerors, are not established as different entities, they are exactly the same; since they are all not other than the dharmadhatu of the same type devoid of truly established entities, they are the same suchness; one should know that such reality, the suchness of the perfection of wisdom, the Tathagatas knew, realized just as it is, and taught to others. By these words of the sutra, one should know that mostly the defining characteristics of knowledge, such as knowing the non-destruction of the world and knowing the behavior of the minds of sentient beings, are explicitly taught in the literal words.

Regarding summarizing their meaning, the meaning of the occurrence of the four verses starting with "At that time..." is: At that time of listening to the sutra of the perfection of wisdom and so forth, these actions of a mara that act as obstacles to the application, such as not possessing the gathering for explaining and listening, will occur. If one asks what those are: At that time of listening to and reflecting upon this dharma and so forth, those sinful maras who are hostile to the dharma will become tormented by suffering and pain; and they, having disturbed the mind-streams of many bhikshus who hold this sutra, by means of various types of methods of making obstacles, many types of dharma that act as obstacles causing one not to hold and reflect upon the meaning of this perfection of wisdom and so forth, which are not explained here, as well as many others, will also occur; one should know all such obstacles to be from maras. Thus also, from the Gaganagañja Sutra: "Son of noble family, engaging in whatever non-virtuous dharmas and discarding whatever virtuous dharmas should all be known as the actions of a mara." Regarding establishing the reason for there being many obstacles by means of an example: Just as whoever has found invaluable things such as a jewel king, they are rare because they are very difficult to find; and at all times of having found and holding them, harms by enemies, thieves, and so forth are also always abundant; similarly, the supreme dharma of the Mother of the Conquerors, the perfection of wisdom, which is invaluable like a precious jewel, is also very rare, and because the dharma is profound, harms are also always abundant. In order to make obstacles for whichever sentient being of small intellect, a beginner newly entered into the Mahayana, who has not previously found such a very rare and profound dharma as this precious sutra of the perfection of wisdom—that is, who has not brought it into their experience—maras will become joyful and will initiate obstacles.

The antidotes that eliminate. Second, regarding the antidotes that eliminate, the meaning of the occurrence of the five lines starting with "The Buddhas of the ten directions..." is: Even though there are many obstacles like that, they will not find an opportunity. If one asks why: Because the Buddhas of the ten directions, whose power that mara exerting himself like that in obstacles is unable to rival even by a fraction, perform the three—guarding, protecting, and hiding—from those obstacles, and thereby apply one to fully holding the perfection of wisdom. From the commentary on the Verses of the Precious Qualities Collection, Clarifying the Suchness of Profound Dependent Arising, Fulfilling the Hopes of the Fortunate, this is the commentary on the eleventh chapter, the chapter on Maras.

translation: Second, regarding teaching the defining characteristics of knowledge of the knowledge of paths, such as emptiness and signlessness, the meaning of the three verses starting with "World of the wise..." is: Whether they are the Bhagavan Buddhas who are wise in the meaning of reality who will occur in the future, or whether they are currently living, maintaining, and abiding in this world system, or have passed into nirvana, this flawless dharmata which is pure from the very beginning, the natural emptiness of dharmas, which cannot be transformed by anyone and is never changing, remains like space as the nature of a non-affirming negation posited merely from the aspect of having negated the object of negation, true establishment; because "bodhisattvas," that is, bodhisattvas, having unmistakably realized this reality, suchness free from proliferations, and practiced it in the union of method and wisdom, one day when their realization reaches culmination, because they have gone or realized the suchness of all dharmas just as it is, the Buddhas have come to be addressed by the name "Tathagata."

Defining characteristics. First, a bodhisattva's yoga embraced by the union of calm abiding and special insight, which has become a method that acts to attain the perfection of wisdom which is the result to be accomplished by it, is the defining characteristic of the yoga of the path perfection of wisdom. Divisions. Second, regarding dividing that, there are ninety-one, because there are forty-eight defining characteristics of knowledge that define the application of the three knowledges, sixteen distinguishing defining characteristics that define the application which is particularly superior to the application of sravakas and pratyekabuddhas, eleven defining characteristics of action that define the application possessing the special action of accomplishing the welfare of others, and sixteen defining characteristics of entity. Among the three even within the first, regarding teaching the first, the sixteen defining characteristics of knowledge of the knowledge of bases, such as the defining characteristic of knowledge of knowing the occurrence of Tathagatas, the meaning of the occurrence of the two verses starting with "Whichever past..." is: If one calls this perfection of wisdom the Mother of the Conquerors, if one asks what the manner of its being a mother is: just as in the world, because of giving birth to a son and establishing him in his activities, one is posited as a mother, similarly, whatever Buddhas are past because they have already appeared previously, whatever present Bhagavan Buddhas, protectors of the world, there are residing in the fields of the ten directions, and whatever Buddhas will occur in future times, because they all arise from this very perfection of wisdom, it has become the Mother of all the Conquerors of the three times. By this, the defining characteristic of knowledge of knowing the occurrence of Tathagatas is taught. That the Buddhas, having seen the reality of the world—that is, all dharmas subsumed by aggregates, constituents, and sense sources—just as it is, teach it to other disciples, also arose in dependence upon this very perfection of wisdom, the generating Mother of the Conquerors. The limitless infinite behaviors of the minds of others in the realms of sentient beings—withdrawn inward, distracted outward, associated with attachment, free from attachment, and so forth—this Mother entirely teaches to her sons, the noble Buddhas; and since the suchness of the five aggregates of the world, the suchness of sravaka arhats, the suchness of pratyekabuddhas, and the suchness of bodhisattvas, the sons of the Conquerors, are not established as different entities, they are exactly the same; since they are all not other than the dharmadhatu of the same type devoid of truly established entities, they are the same suchness; one should know that such reality, the suchness of the perfection of wisdom, the Tathagatas knew, realized just as it is, and taught to others. By these words of the sutra, one should know that mostly the defining characteristics of knowledge, such as knowing the non-destruction of the world and knowing the behavior of the minds of sentient beings, are explicitly taught in the literal words.

heading: **དབྱེ་བ།**
translation: If one asks, "Having realized all dharmas to be empty by nature, what is the manner in which they accomplish the welfare of sentient beings?", this relying upon and abiding in the perfection of wisdom, which is like a divine grove of joy where infinite uncontaminated joy arises, is the domain of the guides, the Buddhas endowed with the ten powers and four fearlessnesses; for although they completely rescue infinite sentient beings from the many sufferings of samsara such as birth, aging, sickness, and death, and from the three bad migrations, for those Buddhas the apprehension of them as truly existent sentient beings will never arise at any time, but rather, while remaining in meditative equipoise on dharmata, the welfare of others occurs effortlessly and spontaneously.

Divisions. Second, regarding dividing that, there are ninety-one, because there are forty-eight defining characteristics of knowledge that define the application of the three knowledges, sixteen distinguishing defining characteristics that define the application which is particularly superior to the application of sravakas and pratyekabuddhas, eleven defining characteristics of action that define the application possessing the special action of accomplishing the welfare of others, and sixteen defining characteristics of entity. Among the three even within the first, regarding teaching the first, the sixteen defining characteristics of knowledge of the knowledge of bases, such as the defining characteristic of knowledge of knowing the occurrence of Tathagatas, the meaning of the occurrence of the two verses starting with "Whichever past..." is: If one calls this perfection of wisdom the Mother of the Conquerors, if one asks what the manner of its being a mother is: just as in the world, because of giving birth to a son and establishing him in his activities, one is posited as a mother, similarly, whatever Buddhas are past because they have already appeared previously, whatever present Bhagavan Buddhas, protectors of the world, there are residing in the fields of the ten directions, and whatever Buddhas will occur in future times, because they all arise from this very perfection of wisdom, it has become the Mother of all the Conquerors of the three times. By this, the defining characteristic of knowledge of knowing the occurrence of Tathagatas is taught. That the Buddhas, having seen the reality of the world—that is, all dharmas subsumed by aggregates, constituents, and sense sources—just as it is, teach it to other disciples, also arose in dependence upon this very perfection of wisdom, the generating Mother of the Conquerors. The limitless infinite behaviors of the minds of others in the realms of sentient beings—withdrawn inward, distracted outward, associated with attachment, free from attachment, and so forth—this Mother entirely teaches to her sons, the noble Buddhas; and since the suchness of the five aggregates of the world, the suchness of sravaka arhats, the suchness of pratyekabuddhas, and the suchness of bodhisattvas, the sons of the Conquerors, are not established as different entities, they are exactly the same; since they are all not other than the dharmadhatu of the same type devoid of truly established entities, they are the same suchness; one should know that such reality, the suchness of the perfection of wisdom, the Tathagatas knew, realized just as it is, and taught to others. By these words of the sutra, one should know that mostly the defining characteristics of knowledge, such as knowing the non-destruction of the world and knowing the behavior of the minds of sentient beings, are explicitly taught in the literal words.

heading: **དབྱེ་བ།**
translation: As for the manner of vanquishing opponents and teaching the dharma of profound emptiness, it is, for example, like the king of beasts, the lion, who, relying upon and abiding in the valleys of snow mountains, without fearing any animal, terrifies many wild beasts such as tigers, leopards, bears, and brown bears, as well as minor animals, and lets out a roar; similarly, the lions among men, the Buddhas, also relying on the meaning of profound emptiness, the perfection of wisdom, terrify the many tirthikas who have fallen into the abyss of the view of a self, and roar the wondrous and vast roar of the ultimate dharma in the world. Furthermore, the bodhisattvas themselves attain Buddhahood by perfecting the ways of the three doors of liberation, and although they rescue infinite sentient beings from the sufferings of the bad migrations, because the apprehension of suffering and sentient beings as ultimately established does not arise, complete non-affliction, non-purification, non-entity, non-nature, and non-support and so forth are taught.

If one asks why all the Buddhas keep them in mind and protect them, establishing that very thing by means of an example is: For example, if a mother becomes ill, all of her many sons will be unhappy, and they will perform services for that mother such as seeking a doctor who removes the illness; similarly, all those Bhagavan Buddhas of the world systems in the ten directions also exert themselves in order to remove the actions of maras and keep in mind this generation of bodhicitta and holy wisdom realizing emptiness which have become their own respective generating Mothers.

[3-181] translation already produced for this document:
Defining characteristics. First, a bodhisattva's yoga embraced by the union of calm abiding and special insight, which has become a method that acts to attain the perfection of wisdom which is the result to be accomplished by it, is the defining characteristic of the yoga of the path perfection of wisdom. This is the general defining characteristic of the application; as for the definiendum, in general terms it is the yoga of the path perfection of wisdom itself; and here, the "application" in "the defining characteristics of the application" is also the path perfection of wisdom itself, and its defining characteristics are called the defining characteristics of the application.

[3-182] translation already produced for this document:
Divisions. Second, regarding dividing that, there are ninety-one, because there are forty-eight defining characteristics of knowledge that define the application of the three knowledges, sixteen distinguishing defining characteristics that define the application which is particularly superior to the application of sravakas and pratyekabuddhas, eleven defining characteristics of action that define the application possessing the special action of accomplishing the welfare of others, and sixteen defining characteristics of entity. Among the three even within the first, regarding teaching the first, the sixteen defining characteristics of knowledge of the knowledge of bases, such as the defining characteristic of knowledge of knowing the occurrence of Tathagatas, the meaning of the occurrence of the two verses starting with "Whichever past..." is: If one calls this perfection of wisdom the Mother of the Conquerors, if one asks what the manner of its being a mother is: just as in the world, because of giving birth to a son and establishing him in his activities, one is posited as a mother, similarly, whatever Buddhas are past because they have already appeared previously, whatever present Bhagavan Buddhas, protectors of the world, there are residing in the fields of the ten directions, and whatever Buddhas will occur in future times, because they all arise from this very perfection of wisdom, it has become the Mother of all the Conquerors of the three times. By this, the defining characteristic of knowledge of knowing the occurrence of Tathagatas is taught. That the Buddhas, having seen the reality of the world—that is, all dharmas subsumed by aggregates, constituents, and sense sources—just as it is, teach it to other disciples, also arose in dependence upon this very perfection of wisdom, the generating Mother of the Conquerors. The limitless infinite behaviors of the minds of others in the realms of sentient beings—withdrawn inward, distracted outward, associated with attachment, free from attachment, and so forth—this Mother entirely teaches to her sons, the noble Buddhas; and since the suchness of the five aggregates of the world, the suchness of sravaka arhats, the suchness of pratyekabuddhas, and the suchness of bodhisattvas, the sons of the Conquerors, are not established as different entities, they are exactly the same; since they are all not other than the dharmadhatu of the same type devoid of truly established entities, they are the same suchness; one should know that such reality, the suchness of the perfection of wisdom, the Tathagatas knew, realized just as it is, and taught to others. By these words of the sutra, one should know that mostly the defining characteristics of knowledge, such as knowing the non-destruction of the world and knowing the behavior of the minds of sentient beings, are explicitly taught in the literal words.

heading: **དབྱེ་བ།**
source: གསུམ་པ་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་མཐོང་ཆོས་ལ་བདེ་བར་གནས་པ་སོགས་རྣམ་མཁྱེན་གྱི་ཤེས་མཚན་སྟོན་པར། དཔེར་ན་ནམ་མཁའ་གནས་པའི་ཞེས་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གསུམ་གསུངས་པའི་དོན། དཔེར་ན་ནམ་མཁར་གནས་པའི་ཉི་མའི་འོད་ཟེར་གྱིས་ནི་ས་འདི་ལ་རླན་གཤེར་ཡོད་པ་སྐེམ་པར་བྱེད་ཅིང་མུན་པ་བསལ་ནས་གཟུགས་རྣམས་ཀྱང་རབ་ཏུ་སྟོན་པར་བྱེད་པའི་བྱེད་ལས་གཉིས་དང་ལྡན་པ་དེ་བཞིན་དུ་ཆོས་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་པོ་སངས་རྒྱས་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་སྨྲ་བའི་ཉི་མས་ཀྱང་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ནམ་མཁའ་ལྟ་བུ་ལ་བརྟེན་ནས་ཟབ་པ་དང་རྒྱ་ཆེ་བའི་ཆོས་ཀྱི་འོད་ཟེར་རྣོན་པོས་སྲིད་པའི་སྲེད་པ་སོགས་ཉེས་པའི་ཆུ་ཀླུང་མཐའ་དག་སྐེམས་ཤིང་ཡོན་ཏན་ཐམས་ཅད་འཕེལ་བར་བྱེད་པའི་ཆོས་རྣམས་ཀྱང་ཡང་དག་པར་རབ་ཏུ་སྟོན་པར་མཛད་དོ། །ཇི་ལྟར་ཆོས་ཉིད་སྟོན་ཅེ་ན། དོན་དམ་དཔྱོད་པའི་རིགས་ཤེས་ཀྱིས་ཕུང་པོ་ལྔའི་གནས་ལུགས་བཙལ་བའི་ཚེ་གཟུགས་རྣམས་དམིགས་སུ་མེད་པས་མི་མཐོང་ལ། དེ་བཞིན་དུ་ཚོར་བ་དག་ཀྱང་མི་མཐོང་ཞིང་། འདུ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་ངོ་བོའང་མཐོང་བ་མེད་ལ་སེམས་པ་མི་མཐོང་ཞིང་།ཆོས་ཉིད་ལ་བརྩེ་གཅིག་ཏུ་མཉམ་པར་བཞག་པའི་འཕགས་པའི་མཉམ་བཞག་ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱིས་ཆོས་ཉིད་གཟིགས་པའི་གཟིགས་ངོར་གང་ལ་རྣམ་པར་ཤེས་པ་དང་སེམས་དང་ཡིད་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ཅི་ཡང་མཐོང་བ་མེད་པ་འདི་ནི་ཕུང་པོ་ལྔའི་གནས་ལུགས་ཆོས་ཉིད་དེ་བཞིན་ཉིད་མཐོང་བ་ཡིན་ཞེས་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་བསྟན་ཏེ། དེ་ཡངདཔེ་ཇི་ལྟ་བུ་ཞེ་ན། འཇིག་རྟེན་པ་དག་གིས་ནམ་མཁའ་མཐོང་ཞེས་ཡིད་ལ་བསམ་ཞིང་སེམས་ཅན་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་ཚིག་ཏུ་རབ་ཏུ་བརྗོད་པ་ནི་ཡོད་མོད་ཀྱི་འོན་ཀྱང་ནམ་མཁའ་ཇི་ལྟར་མཐོང་བར་ནུས་ཞེས་དོན་འདི་ལ་རང་གིས་བརྟག་པར་བགྱིས་དང་། ནམ་མཁའ་ཐོགས་པའི་རེག་བྱ་བཅད་ཙམ་ཡིན་པས་དགག་བྱ་སྒྲིབ་ཐོགས་ཡོད་ན་དམིགས་སུ་རུང་བ་ལས་དེ་མ་མཐོང་པ་ལ་ནམ་མཁའ་མཐོང་ཞེས་བརྗོད་པ་དེ་ལྟར་གཟུགས་ལ་སོགས་པའི་ཆོས་ཉིད་མཐོང་ཞེས་པའང་རིགས་ཤེས་ཀྱིས་བཙལ་བ་ན་གཟུགས་སོགས་མ་རྙེད་པའམ་མ་མཐོང་བ་ནི། དེ་དག་གི་གནས་ལུགས་དེ་བཞིན་ཉིད་མཐོང་བ་ཡིན་ཞེས་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་བསྟན་པ་ཡིན་ལ། མཉམ་བཞག་རྣམ་པར་མི་རྟོག་པའི་ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱིས་ཆོས་ཉིད་མཐོང་བའམ་གཟིགས་ཚུལ་དཔེ་གཞན་གྱིས་ནི་བསྙད་པར་ནུས་པ་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །ཞེས་པ་སྟེ། ཊིཀ་ཆེན་དགོངས་པ་རབ་གསལ་ལས། མི་མཐོང་བ་ཕུང་པ་ོལྔ་དང་། མཐོང་བ་ནི་ཆོས་ཞེས་གསུངས་ལ། དེ་ནི་ཁོ་ན་ཉིད་ཀྱི་དོན་ཏེ་སུས་རྟེན་འབྲེལ་མ་མཐོང་བ་དེས་ཆོས་མཐོང་ངོ་ཞེས་གསུངས་པ་བཞིན་ནོ། །ཞེས་དང་། ཇི་ལྟ་བ་མཁྱེན་པའི་ཡེ་ཤེས་དེས་ཕུང་སོགས་ཀྱི་དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཉིད་མངོན་སུམ་དུ་གཟིགས་པའི་ཕྱིར་དང་། ཕུང་སོགས་རྣམས་གཟིགས་ངོར་མ་གྲུབ་པ་དེ་དག་གི་དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཉིད་ཡིན་པའི་ཕྱིར་དང་། ཕུང་སོགས་མ་གཟིགས་པའི་ཚུལ་གྱིས་དེ་དག་གི་དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཉིད་གཟིགས་དགོས་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཏེ། རང་འགྲེལ་ལས། དངོས་པོ་བྱས་པ་ཅན་ལ་མ་རེག་པར་རང་བཞིན་འབའ་ཞིག་མངོན་སུམ་དུ་མཛད་པས། དེ་ཉིད་ཐུགས་སུ་ཆུད་པའི་ཕྱིར་སངས་རྒྱས་ཞེས་བརྗོད་དོ། །ཞེས་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་དོན་དམ་མཁྱེན་པའི་ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱིས་ཆོས་ཅན་ལ་མ་རེག་པར་ཆོས་ཉིད་འབབ་ཞིག་ཐུགས་སུ་ཆུད་པར་གསུངས་ཏེ། ཕུང་སོགས་མ་གཟིགས་པའི་ཚུལ་གྱིས་དེ་དག་གི་དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཉིད་གཟིགས་པར་གསུངས་པ་དང་དོན་གཅིག་གོ །མཐོང་བ་མེད་པ་ནི་མཐོང་བ་དམ་པའོ། །ཞེས་གསུངས་པའི་དོན་ཡང༌། ཅི་ཡང་མ་མཐོང་བ་མཐོང་བ་མི་བཞེད་ཀྱི། སྔར་བཤད་པ་ལྟར་སྤྲོས་མ་མཐོང་བ་སྤྲོས་བྲལ་མཐོང་བར་འཇོག་པས། མཐོང་མ་མཐོང་གཞི་གཅིག་ལ་བྱེད་པ་མིན་ནོ། །ཞེས་གསུངས་སོ། །བུདྡྷ་ཤྲཱིས་གཟུགས་རྣམས་མི་མཐོང་ཞེས་སོགས་ཁྱད་མཚན་ལ་མར་སྦྱར་ཡང༌། སློབ་དཔོན་གྱིས་ཤེས་མཚན་ལ་སྦྱར་བ་ཉི་ཁྲི་དང་བརྒྱད་སྟོང་སོགས་དང་ཤིན་ཏུ་འགྲིགས་ཞེས་གུང་ཐང་འཇམ་པའི་དབྱངས་ཀྱི་གསུངས་སོ། །ཡོན་ཏན་རིན་པོ་ཆེ་སྡུད་པ་ཚིགས་སུ་བཅད་པའི་འགྲེལ་བ་ཟབ་མོ་རྟེན་འབྱུང་གི་དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཉིད་གསལ་བར་བྱེད་པའི་ནོར་བུའི་སྒྲོན་མེ་སྐལ་བཟང་རེ་སྐོང་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལས་འཇིག་རྟེན་བསྟན་པའི་ལེའུ་སྟེ་བཅུ་གཉིས་པའི་འགྲེལ་པའོ༎  །།
translation: Third, regarding teaching the defining characteristics of knowledge of omniscience, such as the Tathagata dwelling blissfully in the seen dharma, the meaning of the three verses starting with "For example, abiding in the sky..." is: For example, just as the rays of the sun "abiding in the sky" possess the two functions of drying up whatever moisture there is on this earth and, having dispelled darkness, "thoroughly illuminating forms"; similarly, the sun of speech, the Dharma king, the Bhagavan Buddha, also relying upon the sky-like perfection of wisdom, with the sharp light rays of the profound and vast dharma dries up all the rivers of faults such as craving for existence, and correctly "thoroughly illuminates" all the dharmas that cause all qualities to increase. If one asks, "How does he teach dharmata?" When searching for the reality of the five aggregates with rational knowledge that analyzes the ultimate, because forms are without apprehension, one "does not see" them; likewise, one "does not see feelings," one "does not see the nature of discrimination either," one "does not see compositional factors," and in the perspective of the noble one's pristine wisdom of meditative equipoise that is single-pointedly resting in equipoise on dharmata, seeing dharmata, "not seeing anything whatsoever called consciousness, mind, and intellect"—this is the seeing of the reality of the five aggregates, dharmata, suchness, so the Tathagata taught. Furthermore, if one asks what kind of example this is like: Although worldly people think in their minds "we see the sky" and sentient beings "thoroughly express" this in words, examine this point for yourself: "how can the sky be seen?" Because the sky is merely the elimination of obstructive tangible contact, if the object of negation, obstructive covering, existed, it would be suitable to be apprehended; but not seeing that is expressed as "seeing the sky." Similarly, saying "seeing the dharmata of forms and so forth" means that when searching with rational knowledge, not finding or "not seeing" forms and so forth is what the Tathagata taught as seeing their reality, suchness; and this manner of seeing or perceiving dharmata with the non-conceptual pristine wisdom of meditative equipoise "cannot be expressed by another example." From the Great Commentary, Illumination of the Thought: "It is said that what is not seen is the five aggregates, and what is seen is dharma; that is the meaning of reality, just as it is said, 'Whoever does not see dependent origination, they see dharma.'" And: "Because that pristine wisdom which knows reality just as it is directly sees the reality of the aggregates and so forth; and because the aggregates and so forth not being established in the perspective of seeing is their reality; and because by way of not seeing the aggregates and so forth one must see their reality. For, from the Auto-commentary: 'Because, without touching conditioned entities, only the nature is directly realized, and thus reality is understood, one is called a Buddha.' Thus it is said that the Buddha's pristine wisdom knowing the ultimate, without touching the subjects, understands only dharmata; this is synonymous with the statement that by way of not seeing the aggregates and so forth, their reality is seen. Furthermore, the meaning of the statement, 'Non-seeing is the supreme seeing': not seeing anything at all is not considered seeing, but rather, as explained before, not seeing proliferations is posited as seeing freedom from proliferations; therefore, seeing and not seeing do not refer to a single basis." So it is said. Although Buddhaśrī applied "not seeing forms" and so forth to the defining characteristics of superiority, the Master applying it to the defining characteristics of knowledge accords extremely well with the Twenty-five Thousand and the Eight Thousand, so said Gungtang Jamyang. This is the commentary on the twelfth chapter, "Teaching the World," from the Commentary on the Verses of the Precious Qualities Collection, called "The Jewelled Lamp Clarifying the Reality of Profound Dependent Origination, Fulfilling the Hopes of the Fortunate."

Second, regarding teaching the defining characteristics of knowledge of the knowledge of paths, such as emptiness and signlessness, the meaning of the three verses starting with "World of the wise..." is: Whether they are the Bhagavan Buddhas who are wise in the meaning of reality who will occur in the future, or whether they are currently living, maintaining, and abiding in this world system, or have passed into nirvana, this flawless dharmata which is pure from the very beginning, the natural emptiness of dharmas, which cannot be transformed by anyone and is never changing, remains like space as the nature of a non-affirming negation posited merely from the aspect of having negated the object of negation, true establishment; because "bodhisattvas," that is, bodhisattvas, having unmistakably realized this reality, suchness free from proliferations, and practiced it in the union of method and wisdom, one day when their realization reaches culmination, because they have gone or realized the suchness of all dharmas just as it is, the Buddhas have come to be addressed by the name "Tathagata."

As for the manner of vanquishing opponents and teaching the dharma of profound emptiness, it is, for example, like the king of beasts, the lion, who, relying upon and abiding in the valleys of snow mountains, without fearing any animal, terrifies many wild beasts such as tigers, leopards, bears, and brown bears, as well as minor animals, and lets out a roar; similarly, the lions among men, the Buddhas, also relying on the meaning of profound emptiness, the perfection of wisdom, terrify the many tirthikas who have fallen into the abyss of the view of a self, and roar the wondrous and vast roar of the ultimate dharma in the world. Furthermore, the bodhisattvas themselves attain Buddhahood by perfecting the ways of the three doors of liberation, and although they rescue infinite sentient beings from the sufferings of the bad migrations, because the apprehension of suffering and sentient beings as ultimately established does not arise, complete non-affliction, non-purification, non-entity, non-nature, and non-support and so forth are taught.

heading: **དབྱེ་བ།**
translation: Second, regarding explaining the defining characteristics of superiority characterized by the inconceivable and so forth, the meaning of the fourteen verses starting with "Whoever sees in that way..." is: whichever bodhisattva "sees" the dharmata of all dharmas through that "seeing" of the "inconceivable and unequaled" and so forth—meaning that in the perspective of seeing dharmata through the pristine wisdom of meditative equipoise of the Mahayana path of seeing, such as the forbearance of the dharma of suffering and so forth, not seeing forms and so forth is seeing their dharmata—furthermore, regarding how the functions of the knowledge of dharma and so forth operate: Just as a "king" remains equanimous, without making effort in activities, and the great ministers perform all the king's activities; similarly, whatever deeds and enlightened activities of the Buddha and the dharmas of qualities of abandonment and realization of solitary realizers and sravakas there are, all of those are performed by the supreme non-conceptual pristine wisdom, the perfection of wisdom. These demonstrate the defining characteristics of the inconceivable and so forth, and to clearly demonstrate this reality, it was said: "How does the great king," without "going to cities" or "to other kingdoms," abide blissfully "in his own kingdom," inside his palace, "gathering" together "all accumulations such as taxes"? Similarly, the pristine wisdom in the continuum of a bodhisattva realizing profound dharmata, such as the forbearance of the dharma of suffering, does not waver and does not go anywhere else, but by gathering all the qualities of the Buddha level in one's own continuum, is a special dharma of wonderful activity. This demonstrates the defining characteristics of gathering the qualities of abandonment and realization of the three kinds of noble ones and so forth. This is the commentary on the thirteenth chapter, "The Inconceivable," from the Commentary on the Verses of the Precious Qualities Collection, called "The Jewelled Lamp Clarifying the Reality of Profound Dependent Origination, Fulfilling the Hopes of the Fortunate."

དཔེར་ན་ནམ་མཁར་གནས་པའི་ཉི་མའི་འོད་ཟེར་གྱིས་ནི་ས་འདི་ལ་རླན་གཤེར་ཡོད་པ་སྐེམ་པར་བྱེད་ཅིང་མུན་པ་བསལ་ནས་གཟུགས་རྣམས་ཀྱང་རབ་ཏུ་སྟོན་པར་བྱེད་པའི་བྱེད་ལས་གཉིས་དང་ལྡན་པ་དེ་བཞིན་དུ་ཆོས་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་པོ་སངས་རྒྱས་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་སྨྲ་བའི་ཉི་མས་ཀྱང་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ནམ་མཁའ་ལྟ་བུ་ལ་བརྟེན་ནས་ཟབ་པ་དང་རྒྱ་ཆེ་བའི་ཆོས་ཀྱི་འོད་ཟེར་རྣོན་པོས་སྲིད་པའི་སྲེད་པ་སོགས་ཉེས་པའི་ཆུ་ཀླུང་མཐའ་དག་སྐེམས་ཤིང་ཡོན་ཏན་ཐམས་ཅད་འཕེལ་བར་བྱེད་པའི་ཆོས་རྣམས་ཀྱང་ཡང་དག་པར་རབ་ཏུ་སྟོན་པར་མཛད་དོ། །ཇི་ལྟར་ཆོས་ཉིད་སྟོན་ཅེ་ན། དོན་དམ་དཔྱོད་པའི་རིགས་ཤེས་ཀྱིས་ཕུང་པོ་ལྔའི་གནས་ལུགས་བཙལ་བའི་ཚེ་གཟུགས་རྣམས་དམིགས་སུ་མེད་པས་མི་མཐོང་ལ། དེ་བཞིན་དུ་ཚོར་བ་དག་ཀྱང་མི་མཐོང་ཞིང་། འདུ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་ངོ་བོའང་མཐོང་བ་མེད་ལ་སེམས་པ་མི་མཐོང་ཞིང་།ཆོས་ཉིད་ལ་བརྩེ་གཅིག་ཏུ་མཉམ་པར་བཞག་པའི་འཕགས་པའི་མཉམ་བཞག་ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱིས་ཆོས་ཉིད་གཟིགས་པའི་གཟིགས་ངོར་གང་ལ་རྣམ་པར་ཤེས་པ་དང་སེམས་དང་ཡིད་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ཅི་ཡང་མཐོང་བ་མེད་པ་འདི་ནི་ཕུང་པོ་ལྔའི་གནས་ལུགས་ཆོས་ཉིད་དེ་བཞིན་ཉིད་མཐོང་བ་ཡིན་ཞེས་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་བསྟན་ཏེ། དེ་ཡངདཔེ་ཇི་ལྟ་བུ་ཞེ་ན། འཇིག་རྟེན་པ་དག་གིས་ནམ་མཁའ་མཐོང་ཞེས་ཡིད་ལ་བསམ་ཞིང་སེམས་ཅན་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་ཚིག་ཏུ་རབ་ཏུ་བརྗོད་པ་ནི་ཡོད་མོད་ཀྱི་འོན་ཀྱང་ནམ་མཁའ་ཇི་ལྟར་མཐོང་བར་ནུས་ཞེས་དོན་འདི་ལ་རང་གིས་བརྟག་པར་བགྱིས་དང་། ནམ་མཁའ་ཐོགས་པའི་རེག་བྱ་བཅད་ཙམ་ཡིན་པས་དགག་བྱ་སྒྲིབ་ཐོགས་ཡོད་ན་དམིགས་སུ་རུང་བ་ལས་དེ་མ་མཐོང་པ་ལ་ནམ་མཁའ་མཐོང་ཞེས་བརྗོད་པ་དེ་ལྟར་གཟུགས་ལ་སོགས་པའི་ཆོས་ཉིད་མཐོང་ཞེས་པའང་རིགས་ཤེས་ཀྱིས་བཙལ་བ་ན་གཟུགས་སོགས་མ་རྙེད་པའམ་མ་མཐོང་བ་ནི། དེ་དག་གི་གནས་ལུགས་དེ་བཞིན་ཉིད་མཐོང་བ་ཡིན་ཞེས་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་བསྟན་པ་ཡིན་ལ། མཉམ་བཞག་རྣམ་པར་མི་རྟོག་པའི་ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱིས་ཆོས་ཉིད་མཐོང་བའམ་གཟིགས་ཚུལ་དཔེ་གཞན་གྱིས་ནི་བསྙད་པར་ནུས་པ་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །ཞེས་པ་སྟེ། ཊིཀ་ཆེན་དགོངས་པ་རབ་གསལ་ལས། མི་མཐོང་བ་ཕུང་པ་ོལྔ་དང་། མཐོང་བ་ནི་ཆོས་ཞེས་གསུངས་ལ། དེ་ནི་ཁོ་ན་ཉིད་ཀྱི་དོན་ཏེ་སུས་རྟེན་འབྲེལ་མ་མཐོང་བ་དེས་ཆོས་མཐོང་ངོ་ཞེས་གསུངས་པ་བཞིན་ནོ། །ཞེས་དང་། ཇི་ལྟ་བ་མཁྱེན་པའི་ཡེ་ཤེས་དེས་ཕུང་སོགས་ཀྱི་དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཉིད་མངོན་སུམ་དུ་གཟིགས་པའི་ཕྱིར་དང་། ཕུང་སོགས་རྣམས་གཟིགས་ངོར་མ་གྲུབ་པ་དེ་དག་གི་དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཉིད་ཡིན་པའི་ཕྱིར་དང་། ཕུང་སོགས་མ་གཟིགས་པའི་ཚུལ་གྱིས་དེ་དག་གི་དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཉིད་གཟིགས་དགོས་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཏེ། རང་འགྲེལ་ལས། དངོས་པོ་བྱས་པ་ཅན་ལ་མ་རེག་པར་རང་བཞིན་འབའ་ཞིག་མངོན་སུམ་དུ་མཛད་པས། དེ་ཉིད་ཐུགས་སུ་ཆུད་པའི་ཕྱིར་སངས་རྒྱས་ཞེས་བརྗོད་དོ། །ཞེས་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་དོན་དམ་མཁྱེན་པའི་ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱིས་ཆོས་ཅན་ལ་མ་རེག་པར་ཆོས་ཉིད་འབབ་ཞིག་ཐུགས་སུ་ཆུད་པར་གསུངས་ཏེ། ཕུང་སོགས་མ་གཟིགས་པའི་ཚུལ་གྱིས་དེ་དག་གི་དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཉིད་གཟིགས་པར་གསུངས་པ་དང་དོན་གཅིག་གོ །མཐོང་བ་མེད་པ་ནི་མཐོང་བ་དམ་པའོ། །ཞེས་གསུངས་པའི་དོན་ཡང༌། ཅི་ཡང་མ་མཐོང་བ་མཐོང་བ་མི་བཞེད་ཀྱི། སྔར་བཤད་པ་ལྟར་སྤྲོས་མ་མཐོང་བ་སྤྲོས་བྲལ་མཐོང་བར་འཇོག་པས། མཐོང་མ་མཐོང་གཞི་གཅིག་ལ་བྱེད་པ་མིན་ནོ། །ཞེས་གསུངས་སོ། །བུདྡྷ་ཤྲཱིས་གཟུགས་རྣམས་མི་མཐོང་ཞེས་སོགས་ཁྱད་མཚན་ལ་མར་སྦྱར་ཡང༌། སློབ་དཔོན་གྱིས་ཤེས་མཚན་ལ་སྦྱར་བ་ཉི་ཁྲི་དང་བརྒྱད་སྟོང་སོགས་དང་ཤིན་ཏུ་འགྲིགས་ཞེས་གུང་ཐང་འཇམ་པའི་དབྱངས་ཀྱི་གསུངས་སོ། །ཡོན་ཏན་རིན་པོ་ཆེ་སྡུད་པ་ཚིགས་སུ་བཅད་པའི་འགྲེལ་བ་ཟབ་མོ་རྟེན་འབྱུང་གི་དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཉིད་གསལ་བར་བྱེད་པའི་ནོར་བུའི་སྒྲོན་མེ་སྐལ་བཟང་རེ་སྐོང་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལས་འཇིག་རྟེན་བསྟན་པའི་ལེའུ་སྟེ་བཅུ་གཉིས་པའི་འགྲེལ་པའོ༎  །།
[3-186] translation already produced for this document:
Third, regarding teaching the defining characteristics of knowledge of omniscience, such as the Tathagata dwelling blissfully in the seen dharma, the meaning of the three verses starting with "For example, abiding in the sky..." is: For example, just as the rays of the sun "abiding in the sky" possess the two functions of drying up whatever moisture there is on this earth and, having dispelled darkness, "thoroughly illuminating forms"; similarly, the sun of speech, the Dharma king, the Bhagavan Buddha, also relying upon the sky-like perfection of wisdom, with the sharp light rays of the profound and vast dharma dries up all the rivers of faults such as craving for existence, and correctly "thoroughly illuminates" all the dharmas that cause all qualities to increase. If one asks, "How does he teach dharmata?" When searching for the reality of the five aggregates with rational knowledge that analyzes the ultimate, because forms are without apprehension, one "does not see" them; likewise, one "does not see feelings," one "does not see the nature of discrimination either," one "does not see compositional factors," and in the perspective of the noble one's pristine wisdom of meditative equipoise that is single-pointedly resting in equipoise on dharmata, seeing dharmata, "not seeing anything whatsoever called consciousness, mind, and intellect"—this is the seeing of the reality of the five aggregates, dharmata, suchness, so the Tathagata taught. Furthermore, if one asks what kind of example this is like: Although worldly people think in their minds "we see the sky" and sentient beings "thoroughly express" this in words, examine this point for yourself: "how can the sky be seen?" Because the sky is merely the elimination of obstructive tangible contact, if the object of negation, obstructive covering, existed, it would be suitable to be apprehended; but not seeing that is expressed as "seeing the sky." Similarly, saying "seeing the dharmata of forms and so forth" means that when searching with rational knowledge, not finding or "not seeing" forms and so forth is what the Tathagata taught as seeing their reality, suchness; and this manner of seeing or perceiving dharmata with the non-conceptual pristine wisdom of meditative equipoise "cannot be expressed by another example." From the Great Commentary, Illumination of the Thought: "It is said that what is not seen is the five aggregates, and what is seen is dharma; that is the meaning of reality, just as it is said, 'Whoever does not see dependent origination, they see dharma.'" And: "Because that pristine wisdom which knows reality just as it is directly sees the reality of the aggregates and so forth; and because the aggregates and so forth not being established in the perspective of seeing is their reality; and because by way of not seeing the aggregates and so forth one must see their reality. For, from the Auto-commentary: 'Because, without touching conditioned entities, only the nature is directly realized, and thus reality is understood, one is called a Buddha.' Thus it is said that the Buddha's pristine wisdom knowing the ultimate, without touching the subjects, understands only dharmata; this is synonymous with the statement that by way of not seeing the aggregates and so forth, their reality is seen. Furthermore, the meaning of the statement, 'Non-seeing is the supreme seeing': not seeing anything at all is not considered seeing, but rather, as explained before, not seeing proliferations is posited as seeing freedom from proliferations; therefore, seeing and not seeing do not refer to a single basis." So it is said. Although Buddhaśrī applied "not seeing forms" and so forth to the defining characteristics of superiority, the Master applying it to the defining characteristics of knowledge accords extremely well with the Twenty-five Thousand and the Eight Thousand, so said Gungtang Jamyang. This is the commentary on the twelfth chapter, "Teaching the World," from the Commentary on the Verses of the Precious Qualities Collection, called "The Jewelled Lamp Clarifying the Reality of Profound Dependent Origination, Fulfilling the Hopes of the Fortunate."

heading: **དབྱེ་བ།**
translation: Furthermore, if one asks when one obtains the special qualities of a Buddha: Any person who has faith, aspiration, and stable irreversible faith in the Sugatas and bodhisattvas, and out of intention seeks the supreme perfection of wisdom, which is the path to becoming a bodhisattva and a Buddha, and out of application earnestly practices it with joyful effort, then since they possess both method and wisdom, having completely transcended the two straying paths of the sravakas and solitary realizers, they will not be overwhelmed by maras, tirthikas, and so forth, and will swiftly obtain the supreme enlightenment of the Victorious One. Through these, not only do the sravakas and solitary realizers not obtain non-abiding nirvana because they only have one-sided method or wisdom, but they also fall into the extremes of existence and peace; whereas because bodhisattvas practice method and wisdom inseparably—the two truths in the basis, and method and wisdom in combination on the path—they will not fall into the extremes of existence and peace, but will obtain the result, the union of the two kayas; therefore they are supremely elevated above the sravakas and solitary realizers.

Where the commentary quotes or glosses words of the root verses, keep those quoted words recognisable in the translation. Keep proper names in their standard Sanskrit forms (Subhūti, Śāriputra, Maitreya, Haribhadra) and technical terms recognisable (prajñāpāramitā = perfection of wisdom, bodhisattva). Do not add commentary, notes, or explanation of your own.

གསུམ་པ་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་མཐོང་ཆོས་ལ་བདེ་བར་གནས་པ་སོགས་རྣམ་མཁྱེན་གྱི་ཤེས་མཚན་སྟོན་པར། དཔེར་ན་ནམ་མཁའ་གནས་པའི་ཞེས་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གསུམ་གསུངས་པའི་དོན། དཔེར་ན་ནམ་མཁར་གནས་པའི་ཉི་མའི་འོད་ཟེར་གྱིས་ནི་ས་འདི་ལ་རླན་གཤེར་ཡོད་པ་སྐེམ་པར་བྱེད་ཅིང་མུན་པ་བསལ་ནས་གཟུགས་རྣམས་ཀྱང་རབ་ཏུ་སྟོན་པར་བྱེད་པའི་བྱེད་ལས་གཉིས་དང་ལྡན་པ་དེ་བཞིན་དུ་ཆོས་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་པོ་སངས་རྒྱས་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་སྨྲ་བའི་ཉི་མས་ཀྱང་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ནམ་མཁའ་ལྟ་བུ་ལ་བརྟེན་ནས་ཟབ་པ་དང་རྒྱ་ཆེ་བའི་ཆོས་ཀྱི་འོད་ཟེར་རྣོན་པོས་སྲིད་པའི་སྲེད་པ་སོགས་ཉེས་པའི་ཆུ་ཀླུང་མཐའ་དག་སྐེམས་ཤིང་ཡོན་ཏན་ཐམས་ཅད་འཕེལ་བར་བྱེད་པའི་ཆོས་རྣམས་ཀྱང་ཡང་དག་པར་རབ་ཏུ་སྟོན་པར་མཛད་དོ། །ཇི་ལྟར་ཆོས་ཉིད་སྟོན་ཅེ་ན། དོན་དམ་དཔྱོད་པའི་རིགས་ཤེས་ཀྱིས་ཕུང་པོ་ལྔའི་གནས་ལུགས་བཙལ་བའི་ཚེ་གཟུགས་རྣམས་དམིགས་སུ་མེད་པས་མི་མཐོང་ལ། དེ་བཞིན་དུ་ཚོར་བ་དག་ཀྱང་མི་མཐོང་ཞིང་། འདུ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་ངོ་བོའང་མཐོང་བ་མེད་ལ་སེམས་པ་མི་མཐོང་ཞིང་།ཆོས་ཉིད་ལ་བརྩེ་གཅིག་ཏུ་མཉམ་པར་བཞག་པའི་འཕགས་པའི་མཉམ་བཞག་ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱིས་ཆོས་ཉིད་གཟིགས་པའི་གཟིགས་ངོར་གང་ལ་རྣམ་པར་ཤེས་པ་དང་སེམས་དང་ཡིད་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ཅི་ཡང་མཐོང་བ་མེད་པ་འདི་ནི་ཕུང་པོ་ལྔའི་གནས་ལུགས་ཆོས་ཉིད་དེ་བཞིན་ཉིད་མཐོང་བ་ཡིན་ཞེས་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་བསྟན་ཏེ། དེ་ཡངདཔེ་ཇི་ལྟ་བུ་ཞེ་ན། འཇིག་རྟེན་པ་དག་གིས་ནམ་མཁའ་མཐོང་ཞེས་ཡིད་ལ་བསམ་ཞིང་སེམས་ཅན་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་ཚིག་ཏུ་རབ་ཏུ་བརྗོད་པ་ནི་ཡོད་མོད་ཀྱི་འོན་ཀྱང་ནམ་མཁའ་ཇི་ལྟར་མཐོང་བར་ནུས་ཞེས་དོན་འདི་ལ་རང་གིས་བརྟག་པར་བགྱིས་དང་། ནམ་མཁའ་ཐོགས་པའི་རེག་བྱ་བཅད་ཙམ་ཡིན་པས་དགག་བྱ་སྒྲིབ་ཐོགས་ཡོད་ན་དམིགས་སུ་རུང་བ་ལས་དེ་མ་མཐོང་པ་ལ་ནམ་མཁའ་མཐོང་ཞེས་བརྗོད་པ་དེ་ལྟར་གཟུགས་ལ་སོགས་པའི་ཆོས་ཉིད་མཐོང་ཞེས་པའང་རིགས་ཤེས་ཀྱིས་བཙལ་བ་ན་གཟུགས་སོགས་མ་རྙེད་པའམ་མ་མཐོང་བ་ནི། དེ་དག་གི་གནས་ལུགས་དེ་བཞིན་ཉིད་མཐོང་བ་ཡིན་ཞེས་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་བསྟན་པ་ཡིན་ལ། མཉམ་བཞག་རྣམ་པར་མི་རྟོག་པའི་ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱིས་ཆོས་ཉིད་མཐོང་བའམ་གཟིགས་ཚུལ་དཔེ་གཞན་གྱིས་ནི་བསྙད་པར་ནུས་པ་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །ཞེས་པ་སྟེ། ཊིཀ་ཆེན་དགོངས་པ་རབ་གསལ་ལས། མི་མཐོང་བ་ཕུང་པ་ོལྔ་དང་། མཐོང་བ་ནི་ཆོས་ཞེས་གསུངས་ལ། དེ་ནི་ཁོ་ན་ཉིད་ཀྱི་དོན་ཏེ་སུས་རྟེན་འབྲེལ་མ་མཐོང་བ་དེས་ཆོས་མཐོང་ངོ་ཞེས་གསུངས་པ་བཞིན་ནོ། །ཞེས་དང་། ཇི་ལྟ་བ་མཁྱེན་པའི་ཡེ་ཤེས་དེས་ཕུང་སོགས་ཀྱི་དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཉིད་མངོན་སུམ་དུ་གཟིགས་པའི་ཕྱིར་དང་། ཕུང་སོགས་རྣམས་གཟིགས་ངོར་མ་གྲུབ་པ་དེ་དག་གི་དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཉིད་ཡིན་པའི་ཕྱིར་དང་། ཕུང་སོགས་མ་གཟིགས་པའི་ཚུལ་གྱིས་དེ་དག་གི་དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཉིད་གཟིགས་དགོས་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཏེ། རང་འགྲེལ་ལས། དངོས་པོ་བྱས་པ་ཅན་ལ་མ་རེག་པར་རང་བཞིན་འབའ་ཞིག་མངོན་སུམ་དུ་མཛད་པས། དེ་ཉིད་ཐུགས་སུ་ཆུད་པའི་ཕྱིར་སངས་རྒྱས་ཞེས་བརྗོད་དོ། །ཞེས་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་དོན་དམ་མཁྱེན་པའི་ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱིས་ཆོས་ཅན་ལ་མ་རེག་པར་ཆོས་ཉིད་འབབ་ཞིག་ཐུགས་སུ་ཆུད་པར་གསུངས་ཏེ། ཕུང་སོགས་མ་གཟིགས་པའི་ཚུལ་གྱིས་དེ་དག་གི་དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཉིད་གཟིགས་པར་གསུངས་པ་དང་དོན་གཅིག་གོ །མཐོང་བ་མེད་པ་ནི་མཐོང་བ་དམ་པའོ། །ཞེས་གསུངས་པའི་དོན་ཡང༌། ཅི་ཡང་མ་མཐོང་བ་མཐོང་བ་མི་བཞེད་ཀྱི། སྔར་བཤད་པ་ལྟར་སྤྲོས་མ་མཐོང་བ་སྤྲོས་བྲལ་མཐོང་བར་འཇོག་པས། མཐོང་མ་མཐོང་གཞི་གཅིག་ལ་བྱེད་པ་མིན་ནོ། །ཞེས་གསུངས་སོ། །བུདྡྷ་ཤྲཱིས་གཟུགས་རྣམས་མི་མཐོང་ཞེས་སོགས་ཁྱད་མཚན་ལ་མར་སྦྱར་ཡང༌། སློབ་དཔོན་གྱིས་ཤེས་མཚན་ལ་སྦྱར་བ་ཉི་ཁྲི་དང་བརྒྱད་སྟོང་སོགས་དང་ཤིན་ཏུ་འགྲིགས་ཞེས་གུང་ཐང་འཇམ་པའི་དབྱངས་ཀྱི་གསུངས་སོ། །ཡོན་ཏན་རིན་པོ་ཆེ་སྡུད་པ་ཚིགས་སུ་བཅད་པའི་འགྲེལ་བ་ཟབ་མོ་རྟེན་འབྱུང་གི་དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཉིད་གསལ་བར་བྱེད་པའི་ནོར་བུའི་སྒྲོན་མེ་སྐལ་བཟང་རེ་སྐོང་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལས་འཇིག་རྟེན་བསྟན་པའི་ལེའུ་སྟེ་བཅུ་གཉིས་པའི་འགྲེལ་པའོ༎  །།

Third, regarding teaching the defining characteristics of knowledge of omniscience, such as the Tathagata dwelling blissfully in the seen dharma, the meaning of the three verses starting with "For example, abiding in the sky..." is: For example, just as the rays of the sun "abiding in the sky" possess the two functions of drying up whatever moisture there is on this earth and, having dispelled darkness, "thoroughly illuminating forms"; similarly, the sun of speech, the Dharma king, the Bhagavan Buddha, also relying upon the sky-like perfection of wisdom, with the sharp light rays of the profound and vast dharma dries up all the rivers of faults such as craving for existence, and correctly "thoroughly illuminates" all the dharmas that cause all qualities to increase. If one asks, "How does he teach dharmata?" When searching for the reality of the five aggregates with rational knowledge that analyzes the ultimate, because forms are without apprehension, one "does not see" them; likewise, one "does not see feelings," one "does not see the nature of discrimination either," one "does not see compositional factors," and in the perspective of the noble one's pristine wisdom of meditative equipoise that is single-pointedly resting in equipoise on dharmata, seeing dharmata, "not seeing anything whatsoever called consciousness, mind, and intellect"—this is the seeing of the reality of the five aggregates, dharmata, suchness, so the Tathagata taught. Furthermore, if one asks what kind of example this is like: Although worldly people think in their minds "we see the sky" and sentient beings "thoroughly express" this in words, examine this point for yourself: "how can the sky be seen?" Because the sky is merely the elimination of obstructive tangible contact, if the object of negation, obstructive covering, existed, it would be suitable to be apprehended; but not seeing that is expressed as "seeing the sky." Similarly, saying "seeing the dharmata of forms and so forth" means that when searching with rational knowledge, not finding or "not seeing" forms and so forth is what the Tathagata taught as seeing their reality, suchness; and this manner of seeing or perceiving dharmata with the non-conceptual pristine wisdom of meditative equipoise "cannot be expressed by another example." From the Great Commentary, Illumination of the Thought: "It is said that what is not seen is the five aggregates, and what is seen is dharma; that is the meaning of reality, just as it is said, 'Whoever does not see dependent origination, they see dharma.'" And: "Because that pristine wisdom which knows reality just as it is directly sees the reality of the aggregates and so forth; and because the aggregates and so forth not being established in the perspective of seeing is their reality; and because by way of not seeing the aggregates and so forth one must see their reality. For, from the Auto-commentary: 'Because, without touching conditioned entities, only the nature is directly realized, and thus reality is understood, one is called a Buddha.' Thus it is said that the Buddha's pristine wisdom knowing the ultimate, without touching the subjects, understands only dharmata; this is synonymous with the statement that by way of not seeing the aggregates and so forth, their reality is seen. Furthermore, the meaning of the statement, 'Non-seeing is the supreme seeing': not seeing anything at all is not considered seeing, but rather, as explained before, not seeing proliferations is posited as seeing freedom from proliferations; therefore, seeing and not seeing do not refer to a single basis." So it is said. Although Buddhaśrī applied "not seeing forms" and so forth to the defining characteristics of superiority, the Master applying it to the defining characteristics of knowledge accords extremely well with the Twenty-five Thousand and the Eight Thousand, so said Gungtang Jamyang. This is the commentary on the twelfth chapter, "Teaching the World," from the Commentary on the Verses of the Precious Qualities Collection, called "The Jewelled Lamp Clarifying the Reality of Profound Dependent Origination, Fulfilling the Hopes of the Fortunate."

heading: **དབྱེ་བ།**
translation: Therefore, since one cannot accomplish unsurpassed perfect enlightenment with one-sided method or wisdom, establishing through an example the way bodhisattvas must train in a path complete with both method and wisdom is as follows: For example, if a "boat" of "people embarking on the ocean" breaks and falls apart, at that time those people who "do not hold onto a corpse, grass, or a piece of wood" and so forth, remaining as they are, "will be destroyed in the middle of the water," meaning they will die, and will not reach the shore of the ocean; whereas "those who hold onto wood" and so forth, in reliance upon that, "will blissfully reach the other shore of the ocean." "Like that example," any person who possesses faith seeking perfect enlightenment and obtains joyous faith, but who, after finding faith in the perfection of wisdom—the supreme path that brings about the attainment of unsurpassed enlightenment and the mother that generates the Victorious Ones—"does not engage in" practicing it, will not obtain the result of perfect enlightenment; thus, they will constantly wander in the great ocean of samsara, churning with the waves of various kinds of sorrow and suffering such as birth, aging, sickness, death, and mental unhappiness. When that person is embraced by the supreme perfection of wisdom realizing lack of true existence, they will be skilled in the meaning of the abiding nature of entities, and being free from apprehending signs, they will point out ultimate truth without error.

Second, regarding explaining the defining characteristics of superiority characterized by the inconceivable and so forth, the meaning of the fourteen verses starting with "Whoever sees in that way..." is: whichever bodhisattva "sees" the dharmata of all dharmas through that "seeing" of the "inconceivable and unequaled" and so forth—meaning that in the perspective of seeing dharmata through the pristine wisdom of meditative equipoise of the Mahayana path of seeing, such as the forbearance of the dharma of suffering and so forth, not seeing forms and so forth is seeing their dharmata—furthermore, regarding how the functions of the knowledge of dharma and so forth operate: Just as a "king" remains equanimous, without making effort in activities, and the great ministers perform all the king's activities; similarly, whatever deeds and enlightened activities of the Buddha and the dharmas of qualities of abandonment and realization of solitary realizers and sravakas there are, all of those are performed by the supreme non-conceptual pristine wisdom, the perfection of wisdom. These demonstrate the defining characteristics of the inconceivable and so forth, and to clearly demonstrate this reality, it was said: "How does the great king," without "going to cities" or "to other kingdoms," abide blissfully "in his own kingdom," inside his palace, "gathering" together "all accumulations such as taxes"? Similarly, the pristine wisdom in the continuum of a bodhisattva realizing profound dharmata, such as the forbearance of the dharma of suffering, does not waver and does not go anywhere else, but by gathering all the qualities of the Buddha level in one's own continuum, is a special dharma of wonderful activity. This demonstrates the defining characteristics of gathering the qualities of abandonment and realization of the three kinds of noble ones and so forth. This is the commentary on the thirteenth chapter, "The Inconceivable," from the Commentary on the Verses of the Precious Qualities Collection, called "The Jewelled Lamp Clarifying the Reality of Profound Dependent Origination, Fulfilling the Hopes of the Fortunate."

Furthermore, if one asks when one obtains the special qualities of a Buddha: Any person who has faith, aspiration, and stable irreversible faith in the Sugatas and bodhisattvas, and out of intention seeks the supreme perfection of wisdom, which is the path to becoming a bodhisattva and a Buddha, and out of application earnestly practices it with joyful effort, then since they possess both method and wisdom, having completely transcended the two straying paths of the sravakas and solitary realizers, they will not be overwhelmed by maras, tirthikas, and so forth, and will swiftly obtain the supreme enlightenment of the Victorious One. Through these, not only do the sravakas and solitary realizers not obtain non-abiding nirvana because they only have one-sided method or wisdom, but they also fall into the extremes of existence and peace; whereas because bodhisattvas practice method and wisdom inseparably—the two truths in the basis, and method and wisdom in combination on the path—they will not fall into the extremes of existence and peace, but will obtain the result, the union of the two kayas; therefore they are supremely elevated above the sravakas and solitary realizers.

heading: **དབྱེ་བ།**
translation: If those qualities of method, such as their faith seeking perfect enlightenment and compassion, are entirely embraced by wisdom realizing non-apprehension, the two accumulations of merit and pristine wisdom will be completely perfected, and since they do not fall into the domain of sravakas and solitary realizers, they will swiftly touch, meaning obtain, the supremely wonderful enlightenment of the Sugatas.

གཉིས་པ་བསམ་མི་ཁྱབ་སོགས་ཀྱིས་ཁྱད་པར་དུ་བྱས་པའི་ཁྱད་མཚན་འཆད་པར། གང་གིས་དེ་ལྟར་མཐོང་བ་ཞེས་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་བཅུ་བཞི་གསུངས་པའི་དོན་ནི། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གང་གིས་ཐེག་ཆེན་གྱི་མཐོང་ལམ་སྡུག་བསྔལ་ཆོས་བཟོད་ལ་སོགས་པའི་མཉམ་བཞག་ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱིས་ཆོས་ཉིད་གཟིགས་པའི་ངོར་གཟུགས་སོགས་མ་མཐོང་བ་དེ་དག་གི་ཆོས་ཉིད་མཐོང་བ་ཡིན་པ་དེ་ལྟར་བསམ་གྱིས་མི་ཁྱབ་པ་དང་མི་མཉམ་པ་སོགས་མཐོང་བ་དེ་ཡིས་ཆོས་ཀུན་གྱི་ཆོས་ཉིད་མཐོང་བ་ཡིན་ཏེ། ཆོས་ཤེས་ལ་སོགས་པའི་བྱེད་ལས་ཀྱང་ཇི་ལྟར་ན། རྒྱལ་པོ་ནི་བྱ་བ་ལ་འབད་རྩོལ་མེད་པར་བཏང་སྙོམས་སུ་འདུག་ཅིང༌། བློན་པོ་ཆེན་པོས་རྒྱལ་པོའི་བྱ་བ་ཀུན་བྱེད་པ་ལྟར་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱིས་མཛད་པ་འཕྲིན་ལས་དང་རང་རྒྱལ་དང་ཉན་ཐོས་རྣམས་ཀྱི་སྤངས་རྟོགས་ཀྱི་ཡོན་ཏན་གྱི་ཆོས་རྣམས་ཇི་སྙེད་པ་དེ་དག་ཐམས་ཅད་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་རྣམ་པར་མི་རྟོག་པའི་ཡེ་ཤེས་མཆོག་གིས་བྱེད་དོ། །འདི་དག་གིས་བསམ་མི་ཁྱབ་སོགས་ཀྱི་ཁྱད་མཚན་བསྟན་ལ། དེ་ཉིད་གསལ་བར་བསྟན་པའི་ཕྱིར་གསུངས་པ། ཇི་ལྟར་ན་རྒྱལ་པོ་ཆེན་པོ་ནི། གྲོང་ཁྱེར་དུ་འགྲོ་ཞིང་ཡུལ་འཁོར་གཞན་རྣམས་སུ་ཡང་མི་འགྲོ་བར་རང་གི་ཡུལ་ཕོ་བྲང་ནང་ན་བདེ་བར་འདུག་ནས་དཔྱ་ཁྲལ་ལ་སོགས་པའི་འདུ་བ་ཐམས་ཅད་ཚུར་སྡུད་པ་ལྟར། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའི་རྒྱུད་ཀྱི་སྡུག་བསྔལ་ཆོས་བཟོད་སོགས་ཆོས་ཉིད་ཟབ་མོ་རྟོགས་པའི་ཡེ་ཤེས་ནི་མི་གཡོ་ཞིང་གནས་གཞན་གང་དུའང་མི་འགྲོ་ལ་རང་རྒྱུད་ལ་སངས་རྒྱས་ས་ཡི་ཡོན་ཏན་གང་ཡིན་ཐམས་ཅད་སྡུད་ན་བྱ་བ་རྨད་དུ་བྱུང་བའི་ཁྱད་པར་གྱི་ཆོས་སོ། །འདིས་འཕགས་པ་གསུམ་གྱི་སྤངས་རྟོགས་ཀྱི་ཡོན་ཏན་སྡུད་པའི་ཁྱན་མཚན་སོགས་བསྟན་ཏོ། །ཡོན་ཏན་རིན་པོ་ཆེ་སྡུད་པ་ཚིགས་སུ་བཅད་པའི་འགྲེལ་བ་ཟབ་མོ་རྟེན་འབྱུང་གི་དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཉིད་གསལ་བར་བྱེད་པའི་ནོར་བུའི་སྒྲོན་མེ་སྐལ་བཟང་རེ་སྐོང་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལས། བསམ་གྱིས་མི་ཁྱབ་པའི་ལེའུ་སྟེ་བཅུ་གསུམ་པའི་འགྲེལ་བའོ།།   །།

Second, regarding explaining the defining characteristics of superiority characterized by the inconceivable and so forth, the meaning of the fourteen verses starting with "Whoever sees in that way..." is: whichever bodhisattva "sees" the dharmata of all dharmas through that "seeing" of the "inconceivable and unequaled" and so forth—meaning that in the perspective of seeing dharmata through the pristine wisdom of meditative equipoise of the Mahayana path of seeing, such as the forbearance of the dharma of suffering and so forth, not seeing forms and so forth is seeing their dharmata—furthermore, regarding how the functions of the knowledge of dharma and so forth operate: Just as a "king" remains equanimous, without making effort in activities, and the great ministers perform all the king's activities; similarly, whatever deeds and enlightened activities of the Buddha and the dharmas of qualities of abandonment and realization of solitary realizers and sravakas there are, all of those are performed by the supreme non-conceptual pristine wisdom, the perfection of wisdom. These demonstrate the defining characteristics of the inconceivable and so forth, and to clearly demonstrate this reality, it was said: "How does the great king," without "going to cities" or "to other kingdoms," abide blissfully "in his own kingdom," inside his palace, "gathering" together "all accumulations such as taxes"? Similarly, the pristine wisdom in the continuum of a bodhisattva realizing profound dharmata, such as the forbearance of the dharma of suffering, does not waver and does not go anywhere else, but by gathering all the qualities of the Buddha level in one's own continuum, is a special dharma of wonderful activity. This demonstrates the defining characteristics of gathering the qualities of abandonment and realization of the three kinds of noble ones and so forth. This is the commentary on the thirteenth chapter, "The Inconceivable," from the Commentary on the Verses of the Precious Qualities Collection, called "The Jewelled Lamp Clarifying the Reality of Profound Dependent Origination, Fulfilling the Hopes of the Fortunate."

Furthermore, if one asks when one obtains the special qualities of a Buddha: Any person who has faith, aspiration, and stable irreversible faith in the Sugatas and bodhisattvas, and out of intention seeks the supreme perfection of wisdom, which is the path to becoming a bodhisattva and a Buddha, and out of application earnestly practices it with joyful effort, then since they possess both method and wisdom, having completely transcended the two straying paths of the sravakas and solitary realizers, they will not be overwhelmed by maras, tirthikas, and so forth, and will swiftly obtain the supreme enlightenment of the Victorious One. Through these, not only do the sravakas and solitary realizers not obtain non-abiding nirvana because they only have one-sided method or wisdom, but they also fall into the extremes of existence and peace; whereas because bodhisattvas practice method and wisdom inseparably—the two truths in the basis, and method and wisdom in combination on the path—they will not fall into the extremes of existence and peace, but will obtain the result, the union of the two kayas; therefore they are supremely elevated above the sravakas and solitary realizers.

heading: **དབྱེ་བ།**
translation: Furthermore, as another example, if "some ignorant person carries water in an unfired clay vessel"—meaning unbaked by fire—because that vase is fragile and weak, "it will quickly be destroyed." "If one carries water in a fired vase," it will not break or be destroyed along the way without the danger of destruction, and "it will blissfully reach one's home"; "similarly," if any bodhisattva "has much faith" and aspiration seeking perfect enlightenment, "but lacks skill in means" to accomplish it "and the perfection of wisdom" of the path, they will fall into the lower path, degenerate from the Mahayana, and "quickly be ruined." If "faith and wisdom"—meaning both the aspect of method such as faith, and the perfection of wisdom—entirely embrace that person's continuum, they will completely transcend the two levels of sravakas and solitary realizers and "obtain supreme enlightenment," perfect enlightenment.

Second, regarding explaining the defining characteristics of superiority characterized by the inconceivable and so forth, the meaning of the fourteen verses starting with "Whoever sees in that way..." is: whichever bodhisattva "sees" the dharmata of all dharmas through that "seeing" of the "inconceivable and unequaled" and so forth—meaning that in the perspective of seeing dharmata through the pristine wisdom of meditative equipoise of the Mahayana path of seeing, such as the forbearance of the dharma of suffering and so forth, not seeing forms and so forth is seeing their dharmata—furthermore, regarding how the functions of the knowledge of dharma and so forth operate: Just as a "king" remains equanimous, without making effort in activities, and the great ministers perform all the king's activities; similarly, whatever deeds and enlightened activities of the Buddha and the dharmas of qualities of abandonment and realization of solitary realizers and sravakas there are, all of those are performed by the supreme non-conceptual pristine wisdom, the perfection of wisdom. These demonstrate the defining characteristics of the inconceivable and so forth, and to clearly demonstrate this reality, it was said: "How does the great king," without "going to cities" or "to other kingdoms," abide blissfully "in his own kingdom," inside his palace, "gathering" together "all accumulations such as taxes"? Similarly, the pristine wisdom in the continuum of a bodhisattva realizing profound dharmata, such as the forbearance of the dharma of suffering, does not waver and does not go anywhere else, but by gathering all the qualities of the Buddha level in one's own continuum, is a special dharma of wonderful activity. This demonstrates the defining characteristics of gathering the qualities of abandonment and realization of the three kinds of noble ones and so forth. This is the commentary on the thirteenth chapter, "The Inconceivable," from the Commentary on the Verses of the Precious Qualities Collection, called "The Jewelled Lamp Clarifying the Reality of Profound Dependent Origination, Fulfilling the Hopes of the Fortunate."

Furthermore, if one asks when one obtains the special qualities of a Buddha: Any person who has faith, aspiration, and stable irreversible faith in the Sugatas and bodhisattvas, and out of intention seeks the supreme perfection of wisdom, which is the path to becoming a bodhisattva and a Buddha, and out of application earnestly practices it with joyful effort, then since they possess both method and wisdom, having completely transcended the two straying paths of the sravakas and solitary realizers, they will not be overwhelmed by maras, tirthikas, and so forth, and will swiftly obtain the supreme enlightenment of the Victorious One. Through these, not only do the sravakas and solitary realizers not obtain non-abiding nirvana because they only have one-sided method or wisdom, but they also fall into the extremes of existence and peace; whereas because bodhisattvas practice method and wisdom inseparably—the two truths in the basis, and method and wisdom in combination on the path—they will not fall into the extremes of existence and peace, but will obtain the result, the union of the two kayas; therefore they are supremely elevated above the sravakas and solitary realizers.

heading: **དབྱེ་བ།**
translation: To demonstrate yet another example, it was said: For example, if a "boat" has "not been well prepared" with repairs for leaks and patches and so forth, "it will be destroyed in the ocean together with its goods and merchants," and will be ruined; whereas if that boat is well examined and endowed with good repairs and so forth, it will not be destroyed or damaged in the middle of the water, and the merchants together with their wealth "will blissfully reach the shore of the ocean"; similarly, if any bodhisattva's continuum is "entirely endowed with faith and compassion" and so forth, but "does not rely on the perfection of wisdom" of the path, they "will quickly degenerate from perfect enlightenment"; whereas if that very person endowed with wonderful "faith and so forth is endowed with the supreme perfection of wisdom," they will not be harmed by mental engagements of the lower vehicle, and without degenerating from the Mahayana path, "will touch the enlightenment of the Victorious Ones."

Second, regarding explaining the defining characteristics of superiority characterized by the inconceivable and so forth, the meaning of the fourteen verses starting with "Whoever sees in that way..." is: whichever bodhisattva "sees" the dharmata of all dharmas through that "seeing" of the "inconceivable and unequaled" and so forth—meaning that in the perspective of seeing dharmata through the pristine wisdom of meditative equipoise of the Mahayana path of seeing, such as the forbearance of the dharma of suffering and so forth, not seeing forms and so forth is seeing their dharmata—furthermore, regarding how the functions of the knowledge of dharma and so forth operate: Just as a "king" remains equanimous, without making effort in activities, and the great ministers perform all the king's activities; similarly, whatever deeds and enlightened activities of the Buddha and the dharmas of qualities of abandonment and realization of solitary realizers and sravakas there are, all of those are performed by the supreme non-conceptual pristine wisdom, the perfection of wisdom. These demonstrate the defining characteristics of the inconceivable and so forth, and to clearly demonstrate this reality, it was said: "How does the great king," without "going to cities" or "to other kingdoms," abide blissfully "in his own kingdom," inside his palace, "gathering" together "all accumulations such as taxes"? Similarly, the pristine wisdom in the continuum of a bodhisattva realizing profound dharmata, such as the forbearance of the dharma of suffering, does not waver and does not go anywhere else, but by gathering all the qualities of the Buddha level in one's own continuum, is a special dharma of wonderful activity. This demonstrates the defining characteristics of gathering the qualities of abandonment and realization of the three kinds of noble ones and so forth. This is the commentary on the thirteenth chapter, "The Inconceivable," from the Commentary on the Verses of the Precious Qualities Collection, called "The Jewelled Lamp Clarifying the Reality of Profound Dependent Origination, Fulfilling the Hopes of the Fortunate."

Furthermore, if one asks when one obtains the special qualities of a Buddha: Any person who has faith, aspiration, and stable irreversible faith in the Sugatas and bodhisattvas, and out of intention seeks the supreme perfection of wisdom, which is the path to becoming a bodhisattva and a Buddha, and out of application earnestly practices it with joyful effort, then since they possess both method and wisdom, having completely transcended the two straying paths of the sravakas and solitary realizers, they will not be overwhelmed by maras, tirthikas, and so forth, and will swiftly obtain the supreme enlightenment of the Victorious One. Through these, not only do the sravakas and solitary realizers not obtain non-abiding nirvana because they only have one-sided method or wisdom, but they also fall into the extremes of existence and peace; whereas because bodhisattvas practice method and wisdom inseparably—the two truths in the basis, and method and wisdom in combination on the path—they will not fall into the extremes of existence and peace, but will obtain the result, the union of the two kayas; therefore they are supremely elevated above the sravakas and solitary realizers.

heading: **དབྱེ་བ།**
translation: Showing that practicing method and wisdom united without separation is of great importance: For example, if "some person reaches the age of one hundred and twenty," reaching the end of their lifespan, and that person who is "aged and suffering from illness and so forth" is "unable to rise from their seat"; and "even if they are able to stand up," they are "unable to go elsewhere," such as a krośa away, "by their own strength," because they are old and decrepit. "If that person is supported on their right and left sides by two people possessing strength and they go," there is no danger of falling along the way, and "they will easily go to the place they wish to go"; "similarly, if any bodhisattva's wisdom" realizing emptiness "is weak," "even if they have fully entered the Mahayana path, they will degenerate" before obtaining the result of unsurpassed enlightenment; whereas if that very bodhisattva's entire path in their continuum is "entirely embraced by" the aspect of method such as faith and "the supreme wisdom" realizing lack of true existence, they will not degenerate from the supreme path and "will quickly touch the enlightenment of the Tathagatas." Therefore, intelligent bodhisattvas must train in the path complete with method and wisdom and seize the royal seat of supreme enlightenment. This concludes the commentary on the fourteenth chapter, the chapter on examples, from the Lamp of Jewels Illuminating the Suchness of Profound Dependent Origination, Fulfilling the Hopes of the Fortunate, a commentary on the Verses of the Precious Qualities Collection.

Therefore, since one cannot accomplish unsurpassed perfect enlightenment with one-sided method or wisdom, establishing through an example the way bodhisattvas must train in a path complete with both method and wisdom is as follows: For example, if a "boat" of "people embarking on the ocean" breaks and falls apart, at that time those people who "do not hold onto a corpse, grass, or a piece of wood" and so forth, remaining as they are, "will be destroyed in the middle of the water," meaning they will die, and will not reach the shore of the ocean; whereas "those who hold onto wood" and so forth, in reliance upon that, "will blissfully reach the other shore of the ocean." "Like that example," any person who possesses faith seeking perfect enlightenment and obtains joyous faith, but who, after finding faith in the perfection of wisdom—the supreme path that brings about the attainment of unsurpassed enlightenment and the mother that generates the Victorious Ones—"does not engage in" practicing it, will not obtain the result of perfect enlightenment; thus, they will constantly wander in the great ocean of samsara, churning with the waves of various kinds of sorrow and suffering such as birth, aging, sickness, death, and mental unhappiness. When that person is embraced by the supreme perfection of wisdom realizing lack of true existence, they will be skilled in the meaning of the abiding nature of entities, and being free from apprehending signs, they will point out ultimate truth without error.

Furthermore, as another example, if "some ignorant person carries water in an unfired clay vessel"—meaning unbaked by fire—because that vase is fragile and weak, "it will quickly be destroyed." "If one carries water in a fired vase," it will not break or be destroyed along the way without the danger of destruction, and "it will blissfully reach one's home"; "similarly," if any bodhisattva "has much faith" and aspiration seeking perfect enlightenment, "but lacks skill in means" to accomplish it "and the perfection of wisdom" of the path, they will fall into the lower path, degenerate from the Mahayana, and "quickly be ruined." If "faith and wisdom"—meaning both the aspect of method such as faith, and the perfection of wisdom—entirely embrace that person's continuum, they will completely transcend the two levels of sravakas and solitary realizers and "obtain supreme enlightenment," perfect enlightenment.

To demonstrate yet another example, it was said: For example, if a "boat" has "not been well prepared" with repairs for leaks and patches and so forth, "it will be destroyed in the ocean together with its goods and merchants," and will be ruined; whereas if that boat is well examined and endowed with good repairs and so forth, it will not be destroyed or damaged in the middle of the water, and the merchants together with their wealth "will blissfully reach the shore of the ocean"; similarly, if any bodhisattva's continuum is "entirely endowed with faith and compassion" and so forth, but "does not rely on the perfection of wisdom" of the path, they "will quickly degenerate from perfect enlightenment"; whereas if that very person endowed with wonderful "faith and so forth is endowed with the supreme perfection of wisdom," they will not be harmed by mental engagements of the lower vehicle, and without degenerating from the Mahayana path, "will touch the enlightenment of the Victorious Ones."

heading: **དབྱེ་བ།**
translation: To demonstrate that practicing the distinguished Mahayana preparation and bringing it to completion depends on properly relying on a Mahayana spiritual friend, three verses beginning with "bodhisattva" were spoken: Thus, any "bodhisattva abiding on the level of initial action"—meaning abiding on the first level, the Supremely Joyous, and so forth—who, out of a completely pure special resolve desiring to obtain unsurpassed perfect enlightenment for the sake of others, "enters into the preparation" of practicing the distinguished Mahayana preparation by means of seeking "the supreme enlightenment of a Buddha"—those good disciples endowed with faith and respect for the guru, who accomplish whatever is taught according to their word, "must constantly rely on learned gurus" whose view and conduct are supremely excellent and who are able to point out the meaning of the sutras of the perfection of wisdom without error.

Work: ཡོན་ཏན་རིན་པོ་ཆེ་སྡུད་པ་ཚིགས་སུ་བཅད་པའི་འགྲེལ་པ་ཟབ་མོ་རྟེན་འབྱུང་གི་དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཉིད་གསལ་བར་བྱེད་པའི་ནོར་བུའི་སྒྲོན་མེ་སྐལ་བཟང་རེ་སྐོང་། (Khenrab Jamyang, Commentary on the Verses of the Precious Qualities Collection), author: མཁྱེན་རབ་འཇམ་དབྱངས་བློ་བཟང་འཕྲིན་ལས།.
