[3-189] source:
དེས་ན་ཐབས་ཤེས་ཕྱོགས་རེ་བས་བླ་མེད་རྫོགས་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་མི་འགྲུབ་པས་བྱང་སེམས་ཀྱིས་ཐབས་ཤེས་ཆ་ཚང་བའི་ལམ་ལ་སློབ་དགོས་ཚུལ་དཔེས་སྒྲུབ་པ་ནི། དཔེར་ན་རྒྱ་མཚོར་འཇུག་པའི་མི་དག་གི་གྲུ་ནི་ཆག་སྟེ་ཞིག་པར་གྱུར་ལ། དེའི་ཚེ་མི་གང་དག་རོའམ་རྩའམ་ཤིང་ལེབ་སོགས་ནི་མི་འཛིན་པ་རང་གར་ལུས་པ་དེ་དག་ནི་ཆུ་ཡི་དབུས་སུ་འཇིག་པར་འགྱུར་བ་སྟེ་འཆི་བར་འགྱུར་ཞིང་རྒྱ་མཚོའི་ངོགས་སུ་ཕྱིན་པར་མི་འགྱུར་ལ། གང་ཞིག་ཤིང་ལ་སོགས་པ་འཛིན་པ་དེ་ནི་དེ་ལ་བརྟེན་ནས་རྒྱ་མཚོའི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་བདེ་བར་ཕྱིན་པར་འགྱུར་རོ། །དཔེར་དེ་ལྟར་རྫོགས་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་དོན་དུ་གཉེར་བའི་དད་པ་དང་ལྡན་ལ་ཡིད་སྤྲོ་བའི་དད་ལ་ཐོབ་པ་གང་ཞིག་ནི། བླ་མེད་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཐོབ་བྱེད་ཀྱི་ལམ་གྱི་མཆོག་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་རྒྱལ་བ་རྣམས་ཀྱི་བསྐྱེད་པའི་ཡུམ་ལ་དད་པ་རྙེད་ནས་ཉམས་སུ་ལེན་པ་ལ་རྗེས་སུ་མི་འཇུག་པ་ནི། འབྲས་བུ་རྫོགས་བྱང་ཐོབ་པར་འགྱུར་བ་མིན་ཞིང་། འདི་ལྟར་སྐྱེ་རྒ་ན་འཆི་དང་ཡིད་མི་བདེ་བ་སོགས་མྱ་ངན་དང་སྡུག་བསྔལ་རྣམ་པ་སྣ་ཚོགས་ཀྱི་རྦ་རླབས་འཁྲུག་པ་ཡི་འཁོར་བའི་རྒྱ་མཚོ་ཆེན་པོ་དེ་ནི་དུས་རྟག་ཏུ་འཁོར་བར་འགྱུར་བ་ཡིན་ལ། གང་ཟག་གང་ཡིན་པ་དེ་བདེན་མེད་རྟོགས་པའི་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་མཆོག་གིས་ཡོངས་སུ་ཟིན་པར་གྱུར་པ་ན། དངོས་པོའི་རང་བཞིན་གནས་ལུགས་ཀྱི་དོན་ལ་མཁས་ཤིང་མཚན་འཛིན་དང་བྲལ་ནས་དོན་དམ་བདེན་པ་ཕྱིན་ཅི་མ་ལོག་པར་སྟོན་པར་བྱེད་པར་འགྱུར་རོ། །
[3-189] translation already produced for this document:
Therefore, since one cannot accomplish unsurpassed perfect enlightenment with one-sided method or wisdom, establishing through an example the way bodhisattvas must train in a path complete with both method and wisdom is as follows: For example, if a "boat" of "people embarking on the ocean" breaks and falls apart, at that time those people who "do not hold onto a corpse, grass, or a piece of wood" and so forth, remaining as they are, "will be destroyed in the middle of the water," meaning they will die, and will not reach the shore of the ocean; whereas "those who hold onto wood" and so forth, in reliance upon that, "will blissfully reach the other shore of the ocean." "Like that example," any person who possesses faith seeking perfect enlightenment and obtains joyous faith, but who, after finding faith in the perfection of wisdom—the supreme path that brings about the attainment of unsurpassed enlightenment and the mother that generates the Victorious Ones—"does not engage in" practicing it, will not obtain the result of perfect enlightenment; thus, they will constantly wander in the great ocean of samsara, churning with the waves of various kinds of sorrow and suffering such as birth, aging, sickness, death, and mental unhappiness. When that person is embraced by the supreme perfection of wisdom realizing lack of true existence, they will be skilled in the meaning of the abiding nature of entities, and being free from apprehending signs, they will point out ultimate truth without error.

[3-190] source:
དེ་དག་གི་རྫོགས་བྱང་དོན་གཉེར་གྱི་དད་པ་དང་སྙིང་རྗེ་སོགས་ཐབས་ཀྱི་ཡོན་ཏན་དེ་དག་དམིགས་མེད་དུ་རྟོགས་པའི་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱིས་ཡོངས་སུ་ཟིན་པར་འགྱུར་ན་བསོད་ནམས་དང་ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་གཉིས་ཡོངས་སུ་རྫོགས་ཏེ་ཉན་རང་སོགས་ཀྱི་ཡུལ་དུ་མ་གྱུར་བས་མཆོག་ཏུ་རྨད་དུ་བྱུང་བའི་བདེ་བར་གཤེགས་པ་རྣམས་ཀྱི་བྱང་ཆུབ་མྱུར་དུ་རེག་པ་སྟེ་ཐོབ་པར་འགྱུར་རོ། །
[3-190] translation already produced for this document:
If those qualities of method, such as their faith seeking perfect enlightenment and compassion, are entirely embraced by wisdom realizing non-apprehension, the two accumulations of merit and pristine wisdom will be completely perfected, and since they do not fall into the domain of sravakas and solitary realizers, they will swiftly touch, meaning obtain, the supremely wonderful enlightenment of the Sugatas.

[3-191] source:
དེ་ལས་གཞན་ཡང་དཔེར་ན་མི་རྨོངས་པ་ལ་ལས་རྫ་སོ་མ་བཏང་བ་སྟེ་མེར་མ་བསྲེགས་པར་ཆུ་སྐྱེད་པར་བྱས་ན་བུམ་པ་དེ་འཇིག་སླ་བས་ཉམས་ཆུང་བའི་ཕྱིར་ན་མྱུར་དུ་འཇིག་པར་བྱའོ། །སོ་བཏང་བུམ་པར་ཆུ་སྐྱེད་པར་བྱས་ན་ལམ་བར་དུ་ཞིག་ཅིང་འཇིག་པའི་འདོགས་པ་ཡི་འཇིག་པ་མེད་ཅིང་བདེ་བར་རང་གི་ཁྱིམ་དུ་ཕྱིན་པར་འགྱུར་བ་དེ་བཞིན་དུ། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གང་ཞིག་རྫོགས་བྱང་དོན་གཉེར་གྱི་འདུན་པ་དང་དད་པ་མང་བ་དང་ཆེ་བར་གྱུར་ཀྱང་། དེ་སྒྲུབ་བྱེད་ཀྱི་ཐབས་མཁས་དང་ལམ་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལས་རྣམ་པར་ཉམས་པར་གྱུར་ན་དམན་ལམ་དུ་ལྟུང་ནས་ཐེག་པ་ཆེན་པོ་ལས་ཉམས་ཤིང་མྱུར་དུ་མ་རུང་བར་འགྱུར་རོ། །དད་པས་ཤེས་རབ་སྟེ་དད་སོགས་ཐབས་ཀྱི་ཆ་དང་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕར་ཕྱིན་གཉིིས་ཀྱིས་དེ་ནི་གང་ཟག་དེའི་རྒྱུད་ཡོངས་སུ་ཟིན་པར་གྱུར་ན་ཉན་རང་གི་ས་གཉིས་ལས་ཤིན་ཏུ་འདས་ཏེ་བྱང་ཆུབ་མཆོག་རྫོགས་པའི་བྱུང་ཆུབ་ཐོབ་པར་འགྱུར་རོ། །
[3-191] translation already produced for this document:
Furthermore, as another example, if "some ignorant person carries water in an unfired clay vessel"—meaning unbaked by fire—because that vase is fragile and weak, "it will quickly be destroyed." "If one carries water in a fired vase," it will not break or be destroyed along the way without the danger of destruction, and "it will blissfully reach one's home"; "similarly," if any bodhisattva "has much faith" and aspiration seeking perfect enlightenment, "but lacks skill in means" to accomplish it "and the perfection of wisdom" of the path, they will fall into the lower path, degenerate from the Mahayana, and "quickly be ruined." If "faith and wisdom"—meaning both the aspect of method such as faith, and the perfection of wisdom—entirely embrace that person's continuum, they will completely transcend the two levels of sravakas and solitary realizers and "obtain supreme enlightenment," perfect enlightenment.

[3-192] source:
དཔེ་གཞན་ཡང་བསྟན་པའི་ཕྱིར་གསུངས་པ། དཔེར་ན་བུག་རྡོལ་དང་ཟག་ལྷན་སོགས་བཟོ་བཅོས་ལེགས་པར་མ་བྱས་པའི་གྲུ་དེ་ནི་རྒྱུ་མཚོའི་ནང་དུ་ནོར་རྫས་དང་བཅས་ཤིང་ཚོང་བར་བཅས་ཏེ་འཇིག་པར་འགྱུར་ཞིང་མ་རུང་བར་འགྱུར་ལ། གྲུ་དེ་ལེགས་པར་བརྟག་ནས་བཟོ་བཅོས་སོགས་ལེགས་པོར་བྱས་པ་དང་ལྡན་པར་གྱུར་ན། ཆུའི་དབུས་སུ་མི་འཇིག་ཅིང་མི་ཉམས་པར་ཚོང་བ་ནོར་དང་བཅས་པ་རྒྱ་མཆོའི་འགྲམ་གྱི་ངོགས་སུ་བདེ་བར་ཕྱིན་པར་འགྱུར་བ་དེ་ལྟར་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གང་ཞིག་དད་པ་དངསྙིང་རྗེ་ལ་སོགས་པས་རྒྱུད་ཡོངས་སུ་བགོས་ཀྱང༌། ལམ་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལ་བརྟེན་པ་མེད་ན་རྫོགས་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་ལས་ནི་མྱུར་དུ་ཉམས་པར་འགྱུར་ཞིང་། དད་སོགས་རྨད་དུ་བྱུང་བ་དང་ལྡན་པ་དེ་ཉིད་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཕྱིན་པ་མཆོག་དང་ལྡན་པར་འགྱུར་ན། ཐེག་དམན་ཡིད་བྱེད་ཀྱིས་མ་རྨས་ཤིང་ཐེག་པ་ཆེེན་པོའི་ལམ་ལས་མ་ཉམས་པར་རྒྱལ་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་ལ་རེག་པར་འགྱུར་རོ། །
[3-192] translation already produced for this document:
To demonstrate yet another example, it was said: For example, if a "boat" has "not been well prepared" with repairs for leaks and patches and so forth, "it will be destroyed in the ocean together with its goods and merchants," and will be ruined; whereas if that boat is well examined and endowed with good repairs and so forth, it will not be destroyed or damaged in the middle of the water, and the merchants together with their wealth "will blissfully reach the shore of the ocean"; similarly, if any bodhisattva's continuum is "entirely endowed with faith and compassion" and so forth, but "does not rely on the perfection of wisdom" of the path, they "will quickly degenerate from perfect enlightenment"; whereas if that very person endowed with wonderful "faith and so forth is endowed with the supreme perfection of wisdom," they will not be harmed by mental engagements of the lower vehicle, and without degenerating from the Mahayana path, "will touch the enlightenment of the Victorious Ones."

heading: **དབྱེ་བ།**
translation: If one asks why one must rely in that way: because "all qualities"—such as the qualities of being learned in the Mahayana path together with its result, and generating those paths in one's continuum—"arise from that" proper reliance on a spiritual friend; and because those spiritual friends "teach" this perfection of wisdom of the Mahayana path. Therefore, "the Victor", the completely perfect Buddha who possesses the supreme of all qualities, "spoke thus", saying that "the dharmas of a Buddha"—the qualities of abandonment and realization such as the powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unshared dharmas—"rely on the spiritual friend" of the Mahayana, because there is no basis for those qualities to arise without relying on a spiritual friend. Therefore, out of great affection he instructed us, saying, "One must properly rely on a spiritual friend through both thought and action." This shows the distinguishing characteristic of being entirely embraced by the method of a spiritual friend. If one asks what kind of instructions and subsequent teachings the spiritual friends teach: The summary of the Mahayana path that you must practice is the "six perfections". Instructing, "Properly train in the great waves of practice of the perfections—'giving' (giving away one's body, wealth, and all roots of virtue to others), completely pure 'ethical discipline, and patience, and similarly joyous effort, and concentration, and wisdom'—and entirely 'dedicate' the roots of virtue 'to unsurpassed enlightenment' without being tainted by the stain of mental engagements of the lower vehicle," is the instruction on the aspect of method. Furthermore, the instruction, "Do not adhere to and apprehend that ultimate great enlightenment as supreme by strongly adhering to it as truly existent in the uncontaminated aggregates such as the aggregate of ethical discipline," is the instruction on the aspect of wisdom. "That should be taught to that person of initial action" with aspiration "for enlightenment". This shows the distinguishing characteristic of having no savoring through strong adherence.

"If that person is supported on their right and left sides by two people possessing strength and they go," there is no danger of falling along the way, and "they will easily go to the place they wish to go"; "similarly, if any bodhisattva's wisdom" realizing emptiness "is weak," "even if they have fully entered the Mahayana path, they will degenerate" before obtaining the result of unsurpassed enlightenment; whereas if that very bodhisattva's entire path in their continuum is "entirely embraced by" the aspect of method such as faith and "the supreme wisdom" realizing lack of true existence, they will not degenerate from the supreme path and "will quickly touch the enlightenment of the Tathagatas." Therefore, intelligent bodhisattvas must train in the path complete with method and wisdom and seize the royal seat of supreme enlightenment. This concludes the commentary on the fourteenth chapter, the chapter on examples, from the Lamp of Jewels Illuminating the Suchness of Profound Dependent Origination, Fulfilling the Hopes of the Fortunate, a commentary on the Verses of the Precious Qualities Collection.

To demonstrate that practicing the distinguished Mahayana preparation and bringing it to completion depends on properly relying on a Mahayana spiritual friend, three verses beginning with "bodhisattva" were spoken: Thus, any "bodhisattva abiding on the level of initial action"—meaning abiding on the first level, the Supremely Joyous, and so forth—who, out of a completely pure special resolve desiring to obtain unsurpassed perfect enlightenment for the sake of others, "enters into the preparation" of practicing the distinguished Mahayana preparation by means of seeking "the supreme enlightenment of a Buddha"—those good disciples endowed with faith and respect for the guru, who accomplish whatever is taught according to their word, "must constantly rely on learned gurus" whose view and conduct are supremely excellent and who are able to point out the meaning of the sutras of the perfection of wisdom without error.

heading: **དབྱེ་བ།**
translation: Thirdly, to demonstrate the distinguishing characteristic of action endowed with the distinguished functions of benefiting, giving happiness, protecting, and so forth, one verse beginning with "acting thus" was spoken. Its meaning is: By the power of having meditated on the distinguished Mahayana preparation, the great being bodhisattvas who "act thus" as previously explained—that is, who excellently point out the instruction on how to practice the Mahayana path in that way—are equal to an ocean of qualities of abandonment and realization, moons of speech endowed with the light rays of the nectar of the profound and vast Dharma. Because they teach the Dharma that is the cause of benefit and happiness, they have become a "refuge" that dispels the suffering of transmigrators; they have become a "defender" that establishes them in the happiness of liberation; and they have become a "place" that dispels negative actions and obscurations, the causes of suffering. "Similarly," they have become a "support" for proceeding to great enlightenment; they have become an "intellect" that distinguishes good and bad; by establishing those sinking in the river of existence on the dry land of the true path of the holy Dharma, they are an "island"; by teaching the meaning of non-arising, they are like a "captain" who desires the goal or accomplishes the goal of entirely drawing them out of the ocean of cyclic existence; they have become a great "lamp" of Dharma that dispels the darkness of ignorance and clearly illuminates the path of enlightenment; and when they speak on the meaning of emptiness, the supreme profound Dharma, they cannot be disturbed by opponents such as demons and extremists, so they are "undisturbed" and without fear of anything, for having found certainty in the profound Dharma through valid cognition, their eloquence in explaining it is completely perfected to be fully victorious over all opponents. Furthermore, "refuge of transmigrators" demonstrates the characteristic of action of the knowledge of bases, and "defender" and so forth demonstrate the characteristics of action of the knowledge of paths and so forth. In the Aṣṭasāhasrikā as well: "Subhūti, whichever great bodhisattva enters for the sake of benefiting the world, enters for the sake of giving happiness to the world, and enters for the sake of compassion for the world, and having manifestly awakened to unsurpassed completely perfect enlightenment, will become a protector of the world." With this and so forth, the first nine functions of benefiting, giving happiness, protecting, and so forth are briefly demonstrated together, and then it is taught extensively for each with: "Subhūti, if one asks how a great bodhisattva, having manifestly awakened to unsurpassed completely perfect enlightenment, becomes a protector of the world, Subhūti..." and so forth.

If one asks why one must rely in that way: because "all qualities"—such as the qualities of being learned in the Mahayana path together with its result, and generating those paths in one's continuum—"arise from that" proper reliance on a spiritual friend; and because those spiritual friends "teach" this perfection of wisdom of the Mahayana path. Therefore, "the Victor", the completely perfect Buddha who possesses the supreme of all qualities, "spoke thus", saying that "the dharmas of a Buddha"—the qualities of abandonment and realization such as the powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unshared dharmas—"rely on the spiritual friend" of the Mahayana, because there is no basis for those qualities to arise without relying on a spiritual friend. Therefore, out of great affection he instructed us, saying, "One must properly rely on a spiritual friend through both thought and action." This shows the distinguishing characteristic of being entirely embraced by the method of a spiritual friend. If one asks what kind of instructions and subsequent teachings the spiritual friends teach: The summary of the Mahayana path that you must practice is the "six perfections". Instructing, "Properly train in the great waves of practice of the perfections—'giving' (giving away one's body, wealth, and all roots of virtue to others), completely pure 'ethical discipline, and patience, and similarly joyous effort, and concentration, and wisdom'—and entirely 'dedicate' the roots of virtue 'to unsurpassed enlightenment' without being tainted by the stain of mental engagements of the lower vehicle," is the instruction on the aspect of method. Furthermore, the instruction, "Do not adhere to and apprehend that ultimate great enlightenment as supreme by strongly adhering to it as truly existent in the uncontaminated aggregates such as the aggregate of ethical discipline," is the instruction on the aspect of wisdom. "That should be taught to that person of initial action" with aspiration "for enlightenment". This shows the distinguishing characteristic of having no savoring through strong adherence.

heading: **དབྱེ་བ།**
translation: Fourthly, to demonstrate the distinguishing characteristic of essence, six verses beginning with "those possessing great renown" were spoken. Their meaning is: "Those possessing great renown"—who have entered the Mahayana path and whose name "bodhisattva" is of great renown in the fields of the Victors of the ten directions—"don" a great "armor" of extremely difficult deeds, generating the resolve thinking, "I alone shall establish all sentient beings, equal to space, in non-abiding nirvana." Furthermore, they do not don the armor by way of apprehending the essence of dharmas—such as the five aggregates on the side of thorough affliction, the eighteen elements, and the twelve sense sources—as truly existent; they are free from the perception of strongly adhering to the paths of the three vehicles on the side of the remedy, complete purification; and because they abide in the perfection of wisdom without entirely apprehending or grasping any dharma as truly established, they do not degenerate from the perfection of their own purpose, being irreversible from perfect enlightenment, and they do not waver to anything other than the perfection of the purpose of others, the Mahayana path. Since no demons or anyone else can afflict their continuums, they possess the nature of not degenerating from the perfection of the two purposes and being undisturbed.

ཐབས་ཤེས་ཡ་མ་བྲལ་བར་ཟུང་འབྲེལ་དུ་ཉམས་སུ་ལེན་པ་གནད་ཆེ་བར་བསྟན་པ་ནི། དཔེར་ན་སྐྱེ་བུ་གང་ཞིག་ལོ་བརྒྱ་ཉི་ཤུ་ལོན་ཏེ་ཆེའི་མཐར་ཐུག་པའི་རྒས་ཤིང་ནད་ལ་སོགས་པས་སྡུག་བསྔལ་བར་གྱུར་བའི་མི་དེ་ནི་སྟན་ལས་ལྡང་མི་ནུས་པ་ལ་ལངས་ནུས་པར་གྱུར་ཀྱང་བདག་ཉིད་རང་སྟོབས་ཀྱིས་རྒྱང་གྲགས་ལ་སོགས་པར་གཞན་དུ་འགྲོ་བ་ནུས་པ་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ་རྒས་ཤིང་འཁོགས་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །གལ་ཏེ་མི་དེ་ནི་མཆན་གཡས་གཡོན་གཉིས་ནས་མི་སྟོབས་དང་ལྡན་པ་ཡིས་བརྟེན་པར་བྱས་ནས་སོང་ན་ལམ་བར་དུ་འགྱེལ་བའི་འཇིག་པ་མེད་ཅིང་གང་དུ་འགྲོ་བར་འདོད་པའི་གནས་སུ་བདེ་བླག་ཏུ་འགྲོ་བར་འགྱུར་བ་དེ་བཞིན་དུ་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གང་ཞིག་སྟོང་ཉིད་རྟོགས་པའི་ཤེས་རབ་སྟོབས་ཆུང་བ་དེ་ནི་ཐེག་པ་ཆེན་པོའི་ལམ་ལ་རབ་ཏུ་ཞུགས་པར་གྱུར་ཀྱང་འབྲས་བུ་བླ་མེད་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཐོབ་པའི་བར་དུ་ཉམས་པར་འགྱུར་ལ། བྱང་སེམས་དེ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་རྒྱུད་ཀྱི་ལམ་ཐམས་ཅད་དད་སོགས་ཐབས་ཀྱི་ཆ་དང་བདེན་མེད་རྟོགས་པའི་ཤེས་རབ་མཆོག་གིས་ཡོངས་སུ་ཟིན་པར་གྱུར་ན་ཐེག་པ་མཆོག་གི་ལམ་ལས་མི་ཉམས་པར་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་རྣམས་ཀྱི་བྱང་ཆུབ་ལ་མྱུར་དུ་རེག་པར་འགྱུར་རོ། །དེས་ན་བྱང་སེམས་བློ་དང་ལྡན་པ་རྣམས་ཀྱི་ཐབས་ཤེས་ཆ་ཚང་བའི་ལམ་ལ་བསླབ་སྟེ་བྱང་ཆུབ་མཆོག་གི་རྒྱལ་ས་ཟིན་པར་བྱའོ། །ཡོན་ཏན་རིན་པོ་ཆེ་སྡུད་པ་ཚིགས་སུ་བཅད་པའི་འགྲེལ་བ་ཟབ་མོ་རྟེན་འབྱུང་གི་དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཉིད་གསལ་བར་བྱེད་པའི་ནོར་བུའི་སྒྲོན་མེ་སྐལ་མེ་སྐལ་བཟང་རེ་སྐོང་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལས་དཔེའི་ལེའུ་སྟེ་བཅུ་བཞི་པའི་འགྲེལ་བའོ།།   །།
[3-193] translation already produced for this document:
Showing that practicing method and wisdom united without separation is of great importance: For example, if "some person reaches the age of one hundred and twenty," reaching the end of their lifespan, and that person who is "aged and suffering from illness and so forth" is "unable to rise from their seat"; and "even if they are able to stand up," they are "unable to go elsewhere," such as a krośa away, "by their own strength," because they are old and decrepit. "If that person is supported on their right and left sides by two people possessing strength and they go," there is no danger of falling along the way, and "they will easily go to the place they wish to go"; "similarly, if any bodhisattva's wisdom" realizing emptiness "is weak," "even if they have fully entered the Mahayana path, they will degenerate" before obtaining the result of unsurpassed enlightenment; whereas if that very bodhisattva's entire path in their continuum is "entirely embraced by" the aspect of method such as faith and "the supreme wisdom" realizing lack of true existence, they will not degenerate from the supreme path and "will quickly touch the enlightenment of the Tathagatas." Therefore, intelligent bodhisattvas must train in the path complete with method and wisdom and seize the royal seat of supreme enlightenment. This concludes the commentary on the fourteenth chapter, the chapter on examples, from the Lamp of Jewels Illuminating the Suchness of Profound Dependent Origination, Fulfilling the Hopes of the Fortunate, a commentary on the Verses of the Precious Qualities Collection.

ཐེག་ཆེན་གྱི་སྦྱོར་བ་ཁྱད་པར་ཅན་ཉམས་སུ་ལེན་ཅིང་མཐར་ཕྱིན་པར་འགྱུར་བ་ཐེག་པ་ཆེན་པོའི་དགེ་བའི་བཤེས་གཉེན་ཚུལ་བཞིན་དུ་བསྟེན་པ་ལ་རག་ལས་སོ་ཞེས་བསྟན་པའི་ཕྱིར། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཞེས་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གསུམ་གསུངས་ཏེ། འདི་ལྟར་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་དང་པོའི་ལས་ཀྱི་སར་གནས་པ་སྟེ་ས་དང་པོ་རབ་ཏུ་དགའ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པར་གནས་པ་གང་ཞིག །གཞན་གྱི་དོན་དུ་བླ་མེད་རྫོགས་བྱུང་ཐོབ་པར་འདོད་པའི་ལྷག་པའི་བསམ་པ་རྣམ་པར་དག་པས། སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་བྱང་ཆུབ་མཆོག་དོན་དུ་གཉེར་བའི་སྒོ་ནས་ཐེག་ཆེན་གྱི་སྦྱོར་བ་ཁྱད་པར་ཅན་ཉམས་སུ་ལེན་པའི་སྦྱར་བ་ལ་ཞུགས་པ་ཡི་སློབ་མ་བཟང་པོ་བླ་མ་ལ་དད་ཅིང་གུས་པ་དང་ལྡན་པ་ཅི་གསུངས་བཀའ་བཞིན་སྒྲུབ་པ་དེ་དག་གིས། ལྟ་སྤྱོད་མཆོག་ཏུ་བཟང་ཞིང་ཤེར་ཕྱིན་གྱི་མདོའི་དོན་ཕྱིན་ཅི་མ་ལོག་སྟོན་པར་ནུས་པའི་བླ་མ་མཁས་པ་རྣམས་ལ་རྟག་ཏུ་བརྟེན་པར་བྱའོ། །
[3-194] translation already produced for this document:
To demonstrate that practicing the distinguished Mahayana preparation and bringing it to completion depends on properly relying on a Mahayana spiritual friend, three verses beginning with "bodhisattva" were spoken: Thus, any "bodhisattva abiding on the level of initial action"—meaning abiding on the first level, the Supremely Joyous, and so forth—who, out of a completely pure special resolve desiring to obtain unsurpassed perfect enlightenment for the sake of others, "enters into the preparation" of practicing the distinguished Mahayana preparation by means of seeking "the supreme enlightenment of a Buddha"—those good disciples endowed with faith and respect for the guru, who accomplish whatever is taught according to their word, "must constantly rely on learned gurus" whose view and conduct are supremely excellent and who are able to point out the meaning of the sutras of the perfection of wisdom without error.

If one asks why one must rely in that way: because "all qualities"—such as the qualities of being learned in the Mahayana path together with its result, and generating those paths in one's continuum—"arise from that" proper reliance on a spiritual friend; and because those spiritual friends "teach" this perfection of wisdom of the Mahayana path. Therefore, "the Victor", the completely perfect Buddha who possesses the supreme of all qualities, "spoke thus", saying that "the dharmas of a Buddha"—the qualities of abandonment and realization such as the powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unshared dharmas—"rely on the spiritual friend" of the Mahayana, because there is no basis for those qualities to arise without relying on a spiritual friend. Therefore, out of great affection he instructed us, saying, "One must properly rely on a spiritual friend through both thought and action." This shows the distinguishing characteristic of being entirely embraced by the method of a spiritual friend. If one asks what kind of instructions and subsequent teachings the spiritual friends teach: The summary of the Mahayana path that you must practice is the "six perfections". Instructing, "Properly train in the great waves of practice of the perfections—'giving' (giving away one's body, wealth, and all roots of virtue to others), completely pure 'ethical discipline, and patience, and similarly joyous effort, and concentration, and wisdom'—and entirely 'dedicate' the roots of virtue 'to unsurpassed enlightenment' without being tainted by the stain of mental engagements of the lower vehicle," is the instruction on the aspect of method. Furthermore, the instruction, "Do not adhere to and apprehend that ultimate great enlightenment as supreme by strongly adhering to it as truly existent in the uncontaminated aggregates such as the aggregate of ethical discipline," is the instruction on the aspect of wisdom. "That should be taught to that person of initial action" with aspiration "for enlightenment". This shows the distinguishing characteristic of having no savoring through strong adherence.

heading: **དབྱེ་བ།**
translation: Thus, those bodhisattvas are endowed with such profound and hard-to-fathom qualities, and having generated in their continuums the non-conceptual exalted wisdom obtained by the power of meditating on the preparation—the exalted wisdom free from the elaborations of dualistic appearance—they are free from doubt, hesitation, and double-mindedness regarding the Dharma of the Mahayana, and having found certainty in their own path through valid cognition, they possess the meaning of conviction. By the power of that, having heard the profound perfection of wisdom, their minds do not shrink back from its meaning; and because they have deeply found certainty in their own path and integrated it into experience, they do not rely on others—meaning they do not go wherever led by others—and should be known as irreversible from the Mahayana.

Thirdly, to demonstrate the distinguishing characteristic of action endowed with the distinguished functions of benefiting, giving happiness, protecting, and so forth, one verse beginning with "acting thus" was spoken. Its meaning is: By the power of having meditated on the distinguished Mahayana preparation, the great being bodhisattvas who "act thus" as previously explained—that is, who excellently point out the instruction on how to practice the Mahayana path in that way—are equal to an ocean of qualities of abandonment and realization, moons of speech endowed with the light rays of the nectar of the profound and vast Dharma. Because they teach the Dharma that is the cause of benefit and happiness, they have become a "refuge" that dispels the suffering of transmigrators; they have become a "defender" that establishes them in the happiness of liberation; and they have become a "place" that dispels negative actions and obscurations, the causes of suffering. "Similarly," they have become a "support" for proceeding to great enlightenment; they have become an "intellect" that distinguishes good and bad; by establishing those sinking in the river of existence on the dry land of the true path of the holy Dharma, they are an "island"; by teaching the meaning of non-arising, they are like a "captain" who desires the goal or accomplishes the goal of entirely drawing them out of the ocean of cyclic existence; they have become a great "lamp" of Dharma that dispels the darkness of ignorance and clearly illuminates the path of enlightenment; and when they speak on the meaning of emptiness, the supreme profound Dharma, they cannot be disturbed by opponents such as demons and extremists, so they are "undisturbed" and without fear of anything, for having found certainty in the profound Dharma through valid cognition, their eloquence in explaining it is completely perfected to be fully victorious over all opponents. Furthermore, "refuge of transmigrators" demonstrates the characteristic of action of the knowledge of bases, and "defender" and so forth demonstrate the characteristics of action of the knowledge of paths and so forth. In the Aṣṭasāhasrikā as well: "Subhūti, whichever great bodhisattva enters for the sake of benefiting the world, enters for the sake of giving happiness to the world, and enters for the sake of compassion for the world, and having manifestly awakened to unsurpassed completely perfect enlightenment, will become a protector of the world." With this and so forth, the first nine functions of benefiting, giving happiness, protecting, and so forth are briefly demonstrated together, and then it is taught extensively for each with: "Subhūti, if one asks how a great bodhisattva, having manifestly awakened to unsurpassed completely perfect enlightenment, becomes a protector of the world, Subhūti..." and so forth.

Fourthly, to demonstrate the distinguishing characteristic of essence, six verses beginning with "those possessing great renown" were spoken. Their meaning is: "Those possessing great renown"—who have entered the Mahayana path and whose name "bodhisattva" is of great renown in the fields of the Victors of the ten directions—"don" a great "armor" of extremely difficult deeds, generating the resolve thinking, "I alone shall establish all sentient beings, equal to space, in non-abiding nirvana." Furthermore, they do not don the armor by way of apprehending the essence of dharmas—such as the five aggregates on the side of thorough affliction, the eighteen elements, and the twelve sense sources—as truly existent; they are free from the perception of strongly adhering to the paths of the three vehicles on the side of the remedy, complete purification; and because they abide in the perfection of wisdom without entirely apprehending or grasping any dharma as truly established, they do not degenerate from the perfection of their own purpose, being irreversible from perfect enlightenment, and they do not waver to anything other than the perfection of the purpose of others, the Mahayana path. Since no demons or anyone else can afflict their continuums, they possess the nature of not degenerating from the perfection of the two purposes and being undisturbed.

heading: **དབྱེ་བ།**
translation: This perfection of wisdom, the Dharma of the guide Buddhas, is supremely profound. The abiding nature of dharmas, suchness, is difficult to see as it is by a mind with dualistic appearance, and it is not realized directly by any ordinary beings whose continuums are tainted by true grasping; and it is ultimately unobtainable, and will not become obtainable either.

Work: ཡོན་ཏན་རིན་པོ་ཆེ་སྡུད་པ་ཚིགས་སུ་བཅད་པའི་འགྲེལ་པ་ཟབ་མོ་རྟེན་འབྱུང་གི་དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཉིད་གསལ་བར་བྱེད་པའི་ནོར་བུའི་སྒྲོན་མེ་སྐལ་བཟང་རེ་སྐོང་། (Khenrab Jamyang, Commentary on the Verses of the Precious Qualities Collection), author: མཁྱེན་རབ་འཇམ་དབྱངས་བློ་བཟང་འཕྲིན་ལས།. གསུམ་པ་ཕན་བདེ་སྐྱོབ་སོགས་ཀྱི་བྱེད་ལས་ཁྱད་པར་ཅན་དང་ལྡན་པའི་བྱེད་མཚན་སྟོན་པར། དེ་ལྟར་སྤྱོད་པ་ཞེས་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གཅིག་གསུངས་པའི་དོན། ཐེག་ཆེན་སྦྱོར་བ་ཁྱད་པར་ཅན་བསྒོམས་པའི་སྟོབས་ཀྱིས་སྔར་བཤད་པ་དེ་ལྟར་སྤྱོད་པ་སྟེ་དེ་ལྟར་ཐེག་པ་ཆེན་པོའི་ལམ་ཉམས་སུ་ལེན་ཚུལ་གྱི་གདམས་ངག་ལེགས་པར་སྟོན་པའི་བྱང་སེམས་བདག་ཉིད་ཆེན་པོ་སྤངས་རྟོགས་ཀྱི་ཡོན་ཏན་རྒྱ་མཚོ་དང་མཚུངས་པ། ཟབ་རྒྱས་ཆོས་ཀྱི་བདུད་རྩིའི་འོད་ཟེར་དང་ལྡན་པའི་སྨྲ་བའི་ཟླ་བ་རྣམས་ནི། ཕན་བདེའི་རྒྱུ་ཆོས་སྟོན་པས་འགྲོ་བའི་སྔུག་བསྔལ་སེལ་བའི་སྐྱབས་སུ་གྱུར་པ་དང་། ཐར་བའི་བདེ་ལ་འགོད་པའི་དཔུང་གཉེན་དུ་གྱུར་པ་དང་ནི། སྔུག་བསྔལ་གྱི་རྒྱུ་སྡིག་སྒྲིབ་སེལ་བའི་གནས་སུ་གྱུར་པ་ཡིན་ཏེ། དེ་བཞིན་དུ་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཆེན་པོར་འགྲོ་བའི་རྟེན་དུ་གྱུར་པ་དང་། ལེགས་ཉེས་འབྱེད་པའི་བློ་གྲོས་སུ་གྱུར་པ་དང་། སྲིད་པའི་ཆུ་བོར་བྱིང་པ་དམ་པའི་ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྐམ་ས་ཡང་དག་པའི་ལམ་ལ་འགོད་པས་གླིང་དང་། སྐྱེ་མེད་ཀྱི་དོན་བསྟན་པས་འཁོར་བའི་རྒྱ་མཚོ་ལས་ཡོངས་སུ་འདྲེན་པའི་དོན་འདོད་པའམ་དོན་བྱེད་པའི་དད་དཔོན་ལྟ་བུ་ཡིན་པ་དང་། མ་རིག་པའི་མུན་པ་སེལ་ཞིང་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཀྱི་ལམ་རབ་ཏུ་གསལ་བར་བྱེད་པའི་ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྒྲོན་མེ་ཆེན་པོར་གྱུར་པ་དང༌། ཆོས་ཀྱི་མཆོག་ཟབ་མོ་སྟོང་པ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་དོན་སྨྲ་བ་ལ་ཕས་རྒོལ་བདུད་དང་མུ་སྟེགས་ལ་སོགས་པས་འཁྲུགས་པར་མི་ནུས་པས་མི་འཁྲུགས་ཤིང་གང་ལ་ཡང་འཇིག་པ་མེད་པ་ཡིན་ཏེ། ཟབ་མོའི་ཆོས་ལ་ཚད་མས་ངེས་བ་རྙེད་པས་དེའི་འཆད་པ་ལ་ཕྱོགས་ལས་རྣམ་པར་རྒྱལ་བའི་སྤོབས་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་རྫོགས་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །ཞེས་པ་སྟེ། དེ་ཡང་འགྲོ་བའི་སྐྱབས་ཞེས་པས་གཞི་ཤེས་ཀྱི་བྱེད་མཚན་དང་དཔུང་གཉེན་ཞེས་སོགས་ཀྱིས་ལམ་ཤེས་སོགས་ཀྱི་བྱེད་མཚན་སོགས་བསྟན་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །བརྒྱད་སྟོང་པ་ལས་ཀྱང༌། རབ་འབྱོར་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཆེན་པོ་གང་འཇིག་རྟེན་ལ་ཕན་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཞུགས་པ་དང་འཇིག་རྟེན་ལ་བདེ་བའི་ཕྱིར་དང་འཇིག་རྟེན་ལ་སྙིང་བརྩེ་བའི་ཕྱིར་ཞུགས་པ་དང༌། བླ་ན་མེད་པར་ཡང་དག་པར་རྫོགས་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་མངོན་པར་རྫོགས་པར་སངས་རྒྱས་ནས། འཇིག་རྟེན་གྱི་སྐྱོབ་པར་འགྱུར་བ་ཞེས་བྱའོ། །ཞེས་སོགས་ཀྱིས་ཕན་བདེ་སྐྱོབ་སོགས་ཀྱི་བྱེད་པ་དང་པོ་དགུ་མཉམ་དུ་མདོར་བསྟན་ནས། རབ་འབྱོར་ཇི་ལྟར་ན་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཆེེན་པོ་བླ་ན་མེད་པ་ཡང་དག་པར་རྫོགས་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་མངོན་བར་རྫོགས་པར་སངས་རྒྱས་ནས་འཇིག་རྟེན་གྱི་སྐྱོབ་པར་འགྱུར་ཞེ་ན། རབ་འབྱོར་ཞེས་སོགས་ཀྱིས་སོ་སོར་རྒྱས་པར་བསྟན་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །
[3-196] translation already produced for this document:
Thirdly, to demonstrate the distinguishing characteristic of action endowed with the distinguished functions of benefiting, giving happiness, protecting, and so forth, one verse beginning with "acting thus" was spoken. Its meaning is: By the power of having meditated on the distinguished Mahayana preparation, the great being bodhisattvas who "act thus" as previously explained—that is, who excellently point out the instruction on how to practice the Mahayana path in that way—are equal to an ocean of qualities of abandonment and realization, moons of speech endowed with the light rays of the nectar of the profound and vast Dharma. Because they teach the Dharma that is the cause of benefit and happiness, they have become a "refuge" that dispels the suffering of transmigrators; they have become a "defender" that establishes them in the happiness of liberation; and they have become a "place" that dispels negative actions and obscurations, the causes of suffering. "Similarly," they have become a "support" for proceeding to great enlightenment; they have become an "intellect" that distinguishes good and bad; by establishing those sinking in the river of existence on the dry land of the true path of the holy Dharma, they are an "island"; by teaching the meaning of non-arising, they are like a "captain" who desires the goal or accomplishes the goal of entirely drawing them out of the ocean of cyclic existence; they have become a great "lamp" of Dharma that dispels the darkness of ignorance and clearly illuminates the path of enlightenment; and when they speak on the meaning of emptiness, the supreme profound Dharma, they cannot be disturbed by opponents such as demons and extremists, so they are "undisturbed" and without fear of anything, for having found certainty in the profound Dharma through valid cognition, their eloquence in explaining it is completely perfected to be fully victorious over all opponents. Furthermore, "refuge of transmigrators" demonstrates the characteristic of action of the knowledge of bases, and "defender" and so forth demonstrate the characteristics of action of the knowledge of paths and so forth. In the Aṣṭasāhasrikā as well: "Subhūti, whichever great bodhisattva enters for the sake of benefiting the world, enters for the sake of giving happiness to the world, and enters for the sake of compassion for the world, and having manifestly awakened to unsurpassed completely perfect enlightenment, will become a protector of the world." With this and so forth, the first nine functions of benefiting, giving happiness, protecting, and so forth are briefly demonstrated together, and then it is taught extensively for each with: "Subhūti, if one asks how a great bodhisattva, having manifestly awakened to unsurpassed completely perfect enlightenment, becomes a protector of the world, Subhūti..." and so forth.

བཞི་བ་ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་མཚན་སྟོན་པར། གྲགས་ཆེན་ལྡན་རྣམས་ཞེས་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་དྲུག་གསུངས་པ་དེའི་དོན་ནི། ཐེག་པ་ཆེན་པོའི་ལམ་ལ་ཞུགས་ཤིང་ཕྱོགས་བཅུའི་རྒྱལ་བའི་ཞིང་དུ་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཞེས་པའི་མཚན་གྲགས་པ་ཆེན་པོ་དང་ལྡན་པ་རྣམས་ནི་ཤིན་ཏུ་བྱ་དཀའི་གོ་ཆ་ཆེན་པོ་གྱོན་པར་བྱེད་དེ། ནམ་མཁའ་མཉམ་པའི་སེམས་ཅན་ཐམས་ཅད་མི་གནས་པའི་མྱང་འདས་ལ་བདག་ཉིད་གཅིག་པུས་འགོད་པར་བྱའོ་སྙམ་དུ་སེམས་བསྐྱེད་ཅིང་། དེ་ཡང་ཀུན་ནས་ཉོན་མོངས་ཕྱོགས་ཀྱི་ཕུང་པོ་ལྔ་དང་ཁམས་བཅོ་བརྒྱད་དང་སྐྱེ་མཆེད་བཅུ་གཉིས་ལ་སོགས་པའི་ཆོས་རྣམས་ཀྱི་ངོ་བོ་བདེན་པར་དམིགས་པའི་སྒོ་ནས་གོ་ཆ་དགོ་བ་མིན་ལ། གཉེན་པོ་རྣམ་བྱང་གི་ཕྱོགས་ཐེག་པ་གསུམ་གྱི་ལམ་ལ་མངོན་པར་ཞེན་པའི་འདུ་ཤེས་དང་བྲལ་ཞིང་། ཆོས་གང་ཡང་བདེན་གྲུབ་ཏུ་ཡོངས་སུ་དམིགས་པའམ་བཟུང་བ་མེད་པའི་ཤེར་ཕྱིན་ལ་གནས་པའི་ཕྱིར་ན། རང་དོན་ཕུན་ཚོགས་ལས་མི་ཉམས་པར་རྫོགས་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་ལས་ཕྱིར་མི་ལྡོག་པ་དང་། གཞན་དོན་ཕུན་ཚོགས་ཐེག་པ་ཆེན་པོའི་ལམ་ལས་གཞན་དུ་གཡ་ོབ་མེད་ཅིང་། བདུད་ལ་སོགས་པ་གང་གིས་ཀྱང་རྒྱུད་ཉོན་མོངས་པར་བྱ་མི་ནུས་པས་དོན་གཉིས་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་ལས་མི་ཉམས་ཤིང་མི་འཁྲུགས་པའི་ཆོསཅན་ཡིན་ནོ། །

Fourthly, to demonstrate the distinguishing characteristic of essence, six verses beginning with "those possessing great renown" were spoken. Their meaning is: "Those possessing great renown"—who have entered the Mahayana path and whose name "bodhisattva" is of great renown in the fields of the Victors of the ten directions—"don" a great "armor" of extremely difficult deeds, generating the resolve thinking, "I alone shall establish all sentient beings, equal to space, in non-abiding nirvana." Furthermore, they do not don the armor by way of apprehending the essence of dharmas—such as the five aggregates on the side of thorough affliction, the eighteen elements, and the twelve sense sources—as truly existent; they are free from the perception of strongly adhering to the paths of the three vehicles on the side of the remedy, complete purification; and because they abide in the perfection of wisdom without entirely apprehending or grasping any dharma as truly established, they do not degenerate from the perfection of their own purpose, being irreversible from perfect enlightenment, and they do not waver to anything other than the perfection of the purpose of others, the Mahayana path. Since no demons or anyone else can afflict their continuums, they possess the nature of not degenerating from the perfection of the two purposes and being undisturbed.

heading: **དབྱེ་བ།**
translation: Because this profound dharmatā is thus profound and hard to fathom, when the compassionate Buddha, the Bhagavan who accomplishes the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings, attained great unsurpassed enlightenment and manifestly completely awakened, he thought, 'Who among the assemblies of sentient beings will understand such a profound Dharma that I have realized? It is difficult for those of inferior intellect to realize!' Thinking thus, he showed little concern for teaching the Dharma. As it is said in the Lalitavistara Sutra: 'I have found a Dharma like nectar: profound, peaceful, free from elaborations, luminous, and unconditioned. To whomever I teach it, they will not understand, so I shall remain silent and hide in the forest.' Having spoken thus, he acted in the manner of not teaching the Dharma for a while, and then, based on the supplication made by Mahābrahmā, he turned the wheel of Dharma.

Keep proper names in their standard Sanskrit forms (Subhūti, Śāriputra, Maitreya, Haribhadra) and technical terms recognisable (prajñāpāramitā = perfection of wisdom, bodhisattva). གསུམ་པ་ཕན་བདེ་སྐྱོབ་སོགས་ཀྱི་བྱེད་ལས་ཁྱད་པར་ཅན་དང་ལྡན་པའི་བྱེད་མཚན་སྟོན་པར། དེ་ལྟར་སྤྱོད་པ་ཞེས་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གཅིག་གསུངས་པའི་དོན། ཐེག་ཆེན་སྦྱོར་བ་ཁྱད་པར་ཅན་བསྒོམས་པའི་སྟོབས་ཀྱིས་སྔར་བཤད་པ་དེ་ལྟར་སྤྱོད་པ་སྟེ་དེ་ལྟར་ཐེག་པ་ཆེན་པོའི་ལམ་ཉམས་སུ་ལེན་ཚུལ་གྱི་གདམས་ངག་ལེགས་པར་སྟོན་པའི་བྱང་སེམས་བདག་ཉིད་ཆེན་པོ་སྤངས་རྟོགས་ཀྱི་ཡོན་ཏན་རྒྱ་མཚོ་དང་མཚུངས་པ། ཟབ་རྒྱས་ཆོས་ཀྱི་བདུད་རྩིའི་འོད་ཟེར་དང་ལྡན་པའི་སྨྲ་བའི་ཟླ་བ་རྣམས་ནི། ཕན་བདེའི་རྒྱུ་ཆོས་སྟོན་པས་འགྲོ་བའི་སྔུག་བསྔལ་སེལ་བའི་སྐྱབས་སུ་གྱུར་པ་དང་། ཐར་བའི་བདེ་ལ་འགོད་པའི་དཔུང་གཉེན་དུ་གྱུར་པ་དང་ནི། སྔུག་བསྔལ་གྱི་རྒྱུ་སྡིག་སྒྲིབ་སེལ་བའི་གནས་སུ་གྱུར་པ་ཡིན་ཏེ། དེ་བཞིན་དུ་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཆེན་པོར་འགྲོ་བའི་རྟེན་དུ་གྱུར་པ་དང་། ལེགས་ཉེས་འབྱེད་པའི་བློ་གྲོས་སུ་གྱུར་པ་དང་། སྲིད་པའི་ཆུ་བོར་བྱིང་པ་དམ་པའི་ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྐམ་ས་ཡང་དག་པའི་ལམ་ལ་འགོད་པས་གླིང་དང་། སྐྱེ་མེད་ཀྱི་དོན་བསྟན་པས་འཁོར་བའི་རྒྱ་མཚོ་ལས་ཡོངས་སུ་འདྲེན་པའི་དོན་འདོད་པའམ་དོན་བྱེད་པའི་དད་དཔོན་ལྟ་བུ་ཡིན་པ་དང་། མ་རིག་པའི་མུན་པ་སེལ་ཞིང་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཀྱི་ལམ་རབ་ཏུ་གསལ་བར་བྱེད་པའི་ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྒྲོན་མེ་ཆེན་པོར་གྱུར་པ་དང༌། ཆོས་ཀྱི་མཆོག་ཟབ་མོ་སྟོང་པ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་དོན་སྨྲ་བ་ལ་ཕས་རྒོལ་བདུད་དང་མུ་སྟེགས་ལ་སོགས་པས་འཁྲུགས་པར་མི་ནུས་པས་མི་འཁྲུགས་ཤིང་གང་ལ་ཡང་འཇིག་པ་མེད་པ་ཡིན་ཏེ། ཟབ་མོའི་ཆོས་ལ་ཚད་མས་ངེས་བ་རྙེད་པས་དེའི་འཆད་པ་ལ་ཕྱོགས་ལས་རྣམ་པར་རྒྱལ་བའི་སྤོབས་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་རྫོགས་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །ཞེས་པ་སྟེ། དེ་ཡང་འགྲོ་བའི་སྐྱབས་ཞེས་པས་གཞི་ཤེས་ཀྱི་བྱེད་མཚན་དང་དཔུང་གཉེན་ཞེས་སོགས་ཀྱིས་ལམ་ཤེས་སོགས་ཀྱི་བྱེད་མཚན་སོགས་བསྟན་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །བརྒྱད་སྟོང་པ་ལས་ཀྱང༌། རབ་འབྱོར་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཆེན་པོ་གང་འཇིག་རྟེན་ལ་ཕན་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཞུགས་པ་དང་འཇིག་རྟེན་ལ་བདེ་བའི་ཕྱིར་དང་འཇིག་རྟེན་ལ་སྙིང་བརྩེ་བའི་ཕྱིར་ཞུགས་པ་དང༌། བླ་ན་མེད་པར་ཡང་དག་པར་རྫོགས་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་མངོན་པར་རྫོགས་པར་སངས་རྒྱས་ནས། འཇིག་རྟེན་གྱི་སྐྱོབ་པར་འགྱུར་བ་ཞེས་བྱའོ། །ཞེས་སོགས་ཀྱིས་ཕན་བདེ་སྐྱོབ་སོགས་ཀྱི་བྱེད་པ་དང་པོ་དགུ་མཉམ་དུ་མདོར་བསྟན་ནས། རབ་འབྱོར་ཇི་ལྟར་ན་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཆེེན་པོ་བླ་ན་མེད་པ་ཡང་དག་པར་རྫོགས་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་མངོན་བར་རྫོགས་པར་སངས་རྒྱས་ནས་འཇིག་རྟེན་གྱི་སྐྱོབ་པར་འགྱུར་ཞེ་ན། རབ་འབྱོར་ཞེས་སོགས་ཀྱིས་སོ་སོར་རྒྱས་པར་བསྟན་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །

Thirdly, to demonstrate the distinguishing characteristic of action endowed with the distinguished functions of benefiting, giving happiness, protecting, and so forth, one verse beginning with "acting thus" was spoken. Its meaning is: By the power of having meditated on the distinguished Mahayana preparation, the great being bodhisattvas who "act thus" as previously explained—that is, who excellently point out the instruction on how to practice the Mahayana path in that way—are equal to an ocean of qualities of abandonment and realization, moons of speech endowed with the light rays of the nectar of the profound and vast Dharma. Because they teach the Dharma that is the cause of benefit and happiness, they have become a "refuge" that dispels the suffering of transmigrators; they have become a "defender" that establishes them in the happiness of liberation; and they have become a "place" that dispels negative actions and obscurations, the causes of suffering. "Similarly," they have become a "support" for proceeding to great enlightenment; they have become an "intellect" that distinguishes good and bad; by establishing those sinking in the river of existence on the dry land of the true path of the holy Dharma, they are an "island"; by teaching the meaning of non-arising, they are like a "captain" who desires the goal or accomplishes the goal of entirely drawing them out of the ocean of cyclic existence; they have become a great "lamp" of Dharma that dispels the darkness of ignorance and clearly illuminates the path of enlightenment; and when they speak on the meaning of emptiness, the supreme profound Dharma, they cannot be disturbed by opponents such as demons and extremists, so they are "undisturbed" and without fear of anything, for having found certainty in the profound Dharma through valid cognition, their eloquence in explaining it is completely perfected to be fully victorious over all opponents. Furthermore, "refuge of transmigrators" demonstrates the characteristic of action of the knowledge of bases, and "defender" and so forth demonstrate the characteristics of action of the knowledge of paths and so forth. In the Aṣṭasāhasrikā as well: "Subhūti, whichever great bodhisattva enters for the sake of benefiting the world, enters for the sake of giving happiness to the world, and enters for the sake of compassion for the world, and having manifestly awakened to unsurpassed completely perfect enlightenment, will become a protector of the world." With this and so forth, the first nine functions of benefiting, giving happiness, protecting, and so forth are briefly demonstrated together, and then it is taught extensively for each with: "Subhūti, if one asks how a great bodhisattva, having manifestly awakened to unsurpassed completely perfect enlightenment, becomes a protector of the world, Subhūti..." and so forth.

Fourthly, to demonstrate the distinguishing characteristic of essence, six verses beginning with "those possessing great renown" were spoken. Their meaning is: "Those possessing great renown"—who have entered the Mahayana path and whose name "bodhisattva" is of great renown in the fields of the Victors of the ten directions—"don" a great "armor" of extremely difficult deeds, generating the resolve thinking, "I alone shall establish all sentient beings, equal to space, in non-abiding nirvana." Furthermore, they do not don the armor by way of apprehending the essence of dharmas—such as the five aggregates on the side of thorough affliction, the eighteen elements, and the twelve sense sources—as truly existent; they are free from the perception of strongly adhering to the paths of the three vehicles on the side of the remedy, complete purification; and because they abide in the perfection of wisdom without entirely apprehending or grasping any dharma as truly established, they do not degenerate from the perfection of their own purpose, being irreversible from perfect enlightenment, and they do not waver to anything other than the perfection of the purpose of others, the Mahayana path. Since no demons or anyone else can afflict their continuums, they possess the nature of not degenerating from the perfection of the two purposes and being undisturbed.

heading: **དབྱེ་བ།**
translation: If one asks what the reason is that this profound Dharma is difficult to realize: It is like this. Sentient beings, by the power of being habituated to true grasping since beginningless time, to whom whatever appears appears as true and is grasped as truly established, delight in sensory pleasures, which are bases for generating attachment and the rest, and desire objects such as forms and sounds. Abiding in apprehending those as true, they are unskilled in the meaning of suchness, the profound abiding nature, and have become foolish and ignorant, not knowing the profound and vast path as it is, like abiding in the midst of darkness. The dharmas of the path to be obtained abide as lacking true existence, so they do not have even the slightest true establishment, and the non-conceptual exalted wisdom of meditative equipoise does not apprehend them as truly established either, because it unmistakably realizes the meaning of the abiding nature.

Thirdly, to demonstrate the distinguishing characteristic of action endowed with the distinguished functions of benefiting, giving happiness, protecting, and so forth, one verse beginning with "acting thus" was spoken. Its meaning is: By the power of having meditated on the distinguished Mahayana preparation, the great being bodhisattvas who "act thus" as previously explained—that is, who excellently point out the instruction on how to practice the Mahayana path in that way—are equal to an ocean of qualities of abandonment and realization, moons of speech endowed with the light rays of the nectar of the profound and vast Dharma. Because they teach the Dharma that is the cause of benefit and happiness, they have become a "refuge" that dispels the suffering of transmigrators; they have become a "defender" that establishes them in the happiness of liberation; and they have become a "place" that dispels negative actions and obscurations, the causes of suffering. "Similarly," they have become a "support" for proceeding to great enlightenment; they have become an "intellect" that distinguishes good and bad; by establishing those sinking in the river of existence on the dry land of the true path of the holy Dharma, they are an "island"; by teaching the meaning of non-arising, they are like a "captain" who desires the goal or accomplishes the goal of entirely drawing them out of the ocean of cyclic existence; they have become a great "lamp" of Dharma that dispels the darkness of ignorance and clearly illuminates the path of enlightenment; and when they speak on the meaning of emptiness, the supreme profound Dharma, they cannot be disturbed by opponents such as demons and extremists, so they are "undisturbed" and without fear of anything, for having found certainty in the profound Dharma through valid cognition, their eloquence in explaining it is completely perfected to be fully victorious over all opponents. Furthermore, "refuge of transmigrators" demonstrates the characteristic of action of the knowledge of bases, and "defender" and so forth demonstrate the characteristics of action of the knowledge of paths and so forth. In the Aṣṭasāhasrikā as well: "Subhūti, whichever great bodhisattva enters for the sake of benefiting the world, enters for the sake of giving happiness to the world, and enters for the sake of compassion for the world, and having manifestly awakened to unsurpassed completely perfect enlightenment, will become a protector of the world." With this and so forth, the first nine functions of benefiting, giving happiness, protecting, and so forth are briefly demonstrated together, and then it is taught extensively for each with: "Subhūti, if one asks how a great bodhisattva, having manifestly awakened to unsurpassed completely perfect enlightenment, becomes a protector of the world, Subhūti..." and so forth.

heading: **དབྱེ་བ།**
translation: Thus, those supramundane dharmas are discordant with worldly people and particularly exalted, therefore disputes arise with worldly people; this is because worldly people assert them as truly established, whereas the Buddha teaches them as lacking true establishment. Worldly people, not seeing the abiding mode of dharmas, dispute, whereas the Tathāgata, even though dharmas do not exist ultimately, accepts conventional illusion-like dharmas in accordance with worldly conventions. In the sutra, it is said: "I do not dispute with worldly people; whatever is asserted to exist in the world, I also assert to exist." This is the commentary on the fifteenth chapter, the Chapter on Gods, from the commentary on the Verse Summary of the Precious Qualities Collection called The Jewelled Lamp Fulfilling the Hopes of the Fortunate, Clarifying the Suchness of Profound Dependent Arising. As for illustrating with an example that the dharmadhātu is indivisible in essence: Just as the element of space is not established as the essence of form and is not divided into directions and categories, so the eastern direction, the southern direction, and likewise the western direction and the northern direction—the four directions being boundless—are infinite, and likewise above and below and the four intermediate directions; in short, however many limitless extents of the ten directions there are, it exists in them as well, because there is nothing not pervaded by space; and in those spaces there is no essence that has become different, nor is there any difference whatsoever of disparate shapes and so forth. In the same way as that example, whatever is the suchness of the dharmas of the past time, and whatever is the suchness of the unarisen, that is, the future, and whatever is the suchness of the present, and whatever is the suchness of persons such as arhats, and whatever is the suchness of all dharmas of the basis, objects of knowledge, and whatever is the suchness of the result, the Victors, and whatever is the suchness of the dharmas of the path—in all of these there is no difference or distinction of disparate essences whatsoever, because they are of one taste in the dharmadhātu, which is merely the negation of the object to be negated, true establishment. This is what is said.

Because this profound dharmatā is thus profound and hard to fathom, when the compassionate Buddha, the Bhagavan who accomplishes the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings, attained great unsurpassed enlightenment and manifestly completely awakened, he thought, 'Who among the assemblies of sentient beings will understand such a profound Dharma that I have realized? It is difficult for those of inferior intellect to realize!' Thinking thus, he showed little concern for teaching the Dharma. As it is said in the Lalitavistara Sutra: 'I have found a Dharma like nectar: profound, peaceful, free from elaborations, luminous, and unconditioned. To whomever I teach it, they will not understand, so I shall remain silent and hide in the forest.' Having spoken thus, he acted in the manner of not teaching the Dharma for a while, and then, based on the supplication made by Mahābrahmā, he turned the wheel of Dharma.

[3-201] translation already produced for this document:
If one asks what the reason is that this profound Dharma is difficult to realize: It is like this. Sentient beings, by the power of being habituated to true grasping since beginningless time, to whom whatever appears appears as true and is grasped as truly established, delight in sensory pleasures, which are bases for generating attachment and the rest, and desire objects such as forms and sounds. Abiding in apprehending those as true, they are unskilled in the meaning of suchness, the profound abiding nature, and have become foolish and ignorant, not knowing the profound and vast path as it is, like abiding in the midst of darkness. The dharmas of the path to be obtained abide as lacking true existence, so they do not have even the slightest true establishment, and the non-conceptual exalted wisdom of meditative equipoise does not apprehend them as truly established either, because it unmistakably realizes the meaning of the abiding nature.

heading: **དབྱེ་བ།**
source: དེའང་བྱ་དཀའ་གོ་ཆ་གྱོན་ཞེས་སོགས་ཀྱིས་སྒྲུབ་དཀའ་བའི་སྦྱོར་བའི་ངོ་བོ་དང་། ཐེ་ཚོམ་སོམ་ཉི་ཡིད་གཉིས་བྲལ་ཞེས་སོགས་ཀྱིས་འཚང་རྒྱ་བར་ངེས་པའི་སྦྱོར་བ་དང་། སུས་ཀྱང་རྟོགས་པ་མེད་ཅིང་ཞེས་སོགས་ཀྱིས་མི་དམིགས་པའི་སྦྱོར་བ་དང་། མངོན་ཞེན་བཀག་པའི་སྦྱོར་བ་སོགསདང་། སེམས་ཅན་རྣམས་ནི་ཞེས་སོགས་ཀྱིས་འཇིག་རྟེན་ཐམས་ཅད་དང་མི་མཐུན་པའི་སྦྱོར་བའི་ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་མཚན་སོགས་བསྟན་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །དེ་ལྟར་རྣམ་རྫོགས་སྦྱོར་བ་སྤྱིའི་རྣམ་བཞག་བཤད་ཟིན་ནས། དེའི་འོག་ཏུ་ཐར་བ་ཆ་མཐུན་ནས་བཟུང་སྦྱོར་བའི་བར་རྒྱུད་ལ་སྐྱེ་རིམ་བཤད་པ་ལ། དང་པོ་ཐར་པ་ཆ་མཐུན་ནི། རྒྱན་ལས། མཚན་མེད་རབ་ཏུ་སྦྱིན་ལ་སེགས། ནས། ཐར་པའི་ཆ་དང་མཐུན་པ་འདོད། །ཅེས་གསུངས། འདི་ལ་མཚན་ཉིད། དབྱེ་བ། ས་མཚམས་གསུམ་ལས། དང་པོ་ནི། རྣམ་མཁྱེན་རང་རྒྱུད་ལ་སྒྲུབ་པ་ལ་མཁས་པའི་སེམས་དཔའི་རྒྱུད་ཀྱི་ཆོས་མངོན་རྟོགས་དེ། སྐབས་འདིར་དངོས་སུ་བསྟན་པའི་ཐེག་ཆེན་གྱི་ཐར་པ་ཆ་མཐུན་གྱི་མཚན་ཉིད། གཉིས་པ་དེ་ལ་དབྱེ་ན། དེར་གྱུར་བའི་ཆུང་འབྲིང་ཆེན་པོ་གསུམ་ཡོད། གསུམ་པ་ས་མཚམས་ནི། ཐེག་ཆེན་གྱི་ཚོགས་ལམ་ཁོ་ནར་ཡོད།
translation: Furthermore, "don an armor of difficult deeds" and so forth indicates the essence of the preparation of difficult practice; "free from doubt, hesitation, and double-mindedness" and so forth indicates the preparation of being certain to attain enlightenment; "not realized by anyone" and so forth indicates the preparation of non-apprehension; and the preparation of negating strong adherence and so forth; and "sentient beings" and so forth indicate the distinguishing characteristic of essence of the preparation discordant with all the world, and so forth. Having thus explained the general presentation of the preparation of complete realization, following that, regarding the explanation of the stages of generation in the continuum from the aids to liberation up to the preparation: first, as for the aids to liberation, it is said in the Ornament: "Perfectly giving without characteristics and so forth" up to "are asserted as the aids to liberation." For this there are three: definition, divisions, and boundaries. First, the definition of the Mahayana aids to liberation explicitly taught in this context is: a clear realization of Dharma in the continuum of a bodhisattva who is skilled in accomplishing the omniscient exalted wisdom in their own continuum. Second, if that is divided, there are three that have become that: small, medium, and great. Third, as for the boundaries, it exists only on the Mahayana path of accumulation.

Fourthly, to demonstrate the distinguishing characteristic of essence, six verses beginning with "those possessing great renown" were spoken. Their meaning is: "Those possessing great renown"—who have entered the Mahayana path and whose name "bodhisattva" is of great renown in the fields of the Victors of the ten directions—"don" a great "armor" of extremely difficult deeds, generating the resolve thinking, "I alone shall establish all sentient beings, equal to space, in non-abiding nirvana." Furthermore, they do not don the armor by way of apprehending the essence of dharmas—such as the five aggregates on the side of thorough affliction, the eighteen elements, and the twelve sense sources—as truly existent; they are free from the perception of strongly adhering to the paths of the three vehicles on the side of the remedy, complete purification; and because they abide in the perfection of wisdom without entirely apprehending or grasping any dharma as truly established, they do not degenerate from the perfection of their own purpose, being irreversible from perfect enlightenment, and they do not waver to anything other than the perfection of the purpose of others, the Mahayana path. Since no demons or anyone else can afflict their continuums, they possess the nature of not degenerating from the perfection of the two purposes and being undisturbed.

Thus, those bodhisattvas are endowed with such profound and hard-to-fathom qualities, and having generated in their continuums the non-conceptual exalted wisdom obtained by the power of meditating on the preparation—the exalted wisdom free from the elaborations of dualistic appearance—they are free from doubt, hesitation, and double-mindedness regarding the Dharma of the Mahayana, and having found certainty in their own path through valid cognition, they possess the meaning of conviction. By the power of that, having heard the profound perfection of wisdom, their minds do not shrink back from its meaning; and because they have deeply found certainty in their own path and integrated it into experience, they do not rely on others—meaning they do not go wherever led by others—and should be known as irreversible from the Mahayana.

Because this profound dharmatā is thus profound and hard to fathom, when the compassionate Buddha, the Bhagavan who accomplishes the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings, attained great unsurpassed enlightenment and manifestly completely awakened, he thought, 'Who among the assemblies of sentient beings will understand such a profound Dharma that I have realized? It is difficult for those of inferior intellect to realize!' Thinking thus, he showed little concern for teaching the Dharma. As it is said in the Lalitavistara Sutra: 'I have found a Dharma like nectar: profound, peaceful, free from elaborations, luminous, and unconditioned. To whomever I teach it, they will not understand, so I shall remain silent and hide in the forest.' Having spoken thus, he acted in the manner of not teaching the Dharma for a while, and then, based on the supplication made by Mahābrahmā, he turned the wheel of Dharma.

If one asks what the reason is that this profound Dharma is difficult to realize: It is like this. Sentient beings, by the power of being habituated to true grasping since beginningless time, to whom whatever appears appears as true and is grasped as truly established, delight in sensory pleasures, which are bases for generating attachment and the rest, and desire objects such as forms and sounds. Abiding in apprehending those as true, they are unskilled in the meaning of suchness, the profound abiding nature, and have become foolish and ignorant, not knowing the profound and vast path as it is, like abiding in the midst of darkness. The dharmas of the path to be obtained abide as lacking true existence, so they do not have even the slightest true establishment, and the non-conceptual exalted wisdom of meditative equipoise does not apprehend them as truly established either, because it unmistakably realizes the meaning of the abiding nature.

heading: **ཐར་པ་ཆ་མཐུན།**
translation: Aids to liberation. Sixth, as for explaining those very aids to liberation: The meaning of what is stated in the three verses starting with "Sugata enlightenment" is: whatever bodhisattva desires to obtain this ultimate object to be obtained, the enlightenment of a Sugata, which is the dharmatā equal to space, free from diverse dharmas of disparate essences—they must, by being endowed with exceptional methods such as the aspiration seeking perfect enlightenment for the sake of others, also exert themselves in the preparation of the supreme perfection of wisdom that realizes existence and peace as equal in being empty of true establishment, but if this Mother of the Guides, the perfection of wisdom that is the Mother of the Victors, does not exist for them, they will never obtain that great enlightenment. This is because this perfection of wisdom realizing the abiding mode of all dharmas is the supreme cause for obtaining it. For example, if a bird has an extremely large body of one hundred and fifty yojanas, but its wings are ruined and non-existent, so it does not have the strength to be able to fly in the sky, and if that bird thinks, "I will abide here in Jambudvīpa, coming from the abode of the gods of the Thirty-Three," and jumps, at that occasion, there is no other outcome than that the bird will undergo great ruin, such as its body being injured.

Thus, those supramundane dharmas are discordant with worldly people and particularly exalted, therefore disputes arise with worldly people; this is because worldly people assert them as truly established, whereas the Buddha teaches them as lacking true establishment. Worldly people, not seeing the abiding mode of dharmas, dispute, whereas the Tathāgata, even though dharmas do not exist ultimately, accepts conventional illusion-like dharmas in accordance with worldly conventions. In the sutra, it is said: "I do not dispute with worldly people; whatever is asserted to exist in the world, I also assert to exist." This is the commentary on the fifteenth chapter, the Chapter on Gods, from the commentary on the Verse Summary of the Precious Qualities Collection called The Jewelled Lamp Fulfilling the Hopes of the Fortunate, Clarifying the Suchness of Profound Dependent Arising. As for illustrating with an example that the dharmadhātu is indivisible in essence: Just as the element of space is not established as the essence of form and is not divided into directions and categories, so the eastern direction, the southern direction, and likewise the western direction and the northern direction—the four directions being boundless—are infinite, and likewise above and below and the four intermediate directions; in short, however many limitless extents of the ten directions there are, it exists in them as well, because there is nothing not pervaded by space; and in those spaces there is no essence that has become different, nor is there any difference whatsoever of disparate shapes and so forth. In the same way as that example, whatever is the suchness of the dharmas of the past time, and whatever is the suchness of the unarisen, that is, the future, and whatever is the suchness of the present, and whatever is the suchness of persons such as arhats, and whatever is the suchness of all dharmas of the basis, objects of knowledge, and whatever is the suchness of the result, the Victors, and whatever is the suchness of the dharmas of the path—in all of these there is no difference or distinction of disparate essences whatsoever, because they are of one taste in the dharmadhātu, which is merely the negation of the object to be negated, true establishment. This is what is said.

Furthermore, "don an armor of difficult deeds" and so forth indicates the essence of the preparation of difficult practice; "free from doubt, hesitation, and double-mindedness" and so forth indicates the preparation of being certain to attain enlightenment; "not realized by anyone" and so forth indicates the preparation of non-apprehension; and the preparation of negating strong adherence and so forth; and "sentient beings" and so forth indicate the distinguishing characteristic of essence of the preparation discordant with all the world, and so forth. Having thus explained the general presentation of the preparation of complete realization, following that, regarding the explanation of the stages of generation in the continuum from the aids to liberation up to the preparation: first, as for the aids to liberation, it is said in the Ornament: "Perfectly giving without characteristics and so forth" up to "are asserted as the aids to liberation." For this there are three: definition, divisions, and boundaries. First, the definition of the Mahayana aids to liberation explicitly taught in this context is: a clear realization of Dharma in the continuum of a bodhisattva who is skilled in accomplishing the omniscient exalted wisdom in their own continuum. Second, if that is divided, there are three that have become that: small, medium, and great. Third, as for the boundaries, it exists only on the Mahayana path of accumulation.

heading: **ཐར་པ་ཆ་མཐུན།**
translation: Similar to that example, even if they accomplish these five perfections, giving and so forth, the path for obtaining the enlightenment of the Victors, by exerting themselves for a long time, for many tens of millions and hundreds of thousands of eons, and even if they continually rely in this world on vast, limitless aspiration prayers, such as ten hundred thousand countless aspiration prayers of a bodhisattva, they will not be able to obtain great enlightenment without a complete set of method and wisdom; for if they become separated from exceptional method and wisdom, such as the immeasurable skillful methods of dedicating roots of virtue to the omniscient exalted wisdom and so forth, and the wisdom that realizes all dharmas as equal in being empty of true establishment, they will fall to the level of a śrāvaka, just as the bird with a large body but no feathers or wings jumps and falls downward, experiencing suffering. Therefore, one who desires to obtain great enlightenment, having become skilled in the five objects such as faith and so forth, must train in the path complete with method and wisdom. This is what is said.

If one asks what the reason is that this profound Dharma is difficult to realize: It is like this. Sentient beings, by the power of being habituated to true grasping since beginningless time, to whom whatever appears appears as true and is grasped as truly established, delight in sensory pleasures, which are bases for generating attachment and the rest, and desire objects such as forms and sounds. Abiding in apprehending those as true, they are unskilled in the meaning of suchness, the profound abiding nature, and have become foolish and ignorant, not knowing the profound and vast path as it is, like abiding in the midst of darkness. The dharmas of the path to be obtained abide as lacking true existence, so they do not have even the slightest true establishment, and the non-conceptual exalted wisdom of meditative equipoise does not apprehend them as truly established either, because it unmistakably realizes the meaning of the abiding nature.

Thus, those supramundane dharmas are discordant with worldly people and particularly exalted, therefore disputes arise with worldly people; this is because worldly people assert them as truly established, whereas the Buddha teaches them as lacking true establishment. Worldly people, not seeing the abiding mode of dharmas, dispute, whereas the Tathāgata, even though dharmas do not exist ultimately, accepts conventional illusion-like dharmas in accordance with worldly conventions. In the sutra, it is said: "I do not dispute with worldly people; whatever is asserted to exist in the world, I also assert to exist." This is the commentary on the fifteenth chapter, the Chapter on Gods, from the commentary on the Verse Summary of the Precious Qualities Collection called The Jewelled Lamp Fulfilling the Hopes of the Fortunate, Clarifying the Suchness of Profound Dependent Arising. As for illustrating with an example that the dharmadhātu is indivisible in essence: Just as the element of space is not established as the essence of form and is not divided into directions and categories, so the eastern direction, the southern direction, and likewise the western direction and the northern direction—the four directions being boundless—are infinite, and likewise above and below and the four intermediate directions; in short, however many limitless extents of the ten directions there are, it exists in them as well, because there is nothing not pervaded by space; and in those spaces there is no essence that has become different, nor is there any difference whatsoever of disparate shapes and so forth. In the same way as that example, whatever is the suchness of the dharmas of the past time, and whatever is the suchness of the unarisen, that is, the future, and whatever is the suchness of the present, and whatever is the suchness of persons such as arhats, and whatever is the suchness of all dharmas of the basis, objects of knowledge, and whatever is the suchness of the result, the Victors, and whatever is the suchness of the dharmas of the path—in all of these there is no difference or distinction of disparate essences whatsoever, because they are of one taste in the dharmadhātu, which is merely the negation of the object to be negated, true establishment. This is what is said.

དེའང་བྱ་དཀའ་གོ་ཆ་གྱོན་ཞེས་སོགས་ཀྱིས་སྒྲུབ་དཀའ་བའི་སྦྱོར་བའི་ངོ་བོ་དང་། ཐེ་ཚོམ་སོམ་ཉི་ཡིད་གཉིས་བྲལ་ཞེས་སོགས་ཀྱིས་འཚང་རྒྱ་བར་ངེས་པའི་སྦྱོར་བ་དང་། སུས་ཀྱང་རྟོགས་པ་མེད་ཅིང་ཞེས་སོགས་ཀྱིས་མི་དམིགས་པའི་སྦྱོར་བ་དང་། མངོན་ཞེན་བཀག་པའི་སྦྱོར་བ་སོགསདང་། སེམས་ཅན་རྣམས་ནི་ཞེས་སོགས་ཀྱིས་འཇིག་རྟེན་ཐམས་ཅད་དང་མི་མཐུན་པའི་སྦྱོར་བའི་ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་མཚན་སོགས་བསྟན་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །དེ་ལྟར་རྣམ་རྫོགས་སྦྱོར་བ་སྤྱིའི་རྣམ་བཞག་བཤད་ཟིན་ནས། དེའི་འོག་ཏུ་ཐར་བ་ཆ་མཐུན་ནས་བཟུང་སྦྱོར་བའི་བར་རྒྱུད་ལ་སྐྱེ་རིམ་བཤད་པ་ལ། དང་པོ་ཐར་པ་ཆ་མཐུན་ནི། རྒྱན་ལས། མཚན་མེད་རབ་ཏུ་སྦྱིན་ལ་སེགས། ནས། ཐར་པའི་ཆ་དང་མཐུན་པ་འདོད། །ཅེས་གསུངས། འདི་ལ་མཚན་ཉིད། དབྱེ་བ། ས་མཚམས་གསུམ་ལས། དང་པོ་ནི། རྣམ་མཁྱེན་རང་རྒྱུད་ལ་སྒྲུབ་པ་ལ་མཁས་པའི་སེམས་དཔའི་རྒྱུད་ཀྱི་ཆོས་མངོན་རྟོགས་དེ། སྐབས་འདིར་དངོས་སུ་བསྟན་པའི་ཐེག་ཆེན་གྱི་ཐར་པ་ཆ་མཐུན་གྱི་མཚན་ཉིད། གཉིས་པ་དེ་ལ་དབྱེ་ན། དེར་གྱུར་བའི་ཆུང་འབྲིང་ཆེན་པོ་གསུམ་ཡོད། གསུམ་པ་ས་མཚམས་ནི། ཐེག་ཆེན་གྱི་ཚོགས་ལམ་ཁོ་ནར་ཡོད།

Furthermore, "don an armor of difficult deeds" and so forth indicates the essence of the preparation of difficult practice; "free from doubt, hesitation, and double-mindedness" and so forth indicates the preparation of being certain to attain enlightenment; "not realized by anyone" and so forth indicates the preparation of non-apprehension; and the preparation of negating strong adherence and so forth; and "sentient beings" and so forth indicate the distinguishing characteristic of essence of the preparation discordant with all the world, and so forth. Having thus explained the general presentation of the preparation of complete realization, following that, regarding the explanation of the stages of generation in the continuum from the aids to liberation up to the preparation: first, as for the aids to liberation, it is said in the Ornament: "Perfectly giving without characteristics and so forth" up to "are asserted as the aids to liberation." For this there are three: definition, divisions, and boundaries. First, the definition of the Mahayana aids to liberation explicitly taught in this context is: a clear realization of Dharma in the continuum of a bodhisattva who is skilled in accomplishing the omniscient exalted wisdom in their own continuum. Second, if that is divided, there are three that have become that: small, medium, and great. Third, as for the boundaries, it exists only on the Mahayana path of accumulation.

heading: **ངེས་འབྱེད་ཆ་མཐུན།**
source: ངེས་འབྱེད་ཆ་མཐུན།བདུན་པ་ངེས་འབྱེད་ཆ་མཐུན་ནི། རྒྱན་ལས། སངས་རྒྱས་སོགས་དམིགས་དད་པ་དང་། ནས། སྨིན་བྱེད་སོགས་ཀྱིས་ཤེས་པར་བྱ། ཞེས་གསུངས། མཚན་ཉིད། དབྱེ་བ། ས་མཚམས་དང་གསུམ། དང་པོ་ནི། གཙོ་བོ་ཐབས་ཀྱི་ཆས་ཁྱད་པར་དུ་བྱས་པའི་སྐབས་འདིར་དངོས་སུ་བསྟན་པའི་ཐེག་ཆེན་གྱི་དོན་མངོན་རྟོགས་དེ། སྐབས་འདིར་དངོས་སུ་བསྟན་པའི་ཐེག་ཆེན་སྦྱོར་ལམ་གྱི་མཚན་ཉིད། དབྱེ་ན་གདིར་བསྟན་ཐེག་ཆེན་གྱི་སྦྱོར་ལམ་དྲོད་སོགས་བཞི་ཡོད། ས་མཚམས་ཐེག་ཆེན་གྱི་སྦྱོར་ལམ་ཁོ་ནར་ཡོད། དེ་ལྟ་བུའི་ངེས་བྱེད་ཆ་མཐུན་སྟོན་པར། སངས་རྒྱས་ཐེག་པ་ཞེས་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གཅིག་གསུངས་པའི་དོན། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གང་ཞིག་རྒྱལ་བ་ཀུན་གྱི་བགྲོད་པ་གཅིག་པའི་ལམ་པོ་ཆེ་སངས་རྒྱས་ཐེག་པ་བླ་ན་མེད་པ་ངེས་པར་འབྱེད་པའི་ལམ་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་འདི་ལ་བརྟེན་ནས་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཆེན་པོ་ངེས་པར་འབྱུང་བ་སྟེ་ཕྱིན་པར་འདོད་པ་གང་གི་ཐེག་པ་ཆེན་པོའི་ལམ་ལ་ཚུལ་ཇི་ལྟར་དུ་འཇུག་པར་བྱ་ཞེ་ན། སེམས་ཅན་ཐམས་ཅད་ལ་དམིགས་པའི་བྱམས་པ་དང་སྙིང་རྗེ་ཆེན་པོ་བསྐྱེད་ནས་ཕྱིན་དྲུག་སོགས་སློབ་དགོས་པས་ཐོག་མར་མཐའ་ཡས་པའི་འགྲོ་བ་ཀུན་ལ་ཆགས་སྡང་གིས་རིས་སུ་མ་ཆད་པའི་སེམས་ཀྱིས་བཏང་སྙོམས་བསྒོམ་པ་མཉམ་པའི་སེམས་དང་། སྐྱེས་པ་དང་བུ་མེད་རྒན་པ་ལ་ཕ་མའི་འདུ་ཤེས་དང་། མཉམ་པ་སྤུན་དང་སྲིང་མོའི་འདུ་ཤེས་དང་། གཞོན་པ་ལ་བུ་དང་བུ་མོའི་འདུ་ཤེས་དང་། གཞན་ལ་བཤེས་དང་གྲོགས་ཀྱི་འདུ་ཤེས་དང་གཉེན་དང་སྣག་གི་གཉེན་མཚམས་ཀྱི་འདུ་ཤེས་སོགས་ལ་གནས་པ་དང་། བྱང་ཆུབ་ཏུ་འགོད་པར་འདོད་པ་སོགས་གཏན་དུ་ཕན་པའི་སེམས་དང་གནས་སྐབས་སུ་བདེ་བར་འདོད་པ་སོགས་གཏན་དུ་ཕན་པའི་སེམས་དང་གནས་སྐབས་སུ་བདེ་བར་འདོད་པ་བྱམས་པས་ཡིད་ཀྱིས་སེམས་ཅན་གྱི་དོན་ལ་བརྟུལ་བ་སྟེ་བརྩོན་པར་བྱ་ཞིང་། ཁོང་ཁྲོ་བ་དང་འཚེ་བའི་ཐ་བ་མེད་ཅིང་གཡོ་རྒྱུ་མེད་པར་རྒྱུད་དྲང་ལ་ངག་གི་སྒོ་ནས་ཆོས་སྟོན་པ་དང་ཡིད་དུ་འཐད་པའི་ཚིག་འཇམ་པོར་སྨྲ་བར་བྱ་ཞིང་གཞན་ལ་ཕན་པའི་བྱམས་པའི་ལུས་ཀྱི་ལས་སུའང་བྱ་སྟེ་རང་དོན་ཡལ་བར་དོར་ནས་གཞན་གྱི་ཕན་བདེ་མ་ལུས་པ་སྒྲུབ་པ་ལ་འཇུག་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །འདིས་ནི་ཐེག་ཆེན་གྱི་སྦྱོར་ལམ་དྲོད་ཆུང་འབྲིང་ཆེ་གསུམ་གྱི་དམིགས་རྣམས་ཕལ་ཆེར་དངོས་སུ་བསྟན་ནས་རྩེ་མོ་སོགས་ཀྱི་རྣམ་པ་ཤུགས་ལ་འཕངས་སོ། །ཡོན་ཏན་རིན་པོ་ཆེ་སྡུད་པ་ཚིགས་སུ་བཅད་པའི་འགྲེལ་བ་ཟབ་མོ་རྟེན་འབྱུང་གི་དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཉིད་གསལ་བར་བྱེད་པའི་ནོར་བུའི་སྒྲོན་མེ་སྐལ་བཟང་རེ་སྐོང་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལས་དེ་བཞིན་ཉིད་ཀྱི་ལེའུ་སྟེ་བཅུ་དྲུག་པའི་འགྲེལ་བའོ།།  །།
translation: Aids to penetration. Seventh, as for the aids to penetration: it is said in the Ornament: from "Faith focused on the Buddhas and so forth" up to "should be known by the maturing factors and so forth." There are three: definition, divisions, and boundaries. First, the clear realization of meaning of the Mahayana explicitly taught in this context, which is mainly distinguished by the factor of method, is the definition of the Mahayana path of preparation explicitly taught in this context. If divided, there are four Mahayana paths of preparation taught here: heat and so forth. As for the boundaries, it exists only on the Mahayana path of preparation. To teach such aids to penetration, the meaning of the one verse starting with "Buddha vehicle" and so forth is: If one asks how a bodhisattva who desires to definitely emerge into, that is, reach, great enlightenment by relying on this perfection of wisdom—the path of penetration to the unsurpassed "Buddha vehicle", the great path that is the single trajectory of all the Victors—should engage in the path of the Mahayana: Since they must train in the six perfections and so forth after generating love and great compassion focused on all sentient beings, first, meditating on equanimity with a mind not divided into factions by attachment and aversion towards all infinite beings—an "equal mind"; and abiding in the recognition of older men and women as parents, the recognition of peers as brothers and sisters, the recognition of younger ones as sons and daughters, the recognition of others as friends and companions, and the recognition of relatives and blood relations and so forth; and with a mind of ultimate benefit such as desiring to establish them in enlightenment and a mind of ultimate benefit such as desiring happiness in the short term and desiring happiness in the short term, with a loving mind one should exert oneself, that is, strive, for the welfare of sentient beings; and without the stubbornness of anger and harm, and without deceit, with an upright continuum, one should teach the Dharma through speech and speak agreeable, gentle words, and one should also perform physical actions of love that benefit others; thus, discarding one's own welfare, one engages in accomplishing all the benefit and happiness of others without exception. This explicitly teaches for the most part the focal objects of the small, medium, and great Mahayana paths of preparation of heat, and implicitly implies the aspects of peak and so forth. From the commentary on the Verses of the Precious Qualities Collection called The Jewel Lamp Fulfilling the Hopes of the Fortunate, Clarifying the Suchness of Profound Dependent Arising, this is the commentary on the sixteenth chapter, Suchness.

Furthermore, "don an armor of difficult deeds" and so forth indicates the essence of the preparation of difficult practice; "free from doubt, hesitation, and double-mindedness" and so forth indicates the preparation of being certain to attain enlightenment; "not realized by anyone" and so forth indicates the preparation of non-apprehension; and the preparation of negating strong adherence and so forth; and "sentient beings" and so forth indicate the distinguishing characteristic of essence of the preparation discordant with all the world, and so forth. Having thus explained the general presentation of the preparation of complete realization, following that, regarding the explanation of the stages of generation in the continuum from the aids to liberation up to the preparation: first, as for the aids to liberation, it is said in the Ornament: "Perfectly giving without characteristics and so forth" up to "are asserted as the aids to liberation." For this there are three: definition, divisions, and boundaries. First, the definition of the Mahayana aids to liberation explicitly taught in this context is: a clear realization of Dharma in the continuum of a bodhisattva who is skilled in accomplishing the omniscient exalted wisdom in their own continuum. Second, if that is divided, there are three that have become that: small, medium, and great. Third, as for the boundaries, it exists only on the Mahayana path of accumulation.

Aids to liberation. Sixth, as for explaining those very aids to liberation: The meaning of what is stated in the three verses starting with "Sugata enlightenment" is: whatever bodhisattva desires to obtain this ultimate object to be obtained, the enlightenment of a Sugata, which is the dharmatā equal to space, free from diverse dharmas of disparate essences—they must, by being endowed with exceptional methods such as the aspiration seeking perfect enlightenment for the sake of others, also exert themselves in the preparation of the supreme perfection of wisdom that realizes existence and peace as equal in being empty of true establishment, but if this Mother of the Guides, the perfection of wisdom that is the Mother of the Victors, does not exist for them, they will never obtain that great enlightenment. This is because this perfection of wisdom realizing the abiding mode of all dharmas is the supreme cause for obtaining it. For example, if a bird has an extremely large body of one hundred and fifty yojanas, but its wings are ruined and non-existent, so it does not have the strength to be able to fly in the sky, and if that bird thinks, "I will abide here in Jambudvīpa, coming from the abode of the gods of the Thirty-Three," and jumps, at that occasion, there is no other outcome than that the bird will undergo great ruin, such as its body being injured.
