translation: If they say: Even conventionally, it is illogical to attain enlightenment by realization increasing higher and higher; because each individual mind occurring earlier or later lacks the capacity, it does not attain enlightenment; and it is not by all the earlier and later minds gathering simultaneously either, because it is impossible for all earlier and later ones to occur at the same time; nor is it in dependence upon the earlier ones, because without the earlier ones the later ones do not arise - anticipating this dispute from within and teaching the answer to it by way of an example, the meaning taught by the five verses starting with "Wick and oil..." is: "For example," when a "wick and oil" and a blazing "flame of a lamp" meet, that "first moment of the flame alone" does not burn the wick "completely," yet without that first moment of the flame, that wick also does not burn; and the "last" meeting of the flame "alone" also does not burn that wick, yet without the last flame, that wick also does not burn; however, one should understand that from the continuum of all the earlier and later moments of the flame, the wick comes to be completely burned.

translation: Applying that very example that was taught to the meaning of the context, the way of attaining enlightenment: "Likewise," by the "first moment of the mind" of generating bodhicitta "alone," one does not "touch" supreme "enlightenment," yet "without that first mind," one is also unable to "touch that enlightenment"; and by whichever mind is the "last moment" of that mind's continuum "alone," one does not attain the "great enlightenment" where all objects of abandonment are pacified, yet "without that last moment," one is also unable to attain that enlightenment. However, by the true nature of dependent origination, having arisen gradually through the continuum of the earlier and later generations of mind, enlightenment is attained. Having thus generally taught that the collection of earlier and later moments of the path to enlightenment is the cause of enlightenment, now to specifically teach that the first moment of the path to enlightenment is also the principal cause, like a seed, it is said: Thus, "from a seed" a sprout arises, and from that a stalk, flowers, and fruits arise, and at the time its own fruit is established, that "seed is also destroyed," yet it is not the case that the tree that is its fruit would also become non-existent. Just as it is not like that, "likewise" here in the context of the path, the "first mind" initially generated is also a "cause for enlightenment"; at the time enlightenment is attained, it is also destroyed, but it is not the case that the fruit of enlightenment does not exist; rather, one becomes "manifestly and completely enlightened."

To teach the great path of meditation, the meaning of the one verse spoken starting with "That merit also..." is: Although there is conventionally immeasurable merit in explaining the profound dharma concordant with what one meditates on in that way, there is not even the slightest ultimately established thing; thus, "that merit" arising from explaining the dharma is also "thoroughly known" as "hollow" because it is empty of being established by its own defining characteristics, and likewise "empty" because it is empty of inherent nature and empty of the true existence that is the object of negation, and "insubstantial" because it is not established from its own side and arises from the accumulation of causes, conditions, and dependent origination, and "coreless" because its nature is empty of true existence like an illusion. Having thus completely understood, if one "practices the profound practice" of the "perfection of wisdom of the sugatas," which has the nature of the great path of meditation, at the time of engaging in such practice, one "completely grasps" or generates "immeasurable, incalculable merit." To anticipate the doubt that thinks, as raised in the dispute from the Ornament of Clear Realization: "For an inexpressible entity, decrease and increase are not suitable," and so forth, because all dharmas are equal in having no inherent nature within the dharmadhātu, the exhaustion of objects of abandonment and the arising of antidotes are untenable, so therefore the levels of supreme and inferior realizations of the children of the victorious ones are also illogical, the meaning of the one verse spoken starting with "Explained by the buddhas..." is: "Whatever dharmas have been spoken" or taught by the "buddhas, the transcendent conquerors," explaining the meaning in brief, and teaching the meaning of the words extensively by combining examples and meaning, and teaching it with extreme elaboration through infinite reasonings of refutation and proof, "all these" are known as ultimately lacking any object of expression or means of expression to be apprehended, and being conventionally expressed as mere names; and having understood this, even if one were to "express" the profound abiding nature, emptiness, through countless many reasonings of refutation and proof "for many tens of millions of billions of aeons," still, since by that "the dharmadhātu of dharmas" such as the path of meditation "does not decrease" or exhaust, and does not even slightly "increase" or expand, they dispute, thinking, "the exhaustion of objects of abandonment and the arising of antidotes are also untenable." translation: To teach that the second moment is also a cause: thus, the way a result arises in dependence upon a cause is that having "found the seed itself" that possesses the capacity to generate its own result, its result, "various grains" such as "rice" and so forth, "arises," and when the result of that seed ripens, "at that" time that seed does "not exist," yet its own continuum is "also not non-existent." "Likewise, this enlightenment of the victorious ones is also" something that will "arise" from the complete perfection of the aspects of the path such as the generation of bodhicitta, and since it too is devoid of an entity's nature if one searches for the designated object of a conventional designation, one should logically understand it as arising like an illusion as an unanalyzed, unexamined convention.

[3-216] translation already produced for this document:
To teach that conventionally, because the dharmas of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are not permanent, increase and decrease are also suitable like an illusion, the meaning of the one verse spoken starting with "Of the victorious ones..." is: Although those dharmas that are whatever path of the Mahāyāna, such as the six perfections which are the sole path to be traveled by the "victorious ones," are indeed "completely proclaimed" and expressed as mere names as being established by way of their own entities; nevertheless, for a bodhisattva who conventionally "completely dedicates" all roots of virtue to unsurpassable enlightenment and lacks the conceit of adhering to the result to be attained as truly existent and the pride of grasping it as supreme, conventionally, as mere illusions, the cause and effect of dependent origination are infallible, and because they have practiced the path that unites method and wisdom, they "do not decline" from the Mahāyāna, and not only is there nothing untenable about them "touching" the supreme "enlightenment of a buddha," it is highly logical and possesses valid proofs. This concludes the commentary on the eighteenth chapter, on emptiness, from the Commentary on the Verses of the Precious Qualities Collection titled The Jewel Lamp Fulfilling the Hopes of the Fortunate, Clarifying the Suchness of Profound Dependent Origination.

[3-217] translation already produced for this document:
If they say: Even conventionally, it is illogical to attain enlightenment by realization increasing higher and higher; because each individual mind occurring earlier or later lacks the capacity, it does not attain enlightenment; and it is not by all the earlier and later minds gathering simultaneously either, because it is impossible for all earlier and later ones to occur at the same time; nor is it in dependence upon the earlier ones, because without the earlier ones the later ones do not arise - anticipating this dispute from within and teaching the answer to it by way of an example, the meaning taught by the five verses starting with "Wick and oil..." is: "For example," when a "wick and oil" and a blazing "flame of a lamp" meet, that "first moment of the flame alone" does not burn the wick "completely," yet without that first moment of the flame, that wick also does not burn; and the "last" meeting of the flame "alone" also does not burn that wick, yet without the last flame, that wick also does not burn; however, one should understand that from the continuum of all the earlier and later moments of the flame, the wick comes to be completely burned.

[3-218] translation already produced for this document:
Applying that very example that was taught to the meaning of the context, the way of attaining enlightenment: "Likewise," by the "first moment of the mind" of generating bodhicitta "alone," one does not "touch" supreme "enlightenment," yet "without that first mind," one is also unable to "touch that enlightenment"; and by whichever mind is the "last moment" of that mind's continuum "alone," one does not attain the "great enlightenment" where all objects of abandonment are pacified, yet "without that last moment," one is also unable to attain that enlightenment. However, by the true nature of dependent origination, having arisen gradually through the continuum of the earlier and later generations of mind, enlightenment is attained. Having thus generally taught that the collection of earlier and later moments of the path to enlightenment is the cause of enlightenment, now to specifically teach that the first moment of the path to enlightenment is also the principal cause, like a seed, it is said: Thus, "from a seed" a sprout arises, and from that a stalk, flowers, and fruits arise, and at the time its own fruit is established, that "seed is also destroyed," yet it is not the case that the tree that is its fruit would also become non-existent. Just as it is not like that, "likewise" here in the context of the path, the "first mind" initially generated is also a "cause for enlightenment"; at the time enlightenment is attained, it is also destroyed, but it is not the case that the fruit of enlightenment does not exist; rather, one becomes "manifestly and completely enlightened."

heading: **ཕྱིར་མི་ལྡོག་པའི་བྱང་སེམས་ཀྱི་དགེ་འདུན།**
translation: Having extensively taught the way of attaining enlightenment, to summarize the meaning: "For example," as a "pot is filled by the accumulation" of many "drops of water," meaning that it is completely filled gradually, little by little, from the first drop to the last, "likewise," the "first generation of mind" during the state of the path of accumulation "is also" a cause of supreme enlightenment; however, it is not by that alone, but by the later ones, such as the generation of bodhicitta with pure special resolve, traversing the ten grounds gradually starting from the stage of action through belief, and in dependence upon the qualities of the grounds and paths increasing higher and higher, that one becomes a buddha by way of the completion of all white qualities. To teach that conventionally, because the dharmas of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are not permanent, increase and decrease are also suitable like an illusion, the meaning of the one verse spoken starting with "Of the victorious ones..." is: Although those dharmas that are whatever path of the Mahāyāna, such as the six perfections which are the sole path to be traveled by the "victorious ones," are indeed "completely proclaimed" and expressed as mere names as being established by way of their own entities; nevertheless, for a bodhisattva who conventionally "completely dedicates" all roots of virtue to unsurpassable enlightenment and lacks the conceit of adhering to the result to be attained as truly existent and the pride of grasping it as supreme, conventionally, as mere illusions, the cause and effect of dependent origination are infallible, and because they have practiced the path that unites method and wisdom, they "do not decline" from the Mahāyāna, and not only is there nothing untenable about them "touching" the supreme "enlightenment of a buddha," it is highly logical and possesses valid proofs. This concludes the commentary on the eighteenth chapter, on emptiness, from the Commentary on the Verses of the Precious Qualities Collection titled The Jewel Lamp Fulfilling the Hopes of the Fortunate, Clarifying the Suchness of Profound Dependent Origination.

If they say: Even conventionally, it is illogical to attain enlightenment by realization increasing higher and higher; because each individual mind occurring earlier or later lacks the capacity, it does not attain enlightenment; and it is not by all the earlier and later minds gathering simultaneously either, because it is impossible for all earlier and later ones to occur at the same time; nor is it in dependence upon the earlier ones, because without the earlier ones the later ones do not arise - anticipating this dispute from within and teaching the answer to it by way of an example, the meaning taught by the five verses starting with "Wick and oil..." is: "For example," when a "wick and oil" and a blazing "flame of a lamp" meet, that "first moment of the flame alone" does not burn the wick "completely," yet without that first moment of the flame, that wick also does not burn; and the "last" meeting of the flame "alone" also does not burn that wick, yet without the last flame, that wick also does not burn; however, one should understand that from the continuum of all the earlier and later moments of the flame, the wick comes to be completely burned.

Applying that very example that was taught to the meaning of the context, the way of attaining enlightenment: "Likewise," by the "first moment of the mind" of generating bodhicitta "alone," one does not "touch" supreme "enlightenment," yet "without that first mind," one is also unable to "touch that enlightenment"; and by whichever mind is the "last moment" of that mind's continuum "alone," one does not attain the "great enlightenment" where all objects of abandonment are pacified, yet "without that last moment," one is also unable to attain that enlightenment. However, by the true nature of dependent origination, having arisen gradually through the continuum of the earlier and later generations of mind, enlightenment is attained. Having thus generally taught that the collection of earlier and later moments of the path to enlightenment is the cause of enlightenment, now to specifically teach that the first moment of the path to enlightenment is also the principal cause, like a seed, it is said: Thus, "from a seed" a sprout arises, and from that a stalk, flowers, and fruits arise, and at the time its own fruit is established, that "seed is also destroyed," yet it is not the case that the tree that is its fruit would also become non-existent. Just as it is not like that, "likewise" here in the context of the path, the "first mind" initially generated is also a "cause for enlightenment"; at the time enlightenment is attained, it is also destroyed, but it is not the case that the fruit of enlightenment does not exist; rather, one becomes "manifestly and completely enlightened."

heading: **ཕྱིར་མི་ལྡོག་པའི་བྱང་སེམས་ཀྱི་དགེ་འདུན།**
translation: Second, to teach the actual signs of irreversibility because of abiding on the path of meditation, which is the specific attribute that is the main subject of the current context: the meaning of the one verse spoken starting with "Emptiness, signlessness..." is: Thus, "engaging" in the meaning of having realized the profound dharmas of realizing existence and peace as empty of true existence, the realization of the three doors of liberation—such as "emptiness" due to all dharmas not being established by their own entities, "signlessness" due to causes not being truly established, and "wishlessness" by way of not adhering to results as truly established—a bodhisattva endowed with special methods such as great compassion does "not touch" the one-sided peace of nirvāṇa; and although they take rebirth in saṃsāra for the sake of others, because they directly realize existence as empty of true existence and do "not engage in the signs" of manifest adherence, they do not abide in either extreme of existence or peace. This is, "for example," "like" an "expert boatman" carrying goods, going back and forth across the ocean, who neither abides on the two extremes of the far shore or the near shore, nor abides in the ocean. So it is said.

To teach that conventionally, because the dharmas of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are not permanent, increase and decrease are also suitable like an illusion, the meaning of the one verse spoken starting with "Of the victorious ones..." is: Although those dharmas that are whatever path of the Mahāyāna, such as the six perfections which are the sole path to be traveled by the "victorious ones," are indeed "completely proclaimed" and expressed as mere names as being established by way of their own entities; nevertheless, for a bodhisattva who conventionally "completely dedicates" all roots of virtue to unsurpassable enlightenment and lacks the conceit of adhering to the result to be attained as truly existent and the pride of grasping it as supreme, conventionally, as mere illusions, the cause and effect of dependent origination are infallible, and because they have practiced the path that unites method and wisdom, they "do not decline" from the Mahāyāna, and not only is there nothing untenable about them "touching" the supreme "enlightenment of a buddha," it is highly logical and possesses valid proofs. This concludes the commentary on the eighteenth chapter, on emptiness, from the Commentary on the Verses of the Precious Qualities Collection titled The Jewel Lamp Fulfilling the Hopes of the Fortunate, Clarifying the Suchness of Profound Dependent Origination.

If they say: Even conventionally, it is illogical to attain enlightenment by realization increasing higher and higher; because each individual mind occurring earlier or later lacks the capacity, it does not attain enlightenment; and it is not by all the earlier and later minds gathering simultaneously either, because it is impossible for all earlier and later ones to occur at the same time; nor is it in dependence upon the earlier ones, because without the earlier ones the later ones do not arise - anticipating this dispute from within and teaching the answer to it by way of an example, the meaning taught by the five verses starting with "Wick and oil..." is: "For example," when a "wick and oil" and a blazing "flame of a lamp" meet, that "first moment of the flame alone" does not burn the wick "completely," yet without that first moment of the flame, that wick also does not burn; and the "last" meeting of the flame "alone" also does not burn that wick, yet without the last flame, that wick also does not burn; however, one should understand that from the continuum of all the earlier and later moments of the flame, the wick comes to be completely burned.

However, by the true nature of dependent origination, having arisen gradually through the continuum of the earlier and later generations of mind, enlightenment is attained. Having thus generally taught that the collection of earlier and later moments of the path to enlightenment is the cause of enlightenment, now to specifically teach that the first moment of the path to enlightenment is also the principal cause, like a seed, it is said: Thus, "from a seed" a sprout arises, and from that a stalk, flowers, and fruits arise, and at the time its own fruit is established, that "seed is also destroyed," yet it is not the case that the tree that is its fruit would also become non-existent. Just as it is not like that, "likewise" here in the context of the path, the "first mind" initially generated is also a "cause for enlightenment"; at the time enlightenment is attained, it is also destroyed, but it is not the case that the fruit of enlightenment does not exist; rather, one becomes "manifestly and completely enlightened."

translation: The training of the equality of existence and peace. Ninth, to teach the training of the equality of existence and peace: From the Ornament: "Because dharmas are like dreams," up to, "The reply is exactly as explained." So it is said. Regarding this, there are three [topics]: the definition, the divisions, and the boundary of the grounds. First: the yoga of the pure grounds that has exhaustively destroyed the opportunity for manifest true apprehension to arise during the state of subsequent attainment, by way of being embraced by the wisdom that directly realizes existence and peace as empty of true existence—that is the definition of the training of the equality of existence and peace. Second, if that is divided, there are the three wisdoms of the three pure grounds. Third, the boundary of the grounds: it exists only on the three pure grounds. Among the three trainings that accomplish the three bodies, to explain the training of the equality of existence and peace, which accomplishes the dharmakāya: the meaning of the one verse spoken starting with "A bodhisattva engaging thus..." is: "Bodhisattvas engaging" in the path of familiarizing with and directly realizing the equality of existence and peace as empty of true existence "thus", do not have the manifest adherence of thinking, "'I' will be 'prophesied' to unsurpassable enlightenment 'by a victorious one'" endowed with the ten powers, nor the conceited mind of true adherence thinking, "I will touch supreme enlightenment," and if one analyzes and searches with the rational consciousness that investigates the ultimate, one understands that among these dharmas subsumed by both existence and peace, there is "nothing whatsoever" to be removed or abandoned, etc.; having understood this, lacking any unendurable mental "fear" towards the object of abandonment, saṃsāra, and the object of attainment, enlightenment, existing like illusions, and possessing confidence, "engaging thus is engaging" in the profound "wisdom of the Sugatas," the path of realizing existence and peace as empty of true existence. So it is said.

Applying that very example that was taught to the meaning of the context, the way of attaining enlightenment: "Likewise," by the "first moment of the mind" of generating bodhicitta "alone," one does not "touch" supreme "enlightenment," yet "without that first mind," one is also unable to "touch that enlightenment"; and by whichever mind is the "last moment" of that mind's continuum "alone," one does not attain the "great enlightenment" where all objects of abandonment are pacified, yet "without that last moment," one is also unable to attain that enlightenment. However, by the true nature of dependent origination, having arisen gradually through the continuum of the earlier and later generations of mind, enlightenment is attained. Having thus generally taught that the collection of earlier and later moments of the path to enlightenment is the cause of enlightenment, now to specifically teach that the first moment of the path to enlightenment is also the principal cause, like a seed, it is said: Thus, "from a seed" a sprout arises, and from that a stalk, flowers, and fruits arise, and at the time its own fruit is established, that "seed is also destroyed," yet it is not the case that the tree that is its fruit would also become non-existent. Just as it is not like that, "likewise" here in the context of the path, the "first mind" initially generated is also a "cause for enlightenment"; at the time enlightenment is attained, it is also destroyed, but it is not the case that the fruit of enlightenment does not exist; rather, one becomes "manifestly and completely enlightened."

Second, to teach the actual signs of irreversibility because of abiding on the path of meditation, which is the specific attribute that is the main subject of the current context: the meaning of the one verse spoken starting with "Emptiness, signlessness..." is: Thus, "engaging" in the meaning of having realized the profound dharmas of realizing existence and peace as empty of true existence, the realization of the three doors of liberation—such as "emptiness" due to all dharmas not being established by their own entities, "signlessness" due to causes not being truly established, and "wishlessness" by way of not adhering to results as truly established—a bodhisattva endowed with special methods such as great compassion does "not touch" the one-sided peace of nirvāṇa; and although they take rebirth in saṃsāra for the sake of others, because they directly realize existence as empty of true existence and do "not engage in the signs" of manifest adherence, they do not abide in either extreme of existence or peace. This is, "for example," "like" an "expert boatman" carrying goods, going back and forth across the ocean, who neither abides on the two extremes of the far shore or the near shore, nor abides in the ocean. So it is said.

heading: **ཞིང་དག་སྦྱོར་བ།**
source: ཞིང་དག་སྦྱོར་བ།བཅུ་པ་ཞིང་དག་སྦྱོར་བ་ནི། རྒྱན་ལས། སེམས་ཅན་འཇིག་རྟེན་དེ་བཞིན་དུ། ནས། སངས་རྒྱས་ཞིང་ནི་དག་པ་ཡིན། ཞེས་གསུངས། འདི་ལ་མཚན་ཉིད་དབྱེ་བ། ས་མཚམས་གསུམ། དང་པོ་ནི། རང་གང་དུ་འཚང་རྒྱ་འགྱུར་གྱི་ཞིང་ཁྱད་པར་ཅན་འགྲུབ་པའི་སྨོན་ལམ་ལ་སོགས་པའི་དགེ་བའི་རྩ་བ་རང་རྒྱུད་ལ་ནུས་པ་མཐུ་ཅན་དུ་འགྱུར་པའི་དག་སའི་རྣལ་འབྱོར་དེ། ཞིང་དག་སྦྱོར་བའི་མཚན་ཉིད་། གཉིས་པ་དེ་ལ་དབྱེ་ན། སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་ཞིང་གི་སྣོད་དག་པའི་སྦྱོར་བ་དང་། བཅུད་དག་པའི་སྦྱོར་བ་གཉིས་ཡོད། གསུམ་པ་ས་མཚམས་དག་པ་ས་གསུམ་ན་ཡོད། ལོངས་སྐུ་འགྲུབ་བྱེད་ཀྱི་ཞིང་དག་སྦྱོར་བ་དེ་ཉིད་འཆད་པར། འཇིག་རྟེན་དགོན་པའི་ཞེས་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གཅིག་གསུངས་པའི་དོན། ཕྱོགས་བཅུའི་འཇིག་རྟེན་གྱི་ཁམས་འདི་ན་གྲོང་ལས་རིང་དུ་གྱུར་ཅིང་ཆུ་དང་ཟས་ཀྱིས་དབེན་པའི་འབྲོག་དགོན་པའི་ལམ་ཉམ་ང་བ་གཅན་གཟན་གཏུམ་པོས་གང་བ་སོགས་སྣོད་ཀྱི་སྐྱོན་དང་བཅུད་ཀྱི་སེམས་ཅན་རྣམས་ཀྱང་ཟས་གོས་ལོངས་སྤྱོད་ཀྱིས་དབུལ་ཞིང་ཕོངས་པའི་མུ་གེའི་དགོན་པ་དང་། ནང་གི་ཉོན་མོངས་པ་དང་རླུང་ཁྲིས་བད་རྐན་སོགས་ཕྱིའི་ནད་སྣ་ཚོགས་པ་དང་བཅས་པར་མཐོང་ནས་ཀྱང་དེ་ཐམས་ཅད་བདེན་སྟོང་སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟ་བུར་ཤེས་ནས་སྐྲག་པ་མེད་ཅིང་དེ་ནས་འདི་ལྟར་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་ཞིང་སྦྱང་པའི་བསམ་པའི་གོ་ཆ་ཆེན་པོ་གྱོན་ཏེ། ཀྱཻ་མ་སེམས་ཅན་འདི་དག་ནི་ལས་ངན་པ་བསོད་ནམས་མ་བསགས་པས་ནད་དང་སྡུག་བསྔལ་དཔག་ཏུ་མེད་པས་མནར་བ་སྙིང་རེ་རྫེ་བདག་གིས་འདི་དག་ལ་སོགས་པའི་སེམས་ཅན་ཐམས་ཅད་དོན་དུ་རང་གང་དུ་སངས་རྒྱས་པའི་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་ཞིང་ཁྱད་པར་ཅན་དང་སྡུག་བསྔལ་དང་མ་དག་པའི་སྣོད་ཀྱི་སྐྱོན་གང་ཡང་མེད་པར་སྣོད་བཅུད་ཀྱི་འབྱོར་བ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་དེ་ལྟ་བུ་ཞིག་སྒྲུབ་པར་བྱ་ཞིང་དེའི་ཆེད་དུ་ཕར་ཕྱིན་དྲུག་ལ་སོགས་པའི་བསོད་ནམས་དང་ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་བསོགས་པ་ལ་བསྐལ་པ་ཕྱི་མིའི་མུ་མཐར་ཐུག་གི་བར་དུ་རྟག་ཏུ་བརྩོན་པར་བྱ་ཞིང་དེ་དག་རང་བཞིན་མེད་པར་རབ་ཏུ་ཤེས་པའི་སྒོ་ནས་དེ་ལྟ་བུའི་ལམ་ལ་བསླབ་པ་ལ་སྲིང་མོ་གང་གཱའི་ལྷ་མོ་བཞིན་དུ་ཡོངས་སུ་སྐྱོ་བའི་ཡིད་ནི་རྡུལ་ཙམ་ཡང་སྐྱེད་པར་མི་བྱེད་དོ་ཅེས་བསམ་པའི་གོ་ཆ་གྱོན་ཅིང་སྦྱོར་བས་ཉམས་སུ་ལེན་པར་བྱེད་དོ། །ཞེས་སོ། །ཡོན་ཏན་རིན་པོ་ཆེ་སྡུད་པ་ཚིགས་སུ་བཅད་པའི་འགྲེལ་བ་ཟམ་མོ་རྟེན་འབྱུང་གི་དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཉིད་གསལ་བར་བྱེད་པའི་ནོར་བུའི་སྒྲོན་མེ་སྐལ་བཟང་རེ་སྐོང་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལས་གང་གཱའི་ལྷ་མོའི་ལེའུ་སྟེ་བཅུ་དགུ་པའི་འགྲེལ་པའོ།།  །།
translation: The training of pure lands. Tenth, the training of pure lands: From the Ornament: "Likewise the worlds of sentient beings," up to, "The buddhafields are pure." So it is said. Regarding this, there are three [topics]: the definition, the divisions, and the boundary of the grounds. First: the yoga of the pure grounds in which roots of virtue, such as aspiration prayers that accomplish the special field where oneself will become a buddha, become potent in one's own continuum—that is the definition of the training of pure lands. Second, if that is divided, there are two: the training of purifying the environment of the buddhafields, and the training of purifying the inhabitants. Third, the boundary of the grounds: it exists on the three pure grounds. To explain that very training of pure lands, which accomplishes the saṃbhogakāya: the meaning of the one verse spoken starting with "In the wilderness of the world..." is: Although seeing that in this "world"-system of the ten directions there are faults of the environment—such as fearful paths of solitary "wildernesses" that are far from towns, devoid of water and food, and filled with fierce wild animals—and seeing the inhabitants, the sentient beings, in "wildernesses" of famine, destitute and impoverished regarding food, clothing, and resources, as well as possessing inner afflictions and various outer diseases such as wind, bile, and phlegm, one knows that all of them are empty of true existence and "like illusions," and is thus "without fear"; and "then" puts on the great armor of the thought to purify "buddhafields" "thus": "Alas! These sentient beings, having not accumulated merit due to bad karma, are tormented by immeasurable diseases and suffering; how pitiful! For the sake of all these and other sentient beings, I will accomplish a special buddhafield where I will become a buddha, lacking any suffering or faults of an impure environment, with such perfect excellence of environment and inhabitants. And for that purpose, I will always strive to accumulate the collections of merit and wisdom, such as the six perfections, until the limit of future eons. By way of thoroughly knowing them to lack inherent existence, I will not generate even an atom of a completely weary mind toward training on such a path, just 'like' the sister, the 'goddess Gaṅgā'"—putting on the armor of such a thought, one practices through application. So it is said. From the Commentary on the Verses of the Precious Qualities Collection entitled The Jewelled Lamp Fulfilling the Hopes of the Fortunate Ones that Illuminates the Suchness of Profound Dependent Arising, this is the commentary on the nineteenth chapter, the Goddess Gaṅgā.

Second, to teach the actual signs of irreversibility because of abiding on the path of meditation, which is the specific attribute that is the main subject of the current context: the meaning of the one verse spoken starting with "Emptiness, signlessness..." is: Thus, "engaging" in the meaning of having realized the profound dharmas of realizing existence and peace as empty of true existence, the realization of the three doors of liberation—such as "emptiness" due to all dharmas not being established by their own entities, "signlessness" due to causes not being truly established, and "wishlessness" by way of not adhering to results as truly established—a bodhisattva endowed with special methods such as great compassion does "not touch" the one-sided peace of nirvāṇa; and although they take rebirth in saṃsāra for the sake of others, because they directly realize existence as empty of true existence and do "not engage in the signs" of manifest adherence, they do not abide in either extreme of existence or peace. This is, "for example," "like" an "expert boatman" carrying goods, going back and forth across the ocean, who neither abides on the two extremes of the far shore or the near shore, nor abides in the ocean. So it is said.

The training of the equality of existence and peace. Ninth, to teach the training of the equality of existence and peace: From the Ornament: "Because dharmas are like dreams," up to, "The reply is exactly as explained." So it is said. Regarding this, there are three [topics]: the definition, the divisions, and the boundary of the grounds. First: the yoga of the pure grounds that has exhaustively destroyed the opportunity for manifest true apprehension to arise during the state of subsequent attainment, by way of being embraced by the wisdom that directly realizes existence and peace as empty of true existence—that is the definition of the training of the equality of existence and peace. Second, if that is divided, there are the three wisdoms of the three pure grounds. Third, the boundary of the grounds: it exists only on the three pure grounds. Among the three trainings that accomplish the three bodies, to explain the training of the equality of existence and peace, which accomplishes the dharmakāya: the meaning of the one verse spoken starting with "A bodhisattva engaging thus..." is: "Bodhisattvas engaging" in the path of familiarizing with and directly realizing the equality of existence and peace as empty of true existence "thus", do not have the manifest adherence of thinking, "'I' will be 'prophesied' to unsurpassable enlightenment 'by a victorious one'" endowed with the ten powers, nor the conceited mind of true adherence thinking, "I will touch supreme enlightenment," and if one analyzes and searches with the rational consciousness that investigates the ultimate, one understands that among these dharmas subsumed by both existence and peace, there is "nothing whatsoever" to be removed or abandoned, etc.; having understood this, lacking any unendurable mental "fear" towards the object of abandonment, saṃsāra, and the object of attainment, enlightenment, existing like illusions, and possessing confidence, "engaging thus is engaging" in the profound "wisdom of the Sugatas," the path of realizing existence and peace as empty of true existence. So it is said.

heading: **ཐབས་མཁས་སྦྱོར་བ།**
source: ཐབས་མཁས་སྦྱོར་བ།བཅུ་གཅིག་པ་ཐབས་མཁས་སྦྱོར་བ་ནི། རྒྱན་ལས། ཡུལ་དང་སྦྱོར་བ་ཅན་འདི་ནི། ནས། ཐབས་ལ་མཁས་པ་རྣམ་པར་བཅུ། །ཞེས་གསུངས། འདི་ལ་མཚན་ཉིད། དབྱེ་བ། ས་མཚམས་གསུམ། དང་པོ་ནི། འབད་རྩོལ་རགས་པ་ཞི་བའི་སྒོ་ནས་འཕྲིན་ལས་ལྷུན་གྱིས་གྲུབ་པའི་དག་སའི་རྣལ་འབྱོར་དེ། ཐབས་མཁས་སྦྱོར་བའི་མཚན་ཉིད། གཉིས་པ་དེ་ལ་དབྱེ་ན། བདུད་བཞི་ལས་རྒྱལ་བའི་ཐབས་མཁས་སྦྱོར་བ། དོན་དམ་པར་མི་གནས་ཤིང་ཐ་སྙད་དུ་གནས་པའི་དེ་དང་། གཞན་དོན་སྔོན་གྱི་སྨོན་ལམ་གྱི་ཤུགས་ཀྱིས་འཕང་བའི་དེ་དང༌། ཐུན་མོང་མ་ཡིན་བའི་དེ་དང་། མ་ཆགས་པའི་དེ་དང་། མི་དམིགས་པའི་དེ་དང༌། མཚན་མ་མེད་པའི་དེ་དང་། སྨོན་པ་མེད་པའི་དེ་དང་། ཕྱིར་མི་ལྡོག་པའི་རྟགས་ཀྱི་དེ་དང་། ཚད་མེད་པའི་ཐབས་མཁས་སྦྱོར་བ་དང་བཅུ་ཡོད། གསུམ་པ་ས་མཚམས་དག་པ་ས་གསུམ་ཁོ་ནར་ཡོད། སྤྲུལ་སྐུ་འགྲུབ་བྱེད་ཀྱི་ཐབས་མཁས་སྦྱོར་བ་དེ་ཉིད་འཆད་པར། མཁས་བྱའི་ཡུལ་བསྟན་བའི་སྒོ་ནས་ཐབས་མཁས་སྦྱོར་བ་སྤྱིར་སྟོན་པར། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཅེས་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གཅིག་གསུངས་པའི་དོན། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་བདག་ཉིད་ཆེན་པོ་རྣམས་ནི་རྒྱལ་བའི་ཡུམ་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལ་ཐོས་བསམ་བསྒོམ་པས་སྤྱོད་ཅིང་གནས་པར་བྱེད་ལ། དེ་ཡང་ཚུལ་ཇི་ལྟར་ན་གཟུགས་ཀྱི་ཕུང་པོ་ལ་སོགས་པའི་ཆོས་འདི་དག་ཐམས་ཅད་གདོད་མ་ནས་རང་བཞིན་གྱིས་འགྲུབ་པས་སྟོང་ཞིང་བདེན་པའི་སྐྱེ་བ་མེད་པར་མངོན་སུམ་དུ་ཤེས་ནས་ཆོས་ཉིད་དེ་བཞིན་ཉིད་ལ་རྩེ་གཅིག་ཏུ་མཉམ་པར་འཇོག་ཀྱང་སྙིང་རྗེའི་དབང་གིས་བར་དེར། འདིར་བསྟན་ཡང་དག་མཐའ་མངོན་དུ་བྱས་ནས་གཞན་དོན་རྒྱུན་ཆད་པ་མེད་དེ། མཉམ་བཞག་ལས་བཞེངས་ནས་རྗེས་ཐོབ་མཉམ་པར་མ་བཞག་པའི་སྐབས་སུ་གདུལ་བྱའི་སེམས་ཅན་གྱི་ཁམས་ཚད་མེད་པའི་དོན་སྒྲུབ་པར་མཛད་པ་ཡིན་ཏེ། དེ་དག་ལ་སྙིང་རྗེ་ཆེན་པོ་རྒྱུན་ཆགས་སུ་འཇུག་པའི་ཕྱིར། ཞི་བའི་དབྱིངས་ལ་མི་གནས་པར་སེམས་ཅན་གྱི་དོན་དཔག་མེད་བསྒྲུབ་པ་ལ་འཇུག་པའི་བར་སྐབས་དེར་ཡང་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་ཆོས་སྟོབས་བཅུ་མི་འཇིག་པ་བཞི་ལ་སོགས་པ་ལས་ཡོངས་སུ་མི་ཉམས་ཏེ། ཤེས་རབ་དང་སྙིང་རྗེ་ཟུང་དུ་འཇུག་པའི་ཐབས་མཁས་སྟབས་ཀྱིས་སངས་ཀྱི་ཆོས་རྣམས་ཐོབ་པར་འགྱུར་རོ། །ཞེས་བའོ། །
translation: The training of skillful means. Eleventh, the training of skillful means: From the Ornament: "This object and practitioner," up to, "Skillful means has ten aspects." So it is said. Regarding this, there are three [topics]: the definition, the divisions, and the boundary of the grounds. First: the yoga of the pure grounds in which enlightened activity is spontaneously accomplished by way of pacifying coarse effort—that is the definition of the training of skillful means. Second, if that is divided, there are ten: the training of skillful means of overcoming the four māras, that of not abiding in the ultimate but abiding in the conventional, that of others' benefit being propelled by the force of previous aspiration prayers, that which is uncommon, that of non-attachment, that of non-apprehension, that of signlessness, that of wishlessness, that of the sign of non-retrogression, and the training of skillful means that is immeasurable. Third, the boundary of the grounds: it exists only on the three pure grounds. To explain that very training of skillful means, which accomplishes the nirmāṇakāya: to teach the training of skillful means in general by way of teaching the object of skill: the meaning of the one verse spoken starting with "A bodhisattva..." is: "Bodhisattvas," the great beings, engage and abide in the Mother of the Victorious Ones, the perfection of wisdom, through hearing, thinking, and meditating, and how do they do so? Having directly known that all these dharmas, such as the aggregate of form, are empty of being inherently established from the beginning and lack true arising, they rest evenly and one-pointedly in dharmatā, suchness; but by the power of compassion, "in the meantime", having actualized the ultimate limit taught here, the benefit for others is uninterrupted; arising from meditative equipoise, during the state of subsequent attainment when not in meditative equipoise, they accomplish the immeasurable benefit of the realms of sentient beings to be tamed. Because they continuously engage in great compassion for them, they do not abide in the expanse of peace; and even during that interval of engaging in accomplishing the immeasurable benefit of sentient beings, they do not completely degenerate from the qualities of a buddha, such as the ten powers and four fearlessnesses, but through the skillful means that unites wisdom and compassion, they "will attain the qualities of a buddha." So it is said.

སྲིད་ཞི་མཉམ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་སྦྱོར་བ། དགུ་པ་སྲིད་ཞི་མཉམ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་སྦྱོར་བ་སྟོན་པར། རྒྱན་ལས། ཆོས་རྣམས་རྨི་ལམ་འདྲ་བའི་ཕྱིར། ནས། ལན་ནི་ཇི་སྐད་བཤད་པར་ཟད། ཅེས་གསུངས། འདི་ལ་མཚན་ཉིད། དབྱེ་བ། ས་མཚམས་གསུམ། དང་པོ་ནི། སྲིད་ཞི་བདེན་སྟོང་དུ་མངོན་སུམ་དུ་རྟོགས་པའི་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱིས་ཟིན་པའི་སྒོ་ནས་རྗེས་ཐོབ་ཀྱི་གནས་སྐབས་སུ་བདེན་འཛིན་མངོན་འགྱུར་བ་བ་སྐྱེ་བའི་གོ་སྐབས་ཟད་པར་བཅོམ་པའི་དག་སའི་རྣལ་འབྱོར་དེ། སྲིད་ཞི་མཉམ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་སྦྱོར་བའི་མཚན་ཉིད། གཉིས་པ་དེ་ལ་དབྱེ་ན་དག་པ་ས་གསུམ་གྱི་ཡེ་ཤེས་གསུམ་ཡོད། གསུམ་པ་ས་ས་མཚམས་དག་པས་ས་གསུམ་ཁོ་ནར་ཡོད། སྐུ་གསུམ་འགྲུབ་བྱེད་ཀྱི་སྦྱོར་བ་གསུམ་ལས་ཆོས་སྐུ་འགྲུབ་བྱེད་སྲིད་ཞི་མཉམ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་སྦྱོར་བ་འཆད་པར། དེ་ལྟར་སྤྱོད་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཞེས་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གཅིག་གསུངས་པའི་དོན། དེ་ལྟར་སྲིད་ཞི་བདེན་སྟོང་མཉམ་པ་ཉིད་མངོན་སུམ་དུ་རྟོགས་ཤིང་གོམས་པའི་ལམ་ལ་སྤྱོད་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་རྣམས་ནི་འདི་སྙམ་དུ་བདག་སྟོབས་བཅུ་མངའ་བ་རྒྱལ་བས་བླ་མེད་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཏུ་ལུང་བསྟན་པར་འགྱུར་རོ་སྙམ་དུ་མངོན་པར་ཞེན་པ་དང་། བྱང་ཆུབ་མཆོག་ལ་རེག་པར་འགྱུར་རོ་སྙམ་པའི་བདེན་བཞེན་གྱི་རློམ་སེམས་མེད་ཅིང་། དོན་དམ་དཔྱོད་བྱེད་ཀྱི་རིགས་ཤེས་ཀྱིས་དཔྱད་ཅིང་བཙལ་ན་སྲིད་ཞི་གཉིས་ཀྱིས་བསྡུས་པའི་ཆོས་འདི་དག་ལ་བསལ་བྱ་དང་སྤང་བྱ་སོགས་ཅིི་ཡང་མེད་དོ་ཅེས་ཁོང་དུ་ཆུད་ནས་སྤངས་བྱ་འཁོར་བ་དང་ཐོབ་བྱ་བྱང་ཆུབ་སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟ་བུར་གནས་པ་ལ་བློས་མི་བཟོད་པའི་སྐྲག་པ་མེད་པར་གདེངས་དང་ལྡན་པར་དེ་ལྟར་སྤྱོད་པ་ནི་བདེ་བར་གཤེགས་པའི་ཤེས་རབ་ཟབ་མོ་སྲིད་ཞི་བདེན་སྟོང་དུ་རྟོགས་པའི་ལམ་ལ་སྤྱོད་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །ཞེས་སོ། །

The training of the equality of existence and peace. Ninth, to teach the training of the equality of existence and peace: From the Ornament: "Because dharmas are like dreams," up to, "The reply is exactly as explained." So it is said. Regarding this, there are three [topics]: the definition, the divisions, and the boundary of the grounds. First: the yoga of the pure grounds that has exhaustively destroyed the opportunity for manifest true apprehension to arise during the state of subsequent attainment, by way of being embraced by the wisdom that directly realizes existence and peace as empty of true existence—that is the definition of the training of the equality of existence and peace. Second, if that is divided, there are the three wisdoms of the three pure grounds. Third, the boundary of the grounds: it exists only on the three pure grounds. Among the three trainings that accomplish the three bodies, to explain the training of the equality of existence and peace, which accomplishes the dharmakāya: the meaning of the one verse spoken starting with "A bodhisattva engaging thus..." is: "Bodhisattvas engaging" in the path of familiarizing with and directly realizing the equality of existence and peace as empty of true existence "thus", do not have the manifest adherence of thinking, "'I' will be 'prophesied' to unsurpassable enlightenment 'by a victorious one'" endowed with the ten powers, nor the conceited mind of true adherence thinking, "I will touch supreme enlightenment," and if one analyzes and searches with the rational consciousness that investigates the ultimate, one understands that among these dharmas subsumed by both existence and peace, there is "nothing whatsoever" to be removed or abandoned, etc.; having understood this, lacking any unendurable mental "fear" towards the object of abandonment, saṃsāra, and the object of attainment, enlightenment, existing like illusions, and possessing confidence, "engaging thus is engaging" in the profound "wisdom of the Sugatas," the path of realizing existence and peace as empty of true existence. So it is said.

ཞིང་དག་སྦྱོར་བ།བཅུ་པ་ཞིང་དག་སྦྱོར་བ་ནི། རྒྱན་ལས། སེམས་ཅན་འཇིག་རྟེན་དེ་བཞིན་དུ། ནས། སངས་རྒྱས་ཞིང་ནི་དག་པ་ཡིན། ཞེས་གསུངས། འདི་ལ་མཚན་ཉིད་དབྱེ་བ། ས་མཚམས་གསུམ། དང་པོ་ནི། རང་གང་དུ་འཚང་རྒྱ་འགྱུར་གྱི་ཞིང་ཁྱད་པར་ཅན་འགྲུབ་པའི་སྨོན་ལམ་ལ་སོགས་པའི་དགེ་བའི་རྩ་བ་རང་རྒྱུད་ལ་ནུས་པ་མཐུ་ཅན་དུ་འགྱུར་པའི་དག་སའི་རྣལ་འབྱོར་དེ། ཞིང་དག་སྦྱོར་བའི་མཚན་ཉིད་། གཉིས་པ་དེ་ལ་དབྱེ་ན། སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་ཞིང་གི་སྣོད་དག་པའི་སྦྱོར་བ་དང་། བཅུད་དག་པའི་སྦྱོར་བ་གཉིས་ཡོད། གསུམ་པ་ས་མཚམས་དག་པ་ས་གསུམ་ན་ཡོད། ལོངས་སྐུ་འགྲུབ་བྱེད་ཀྱི་ཞིང་དག་སྦྱོར་བ་དེ་ཉིད་འཆད་པར། འཇིག་རྟེན་དགོན་པའི་ཞེས་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གཅིག་གསུངས་པའི་དོན། ཕྱོགས་བཅུའི་འཇིག་རྟེན་གྱི་ཁམས་འདི་ན་གྲོང་ལས་རིང་དུ་གྱུར་ཅིང་ཆུ་དང་ཟས་ཀྱིས་དབེན་པའི་འབྲོག་དགོན་པའི་ལམ་ཉམ་ང་བ་གཅན་གཟན་གཏུམ་པོས་གང་བ་སོགས་སྣོད་ཀྱི་སྐྱོན་དང་བཅུད་ཀྱི་སེམས་ཅན་རྣམས་ཀྱང་ཟས་གོས་ལོངས་སྤྱོད་ཀྱིས་དབུལ་ཞིང་ཕོངས་པའི་མུ་གེའི་དགོན་པ་དང་། ནང་གི་ཉོན་མོངས་པ་དང་རླུང་ཁྲིས་བད་རྐན་སོགས་ཕྱིའི་ནད་སྣ་ཚོགས་པ་དང་བཅས་པར་མཐོང་ནས་ཀྱང་དེ་ཐམས་ཅད་བདེན་སྟོང་སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟ་བུར་ཤེས་ནས་སྐྲག་པ་མེད་ཅིང་དེ་ནས་འདི་ལྟར་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་ཞིང་སྦྱང་པའི་བསམ་པའི་གོ་ཆ་ཆེན་པོ་གྱོན་ཏེ། ཀྱཻ་མ་སེམས་ཅན་འདི་དག་ནི་ལས་ངན་པ་བསོད་ནམས་མ་བསགས་པས་ནད་དང་སྡུག་བསྔལ་དཔག་ཏུ་མེད་པས་མནར་བ་སྙིང་རེ་རྫེ་བདག་གིས་འདི་དག་ལ་སོགས་པའི་སེམས་ཅན་ཐམས་ཅད་དོན་དུ་རང་གང་དུ་སངས་རྒྱས་པའི་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་ཞིང་ཁྱད་པར་ཅན་དང་སྡུག་བསྔལ་དང་མ་དག་པའི་སྣོད་ཀྱི་སྐྱོན་གང་ཡང་མེད་པར་སྣོད་བཅུད་ཀྱི་འབྱོར་བ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་དེ་ལྟ་བུ་ཞིག་སྒྲུབ་པར་བྱ་ཞིང་དེའི་ཆེད་དུ་ཕར་ཕྱིན་དྲུག་ལ་སོགས་པའི་བསོད་ནམས་དང་ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་བསོགས་པ་ལ་བསྐལ་པ་ཕྱི་མིའི་མུ་མཐར་ཐུག་གི་བར་དུ་རྟག་ཏུ་བརྩོན་པར་བྱ་ཞིང་དེ་དག་རང་བཞིན་མེད་པར་རབ་ཏུ་ཤེས་པའི་སྒོ་ནས་དེ་ལྟ་བུའི་ལམ་ལ་བསླབ་པ་ལ་སྲིང་མོ་གང་གཱའི་ལྷ་མོ་བཞིན་དུ་ཡོངས་སུ་སྐྱོ་བའི་ཡིད་ནི་རྡུལ་ཙམ་ཡང་སྐྱེད་པར་མི་བྱེད་དོ་ཅེས་བསམ་པའི་གོ་ཆ་གྱོན་ཅིང་སྦྱོར་བས་ཉམས་སུ་ལེན་པར་བྱེད་དོ། །ཞེས་སོ། །ཡོན་ཏན་རིན་པོ་ཆེ་སྡུད་པ་ཚིགས་སུ་བཅད་པའི་འགྲེལ་བ་ཟམ་མོ་རྟེན་འབྱུང་གི་དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཉིད་གསལ་བར་བྱེད་པའི་ནོར་བུའི་སྒྲོན་མེ་སྐལ་བཟང་རེ་སྐོང་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལས་གང་གཱའི་ལྷ་མོའི་ལེའུ་སྟེ་བཅུ་དགུ་པའི་འགྲེལ་པའོ།།  །།

The training of pure lands. Tenth, the training of pure lands: From the Ornament: "Likewise the worlds of sentient beings," up to, "The buddhafields are pure." So it is said. Regarding this, there are three [topics]: the definition, the divisions, and the boundary of the grounds. First: the yoga of the pure grounds in which roots of virtue, such as aspiration prayers that accomplish the special field where oneself will become a buddha, become potent in one's own continuum—that is the definition of the training of pure lands. Second, if that is divided, there are two: the training of purifying the environment of the buddhafields, and the training of purifying the inhabitants. Third, the boundary of the grounds: it exists on the three pure grounds. To explain that very training of pure lands, which accomplishes the saṃbhogakāya: the meaning of the one verse spoken starting with "In the wilderness of the world..." is: Although seeing that in this "world"-system of the ten directions there are faults of the environment—such as fearful paths of solitary "wildernesses" that are far from towns, devoid of water and food, and filled with fierce wild animals—and seeing the inhabitants, the sentient beings, in "wildernesses" of famine, destitute and impoverished regarding food, clothing, and resources, as well as possessing inner afflictions and various outer diseases such as wind, bile, and phlegm, one knows that all of them are empty of true existence and "like illusions," and is thus "without fear"; and "then" puts on the great armor of the thought to purify "buddhafields" "thus": "Alas! These sentient beings, having not accumulated merit due to bad karma, are tormented by immeasurable diseases and suffering; how pitiful! For the sake of all these and other sentient beings, I will accomplish a special buddhafield where I will become a buddha, lacking any suffering or faults of an impure environment, with such perfect excellence of environment and inhabitants. And for that purpose, I will always strive to accumulate the collections of merit and wisdom, such as the six perfections, until the limit of future eons. By way of thoroughly knowing them to lack inherent existence, I will not generate even an atom of a completely weary mind toward training on such a path, just 'like' the sister, the 'goddess Gaṅgā'"—putting on the armor of such a thought, one practices through application. So it is said. From the Commentary on the Verses of the Precious Qualities Collection entitled The Jewelled Lamp Fulfilling the Hopes of the Fortunate Ones that Illuminates the Suchness of Profound Dependent Arising, this is the commentary on the nineteenth chapter, the Goddess Gaṅgā.

The training of the equality of existence and peace. Ninth, to teach the training of the equality of existence and peace: From the Ornament: "Because dharmas are like dreams," up to, "The reply is exactly as explained." So it is said. Regarding this, there are three [topics]: the definition, the divisions, and the boundary of the grounds. First: the yoga of the pure grounds that has exhaustively destroyed the opportunity for manifest true apprehension to arise during the state of subsequent attainment, by way of being embraced by the wisdom that directly realizes existence and peace as empty of true existence—that is the definition of the training of the equality of existence and peace. Second, if that is divided, there are the three wisdoms of the three pure grounds. Third, the boundary of the grounds: it exists only on the three pure grounds. Among the three trainings that accomplish the three bodies, to explain the training of the equality of existence and peace, which accomplishes the dharmakāya: the meaning of the one verse spoken starting with "A bodhisattva engaging thus..." is: "Bodhisattvas engaging" in the path of familiarizing with and directly realizing the equality of existence and peace as empty of true existence "thus", do not have the manifest adherence of thinking, "'I' will be 'prophesied' to unsurpassable enlightenment 'by a victorious one'" endowed with the ten powers, nor the conceited mind of true adherence thinking, "I will touch supreme enlightenment," and if one analyzes and searches with the rational consciousness that investigates the ultimate, one understands that among these dharmas subsumed by both existence and peace, there is "nothing whatsoever" to be removed or abandoned, etc.; having understood this, lacking any unendurable mental "fear" towards the object of abandonment, saṃsāra, and the object of attainment, enlightenment, existing like illusions, and possessing confidence, "engaging thus is engaging" in the profound "wisdom of the Sugatas," the path of realizing existence and peace as empty of true existence. So it is said.

The training of pure lands. Tenth, the training of pure lands: From the Ornament: "Likewise the worlds of sentient beings," up to, "The buddhafields are pure." So it is said. Regarding this, there are three [topics]: the definition, the divisions, and the boundary of the grounds. First: the yoga of the pure grounds in which roots of virtue, such as aspiration prayers that accomplish the special field where oneself will become a buddha, become potent in one's own continuum—that is the definition of the training of pure lands. Second, if that is divided, there are two: the training of purifying the environment of the buddhafields, and the training of purifying the inhabitants. Third, the boundary of the grounds: it exists on the three pure grounds. To explain that very training of pure lands, which accomplishes the saṃbhogakāya: the meaning of the one verse spoken starting with "In the wilderness of the world..." is: Although seeing that in this "world"-system of the ten directions there are faults of the environment—such as fearful paths of solitary "wildernesses" that are far from towns, devoid of water and food, and filled with fierce wild animals—and seeing the inhabitants, the sentient beings, in "wildernesses" of famine, destitute and impoverished regarding food, clothing, and resources, as well as possessing inner afflictions and various outer diseases such as wind, bile, and phlegm, one knows that all of them are empty of true existence and "like illusions," and is thus "without fear"; and "then" puts on the great armor of the thought to purify "buddhafields" "thus": "Alas! These sentient beings, having not accumulated merit due to bad karma, are tormented by immeasurable diseases and suffering; how pitiful! For the sake of all these and other sentient beings, I will accomplish a special buddhafield where I will become a buddha, lacking any suffering or faults of an impure environment, with such perfect excellence of environment and inhabitants. And for that purpose, I will always strive to accumulate the collections of merit and wisdom, such as the six perfections, until the limit of future eons. By way of thoroughly knowing them to lack inherent existence, I will not generate even an atom of a completely weary mind toward training on such a path, just 'like' the sister, the 'goddess Gaṅgā'"—putting on the armor of such a thought, one practices through application. So it is said. From the Commentary on the Verses of the Precious Qualities Collection entitled The Jewelled Lamp Fulfilling the Hopes of the Fortunate Ones that Illuminates the Suchness of Profound Dependent Arising, this is the commentary on the nineteenth chapter, the Goddess Gaṅgā.

heading: **བདུད་བཞི་ལས་རྒྱལ་བའི་ཐབས་མཁས་སྦྱོར་བ།**
translation: The training of skillful means of overcoming the four māras. To explain the training of skillful means of overcoming the four māras: the meaning of the three verses spoken starting with "For example, a person..." is: among the explanations of the manner of training in the skillful means that unites compassion and wisdom by way of multiple examples, the first is: "For example, a person" who is skilled in the means of taming enemies, protecting his own side, and so forth, who possesses all qualities such as great courage, and who is endowed with the strength and capability to accomplish great deeds, has exerted himself in deeds that cannot be overcome by others. What is he like? Like this: he has become knowledgeable in the deeds or methods of arts such as running fast and jumping; he has perfected archery, such as shooting arrows, and many worldly fields of craft; and knowing how to emanate or produce various illusions, one who wishes to thoroughly accomplish the benefit of beings, such as protecting his relatives, has completely gathered and led his relatives, including his father, mother, and wife, and travelled on a road through an unpopulated wilderness where there are many who cause injury, such as enemies, robbers, and thieves who would harm him. And when those enemies and so forth have come there, without forsaking his relatives, by means of great courage, that person emanates many people who are extremely brave and possess the valor capable of attacking the enemies. Having ensured that harm from enemies and so forth does not arise, he goes safely in the direction he wishes to go, and also returns safely to his own home. Just like that example, at the time of practising the path and accomplishing the benefit of beings, a "bodhisattva" who is "skilled in means" continually generates great compassion for the realms of sentient beings and accomplishes immeasurable temporary and ultimate benefit and bliss. Having completely passed beyond the hindrances to the path—the "four māras", such as the māra of the son of the gods, and the two [vehicles] of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas—and abiding in the supreme samādhi that causes the attainment of buddhahood, he does "not touch enlightenment" by resting evenly in such a way that he does not rise again from the expanse of peace prematurely. Thus, it directly teaches that noble bodhisattvas do not actualize the ultimate limit taught here without having [completed] the three—perfecting, ripening, and purifying—and thereby implicitly indicates that they do actualize it after having [completed] the three—perfecting, ripening, and purifying.

The training of skillful means. Eleventh, the training of skillful means: From the Ornament: "This object and practitioner," up to, "Skillful means has ten aspects." So it is said. Regarding this, there are three [topics]: the definition, the divisions, and the boundary of the grounds. First: the yoga of the pure grounds in which enlightened activity is spontaneously accomplished by way of pacifying coarse effort—that is the definition of the training of skillful means. Second, if that is divided, there are ten: the training of skillful means of overcoming the four māras, that of not abiding in the ultimate but abiding in the conventional, that of others' benefit being propelled by the force of previous aspiration prayers, that which is uncommon, that of non-attachment, that of non-apprehension, that of signlessness, that of wishlessness, that of the sign of non-retrogression, and the training of skillful means that is immeasurable. Third, the boundary of the grounds: it exists only on the three pure grounds. To explain that very training of skillful means, which accomplishes the nirmāṇakāya: to teach the training of skillful means in general by way of teaching the object of skill: the meaning of the one verse spoken starting with "A bodhisattva..." is: "Bodhisattvas," the great beings, engage and abide in the Mother of the Victorious Ones, the perfection of wisdom, through hearing, thinking, and meditating, and how do they do so? Having directly known that all these dharmas, such as the aggregate of form, are empty of being inherently established from the beginning and lack true arising, they rest evenly and one-pointedly in dharmatā, suchness; but by the power of compassion, "in the meantime", having actualized the ultimate limit taught here, the benefit for others is uninterrupted; arising from meditative equipoise, during the state of subsequent attainment when not in meditative equipoise, they accomplish the immeasurable benefit of the realms of sentient beings to be tamed. Because they continuously engage in great compassion for them, they do not abide in the expanse of peace; and even during that interval of engaging in accomplishing the immeasurable benefit of sentient beings, they do not completely degenerate from the qualities of a buddha, such as the ten powers and four fearlessnesses, but through the skillful means that unites wisdom and compassion, they "will attain the qualities of a buddha." So it is said.

Among the ten actual trainings of skillful means:

heading: **མི་གནས་པའི་ཐབས་མཁས་སྦྱོར་བ།**
translation: The training of skillful means of non-abiding. To explain the second, the training of skillful means of non-abiding: two verses are spoken starting with "The wind supported by space..." It is like this: when the world is formed, first the maṇḍala of "wind" forms, "supported by space"; the mass of "water" is supported by that wind; the golden ground is supported by the water; this "great earth" is supported by that; and the beings of the essence, the four continents, the eight subcontinents, and so forth, remain supported by that earth. Such is the cause or basis for experiencing the result of the accumulation of the common karma of sentient beings. Having investigated, thinking, "Although the other maṇḍalas of the four elements are established in dependence on one another, upon what else is space supported and remaining?", you should reflect upon this meaning! And because it is not established as a physical entity, you will understand the manner in which it is not supported by anything at all. In "that manner", a "bodhisattva" who remains one-pointedly in "emptiness" "like space", even at that time, does not set his mind on the bliss of peace, but rather, having the support of objectless great love and compassion—without the apprehension of perceiving those who are tormented by suffering as truly existent sentient beings—and having attained immeasurable previous generation of the mind and aspirations, displays by the power of those "aspirations" immeasurable arrays of emanations that accomplish multiple "various" deeds that increase the excellent collections of the benefit and bliss of "beings". "By means of" the "skill in means" as explained, he does "not touch" the one-sided peace of "nirvāṇa", nor does he truly "abide in emptiness".

The training of skillful means of overcoming the four māras. To explain the training of skillful means of overcoming the four māras: the meaning of the three verses spoken starting with "For example, a person..." is: among the explanations of the manner of training in the skillful means that unites compassion and wisdom by way of multiple examples, the first is: "For example, a person" who is skilled in the means of taming enemies, protecting his own side, and so forth, who possesses all qualities such as great courage, and who is endowed with the strength and capability to accomplish great deeds, has exerted himself in deeds that cannot be overcome by others. What is he like? Like this: he has become knowledgeable in the deeds or methods of arts such as running fast and jumping; he has perfected archery, such as shooting arrows, and many worldly fields of craft; and knowing how to emanate or produce various illusions, one who wishes to thoroughly accomplish the benefit of beings, such as protecting his relatives, has completely gathered and led his relatives, including his father, mother, and wife, and travelled on a road through an unpopulated wilderness where there are many who cause injury, such as enemies, robbers, and thieves who would harm him. And when those enemies and so forth have come there, without forsaking his relatives, by means of great courage, that person emanates many people who are extremely brave and possess the valor capable of attacking the enemies. Having ensured that harm from enemies and so forth does not arise, he goes safely in the direction he wishes to go, and also returns safely to his own home. Just like that example, at the time of practising the path and accomplishing the benefit of beings, a "bodhisattva" who is "skilled in means" continually generates great compassion for the realms of sentient beings and accomplishes immeasurable temporary and ultimate benefit and bliss. Having completely passed beyond the hindrances to the path—the "four māras", such as the māra of the son of the gods, and the two [vehicles] of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas—and abiding in the supreme samādhi that causes the attainment of buddhahood, he does "not touch enlightenment" by resting evenly in such a way that he does not rise again from the expanse of peace prematurely. Thus, it directly teaches that noble bodhisattvas do not actualize the ultimate limit taught here without having [completed] the three—perfecting, ripening, and purifying—and thereby implicitly indicates that they do actualize it after having [completed] the three—perfecting, ripening, and purifying.

heading: **གཞན་དོན་སྨོན་ལམ་ཤུགས་ཀྱིས་འཕངས་པའི་ཐབས་མཁས་སྦྱོར་བ།**
translation: The training of skillful means implicitly indicated by aspirations for the benefit of others. To explain the third, the training of skillful means implicitly indicated by aspirations for the benefit of others: the meaning of the single verse spoken starting with "Whenever..." is: "Whenever" they train on the path of the Mahāyāna, thus "bodhisattvas" who are skilled in the meaning of the profound abiding nature, emptiness, and "who", having dispelled the darkness of the ignorance of other disciples, "illuminate" the excellent path of the Mahāyāna, directly realize that all phenomena are empty by nature, and practice by way of resting evenly in "this" supreme "samādhi of the heroic stride" in which the elaborations of dualistic appearance are entirely "pacified". At the time of cultivating the path, they "do not cultivate" even the slightest mark of conventional elaborations; remaining in the meaning of the "signless" object of negation (truly existent marks), they practice the pacification of the conceptualization that adheres to nirvāṇa as truly something to be attained, and the complete pacification of the conceptualization that grasps saṃsāra as truly something to be abandoned. The "non-abiding" in either extreme of existence or peace "arises from the power of cultivating" the path of the special training of "skillful means".

The training of skillful means of overcoming the four māras. To explain the training of skillful means of overcoming the four māras: the meaning of the three verses spoken starting with "For example, a person..." is: among the explanations of the manner of training in the skillful means that unites compassion and wisdom by way of multiple examples, the first is: "For example, a person" who is skilled in the means of taming enemies, protecting his own side, and so forth, who possesses all qualities such as great courage, and who is endowed with the strength and capability to accomplish great deeds, has exerted himself in deeds that cannot be overcome by others. What is he like? Like this: he has become knowledgeable in the deeds or methods of arts such as running fast and jumping; he has perfected archery, such as shooting arrows, and many worldly fields of craft; and knowing how to emanate or produce various illusions, one who wishes to thoroughly accomplish the benefit of beings, such as protecting his relatives, has completely gathered and led his relatives, including his father, mother, and wife, and travelled on a road through an unpopulated wilderness where there are many who cause injury, such as enemies, robbers, and thieves who would harm him. And when those enemies and so forth have come there, without forsaking his relatives, by means of great courage, that person emanates many people who are extremely brave and possess the valor capable of attacking the enemies. Having ensured that harm from enemies and so forth does not arise, he goes safely in the direction he wishes to go, and also returns safely to his own home. Just like that example, at the time of practising the path and accomplishing the benefit of beings, a "bodhisattva" who is "skilled in means" continually generates great compassion for the realms of sentient beings and accomplishes immeasurable temporary and ultimate benefit and bliss. Having completely passed beyond the hindrances to the path—the "four māras", such as the māra of the son of the gods, and the two [vehicles] of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas—and abiding in the supreme samādhi that causes the attainment of buddhahood, he does "not touch enlightenment" by resting evenly in such a way that he does not rise again from the expanse of peace prematurely. Thus, it directly teaches that noble bodhisattvas do not actualize the ultimate limit taught here without having [completed] the three—perfecting, ripening, and purifying—and thereby implicitly indicates that they do actualize it after having [completed] the three—perfecting, ripening, and purifying.

heading: **ཐུན་མོང་མ་ཡིན་པའི་ཐབས་མཁས་སྦྱོར་བ།**
translation: The uncommon training of skillful means. To explain the fourth, the uncommon training of skillful means: the meaning of the single verse spoken starting with "flying in the air..." is: "For example", for a "bird flying in the air", there is no place or basis upon which to be supported, so it does "not remain" in that "space", "yet" by the power of its two wings it "does not fall to the ground". "Like that", a "bodhisattva practices" or abides "at the doors of the three liberations"—"emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness"—yet due to skillful means he "does not touch" the extreme of "nirvāṇa"; and due to the wisdom that realizes the abiding nature, he "does not practice the path" of grasping at marks "in existence". That he does not abide in the two extremes "is by the power of skillful means."

[3-226] translation already produced for this document:
The training of skillful means of overcoming the four māras. To explain the training of skillful means of overcoming the four māras: the meaning of the three verses spoken starting with "For example, a person..." is: among the explanations of the manner of training in the skillful means that unites compassion and wisdom by way of multiple examples, the first is: "For example, a person" who is skilled in the means of taming enemies, protecting his own side, and so forth, who possesses all qualities such as great courage, and who is endowed with the strength and capability to accomplish great deeds, has exerted himself in deeds that cannot be overcome by others. What is he like? Like this: he has become knowledgeable in the deeds or methods of arts such as running fast and jumping; he has perfected archery, such as shooting arrows, and many worldly fields of craft; and knowing how to emanate or produce various illusions, one who wishes to thoroughly accomplish the benefit of beings, such as protecting his relatives, has completely gathered and led his relatives, including his father, mother, and wife, and travelled on a road through an unpopulated wilderness where there are many who cause injury, such as enemies, robbers, and thieves who would harm him. And when those enemies and so forth have come there, without forsaking his relatives, by means of great courage, that person emanates many people who are extremely brave and possess the valor capable of attacking the enemies. Having ensured that harm from enemies and so forth does not arise, he goes safely in the direction he wishes to go, and also returns safely to his own home. Just like that example, at the time of practising the path and accomplishing the benefit of beings, a "bodhisattva" who is "skilled in means" continually generates great compassion for the realms of sentient beings and accomplishes immeasurable temporary and ultimate benefit and bliss. Having completely passed beyond the hindrances to the path—the "four māras", such as the māra of the son of the gods, and the two [vehicles] of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas—and abiding in the supreme samādhi that causes the attainment of buddhahood, he does "not touch enlightenment" by resting evenly in such a way that he does not rise again from the expanse of peace prematurely. Thus, it directly teaches that noble bodhisattvas do not actualize the ultimate limit taught here without having [completed] the three—perfecting, ripening, and purifying—and thereby implicitly indicates that they do actualize it after having [completed] the three—perfecting, ripening, and purifying.

[3-226] translation already produced for this document:
The training of skillful means of overcoming the four māras. To explain the training of skillful means of overcoming the four māras: the meaning of the three verses spoken starting with "For example, a person..." is: among the explanations of the manner of training in the skillful means that unites compassion and wisdom by way of multiple examples, the first is: "For example, a person" who is skilled in the means of taming enemies, protecting his own side, and so forth, who possesses all qualities such as great courage, and who is endowed with the strength and capability to accomplish great deeds, has exerted himself in deeds that cannot be overcome by others. What is he like? Like this: he has become knowledgeable in the deeds or methods of arts such as running fast and jumping; he has perfected archery, such as shooting arrows, and many worldly fields of craft; and knowing how to emanate or produce various illusions, one who wishes to thoroughly accomplish the benefit of beings, such as protecting his relatives, has completely gathered and led his relatives, including his father, mother, and wife, and travelled on a road through an unpopulated wilderness where there are many who cause injury, such as enemies, robbers, and thieves who would harm him. And when those enemies and so forth have come there, without forsaking his relatives, by means of great courage, that person emanates many people who are extremely brave and possess the valor capable of attacking the enemies. Having ensured that harm from enemies and so forth does not arise, he goes safely in the direction he wishes to go, and also returns safely to his own home. Just like that example, at the time of practising the path and accomplishing the benefit of beings, a "bodhisattva" who is "skilled in means" continually generates great compassion for the realms of sentient beings and accomplishes immeasurable temporary and ultimate benefit and bliss. Having completely passed beyond the hindrances to the path—the "four māras", such as the māra of the son of the gods, and the two [vehicles] of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas—and abiding in the supreme samādhi that causes the attainment of buddhahood, he does "not touch enlightenment" by resting evenly in such a way that he does not rise again from the expanse of peace prematurely. Thus, it directly teaches that noble bodhisattvas do not actualize the ultimate limit taught here without having [completed] the three—perfecting, ripening, and purifying—and thereby implicitly indicates that they do actualize it after having [completed] the three—perfecting, ripening, and purifying.

heading: **མ་ཆགས་པའི་ཐབས་མཁས་སྦྱོར་བ།**
translation: The fifth, the training of skillful means of non-attachment: Although slightly different from Buddhaśrī, according to the system of the Master (Haribhadra), it is explained by two verses starting with "For example, trained in archery..." Furthermore, "for example", a man who has properly "trained" and become skilled in the "archery" of shooting arrows shoots an "arrow" into the sky together with a wooden board; and again, by shooting other arrows after that, attaching them completely in continuous succession behind each previous arrow, by being held by those shot unceasingly, that earlier arrow finds no opportunity to "fall to the ground". But when that man desires it to fall to the ground and does not shoot an arrow, that arrow will fall to the ground.

The training of skillful means of non-abiding. To explain the second, the training of skillful means of non-abiding: two verses are spoken starting with "The wind supported by space..." It is like this: when the world is formed, first the maṇḍala of "wind" forms, "supported by space"; the mass of "water" is supported by that wind; the golden ground is supported by the water; this "great earth" is supported by that; and the beings of the essence, the four continents, the eight subcontinents, and so forth, remain supported by that earth. Such is the cause or basis for experiencing the result of the accumulation of the common karma of sentient beings. Having investigated, thinking, "Although the other maṇḍalas of the four elements are established in dependence on one another, upon what else is space supported and remaining?", you should reflect upon this meaning! And because it is not established as a physical entity, you will understand the manner in which it is not supported by anything at all. In "that manner", a "bodhisattva" who remains one-pointedly in "emptiness" "like space", even at that time, does not set his mind on the bliss of peace, but rather, having the support of objectless great love and compassion—without the apprehension of perceiving those who are tormented by suffering as truly existent sentient beings—and having attained immeasurable previous generation of the mind and aspirations, displays by the power of those "aspirations" immeasurable arrays of emanations that accomplish multiple "various" deeds that increase the excellent collections of the benefit and bliss of "beings". "By means of" the "skill in means" as explained, he does "not touch" the one-sided peace of "nirvāṇa", nor does he truly "abide in emptiness".

The training of skillful means implicitly indicated by aspirations for the benefit of others. To explain the third, the training of skillful means implicitly indicated by aspirations for the benefit of others: the meaning of the single verse spoken starting with "Whenever..." is: "Whenever" they train on the path of the Mahāyāna, thus "bodhisattvas" who are skilled in the meaning of the profound abiding nature, emptiness, and "who", having dispelled the darkness of the ignorance of other disciples, "illuminate" the excellent path of the Mahāyāna, directly realize that all phenomena are empty by nature, and practice by way of resting evenly in "this" supreme "samādhi of the heroic stride" in which the elaborations of dualistic appearance are entirely "pacified". At the time of cultivating the path, they "do not cultivate" even the slightest mark of conventional elaborations; remaining in the meaning of the "signless" object of negation (truly existent marks), they practice the pacification of the conceptualization that adheres to nirvāṇa as truly something to be attained, and the complete pacification of the conceptualization that grasps saṃsāra as truly something to be abandoned. The "non-abiding" in either extreme of existence or peace "arises from the power of cultivating" the path of the special training of "skillful means".

The uncommon training of skillful means. To explain the fourth, the uncommon training of skillful means: the meaning of the single verse spoken starting with "flying in the air..." is: "For example", for a "bird flying in the air", there is no place or basis upon which to be supported, so it does "not remain" in that "space", "yet" by the power of its two wings it "does not fall to the ground". "Like that", a "bodhisattva practices" or abides "at the doors of the three liberations"—"emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness"—yet due to skillful means he "does not touch" the extreme of "nirvāṇa"; and due to the wisdom that realizes the abiding nature, he "does not practice the path" of grasping at marks "in existence". That he does not abide in the two extremes "is by the power of skillful means."

translation: "Like" that "example", that "great being", a "bodhisattva practicing" the "supreme perfection of wisdom", during the time of training on the path of the Mahāyāna, possesses the wisdom that realizes emptiness and means such as "great compassion", aspirations, and complete dedication; and those of vast intellect who consider and completely investigate by means of the powers of faith and so forth and clairvoyances and "miraculous abilities", "as long as" the "roots of virtue" that culminate in the three—completion, ripening, and purification—are "not completed", for "that long" they "do not" manifest or attain that "supreme emptiness" or the "authentic limit in the meantime".

མི་གནས་པའི་ཐབས་མཁས་སྦྱོར་བ། གཉིས་པ་མི་གནས་པའི་ཐབས་མཁས་སྦྱོར་བ་འཆད་པར། མཁའ་ལ་རླུང་བརྟེན་ཞེས་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གཉིས་གསུངས། དེ་ཡང་འདི་ལྟར་འཇིག་རྟེན་ཆགས་པའི་ཚེ་ཐོག་མར་ནམ་མཁའ་ལ་རླུང་གི་དཀྱིལ་འཁོར་བརྟེན་ཏེ་ཆགས་ལ་རླུང་དེ་ལ་ཆུ་ཡི་ཕུང་པོ་བརྟེན་པ་དང་ཆུ་ལ་གསེར་གྱིས་གཞི་དང་དེ་ལ་ས་ཆེན་པོ་འདི་ལ་བརྟེན་ཅིང་ས་དེ་ལ་བཅུད་ཀྱི་འགྲོ་བ་གླིང་བཞི་གླིང་ཕྲན་བརྒྱད་སོགས་བརྟེན་ནས་གནས་པ་ཡིན་ཏེ། སེམས་ཅན་རྣམས་ཀྱི་སྤྱི་མཐུན་གྱི་ལས་བསགས་པའི་འབྲས་བུ་ལ་སྤྱོད་པའི་རྒྱུའམ་གཞི་ནི་དེ་འདྲ་ཡིན་པ་སྟེ་འབྱུང་བཞིའི་དཀྱིལ་འཁོར་གཞན་རྣམས་གཅིག་ལ་གཅིག་བརྟེན་གྱིས་གྲུབ་ཀྱང་ནམ་མཁའ་གཞན་གང་ལ་བརྟེན་ནས་གནས་པ་ཡིན་སྙམ་དུ་བརྟགས་ནས་དོན་འདི་བསམ་པར་གྱིས་ཤིག་དང་དེ་ནི་གཟུགས་ཅན་གྱི་དངོས་པོར་མ་གྲུབ་པས་གང་ལ་ཡང་མ་བརྟེན་པའི་ཚུལ་ཤེས་པར་འགྱུར་རོ། །ཚུལ་དེ་བཞིན་དུ་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ནམ་མཁའ་ལྟར་སྟོང་པ་ཉིད་ལ་རྩེ་གཅིག་ཏུ་གནས་པ་དེའི་ཚེ་ནའང་ཞི་བདེ་ལ་ཐུགས་མི་གཞོལ་བར་སྡུག་བསྔལ་གྱི་མནར་བའི་འགྲོ་བ་རྣམས་ལ་སེམས་ཅན་དུ་བདེན་པར་འདུ་ཤེས་པའི་དམིགས་པ་མེད་པའི་བརྩེ་བ་སྙིང་རྗེ་ཆེན་པོ་དང་སྔོན་གྱི་ཐུགས་བསྐྱེད་དང་སྨོན་ལམ་ཚད་མེད་པ་བརྙེས་པའི་རྟེན་ཅན་ཏེ་སྨོན་ལམ་གྱི་མཐུ་ལས་འགྲོ་བའི་ཕན་བདེ་ལེགས་ཚོགས་སྤེལ་བའི་བྱ་བ་རྣམ་པ་སྣ་ཚོགས་པ་དུ་མ་སྒྲུབ་པའི་སྤྲུལ་པའིབཀོད་པ་དཔག་ཏུ་མེད་པར་སྟོན་པར་བྱེད་ཅིང་། ཇིསྐད་བཤད་པའི་ཐབས་ལ་མཁས་པས་ཞི་བ་ཕྱོགས་གཅིག་པའི་མྱ་ངན་ལས་འདས་པ་ལ་མི་རེག་ལ་སྟོང་པ་ཉིད་ལ་བདེན་གྱིས་གནས་པའང་མེད་དོ། །ཅེས་པའོ། །
[3-227] translation already produced for this document:
The training of skillful means of non-abiding. To explain the second, the training of skillful means of non-abiding: two verses are spoken starting with "The wind supported by space..." It is like this: when the world is formed, first the maṇḍala of "wind" forms, "supported by space"; the mass of "water" is supported by that wind; the golden ground is supported by the water; this "great earth" is supported by that; and the beings of the essence, the four continents, the eight subcontinents, and so forth, remain supported by that earth. Such is the cause or basis for experiencing the result of the accumulation of the common karma of sentient beings. Having investigated, thinking, "Although the other maṇḍalas of the four elements are established in dependence on one another, upon what else is space supported and remaining?", you should reflect upon this meaning! And because it is not established as a physical entity, you will understand the manner in which it is not supported by anything at all. In "that manner", a "bodhisattva" who remains one-pointedly in "emptiness" "like space", even at that time, does not set his mind on the bliss of peace, but rather, having the support of objectless great love and compassion—without the apprehension of perceiving those who are tormented by suffering as truly existent sentient beings—and having attained immeasurable previous generation of the mind and aspirations, displays by the power of those "aspirations" immeasurable arrays of emanations that accomplish multiple "various" deeds that increase the excellent collections of the benefit and bliss of "beings". "By means of" the "skill in means" as explained, he does "not touch" the one-sided peace of "nirvāṇa", nor does he truly "abide in emptiness".

གཞན་དོན་སྨོན་ལམ་ཤུགས་ཀྱིས་འཕངས་པའི་ཐབས་མཁས་སྦྱོར་བ། གསུམ་པ་གཞན་དོན་སྨོན་ལམ་ཤུགས་ཀྱིས་འཕངས་པའི་ཐབས་མཁས་སྦྱོར་བ་འཆད་པར། གང་གི་ཚེ་ན་ཞེས་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གཅིག་གསུངས་པའི་དོན། ཐེག་པ་ཆེན་པོའི་ལམ་ལ་སློབ་པ་གང་གི་ཚེ་ན་འདི་ལྟར་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གནས་ལུགས་ཟབ་མོ་སྟོང་པ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་དོན་ལ་མཁས་ཤིང་། གདུལ་བྱ་གཞན་གྱི་རྨོངས་བའི་མུན་པ་བསལ་ནས་ཐེག་པ་ཆེན་པོའི་ལམ་བཟང་གསལ་བར་བྱེད་པ་རྣམས་ནི་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་རང་བཞིན་གྱིས་སྟོང་པ་མངོན་སུམ་དུ་རྟོགས་ནས་གཉིས་སྣང་གི་སྤྲོས་པ་མ་ལུས་པ་ཞི་བའི་དཔའ་བར་འགྲོ་བའི་ཏིང་ངེ་འཛིན་དམ་པ་འདི་ལ་མཉམ་པར་བཞག་པའི་སྒོ་ནས་སྤྱོད་པ་འདི་ནི་ལམ་སྒོམ་པའི་བར་སྐབས་དེར་ནི་ཀུན་རྫོབ་སྤྲོས་བཅས་ཀྱི་མཚན་མ་ཅུང་ཟད་ཙམ་ཡང་རབ་ཏུ་སྒོམ་པར་མི་བྱེད་དེ་དགག་བྱ་བདེན་གྲུབ་ཀྱི་མཚན་མ་མེད་པའི་དོན་ལ་གནས་ཤིང་མྱང་འདས་ལ་ཐོབ་བྱར་བདེན་པར་ཞེན་པའི་རྟོག་པ་ཞི་ལ་འཁོར་བ་ལ་སྤང་བྱར་བདེན་པར་འཛིན་པའི་རྟོག་པ་རབ་ཏུ་ཞི་བ་ལ་སྤྱོད་ཅིང་སྲིད་ཞི་གཉིས་ཀྱི་མཐའ་གང་ལ་ཡང་མི་གནས་པ་ནི་ཐབས་ལ་མཁས་པའི་སྦྱོར་བ་ཁྱད་པར་ཅན་གྱི་ལམ་སྒོམ་པའི་སྟོབས་ལས་བྱུང་བ་ཡིན་ནོ། །ཞེས་སོ། །
