The training of skillful means implicitly indicated by aspirations for the benefit of others. To explain the third, the training of skillful means implicitly indicated by aspirations for the benefit of others: the meaning of the single verse spoken starting with "Whenever..." is: "Whenever" they train on the path of the Mahāyāna, thus "bodhisattvas" who are skilled in the meaning of the profound abiding nature, emptiness, and "who", having dispelled the darkness of the ignorance of other disciples, "illuminate" the excellent path of the Mahāyāna, directly realize that all phenomena are empty by nature, and practice by way of resting evenly in "this" supreme "samādhi of the heroic stride" in which the elaborations of dualistic appearance are entirely "pacified". At the time of cultivating the path, they "do not cultivate" even the slightest mark of conventional elaborations; remaining in the meaning of the "signless" object of negation (truly existent marks), they practice the pacification of the conceptualization that adheres to nirvāṇa as truly something to be attained, and the complete pacification of the conceptualization that grasps saṃsāra as truly something to be abandoned. The "non-abiding" in either extreme of existence or peace "arises from the power of cultivating" the path of the special training of "skillful means".

[3-229] translation already produced for this document:
The uncommon training of skillful means. To explain the fourth, the uncommon training of skillful means: the meaning of the single verse spoken starting with "flying in the air..." is: "For example", for a "bird flying in the air", there is no place or basis upon which to be supported, so it does "not remain" in that "space", "yet" by the power of its two wings it "does not fall to the ground". "Like that", a "bodhisattva practices" or abides "at the doors of the three liberations"—"emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness"—yet due to skillful means he "does not touch" the extreme of "nirvāṇa"; and due to the wisdom that realizes the abiding nature, he "does not practice the path" of grasping at marks "in existence". That he does not abide in the two extremes "is by the power of skillful means."

heading: **མི་དམིགས་པའི་ཐབས་མཁས་སྦྱོར་བ།**
translation: The training of skillful means of non-apprehension. To explain the sixth, the training of skillful means of non-apprehension: the meaning of the two verses spoken starting with "For example, a monk..." "For example", a "monk" without afflictions, who possesses supreme powers of "miraculous abilities", remains in "space" and simultaneously manifests "various" arrays of miracles to tame beings, "displaying" multiple actions such as "walking, pacing, lying down, and sitting"; "yet" his mind has no weariness from those "various" behaviors, "nor does his body have" any "fatigue". "Like that example", a "bodhisattva" who is "skilled in means" remains in the door of liberation, "emptiness", and having "reached the far shore" of the "miraculous ability" of the primordial wisdom that knows the conventional and the ultimate, does not remain with true adherence to any object at all; "yet" he displays infinite types of deeds of benefit and bliss to "beings" in accordance with their respective fortunes, and although he exerts himself for the welfare of beings for "immeasurable millions of eons", there is no weariness in his mind "nor is there any exhaustion or fatigue of the body"; this is "by the power" of extraordinary means and wisdom.

It is like this: when the world is formed, first the maṇḍala of "wind" forms, "supported by space"; the mass of "water" is supported by that wind; the golden ground is supported by the water; this "great earth" is supported by that; and the beings of the essence, the four continents, the eight subcontinents, and so forth, remain supported by that earth. Such is the cause or basis for experiencing the result of the accumulation of the common karma of sentient beings. Having investigated, thinking, "Although the other maṇḍalas of the four elements are established in dependence on one another, upon what else is space supported and remaining?", you should reflect upon this meaning! And because it is not established as a physical entity, you will understand the manner in which it is not supported by anything at all. In "that manner", a "bodhisattva" who remains one-pointedly in "emptiness" "like space", even at that time, does not set his mind on the bliss of peace, but rather, having the support of objectless great love and compassion—without the apprehension of perceiving those who are tormented by suffering as truly existent sentient beings—and having attained immeasurable previous generation of the mind and aspirations, displays by the power of those "aspirations" immeasurable arrays of emanations that accomplish multiple "various" deeds that increase the excellent collections of the benefit and bliss of "beings". "By means of" the "skill in means" as explained, he does "not touch" the one-sided peace of "nirvāṇa", nor does he truly "abide in emptiness".

To explain the third, the training of skillful means implicitly indicated by aspirations for the benefit of others: the meaning of the single verse spoken starting with "Whenever..." is: "Whenever" they train on the path of the Mahāyāna, thus "bodhisattvas" who are skilled in the meaning of the profound abiding nature, emptiness, and "who", having dispelled the darkness of the ignorance of other disciples, "illuminate" the excellent path of the Mahāyāna, directly realize that all phenomena are empty by nature, and practice by way of resting evenly in "this" supreme "samādhi of the heroic stride" in which the elaborations of dualistic appearance are entirely "pacified". The "non-abiding" in either extreme of existence or peace "arises from the power of cultivating" the path of the special training of "skillful means".

"Like that", a "bodhisattva practices" or abides "at the doors of the three liberations"—"emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness"—yet due to skillful means he "does not touch" the extreme of "nirvāṇa"; and due to the wisdom that realizes the abiding nature, he "does not practice the path" of grasping at marks "in existence". That he does not abide in the two extremes "is by the power of skillful means."

translation: The training of skillful means of signlessness. The seventh, the training of skillful means of signlessness: the meaning explained by the two verses starting with "For example, some men..." "For example", if "some men" stand on the edge of a great abyss, holding two umbrellas in both hands, and jump into the space of the abyss, casting their bodies into the great abyss, by the power of the wind lifting those two umbrellas, they do not "fall to the ground" immediately, and not only are their bodies not injured, but they safely arrive in the meantime and go to wherever they wish. "Like that", a "bodhisattva" who is skilled in the meaning of the abiding nature and abides in love and compassion completely "holds the umbrellas" of the two—means and wisdom—and remains; by the power of wisdom, he realizes all phenomena as empty by nature, signless, and wishless; and by the power of special means, he "does not touch" the extreme of peace, nirvāṇa, and also "sees all" knowable "phenomena" as explained.

The training of skillful means of non-abiding. To explain the second, the training of skillful means of non-abiding: two verses are spoken starting with "The wind supported by space..." It is like this: when the world is formed, first the maṇḍala of "wind" forms, "supported by space"; the mass of "water" is supported by that wind; the golden ground is supported by the water; this "great earth" is supported by that; and the beings of the essence, the four continents, the eight subcontinents, and so forth, remain supported by that earth. Such is the cause or basis for experiencing the result of the accumulation of the common karma of sentient beings. Having investigated, thinking, "Although the other maṇḍalas of the four elements are established in dependence on one another, upon what else is space supported and remaining?", you should reflect upon this meaning! And because it is not established as a physical entity, you will understand the manner in which it is not supported by anything at all. In "that manner", a "bodhisattva" who remains one-pointedly in "emptiness" "like space", even at that time, does not set his mind on the bliss of peace, but rather, having the support of objectless great love and compassion—without the apprehension of perceiving those who are tormented by suffering as truly existent sentient beings—and having attained immeasurable previous generation of the mind and aspirations, displays by the power of those "aspirations" immeasurable arrays of emanations that accomplish multiple "various" deeds that increase the excellent collections of the benefit and bliss of "beings". "By means of" the "skill in means" as explained, he does "not touch" the one-sided peace of "nirvāṇa", nor does he truly "abide in emptiness".

The training of skillful means implicitly indicated by aspirations for the benefit of others. To explain the third, the training of skillful means implicitly indicated by aspirations for the benefit of others: the meaning of the single verse spoken starting with "Whenever..." is: "Whenever" they train on the path of the Mahāyāna, thus "bodhisattvas" who are skilled in the meaning of the profound abiding nature, emptiness, and "who", having dispelled the darkness of the ignorance of other disciples, "illuminate" the excellent path of the Mahāyāna, directly realize that all phenomena are empty by nature, and practice by way of resting evenly in "this" supreme "samādhi of the heroic stride" in which the elaborations of dualistic appearance are entirely "pacified". At the time of cultivating the path, they "do not cultivate" even the slightest mark of conventional elaborations; remaining in the meaning of the "signless" object of negation (truly existent marks), they practice the pacification of the conceptualization that adheres to nirvāṇa as truly something to be attained, and the complete pacification of the conceptualization that grasps saṃsāra as truly something to be abandoned. translation: The training of skillful means of wishlessness. Eighth, to explain the training of skillful means of wishlessness: two verses are spoken starting with "For example, a jewel..." Furthermore, "for example", a man of great strength and noble character, desiring jewels in order to make his relatives happy, goes to an island of jewels, and having arrived and found many jewels, when he returns to his own home again, it is not the case that the merchant himself alone lives happily with what he has found and gives nothing at all to his other relatives and friends, leaving them unhappy. "Like that example", a "bodhisattva" goes to the "island of jewels" of the primordial wisdom realizing profound emptiness, which is the source of all qualities, and when he attains immeasurable phenomena of qualities such as the joy and bliss of concentration, the five faculties such as faith, and the five powers, he does not delight in merely himself touching the nirvāṇa where all suffering without exception is pacified, and without accomplishing the benefit and bliss of other sentient beings, leave them as possessors of minds tormented by suffering; for by great compassion he establishes all beings in ripening and liberation.

translation: The training of skillful means of the mark of non-reversal. Ninth, to explain the training of skillful means of the mark of non-reversal: the meaning of the two verses spoken starting with "For example, seeking..." "For example", in order for "merchants seeking jewels" to know the conditions of the road and the value of goods for buying and selling, they travel to whatever "large cities", "towns, and villages" lie between their home country and the island of jewels, yet they do not stay there long; "nor do they remain permanently on the island of jewels"; having set out on the path, they know and understand the conditions of the path, and "without remaining in their own homes either", being skilled in how to travel the path and exerting themselves, they arrive at their desired destination.

To explain the sixth, the training of skillful means of non-apprehension: the meaning of the two verses spoken starting with "For example, a monk..." "For example", a "monk" without afflictions, who possesses supreme powers of "miraculous abilities", remains in "space" and simultaneously manifests "various" arrays of miracles to tame beings, "displaying" multiple actions such as "walking, pacing, lying down, and sitting"; "yet" his mind has no weariness from those "various" behaviors, "nor does his body have" any "fatigue". "Like that example", a "bodhisattva" who is "skilled in means" remains in the door of liberation, "emptiness", and having "reached the far shore" of the "miraculous ability" of the primordial wisdom that knows the conventional and the ultimate, does not remain with true adherence to any object at all; "yet" he displays infinite types of deeds of benefit and bliss to "beings" in accordance with their respective fortunes, and although he exerts himself for the welfare of beings for "immeasurable millions of eons", there is no weariness in his mind "nor is there any exhaustion or fatigue of the body"; this is "by the power" of extraordinary means and wisdom.

The training of skillful means of signlessness. The seventh, the training of skillful means of signlessness: the meaning explained by the two verses starting with "For example, some men..." "For example", if "some men" stand on the edge of a great abyss, holding two umbrellas in both hands, and jump into the space of the abyss, casting their bodies into the great abyss, by the power of the wind lifting those two umbrellas, they do not "fall to the ground" immediately, and not only are their bodies not injured, but they safely arrive in the meantime and go to wherever they wish. "Like that", a "bodhisattva" who is skilled in the meaning of the abiding nature and abides in love and compassion completely "holds the umbrellas" of the two—means and wisdom—and remains; by the power of wisdom, he realizes all phenomena as empty by nature, signless, and wishless; and by the power of special means, he "does not touch" the extreme of peace, nirvāṇa, and also "sees all" knowable "phenomena" as explained.

heading: **ཕྱིར་མ་ལྡོག་པའི་རྟགས་ཀྱི་ཐབས་མཁས་སྦྱོར་བ།**
translation: "Like that example", a "bodhisattva" who constantly exerts himself in accomplishing the welfare of others, who is clear-minded, that is, skilled in the path of means and wisdom, having accomplished the welfare of sentient beings to be tamed by them, does "not remain" himself in the path or fruit of the lower vehicles; nor does he remain in the "buddha's primordial wisdom", which is like the island of jewels, without having performed the three—completion, ripening, and purification; "nor does he remain" with true adherence in the unconditioned dharmadhātu, which is like one's own home, "yet" having understood the modes of the paths of the three vehicles, it should be known that he acts for the welfare of immeasurable sentient beings, such as the trainees of the three classes. Such is the mark of non-reversal, the uncommon distinguishing characteristic of a bodhisattva.

[3-229] translation already produced for this document:
The uncommon training of skillful means. To explain the fourth, the uncommon training of skillful means: the meaning of the single verse spoken starting with "flying in the air..." is: "For example", for a "bird flying in the air", there is no place or basis upon which to be supported, so it does "not remain" in that "space", "yet" by the power of its two wings it "does not fall to the ground". "Like that", a "bodhisattva practices" or abides "at the doors of the three liberations"—"emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness"—yet due to skillful means he "does not touch" the extreme of "nirvāṇa"; and due to the wisdom that realizes the abiding nature, he "does not practice the path" of grasping at marks "in existence". That he does not abide in the two extremes "is by the power of skillful means."

[3-231] translation already produced for this document:
The fifth, the training of skillful means of non-attachment: Although slightly different from Buddhaśrī, according to the system of the Master (Haribhadra), it is explained by two verses starting with "For example, trained in archery..." Furthermore, "for example", a man who has properly "trained" and become skilled in the "archery" of shooting arrows shoots an "arrow" into the sky together with a wooden board; and again, by shooting other arrows after that, attaching them completely in continuous succession behind each previous arrow, by being held by those shot unceasingly, that earlier arrow finds no opportunity to "fall to the ground". But when that man desires it to fall to the ground and does not shoot an arrow, that arrow will fall to the ground.

[3-233] translation already produced for this document:
The training of skillful means of non-apprehension. To explain the sixth, the training of skillful means of non-apprehension: the meaning of the two verses spoken starting with "For example, a monk..." "For example", a "monk" without afflictions, who possesses supreme powers of "miraculous abilities", remains in "space" and simultaneously manifests "various" arrays of miracles to tame beings, "displaying" multiple actions such as "walking, pacing, lying down, and sitting"; "yet" his mind has no weariness from those "various" behaviors, "nor does his body have" any "fatigue". "Like that example", a "bodhisattva" who is "skilled in means" remains in the door of liberation, "emptiness", and having "reached the far shore" of the "miraculous ability" of the primordial wisdom that knows the conventional and the ultimate, does not remain with true adherence to any object at all; "yet" he displays infinite types of deeds of benefit and bliss to "beings" in accordance with their respective fortunes, and although he exerts himself for the welfare of beings for "immeasurable millions of eons", there is no weariness in his mind "nor is there any exhaustion or fatigue of the body"; this is "by the power" of extraordinary means and wisdom.

"For example", if "some men" stand on the edge of a great abyss, holding two umbrellas in both hands, and jump into the space of the abyss, casting their bodies into the great abyss, by the power of the wind lifting those two umbrellas, they do not "fall to the ground" immediately, and not only are their bodies not injured, but they safely arrive in the meantime and go to wherever they wish. "Like that", a "bodhisattva" who is skilled in the meaning of the abiding nature and abides in love and compassion completely "holds the umbrellas" of the two—means and wisdom—and remains; by the power of wisdom, he realizes all phenomena as empty by nature, signless, and wishless; and by the power of special means, he "does not touch" the extreme of peace, nirvāṇa, and also "sees all" knowable "phenomena" as explained.

heading: **ཚད་མེད་པའི་ཐབས་མཁས་སྦྱོར་བ།**
translation: "For example", "the body of an emanated man" is not such that it does not appear to anyone; and although by its own essence "it is empty", it can "also be designated by a name", and in the world "there are also those who express its manner". "Like that", a "bodhisattva practicing" in the doors of the three liberations does not abide in the two extremes of existence or peace, "yet" he appears in the world and can "also be designated by a name".

The training of skillful means of signlessness. The seventh, the training of skillful means of signlessness: the meaning explained by the two verses starting with "For example, some men..." "For example", if "some men" stand on the edge of a great abyss, holding two umbrellas in both hands, and jump into the space of the abyss, casting their bodies into the great abyss, by the power of the wind lifting those two umbrellas, they do not "fall to the ground" immediately, and not only are their bodies not injured, but they safely arrive in the meantime and go to wherever they wish. "Like that", a "bodhisattva" who is skilled in the meaning of the abiding nature and abides in love and compassion completely "holds the umbrellas" of the two—means and wisdom—and remains; by the power of wisdom, he realizes all phenomena as empty by nature, signless, and wishless; and by the power of special means, he "does not touch" the extreme of peace, nirvāṇa, and also "sees all" knowable "phenomena" as explained.

heading: **ཚད་མེད་པའི་ཐབས་མཁས་སྦྱོར་བ།**
translation: Teaching the limitless skillful means by way of a summary: "If someone" completely "asks" a bodhisattva what the "deeds to be practiced by the sons of the victorious ones are like" "and" how the elements, intentions, and sharp or dull faculties, and so forth, of the trainees are, if the "bodhisattva" does "not know" the elements, inclinations, and so forth, of the trainees, and does "not completely teach" the profound dharmas of emptiness and signlessness to be taught, and does "not explain", meaning is unable to explain, "the dharmas", marks, aspects, and so forth "of the stage of non-reversal" by which one can ascertain that bodhisattva as non-reversing, "it should be known that" he has "not been prophesied" as non-reversing; whereas knowing those and being skilled in teaching the dharma appropriately to the minds of the trainees should be known as being one who has attained the mark of non-reversal. Having thus finished explaining the eleven phenomena that characterize the application of the complete realization of all aspects, the conclusion of the chapter: this is the commentary on the fourth chapter from The Fulfilling the Hopes of the Fortunate: A Jewel Lamp Illuminating the Suchness of Profound Dependent Arising, a Commentary on the Verses of the Precious Qualities Collection.

[3-235] translation already produced for this document:
The training of skillful means of wishlessness. Eighth, to explain the training of skillful means of wishlessness: two verses are spoken starting with "For example, a jewel..." Furthermore, "for example", a man of great strength and noble character, desiring jewels in order to make his relatives happy, goes to an island of jewels, and having arrived and found many jewels, when he returns to his own home again, it is not the case that the merchant himself alone lives happily with what he has found and gives nothing at all to his other relatives and friends, leaving them unhappy. "Like that example", a "bodhisattva" goes to the "island of jewels" of the primordial wisdom realizing profound emptiness, which is the source of all qualities, and when he attains immeasurable phenomena of qualities such as the joy and bliss of concentration, the five faculties such as faith, and the five powers, he does not delight in merely himself touching the nirvāṇa where all suffering without exception is pacified, and without accomplishing the benefit and bliss of other sentient beings, leave them as possessors of minds tormented by suffering; for by great compassion he establishes all beings in ripening and liberation.

[3-236] translation already produced for this document:
The training of skillful means of the mark of non-reversal. Ninth, to explain the training of skillful means of the mark of non-reversal: the meaning of the two verses spoken starting with "For example, seeking..." "For example", in order for "merchants seeking jewels" to know the conditions of the road and the value of goods for buying and selling, they travel to whatever "large cities", "towns, and villages" lie between their home country and the island of jewels, yet they do not stay there long; "nor do they remain permanently on the island of jewels"; having set out on the path, they know and understand the conditions of the path, and "without remaining in their own homes either", being skilled in how to travel the path and exerting themselves, they arrive at their desired destination.

[3-237] translation already produced for this document:
"Like that example", a "bodhisattva" who constantly exerts himself in accomplishing the welfare of others, who is clear-minded, that is, skilled in the path of means and wisdom, having accomplished the welfare of sentient beings to be tamed by them, does "not remain" himself in the path or fruit of the lower vehicles; nor does he remain in the "buddha's primordial wisdom", which is like the island of jewels, without having performed the three—completion, ripening, and purification; "nor does he remain" with true adherence in the unconditioned dharmadhātu, which is like one's own home, "yet" having understood the modes of the paths of the three vehicles, it should be known that he acts for the welfare of immeasurable sentient beings, such as the trainees of the three classes. Such is the mark of non-reversal, the uncommon distinguishing characteristic of a bodhisattva.

The training of skillful means of the immeasurables. Tenth, to explain the training of skillful means of the immeasurables: the meaning of the three verses spoken starting with "Whenever towards beings..." "Whenever" training in the deeds of a bodhisattva, having connected with all "beings", sentient beings, through generating great love that wishes them to meet with happiness, a "bodhisattva" who "practices" the "supreme concentration", the nature of being naturally empty, without the mark of the cause being truly established, and without the wish of the result being truly established, that he would attain the unconditioned expanse, nirvāṇa, for his own sake alone, or that he could be designated as one belonging to conditioned saṃsāra, is impossible. In order to clearly teach this very thing by way of an example:

"For example", "the body of an emanated man" is not such that it does not appear to anyone; and although by its own essence "it is empty", it can "also be designated by a name", and in the world "there are also those who express its manner". "Like that", a "bodhisattva practicing" in the doors of the three liberations does not abide in the two extremes of existence or peace, "yet" he appears in the world and can "also be designated by a name".

[3-235] translation already produced for this document:
The training of skillful means of wishlessness. Eighth, to explain the training of skillful means of wishlessness: two verses are spoken starting with "For example, a jewel..." Furthermore, "for example", a man of great strength and noble character, desiring jewels in order to make his relatives happy, goes to an island of jewels, and having arrived and found many jewels, when he returns to his own home again, it is not the case that the merchant himself alone lives happily with what he has found and gives nothing at all to his other relatives and friends, leaving them unhappy. "Like that example", a "bodhisattva" goes to the "island of jewels" of the primordial wisdom realizing profound emptiness, which is the source of all qualities, and when he attains immeasurable phenomena of qualities such as the joy and bliss of concentration, the five faculties such as faith, and the five powers, he does not delight in merely himself touching the nirvāṇa where all suffering without exception is pacified, and without accomplishing the benefit and bliss of other sentient beings, leave them as possessors of minds tormented by suffering; for by great compassion he establishes all beings in ripening and liberation.

The training of skillful means of the mark of non-reversal. Ninth, to explain the training of skillful means of the mark of non-reversal: the meaning of the two verses spoken starting with "For example, seeking..." "For example", in order for "merchants seeking jewels" to know the conditions of the road and the value of goods for buying and selling, they travel to whatever "large cities", "towns, and villages" lie between their home country and the island of jewels, yet they do not stay there long; "nor do they remain permanently on the island of jewels"; having set out on the path, they know and understand the conditions of the path, and "without remaining in their own homes either", being skilled in how to travel the path and exerting themselves, they arrive at their desired destination.

[3-237] translation already produced for this document:
"Like that example", a "bodhisattva" who constantly exerts himself in accomplishing the welfare of others, who is clear-minded, that is, skilled in the path of means and wisdom, having accomplished the welfare of sentient beings to be tamed by them, does "not remain" himself in the path or fruit of the lower vehicles; nor does he remain in the "buddha's primordial wisdom", which is like the island of jewels, without having performed the three—completion, ripening, and purification; "nor does he remain" with true adherence in the unconditioned dharmadhātu, which is like one's own home, "yet" having understood the modes of the paths of the three vehicles, it should be known that he acts for the welfare of immeasurable sentient beings, such as the trainees of the three classes. Such is the mark of non-reversal, the uncommon distinguishing characteristic of a bodhisattva.

The training of skillful means of the immeasurables. Tenth, to explain the training of skillful means of the immeasurables: the meaning of the three verses spoken starting with "Whenever towards beings..." "Whenever" training in the deeds of a bodhisattva, having connected with all "beings", sentient beings, through generating great love that wishes them to meet with happiness, a "bodhisattva" who "practices" the "supreme concentration", the nature of being naturally empty, without the mark of the cause being truly established, and without the wish of the result being truly established, that he would attain the unconditioned expanse, nirvāṇa, for his own sake alone, or that he could be designated as one belonging to conditioned saṃsāra, is impossible. In order to clearly teach this very thing by way of an example:

translation: The result, the peak application. Second, to explain the result to be mastered, the peak application: it is stated in the Ornament of Clear Realization (Abhisamayālaṃkāra), "The realization of that and the increase of aspects..." up to "...the clear realization at the peak." That yoga of a bodhisattva held by wisdom that has become superior to the Mahāyāna path of accumulation in summarizing and cultivating the three kinds of exalted knowledge is the definition of the peak application. That and the achievement of engagement are synonymous. There are eight phenomena that characterize the peak application: because there are the four peak applications of the four paths of preparation (heat and so forth), the peak application of the path of seeing, the peak application of the path of meditation, the uninterrupted peak application, and the mistaken achievement to be cleared away, making eight. Its boundaries are from the heat of the Mahāyāna path of preparation up to the end of the continuum.

The training of skillful means of wishlessness. Eighth, to explain the training of skillful means of wishlessness: two verses are spoken starting with "For example, a jewel..." Furthermore, "for example", a man of great strength and noble character, desiring jewels in order to make his relatives happy, goes to an island of jewels, and having arrived and found many jewels, when he returns to his own home again, it is not the case that the merchant himself alone lives happily with what he has found and gives nothing at all to his other relatives and friends, leaving them unhappy. "Like that example", a "bodhisattva" goes to the "island of jewels" of the primordial wisdom realizing profound emptiness, which is the source of all qualities, and when he attains immeasurable phenomena of qualities such as the joy and bliss of concentration, the five faculties such as faith, and the five powers, he does not delight in merely himself touching the nirvāṇa where all suffering without exception is pacified, and without accomplishing the benefit and bliss of other sentient beings, leave them as possessors of minds tormented by suffering; for by great compassion he establishes all beings in ripening and liberation.

source: དྲོད་རྩེ་སྦྱོར།དེ་རྣམས་ཀྱི་ནང་ནས་དང་པོ་དྲོད་རྩེ་སྦྱོར་འཆད་པ། མངོན་རྟོགས་རྒྱན་ལས། རྨི་ལམ་ན་ཡང་ཆོས་རྣམས་ཀུན། ནས། རྣམ་པ་བཅུ་གཉིས་ངག་ཏུ་བཞེད། །ཅེས་གསུངས། འདི་ལ་མཚན་ཉིད། དབྱེ་བ། ས་མཚམས་གསུམ་ལས། དང་པོ་ནི། རྩེ་སྦྱོར་ཐོབ་པའི་རྟགས་བཅུ་གཉིས་པོ་གང་རུང་ཐོབ་པའི་ཐེག་ཆེན་གྱི་ངེས་འབྱེད་ཆ་མཐུན་དང་པོ་དེ། དྲོད་རྩེ་སྦྱོར་གྱི་མཚན་ཉིད། གཉིས་པ་དེ་ལ་དབྱེ་ན། དྲོད་ཆུང་འབྲིང་ཆེ་གསུམ་ཡོད། གསུམ་པ་ས་མཚམས་ཐེག་ཆེན་གྱི་སྦྱོར་ལམ་དྲོད་ཁོ་ནར་ཡོད། རྨི་ལམ་ན་ཡང་འཁོར་བ་ལ་ཡིད་འབྱུང་ཞིང་ཆོས་རྣམས་རྨི་ལམ་ལྟ་བུར་བལྟ་བ་དང་། བདེན་ཚིག་གིས་འགྲོ་བའི་ཉེར་འཚེ་ཞི་བ་སོགས་རྟགས་བཅུ་གཉིས་ཀྱིས་མཚོན་པའི་དྲོད་རྩེ་སྦྱོར་འཆད་པ་ལ་རྟགས་དང་པོ་བརྒྱད་འཆད་པ་དང༌། འཕྲོས་དོན་གཉིས་ལས།
translation: The peak application of heat. To explain the first among those, the peak application of heat: it is stated in the Ornament of Clear Realization, "Even in dreams, all phenomena..." up to "...twelve aspects are asserted in speech." Here, concerning the three: definition, divisions, and boundaries; first, the definition of the peak application of heat is: the first Mahāyāna aid to penetration that has attained any of the twelve marks of attaining the peak application. Second, if divided, there are three: small, medium, and great heat. Third, its boundaries: it exists only on the Mahāyāna path of preparation of heat. To explain the peak application of heat, which is characterized by the twelve marks, such as experiencing revulsion towards saṃsāra and viewing phenomena as like a dream "even in dreams," and pacifying the afflictions of beings by words of truth and so forth, there are two parts: explaining the first eight marks, and related topics.

[3-235] translation already produced for this document:
The training of skillful means of wishlessness. Eighth, to explain the training of skillful means of wishlessness: two verses are spoken starting with "For example, a jewel..." Furthermore, "for example", a man of great strength and noble character, desiring jewels in order to make his relatives happy, goes to an island of jewels, and having arrived and found many jewels, when he returns to his own home again, it is not the case that the merchant himself alone lives happily with what he has found and gives nothing at all to his other relatives and friends, leaving them unhappy. "Like that example", a "bodhisattva" goes to the "island of jewels" of the primordial wisdom realizing profound emptiness, which is the source of all qualities, and when he attains immeasurable phenomena of qualities such as the joy and bliss of concentration, the five faculties such as faith, and the five powers, he does not delight in merely himself touching the nirvāṇa where all suffering without exception is pacified, and without accomplishing the benefit and bliss of other sentient beings, leave them as possessors of minds tormented by suffering; for by great compassion he establishes all beings in ripening and liberation.

The training of skillful means of the mark of non-reversal. Ninth, to explain the training of skillful means of the mark of non-reversal: the meaning of the two verses spoken starting with "For example, seeking..." "For example", in order for "merchants seeking jewels" to know the conditions of the road and the value of goods for buying and selling, they travel to whatever "large cities", "towns, and villages" lie between their home country and the island of jewels, yet they do not stay there long; "nor do they remain permanently on the island of jewels"; having set out on the path, they know and understand the conditions of the path, and "without remaining in their own homes either", being skilled in how to travel the path and exerting themselves, they arrive at their desired destination.

[3-237] translation already produced for this document:
"Like that example", a "bodhisattva" who constantly exerts himself in accomplishing the welfare of others, who is clear-minded, that is, skilled in the path of means and wisdom, having accomplished the welfare of sentient beings to be tamed by them, does "not remain" himself in the path or fruit of the lower vehicles; nor does he remain in the "buddha's primordial wisdom", which is like the island of jewels, without having performed the three—completion, ripening, and purification; "nor does he remain" with true adherence in the unconditioned dharmadhātu, which is like one's own home, "yet" having understood the modes of the paths of the three vehicles, it should be known that he acts for the welfare of immeasurable sentient beings, such as the trainees of the three classes. Such is the mark of non-reversal, the uncommon distinguishing characteristic of a bodhisattva.

The training of skillful means of the immeasurables. Tenth, to explain the training of skillful means of the immeasurables: the meaning of the three verses spoken starting with "Whenever towards beings..." "Whenever" training in the deeds of a bodhisattva, having connected with all "beings", sentient beings, through generating great love that wishes them to meet with happiness, a "bodhisattva" who "practices" the "supreme concentration", the nature of being naturally empty, without the mark of the cause being truly established, and without the wish of the result being truly established, that he would attain the unconditioned expanse, nirvāṇa, for his own sake alone, or that he could be designated as one belonging to conditioned saṃsāra, is impossible. In order to clearly teach this very thing by way of an example:

"For example", "the body of an emanated man" is not such that it does not appear to anyone; and although by its own essence "it is empty", it can "also be designated by a name", and in the world "there are also those who express its manner". "Like that", a "bodhisattva practicing" in the doors of the three liberations does not abide in the two extremes of existence or peace, "yet" he appears in the world and can "also be designated by a name".

heading: **རྟགས་ཀྱི་རབ་ཏུ་དབྱེ་བ།**
translation: The thorough division of marks. First: the meaning taught by the three verses starting with "The arhats and..." By the power of having become accustomed to the Mahāyāna path of the unity of means and wisdom for a long time, let alone in actuality, "even in dreams he does not desire" the stage of a śrāvaka "arhat and" the "pratyekabuddha", that is, the primordial wisdom of a solitary realizer of the lower vehicles, nor the qualities and happiness of saṃsāra in the three realms. And seeing "in dreams" and so forth "buddhas" surrounded by an ocean of retinues, whichever bodhisattva sees those buddhas "also teaching the dharma to beings", "it should be known that" this is the "mark of having been prophesied by the buddhas" as not reversing to the lower paths away from the Mahāyāna enlightenment, or of having attained the peak application. Thus, the first two lines teach the realization of means, and the next two lines teach the mark of seeing buddhas and the second mark of them teaching.

The training of skillful means of wishlessness. Eighth, to explain the training of skillful means of wishlessness: two verses are spoken starting with "For example, a jewel..." Furthermore, "for example", a man of great strength and noble character, desiring jewels in order to make his relatives happy, goes to an island of jewels, and having arrived and found many jewels, when he returns to his own home again, it is not the case that the merchant himself alone lives happily with what he has found and gives nothing at all to his other relatives and friends, leaving them unhappy. "Like that example", a "bodhisattva" goes to the "island of jewels" of the primordial wisdom realizing profound emptiness, which is the source of all qualities, and when he attains immeasurable phenomena of qualities such as the joy and bliss of concentration, the five faculties such as faith, and the five powers, he does not delight in merely himself touching the nirvāṇa where all suffering without exception is pacified, and without accomplishing the benefit and bliss of other sentient beings, leave them as possessors of minds tormented by suffering; for by great compassion he establishes all beings in ripening and liberation.

The training of skillful means of the mark of non-reversal. Ninth, to explain the training of skillful means of the mark of non-reversal: the meaning of the two verses spoken starting with "For example, seeking..." "For example", in order for "merchants seeking jewels" to know the conditions of the road and the value of goods for buying and selling, they travel to whatever "large cities", "towns, and villages" lie between their home country and the island of jewels, yet they do not stay there long; "nor do they remain permanently on the island of jewels"; having set out on the path, they know and understand the conditions of the path, and "without remaining in their own homes either", being skilled in how to travel the path and exerting themselves, they arrive at their desired destination.

[3-237] translation already produced for this document:
"Like that example", a "bodhisattva" who constantly exerts himself in accomplishing the welfare of others, who is clear-minded, that is, skilled in the path of means and wisdom, having accomplished the welfare of sentient beings to be tamed by them, does "not remain" himself in the path or fruit of the lower vehicles; nor does he remain in the "buddha's primordial wisdom", which is like the island of jewels, without having performed the three—completion, ripening, and purification; "nor does he remain" with true adherence in the unconditioned dharmadhātu, which is like one's own home, "yet" having understood the modes of the paths of the three vehicles, it should be known that he acts for the welfare of immeasurable sentient beings, such as the trainees of the three classes. Such is the mark of non-reversal, the uncommon distinguishing characteristic of a bodhisattva.

[3-238] translation already produced for this document:
The training of skillful means of the immeasurables. Tenth, to explain the training of skillful means of the immeasurables: the meaning of the three verses spoken starting with "Whenever towards beings..." "Whenever" training in the deeds of a bodhisattva, having connected with all "beings", sentient beings, through generating great love that wishes them to meet with happiness, a "bodhisattva" who "practices" the "supreme concentration", the nature of being naturally empty, without the mark of the cause being truly established, and without the wish of the result being truly established, that he would attain the unconditioned expanse, nirvāṇa, for his own sake alone, or that he could be designated as one belonging to conditioned saṃsāra, is impossible. translation: Furthermore, when that bodhisattva sees many sentient beings abiding in the three lower realms "in dreams," out of compassion, in "that instant" he makes aspirations "to cut off the continuation" of the lower realms, and by its power he sees their sufferings pacified; "and" also, when awake, if he sees a town and so forth burning with fire, and without fear he says, "If it is true that I have been prophesied as non-reversing, by this truth and words of truth may this fire be pacified!" and thus by the blessing of expressing the power of truth the ability to "pacify the mass of fire" is accomplished, "it should be known that" he is one who has been "prophesied by the victorious ones of the past" as non-reversing from complete enlightenment. This verse teaches the two marks of abandoning the lower realms and of pacifying fire and so forth by truth. "Likewise, in the human realm," when one sees sentient beings harmed by "the demons of spirits" and tormented by "many different kinds of diseases," that bodhisattva endowed with love who wishes to permanently benefit and temporarily save them from suffering, by the blessing of pronouncing words of truth and so forth, "those will be pacified"; "yet" he does "not become conceited" by that ability, thinking "My power is extremely great," and does "not generate pride" holding himself supreme; "it should be known that" this is a mark of having been prophesied as non-reversing or of having attained the peak application. This teaches the mark of the peak application of pacifying the demons of spirits and so forth merely by uttering words of truth. When the first eight marks are explained in the Eight Thousand Stanza Perfection of Wisdom: it is taught extensively from, "Subhūti, if a bodhisattva, a great being, even in dreams perfectly views all phenomena as like a dream and does not actualize them, Subhūti, this too is of a non-reversing great bodhisattva," up to "...the twentieth chapter, on skillful means." The commentary on the twentieth chapter, on skillful means, from The Fulfilling the Hopes of the Fortunate: A Jewel Lamp Illuminating the Suchness of Profound Dependent Arising, a Commentary on the Verses of the Precious Qualities Collection.

heading: **འཕྲོས་དོན།**
translation: Teaching the actions of Māra that arise from a basis of names. The demon of generating conceit and pride arises from a basis of names as well. Thus, if "sinful Māra approaches before" that bodhisattva in the guise of a buddha, a fully ordained monk, and so forth, he will say this: "Such are 'your and your parents' names', and the names 'up through the lineage of your ancestors for seven generations' are this," thus speaking their names; and in accordance with what he previously thought in his mind, he says, "Whenever you 'become a buddha, your name will be this'." And he clearly states just how that person will currently possess qualities such as the ascetic qualities of being an "alms-beggar" and one who wears "rags from a dust heap" and so forth, possessing the vows of a novice or fully ordained monk, and possessing the yoga of calm abiding and special insight; and he says, "'Also in your former times,' the manner of your qualities, such as ascetic qualities, was 'similar to this' present one." Having heard those words spoken at that time, "whichever bodhisattva" generates overt "pride" and "conceit" based on that basis or cause of merely naming the expression of his own qualities, "it should be known that" his "conceit" has been thoroughly "incited by Māra" and he has a "small mind" or is inferior.

heading: **འཕྲོས་དོན།**
translation: How Māra enters even when one is practicing isolation. In general, there are two kinds of isolation: outer isolation from crowds, and inner isolation from distraction. Among these, for a bodhisattva, the primary isolation is to be isolated from inferior mental engagements that distract one from the Mahāyāna; therefore, without that, even if one fully relies upon and abides in places "thoroughly isolated" from crowds—such as a "wilderness" situated far from "villages and great cities," "mountain valleys," and "forests" isolated from the coming and going and clamour of people—a bodhisattva who generates conceit, thinking, "'I abide in isolation highly praised by the Sugata'," and praises himself while "despising other bodhisattvas who abide in villages," "it should be known that" his mental continuum has been completely corrupted or generated "by Māra," and he has a "small mind" and is not good.

The thorough division of marks. First: the meaning taught by the three verses starting with "The arhats and..." By the power of having become accustomed to the Mahāyāna path of the unity of means and wisdom for a long time, let alone in actuality, "even in dreams he does not desire" the stage of a śrāvaka "arhat and" the "pratyekabuddha", that is, the primordial wisdom of a solitary realizer of the lower vehicles, nor the qualities and happiness of saṃsāra in the three realms. And seeing "in dreams" and so forth "buddhas" surrounded by an ocean of retinues, whichever bodhisattva sees those buddhas "also teaching the dharma to beings", "it should be known that" this is the "mark of having been prophesied by the buddhas" as not reversing to the lower paths away from the Mahāyāna enlightenment, or of having attained the peak application. Thus, the first two lines teach the realization of means, and the next two lines teach the mark of seeing buddhas and the second mark of them teaching.

གཞན་ཡང་བྱང་སེམས་དེས་རྨི་ལམན་ནི་སེམས་ཅན་མང་པོ་ངན་སོང་གསུམ་དུ་གནས་པ་མཐོང་ནས་སྙིང་བརྩེ་བས་སྐད་ཅིག་དེ་ལ་ངན་སོང་རྣམས་རྒྱུན་གཅོད་པའི་སྨོན་ལམ་འདེབས་པར་བྱེད་ཅིང་དེས་སྟོབས་ཀྱི་སྡུག་བསྔལ་རྣམས་ཞི་བར་མཐོང་བ་དང་། ཡང་རྨི་ལམ་སད་པའི་གནས་སྐབས་ན་གྲོང་སོགས་མེས་ཚིག་པ་མཐོང་ན་སྐྲག་པ་མེད་པར་བདག་ཕྱིར་མི་ལྡོག་པ་ལུང་བསྟན་པ་ཡིན་ན་བདེན་པ་དང་བདེན་པའི་ཚིགས་འདིས་མེ་འདི་ཞི་བར་གྱུར་ཅིག་ཅེས་པ་ལྟ་བུའི་བདེན་པའི་སྟོབས་བརྗོད་པའི་བྱིན་གྱི་རླབས་ཀྱིས་མེ་ཡི་ཕུང་པོ་ཞི་བའི་མཐུ་གྲུབ་པདེ་ནི་སྔོན་གྱི་རྒྱལ་བ་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་རྫོགས་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་ལས་ཕྱིར་མི་ལྡོག་པར་ལུང་བསྟན་པ་ཡིན་པར་རིག་པར་བྱའོ། །ཚིགས་བཅད་འདིས་ངན་སོང་སྤོང་བའི་དེ་དང་། བདེན་པས་མེ་སོགས་ཞི་བར་བྱེད་པའི་རྟགས་གཉིས་བསྟན། དེ་བཞིནདུ་མི་ཡི་འཇིག་རྟེན་གྱི་ཁམས་ན་སེམས་ཅན་རྣམས་འབྱུང་པོའི་གདོན་གྱིས་གནོད་པ་དང་ནད་ཀྱི་རིགས་མི་འདྲ་བ་མང་པོས་མནར་བ་མཐོང་བ་ན། གཏན་དུ་ཕན་པ་དང་གནས་སྐབས་སྡུག་བསྔལ་ལས་བསྐྱབ་པར་འདོད་པའི་སྙིང་རྩེར་ལྡན་པའི་བྱང་སེམས་དེ་ཡིས་བདེན་པའི་ཚིག་བརྗོད་པ་སོགས་ཀྱི་བྱིན་རླབས་ཀྱིས་དེ་དག་ཞི་བར་འགྱུར་ལ། འོན་ཀྱང་བདག་ནི་ནུས་མཐུ་ཤིན་ཏུ་ཆེའོ་སྙམ་དུ་ནུས་པ་དེས་རློམ་སེམས་སུ་གྱུར་པ་མེད་ཅིང་རང་ཉིད་མཆོག་ཏུ་འཛིན་པའི་ང་རྒྱལ་སྐྱེ་བ་མེད་པ་དེ་ནི་ཕྱིར་མི་ལྡོག་པར་ལུང་བསྟན་པའམ་རྩེ་སྦྱོར་ཐོབ་པའི་རྟགས་ཡིན་པར་རིགས་པར་བྱའོ། །འདིས་འབྱུང་པོའི་གདོན་སོགས་བདེན་ཚིག་བརྗོད་པ་ཙམ་གྱིས་ཞི་བར་བྱེད་པའི་རྩེ་སྦྱོར་གྱི་རྟགས་བསྟན་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །རྟགས་དང་པོ་བརྒྱད་བརྒྱད་སྟོང་པར་འཆད་པའི་ཚེ། རབ་འབྱོར་གལ་ཏེ་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཆེན་པོ་རྨི་ལམ་ན་ཡང་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་རྨི་ལམ་ལྟར་ཡང་དག་པར་ལྟ་ཞིང་མངོན་དུའང་མི་བྱེད་ན། རབ་འབྱོར་འདི་ཡང་ཕྱིར་མི་ལྡོག་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཆེན་པོའི་ཞེས་པ་ནས་ཐབས་ལ་མཁས་པའི་ལེའུ་སྟེ་ཉི་ཤུ་པའོ། །ཞེས་པའི་བར་གྱིས་རྒྱས་པར་བསྟན་ཏོ། །ཡོན་ཏན་རིན་པོ་ཆེ་སྡུད་པ་ཚིགས་སུ་བཅད་པའི་འགྲེལ་བ་ཟབ་མོ་རྟེན་འབྱུང་གི་དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཉིད་གསལ་བར་བྱེད་པའི་ནོར་བུའི་སྒྲོན་མེ་སྐལ་བཟང་རེ་སྐོང་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལས། ཐབས་ལ་མཁས་པའི་ལེའུ་སྟེ་ཉི་ཤུ་པའི་འགྲེལ་པའོ།།   །།

Furthermore, when that bodhisattva sees many sentient beings abiding in the three lower realms "in dreams," out of compassion, in "that instant" he makes aspirations "to cut off the continuation" of the lower realms, and by its power he sees their sufferings pacified; "and" also, when awake, if he sees a town and so forth burning with fire, and without fear he says, "If it is true that I have been prophesied as non-reversing, by this truth and words of truth may this fire be pacified!" and thus by the blessing of expressing the power of truth the ability to "pacify the mass of fire" is accomplished, "it should be known that" he is one who has been "prophesied by the victorious ones of the past" as non-reversing from complete enlightenment. This verse teaches the two marks of abandoning the lower realms and of pacifying fire and so forth by truth. "Likewise, in the human realm," when one sees sentient beings harmed by "the demons of spirits" and tormented by "many different kinds of diseases," that bodhisattva endowed with love who wishes to permanently benefit and temporarily save them from suffering, by the blessing of pronouncing words of truth and so forth, "those will be pacified"; "yet" he does "not become conceited" by that ability, thinking "My power is extremely great," and does "not generate pride" holding himself supreme; "it should be known that" this is a mark of having been prophesied as non-reversing or of having attained the peak application. This teaches the mark of the peak application of pacifying the demons of spirits and so forth merely by uttering words of truth. When the first eight marks are explained in the Eight Thousand Stanza Perfection of Wisdom: it is taught extensively from, "Subhūti, if a bodhisattva, a great being, even in dreams perfectly views all phenomena as like a dream and does not actualize them, Subhūti, this too is of a non-reversing great bodhisattva," up to "...the twentieth chapter, on skillful means." heading: **འཕྲོས་དོན།**
translation: Teaching the specific identification of a bodhisattva's isolation, the example of its pointlessness if it does not occur, and how it is unsuitable to despise based on appearances if it does occur. If one "always" abides in "villages" such as Videha and so forth, "countries" such as Campaka and so forth, and "cities" such as Pāṭaliputra and so forth, and even while abiding there, apart from striving to ripen the unripened disciples among sentient beings, to liberate those who are ripened, and to accomplish unsurpassed awakening, that bodhisattva "never," i.e., at no time, "generates the desire for" a śrāvaka arhat and "pratyekabuddha"; this is taught to be "the genuine isolation of the bodhisattvas," the "sons of the Sugatas." If one's own mind is isolated from inferior vehicle mental engagements, no matter where one abides, such as in towns or villages, one abides in supreme isolation. Not abiding in such isolation, "whichever bodhisattva" abides in a place extending for "five hundred yojanas," a "mountain valley thoroughly isolated" from the bustling of people, "wherever" it is, a place unpopulated by humans and filled with poisonous snakes and so forth, "even for many tens of millions of years," that bodhisattva "who does not know this" inner isolation generates, i.e., "acquires, overweening pride," thinking, "My abiding in isolation is supreme!" and abides similarly to inferior vehicle mental engagement; that is not abiding in the isolation of a bodhisattva, because it is corrupted by inferior mental engagement. Under the influence of such pride, towards "other bodhisattvas" who strive for the welfare of transmigrators and who, having attained the "four dhyānas," the "five powers," the "five faculties" such as faith, the "three doors of liberation," the "heroic stride samādhi," and so forth, roam in villages and cities for the sake of others, establishing sentient beings in ripening and liberation, not knowing their intent and conduct, one who "despises" them, thinking, "This one is not practicing in wilderness and isolation," is "the object of Māra's activity," that is, they have come to abide in an object where Māra has found an opportunity; so "the Victors have taught."

Teaching the actions of Māra that arise from a basis of names. The demon of generating conceit and pride arises from a basis of names as well. Thus, if "sinful Māra approaches before" that bodhisattva in the guise of a buddha, a fully ordained monk, and so forth, he will say this: "Such are 'your and your parents' names', and the names 'up through the lineage of your ancestors for seven generations' are this," thus speaking their names; and in accordance with what he previously thought in his mind, he says, "Whenever you 'become a buddha, your name will be this'." And he clearly states just how that person will currently possess qualities such as the ascetic qualities of being an "alms-beggar" and one who wears "rags from a dust heap" and so forth, possessing the vows of a novice or fully ordained monk, and possessing the yoga of calm abiding and special insight; and he says, "'Also in your former times,' the manner of your qualities, such as ascetic qualities, was 'similar to this' present one." Having heard those words spoken at that time, "whichever bodhisattva" generates overt "pride" and "conceit" based on that basis or cause of merely naming the expression of his own qualities, "it should be known that" his "conceit" has been thoroughly "incited by Māra" and he has a "small mind" or is inferior.

How Māra enters even when one is practicing isolation. In general, there are two kinds of isolation: outer isolation from crowds, and inner isolation from distraction. Among these, for a bodhisattva, the primary isolation is to be isolated from inferior mental engagements that distract one from the Mahāyāna; therefore, without that, even if one fully relies upon and abides in places "thoroughly isolated" from crowds—such as a "wilderness" situated far from "villages and great cities," "mountain valleys," and "forests" isolated from the coming and going and clamour of people—a bodhisattva who generates conceit, thinking, "'I abide in isolation highly praised by the Sugata'," and praises himself while "despising other bodhisattvas who abide in villages," "it should be known that" his mental continuum has been completely corrupted or generated "by Māra," and he has a "small mind" and is not good.

heading: **འཕྲོས་དོན།**
translation: Well then, if abiding alone is not isolation, what is isolation? "Whichever bodhisattva," whether his body abides in a "village or else in a wilderness," if his mind is free from the thought desiring to attain either of the two vehicles of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and becomes singularly ascertained in the path of supreme awakening, this manner is the completely pure isolation of bodhisattvas who have engaged in the welfare of transmigrators. Not knowing this, one such as the previous bodhisattva who assesses the measure, i.e., "gauges the level," of that bodhisattva who abides in such isolation, and appraises them, thinking, "This one is not abiding in isolation," will themselves degenerate from the qualities of the grounds and paths. Therefore, the Capable One, the Buddha Bhagavat, has stated: "Apart from those like me, individuals should not assess the measure of individuals, lest they degenerate," and "A bodhisattva should examine their own continuum but should not look for faults in others." Having understood according to what is taught in the sūtras, generating the perception of all sentient beings as the Teacher and paying respect is the primary training for bodhisattvas. This is the commentary on the twenty-first chapter, the Chapter on Māra, from the Commentary on the Verse Summary of the Perfection of Wisdom, entitled A Jeweled Lamp Fulfilling the Hopes of the Fortunate, Illuminating the Suchness of Profound Dependent Arising.

Teaching the actions of Māra that arise from a basis of names. The demon of generating conceit and pride arises from a basis of names as well. Thus, if "sinful Māra approaches before" that bodhisattva in the guise of a buddha, a fully ordained monk, and so forth, he will say this: "Such are 'your and your parents' names', and the names 'up through the lineage of your ancestors for seven generations' are this," thus speaking their names; and in accordance with what he previously thought in his mind, he says, "Whenever you 'become a buddha, your name will be this'." And he clearly states just how that person will currently possess qualities such as the ascetic qualities of being an "alms-beggar" and one who wears "rags from a dust heap" and so forth, possessing the vows of a novice or fully ordained monk, and possessing the yoga of calm abiding and special insight; and he says, "'Also in your former times,' the manner of your qualities, such as ascetic qualities, was 'similar to this' present one." Having heard those words spoken at that time, "whichever bodhisattva" generates overt "pride" and "conceit" based on that basis or cause of merely naming the expression of his own qualities, "it should be known that" his "conceit" has been thoroughly "incited by Māra" and he has a "small mind" or is inferior.

How Māra enters even when one is practicing isolation. In general, there are two kinds of isolation: outer isolation from crowds, and inner isolation from distraction. Among these, for a bodhisattva, the primary isolation is to be isolated from inferior mental engagements that distract one from the Mahāyāna; therefore, without that, even if one fully relies upon and abides in places "thoroughly isolated" from crowds—such as a "wilderness" situated far from "villages and great cities," "mountain valleys," and "forests" isolated from the coming and going and clamour of people—a bodhisattva who generates conceit, thinking, "'I abide in isolation highly praised by the Sugata'," and praises himself while "despising other bodhisattvas who abide in villages," "it should be known that" his mental continuum has been completely corrupted or generated "by Māra," and he has a "small mind" and is not good.

heading: **འཕྲོས་དོན།**
translation: Second, since the non-occurrence of such things also depends upon relying on a spiritual friend, the meaning of what is stated in two verses starting with "Therefore" and so forth, in order to advise the necessity of relying on a spiritual friend and to explain the signs of an irreversible one who is like that: Because many deeds of Māra occur that cause hindrances when practicing the path of the Mahāyāna, "therefore," having understood that, one must turn them back, and so one should rely on outer and inner tutors. Moreover, the one who relies has a strong intention "seeking" "supreme awakening"—unsurpassed awakening—for the sake of others, and is skilled in the means to accomplish it; as for the manner in which to rely, by "definitely destroying" "pride" that holds oneself as supreme and so forth, for example, just as "in the world" "a host of sick people" "rely upon" another, "a skilled physician," "to cure their illness," one should properly rely upon a qualified spiritual friend, unfalteringly through both intention and application, by relying on the perceptions of oneself as a sick person, the Dharma speaker as a physician, the Dharma as medicine, earnest practice as curing the illness, the Tathāgata as a supreme being, and the Dharma system as remaining for a long time.

Teaching the specific identification of a bodhisattva's isolation, the example of its pointlessness if it does not occur, and how it is unsuitable to despise based on appearances if it does occur. If one "always" abides in "villages" such as Videha and so forth, "countries" such as Campaka and so forth, and "cities" such as Pāṭaliputra and so forth, and even while abiding there, apart from striving to ripen the unripened disciples among sentient beings, to liberate those who are ripened, and to accomplish unsurpassed awakening, that bodhisattva "never," i.e., at no time, "generates the desire for" a śrāvaka arhat and "pratyekabuddha"; this is taught to be "the genuine isolation of the bodhisattvas," the "sons of the Sugatas." If one's own mind is isolated from inferior vehicle mental engagements, no matter where one abides, such as in towns or villages, one abides in supreme isolation. Not abiding in such isolation, "whichever bodhisattva" abides in a place extending for "five hundred yojanas," a "mountain valley thoroughly isolated" from the bustling of people, "wherever" it is, a place unpopulated by humans and filled with poisonous snakes and so forth, "even for many tens of millions of years," that bodhisattva "who does not know this" inner isolation generates, i.e., "acquires, overweening pride," thinking, "My abiding in isolation is supreme!" and abides similarly to inferior vehicle mental engagement; that is not abiding in the isolation of a bodhisattva, because it is corrupted by inferior mental engagement. Under the influence of such pride, towards "other bodhisattvas" who strive for the welfare of transmigrators and who, having attained the "four dhyānas," the "five powers," the "five faculties" such as faith, the "three doors of liberation," the "heroic stride samādhi," and so forth, roam in villages and cities for the sake of others, establishing sentient beings in ripening and liberation, not knowing their intent and conduct, one who "despises" them, thinking, "This one is not practicing in wilderness and isolation," is "the object of Māra's activity," that is, they have come to abide in an object where Māra has found an opportunity; so "the Victors have taught."

Well then, if abiding alone is not isolation, what is isolation? "Whichever bodhisattva," whether his body abides in a "village or else in a wilderness," if his mind is free from the thought desiring to attain either of the two vehicles of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and becomes singularly ascertained in the path of supreme awakening, this manner is the completely pure isolation of bodhisattvas who have engaged in the welfare of transmigrators. Not knowing this, one such as the previous bodhisattva who assesses the measure, i.e., "gauges the level," of that bodhisattva who abides in such isolation, and appraises them, thinking, "This one is not abiding in isolation," will themselves degenerate from the qualities of the grounds and paths. Therefore, the Capable One, the Buddha Bhagavat, has stated: "Apart from those like me, individuals should not assess the measure of individuals, lest they degenerate," and "A bodhisattva should examine their own continuum but should not look for faults in others." Having understood according to what is taught in the sūtras, generating the perception of all sentient beings as the Teacher and paying respect is the primary training for bodhisattvas. This is the commentary on the twenty-first chapter, the Chapter on Māra, from the Commentary on the Verse Summary of the Perfection of Wisdom, entitled A Jeweled Lamp Fulfilling the Hopes of the Fortunate, Illuminating the Suchness of Profound Dependent Arising.

heading: **འཕྲོས་དོན།**
source: བསྟེན་པར་བྱ་བའི་གཤེས་གཉེན་དེ་ཡང་གང་ཞེས་ན། ཕྱིའི་ཡོངས་འཛིན་སངས་རྒྱས་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་རྣམས་དང་བྱང་ཆུབ་མཆོག་གི་ལམ་ཉམས་སུ་ལེན་པ་ལ་ཞུགས་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་དག་དང༌། ནང་གི་ཡོངས་འཛིན་ལམ་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་དྲུག་དང་བཅས་ཏེ་དགེ་བའི་བཤེས་སུ་བསྟེན་པར་བྱའོ། །དེ་ཡང་སངས་རྒྱས་བྱང་སེམས་དེ་དག་ནི་ཐེག་པ་ཆེན་པོའི་ལམ་རྗེས་སུ་སྟོན་པར་བྱེད་པ་པོ་ཡིན་པས་ཕྱིའི་ཡོངས་འཛིན་ཞེས་བྱ་ལ། ལམ་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་དྲུག་པོ་འདི་ནི་ཉམས་སུ་བླང་བྱ་དང་བསྒྲུབ་པར་བྱ་བའི་སུ་ཡིན་པས་ནང་གི་ཡོངས་འཛིན་ཞེས་བྱའོ། །དེ་གཉིས་ཀྱིས་དམན་ལམ་སོགས་སུ་མི་ལྟུང་བར་འཛིན་པར་བྱེད་པས་ཡོངས་འཛིན་གཉིས་པ་དེ་བསྟེན་པའི་རྒྱུ་རྣམ་པ་གཉིས་ཀྱིས་བླ་ན་མེད་པའི་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་བྱང་ཆུབ་མྱུར་དུ་རྟོགས་པར་འགྱུར་ཏེ།ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་ཚང་བ་ལས་རང་གི་འབྲས་བུ་འབྱུང་བ་རྟེན་འབྲེལ་ཆོས་ཉིད་ཡིན་པའི་ཕྱིར། ཞེས་པའོ། །བརྒྱད་སྟོང་པ་ལས་ཀྱང་། དེ་ནས་ཡང་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཞེས་པ་ནས། དང་པོ་ཉིད་དུ་དགེ་བའི་བཤེས་གཉེན་ལ་བརྟེན་པར་བྱ་གུས་པར་བྱ། ཞེས་སོགས་ཀྱིས་བཤད་དོ། །ནང་གི་ཡོངས་འཛིན་ཤེར་ཕྱིན་ལ་སློབ་པའི་རྟགས་དེ་ཉིད་འཆད་པར་། རྒྱལ་བ་འདས་དང་ཞེས་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གཅིག་གསུངས་པའི་དོན། ཕར་ཕྱིན་དྲུག་གིས་ནང་གི་ཡོངས་འཛིན་བྱེད་ཚུལ་ནི། རྒྱལ་བ་ཡང་དག་པར་རྫོགས་པའི་སངས་རྒྱས་གང་དག་སྔར་འདས་པའི་དུས་སུ་བྱོན་ཟིན་པ་དང་། མ་བྱོན་པ་མ་འོངས་པའི་སངས་རྒྱས་དང་། ད་ལྟ་ཕྱོགས་བཅུ་དག་ན་ཆོས་སྟོན་བཞིན་དུ་གང་དག་བཞུགས་པ་སྟེ་དུས་གསུམ་གྱི་རྒྱལ་བ་ཀུན་གྱི་བགྲོད་པ་གཅིག་པའི་ལམ་པོ་ཆེ་ནི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་དྲུག་པོ་འདི་ཉིད་ཡིན་གྱི་འདི་ལས་གཞན་ནི་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ་ཕར་ཕྱིན་དྲུག་ལ་མ་བསྟེན་པར་ཚང་རྒྱ་བ་མི་སྲིད་ཅིང་དེ་ལས་གཞན་པའི་ལམ་གྱི་འཚང་མི་ནུས་པའི་ཕྱིར། ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་དྲུག་པོ་འདི་ནི་བྱང་ཆུབ་མཆོག་གི་ལམ་མམ་ཚུལ་ལ་ཞུགས་པ་རྣམས་ཀྱི་ཉོན་མངས་པའི་སྒྲིབ་པའི་མུན་པ་སེལ་བར་བྱེད་ཅིང་བདག་མེད་རྟོགས་པའི་ལམ་གསལ་བའི་གསལ་བྱེད་གྱུར་པ་དང་། ཤེས་བྱའི་སྒྲིབ་པའི་མུན་པ་བསལ་བས་ན་སྒྲོན་མ་དང་མཐོང་ལམ་གྱིས་སྣང་བར་བྱེད་པས་ན་སྣང་བར་གྱུར་པ་དང་། སྒོམ་ལམ་སོགས་ཐེག་པ་མཆོག་གི་ལམ་ཡོངས་སུ་རྫོགས་པར་བྱེད་པས་ན་སྟོན་པ་མཆོག་ཏུ་གྱུར་པ་ཡིན་ནོ་ཞེས་རྒྱལ་བ་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་བཤད་པ་ཡིན་ཏེ།དེ་ལྟར་བརྒྱད་སྟོང་པ་ལས། ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་དྲུག་པོ་འདི་ཉིད་སྟོན་པའོ། །ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་དྲུག་ནི་ལམ་མོ། །ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་དྲུག་ནི་སྣང་བའོ། །ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་དྲུག་ནི་སྒྲོན་མའོ། །ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་དྲུག་ནི་འོད་དོ། །ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་དྲུག་ནི་སྐྱོབ་པའོ། །སྐྱབས་སོ། །གནས་སོ་ཞེས་སོགས་གསུངས་སོ། །མདོར་བསྡུ་ན་སངས་རྒྱས་ཐོབ་པ་ལ་ཕར་ཕྱིན་དྲུག་རྗེས་སུ་སྟོན་པའི་བཤེས་གཉེན་དང༌། རང་གིས་སྒྲུབ་པའམ་སྤྱོད་པ་སྟེ་རྒྱུ་གཉིས་པོ་དེ་མེད་མི་རུང་བ་ཡིན་ཞིང་།
translation: If one asks, "Who is that spiritual friend to be relied upon?": the outer tutors, the Buddhas Bhagavats and the bodhisattvas who have engaged in practicing the path of supreme awakening, together with the inner tutor, the path of the six perfections, should be relied upon as spiritual friends. Moreover, because those Buddhas and bodhisattvas are the ones who teach the path of the Mahāyāna, they are called outer tutors, and because this path of the six perfections is what is to be practiced and accomplished, it is called the inner tutor. Because those two hold one back from falling into the inferior paths and so forth, by the two types of causes of relying upon those two tutors, one will quickly realize the unsurpassable awakening of a Buddha, "because it is the nature of dependent arising that its own result arises from complete perfection." Also, from the Aṣṭasāhasrikā: from "Then again, Bhagavat..." down to "At the very beginning, one should rely upon and pay respect to a spiritual friend," and so forth, this is explained. In order to explain the signs of training in the perfection of wisdom, which is the inner tutor, the meaning of what is stated in one verse starting with "Past Jinas" and so forth: The manner in which the six perfections act as inner tutors is as follows. The completely perfect Buddhas, the "Jinas," who have "past," having already appeared in the past, and the "un-arisen," future Buddhas, and those who are "abiding," currently teaching the Dharma in the "ten directions"—the great path traveled by all the Jinas of the three times is solely these six perfections and none other than this, because without relying on the six perfections it is impossible to attain Buddhahood, and by a path other than this one cannot attain Buddhahood. These six perfections dispel the darkness of the afflictive obscurations of those who have engaged in the path or method of supreme awakening, and become the "illuminator" that illuminates the path of realizing selflessness; because they clear away the darkness of cognitive obscurations, they are a "lamp"; because they make things apparent through the path of seeing, they become "light"; and because they bring the paths of the supreme vehicle, such as the path of meditation, to full completion, they become the supreme "teacher"—thus the Jinas have explained. Likewise, the Aṣṭasāhasrikā states: "These very six perfections are the teacher. The six perfections are the path. The six perfections are the light. The six perfections are the lamp. The six perfections are the illumination. The six perfections are the protector, the refuge, the resting place," and so forth. In brief, for attaining Buddhahood, the two causes—the spiritual friend who teaches the six perfections and one's own accomplishment or practice—are indispensable, and...

Well then, if abiding alone is not isolation, what is isolation? "Whichever bodhisattva," whether his body abides in a "village or else in a wilderness," if his mind is free from the thought desiring to attain either of the two vehicles of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and becomes singularly ascertained in the path of supreme awakening, this manner is the completely pure isolation of bodhisattvas who have engaged in the welfare of transmigrators. Not knowing this, one such as the previous bodhisattva who assesses the measure, i.e., "gauges the level," of that bodhisattva who abides in such isolation, and appraises them, thinking, "This one is not abiding in isolation," will themselves degenerate from the qualities of the grounds and paths. Therefore, the Capable One, the Buddha Bhagavat, has stated: "Apart from those like me, individuals should not assess the measure of individuals, lest they degenerate," and "A bodhisattva should examine their own continuum but should not look for faults in others." Having understood according to what is taught in the sūtras, generating the perception of all sentient beings as the Teacher and paying respect is the primary training for bodhisattvas. This is the commentary on the twenty-first chapter, the Chapter on Māra, from the Commentary on the Verse Summary of the Perfection of Wisdom, entitled A Jeweled Lamp Fulfilling the Hopes of the Fortunate, Illuminating the Suchness of Profound Dependent Arising.

Second, since the non-occurrence of such things also depends upon relying on a spiritual friend, the meaning of what is stated in two verses starting with "Therefore" and so forth, in order to advise the necessity of relying on a spiritual friend and to explain the signs of an irreversible one who is like that: Because many deeds of Māra occur that cause hindrances when practicing the path of the Mahāyāna, "therefore," having understood that, one must turn them back, and so one should rely on outer and inner tutors. Moreover, the one who relies has a strong intention "seeking" "supreme awakening"—unsurpassed awakening—for the sake of others, and is skilled in the means to accomplish it; as for the manner in which to rely, by "definitely destroying" "pride" that holds oneself as supreme and so forth, for example, just as "in the world" "a host of sick people" "rely upon" another, "a skilled physician," "to cure their illness," one should properly rely upon a qualified spiritual friend, unfalteringly through both intention and application, by relying on the perceptions of oneself as a sick person, the Dharma speaker as a physician, the Dharma as medicine, earnest practice as curing the illness, the Tathāgata as a supreme being, and the Dharma system as remaining for a long time.

heading: **འཕྲོས་དོན།**
translation: If those are complete, even though one attains the signs, manifest clinging does not arise; and in order to explain that very realization of having no manifest clinging, such as the manner in which all faults and qualities arise merely through being imputed by conception, the meaning of what is stated in four verses starting with "Just as wisdom" and so forth: Moreover, just as the Aṣṭasāhasrikā states, "The perfection of wisdom has the characteristic of emptiness," "just as" the essence or characteristic of the perfection of wisdom is inherently empty because it is devoid of a nature of being truly established as one or many, "likewise," all these phenomena, "form and so forth," in their mode of abiding or characteristic, are known to be inherently empty, similar to that perfection of wisdom; and if one thoroughly knows all phenomena from form up to omniscience to be empty of their own essence and without the mark of true establishment, then "at that time" when one practices the signs of attaining the peak application as taught above, or practices "here" in that way, one is "practicing the perfection of wisdom of the Sugatas."

གཉིས་པ་དེ་ལྟ་བུ་མི་འབྱུང་བའང་དགེ་བའི་བཤེས་གཉེན་བསྟེན་པ་ལ་རག་ལས་པས། བཤེས་གཉེན་བསྟན་དགོས་པར་གདམས་པ་དང་། དེ་འདྲའི་ཕྱིར་མི་ལྡོག་པའི་རྟགས་འཆད་བར། དེ་ལྟ་བས་ན་ཞེས་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གཉིས་གཉིས་གསུངས་པའི་དོན། ཐེག་པ་ཆེན་པོའི་ལམ་ཉམས་སུ་ལེན་པ་ལ་བར་དུ་གཅོད་པའི་བདུད་ལས་མང་དུ་འབྱུང་བ་དེ་ལྟ་བུས་ན། དེ་ཉིད་ཤེས་པར་བྱས་ནས་བཟློག་དགོས་པས་ཕྱི་ནང་གི་ཡོངས་འཛིན་བསྟེན་པར་བྱའོ། །དེ་ཡང་གང་གིས་བསྟེན་པ་པོ་ནི་བྱང་ཆུབ་དམ་པ་བླ་ན་མེད་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་གཞན་དོན་དུ་འཆོལ་བ་ཡི་བསམ་པ་ཤུགས་དྲག་པོ་དང་ལྡན་ཞིང་དེ་སྒྲུབ་པའི་ཐབས་ལ་མཁས་པས། ཚུལ་ཇི་ལྟར་བསྟན་ན་རང་ཉིད་མཆོག་ཏུ་འཛིན་པའི་ང་རྒྱལ་སོགས་ངེས་པར་བཅོམ་སྟེ། དཔེ་ཇི་ལྟར་ན་འཇིག་རྟེན་ན་ནད་པའི་ཚོགས་ཀྱིས་རང་གི་ནད་གསོ་བའི་ཕྱིར་གཞན་སྨན་པ་མཁས་པ་བསྟེན་པ་ལྟར་རང་ལ་ནད་པ་དང་ཆོས་སྨྲ་བ་པོ་ལ་སྨན་པ་དང་ཆོས་ལ་སྨན་དང་ནན་ཏན་ཉམས་སུ་ལེན་པ་ལ་ནད་གསོ་བ་དང་། དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ལ་སྐྱེས་བུ་དམ་པ་དང༌། ཆོས་ཀྱི་ཚུལ་ལ་རིང་དུ་གནས་པའི་འདུ་ཤེས་བརྟེན་པ་སོགས་བསམ་སྦྱོར་གཉིས་ཀྱིས་གཡེལ་བ་མེད་པར་དགེ་བའི་བཤེས་གཉེན་མཚན་ཉིད་དང་ལྡན་བ་ཚུལ་བཞིན་དུ་བསྟེན་པར་བྱའོ། །

Second, since the non-occurrence of such things also depends upon relying on a spiritual friend, the meaning of what is stated in two verses starting with "Therefore" and so forth, in order to advise the necessity of relying on a spiritual friend and to explain the signs of an irreversible one who is like that: Because many deeds of Māra occur that cause hindrances when practicing the path of the Mahāyāna, "therefore," having understood that, one must turn them back, and so one should rely on outer and inner tutors. Moreover, the one who relies has a strong intention "seeking" "supreme awakening"—unsurpassed awakening—for the sake of others, and is skilled in the means to accomplish it; as for the manner in which to rely, by "definitely destroying" "pride" that holds oneself as supreme and so forth, for example, just as "in the world" "a host of sick people" "rely upon" another, "a skilled physician," "to cure their illness," one should properly rely upon a qualified spiritual friend, unfalteringly through both intention and application, by relying on the perceptions of oneself as a sick person, the Dharma speaker as a physician, the Dharma as medicine, earnest practice as curing the illness, the Tathāgata as a supreme being, and the Dharma system as remaining for a long time.

བསྟེན་པར་བྱ་བའི་གཤེས་གཉེན་དེ་ཡང་གང་ཞེས་ན། ཕྱིའི་ཡོངས་འཛིན་སངས་རྒྱས་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་རྣམས་དང་བྱང་ཆུབ་མཆོག་གི་ལམ་ཉམས་སུ་ལེན་པ་ལ་ཞུགས་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་དག་དང༌། ནང་གི་ཡོངས་འཛིན་ལམ་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་དྲུག་དང་བཅས་ཏེ་དགེ་བའི་བཤེས་སུ་བསྟེན་པར་བྱའོ། །དེ་ཡང་སངས་རྒྱས་བྱང་སེམས་དེ་དག་ནི་ཐེག་པ་ཆེན་པོའི་ལམ་རྗེས་སུ་སྟོན་པར་བྱེད་པ་པོ་ཡིན་པས་ཕྱིའི་ཡོངས་འཛིན་ཞེས་བྱ་ལ། ལམ་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་དྲུག་པོ་འདི་ནི་ཉམས་སུ་བླང་བྱ་དང་བསྒྲུབ་པར་བྱ་བའི་སུ་ཡིན་པས་ནང་གི་ཡོངས་འཛིན་ཞེས་བྱའོ། །དེ་གཉིས་ཀྱིས་དམན་ལམ་སོགས་སུ་མི་ལྟུང་བར་འཛིན་པར་བྱེད་པས་ཡོངས་འཛིན་གཉིས་པ་དེ་བསྟེན་པའི་རྒྱུ་རྣམ་པ་གཉིས་ཀྱིས་བླ་ན་མེད་པའི་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་བྱང་ཆུབ་མྱུར་དུ་རྟོགས་པར་འགྱུར་ཏེ།ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་ཚང་བ་ལས་རང་གི་འབྲས་བུ་འབྱུང་བ་རྟེན་འབྲེལ་ཆོས་ཉིད་ཡིན་པའི་ཕྱིར། ཞེས་པའོ། །བརྒྱད་སྟོང་པ་ལས་ཀྱང་། དེ་ནས་ཡང་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཞེས་པ་ནས། དང་པོ་ཉིད་དུ་དགེ་བའི་བཤེས་གཉེན་ལ་བརྟེན་པར་བྱ་གུས་པར་བྱ། ཞེས་སོགས་ཀྱིས་བཤད་དོ། །ནང་གི་ཡོངས་འཛིན་ཤེར་ཕྱིན་ལ་སློབ་པའི་རྟགས་དེ་ཉིད་འཆད་པར་། རྒྱལ་བ་འདས་དང་ཞེས་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གཅིག་གསུངས་པའི་དོན། ཕར་ཕྱིན་དྲུག་གིས་ནང་གི་ཡོངས་འཛིན་བྱེད་ཚུལ་ནི། རྒྱལ་བ་ཡང་དག་པར་རྫོགས་པའི་སངས་རྒྱས་གང་དག་སྔར་འདས་པའི་དུས་སུ་བྱོན་ཟིན་པ་དང་། མ་བྱོན་པ་མ་འོངས་པའི་སངས་རྒྱས་དང་། ད་ལྟ་ཕྱོགས་བཅུ་དག་ན་ཆོས་སྟོན་བཞིན་དུ་གང་དག་བཞུགས་པ་སྟེ་དུས་གསུམ་གྱི་རྒྱལ་བ་ཀུན་གྱི་བགྲོད་པ་གཅིག་པའི་ལམ་པོ་ཆེ་ནི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་དྲུག་པོ་འདི་ཉིད་ཡིན་གྱི་འདི་ལས་གཞན་ནི་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ་ཕར་ཕྱིན་དྲུག་ལ་མ་བསྟེན་པར་ཚང་རྒྱ་བ་མི་སྲིད་ཅིང་དེ་ལས་གཞན་པའི་ལམ་གྱི་འཚང་མི་ནུས་པའི་ཕྱིར། ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་དྲུག་པོ་འདི་ནི་བྱང་ཆུབ་མཆོག་གི་ལམ་མམ་ཚུལ་ལ་ཞུགས་པ་རྣམས་ཀྱི་ཉོན་མངས་པའི་སྒྲིབ་པའི་མུན་པ་སེལ་བར་བྱེད་ཅིང་བདག་མེད་རྟོགས་པའི་ལམ་གསལ་བའི་གསལ་བྱེད་གྱུར་པ་དང་། ཤེས་བྱའི་སྒྲིབ་པའི་མུན་པ་བསལ་བས་ན་སྒྲོན་མ་དང་མཐོང་ལམ་གྱིས་སྣང་བར་བྱེད་པས་ན་སྣང་བར་གྱུར་པ་དང་། སྒོམ་ལམ་སོགས་ཐེག་པ་མཆོག་གི་ལམ་ཡོངས་སུ་རྫོགས་པར་བྱེད་པས་ན་སྟོན་པ་མཆོག་ཏུ་གྱུར་པ་ཡིན་ནོ་ཞེས་རྒྱལ་བ་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་བཤད་པ་ཡིན་ཏེ།དེ་ལྟར་བརྒྱད་སྟོང་པ་ལས། ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་དྲུག་པོ་འདི་ཉིད་སྟོན་པའོ། །ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་དྲུག་ནི་ལམ་མོ། །ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་དྲུག་ནི་སྣང་བའོ། །ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་དྲུག་ནི་སྒྲོན་མའོ། །ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་དྲུག་ནི་འོད་དོ། །ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་དྲུག་ནི་སྐྱོབ་པའོ། །སྐྱབས་སོ། །གནས་སོ་ཞེས་སོགས་གསུངས་སོ། །མདོར་བསྡུ་ན་སངས་རྒྱས་ཐོབ་པ་ལ་ཕར་ཕྱིན་དྲུག་རྗེས་སུ་སྟོན་པའི་བཤེས་གཉེན་དང༌། རང་གིས་སྒྲུབ་པའམ་སྤྱོད་པ་སྟེ་རྒྱུ་གཉིས་པོ་དེ་མེད་མི་རུང་བ་ཡིན་ཞིང་།
