If one asks, "Who is that spiritual friend to be relied upon?": the outer tutors, the Buddhas Bhagavats and the bodhisattvas who have engaged in practicing the path of supreme awakening, together with the inner tutor, the path of the six perfections, should be relied upon as spiritual friends. Moreover, because those Buddhas and bodhisattvas are the ones who teach the path of the Mahāyāna, they are called outer tutors, and because this path of the six perfections is what is to be practiced and accomplished, it is called the inner tutor. Because those two hold one back from falling into the inferior paths and so forth, by the two types of causes of relying upon those two tutors, one will quickly realize the unsurpassable awakening of a Buddha, "because it is the nature of dependent arising that its own result arises from complete perfection." Also, from the Aṣṭasāhasrikā: from "Then again, Bhagavat..." down to "At the very beginning, one should rely upon and pay respect to a spiritual friend," and so forth, this is explained. In order to explain the signs of training in the perfection of wisdom, which is the inner tutor, the meaning of what is stated in one verse starting with "Past Jinas" and so forth: The manner in which the six perfections act as inner tutors is as follows. The completely perfect Buddhas, the "Jinas," who have "past," having already appeared in the past, and the "un-arisen," future Buddhas, and those who are "abiding," currently teaching the Dharma in the "ten directions"—the great path traveled by all the Jinas of the three times is solely these six perfections and none other than this, because without relying on the six perfections it is impossible to attain Buddhahood, and by a path other than this one cannot attain Buddhahood. These six perfections dispel the darkness of the afflictive obscurations of those who have engaged in the path or method of supreme awakening, and become the "illuminator" that illuminates the path of realizing selflessness; because they clear away the darkness of cognitive obscurations, they are a "lamp"; because they make things apparent through the path of seeing, they become "light"; and because they bring the paths of the supreme vehicle, such as the path of meditation, to full completion, they become the supreme "teacher"—thus the Jinas have explained. Likewise, the Aṣṭasāhasrikā states: "These very six perfections are the teacher. The six perfections are the path. The six perfections are the light. The six perfections are the lamp. The six perfections are the illumination. The six perfections are the protector, the refuge, the resting place," and so forth. heading: **འཕྲོས་དོན།**
translation: If one asks, "If all phenomena are inherently empty, how do sentient beings become completely afflicted or completely purified?", in order to teach the answer to that: ordinary sentient beings excessively superimpose pleasantness and unpleasantness and "completely conceptualize" through improper mental engagement, and by the force of that, they generate craving desire for the food of the sensory qualities such as form, sound, smell, taste, and tangibles, and those possessing minds attached to saṃsāra, such as sensory qualities, constantly cycle from the peak of existence down to the Avīci hell, like flies swarming around the smell of filth, and therefore become completely afflicted; moreover, except for being established merely conventionally like an illusion, both the "self" and the virtuous phenomena of a self are not genuinely established and are inherently empty, because they are ultimately unproduced. Nevertheless, foolish "beings" who are unskilled in the meaning of the abiding nature apprehend what is ultimately non-existent as existent, for example, becoming like some people who think they have "tied a knot in space"; therefore, beings whose mind-streams are bound by erroneous conceptions are difficult to liberate—thus the side of complete affliction is tenable; and as for how they suffer in saṃsāra by the power of grasping at true existence, which holds things to be established in that way even though they are not ultimately established: "for example," when a manifest concept arises from an erroneous mind due to one's own perception of suspicion that "poison has flared up" or "poison has entered the stomach," even though in reality poison has not entered the stomach, by the power of that conception suffering arises and one faints from fear, just as cowards tremble with fear merely upon being told by an enemy or the like, "I will kill you."

If one asks, "Who is that spiritual friend to be relied upon?": the outer tutors, the Buddhas Bhagavats and the bodhisattvas who have engaged in practicing the path of supreme awakening, together with the inner tutor, the path of the six perfections, should be relied upon as spiritual friends. Moreover, because those Buddhas and bodhisattvas are the ones who teach the path of the Mahāyāna, they are called outer tutors, and because this path of the six perfections is what is to be practiced and accomplished, it is called the inner tutor. Because those two hold one back from falling into the inferior paths and so forth, by the two types of causes of relying upon those two tutors, one will quickly realize the unsurpassable awakening of a Buddha, "because it is the nature of dependent arising that its own result arises from complete perfection." Also, from the Aṣṭasāhasrikā: from "Then again, Bhagavat..." down to "At the very beginning, one should rely upon and pay respect to a spiritual friend," and so forth, this is explained. In order to explain the signs of training in the perfection of wisdom, which is the inner tutor, the meaning of what is stated in one verse starting with "Past Jinas" and so forth: The manner in which the six perfections act as inner tutors is as follows. The completely perfect Buddhas, the "Jinas," who have "past," having already appeared in the past, and the "un-arisen," future Buddhas, and those who are "abiding," currently teaching the Dharma in the "ten directions"—the great path traveled by all the Jinas of the three times is solely these six perfections and none other than this, because without relying on the six perfections it is impossible to attain Buddhahood, and by a path other than this one cannot attain Buddhahood. These six perfections dispel the darkness of the afflictive obscurations of those who have engaged in the path or method of supreme awakening, and become the "illuminator" that illuminates the path of realizing selflessness; because they clear away the darkness of cognitive obscurations, they are a "lamp"; because they make things apparent through the path of seeing, they become "light"; and because they bring the paths of the supreme vehicle, such as the path of meditation, to full completion, they become the supreme "teacher"—thus the Jinas have explained. Likewise, the Aṣṭasāhasrikā states: "These very six perfections are the teacher. The six perfections are the path. The six perfections are the light. The six perfections are the lamp. The six perfections are the illumination. The six perfections are the protector, the refuge, the resting place," and so forth. heading: **འཕྲོས་དོན།**
translation: Just like that example, foolish ordinary beings who have not attained the noble path apprehend a self as inherently existent even though it is not ultimately established, and by focusing on the eye, nose, and so forth, they accept them as belonging to a self; from habituation to that, there arises the untrue complete conceptualization that perceives the self and what belongs to a self as true, and by the power of that, they accumulate karma, take birth again and again in existence, and continuously experience various sufferings such as perishing—that is, death—decline, and mental unhappiness. Just as it was taught that grasping at a self and what belongs to a self as existent even though they do not exist in the mode of abiding leads to complete affliction by the power of all-obscuring ignorance, it is stated that a bodhisattva who directly realizes the meaning of selflessness—that is, the non-apprehension of self and what belongs to a self in accordance with the unmistaken mode of abiding—knows the abiding nature and habituates to it, and thereby will attain the state of liberation, which is complete purification; moreover, that is conventional, but ultimately, a bodhisattva who genuinely knows that in this regard no person whatsoever becomes afflicted or completely pure will subsequently realize the perfection of wisdom, which realizes existence and peace as equal in being empty of true existence, thus it is said. The explanation of this is taught in the Aṣṭasāhasrikā by Subhūti asking, "Lord, what is the characteristic of the perfection of wisdom?" and so forth.

If those are complete, even though one attains the signs, manifest clinging does not arise; and in order to explain that very realization of having no manifest clinging, such as the manner in which all faults and qualities arise merely through being imputed by conception, the meaning of what is stated in four verses starting with "Just as wisdom" and so forth: Moreover, just as the Aṣṭasāhasrikā states, "The perfection of wisdom has the characteristic of emptiness," "just as" the essence or characteristic of the perfection of wisdom is inherently empty because it is devoid of a nature of being truly established as one or many, "likewise," all these phenomena, "form and so forth," in their mode of abiding or characteristic, are known to be inherently empty, similar to that perfection of wisdom; and if one thoroughly knows all phenomena from form up to omniscience to be empty of their own essence and without the mark of true establishment, then "at that time" when one practices the signs of attaining the peak application as taught above, or practices "here" in that way, one is "practicing the perfection of wisdom of the Sugatas."

If one asks, "If all phenomena are inherently empty, how do sentient beings become completely afflicted or completely purified?", in order to teach the answer to that: ordinary sentient beings excessively superimpose pleasantness and unpleasantness and "completely conceptualize" through improper mental engagement, and by the force of that, they generate craving desire for the food of the sensory qualities such as form, sound, smell, taste, and tangibles, and those possessing minds attached to saṃsāra, such as sensory qualities, constantly cycle from the peak of existence down to the Avīci hell, like flies swarming around the smell of filth, and therefore become completely afflicted; moreover, except for being established merely conventionally like an illusion, both the "self" and the virtuous phenomena of a self are not genuinely established and are inherently empty, because they are ultimately unproduced. Nevertheless, foolish "beings" who are unskilled in the meaning of the abiding nature apprehend what is ultimately non-existent as existent, for example, becoming like some people who think they have "tied a knot in space"; therefore, beings whose mind-streams are bound by erroneous conceptions are difficult to liberate—thus the side of complete affliction is tenable; and as for how they suffer in saṃsāra by the power of grasping at true existence, which holds things to be established in that way even though they are not ultimately established: "for example," when a manifest concept arises from an erroneous mind due to one's own perception of suspicion that "poison has flared up" or "poison has entered the stomach," even though in reality poison has not entered the stomach, by the power of that conception suffering arises and one faints from fear, just as cowards tremble with fear merely upon being told by an enemy or the like, "I will kill you."

heading: **རྩེ་མོའི་སྦྱོར་བ།**
source: རྩེ་མོའི་སྦྱོར་བ། གཉིས་པ་རྩེ་མོའི་སྦྱོར་བ་ནི།རྒྱན་ལས། འཛམ་བུ་གླིང་གི་སྐྱེ་བོ་སྙིང་། །ནས། རྣམ་འཕེལ་བཅུ་དྲུག་བདག་ཉིད་དོ། །ཞེས་གསུངས། འདི་ལ་གསུམ་ལས། དང་པ་ནི། སྟོང་གསུམ་གྱི་སེམས་ཅན་དང་མཉམ་པའི་སངས་རྒྱས་མཆོད་པ་ལས་ལྷག་པའི་བསོད་ནམས་རྣམ་པར་འཕེལ་བ་བཅུ་དྲུག་ཐོབ་པའི་ཐེག་ཆེན་གྱི་ངེས་འབྱེད་ཆ་མཐུན་གཉིས་པ་དེ། རྩེ་མོ་རྩེ་སྦྱོར་གྱི་མཚན་ཉིད། གཉིས་པ་དེ་ལ་དབྱེ་ན། རྩེ་མོའི་རྩེ་སྦྱོར་ཆུང་འབྲིང་ཆེ་གསུམ་ཡོད། ས་མཚམས་ཐེག་ཆེན་གྱི་སྦྱོར་ལམ་རྩེ་མོ་ཁོ་ནར་ཡོད། རྩེ་མོའི་རྩེ་སྦྱོར་ལ་བསོད་ནམས་རྣམ་པར་འཕེལ་བ་བཅུ་དྲུག་ཡོད་པ་ལས། དང་པོ་ནི། འཛམ་བུ་གླིང་སོགས་སྟོང་གསུམ་གྱི་སེམས་ཅན་གྱིས་སངས་རྒྱས་མཆོད་པ་ལས་ལྷག་པའི་བསོད་ནམས་རྣམ་པར་འཕེལ་བའི་རྩེ་སྦྱོར་ནི། འཛམ་བུའི་གླིང་ན་ཞེས་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གཉིས་གསུངས་པའི་དོན། བརྟག་པ་མཐའ་བཟུང་གི་དབང་དུ་བཏང་ནས་དཔེར་བྱས་ན། འཛམ་བུ་གླིང་ན་ཡོད་པའི་སེམས་ཅན་གྱིས་མཚོན་བའི་སྟོང་གསུམ་གྱི་སེམས་ཅན་ཇི་སྙེད་མ་ལུས་པ་དེ་དག་གིས་མི་ཡི་ལུས་ཐོབ་སྟེ། དེ་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་བླ་ན་མེད་པར་ཡང་དག་པར་རྫོགས་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་མཆོག་ཏུ་སེམས་བསྐྱེད་ནས། ལོ་སྟོང་བྱེ་བ་མང་པོ་སངས་རྒྱས་དང་བྱང་སེམས་ལ་མཆོད་པ་རྒྱ་ཆེན་པ་ོདང་སེམས་ཅན་རྣམས་ལ་སྦྱིན་པ་ཚད་མེད་པ་བྱིན་པར་བྱས་ལ་དགེ་བའི་རྩ་བ་དེ་དག་ཀུན་ཀྱང་འགྲོ་བའི་དོན་གྱི་ཕྱིར་དུ་བྱང་ཆུབ་མཆོག་གི་རྒྱུར་ཡོངས་སུ་བསྔོ་བར་བྱས་ན་དེ་ལ་ཡང་བསོད་ནམས་དཔག་ཏུ་མེད་པ་ཡོད་ཀྱང་། བྱང་སེམས་གང་ཞིག་གིས་རྩེ་མོའི་མངོན་པར་རྟོགས་པའི་རང་བཞིན་གྱི་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་མཆོག་ལ་མངོན་པར་བརྩོན་པ་ན་དུས་རིང་པོར་ཕར་ཞོག །ཐ་ན་ཉི་མ་གཅིག་གཅིག་ཙམ་ལ་ཤེར་ཕྱིན་དེའི་རྗེས་སུ་མཐུན་པར་ལམ་སྒོམ་ཤིང་གཞན་ལ་སྟོན་པ་སོགས་བྱེད་ན་དེའི་བསོད་ནམས་དེ་ལ་གོང་དུ་བཤད་མ་ཐག་པའི་སྦྱིན་པའི་ཕུང་པོས་བསོད་ནམས་དེའི་ཆར་ཡང་འགྲན་པར་མི་ཕོད་པ་སྟེ་འགྲན་པར་མི་ནུས་པ་ཡིན་པ་དེ་ཡིས་ཕྱིར་ན་གཡེལ་བ་མེད་པར་དུས་རྟག་ཏུ་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕར་ཕྱིན་ནམ་རྩེ་སྦྱོར་བསྒོམ་པ་འདི་ལ་འཇུག་པར་བྱ་དགོས་སོ། །ཞེས་པའོ། །
translation: Peak application. Second, the peak application: the Ornament states, from "If the beings of Jambudvīpa..." up to "...has the nature of sixteen increases." In this there are three parts: First, the characteristic of the peak stage of the peak application is the second Mahāyāna aid to penetration, which attains the sixteen increases of merit that surpass making offerings to Buddhas equal to the sentient beings of a trichiliocosm. Second, if divided: there are three peak stages of the peak application: small, medium, and great. The boundary is solely on the Mahāyāna path of preparation of peak. Among the sixteen increases of merit in the peak stage of the peak application, the first: the peak application where the increase of merit surpasses sentient beings of a trichiliocosm, such as those in Jambudvīpa, making offerings to Buddhas: the meaning of the two verses stated starting with "If in Jambudvīpa": Taking a hypothetical extreme as an example, "if" all the sentient beings without exception in a trichiliocosm, illustrated by the sentient beings "in Jambudvīpa," were to attain a human body, and all of them were to generate the mind for unsurpassed, perfectly complete supreme awakening, and for "many tens of millions of thousands of years" they were to make extensive offerings to Buddhas and bodhisattvas and give immeasurable generosity to sentient beings, and they were to fully dedicate all those roots of virtue as causes for supreme awakening for the sake of beings, even though they would have immeasurable merit; "if" any bodhisattva manifests endeavor in the supreme perfection of wisdom, which has the nature of the clear realization of the peak, let alone for a long time, if they meditate on the path in accordance with that perfection of wisdom and teach it to others and so forth for even just "a single day," the mass of generosity just explained above would "not dare to compete" with even a fraction of that merit, that is, it would be unable to compete; "therefore," one should without distraction and constantly engage in this meditation on the perfection of wisdom, or peak application. Thus it is said.

If those are complete, even though one attains the signs, manifest clinging does not arise; and in order to explain that very realization of having no manifest clinging, such as the manner in which all faults and qualities arise merely through being imputed by conception, the meaning of what is stated in four verses starting with "Just as wisdom" and so forth: Moreover, just as the Aṣṭasāhasrikā states, "The perfection of wisdom has the characteristic of emptiness," "just as" the essence or characteristic of the perfection of wisdom is inherently empty because it is devoid of a nature of being truly established as one or many, "likewise," all these phenomena, "form and so forth," in their mode of abiding or characteristic, are known to be inherently empty, similar to that perfection of wisdom; and if one thoroughly knows all phenomena from form up to omniscience to be empty of their own essence and without the mark of true establishment, then "at that time" when one practices the signs of attaining the peak application as taught above, or practices "here" in that way, one is "practicing the perfection of wisdom of the Sugatas."

If one asks, "If all phenomena are inherently empty, how do sentient beings become completely afflicted or completely purified?", in order to teach the answer to that: ordinary sentient beings excessively superimpose pleasantness and unpleasantness and "completely conceptualize" through improper mental engagement, and by the force of that, they generate craving desire for the food of the sensory qualities such as form, sound, smell, taste, and tangibles, and those possessing minds attached to saṃsāra, such as sensory qualities, constantly cycle from the peak of existence down to the Avīci hell, like flies swarming around the smell of filth, and therefore become completely afflicted; moreover, except for being established merely conventionally like an illusion, both the "self" and the virtuous phenomena of a self are not genuinely established and are inherently empty, because they are ultimately unproduced. Nevertheless, foolish "beings" who are unskilled in the meaning of the abiding nature apprehend what is ultimately non-existent as existent, for example, becoming like some people who think they have "tied a knot in space"; therefore, beings whose mind-streams are bound by erroneous conceptions are difficult to liberate—thus the side of complete affliction is tenable; and as for how they suffer in saṃsāra by the power of grasping at true existence, which holds things to be established in that way even though they are not ultimately established: "for example," when a manifest concept arises from an erroneous mind due to one's own perception of suspicion that "poison has flared up" or "poison has entered the stomach," even though in reality poison has not entered the stomach, by the power of that conception suffering arises and one faints from fear, just as cowards tremble with fear merely upon being told by an enemy or the like, "I will kill you."

heading: **རྩེ་མོའི་སྦྱོར་བ།**
translation: The increase of merit of the union of method and wisdom is explained by one verse starting with "The perfection of wisdom". Those yogis who course in the supreme perfection of wisdom that has the nature of the peak stage of the peak application generate great compassion for all sentient beings tormented by suffering and accomplish the benefit of beings, yet they do not have the perception of sentient beings as truly existent; when they possess the excellent path in which such non-apprehending compassion and wisdom are united, those bodhisattvas who are skilled in method become unsurpassed objects of generosity, or fields of merit, for all beings, and constantly fully consume meaningful alms and so forth desired from the realms.

Just like that example, foolish ordinary beings who have not attained the noble path apprehend a self as inherently existent even though it is not ultimately established, and by focusing on the eye, nose, and so forth, they accept them as belonging to a self; from habituation to that, there arises the untrue complete conceptualization that perceives the self and what belongs to a self as true, and by the power of that, they accumulate karma, take birth again and again in existence, and continuously experience various sufferings such as perishing—that is, death—decline, and mental unhappiness. Just as it was taught that grasping at a self and what belongs to a self as existent even though they do not exist in the mode of abiding leads to complete affliction by the power of all-obscuring ignorance, it is stated that a bodhisattva who directly realizes the meaning of selflessness—that is, the non-apprehension of self and what belongs to a self in accordance with the unmistaken mode of abiding—knows the abiding nature and habituates to it, and thereby will attain the state of liberation, which is complete purification; moreover, that is conventional, but ultimately, a bodhisattva who genuinely knows that in this regard no person whatsoever becomes afflicted or completely pure will subsequently realize the perfection of wisdom, which realizes existence and peace as equal in being empty of true existence, thus it is said. The explanation of this is taught in the Aṣṭasāhasrikā by Subhūti asking, "Lord, what is the characteristic of the perfection of wisdom?" and so forth.

རྩེ་མོའི་སྦྱོར་བ། གཉིས་པ་རྩེ་མོའི་སྦྱོར་བ་ནི།རྒྱན་ལས། འཛམ་བུ་གླིང་གི་སྐྱེ་བོ་སྙིང་། །ནས། རྣམ་འཕེལ་བཅུ་དྲུག་བདག་ཉིད་དོ། །ཞེས་གསུངས། འདི་ལ་གསུམ་ལས། དང་པ་ནི། སྟོང་གསུམ་གྱི་སེམས་ཅན་དང་མཉམ་པའི་སངས་རྒྱས་མཆོད་པ་ལས་ལྷག་པའི་བསོད་ནམས་རྣམ་པར་འཕེལ་བ་བཅུ་དྲུག་ཐོབ་པའི་ཐེག་ཆེན་གྱི་ངེས་འབྱེད་ཆ་མཐུན་གཉིས་པ་དེ། རྩེ་མོ་རྩེ་སྦྱོར་གྱི་མཚན་ཉིད། གཉིས་པ་དེ་ལ་དབྱེ་ན། རྩེ་མོའི་རྩེ་སྦྱོར་ཆུང་འབྲིང་ཆེ་གསུམ་ཡོད། ས་མཚམས་ཐེག་ཆེན་གྱི་སྦྱོར་ལམ་རྩེ་མོ་ཁོ་ནར་ཡོད། རྩེ་མོའི་རྩེ་སྦྱོར་ལ་བསོད་ནམས་རྣམ་པར་འཕེལ་བ་བཅུ་དྲུག་ཡོད་པ་ལས། དང་པོ་ནི། འཛམ་བུ་གླིང་སོགས་སྟོང་གསུམ་གྱི་སེམས་ཅན་གྱིས་སངས་རྒྱས་མཆོད་པ་ལས་ལྷག་པའི་བསོད་ནམས་རྣམ་པར་འཕེལ་བའི་རྩེ་སྦྱོར་ནི། འཛམ་བུའི་གླིང་ན་ཞེས་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གཉིས་གསུངས་པའི་དོན། བརྟག་པ་མཐའ་བཟུང་གི་དབང་དུ་བཏང་ནས་དཔེར་བྱས་ན། འཛམ་བུ་གླིང་ན་ཡོད་པའི་སེམས་ཅན་གྱིས་མཚོན་བའི་སྟོང་གསུམ་གྱི་སེམས་ཅན་ཇི་སྙེད་མ་ལུས་པ་དེ་དག་གིས་མི་ཡི་ལུས་ཐོབ་སྟེ། དེ་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་བླ་ན་མེད་པར་ཡང་དག་པར་རྫོགས་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་མཆོག་ཏུ་སེམས་བསྐྱེད་ནས། ལོ་སྟོང་བྱེ་བ་མང་པོ་སངས་རྒྱས་དང་བྱང་སེམས་ལ་མཆོད་པ་རྒྱ་ཆེན་པ་ོདང་སེམས་ཅན་རྣམས་ལ་སྦྱིན་པ་ཚད་མེད་པ་བྱིན་པར་བྱས་ལ་དགེ་བའི་རྩ་བ་དེ་དག་ཀུན་ཀྱང་འགྲོ་བའི་དོན་གྱི་ཕྱིར་དུ་བྱང་ཆུབ་མཆོག་གི་རྒྱུར་ཡོངས་སུ་བསྔོ་བར་བྱས་ན་དེ་ལ་ཡང་བསོད་ནམས་དཔག་ཏུ་མེད་པ་ཡོད་ཀྱང་། བྱང་སེམས་གང་ཞིག་གིས་རྩེ་མོའི་མངོན་པར་རྟོགས་པའི་རང་བཞིན་གྱི་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་མཆོག་ལ་མངོན་པར་བརྩོན་པ་ན་དུས་རིང་པོར་ཕར་ཞོག །ཐ་ན་ཉི་མ་གཅིག་གཅིག་ཙམ་ལ་ཤེར་ཕྱིན་དེའི་རྗེས་སུ་མཐུན་པར་ལམ་སྒོམ་ཤིང་གཞན་ལ་སྟོན་པ་སོགས་བྱེད་ན་དེའི་བསོད་ནམས་དེ་ལ་གོང་དུ་བཤད་མ་ཐག་པའི་སྦྱིན་པའི་ཕུང་པོས་བསོད་ནམས་དེའི་ཆར་ཡང་འགྲན་པར་མི་ཕོད་པ་སྟེ་འགྲན་པར་མི་ནུས་པ་ཡིན་པ་དེ་ཡིས་ཕྱིར་ན་གཡེལ་བ་མེད་པར་དུས་རྟག་ཏུ་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕར་ཕྱིན་ནམ་རྩེ་སྦྱོར་བསྒོམ་པ་འདི་ལ་འཇུག་པར་བྱ་དགོས་སོ། །ཞེས་པའོ། །

Peak application. Second, the peak application: the Ornament states, from "If the beings of Jambudvīpa..." up to "...has the nature of sixteen increases." In this there are three parts: First, the characteristic of the peak stage of the peak application is the second Mahāyāna aid to penetration, which attains the sixteen increases of merit that surpass making offerings to Buddhas equal to the sentient beings of a trichiliocosm. Second, if divided: there are three peak stages of the peak application: small, medium, and great. The boundary is solely on the Mahāyāna path of preparation of peak. Among the sixteen increases of merit in the peak stage of the peak application, the first: the peak application where the increase of merit surpasses sentient beings of a trichiliocosm, such as those in Jambudvīpa, making offerings to Buddhas: the meaning of the two verses stated starting with "If in Jambudvīpa": Taking a hypothetical extreme as an example, "if" all the sentient beings without exception in a trichiliocosm, illustrated by the sentient beings "in Jambudvīpa," were to attain a human body, and all of them were to generate the mind for unsurpassed, perfectly complete supreme awakening, and for "many tens of millions of thousands of years" they were to make extensive offerings to Buddhas and bodhisattvas and give immeasurable generosity to sentient beings, and they were to fully dedicate all those roots of virtue as causes for supreme awakening for the sake of beings, even though they would have immeasurable merit; "if" any bodhisattva manifests endeavor in the supreme perfection of wisdom, which has the nature of the clear realization of the peak, let alone for a long time, if they meditate on the path in accordance with that perfection of wisdom and teach it to others and so forth for even just "a single day," the mass of generosity just explained above would "not dare to compete" with even a fraction of that merit, that is, it would be unable to compete; "therefore," one should without distraction and constantly engage in this meditation on the perfection of wisdom, or peak application. Thus it is said.

heading: **རྩེ་མོའི་སྦྱོར་བ།**
translation: The way one must endeavor in that path of the union of method and wisdom along with an example: the meaning of the three verses stated starting with "A bodhisattva". "Any bodhisattva" abiding in the peak application and so forth, in order to liberate from the bondage of karma and afflictions and from the suffering of saṃsāra the sentient beings subsumed by the five continuums—the transmigrators of gods, humans, and the three lower realms—who have been connected as fathers, mothers, and so forth since long ago in this place of saṃsāra, out of a desire to teach the realm of sentient beings that very non-abiding nirvāṇa which is the further shore of the ocean of saṃsāra by relying on the "broad path," that is, the extensive path of the Mahāyāna, should endeavor in the perfection of wisdom that realizes emptiness, together with compassion, "day and night" without distraction.

Just like that example, foolish ordinary beings who have not attained the noble path apprehend a self as inherently existent even though it is not ultimately established, and by focusing on the eye, nose, and so forth, they accept them as belonging to a self; from habituation to that, there arises the untrue complete conceptualization that perceives the self and what belongs to a self as true, and by the power of that, they accumulate karma, take birth again and again in existence, and continuously experience various sufferings such as perishing—that is, death—decline, and mental unhappiness. Just as it was taught that grasping at a self and what belongs to a self as existent even though they do not exist in the mode of abiding leads to complete affliction by the power of all-obscuring ignorance, it is stated that a bodhisattva who directly realizes the meaning of selflessness—that is, the non-apprehension of self and what belongs to a self in accordance with the unmistaken mode of abiding—knows the abiding nature and habituates to it, and thereby will attain the state of liberation, which is complete purification; moreover, that is conventional, but ultimately, a bodhisattva who genuinely knows that in this regard no person whatsoever becomes afflicted or completely pure will subsequently realize the perfection of wisdom, which realizes existence and peace as equal in being empty of true existence, thus it is said. The explanation of this is taught in the Aṣṭasāhasrikā by Subhūti asking, "Lord, what is the characteristic of the perfection of wisdom?" and so forth.

རྩེ་མོའི་སྦྱོར་བ། གཉིས་པ་རྩེ་མོའི་སྦྱོར་བ་ནི།རྒྱན་ལས། འཛམ་བུ་གླིང་གི་སྐྱེ་བོ་སྙིང་། །ནས། རྣམ་འཕེལ་བཅུ་དྲུག་བདག་ཉིད་དོ། །ཞེས་གསུངས། འདི་ལ་གསུམ་ལས། དང་པ་ནི། སྟོང་གསུམ་གྱི་སེམས་ཅན་དང་མཉམ་པའི་སངས་རྒྱས་མཆོད་པ་ལས་ལྷག་པའི་བསོད་ནམས་རྣམ་པར་འཕེལ་བ་བཅུ་དྲུག་ཐོབ་པའི་ཐེག་ཆེན་གྱི་ངེས་འབྱེད་ཆ་མཐུན་གཉིས་པ་དེ། རྩེ་མོ་རྩེ་སྦྱོར་གྱི་མཚན་ཉིད། གཉིས་པ་དེ་ལ་དབྱེ་ན། རྩེ་མོའི་རྩེ་སྦྱོར་ཆུང་འབྲིང་ཆེ་གསུམ་ཡོད། ས་མཚམས་ཐེག་ཆེན་གྱི་སྦྱོར་ལམ་རྩེ་མོ་ཁོ་ནར་ཡོད། རྩེ་མོའི་རྩེ་སྦྱོར་ལ་བསོད་ནམས་རྣམ་པར་འཕེལ་བ་བཅུ་དྲུག་ཡོད་པ་ལས། དང་པོ་ནི། འཛམ་བུ་གླིང་སོགས་སྟོང་གསུམ་གྱི་སེམས་ཅན་གྱིས་སངས་རྒྱས་མཆོད་པ་ལས་ལྷག་པའི་བསོད་ནམས་རྣམ་པར་འཕེལ་བའི་རྩེ་སྦྱོར་ནི། འཛམ་བུའི་གླིང་ན་ཞེས་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གཉིས་གསུངས་པའི་དོན། བརྟག་པ་མཐའ་བཟུང་གི་དབང་དུ་བཏང་ནས་དཔེར་བྱས་ན། འཛམ་བུ་གླིང་ན་ཡོད་པའི་སེམས་ཅན་གྱིས་མཚོན་བའི་སྟོང་གསུམ་གྱི་སེམས་ཅན་ཇི་སྙེད་མ་ལུས་པ་དེ་དག་གིས་མི་ཡི་ལུས་ཐོབ་སྟེ། དེ་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་བླ་ན་མེད་པར་ཡང་དག་པར་རྫོགས་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་མཆོག་ཏུ་སེམས་བསྐྱེད་ནས། ལོ་སྟོང་བྱེ་བ་མང་པོ་སངས་རྒྱས་དང་བྱང་སེམས་ལ་མཆོད་པ་རྒྱ་ཆེན་པ་ོདང་སེམས་ཅན་རྣམས་ལ་སྦྱིན་པ་ཚད་མེད་པ་བྱིན་པར་བྱས་ལ་དགེ་བའི་རྩ་བ་དེ་དག་ཀུན་ཀྱང་འགྲོ་བའི་དོན་གྱི་ཕྱིར་དུ་བྱང་ཆུབ་མཆོག་གི་རྒྱུར་ཡོངས་སུ་བསྔོ་བར་བྱས་ན་དེ་ལ་ཡང་བསོད་ནམས་དཔག་ཏུ་མེད་པ་ཡོད་ཀྱང་། བྱང་སེམས་གང་ཞིག་གིས་རྩེ་མོའི་མངོན་པར་རྟོགས་པའི་རང་བཞིན་གྱི་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་མཆོག་ལ་མངོན་པར་བརྩོན་པ་ན་དུས་རིང་པོར་ཕར་ཞོག །ཐ་ན་ཉི་མ་གཅིག་གཅིག་ཙམ་ལ་ཤེར་ཕྱིན་དེའི་རྗེས་སུ་མཐུན་པར་ལམ་སྒོམ་ཤིང་གཞན་ལ་སྟོན་པ་སོགས་བྱེད་ན་དེའི་བསོད་ནམས་དེ་ལ་གོང་དུ་བཤད་མ་ཐག་པའི་སྦྱིན་པའི་ཕུང་པོས་བསོད་ནམས་དེའི་ཆར་ཡང་འགྲན་པར་མི་ཕོད་པ་སྟེ་འགྲན་པར་མི་ནུས་པ་ཡིན་པ་དེ་ཡིས་ཕྱིར་ན་གཡེལ་བ་མེད་པར་དུས་རྟག་ཏུ་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕར་ཕྱིན་ནམ་རྩེ་སྦྱོར་བསྒོམ་པ་འདི་ལ་འཇུག་པར་བྱ་དགོས་སོ། །ཞེས་པའོ། །

Peak application. Second, the peak application: the Ornament states, from "If the beings of Jambudvīpa..." up to "...has the nature of sixteen increases." In this there are three parts: First, the characteristic of the peak stage of the peak application is the second Mahāyāna aid to penetration, which attains the sixteen increases of merit that surpass making offerings to Buddhas equal to the sentient beings of a trichiliocosm. Second, if divided: there are three peak stages of the peak application: small, medium, and great. The boundary is solely on the Mahāyāna path of preparation of peak. Among the sixteen increases of merit in the peak stage of the peak application, the first: the peak application where the increase of merit surpasses sentient beings of a trichiliocosm, such as those in Jambudvīpa, making offerings to Buddhas: the meaning of the two verses stated starting with "If in Jambudvīpa": Taking a hypothetical extreme as an example, "if" all the sentient beings without exception in a trichiliocosm, illustrated by the sentient beings "in Jambudvīpa," were to attain a human body, and all of them were to generate the mind for unsurpassed, perfectly complete supreme awakening, and for "many tens of millions of thousands of years" they were to make extensive offerings to Buddhas and bodhisattvas and give immeasurable generosity to sentient beings, and they were to fully dedicate all those roots of virtue as causes for supreme awakening for the sake of beings, even though they would have immeasurable merit; "if" any bodhisattva manifests endeavor in the supreme perfection of wisdom, which has the nature of the clear realization of the peak, let alone for a long time, if they meditate on the path in accordance with that perfection of wisdom and teach it to others and so forth for even just "a single day," the mass of generosity just explained above would "not dare to compete" with even a fraction of that merit, that is, it would be unable to compete; "therefore," one should without distraction and constantly engage in this meditation on the perfection of wisdom, or peak application. Thus it is said.

heading: **རྩེ་མོའི་སྦྱོར་བ།**
translation: Explaining the sign of bringing the perfection of wisdom to mind by way of clarifying that very meaning with an example: "For example, if a person" who "had not found it previously," that is, a "supreme jewel" that is difficult to find, were to find it at another time, their mind would be intensely joyful, but if as soon as they found it they fell under the sway of careless distraction and that jewel were "lost," since it was lost they would manifest a desire in their mind thinking, "When will I find that jewel?" and they would "always be miserable." Like that "example," a "bodhisattva" who has entered the path of "supreme awakening," having found this "perfection of wisdom" which is like a supreme jewel that is very difficult to find and of great significance, should "practice yoga" in it and "never abandon" it; "for example," just as finding again later that lost jewel, joyfully taking it, wrapping it in cloth and so forth with intense endeavor, and quickly going to one's own home for fear of losing it or having it stolen by others, and cherishing it, pacifies the sorrow of being parted from the jewel and the suffering of poverty, similarly if a bodhisattva constantly endeavors in meditation on the perfection of wisdom, they will quickly attain unsurpassed awakening. Thus it is said. This is the commentary on the twenty-second chapter, the Chapter on the Spiritual Friend, from the Commentary on the Verses of the Precious Qualities Collection, the Jewel Lamp Fulfilling the Hopes of the Fortunate Ones that Clarifies the Reality of Profound Dependent Arising.

Work: ཡོན་ཏན་རིན་པོ་ཆེ་སྡུད་པ་ཚིགས་སུ་བཅད་པའི་འགྲེལ་པ་ཟབ་མོ་རྟེན་འབྱུང་གི་དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཉིད་གསལ་བར་བྱེད་པའི་ནོར་བུའི་སྒྲོན་མེ་སྐལ་བཟང་རེ་སྐོང་། (Khenrab Jamyang, Commentary on the Verses of the Precious Qualities Collection), author: མཁྱེན་རབ་འཇམ་དབྱངས་བློ་བཟང་འཕྲིན་ལས།. དཔེ་དེ་བཞིན་དུ་འཕགས་ལམ་མ་ཐོབ་པའ་ིབྱིས་པ་སོ་སོའི་སྐྱེ་བོ་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་དོན་དམ་པར་གྲུབ་པ་མེད་བཞིན་དུ་བདག་རང་བཞིན་གྱིས་ཡོད་པར་བཟུང་བ་དང་མིག་སྣ་སོགས་ལ་དམིགས་ནས་བདག་གིར་ཁས་ལེན་པ་གོམས་ལམ་པ་ལས་བདག་དང་བདག་གིར་བ་དེར་བདེན་པར་འདུ་ཤེས་པ་ཡང་དག་པ་མིན་པའི་ཀུན་རྟོག་འབྱུང་ཞིང་དེའི་དབང་གིས་ལས་བསགས་ཏེ། སྲིད་པར་ཡང་ནས་ཡང་དུ་སྐྱེ་ཞིང་འཇིག་པ་སྟེ་འཆི་བ་དང་རྒུད་པ་དང་ཡིད་མི་བདེ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་སྡུག་བསྔལ་སྣ་ཚོགས་རྒྱུད་མར་མྱོང་བར་འགྱུར་རོ། །ཇི་ལྟར་གནས་ཚུལ་ལ་མེད་ཀྱང་བདག་དང་བདག་གི་བ་ཡོད་པར་འཛིན་པ་དེ་ལྟར་ཀུན་རྨོངས་མ་རིག་པའི་དབང་གིས་ཀུན་ནས་ཉོན་མངས་པར་བསྟན་ནས་ཕྱིན་ཅི་མ་ལོག་པའི་གནས་ཚུལ་ལྟར་བདག་དང་བདག་གིར་མི་དམིགས་པ་སྟེ་བདག་མེད་པའི་དོན་མངོན་སུམ་དུ་རྟོགས་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔས་གནས་ལུགས་ཀྱི་ཤེས་ཤིང་གོམས་པར་བྱས་པས་རྣམ་པར་བྱང་བ་ཐར་པའི་གོ་འཕང་ཐོབ་པར་འགྱུར་བར་གསུངས་ཏེ། དེའང་ཀུན་རྫོབ་ཏུ་ཡིན་གྱི་དོན་དམ་པར་ནི། འདི་ལ་གང་ཟག་གང་ཡང་ཉོན་མོངས་པ་དང་རྣམ་པར་དག་པ་ཉིད་དུ་འགྱུར་བ་མེད་པར་ཡང་དག་པར་ཤེས་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔས་སྲིད་ཞི་བདེན་སྟོང་མཉམ་པ་ཉིད་དུ་རྟོགས་པའི་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་རྗེས་སུ་རྟོགས་པར་འགྱུར་བ་ཡིན་ནོ། །ཞེས་སོ། །འདི་འཆད་པ་བརྒྱད་སྟོང་པ་ལས། རབ་འབྱོར་གྱིས་གསོལ་བ། བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པའི་མཚན་ཉིད་གང་ལགས་ཞེས་སོགས་ཀྱིས་བསྟན་ཏོ། །

Just like that example, foolish ordinary beings who have not attained the noble path apprehend a self as inherently existent even though it is not ultimately established, and by focusing on the eye, nose, and so forth, they accept them as belonging to a self; from habituation to that, there arises the untrue complete conceptualization that perceives the self and what belongs to a self as true, and by the power of that, they accumulate karma, take birth again and again in existence, and continuously experience various sufferings such as perishing—that is, death—decline, and mental unhappiness. Just as it was taught that grasping at a self and what belongs to a self as existent even though they do not exist in the mode of abiding leads to complete affliction by the power of all-obscuring ignorance, it is stated that a bodhisattva who directly realizes the meaning of selflessness—that is, the non-apprehension of self and what belongs to a self in accordance with the unmistaken mode of abiding—knows the abiding nature and habituates to it, and thereby will attain the state of liberation, which is complete purification; moreover, that is conventional, but ultimately, a bodhisattva who genuinely knows that in this regard no person whatsoever becomes afflicted or completely pure will subsequently realize the perfection of wisdom, which realizes existence and peace as equal in being empty of true existence, thus it is said. The explanation of this is taught in the Aṣṭasāhasrikā by Subhūti asking, "Lord, what is the characteristic of the perfection of wisdom?" and so forth.

རྩེ་མོའི་སྦྱོར་བ། གཉིས་པ་རྩེ་མོའི་སྦྱོར་བ་ནི།རྒྱན་ལས། འཛམ་བུ་གླིང་གི་སྐྱེ་བོ་སྙིང་། །ནས། རྣམ་འཕེལ་བཅུ་དྲུག་བདག་ཉིད་དོ། །ཞེས་གསུངས། འདི་ལ་གསུམ་ལས། དང་པ་ནི། སྟོང་གསུམ་གྱི་སེམས་ཅན་དང་མཉམ་པའི་སངས་རྒྱས་མཆོད་པ་ལས་ལྷག་པའི་བསོད་ནམས་རྣམ་པར་འཕེལ་བ་བཅུ་དྲུག་ཐོབ་པའི་ཐེག་ཆེན་གྱི་ངེས་འབྱེད་ཆ་མཐུན་གཉིས་པ་དེ། རྩེ་མོ་རྩེ་སྦྱོར་གྱི་མཚན་ཉིད། གཉིས་པ་དེ་ལ་དབྱེ་ན། རྩེ་མོའི་རྩེ་སྦྱོར་ཆུང་འབྲིང་ཆེ་གསུམ་ཡོད། ས་མཚམས་ཐེག་ཆེན་གྱི་སྦྱོར་ལམ་རྩེ་མོ་ཁོ་ནར་ཡོད། རྩེ་མོའི་རྩེ་སྦྱོར་ལ་བསོད་ནམས་རྣམ་པར་འཕེལ་བ་བཅུ་དྲུག་ཡོད་པ་ལས། དང་པོ་ནི། འཛམ་བུ་གླིང་སོགས་སྟོང་གསུམ་གྱི་སེམས་ཅན་གྱིས་སངས་རྒྱས་མཆོད་པ་ལས་ལྷག་པའི་བསོད་ནམས་རྣམ་པར་འཕེལ་བའི་རྩེ་སྦྱོར་ནི། འཛམ་བུའི་གླིང་ན་ཞེས་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གཉིས་གསུངས་པའི་དོན། བརྟག་པ་མཐའ་བཟུང་གི་དབང་དུ་བཏང་ནས་དཔེར་བྱས་ན། འཛམ་བུ་གླིང་ན་ཡོད་པའི་སེམས་ཅན་གྱིས་མཚོན་བའི་སྟོང་གསུམ་གྱི་སེམས་ཅན་ཇི་སྙེད་མ་ལུས་པ་དེ་དག་གིས་མི་ཡི་ལུས་ཐོབ་སྟེ། དེ་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་བླ་ན་མེད་པར་ཡང་དག་པར་རྫོགས་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་མཆོག་ཏུ་སེམས་བསྐྱེད་ནས། ལོ་སྟོང་བྱེ་བ་མང་པོ་སངས་རྒྱས་དང་བྱང་སེམས་ལ་མཆོད་པ་རྒྱ་ཆེན་པ་ོདང་སེམས་ཅན་རྣམས་ལ་སྦྱིན་པ་ཚད་མེད་པ་བྱིན་པར་བྱས་ལ་དགེ་བའི་རྩ་བ་དེ་དག་ཀུན་ཀྱང་འགྲོ་བའི་དོན་གྱི་ཕྱིར་དུ་བྱང་ཆུབ་མཆོག་གི་རྒྱུར་ཡོངས་སུ་བསྔོ་བར་བྱས་ན་དེ་ལ་ཡང་བསོད་ནམས་དཔག་ཏུ་མེད་པ་ཡོད་ཀྱང་། བྱང་སེམས་གང་ཞིག་གིས་རྩེ་མོའི་མངོན་པར་རྟོགས་པའི་རང་བཞིན་གྱི་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་མཆོག་ལ་མངོན་པར་བརྩོན་པ་ན་དུས་རིང་པོར་ཕར་ཞོག །ཐ་ན་ཉི་མ་གཅིག་གཅིག་ཙམ་ལ་ཤེར་ཕྱིན་དེའི་རྗེས་སུ་མཐུན་པར་ལམ་སྒོམ་ཤིང་གཞན་ལ་སྟོན་པ་སོགས་བྱེད་ན་དེའི་བསོད་ནམས་དེ་ལ་གོང་དུ་བཤད་མ་ཐག་པའི་སྦྱིན་པའི་ཕུང་པོས་བསོད་ནམས་དེའི་ཆར་ཡང་འགྲན་པར་མི་ཕོད་པ་སྟེ་འགྲན་པར་མི་ནུས་པ་ཡིན་པ་དེ་ཡིས་ཕྱིར་ན་གཡེལ་བ་མེད་པར་དུས་རྟག་ཏུ་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕར་ཕྱིན་ནམ་རྩེ་སྦྱོར་བསྒོམ་པ་འདི་ལ་འཇུག་པར་བྱ་དགོས་སོ། །ཞེས་པའོ། །

Peak application. Second, the peak application: the Ornament states, from "If the beings of Jambudvīpa..." up to "...has the nature of sixteen increases." In this there are three parts: First, the characteristic of the peak stage of the peak application is the second Mahāyāna aid to penetration, which attains the sixteen increases of merit that surpass making offerings to Buddhas equal to the sentient beings of a trichiliocosm. Second, if divided: there are three peak stages of the peak application: small, medium, and great. The boundary is solely on the Mahāyāna path of preparation of peak. Among the sixteen increases of merit in the peak stage of the peak application, the first: the peak application where the increase of merit surpasses sentient beings of a trichiliocosm, such as those in Jambudvīpa, making offerings to Buddhas: the meaning of the two verses stated starting with "If in Jambudvīpa": Taking a hypothetical extreme as an example, "if" all the sentient beings without exception in a trichiliocosm, illustrated by the sentient beings "in Jambudvīpa," were to attain a human body, and all of them were to generate the mind for unsurpassed, perfectly complete supreme awakening, and for "many tens of millions of thousands of years" they were to make extensive offerings to Buddhas and bodhisattvas and give immeasurable generosity to sentient beings, and they were to fully dedicate all those roots of virtue as causes for supreme awakening for the sake of beings, even though they would have immeasurable merit; "if" any bodhisattva manifests endeavor in the supreme perfection of wisdom, which has the nature of the clear realization of the peak, let alone for a long time, if they meditate on the path in accordance with that perfection of wisdom and teach it to others and so forth for even just "a single day," the mass of generosity just explained above would "not dare to compete" with even a fraction of that merit, that is, it would be unable to compete; "therefore," one should without distraction and constantly engage in this meditation on the perfection of wisdom, or peak application. Thus it is said.

heading: **རྩེ་མོའི་སྦྱོར་བ།**
translation: To explain, by combining three increases of merit, the way that path of the union of method and wisdom outshines discordant factors, the patience towards non-arising phenomena, and so forth: the meaning of the two verses stated starting with "The sun and clouds". "For example", when "the sun" parted from "clouds", extremely bright and possessing a net of light rays, rises, vanquishing all the dense black darkness, it "outshines" fireflies that have only a tiny amount of light, the light of all living beings who are able to clear away only the darkness in their vicinity with the light of their own bodies, the host of stars that illuminate a little, the light of the moon, and all the rest. Similarly, the "bodhisattva" who courses in the supreme perfection of wisdom endowed with all supreme aspects, who is like the sun parted from the clouds of obscurations, by naturally "coursing in emptiness and the signless", is a wise one who, by radiating the light rays of speech that teaches the selflessness of phenomena and persons, completely destroys the dense darkness of views such as the view of the transitory collection, and outshines all transmigrators who are like fireflies, śrāvaka arhats who are like other living beings, pratyekabuddhas who are like stars, and many other bodhisattvas lacking skill in method who are like the moon, and is thereby specially exalted. By that statement "coursing in emptiness and the signless", it teaches the increase of merit of patience towards non-arising phenomena and the two which are the non-apprehending of awakening and that which awakens, and it teaches the increase of merit that is specially exalted above arhats, pratyekabuddhas, and so forth.

[3-259] translation already produced for this document:
Explaining the sign of bringing the perfection of wisdom to mind by way of clarifying that very meaning with an example: "For example, if a person" who "had not found it previously," that is, a "supreme jewel" that is difficult to find, were to find it at another time, their mind would be intensely joyful, but if as soon as they found it they fell under the sway of careless distraction and that jewel were "lost," since it was lost they would manifest a desire in their mind thinking, "When will I find that jewel?" and they would "always be miserable." Like that "example," a "bodhisattva" who has entered the path of "supreme awakening," having found this "perfection of wisdom" which is like a supreme jewel that is very difficult to find and of great significance, should "practice yoga" in it and "never abandon" it; "for example," just as finding again later that lost jewel, joyfully taking it, wrapping it in cloth and so forth with intense endeavor, and quickly going to one's own home for fear of losing it or having it stolen by others, and cherishing it, pacifies the sorrow of being parted from the jewel and the suffering of poverty, similarly if a bodhisattva constantly endeavors in meditation on the perfection of wisdom, they will quickly attain unsurpassed awakening. Thus it is said. This is the commentary on the twenty-second chapter, the Chapter on the Spiritual Friend, from the Commentary on the Verses of the Precious Qualities Collection, the Jewel Lamp Fulfilling the Hopes of the Fortunate Ones that Clarifies the Reality of Profound Dependent Arising.

heading: **རྩེ་མོའི་སྦྱོར་བ།**
translation: To explain the way of ripening other trainees and the increase of merit of all classes of gods drawing near: two verses are stated starting with "For example, a king's". The meaning is: "For example," a "king's" son who gives away wealth in order to benefit the subjects, who desires to protect all beings from harm and to accomplish the goal of their benefit and happiness, who is skilled in method and of good character, becomes the chief of all the king's sons, is revered by all the subject beings, and becomes worthy of their going to his presence, each hoping to accomplish their own goals; if that prince brings benefit and joy to many sentient beings even now when he has not yet become king, "what need is there to mention" that he will accomplish the benefit of beings and bring them joy when he is consecrated as king, obtains the methods of sovereignty, and becomes a king abiding in sovereignty? Like that example, a wise "bodhisattva" who courses in the deeds of a prince with wisdom and compassion, gives the nectar of Dharma to hosts of fortunate beings and brings joy to gods and humans by establishing them on the path and so forth, so that the six classes of desire realm gods and so forth will come to their presence to listen to the Dharma and show reverence; if this bodhisattva endeavors to accomplish the benefit and happiness of many sentient beings even now during the phase of the path of training, what need is there to mention that they will bring benefit to all transmigrators when they become a Buddha, a Dharma King, and abide in the exalted wisdom of omniscient knowledge? Because it goes without saying. This is the commentary on the twenty-third chapter, the Chapter on Śakra, from the Commentary on the Verses of the Precious Qualities Collection, the Jewel Lamp Fulfilling the Hopes of the Fortunate Ones that Clarifies the Reality of Profound Dependent Arising.

The increase of merit of the union of method and wisdom is explained by one verse starting with "The perfection of wisdom". Those yogis who course in the supreme perfection of wisdom that has the nature of the peak stage of the peak application generate great compassion for all sentient beings tormented by suffering and accomplish the benefit of beings, yet they do not have the perception of sentient beings as truly existent; when they possess the excellent path in which such non-apprehending compassion and wisdom are united, those bodhisattvas who are skilled in method become unsurpassed objects of generosity, or fields of merit, for all beings, and constantly fully consume meaningful alms and so forth desired from the realms.

[3-259] translation already produced for this document:
Explaining the sign of bringing the perfection of wisdom to mind by way of clarifying that very meaning with an example: "For example, if a person" who "had not found it previously," that is, a "supreme jewel" that is difficult to find, were to find it at another time, their mind would be intensely joyful, but if as soon as they found it they fell under the sway of careless distraction and that jewel were "lost," since it was lost they would manifest a desire in their mind thinking, "When will I find that jewel?" and they would "always be miserable." Like that "example," a "bodhisattva" who has entered the path of "supreme awakening," having found this "perfection of wisdom" which is like a supreme jewel that is very difficult to find and of great significance, should "practice yoga" in it and "never abandon" it; "for example," just as finding again later that lost jewel, joyfully taking it, wrapping it in cloth and so forth with intense endeavor, and quickly going to one's own home for fear of losing it or having it stolen by others, and cherishing it, pacifies the sorrow of being parted from the jewel and the suffering of poverty, similarly if a bodhisattva constantly endeavors in meditation on the perfection of wisdom, they will quickly attain unsurpassed awakening. Thus it is said. This is the commentary on the twenty-second chapter, the Chapter on the Spiritual Friend, from the Commentary on the Verses of the Precious Qualities Collection, the Jewel Lamp Fulfilling the Hopes of the Fortunate Ones that Clarifies the Reality of Profound Dependent Arising.

heading: **རྩེ་མོའི་སྦྱོར་བ།**
translation: To explain the two increases of merit of outshining all māras and revering other bodhisattvas as similar to the Teacher and abiding in equal training with them: the meaning of the six verses stated starting with "At that time". "At that time" when coursing on the path of the union of method and wisdom that cannot be overpowered by discordant factors, the "evil māras" abiding in the trichiliocosm think, "This bodhisattva has passed beyond my domain and, having awakened, will cause many sentient beings to pass beyond as well, so my domain will become empty," and their minds become endowed with "agony", and thinking "I am unable to cause interruptions," they are stricken with "sorrow", and due to that, they experience physical suffering and mental displeasure, and become "faint-hearted" and weak; and unable to bear being tormented by suffering in that way, they think, "What can be done so that this bodhisattva's mind will shrink back and turn away from the path of the Great Vehicle?", and they cause interruptions, and in order to display great terror to that bodhisattva, they display various miracles, such as burning the directions with fire and casting meteors.

To explain, by combining three increases of merit, the way that path of the union of method and wisdom outshines discordant factors, the patience towards non-arising phenomena, and so forth: the meaning of the two verses stated starting with "The sun and clouds". "For example", when "the sun" parted from "clouds", extremely bright and possessing a net of light rays, rises, vanquishing all the dense black darkness, it "outshines" fireflies that have only a tiny amount of light, the light of all living beings who are able to clear away only the darkness in their vicinity with the light of their own bodies, the host of stars that illuminate a little, the light of the moon, and all the rest. Similarly, the "bodhisattva" who courses in the supreme perfection of wisdom endowed with all supreme aspects, who is like the sun parted from the clouds of obscurations, by naturally "coursing in emptiness and the signless", is a wise one who, by radiating the light rays of speech that teaches the selflessness of phenomena and persons, completely destroys the dense darkness of views such as the view of the transitory collection, and outshines all transmigrators who are like fireflies, śrāvaka arhats who are like other living beings, pratyekabuddhas who are like stars, and many other bodhisattvas lacking skill in method who are like the moon, and is thereby specially exalted. By that statement "coursing in emptiness and the signless", it teaches the increase of merit of patience towards non-arising phenomena and the two which are the non-apprehending of awakening and that which awakens, and it teaches the increase of merit that is specially exalted above arhats, pratyekabuddhas, and so forth.

To explain the way of ripening other trainees and the increase of merit of all classes of gods drawing near: two verses are stated starting with "For example, a king's". The meaning is: "For example," a "king's" son who gives away wealth in order to benefit the subjects, who desires to protect all beings from harm and to accomplish the goal of their benefit and happiness, who is skilled in method and of good character, becomes the chief of all the king's sons, is revered by all the subject beings, and becomes worthy of their going to his presence, each hoping to accomplish their own goals; if that prince brings benefit and joy to many sentient beings even now when he has not yet become king, "what need is there to mention" that he will accomplish the benefit of beings and bring them joy when he is consecrated as king, obtains the methods of sovereignty, and becomes a king abiding in sovereignty? Like that example, a wise "bodhisattva" who courses in the deeds of a prince with wisdom and compassion, gives the nectar of Dharma to hosts of fortunate beings and brings joy to gods and humans by establishing them on the path and so forth, so that the six classes of desire realm gods and so forth will come to their presence to listen to the Dharma and show reverence; if this bodhisattva endeavors to accomplish the benefit and happiness of many sentient beings even now during the phase of the path of training, what need is there to mention that they will bring benefit to all transmigrators when they become a Buddha, a Dharma King, and abide in the exalted wisdom of omniscient knowledge? Because it goes without saying. This is the commentary on the twenty-third chapter, the Chapter on Śakra, from the Commentary on the Verses of the Precious Qualities Collection, the Jewel Lamp Fulfilling the Hopes of the Fortunate Ones that Clarifies the Reality of Profound Dependent Arising.

heading: **རྩེ་མོའི་སྦྱོར་བ།**
translation: Who is the bodhisattva against whom the māras do not find an opportunity, even if they act in that way? "At whatever time" those "bodhisattvas" who are "skilled in wisdom and method", endowed with an intensely strong, unyielding intention for the path of the Great Vehicle, "constantly day and night look upon" and consider the meaning of the supreme "perfection of wisdom"; "at that time" when acting in that way, "the bodies and minds" of those bodhisattvas course "like birds" going in the sky, without fear of the precipices of existence and peace, because they abide on the path of the union of method and wisdom. Therefore, "how could" the evil "māras" and other partisans of the dark "find an opportunity" against those bodhisattvas? They will not.

གདུལ་བྱ་གཞན་སྨིན་པར་བྱེད་ཚུལ་དང་། ལྷའི་རིས་ཐམས་ཅད་ཉེར་བར་འོངས་བའི་རྣམས་འཕེལ་འཆད་པར། དཔེ་ན་རྒྱལ་པོའི་ཞེས་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གཉིས་གསུངས། དོན་ནི། དཔེར་ན་རྒྱལ་པོའི་བུ་ཞིག་འབང་ས་ལ་ཕན་ཕྱིར་ནོར་རྣམས་སྦྱིན་པ་གཏོང་བ་དང་། སྐྱ་ེབོ་ཀུན་གནད་འཚེ་ལས་སྐྱབས་པ་དང་ཕན་པ་དང་བདེ་བའི་དོན་སྒྲུབ་པར་འདོད་པ་ཐབས་ལ་མཁས་ཤིང་ངང་ཚུལ་བཟང་བ་དེ་ནི་རྒྱལ་པོའི་སྲས་ཀུན་གྱི་གཙོ་བོར་གྱུར་ཏེ། འབངས་ཀྱི་སྐྱེ་བོ་ཀུན་གྱིས་བཀུར་ཞིང་རང་གི་དོན་འགྲུབ་པ་རེ་རེ་བས་དེ་ཡི་དྲུང་དུ་མངོན་པར་འགྲོ་བར་བྱ་བའི་འོས་སུ་གྱུར་ཏེ། རྒྱལ་བུ་དེ་ནི་ད་ལྟ་རྒྱལ་པོར་མ་གྱུར་བའི་དུས་ན་ཡང་སེམས་ཅན་མང་པོ་ལ་ཕན་འདོགས་ཤིང་དགའ་བར་བྱེད་ན། རྒྱལ་པོར་དབང་བསྐུར་ཏེ་རྒྱལ་སྲིད་ཀྱི་ཐབས་ཐོབ་པར་གྱུར་ཏེ་རྒྱལ་སྲིད་ལ་གནས་པའི་རྒྱལ་པོར་གྱུར་བ་ན་སྐྱེ་དགུ་རྣམས་ཀྱི་དོན་བྱེད་ཅིང་དགའ་བར་བྱེད་པ་སྨྲོས་ཅི་དགོས། དཔེ་དེ་ལྟར་དུ་ཤེས་རབ་སྙིང་བརྩེར་བཅས་པར་རྒྱལ་སྲས་ཀྱི་སྤྱད་པ་སྤྱོད་པའི་མཁས་པ་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཡང༌། སྐལ་ལྡན་གྱི་སྐྱེ་བོའི་ཚོགས་ལ་ཆོས་ཀྱི་བདུད་རྩི་སྦྱིན་པར་བྱེད་ཅིང་ལམ་ལ་འགོད་པ་སོགས་ཀྱི་སྒོ་ནས་ལྷ་དང་མི་རྣམས་དགའ་བར་བྱེད་པས་འདོད་ལྷ་རིགས་དྲུག་སོགས་དེ་ཡི་དྲུང་དུ་འོང་ནས་ཆོས་ཉན་པ་དང་བཀུར་སྟི་བྱེད་པར་འགྱུར་ལ། བྱང་སེམས་འདི་ནི་སློབ་ལམ་གྱི་གནས་སྐབས་ད་ལྟ་ན་ཡང་སེམས་ཅན་མང་པོའི་ཕན་བདེ་སྒྲུབ་པར་བརྩོན་པར་བྱེད་ན་ཆོས་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་པོ་སངས་རྒྱས་སུ་གྱུར་ཏེ་རྣམ་པ་ཐམས་ཅད་མཁྱེན་པའི་ཡེ་ཤེས་ལ་གནས་པར་གྱུར་ན་འགྲོ་བ་ཀུན་ལ་ཕན་པ་མཛད་པ་སྨོས་ཅི་དགོས་ཏེ་སྨོས་མིདགོས་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །ཡོན་ཏན་རིན་པོ་ཆེ་སྡུད་པ་ཚིགས་སུ་བཅད་པའི་འགྲེལ་བ་ཟབ་མོ་རྟེན་འབྱུང་གི་དེ་་ཁོ་ན་ཉིད་གསལ་བར་བྱེད་པའི་ནོར་བུའི་སྒྲོན་མེ་སྐལ་བཟང་རེ་སྐོང་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལས་བརྒྱ་བྱིན་གྱི་ལེའུ་སྟེ་ཉེར་གསུམ་པའི་འགྲེལ་བའོ༎  །།
[3-261] translation already produced for this document:
To explain the way of ripening other trainees and the increase of merit of all classes of gods drawing near: two verses are stated starting with "For example, a king's". The meaning is: "For example," a "king's" son who gives away wealth in order to benefit the subjects, who desires to protect all beings from harm and to accomplish the goal of their benefit and happiness, who is skilled in method and of good character, becomes the chief of all the king's sons, is revered by all the subject beings, and becomes worthy of their going to his presence, each hoping to accomplish their own goals; if that prince brings benefit and joy to many sentient beings even now when he has not yet become king, "what need is there to mention" that he will accomplish the benefit of beings and bring them joy when he is consecrated as king, obtains the methods of sovereignty, and becomes a king abiding in sovereignty? Like that example, a wise "bodhisattva" who courses in the deeds of a prince with wisdom and compassion, gives the nectar of Dharma to hosts of fortunate beings and brings joy to gods and humans by establishing them on the path and so forth, so that the six classes of desire realm gods and so forth will come to their presence to listen to the Dharma and show reverence; if this bodhisattva endeavors to accomplish the benefit and happiness of many sentient beings even now during the phase of the path of training, what need is there to mention that they will bring benefit to all transmigrators when they become a Buddha, a Dharma King, and abide in the exalted wisdom of omniscient knowledge? Because it goes without saying. This is the commentary on the twenty-third chapter, the Chapter on Śakra, from the Commentary on the Verses of the Precious Qualities Collection, the Jewel Lamp Fulfilling the Hopes of the Fortunate Ones that Clarifies the Reality of Profound Dependent Arising.

[3-262] translation already produced for this document:
To explain the two increases of merit of outshining all māras and revering other bodhisattvas as similar to the Teacher and abiding in equal training with them: the meaning of the six verses stated starting with "At that time". "At that time" when coursing on the path of the union of method and wisdom that cannot be overpowered by discordant factors, the "evil māras" abiding in the trichiliocosm think, "This bodhisattva has passed beyond my domain and, having awakened, will cause many sentient beings to pass beyond as well, so my domain will become empty," and their minds become endowed with "agony", and thinking "I am unable to cause interruptions," they are stricken with "sorrow", and due to that, they experience physical suffering and mental displeasure, and become "faint-hearted" and weak; and unable to bear being tormented by suffering in that way, they think, "What can be done so that this bodhisattva's mind will shrink back and turn away from the path of the Great Vehicle?", and they cause interruptions, and in order to display great terror to that bodhisattva, they display various miracles, such as burning the directions with fire and casting meteors.

heading: **རྩེ་མོའི་སྦྱོར་བ།**
source: རང་གི་སྤྱོད་པ་ལ་སྐྱོན་ཞུགས་ན་གླགས་རྙེད་ཚུལ་ནི། དུས་གང་གི་ཚེ་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ནང་ཕན་ཚུན་ཁྲོས་ཏེ་ལུས་ཀྱིས་རྡེག་པ་ལ་སོགས་པ་བྱེད་པའི་འཐབ་པ་དང་ངག་གིས་མཚང་འབྲུ་བ་དང་རྒྱལ་པོའི་དྲུང་དུ་ཞལ་ལྕེ་གཅོད་པར་འགྱུར་བའི་རྩོད་པར་གྱུར་ཅིང་ཕན་ཚུན་མི་མཐུན་པར་ཞེ་སྡང་གིས་ཁྲོས་པའི་སེམས་དང་ལྡན་པར་འགྱུར་པ་དེ་ཡི་ཚེ་བདུད་སྡིག་ཅན་དེ་ནི་མཆོག་ཏུ་དགའ་ཞིང་ཉམས་བདེ་བར་འགྱུར་ཏེ། དེ་ཡི་རྒྱུ་མཚན་ཡང་བྱང་ཆུབ་་སེམས་དཔའ་དེ་གཉིས་ཀའང་འཐབ་རྩོད་བྱས་པའི་ཉེས་པས་རྒྱལ་བའི་ཡེ་ཤེས་ལས་ནི་ཐག་རིང་དུ་འགྱུར་ཞིང་ཐེག་པ་ཆེན་པོའི་ལམ་གྱི་བར་ཆད་དུ་འགྱུར་རོ་སྙམ་པའི་ཕྱིར། དེ་ལྟར་དེ་གཉིས་ཀ་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་ཡེ་ཤེས་ལས་རིང་དུ་འགྱུར་ཞིང་རྒྱུད་མ་རུང་བར་གནོད་འཚེ་བྱེད་པའི་སྲིན་པོ་དང་ཤ་ཟ་རྣམས་དང་འདྲ་བར་འགྱུར་ལ། དེ་གཉིས་ཀ་ཡང་སེམས་ཅན་ལ་ཕན་བདེ་སྒྲུབ་པའི་རང་གི་དམ་བཅས་དེ་རྩོད་པས་ཉམས་པར་བྱེད་པར་འགྱུར་རོ། །སྙིང་རྗེ་དང་བྱམས་པ་དང་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཀྱི་སེམས་སོགས་ཉམས་པར་འགྱུར་བའི་ཞེ་སྡང་དང་དེའི་གཉེན་པོ་བཟོད་པ་བསྒོམ་པ་དང་བྲལ་བ་ལ་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཐོབ་པ་ག་ལ་ཡོད་དེ། ས་བོན་མེས་ཚིག་པ་ལ་མྱུ་གུ་མི་འབྱུང་བ་བཞིན་ནོ། །བྱང་སེམས་རྣམས་ཕན་ཚུན་རྩོད་པར་གྱུར་བ་དེ་ཡི་ཚེ་བདུད་རྣམས་རང་གི་འཁོར་རམ་ཕྱོགས་དང་བཅས་ཏེ་རབ་ཏུ་དགའ་བར་འགྱུར་རོ། །དེས་ན་བྱང་སེམས་ལ་འདོད་ཆགས་ཀྱི་ཉེས་པ་ཆེན་པོ་དུས་ཡུན་རིང་བ་བྱུང་བ་ལས་ཁོང་ཁྲོ་སྐད་ཅིག་ཙམ་སྐྱེས་པས་བྱམས་སྙིང་རྗེ་ཉམས་ཤིང་དགེ་རྩ་འཇོམས་པ་སོགས་ཉེས་དམིགས་ཆེ་བར་མདོ་ལས་རྒྱ་ཆེར་གསུངས་ཏེ། ཟླ་བ་སྒྲོན་མའི་མདོ། མད་ོབཏུས་སུ་དྲངས་པ་ལས། ཕན་ཚུན་གནོད་པའི་སེམས་སུ་གང་བྱེད་པ། དེ་ལ་ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་ཐོས་པས་སྐྱོབ་མི་བྱེ་བསམ་གཏན་དང་ནི་དགོན་གནས་མི་སྐྱོབ་སྟེ། སྦྱིན་དང་སངས་རྒྱས་མཆོད་པའང་སྐྱོབ་མི་བྱེད། ཞེས་དང་། འཇམ་དཔལ་རྣམ་པར་རོལ་བའི་མདོ་ལས། འཇམ་དཔལ་ཁོང་ཁྲོ་བ་ཁོང་ཁྲོ་བ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི། བསྐལ་བ་བརྒྱར་བསགས་པའི་དགེ་བ་ཉེ་བར་འཇོམས་པར་བྱེད་པ་དེའི་ཕྱིར། ཁོང་ཁྲོ་བ་ཞེས་བྱའོ། །ཞེས་དང་། བྱམས་པ་སེངྒེའི་སྒྲ་ཆེན་པོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་མདོ་ལས་ཀྱང་། ཞེ་སྡང་གི་རྩོད་པ་དང་བཅས་པའི་གནས་ལས་དཔག་ཚད་བརྒྱར་འབྱོལ་བར་བྱ་སྟེ།ཞེ་ལྡང་གི་སེམས་བསྐྱེད་པར་མི་བྱའོ། །སྟོང་གསུམ་གྱི་སྟོང་ཆེན་པོའི་འཇིག་རྟེན་ཁམས་ཀྱི་སེམས་ཅན་ཐམས་ཅད་ལ་སྤྱོད་ཤིང་བརྡེག་ལ་མཚོན་གྱིས་བཏབ་པས་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གཞན་ལ་ཐ་བ་དང་ཞེས་སྡང་གི་སེམས་བསྐྱེད་པ་དེ་ཆེས་ཉེས་པ་ལྕི་ཞིང་དེས་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་རྨས་པ་དང་ཉམས་པར་འགྱུར་ཏ་རེ། དཔེར་ན་ལྕགས་ནི་ལྕགས་ལས་གཞན་བོང་བ་སོགས་ཀྱིས་མི་ཆོད་པ་ལྟར།བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའི་དགེ་བའི་རྩ་བ་ཡང་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཅིག་ཤོས་ཞེ་སྡང་བས་ཟད་པར་བྱེད་ཀྱིས་གཞན་གྱིས་ཟད་མི་ནུས་པས་ན། གཅིག་གིས་གཅིག་ལ་ཞེ་ས་དང་གུས་པ་དང་བཅས་པར་བྱ་སྟེ་སེམས་དང་པོ་བསྐྱེད་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ལ་ཡང་སྟོན་པའི་འདུ་ཤེས་བསྐྱེད་པར་བྱའོ། །ཞེས་གསུངས་སོ། །ཁྱད་པར་ལུང་བསྟན་ཐོབ་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ལ་ཁྲོ་བ་ནི་ཉེས་པ་ཤིན་ཏུ་ཆེ་སྟེ། ཐེག་པ་ཆེན་པོ་ལས་ཕྱིར་མི་ལྡོག་པར་ལུང་བསྟན་མ་ཐོབ་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གང་ཞིག་གིས་ཕྱིར་མི་ལྡོག་པར་ལུང་བསྟན་པའམ་རྟགས་ཐོབ་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ལ་སེམས་ཁྲོས་ནས་ལུས་ངག་གི་རྩོད་པ་རྩོམ་པར་བྱེད་ཅིང་དེ་ལ་འགྱོད་བཤགས་སོགས་མི་བྱེད་ཅིང་ཁྲོ་བའི་སེམས་མ་བཏད་ན། དགེ་བའི་ལོ་ཏོག་མི་སྐྱེ་བའི་ཞིང་ཐ་བ་ལྟ་བུའི་སྐྱོན་དང་ལྡན་པའི་ཁོང་ཁྲོ་སེམས་ཀྱི་སྐད་ཅིག་མ་ཅི་ཙམ་ཞིག་སྐྱེས་པ་ཇི་སྙེད་པ་དེ་སྙེད་ཀྱི་གྲངས་དང་མཉམ་པའི་བསྐལ་བར་ཞི་ནས་ལམ་ལ་བསླབ་པ་དང་ལམ་ལ་འཇུག་བའི་གོ་ཆ་བགོ་དགོས་སོ། །མདོ་ཀུན་ལས་བཏུས་སུ་བྱམས་པ་སེངྒེ་སྒྲས་མདོ་དྲངས་བ་ལས་ཀྱང་། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གང་ལ་ལ་ཞིག་གིས། སྟོང་གསུམ་གྱི་སྟོང་ཆེན་པོའི་འཇིག་རྟེན་གྱི་ཁམས་སུ་གཏོགས་པའི་སེམས་ཅན་ཐམས་ཅད་ལ་སྤྱོས་པ་དང་། བརྒྱད་པ་དང་དབྱུག་པ་དང་། ཁུར་ཚུར་གྱིས་བརྡེགས་པ་དེ་ཙམ་གྱིས། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ལ་རྨ་བྱུང་ཞིང་རྨས་པར་མི་འགྱུར་གྱི། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གང་གིས་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གཅིག་ལ།ཐ་ན་གནོད་སེམས་དང་། ཐ་བ་དང་ཞེ་སྡང་གི་སེམས་བསྐྱེད་པ་དེ་ཙམ་གྱིས། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ལ་རྨ་བྱུང་ཞིང་རྨས་པར་འགྱུར་རོ། །དེ་ཅིའི་ཕྱིར་ཞེ་ན། གལ་ཏེ་དེས་ཐམས་ཅད་མཁྱེན་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་མ་བཏང་ན། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔས་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གཅིག་ཤོས་ལ་གནོད་སེམས་དང་། ཐ་བ་དང་སྡང་བའི་སེམས་ཇི་སྙད་དུ་བསྐྱེད་པ་དེ་སྙེད་ཀྱི་བསྐལ་པར་གོ་ཆ་བཟོད་ཡང་བགོ་དགོས་སོ། །ཞེས་གསུངས་སོ། །དེ་བས་ན་ཐེག་པ་ཆེན་པོའི་ལམ་ཉམས་སུ་ལེན་པར་འདོད་པའི་གང་ཟག་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་སྲོག་ལ་བབས་ཀྱང་ཁྲོ་བོའི་གོ་སྐབས་དབྱེ་བར་མི་བྱ་ཞིང་བྱམས་སྙིང་རྗེ་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཀྱི་སེམས་ལ་ཉམས་ལེན་གྱི་མཐིལ་དུ་བྱའོ། །
translation: The way an opportunity is found if a fault enters one's behavior: "At whatever time" "bodhisattvas" become mutually enraged and engage in physical "fighting" by striking each other and so forth, or "disputing" by verbally exposing each other's faults or litigating before a king, and become mutually discordant, endowed with minds enraged with hatred; "at that time" "the evil māras" become "supremely joyous" and delighted. The reason for this is because they think: "Due to the fault of engaging in fighting and disputing, 'both' of those bodhisattvas 'will become distant from the Victor's exalted wisdom' and it will become an interruption to the path of the Great Vehicle." In that way, "both" of them "will become distant from the Buddha's exalted wisdom", and with their minds becoming corrupted, they become similar to harm-inflicting rākṣasas and piśācas. "Both" of them also cause their own vow to accomplish the benefit and happiness of sentient beings to degenerate through their "disputing." How could they attain awakening when they are endowed with hatred, which degenerates compassion, love, bodhicitta, and so forth, and are devoid of meditating on its antidote, patience? It is like a sprout not emerging from a seed burnt by fire. "At that time" when bodhisattvas engage in mutual disputes, "the māras together with their retinues" or partisans "will become intensely joyous." Therefore, it is taught extensively in the sutras that the disadvantages of a single instant of anger arising in a bodhisattva are greater than a great fault of attachment occurring for a long time, as it destroys love and compassion and annihilates roots of virtue and so forth. As quoted in the Sūtrasamuccaya from the Candrapradīpa Sūtra: "Whoever harbors a mind of mutual harm, they are not saved by ethical discipline and learning, they are not saved by concentration and dwelling in the wilderness, nor are they saved by generosity and making offerings to the Buddha." And from the Mañjuśrīvikrīḍita Sūtra: "Mañjuśrī, that which is called anger, anger, because it thoroughly destroys the virtue accumulated over a hundred eons, it is called anger." Also from the Sūtra of Maitreya's Great Lion's Roar: "One should avoid a place with angry disputes by a hundred yojanas, and one should not generate a mind of hatred. Generating a mind of malice and hatred towards another bodhisattva is a far heavier fault than scolding, striking, or stabbing with weapons all the sentient beings of the great trichiliocosm, and it will injure and corrupt the bodhisattva. Just as, for example, iron cannot be cut by anything other than iron, such as clods of earth, the roots of virtue of a bodhisattva are exhausted by hating another bodhisattva, but cannot be exhausted by anything else. Therefore, they should mutually show respect and reverence to one another, and should generate the recognition of the Teacher even towards a bodhisattva who has newly generated the mind [of awakening]." In particular, becoming angry at a bodhisattva who has received prophecy is an extremely great fault: if any bodhisattva who has not received the prophecy of irreversibility from the Great Vehicle becomes mentally enraged at a bodhisattva who has received the prophecy of irreversibility or has obtained the signs, and initiates physical or verbal disputes, and does not feel regret or confess it and so forth, and does not let go of the angry mind, they must don the armor of engaging in the path and train on the path after calming themselves, for a number of eons equal in number to however many instants of anger arose in them, endowed with faults like a barren field where crops of virtue do not grow. Furthermore, from the Sūtra of Maitreya's Lion's Roar quoted in the Sūtrasamuccaya: "If any bodhisattva scolds, reprimands, or strikes with a stick or fist all sentient beings belonging to the great trichiliocosm, merely by that, the bodhisattva will not incur a wound or become injured; but if any bodhisattva generates a malicious mind, or even a mind of malice and hatred, toward one bodhisattva, merely by that, the bodhisattva will incur a wound and become injured. Why is that? If they do not completely abandon omniscience, for as many times as the bodhisattva generated a malicious mind, or a mind of malice and hatred, toward the other bodhisattva, they must repeatedly don the armor for that many eons." Therefore, individuals who desire to practice the path of the Great Vehicle should not allow an opportunity for anger even at the cost of their lives, and should make love, compassion, and bodhicitta the core of their practice.

To explain the way of ripening other trainees and the increase of merit of all classes of gods drawing near: two verses are stated starting with "For example, a king's". The meaning is: "For example," a "king's" son who gives away wealth in order to benefit the subjects, who desires to protect all beings from harm and to accomplish the goal of their benefit and happiness, who is skilled in method and of good character, becomes the chief of all the king's sons, is revered by all the subject beings, and becomes worthy of their going to his presence, each hoping to accomplish their own goals; if that prince brings benefit and joy to many sentient beings even now when he has not yet become king, "what need is there to mention" that he will accomplish the benefit of beings and bring them joy when he is consecrated as king, obtains the methods of sovereignty, and becomes a king abiding in sovereignty? Like that example, a wise "bodhisattva" who courses in the deeds of a prince with wisdom and compassion, gives the nectar of Dharma to hosts of fortunate beings and brings joy to gods and humans by establishing them on the path and so forth, so that the six classes of desire realm gods and so forth will come to their presence to listen to the Dharma and show reverence; if this bodhisattva endeavors to accomplish the benefit and happiness of many sentient beings even now during the phase of the path of training, what need is there to mention that they will bring benefit to all transmigrators when they become a Buddha, a Dharma King, and abide in the exalted wisdom of omniscient knowledge? Because it goes without saying. This is the commentary on the twenty-third chapter, the Chapter on Śakra, from the Commentary on the Verses of the Precious Qualities Collection, the Jewel Lamp Fulfilling the Hopes of the Fortunate Ones that Clarifies the Reality of Profound Dependent Arising.

To explain the two increases of merit of outshining all māras and revering other bodhisattvas as similar to the Teacher and abiding in equal training with them: the meaning of the six verses stated starting with "At that time". "At that time" when coursing on the path of the union of method and wisdom that cannot be overpowered by discordant factors, the "evil māras" abiding in the trichiliocosm think, "This bodhisattva has passed beyond my domain and, having awakened, will cause many sentient beings to pass beyond as well, so my domain will become empty," and their minds become endowed with "agony", and thinking "I am unable to cause interruptions," they are stricken with "sorrow", and due to that, they experience physical suffering and mental displeasure, and become "faint-hearted" and weak; and unable to bear being tormented by suffering in that way, they think, "What can be done so that this bodhisattva's mind will shrink back and turn away from the path of the Great Vehicle?", and they cause interruptions, and in order to display great terror to that bodhisattva, they display various miracles, such as burning the directions with fire and casting meteors.

"At whatever time" those "bodhisattvas" who are "skilled in wisdom and method", endowed with an intensely strong, unyielding intention for the path of the Great Vehicle, "constantly day and night look upon" and consider the meaning of the supreme "perfection of wisdom"; "at that time" when acting in that way, "the bodies and minds" of those bodhisattvas course "like birds" going in the sky, without fear of the precipices of existence and peace, because they abide on the path of the union of method and wisdom. heading: **རྩེ་མོའི་སྦྱོར་བ།**
translation: The way one must rely on patience, since the faults of anger are as explained above: Since "the Buddhas touched" or attained "great awakening through the perfection of patience," "this angry mind," which is its discordant class, "is not good." Generating the mindfulness of thinking, "It destroys the roots of virtue accumulated over many eons and causes love and compassion to degenerate," one individually confesses that sin with intense regret and vows not to commit such faults again in the future. Thinking, "I must not give this corrupt mind an opportunity to arise in my continuum," one does not delight in fighting, disputes, and so forth; this is to "arrive at this path of the Great Vehicle, the dharma of the Buddha." Thus it is said. From the Commentary on the Verses of the Precious Qualities Collection Fulfilling the Hopes of the Fortunate: A Jeweled Lamp Illuminating the Suchness of Profound Dependent Arising, this is the commentary on the twenty-fourth chapter, the Chapter on Pride.

དེ་ལྟར་དེ་གཉིས་ཀ་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་ཡེ་ཤེས་ལས་རིང་དུ་འགྱུར་ཞིང་རྒྱུད་མ་རུང་བར་གནོད་འཚེ་བྱེད་པའི་སྲིན་པོ་དང་ཤ་ཟ་རྣམས་དང་འདྲ་བར་འགྱུར་ལ། མད་ོབཏུས་སུ་དྲངས་པ་ལས། ཕན་ཚུན་གནོད་པའི་སེམས་སུ་གང་བྱེད་པ། དེ་ལ་ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་ཐོས་པས་སྐྱོབ་མི་བྱེ་བསམ་གཏན་དང་ནི་དགོན་གནས་མི་སྐྱོབ་སྟེ། སྦྱིན་དང་སངས་རྒྱས་མཆོད་པའང་སྐྱོབ་མི་བྱེད། ཞེས་དང་། འཇམ་དཔལ་རྣམ་པར་རོལ་བའི་མདོ་ལས། འཇམ་དཔལ་ཁོང་ཁྲོ་བ་ཁོང་ཁྲོ་བ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི། བསྐལ་བ་བརྒྱར་བསགས་པའི་དགེ་བ་ཉེ་བར་འཇོམས་པར་བྱེད་པ་དེའི་ཕྱིར། ཁོང་ཁྲོ་བ་ཞེས་བྱའོ། །ཞེས་དང་། བྱམས་པ་སེངྒེའི་སྒྲ་ཆེན་པོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་མདོ་ལས་ཀྱང་། ཞེ་སྡང་གི་རྩོད་པ་དང་བཅས་པའི་གནས་ལས་དཔག་ཚད་བརྒྱར་འབྱོལ་བར་བྱ་སྟེ།ཞེ་ལྡང་གི་སེམས་བསྐྱེད་པར་མི་བྱའོ། །སྟོང་གསུམ་གྱི་སྟོང་ཆེན་པོའི་འཇིག་རྟེན་ཁམས་ཀྱི་སེམས་ཅན་ཐམས་ཅད་ལ་སྤྱོད་ཤིང་བརྡེག་ལ་མཚོན་གྱིས་བཏབ་པས་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གཞན་ལ་ཐ་བ་དང་ཞེས་སྡང་གི་སེམས་བསྐྱེད་པ་དེ་ཆེས་ཉེས་པ་ལྕི་ཞིང་དེས་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་རྨས་པ་དང་ཉམས་པར་འགྱུར་ཏ་རེ། དཔེར་ན་ལྕགས་ནི་ལྕགས་ལས་གཞན་བོང་བ་སོགས་ཀྱིས་མི་ཆོད་པ་ལྟར།བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའི་དགེ་བའི་རྩ་བ་ཡང་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཅིག་ཤོས་ཞེ་སྡང་བས་ཟད་པར་བྱེད་ཀྱིས་གཞན་གྱིས་ཟད་མི་ནུས་པས་ན། གཅིག་གིས་གཅིག་ལ་ཞེ་ས་དང་གུས་པ་དང་བཅས་པར་བྱ་སྟེ་སེམས་དང་པོ་བསྐྱེད་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ལ་ཡང་སྟོན་པའི་འདུ་ཤེས་བསྐྱེད་པར་བྱའོ། །ཞེས་གསུངས་སོ། །ཁྱད་པར་ལུང་བསྟན་ཐོབ་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ལ་ཁྲོ་བ་ནི་ཉེས་པ་ཤིན་ཏུ་ཆེ་སྟེ། ཐེག་པ་ཆེན་པོ་ལས་ཕྱིར་མི་ལྡོག་པར་ལུང་བསྟན་མ་ཐོབ་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གང་ཞིག་གིས་ཕྱིར་མི་ལྡོག་པར་ལུང་བསྟན་པའམ་རྟགས་ཐོབ་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ལ་སེམས་ཁྲོས་ནས་ལུས་ངག་གི་རྩོད་པ་རྩོམ་པར་བྱེད་ཅིང་དེ་ལ་འགྱོད་བཤགས་སོགས་མི་བྱེད་ཅིང་ཁྲོ་བའི་སེམས་མ་བཏད་ན། དགེ་བའི་ལོ་ཏོག་མི་སྐྱེ་བའི་ཞིང་ཐ་བ་ལྟ་བུའི་སྐྱོན་དང་ལྡན་པའི་ཁོང་ཁྲོ་སེམས་ཀྱི་སྐད་ཅིག་མ་ཅི་ཙམ་ཞིག་སྐྱེས་པ་ཇི་སྙེད་པ་དེ་སྙེད་ཀྱི་གྲངས་དང་མཉམ་པའི་བསྐལ་བར་ཞི་ནས་ལམ་ལ་བསླབ་པ་དང་ལམ་ལ་འཇུག་བའི་གོ་ཆ་བགོ་དགོས་སོ། །མདོ་ཀུན་ལས་བཏུས་སུ་བྱམས་པ་སེངྒེ་སྒྲས་མདོ་དྲངས་བ་ལས་ཀྱང་། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གང་ལ་ལ་ཞིག་གིས། སྟོང་གསུམ་གྱི་སྟོང་ཆེན་པོའི་འཇིག་རྟེན་གྱི་ཁམས་སུ་གཏོགས་པའི་སེམས་ཅན་ཐམས་ཅད་ལ་སྤྱོས་པ་དང་། བརྒྱད་པ་དང་དབྱུག་པ་དང་། ཁུར་ཚུར་གྱིས་བརྡེགས་པ་དེ་ཙམ་གྱིས། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ལ་རྨ་བྱུང་ཞིང་རྨས་པར་མི་འགྱུར་གྱི། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གང་གིས་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གཅིག་ལ།ཐ་ན་གནོད་སེམས་དང་། ཐ་བ་དང་ཞེ་སྡང་གི་སེམས་བསྐྱེད་པ་དེ་ཙམ་གྱིས། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ལ་རྨ་བྱུང་ཞིང་རྨས་པར་འགྱུར་རོ། །དེ་ཅིའི་ཕྱིར་ཞེ་ན། གལ་ཏེ་དེས་ཐམས་ཅད་མཁྱེན་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་མ་བཏང་ན། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔས་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གཅིག་ཤོས་ལ་གནོད་སེམས་དང་། ཐ་བ་དང་སྡང་བའི་སེམས་ཇི་སྙད་དུ་བསྐྱེད་པ་དེ་སྙེད་ཀྱི་བསྐལ་པར་གོ་ཆ་བཟོད་ཡང་བགོ་དགོས་སོ། །ཞེས་གསུངས་སོ། །དེ་བས་ན་ཐེག་པ་ཆེན་པོའི་ལམ་ཉམས་སུ་ལེན་པར་འདོད་པའི་གང་ཟག་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་སྲོག་ལ་བབས་ཀྱང་ཁྲོ་བོའི་གོ་སྐབས་དབྱེ་བར་མི་བྱ་ཞིང་བྱམས་སྙིང་རྗེ་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཀྱི་སེམས་ལ་ཉམས་ལེན་གྱི་མཐིལ་དུ་བྱའོ། །

The way an opportunity is found if a fault enters one's behavior: "At whatever time" "bodhisattvas" become mutually enraged and engage in physical "fighting" by striking each other and so forth, or "disputing" by verbally exposing each other's faults or litigating before a king, and become mutually discordant, endowed with minds enraged with hatred; "at that time" "the evil māras" become "supremely joyous" and delighted. The reason for this is because they think: "Due to the fault of engaging in fighting and disputing, 'both' of those bodhisattvas 'will become distant from the Victor's exalted wisdom' and it will become an interruption to the path of the Great Vehicle." In that way, "both" of them "will become distant from the Buddha's exalted wisdom", and with their minds becoming corrupted, they become similar to harm-inflicting rākṣasas and piśācas. "Both" of them also cause their own vow to accomplish the benefit and happiness of sentient beings to degenerate through their "disputing." How could they attain awakening when they are endowed with hatred, which degenerates compassion, love, bodhicitta, and so forth, and are devoid of meditating on its antidote, patience? It is like a sprout not emerging from a seed burnt by fire. "At that time" when bodhisattvas engage in mutual disputes, "the māras together with their retinues" or partisans "will become intensely joyous." Therefore, it is taught extensively in the sutras that the disadvantages of a single instant of anger arising in a bodhisattva are greater than a great fault of attachment occurring for a long time, as it destroys love and compassion and annihilates roots of virtue and so forth. As quoted in the Sūtrasamuccaya from the Candrapradīpa Sūtra: "Whoever harbors a mind of mutual harm, they are not saved by ethical discipline and learning, they are not saved by concentration and dwelling in the wilderness, nor are they saved by generosity and making offerings to the Buddha." And from the Mañjuśrīvikrīḍita Sūtra: "Mañjuśrī, that which is called anger, anger, because it thoroughly destroys the virtue accumulated over a hundred eons, it is called anger." Also from the Sūtra of Maitreya's Great Lion's Roar: "One should avoid a place with angry disputes by a hundred yojanas, and one should not generate a mind of hatred. Generating a mind of malice and hatred towards another bodhisattva is a far heavier fault than scolding, striking, or stabbing with weapons all the sentient beings of the great trichiliocosm, and it will injure and corrupt the bodhisattva. Just as, for example, iron cannot be cut by anything other than iron, such as clods of earth, the roots of virtue of a bodhisattva are exhausted by hating another bodhisattva, but cannot be exhausted by anything else. Therefore, they should mutually show respect and reverence to one another, and should generate the recognition of the Teacher even towards a bodhisattva who has newly generated the mind [of awakening]." In particular, becoming angry at a bodhisattva who has received prophecy is an extremely great fault: if any bodhisattva who has not received the prophecy of irreversibility from the Great Vehicle becomes mentally enraged at a bodhisattva who has received the prophecy of irreversibility or has obtained the signs, and initiates physical or verbal disputes, and does not feel regret or confess it and so forth, and does not let go of the angry mind, they must don the armor of engaging in the path and train on the path after calming themselves, for a number of eons equal in number to however many instants of anger arose in them, endowed with faults like a barren field where crops of virtue do not grow. Furthermore, from the Sūtra of Maitreya's Lion's Roar quoted in the Sūtrasamuccaya: "If any bodhisattva scolds, reprimands, or strikes with a stick or fist all sentient beings belonging to the great trichiliocosm, merely by that, the bodhisattva will not incur a wound or become injured; but if any bodhisattva generates a malicious mind, or even a mind of malice and hatred, toward one bodhisattva, merely by that, the bodhisattva will incur a wound and become injured. Why is that? If they do not completely abandon omniscience, for as many times as the bodhisattva generated a malicious mind, or a mind of malice and hatred, toward the other bodhisattva, they must repeatedly don the armor for that many eons." Therefore, individuals who desire to practice the path of the Great Vehicle should not allow an opportunity for anger even at the cost of their lives, and should make love, compassion, and bodhicitta the core of their practice.

heading: **རྩེ་མོའི་སྦྱོར་བ།**
translation: To teach the increase that is foremost among the inner ones, such as the two increases, by reason of becoming one possessing the lineage of the Buddha and attaining the fruition of Buddhahood itself, the meaning of the two verses stated starting with "Whoever, when training" is as follows: "When whoever," meaning a bodhisattva, "trains" on the path of the Great Vehicle, they do not accept any of the dharmas to be trained in—the three trainings, the six perfections, and so forth—ultimately, and they do not apprehend the training self and the dharmas to be trained in by it as truly existent. "Whoever trains like that," knowing "both these"—the antidote, the training of the bodhisattva, and its discordant class, "non-training," such as anger—as equally empty of true existence, "without conceptualizing" them as truly existent, "that is the unmistaken training in this perfection," the dharma that brings about the attainment of the state of a Buddha.

དུས་གང་གི་ཚེ་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ནང་ཕན་ཚུན་ཁྲོས་ཏེ་ལུས་ཀྱིས་རྡེག་པ་ལ་སོགས་པ་བྱེད་པའི་འཐབ་པ་དང་ངག་གིས་མཚང་འབྲུ་བ་དང་རྒྱལ་པོའི་དྲུང་དུ་ཞལ་ལྕེ་གཅོད་པར་འགྱུར་བའི་རྩོད་པར་གྱུར་ཅིང་ཕན་ཚུན་མི་མཐུན་པར་ཞེ་སྡང་གིས་ཁྲོས་པའི་སེམས་དང་ལྡན་པར་འགྱུར་པ་དེ་ཡི་ཚེ་བདུད་སྡིག་ཅན་དེ་ནི་མཆོག་ཏུ་དགའ་ཞིང་ཉམས་བདེ་བར་འགྱུར་ཏེ། དེ་ལྟར་དེ་གཉིས་ཀ་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་ཡེ་ཤེས་ལས་རིང་དུ་འགྱུར་ཞིང་རྒྱུད་མ་རུང་བར་གནོད་འཚེ་བྱེད་པའི་སྲིན་པོ་དང་ཤ་ཟ་རྣམས་དང་འདྲ་བར་འགྱུར་ལ།
