།སྙིང་རྗེ་དང་བྱམས་པ་དང་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཀྱི་སེམས་སོགས་ཉམས་པར་འགྱུར་བའི་ཞེ་སྡང་དང་དེའི་གཉེན་པོ་བཟོད་པ་བསྒོམ་པ་དང་བྲལ་བ་ལ་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཐོབ་པ་ག་ལ་ཡོད་དེ། ས་བོན་མེས་ཚིག་པ་ལ་མྱུ་གུ་མི་འབྱུང་བ་བཞིན་ནོ། །བྱང་སེམས་རྣམས་ཕན་ཚུན་རྩོད་པར་གྱུར་བ་དེ་ཡི་ཚེ་བདུད་རྣམས་རང་གི་འཁོར་རམ་ཕྱོགས་དང་བཅས་ཏེ་རབ་ཏུ་དགའ་བར་འགྱུར་རོ། །དེས་ན་བྱང་སེམས་ལ་འདོད་ཆགས་ཀྱི་ཉེས་པ་ཆེན་པོ་དུས་ཡུན་རིང་བ་བྱུང་བ་ལས་ཁོང་ཁྲོ་སྐད་ཅིག་ཙམ་སྐྱེས་པས་བྱམས་སྙིང་རྗེ་ཉམས་ཤིང་དགེ་རྩ་འཇོམས་པ་སོགས་ཉེས་དམིགས་ཆེ་བར་མདོ་ལས་རྒྱ་ཆེར་གསུངས་ཏེ། ཟླ་བ་སྒྲོན་མའི་མདོ། མད་ོབཏུས་སུ་དྲངས་པ་ལས། ཕན་ཚུན་གནོད་པའི་སེམས་སུ་གང་བྱེད་པ། དེ་ལ་ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་ཐོས་པས་སྐྱོབ་མི་བྱེ་བསམ་གཏན་དང་ནི་དགོན་གནས་མི་སྐྱོབ་སྟེ། སྦྱིན་དང་སངས་རྒྱས་མཆོད་པའང་སྐྱོབ་མི་བྱེད། ཞེས་དང་། འཇམ་དཔལ་རྣམ་པར་རོལ་བའི་མདོ་ལས། འཇམ་དཔལ་ཁོང་ཁྲོ་བ་ཁོང་ཁྲོ་བ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི། བསྐལ་བ་བརྒྱར་བསགས་པའི་དགེ་བ་ཉེ་བར་འཇོམས་པར་བྱེད་པ་དེའི་ཕྱིར། ཁོང་ཁྲོ་བ་ཞེས་བྱའོ། །ཞེས་དང་། བྱམས་པ་སེངྒེའི་སྒྲ་ཆེན་པོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་མདོ་ལས་ཀྱང་། ཞེ་སྡང་གི་རྩོད་པ་དང་བཅས་པའི་གནས་ལས་དཔག་ཚད་བརྒྱར་འབྱོལ་བར་བྱ་སྟེ།ཞེ་ལྡང་གི་སེམས་བསྐྱེད་པར་མི་བྱའོ། །སྟོང་གསུམ་གྱི་སྟོང་ཆེན་པོའི་འཇིག་རྟེན་ཁམས་ཀྱི་སེམས་ཅན་ཐམས་ཅད་ལ་སྤྱོད་ཤིང་བརྡེག་ལ་མཚོན་གྱིས་བཏབ་པས་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གཞན་ལ་ཐ་བ་དང་ཞེས་སྡང་གི་སེམས་བསྐྱེད་པ་དེ་ཆེས་ཉེས་པ་ལྕི་ཞིང་དེས་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་རྨས་པ་དང་ཉམས་པར་འགྱུར་ཏ་རེ། དཔེར་ན་ལྕགས་ནི་ལྕགས་ལས་གཞན་བོང་བ་སོགས་ཀྱིས་མི་ཆོད་པ་ལྟར།བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའི་དགེ་བའི་རྩ་བ་ཡང་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཅིག་ཤོས་ཞེ་སྡང་བས་ཟད་པར་བྱེད་ཀྱིས་གཞན་གྱིས་ཟད་མི་ནུས་པས་ན། གཅིག་གིས་གཅིག་ལ་ཞེ་ས་དང་གུས་པ་དང་བཅས་པར་བྱ་སྟེ་སེམས་དང་པོ་བསྐྱེད་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ལ་ཡང་སྟོན་པའི་འདུ་ཤེས་བསྐྱེད་པར་བྱའོ། །ཞེས་གསུངས་སོ། །ཁྱད་པར་ལུང་བསྟན་ཐོབ་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ལ་ཁྲོ་བ་ནི་ཉེས་པ་ཤིན་ཏུ་ཆེ་སྟེ། ཐེག་པ་ཆེན་པོ་ལས་ཕྱིར་མི་ལྡོག་པར་ལུང་བསྟན་མ་ཐོབ་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གང་ཞིག་གིས་ཕྱིར་མི་ལྡོག་པར་ལུང་བསྟན་པའམ་རྟགས་ཐོབ་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ལ་སེམས་ཁྲོས་ནས་ལུས་ངག་གི་རྩོད་པ་རྩོམ་པར་བྱེད་ཅིང་དེ་ལ་འགྱོད་བཤགས་སོགས་མི་བྱེད་ཅིང་ཁྲོ་བའི་སེམས་མ་བཏད་ན། དགེ་བའི་ལོ་ཏོག་མི་སྐྱེ་བའི་ཞིང་ཐ་བ་ལྟ་བུའི་སྐྱོན་དང་ལྡན་པའི་ཁོང་ཁྲོ་སེམས་ཀྱི་སྐད་ཅིག་མ་ཅི་ཙམ་ཞིག་སྐྱེས་པ་ཇི་སྙེད་པ་དེ་སྙེད་ཀྱི་གྲངས་དང་མཉམ་པའི་བསྐལ་བར་ཞི་ནས་ལམ་ལ་བསླབ་པ་དང་ལམ་ལ་འཇུག་བའི་གོ་ཆ་བགོ་དགོས་སོ། །མདོ་ཀུན་ལས་བཏུས་སུ་བྱམས་པ་སེངྒེ་སྒྲས་མདོ་དྲངས་བ་ལས་ཀྱང་། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གང་ལ་ལ་ཞིག་གིས། སྟོང་གསུམ་གྱི་སྟོང་ཆེན་པོའི་འཇིག་རྟེན་གྱི་ཁམས་སུ་གཏོགས་པའི་སེམས་ཅན་ཐམས་ཅད་ལ་སྤྱོས་པ་དང་། བརྒྱད་པ་དང་དབྱུག་པ་དང་། ཁུར་ཚུར་གྱིས་བརྡེགས་པ་དེ་ཙམ་གྱིས། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ལ་རྨ་བྱུང་ཞིང་རྨས་པར་མི་འགྱུར་གྱི། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གང་གིས་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གཅིག་ལ།ཐ་ན་གནོད་སེམས་དང་། ཐ་བ་དང་ཞེ་སྡང་གི་སེམས་བསྐྱེད་པ་དེ་ཙམ་གྱིས། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ལ་རྨ་བྱུང་ཞིང་རྨས་པར་འགྱུར་རོ། །དེ་ཅིའི་ཕྱིར་ཞེ་ན། གལ་ཏེ་དེས་ཐམས་ཅད་མཁྱེན་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་མ་བཏང་ན། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔས་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གཅིག་ཤོས་ལ་གནོད་སེམས་དང་། ཐ་བ་དང་སྡང་བའི་སེམས་ཇི་སྙད་དུ་བསྐྱེད་པ་དེ་སྙེད་ཀྱི་བསྐལ་པར་གོ་ཆ་བཟོད་ཡང་བགོ་དགོས་སོ། །ཞེས་གསུངས་སོ། །དེ་བས་ན་ཐེག་པ་ཆེན་པོའི་ལམ་ཉམས་སུ་ལེན་པར་འདོད་པའི་གང་ཟག་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་སྲོག་ལ་བབས་ཀྱང་ཁྲོ་བོའི་གོ་སྐབས་དབྱེ་བར་མི་བྱ་ཞིང་བྱམས་སྙིང་རྗེ་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཀྱི་སེམས་ལ་ཉམས་ལེན་གྱི་མཐིལ་དུ་བྱའོ། །
[3-264] translation already produced for this document:
The way an opportunity is found if a fault enters one's behavior: "At whatever time" "bodhisattvas" become mutually enraged and engage in physical "fighting" by striking each other and so forth, or "disputing" by verbally exposing each other's faults or litigating before a king, and become mutually discordant, endowed with minds enraged with hatred; "at that time" "the evil māras" become "supremely joyous" and delighted. The reason for this is because they think: "Due to the fault of engaging in fighting and disputing, 'both' of those bodhisattvas 'will become distant from the Victor's exalted wisdom' and it will become an interruption to the path of the Great Vehicle." In that way, "both" of them "will become distant from the Buddha's exalted wisdom", and with their minds becoming corrupted, they become similar to harm-inflicting rākṣasas and piśācas. "Both" of them also cause their own vow to accomplish the benefit and happiness of sentient beings to degenerate through their "disputing." How could they attain awakening when they are endowed with hatred, which degenerates compassion, love, bodhicitta, and so forth, and are devoid of meditating on its antidote, patience? It is like a sprout not emerging from a seed burnt by fire. "At that time" when bodhisattvas engage in mutual disputes, "the māras together with their retinues" or partisans "will become intensely joyous." Therefore, it is taught extensively in the sutras that the disadvantages of a single instant of anger arising in a bodhisattva are greater than a great fault of attachment occurring for a long time, as it destroys love and compassion and annihilates roots of virtue and so forth. As quoted in the Sūtrasamuccaya from the Candrapradīpa Sūtra: "Whoever harbors a mind of mutual harm, they are not saved by ethical discipline and learning, they are not saved by concentration and dwelling in the wilderness, nor are they saved by generosity and making offerings to the Buddha." And from the Mañjuśrīvikrīḍita Sūtra: "Mañjuśrī, that which is called anger, anger, because it thoroughly destroys the virtue accumulated over a hundred eons, it is called anger." Also from the Sūtra of Maitreya's Great Lion's Roar: "One should avoid a place with angry disputes by a hundred yojanas, and one should not generate a mind of hatred. Generating a mind of malice and hatred towards another bodhisattva is a far heavier fault than scolding, striking, or stabbing with weapons all the sentient beings of the great trichiliocosm, and it will injure and corrupt the bodhisattva. Just as, for example, iron cannot be cut by anything other than iron, such as clods of earth, the roots of virtue of a bodhisattva are exhausted by hating another bodhisattva, but cannot be exhausted by anything else. Therefore, they should mutually show respect and reverence to one another, and should generate the recognition of the Teacher even towards a bodhisattva who has newly generated the mind [of awakening]." In particular, becoming angry at a bodhisattva who has received prophecy is an extremely great fault: if any bodhisattva who has not received the prophecy of irreversibility from the Great Vehicle becomes mentally enraged at a bodhisattva who has received the prophecy of irreversibility or has obtained the signs, and initiates physical or verbal disputes, and does not feel regret or confess it and so forth, and does not let go of the angry mind, they must don the armor of engaging in the path and train on the path after calming themselves, for a number of eons equal in number to however many instants of anger arose in them, endowed with faults like a barren field where crops of virtue do not grow. Furthermore, from the Sūtra of Maitreya's Lion's Roar quoted in the Sūtrasamuccaya: "If any bodhisattva scolds, reprimands, or strikes with a stick or fist all sentient beings belonging to the great trichiliocosm, merely by that, the bodhisattva will not incur a wound or become injured; but if any bodhisattva generates a malicious mind, or even a mind of malice and hatred, toward one bodhisattva, merely by that, the bodhisattva will incur a wound and become injured. Why is that? If they do not completely abandon omniscience, for as many times as the bodhisattva generated a malicious mind, or a mind of malice and hatred, toward the other bodhisattva, they must repeatedly don the armor for that many eons." Therefore, individuals who desire to practice the path of the Great Vehicle should not allow an opportunity for anger even at the cost of their lives, and should make love, compassion, and bodhicitta the core of their practice.

heading: **རྩེ་མོའི་སྦྱོར་བ།**
translation: Any bodhisattva who "knows this training" without transgressing the stages of the two truths in that way, "this one will never," meaning at no time, degenerate from the trainings of wisdom and concentration, "and will not become of corrupted ethical discipline"—thus they become of the lineage of the Buddha. And it teaches the reason for attaining Buddhahood itself, stating, "Such a bodhisattva 'trains in this,'" such a path of the supreme vehicle, "in order to find" or attain "the dharmas of the Buddha," the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and so forth. This is because that bodhisattva will exceptionally increase in the training of concentration and the training of ethical discipline, and will be skilled in the training of wisdom. The reason for this is because they train by way of knowing them to be devoid of true existence, without even the slightest apprehension of their three spheres as truly existent. Thus it is said.

Do not add commentary, notes, or explanation of your own.

Work: ཡོན་ཏན་རིན་པོ་ཆེ་སྡུད་པ་ཚིགས་སུ་བཅད་པའི་འགྲེལ་པ་ཟབ་མོ་རྟེན་འབྱུང་གི་དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཉིད་གསལ་བར་བྱེད་པའི་ནོར་བུའི་སྒྲོན་མེ་སྐལ་བཟང་རེ་སྐོང་། (Khenrab Jamyang, Commentary on the Verses of the Precious Qualities Collection), author: མཁྱེན་རབ་འཇམ་དབྱངས་བློ་བཟང་འཕྲིན་ལས།. རང་གི་སྤྱོད་པ་ལ་སྐྱོན་ཞུགས་ན་གླགས་རྙེད་ཚུལ་ནི། དུས་གང་གི་ཚེ་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ནང་ཕན་ཚུན་ཁྲོས་ཏེ་ལུས་ཀྱིས་རྡེག་པ་ལ་སོགས་པ་བྱེད་པའི་འཐབ་པ་དང་ངག་གིས་མཚང་འབྲུ་བ་དང་རྒྱལ་པོའི་དྲུང་དུ་ཞལ་ལྕེ་གཅོད་པར་འགྱུར་བའི་རྩོད་པར་གྱུར་ཅིང་ཕན་ཚུན་མི་མཐུན་པར་ཞེ་སྡང་གིས་ཁྲོས་པའི་སེམས་དང་ལྡན་པར་འགྱུར་པ་དེ་ཡི་ཚེ་བདུད་སྡིག་ཅན་དེ་ནི་མཆོག་ཏུ་དགའ་ཞིང་ཉམས་བདེ་བར་འགྱུར་ཏེ། དེ་ཡི་རྒྱུ་མཚན་ཡང་བྱང་ཆུབ་་སེམས་དཔའ་དེ་གཉིས་ཀའང་འཐབ་རྩོད་བྱས་པའི་ཉེས་པས་རྒྱལ་བའི་ཡེ་ཤེས་ལས་ནི་ཐག་རིང་དུ་འགྱུར་ཞིང་ཐེག་པ་ཆེན་པོའི་ལམ་གྱི་བར་ཆད་དུ་འགྱུར་རོ་སྙམ་པའི་ཕྱིར། དེ་ལྟར་དེ་གཉིས་ཀ་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་ཡེ་ཤེས་ལས་རིང་དུ་འགྱུར་ཞིང་རྒྱུད་མ་རུང་བར་གནོད་འཚེ་བྱེད་པའི་སྲིན་པོ་དང་ཤ་ཟ་རྣམས་དང་འདྲ་བར་འགྱུར་ལ། དེ་གཉིས་ཀ་ཡང་སེམས་ཅན་ལ་ཕན་བདེ་སྒྲུབ་པའི་རང་གི་དམ་བཅས་དེ་རྩོད་པས་ཉམས་པར་བྱེད་པར་འགྱུར་རོ། །སྙིང་རྗེ་དང་བྱམས་པ་དང་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཀྱི་སེམས་སོགས་ཉམས་པར་འགྱུར་བའི་ཞེ་སྡང་དང་དེའི་གཉེན་པོ་བཟོད་པ་བསྒོམ་པ་དང་བྲལ་བ་ལ་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཐོབ་པ་ག་ལ་ཡོད་དེ། ས་བོན་མེས་ཚིག་པ་ལ་མྱུ་གུ་མི་འབྱུང་བ་བཞིན་ནོ། །བྱང་སེམས་རྣམས་ཕན་ཚུན་རྩོད་པར་གྱུར་བ་དེ་ཡི་ཚེ་བདུད་རྣམས་རང་གི་འཁོར་རམ་ཕྱོགས་དང་བཅས་ཏེ་རབ་ཏུ་དགའ་བར་འགྱུར་རོ། །དེས་ན་བྱང་སེམས་ལ་འདོད་ཆགས་ཀྱི་ཉེས་པ་ཆེན་པོ་དུས་ཡུན་རིང་བ་བྱུང་བ་ལས་ཁོང་ཁྲོ་སྐད་ཅིག་ཙམ་སྐྱེས་པས་བྱམས་སྙིང་རྗེ་ཉམས་ཤིང་དགེ་རྩ་འཇོམས་པ་སོགས་ཉེས་དམིགས་ཆེ་བར་མདོ་ལས་རྒྱ་ཆེར་གསུངས་ཏེ། ཟླ་བ་སྒྲོན་མའི་མདོ། མད་ོབཏུས་སུ་དྲངས་པ་ལས། ཕན་ཚུན་གནོད་པའི་སེམས་སུ་གང་བྱེད་པ། དེ་ལ་ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་ཐོས་པས་སྐྱོབ་མི་བྱེ་བསམ་གཏན་དང་ནི་དགོན་གནས་མི་སྐྱོབ་སྟེ། སྦྱིན་དང་སངས་རྒྱས་མཆོད་པའང་སྐྱོབ་མི་བྱེད། ཞེས་དང་། འཇམ་དཔལ་རྣམ་པར་རོལ་བའི་མདོ་ལས། འཇམ་དཔལ་ཁོང་ཁྲོ་བ་ཁོང་ཁྲོ་བ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི། བསྐལ་བ་བརྒྱར་བསགས་པའི་དགེ་བ་ཉེ་བར་འཇོམས་པར་བྱེད་པ་དེའི་ཕྱིར། ཁོང་ཁྲོ་བ་ཞེས་བྱའོ། །ཞེས་དང་། བྱམས་པ་སེངྒེའི་སྒྲ་ཆེན་པོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་མདོ་ལས་ཀྱང་། ཞེ་སྡང་གི་རྩོད་པ་དང་བཅས་པའི་གནས་ལས་དཔག་ཚད་བརྒྱར་འབྱོལ་བར་བྱ་སྟེ།ཞེ་ལྡང་གི་སེམས་བསྐྱེད་པར་མི་བྱའོ། །སྟོང་གསུམ་གྱི་སྟོང་ཆེན་པོའི་འཇིག་རྟེན་ཁམས་ཀྱི་སེམས་ཅན་ཐམས་ཅད་ལ་སྤྱོད་ཤིང་བརྡེག་ལ་མཚོན་གྱིས་བཏབ་པས་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གཞན་ལ་ཐ་བ་དང་ཞེས་སྡང་གི་སེམས་བསྐྱེད་པ་དེ་ཆེས་ཉེས་པ་ལྕི་ཞིང་དེས་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་རྨས་པ་དང་ཉམས་པར་འགྱུར་ཏ་རེ། དཔེར་ན་ལྕགས་ནི་ལྕགས་ལས་གཞན་བོང་བ་སོགས་ཀྱིས་མི་ཆོད་པ་ལྟར།བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའི་དགེ་བའི་རྩ་བ་ཡང་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཅིག་ཤོས་ཞེ་སྡང་བས་ཟད་པར་བྱེད་ཀྱིས་གཞན་གྱིས་ཟད་མི་ནུས་པས་ན། གཅིག་གིས་གཅིག་ལ་ཞེ་ས་དང་གུས་པ་དང་བཅས་པར་བྱ་སྟེ་སེམས་དང་པོ་བསྐྱེད་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ལ་ཡང་སྟོན་པའི་འདུ་ཤེས་བསྐྱེད་པར་བྱའོ། །ཞེས་གསུངས་སོ། །ཁྱད་པར་ལུང་བསྟན་ཐོབ་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ལ་ཁྲོ་བ་ནི་ཉེས་པ་ཤིན་ཏུ་ཆེ་སྟེ། ཐེག་པ་ཆེན་པོ་ལས་ཕྱིར་མི་ལྡོག་པར་ལུང་བསྟན་མ་ཐོབ་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གང་ཞིག་གིས་ཕྱིར་མི་ལྡོག་པར་ལུང་བསྟན་པའམ་རྟགས་ཐོབ་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ལ་སེམས་ཁྲོས་ནས་ལུས་ངག་གི་རྩོད་པ་རྩོམ་པར་བྱེད་ཅིང་དེ་ལ་འགྱོད་བཤགས་སོགས་མི་བྱེད་ཅིང་ཁྲོ་བའི་སེམས་མ་བཏད་ན། དགེ་བའི་ལོ་ཏོག་མི་སྐྱེ་བའི་ཞིང་ཐ་བ་ལྟ་བུའི་སྐྱོན་དང་ལྡན་པའི་ཁོང་ཁྲོ་སེམས་ཀྱི་སྐད་ཅིག་མ་ཅི་ཙམ་ཞིག་སྐྱེས་པ་ཇི་སྙེད་པ་དེ་སྙེད་ཀྱི་གྲངས་དང་མཉམ་པའི་བསྐལ་བར་ཞི་ནས་ལམ་ལ་བསླབ་པ་དང་ལམ་ལ་འཇུག་བའི་གོ་ཆ་བགོ་དགོས་སོ། །མདོ་ཀུན་ལས་བཏུས་སུ་བྱམས་པ་སེངྒེ་སྒྲས་མདོ་དྲངས་བ་ལས་ཀྱང་། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གང་ལ་ལ་ཞིག་གིས། སྟོང་གསུམ་གྱི་སྟོང་ཆེན་པོའི་འཇིག་རྟེན་གྱི་ཁམས་སུ་གཏོགས་པའི་སེམས་ཅན་ཐམས་ཅད་ལ་སྤྱོས་པ་དང་། བརྒྱད་པ་དང་དབྱུག་པ་དང་། ཁུར་ཚུར་གྱིས་བརྡེགས་པ་དེ་ཙམ་གྱིས། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ལ་རྨ་བྱུང་ཞིང་རྨས་པར་མི་འགྱུར་གྱི། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གང་གིས་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གཅིག་ལ།ཐ་ན་གནོད་སེམས་དང་། ཐ་བ་དང་ཞེ་སྡང་གི་སེམས་བསྐྱེད་པ་དེ་ཙམ་གྱིས། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ལ་རྨ་བྱུང་ཞིང་རྨས་པར་འགྱུར་རོ། །དེ་ཅིའི་ཕྱིར་ཞེ་ན། གལ་ཏེ་དེས་ཐམས་ཅད་མཁྱེན་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་མ་བཏང་ན། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔས་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གཅིག་ཤོས་ལ་གནོད་སེམས་དང་། ཐ་བ་དང་སྡང་བའི་སེམས་ཇི་སྙད་དུ་བསྐྱེད་པ་དེ་སྙེད་ཀྱི་བསྐལ་པར་གོ་ཆ་བཟོད་ཡང་བགོ་དགོས་སོ། །ཞེས་གསུངས་སོ། །དེ་བས་ན་ཐེག་པ་ཆེན་པོའི་ལམ་ཉམས་སུ་ལེན་པར་འདོད་པའི་གང་ཟག་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་སྲོག་ལ་བབས་ཀྱང་ཁྲོ་བོའི་གོ་སྐབས་དབྱེ་བར་མི་བྱ་ཞིང་བྱམས་སྙིང་རྗེ་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཀྱི་སེམས་ལ་ཉམས་ལེན་གྱི་མཐིལ་དུ་བྱའོ། །
[3-264] translation already produced for this document:
The way an opportunity is found if a fault enters one's behavior: "At whatever time" "bodhisattvas" become mutually enraged and engage in physical "fighting" by striking each other and so forth, or "disputing" by verbally exposing each other's faults or litigating before a king, and become mutually discordant, endowed with minds enraged with hatred; "at that time" "the evil māras" become "supremely joyous" and delighted. The reason for this is because they think: "Due to the fault of engaging in fighting and disputing, 'both' of those bodhisattvas 'will become distant from the Victor's exalted wisdom' and it will become an interruption to the path of the Great Vehicle." In that way, "both" of them "will become distant from the Buddha's exalted wisdom", and with their minds becoming corrupted, they become similar to harm-inflicting rākṣasas and piśācas. "Both" of them also cause their own vow to accomplish the benefit and happiness of sentient beings to degenerate through their "disputing." How could they attain awakening when they are endowed with hatred, which degenerates compassion, love, bodhicitta, and so forth, and are devoid of meditating on its antidote, patience? It is like a sprout not emerging from a seed burnt by fire. "At that time" when bodhisattvas engage in mutual disputes, "the māras together with their retinues" or partisans "will become intensely joyous." Therefore, it is taught extensively in the sutras that the disadvantages of a single instant of anger arising in a bodhisattva are greater than a great fault of attachment occurring for a long time, as it destroys love and compassion and annihilates roots of virtue and so forth. As quoted in the Sūtrasamuccaya from the Candrapradīpa Sūtra: "Whoever harbors a mind of mutual harm, they are not saved by ethical discipline and learning, they are not saved by concentration and dwelling in the wilderness, nor are they saved by generosity and making offerings to the Buddha." And from the Mañjuśrīvikrīḍita Sūtra: "Mañjuśrī, that which is called anger, anger, because it thoroughly destroys the virtue accumulated over a hundred eons, it is called anger." Also from the Sūtra of Maitreya's Great Lion's Roar: "One should avoid a place with angry disputes by a hundred yojanas, and one should not generate a mind of hatred. Generating a mind of malice and hatred towards another bodhisattva is a far heavier fault than scolding, striking, or stabbing with weapons all the sentient beings of the great trichiliocosm, and it will injure and corrupt the bodhisattva. Just as, for example, iron cannot be cut by anything other than iron, such as clods of earth, the roots of virtue of a bodhisattva are exhausted by hating another bodhisattva, but cannot be exhausted by anything else. Therefore, they should mutually show respect and reverence to one another, and should generate the recognition of the Teacher even towards a bodhisattva who has newly generated the mind [of awakening]." In particular, becoming angry at a bodhisattva who has received prophecy is an extremely great fault: if any bodhisattva who has not received the prophecy of irreversibility from the Great Vehicle becomes mentally enraged at a bodhisattva who has received the prophecy of irreversibility or has obtained the signs, and initiates physical or verbal disputes, and does not feel regret or confess it and so forth, and does not let go of the angry mind, they must don the armor of engaging in the path and train on the path after calming themselves, for a number of eons equal in number to however many instants of anger arose in them, endowed with faults like a barren field where crops of virtue do not grow. Furthermore, from the Sūtra of Maitreya's Lion's Roar quoted in the Sūtrasamuccaya: "If any bodhisattva scolds, reprimands, or strikes with a stick or fist all sentient beings belonging to the great trichiliocosm, merely by that, the bodhisattva will not incur a wound or become injured; but if any bodhisattva generates a malicious mind, or even a mind of malice and hatred, toward one bodhisattva, merely by that, the bodhisattva will incur a wound and become injured. Why is that? If they do not completely abandon omniscience, for as many times as the bodhisattva generated a malicious mind, or a mind of malice and hatred, toward the other bodhisattva, they must repeatedly don the armor for that many eons." Therefore, individuals who desire to practice the path of the Great Vehicle should not allow an opportunity for anger even at the cost of their lives, and should make love, compassion, and bodhicitta the core of their practice.

heading: **རྩེ་མོའི་སྦྱོར་བ།**
translation: Regarding the teaching on the increase of the non-arising of discordant classes such as miserliness, the meaning of the two verses stated starting with "The wise ones, makers of light": "When the wise ones," bodhisattvas who are skilled in the meaning of the two truths in that way, "the makers of light" who illuminate the dharma of profound emptiness, "train thus" in the perfection of wisdom, they do not generate even a single non-virtuous mind of afflictive conceptualizations, such as true grasping, miserliness, and so forth, which contradict the path of omniscience. Since their continuums are pervaded by the light of wisdom realizing profound emptiness, there is no refuge where the darkness of bad conceptualizations can abide. It is like how "even a slight amount of darkness does not abide in the space before the sun traveling in the sky, being overpowered by its light rays." Thus it is said.

དེ་ལྟར་དེ་གཉིས་ཀ་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་ཡེ་ཤེས་ལས་རིང་དུ་འགྱུར་ཞིང་རྒྱུད་མ་རུང་བར་གནོད་འཚེ་བྱེད་པའི་སྲིན་པོ་དང་ཤ་ཟ་རྣམས་དང་འདྲ་བར་འགྱུར་ལ། འཇམ་དཔལ་རྣམ་པར་རོལ་བའི་མདོ་ལས། འཇམ་དཔལ་ཁོང་ཁྲོ་བ་ཁོང་ཁྲོ་བ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི། བསྐལ་བ་བརྒྱར་བསགས་པའི་དགེ་བ་ཉེ་བར་འཇོམས་པར་བྱེད་པ་དེའི་ཕྱིར། ཁོང་ཁྲོ་བ་ཞེས་བྱའོ། །ཞེས་དང་། བྱམས་པ་སེངྒེའི་སྒྲ་ཆེན་པོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་མདོ་ལས་ཀྱང་། ཞེ་སྡང་གི་རྩོད་པ་དང་བཅས་པའི་གནས་ལས་དཔག་ཚད་བརྒྱར་འབྱོལ་བར་བྱ་སྟེ།ཞེ་ལྡང་གི་སེམས་བསྐྱེད་པར་མི་བྱའོ། །སྟོང་གསུམ་གྱི་སྟོང་ཆེན་པོའི་འཇིག་རྟེན་ཁམས་ཀྱི་སེམས་ཅན་ཐམས་ཅད་ལ་སྤྱོད་ཤིང་བརྡེག་ལ་མཚོན་གྱིས་བཏབ་པས་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གཞན་ལ་ཐ་བ་དང་ཞེས་སྡང་གི་སེམས་བསྐྱེད་པ་དེ་ཆེས་ཉེས་པ་ལྕི་ཞིང་དེས་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་རྨས་པ་དང་ཉམས་པར་འགྱུར་ཏ་རེ། དཔེར་ན་ལྕགས་ནི་ལྕགས་ལས་གཞན་བོང་བ་སོགས་ཀྱིས་མི་ཆོད་པ་ལྟར།བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའི་དགེ་བའི་རྩ་བ་ཡང་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཅིག་ཤོས་ཞེ་སྡང་བས་ཟད་པར་བྱེད་ཀྱིས་གཞན་གྱིས་ཟད་མི་ནུས་པས་ན། གཅིག་གིས་གཅིག་ལ་ཞེ་ས་དང་གུས་པ་དང་བཅས་པར་བྱ་སྟེ་སེམས་དང་པོ་བསྐྱེད་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ལ་ཡང་སྟོན་པའི་འདུ་ཤེས་བསྐྱེད་པར་བྱའོ། །ཞེས་གསུངས་སོ། །ཁྱད་པར་ལུང་བསྟན་ཐོབ་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ལ་ཁྲོ་བ་ནི་ཉེས་པ་ཤིན་ཏུ་ཆེ་སྟེ། ཐེག་པ་ཆེན་པོ་ལས་ཕྱིར་མི་ལྡོག་པར་ལུང་བསྟན་མ་ཐོབ་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གང་ཞིག་གིས་ཕྱིར་མི་ལྡོག་པར་ལུང་བསྟན་པའམ་རྟགས་ཐོབ་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ལ་སེམས་ཁྲོས་ནས་ལུས་ངག་གི་རྩོད་པ་རྩོམ་པར་བྱེད་ཅིང་དེ་ལ་འགྱོད་བཤགས་སོགས་མི་བྱེད་ཅིང་ཁྲོ་བའི་སེམས་མ་བཏད་ན། དགེ་བའི་ལོ་ཏོག་མི་སྐྱེ་བའི་ཞིང་ཐ་བ་ལྟ་བུའི་སྐྱོན་དང་ལྡན་པའི་ཁོང་ཁྲོ་སེམས་ཀྱི་སྐད་ཅིག་མ་ཅི་ཙམ་ཞིག་སྐྱེས་པ་ཇི་སྙེད་པ་དེ་སྙེད་ཀྱི་གྲངས་དང་མཉམ་པའི་བསྐལ་བར་ཞི་ནས་ལམ་ལ་བསླབ་པ་དང་ལམ་ལ་འཇུག་བའི་གོ་ཆ་བགོ་དགོས་སོ། །མདོ་ཀུན་ལས་བཏུས་སུ་བྱམས་པ་སེངྒེ་སྒྲས་མདོ་དྲངས་བ་ལས་ཀྱང་། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གང་ལ་ལ་ཞིག་གིས། སྟོང་གསུམ་གྱི་སྟོང་ཆེན་པོའི་འཇིག་རྟེན་གྱི་ཁམས་སུ་གཏོགས་པའི་སེམས་ཅན་ཐམས་ཅད་ལ་སྤྱོས་པ་དང་། བརྒྱད་པ་དང་དབྱུག་པ་དང་། ཁུར་ཚུར་གྱིས་བརྡེགས་པ་དེ་ཙམ་གྱིས། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ལ་རྨ་བྱུང་ཞིང་རྨས་པར་མི་འགྱུར་གྱི། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གང་གིས་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གཅིག་ལ།ཐ་ན་གནོད་སེམས་དང་། ཐ་བ་དང་ཞེ་སྡང་གི་སེམས་བསྐྱེད་པ་དེ་ཙམ་གྱིས། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ལ་རྨ་བྱུང་ཞིང་རྨས་པར་འགྱུར་རོ། །དེ་ཅིའི་ཕྱིར་ཞེ་ན། གལ་ཏེ་དེས་ཐམས་ཅད་མཁྱེན་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་མ་བཏང་ན། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔས་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གཅིག་ཤོས་ལ་གནོད་སེམས་དང་། ཐ་བ་དང་སྡང་བའི་སེམས་ཇི་སྙད་དུ་བསྐྱེད་པ་དེ་སྙེད་ཀྱི་བསྐལ་པར་གོ་ཆ་བཟོད་ཡང་བགོ་དགོས་སོ། །ཞེས་གསུངས་སོ། །དེ་བས་ན་ཐེག་པ་ཆེན་པོའི་ལམ་ཉམས་སུ་ལེན་པར་འདོད་པའི་གང་ཟག་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་སྲོག་ལ་བབས་ཀྱང་ཁྲོ་བོའི་གོ་སྐབས་དབྱེ་བར་མི་བྱ་ཞིང་བྱམས་སྙིང་རྗེ་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཀྱི་སེམས་ལ་ཉམས་ལེན་གྱི་མཐིལ་དུ་བྱའོ། །

The way an opportunity is found if a fault enters one's behavior: "At whatever time" "bodhisattvas" become mutually enraged and engage in physical "fighting" by striking each other and so forth, or "disputing" by verbally exposing each other's faults or litigating before a king, and become mutually discordant, endowed with minds enraged with hatred; "at that time" "the evil māras" become "supremely joyous" and delighted. The reason for this is because they think: "Due to the fault of engaging in fighting and disputing, 'both' of those bodhisattvas 'will become distant from the Victor's exalted wisdom' and it will become an interruption to the path of the Great Vehicle." In that way, "both" of them "will become distant from the Buddha's exalted wisdom", and with their minds becoming corrupted, they become similar to harm-inflicting rākṣasas and piśācas. "Both" of them also cause their own vow to accomplish the benefit and happiness of sentient beings to degenerate through their "disputing." How could they attain awakening when they are endowed with hatred, which degenerates compassion, love, bodhicitta, and so forth, and are devoid of meditating on its antidote, patience? It is like a sprout not emerging from a seed burnt by fire. "At that time" when bodhisattvas engage in mutual disputes, "the māras together with their retinues" or partisans "will become intensely joyous." Therefore, it is taught extensively in the sutras that the disadvantages of a single instant of anger arising in a bodhisattva are greater than a great fault of attachment occurring for a long time, as it destroys love and compassion and annihilates roots of virtue and so forth. As quoted in the Sūtrasamuccaya from the Candrapradīpa Sūtra: "Whoever harbors a mind of mutual harm, they are not saved by ethical discipline and learning, they are not saved by concentration and dwelling in the wilderness, nor are they saved by generosity and making offerings to the Buddha." And from the Mañjuśrīvikrīḍita Sūtra: "Mañjuśrī, that which is called anger, anger, because it thoroughly destroys the virtue accumulated over a hundred eons, it is called anger." Also from the Sūtra of Maitreya's Great Lion's Roar: "One should avoid a place with angry disputes by a hundred yojanas, and one should not generate a mind of hatred. Generating a mind of malice and hatred towards another bodhisattva is a far heavier fault than scolding, striking, or stabbing with weapons all the sentient beings of the great trichiliocosm, and it will injure and corrupt the bodhisattva. Just as, for example, iron cannot be cut by anything other than iron, such as clods of earth, the roots of virtue of a bodhisattva are exhausted by hating another bodhisattva, but cannot be exhausted by anything else. Therefore, they should mutually show respect and reverence to one another, and should generate the recognition of the Teacher even towards a bodhisattva who has newly generated the mind [of awakening]." In particular, becoming angry at a bodhisattva who has received prophecy is an extremely great fault: if any bodhisattva who has not received the prophecy of irreversibility from the Great Vehicle becomes mentally enraged at a bodhisattva who has received the prophecy of irreversibility or has obtained the signs, and initiates physical or verbal disputes, and does not feel regret or confess it and so forth, and does not let go of the angry mind, they must don the armor of engaging in the path and train on the path after calming themselves, for a number of eons equal in number to however many instants of anger arose in them, endowed with faults like a barren field where crops of virtue do not grow. Furthermore, from the Sūtra of Maitreya's Lion's Roar quoted in the Sūtrasamuccaya: "If any bodhisattva scolds, reprimands, or strikes with a stick or fist all sentient beings belonging to the great trichiliocosm, merely by that, the bodhisattva will not incur a wound or become injured; but if any bodhisattva generates a malicious mind, or even a mind of malice and hatred, toward one bodhisattva, merely by that, the bodhisattva will incur a wound and become injured. Why is that? If they do not completely abandon omniscience, for as many times as the bodhisattva generated a malicious mind, or a mind of malice and hatred, toward the other bodhisattva, they must repeatedly don the armor for that many eons." Therefore, individuals who desire to practice the path of the Great Vehicle should not allow an opportunity for anger even at the cost of their lives, and should make love, compassion, and bodhicitta the core of their practice.

heading: **རྩེ་མོའི་སྦྱོར་བ།**
translation: To teach the increase of knowing the way to practice by subsuming all perfections within the perfection of wisdom, together with an example, the two verses starting with "The perfection of wisdom" were stated. The meaning is: For those who train unmistakenly in the perfection of wisdom in this way, "all perfections, giving and so forth, are subsumed within this perfection of wisdom" realizing the non-apprehension of the three spheres. "For example, regarding the view of the transitory collection," just as it is stated in the Sūtra Requested by Brahmājāla that "all those sixty-two bad views" based on the extremes of past and future, such as the view that the self and the world are eternal, "are subsumed" within it, "similarly" to that example, it is stated that "all these perfections, giving and so forth," are subsumed within the practice of the perfection of wisdom realizing emptiness endowed with all supreme aspects, which is embraced by not lacking any aspect of method.

The way one must rely on patience, since the faults of anger are as explained above: Since "the Buddhas touched" or attained "great awakening through the perfection of patience," "this angry mind," which is its discordant class, "is not good." Generating the mindfulness of thinking, "It destroys the roots of virtue accumulated over many eons and causes love and compassion to degenerate," one individually confesses that sin with intense regret and vows not to commit such faults again in the future. Thinking, "I must not give this corrupt mind an opportunity to arise in my continuum," one does not delight in fighting, disputes, and so forth; this is to "arrive at this path of the Great Vehicle, the dharma of the Buddha." Thus it is said. From the Commentary on the Verses of the Precious Qualities Collection Fulfilling the Hopes of the Fortunate: A Jeweled Lamp Illuminating the Suchness of Profound Dependent Arising, this is the commentary on the twenty-fourth chapter, the Chapter on Pride.

[3-266] translation already produced for this document:
To teach the increase that is foremost among the inner ones, such as the two increases, by reason of becoming one possessing the lineage of the Buddha and attaining the fruition of Buddhahood itself, the meaning of the two verses stated starting with "Whoever, when training" is as follows: "When whoever," meaning a bodhisattva, "trains" on the path of the Great Vehicle, they do not accept any of the dharmas to be trained in—the three trainings, the six perfections, and so forth—ultimately, and they do not apprehend the training self and the dharmas to be trained in by it as truly existent. "Whoever trains like that," knowing "both these"—the antidote, the training of the bodhisattva, and its discordant class, "non-training," such as anger—as equally empty of true existence, "without conceptualizing" them as truly existent, "that is the unmistaken training in this perfection," the dharma that brings about the attainment of the state of a Buddha.

Any bodhisattva who "knows this training" without transgressing the stages of the two truths in that way, "this one will never," meaning at no time, degenerate from the trainings of wisdom and concentration, "and will not become of corrupted ethical discipline"—thus they become of the lineage of the Buddha. And it teaches the reason for attaining Buddhahood itself, stating, "Such a bodhisattva 'trains in this,'" such a path of the supreme vehicle, "in order to find" or attain "the dharmas of the Buddha," the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and so forth. This is because that bodhisattva will exceptionally increase in the training of concentration and the training of ethical discipline, and will be skilled in the training of wisdom. The reason for this is because they train by way of knowing them to be devoid of true existence, without even the slightest apprehension of their three spheres as truly existent. Thus it is said.

[3-268] translation already produced for this document:
Regarding the teaching on the increase of the non-arising of discordant classes such as miserliness, the meaning of the two verses stated starting with "The wise ones, makers of light": "When the wise ones," bodhisattvas who are skilled in the meaning of the two truths in that way, "the makers of light" who illuminate the dharma of profound emptiness, "train thus" in the perfection of wisdom, they do not generate even a single non-virtuous mind of afflictive conceptualizations, such as true grasping, miserliness, and so forth, which contradict the path of omniscience. Since their continuums are pervaded by the light of wisdom realizing profound emptiness, there is no refuge where the darkness of bad conceptualizations can abide. It is like how "even a slight amount of darkness does not abide in the space before the sun traveling in the sky, being overpowered by its light rays." Thus it is said.

heading: **རྩེ་མོའི་སྦྱོར་བ།**
translation: "For example, if the life faculty is stopped, all however many other faculties there are, such as the eye faculty and so forth, will also stop." Just so, for "whoever practices the perfection of wisdom," meaning the bodhisattvas who have become supremely skilled in the way of practicing the path of the Great Vehicle, "all" other "perfection" trainings "are subsumed within this" practice of the perfection of wisdom, and it is stated that without this perfection of wisdom, all others are absent. Thus it is said.

The way one must rely on patience, since the faults of anger are as explained above: Since "the Buddhas touched" or attained "great awakening through the perfection of patience," "this angry mind," which is its discordant class, "is not good." Generating the mindfulness of thinking, "It destroys the roots of virtue accumulated over many eons and causes love and compassion to degenerate," one individually confesses that sin with intense regret and vows not to commit such faults again in the future. Thinking, "I must not give this corrupt mind an opportunity to arise in my continuum," one does not delight in fighting, disputes, and so forth; this is to "arrive at this path of the Great Vehicle, the dharma of the Buddha." Thus it is said. From the Commentary on the Verses of the Precious Qualities Collection Fulfilling the Hopes of the Fortunate: A Jeweled Lamp Illuminating the Suchness of Profound Dependent Arising, this is the commentary on the twenty-fourth chapter, the Chapter on Pride.

[3-266] translation already produced for this document:
To teach the increase that is foremost among the inner ones, such as the two increases, by reason of becoming one possessing the lineage of the Buddha and attaining the fruition of Buddhahood itself, the meaning of the two verses stated starting with "Whoever, when training" is as follows: "When whoever," meaning a bodhisattva, "trains" on the path of the Great Vehicle, they do not accept any of the dharmas to be trained in—the three trainings, the six perfections, and so forth—ultimately, and they do not apprehend the training self and the dharmas to be trained in by it as truly existent. "Whoever trains like that," knowing "both these"—the antidote, the training of the bodhisattva, and its discordant class, "non-training," such as anger—as equally empty of true existence, "without conceptualizing" them as truly existent, "that is the unmistaken training in this perfection," the dharma that brings about the attainment of the state of a Buddha.

Any bodhisattva who "knows this training" without transgressing the stages of the two truths in that way, "this one will never," meaning at no time, degenerate from the trainings of wisdom and concentration, "and will not become of corrupted ethical discipline"—thus they become of the lineage of the Buddha. And it teaches the reason for attaining Buddhahood itself, stating, "Such a bodhisattva 'trains in this,'" such a path of the supreme vehicle, "in order to find" or attain "the dharmas of the Buddha," the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and so forth. This is because that bodhisattva will exceptionally increase in the training of concentration and the training of ethical discipline, and will be skilled in the training of wisdom. The reason for this is because they train by way of knowing them to be devoid of true existence, without even the slightest apprehension of their three spheres as truly existent. Thus it is said.

[3-268] translation already produced for this document:
Regarding the teaching on the increase of the non-arising of discordant classes such as miserliness, the meaning of the two verses stated starting with "The wise ones, makers of light": "When the wise ones," bodhisattvas who are skilled in the meaning of the two truths in that way, "the makers of light" who illuminate the dharma of profound emptiness, "train thus" in the perfection of wisdom, they do not generate even a single non-virtuous mind of afflictive conceptualizations, such as true grasping, miserliness, and so forth, which contradict the path of omniscience. Since their continuums are pervaded by the light of wisdom realizing profound emptiness, there is no refuge where the darkness of bad conceptualizations can abide. It is like how "even a slight amount of darkness does not abide in the space before the sun traveling in the sky, being overpowered by its light rays." Thus it is said.

heading: **རྩེ་མོའི་སྦྱོར་བ།**
translation: To explain the two increases—the increase of attaining all excellences and the increase of nearing awakening—one verse starting with "Wise bodhisattvas" was stated. The meaning is: That "bodhisattva skilled" in method and wisdom "trains" in "whatever are the qualities of the grounds and paths of the hearers, and likewise, all the qualities of the solitary realizers," in order to care for the trainees to be tamed by them. And although they care for those trainees, those bodhisattvas "do not abide" in that path of the lesser vehicle "and do not generate the desire to attain their fruitions." Thinking, "This path is merely to be known or trained in by me for the sake of caring for other trainees, but is not to be actualized," "therefore," they train in "all" the paths of the three vehicles. These increases are explained in the Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines by the passage: "Subhūti, moreover, if all however many sentient beings there are in Jambudvīpa were to simultaneously obtain a human body, and having obtained a human body, were to generate the mind set on unexcelled, perfect awakening..." and so forth. It is like how "even a slight amount of darkness does not abide in the space before the sun traveling in the sky, being overpowered by its light rays." Thus it is said.

translation: Peak training of patience. Third, regarding the peak training of patience: It is stated in the Ornament, from "Of the phenomena of the three omnisciences..." up to "...is plainly called stability." Among the three aspects of this—definition, divisions, and boundary—first: The definition of the peak training of patience is the third aid to penetration of the vehicle, which is the wisdom completely conforming to the three omnisciences and the attainment of stability not diverted from the welfare of others. Second, if that is divided, there are three peak trainings of patience: small, middling, and great. The boundary is solely on [the level of] patience. To explain this very stability or peak training of patience, which is the firm attainment of the realization of method and wisdom, one verse starting with "Irreversible awakening" was stated. Although Buddhaśrī applies [the text] from here onwards to the state of mind continually abiding, it is as the Master applied it to stability. Moreover, if someone else rejoices from the depths of their heart at the mind generation of that person—a bodhisattva who, having stably attained the realization of method and wisdom, possesses a stable, intense mind generation (the intention desiring to establish beings in supreme awakening without turning back from the Great Vehicle) and who has thoroughly engaged by means of the application of practicing the perfections and so forth—then, while it is possible to capture the measure by weighing on a scale the kings of mountains, the Mount Merus, present in this great trichiliocosm, that virtue of rejoicing in the bodhisattva's roots of virtue cannot be thus measured, because it is limitless. Gungtang Jamyang stated that this is the hidden meaning, because it teaches that rejoicing illustrates their firm realization of method and wisdom.

To explain the two increases—the increase of attaining all excellences and the increase of nearing awakening—one verse starting with "Wise bodhisattvas" was stated. The meaning is: That "bodhisattva skilled" in method and wisdom "trains" in "whatever are the qualities of the grounds and paths of the hearers, and likewise, all the qualities of the solitary realizers," in order to care for the trainees to be tamed by them. And although they care for those trainees, those bodhisattvas "do not abide" in that path of the lesser vehicle "and do not generate the desire to attain their fruitions." Thinking, "This path is merely to be known or trained in by me for the sake of caring for other trainees, but is not to be actualized," "therefore," they train in "all" the paths of the three vehicles. These increases are explained in the Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines by the passage: "Subhūti, moreover, if all however many sentient beings there are in Jambudvīpa were to simultaneously obtain a human body, and having obtained a human body, were to generate the mind set on unexcelled, perfect awakening..." and so forth. From the Commentary on the Verses of the Precious Qualities Collection Fulfilling the Hopes of the Fortunate: A Jeweled Lamp Illuminating the Suchness of Profound Dependent Arising, this is the commentary on the twenty-fifth chapter, the Chapter on Training.

translation: Peak training of supreme dharma. Fourth, regarding the peak training of supreme dharma: It is stated in the Ornament, from "Those in four continents, a thousand..." up to "...are proclaimed to be the meditative concentration." Among the three aspects of this, first: The definition of the peak training of supreme dharma is the fourth aid to penetration of the Great Vehicle, which attains the state of mind continually abiding in meditative concentration passed beyond extremes, from the perspective of having ripened the capacity to generate the path of seeing of the Great Vehicle, which is its fruition. Second, if that is divided, there are three supreme dharmas: small, middling, and great. Third, the boundary is solely on [the level of] supreme dharma of the path of preparation of the Great Vehicle.

Regarding the teaching on the increase of the non-arising of discordant classes such as miserliness, the meaning of the two verses stated starting with "The wise ones, makers of light": "When the wise ones," bodhisattvas who are skilled in the meaning of the two truths in that way, "the makers of light" who illuminate the dharma of profound emptiness, "train thus" in the perfection of wisdom, they do not generate even a single non-virtuous mind of afflictive conceptualizations, such as true grasping, miserliness, and so forth, which contradict the path of omniscience. Since their continuums are pervaded by the light of wisdom realizing profound emptiness, there is no refuge where the darkness of bad conceptualizations can abide. To explain the two increases—the increase of attaining all excellences and the increase of nearing awakening—one verse starting with "Wise bodhisattvas" was stated. The meaning is: That "bodhisattva skilled" in method and wisdom "trains" in "whatever are the qualities of the grounds and paths of the hearers, and likewise, all the qualities of the solitary realizers," in order to care for the trainees to be tamed by them. And although they care for those trainees, those bodhisattvas "do not abide" in that path of the lesser vehicle "and do not generate the desire to attain their fruitions." Thinking, "This path is merely to be known or trained in by me for the sake of caring for other trainees, but is not to be actualized," "therefore," they train in "all" the paths of the three vehicles. These increases are explained in the Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines by the passage: "Subhūti, moreover, if all however many sentient beings there are in Jambudvīpa were to simultaneously obtain a human body, and having obtained a human body, were to generate the mind set on unexcelled, perfect awakening..." and so forth. From the Commentary on the Verses of the Precious Qualities Collection Fulfilling the Hopes of the Fortunate: A Jeweled Lamp Illuminating the Suchness of Profound Dependent Arising, this is the commentary on the twenty-fifth chapter, the Chapter on Training.

heading: **ཆོས་མཆོག་གི་རྩེ་སྦྱོར།**
translation: To explain the peak training of the state of mind continually abiding, the meaning of the one verse stated starting with "Seeking virtue" is: If one asks what the reason is that rejoicing in the roots of virtue of a bodhisattva in that way has such great benefits: By directly rejoicing solely in that virtue of the bodhisattvas, one indirectly comes to rejoice in the aggregate of merit of all however many sentient beings there are in the world who "seek virtue" for themselves and who desire to benefit other beings. Why is that? It is because whatever virtue bodhisattvas accumulate is for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings. Those irreversible bodhisattvas, by the power of that excellent path, will attain all the qualities of the omniscient victors, and in order to exhaust without remainder the suffering of sentient beings wandering in cyclic existence, they give the gift of dharma in all worlds and establish beings without remainder on the path of awakening. Thus it is said.

[3-268] translation already produced for this document:
Regarding the teaching on the increase of the non-arising of discordant classes such as miserliness, the meaning of the two verses stated starting with "The wise ones, makers of light": "When the wise ones," bodhisattvas who are skilled in the meaning of the two truths in that way, "the makers of light" who illuminate the dharma of profound emptiness, "train thus" in the perfection of wisdom, they do not generate even a single non-virtuous mind of afflictive conceptualizations, such as true grasping, miserliness, and so forth, which contradict the path of omniscience. Since their continuums are pervaded by the light of wisdom realizing profound emptiness, there is no refuge where the darkness of bad conceptualizations can abide. It is like how "even a slight amount of darkness does not abide in the space before the sun traveling in the sky, being overpowered by its light rays." Thus it is said.

To teach the increase of knowing the way to practice by subsuming all perfections within the perfection of wisdom, together with an example, the two verses starting with "The perfection of wisdom" were stated. The meaning is: For those who train unmistakenly in the perfection of wisdom in this way, "all perfections, giving and so forth, are subsumed within this perfection of wisdom" realizing the non-apprehension of the three spheres. "For example, regarding the view of the transitory collection," just as it is stated in the Sūtra Requested by Brahmājāla that "all those sixty-two bad views" based on the extremes of past and future, such as the view that the self and the world are eternal, "are subsumed" within it, "similarly" to that example, it is stated that "all these perfections, giving and so forth," are subsumed within the practice of the perfection of wisdom realizing emptiness endowed with all supreme aspects, which is embraced by not lacking any aspect of method.

[3-271] translation already produced for this document:
To explain the two increases—the increase of attaining all excellences and the increase of nearing awakening—one verse starting with "Wise bodhisattvas" was stated. The meaning is: That "bodhisattva skilled" in method and wisdom "trains" in "whatever are the qualities of the grounds and paths of the hearers, and likewise, all the qualities of the solitary realizers," in order to care for the trainees to be tamed by them. And although they care for those trainees, those bodhisattvas "do not abide" in that path of the lesser vehicle "and do not generate the desire to attain their fruitions." Thinking, "This path is merely to be known or trained in by me for the sake of caring for other trainees, but is not to be actualized," "therefore," they train in "all" the paths of the three vehicles. These increases are explained in the Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines by the passage: "Subhūti, moreover, if all however many sentient beings there are in Jambudvīpa were to simultaneously obtain a human body, and having obtained a human body, were to generate the mind set on unexcelled, perfect awakening..." and so forth. From the Commentary on the Verses of the Precious Qualities Collection Fulfilling the Hopes of the Fortunate: A Jeweled Lamp Illuminating the Suchness of Profound Dependent Arising, this is the commentary on the twenty-fifth chapter, the Chapter on Training.

source: མཐོང་ལམ་གྱི་རྩེ་སྦྱོར།ལྔ་པ་མཐོང་ལམ་གྱི་རྩེ་སྦྱོར་སྟོན་པར། རྒྱན་ལས། འཇུག་པ་དང་ནི་ལྡོག་པ་ལ། །ནས། བསྡུས་པ་དེ་འདིར་མཐོང་བའི་ལམ། །ཞེས་གསུངས། འདི་ལ་གསུམ་ལས། དང་པོ་ནི། མཐོང་སྤངས་རྟོག་བའི་ས་བོན་གྱི་དངོས་གཉེན་གྱི་རིགས་སུ་གནས་པའི་ཐེག་ཆེན་གྱི་བདེན་པ་མངོན་རྟོགས་དེ། མཐོང་ལམ་རྩེ་སྦྱོར་གྱི་མཚན་ཉིད། གཉིས་པ་དེ་ལ་དབྱེ་ན། མཉམ་རྗེས་གཉིས་དང་། སྤངས་བྱའི་སྒོ་ནས་དབྱེ་ན་མཐོང་སྤངས་རྣམ་རྟོག་བཞིའི་གཉེན་པོ་མཐོང་ལམ་རྩེ་སྦྱོར་བཞི་ཡོད། གསུམ་པ་ས་མཚམས་ཐེག་ཆེན་གྱི་མཐེང་ལམ་ཁོ་ནར་ཡོད། མཐོང་ལམ་རྩེ་སྦྱོར་འཆད་པར། སྤངས་བྱ་རྟོག་པ་བཤད་པ་དང་། གཉེན་པོ་མཐོང་ལམ་བཤད་པའོ། །
translation: Peak training of the path of seeing. Fifth, to teach the peak training of the path of seeing: It is stated in the Ornament, from "On engaging and turning back..." up to "...summarized, that is the path of seeing here." Among the three aspects of this, first: The definition of the peak training of the path of seeing is the clear realization of the truth of the Great Vehicle that abides in the class of being the direct antidote to the seeds of the conceptions to be abandoned on the path of seeing. Second, if that is divided, there are two: meditative equipoise and subsequent attainment; and if divided by way of what is to be abandoned, there are four peak trainings of the path of seeing that are the antidotes to the four conceptions to be abandoned on the path of seeing. Third, the boundary is solely on the path of seeing of the Great Vehicle. To explain the peak training of the path of seeing, there is the explanation of the conceptions to be abandoned and the explanation of the path of seeing that is the antidote.

Peak training of patience. Third, regarding the peak training of patience: It is stated in the Ornament, from "Of the phenomena of the three omnisciences..." up to "...is plainly called stability." Among the three aspects of this—definition, divisions, and boundary—first: The definition of the peak training of patience is the third aid to penetration of the vehicle, which is the wisdom completely conforming to the three omnisciences and the attainment of stability not diverted from the welfare of others. Second, if that is divided, there are three peak trainings of patience: small, middling, and great. The boundary is solely on [the level of] patience. To explain this very stability or peak training of patience, which is the firm attainment of the realization of method and wisdom, one verse starting with "Irreversible awakening" was stated. Although Buddhaśrī applies [the text] from here onwards to the state of mind continually abiding, it is as the Master applied it to stability. Moreover, if someone else rejoices from the depths of their heart at the mind generation of that person—a bodhisattva who, having stably attained the realization of method and wisdom, possesses a stable, intense mind generation (the intention desiring to establish beings in supreme awakening without turning back from the Great Vehicle) and who has thoroughly engaged by means of the application of practicing the perfections and so forth—then, while it is possible to capture the measure by weighing on a scale the kings of mountains, the Mount Merus, present in this great trichiliocosm, that virtue of rejoicing in the bodhisattva's roots of virtue cannot be thus measured, because it is limitless. Gungtang Jamyang stated that this is the hidden meaning, because it teaches that rejoicing illustrates their firm realization of method and wisdom.

Peak training of supreme dharma. Fourth, regarding the peak training of supreme dharma: It is stated in the Ornament, from "Those in four continents, a thousand..." up to "...are proclaimed to be the meditative concentration." Among the three aspects of this, first: The definition of the peak training of supreme dharma is the fourth aid to penetration of the Great Vehicle, which attains the state of mind continually abiding in meditative concentration passed beyond extremes, from the perspective of having ripened the capacity to generate the path of seeing of the Great Vehicle, which is its fruition. Second, if that is divided, there are three supreme dharmas: small, middling, and great. To explain the peak training of the state of mind continually abiding, the meaning of the one verse stated starting with "Seeking virtue" is: If one asks what the reason is that rejoicing in the roots of virtue of a bodhisattva in that way has such great benefits: By directly rejoicing solely in that virtue of the bodhisattvas, one indirectly comes to rejoice in the aggregate of merit of all however many sentient beings there are in the world who "seek virtue" for themselves and who desire to benefit other beings. Why is that? It is because whatever virtue bodhisattvas accumulate is for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings. Thus it is said.

Peak training of patience. Third, regarding the peak training of patience: It is stated in the Ornament, from "Of the phenomena of the three omnisciences..." up to "...is plainly called stability." Among the three aspects of this—definition, divisions, and boundary—first: The definition of the peak training of patience is the third aid to penetration of the vehicle, which is the wisdom completely conforming to the three omnisciences and the attainment of stability not diverted from the welfare of others. Second, if that is divided, there are three peak trainings of patience: small, middling, and great. The boundary is solely on [the level of] patience. To explain this very stability or peak training of patience, which is the firm attainment of the realization of method and wisdom, one verse starting with "Irreversible awakening" was stated. Although Buddhaśrī applies [the text] from here onwards to the state of mind continually abiding, it is as the Master applied it to stability. Moreover, if someone else rejoices from the depths of their heart at the mind generation of that person—a bodhisattva who, having stably attained the realization of method and wisdom, possesses a stable, intense mind generation (the intention desiring to establish beings in supreme awakening without turning back from the Great Vehicle) and who has thoroughly engaged by means of the application of practicing the perfections and so forth—then, while it is possible to capture the measure by weighing on a scale the kings of mountains, the Mount Merus, present in this great trichiliocosm, that virtue of rejoicing in the bodhisattva's roots of virtue cannot be thus measured, because it is limitless. Gungtang Jamyang stated that this is the hidden meaning, because it teaches that rejoicing illustrates their firm realization of method and wisdom.

Fourth, regarding the peak training of supreme dharma: It is stated in the Ornament, from "Those in four continents, a thousand..." up to "...are proclaimed to be the meditative concentration." To explain the peak training of the state of mind continually abiding, the meaning of the one verse stated starting with "Seeking virtue" is: If one asks what the reason is that rejoicing in the roots of virtue of a bodhisattva in that way has such great benefits: By directly rejoicing solely in that virtue of the bodhisattvas, one indirectly comes to rejoice in the aggregate of merit of all however many sentient beings there are in the world who "seek virtue" for themselves and who desire to benefit other beings. Why is that? It is because whatever virtue bodhisattvas accumulate is for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings. Those irreversible bodhisattvas, by the power of that excellent path, will attain all the qualities of the omniscient victors, and in order to exhaust without remainder the suffering of sentient beings wandering in cyclic existence, they give the gift of dharma in all worlds and establish beings without remainder on the path of awakening. Thus it is said.

Peak training of patience. Third, regarding the peak training of patience: It is stated in the Ornament, from "Of the phenomena of the three omnisciences..." up to "...is plainly called stability." Among the three aspects of this—definition, divisions, and boundary—first: The definition of the peak training of patience is the third aid to penetration of the vehicle, which is the wisdom completely conforming to the three omnisciences and the attainment of stability not diverted from the welfare of others. Second, if that is divided, there are three peak trainings of patience: small, middling, and great. The boundary is solely on [the level of] patience. To explain this very stability or peak training of patience, which is the firm attainment of the realization of method and wisdom, one verse starting with "Irreversible awakening" was stated. Although Buddhaśrī applies [the text] from here onwards to the state of mind continually abiding, it is as the Master applied it to stability. Moreover, if someone else rejoices from the depths of their heart at the mind generation of that person—a bodhisattva who, having stably attained the realization of method and wisdom, possesses a stable, intense mind generation (the intention desiring to establish beings in supreme awakening without turning back from the Great Vehicle) and who has thoroughly engaged by means of the application of practicing the perfections and so forth—then, while it is possible to capture the measure by weighing on a scale the kings of mountains, the Mount Merus, present in this great trichiliocosm, that virtue of rejoicing in the bodhisattva's roots of virtue cannot be thus measured, because it is limitless. Gungtang Jamyang stated that this is the hidden meaning, because it teaches that rejoicing illustrates their firm realization of method and wisdom.

Peak training of supreme dharma. Fourth, regarding the peak training of supreme dharma: It is stated in the Ornament, from "Those in four continents, a thousand..." up to "...are proclaimed to be the meditative concentration." Among the three aspects of this, first: The definition of the peak training of supreme dharma is the fourth aid to penetration of the Great Vehicle, which attains the state of mind continually abiding in meditative concentration passed beyond extremes, from the perspective of having ripened the capacity to generate the path of seeing of the Great Vehicle, which is its fruition. To explain the peak training of the state of mind continually abiding, the meaning of the one verse stated starting with "Seeking virtue" is: If one asks what the reason is that rejoicing in the roots of virtue of a bodhisattva in that way has such great benefits: By directly rejoicing solely in that virtue of the bodhisattvas, one indirectly comes to rejoice in the aggregate of merit of all however many sentient beings there are in the world who "seek virtue" for themselves and who desire to benefit other beings. Why is that? It is because whatever virtue bodhisattvas accumulate is for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings. Those irreversible bodhisattvas, by the power of that excellent path, will attain all the qualities of the omniscient victors, and in order to exhaust without remainder the suffering of sentient beings wandering in cyclic existence, they give the gift of dharma in all worlds and establish beings without remainder on the path of awakening. Thus it is said.

Peak training of patience. Third, regarding the peak training of patience: It is stated in the Ornament, from "Of the phenomena of the three omnisciences..." up to "...is plainly called stability." Among the three aspects of this—definition, divisions, and boundary—first: The definition of the peak training of patience is the third aid to penetration of the vehicle, which is the wisdom completely conforming to the three omnisciences and the attainment of stability not diverted from the welfare of others. Second, if that is divided, there are three peak trainings of patience: small, middling, and great. The boundary is solely on [the level of] patience. To explain this very stability or peak training of patience, which is the firm attainment of the realization of method and wisdom, one verse starting with "Irreversible awakening" was stated. Although Buddhaśrī applies [the text] from here onwards to the state of mind continually abiding, it is as the Master applied it to stability. Moreover, if someone else rejoices from the depths of their heart at the mind generation of that person—a bodhisattva who, having stably attained the realization of method and wisdom, possesses a stable, intense mind generation (the intention desiring to establish beings in supreme awakening without turning back from the Great Vehicle) and who has thoroughly engaged by means of the application of practicing the perfections and so forth—then, while it is possible to capture the measure by weighing on a scale the kings of mountains, the Mount Merus, present in this great trichiliocosm, that virtue of rejoicing in the bodhisattva's roots of virtue cannot be thus measured, because it is limitless. Gungtang Jamyang stated that this is the hidden meaning, because it teaches that rejoicing illustrates their firm realization of method and wisdom.

Fourth, regarding the peak training of supreme dharma: It is stated in the Ornament, from "Those in four continents, a thousand..." up to "...are proclaimed to be the meditative concentration." To explain the peak training of the state of mind continually abiding, the meaning of the one verse stated starting with "Seeking virtue" is: If one asks what the reason is that rejoicing in the roots of virtue of a bodhisattva in that way has such great benefits: By directly rejoicing solely in that virtue of the bodhisattvas, one indirectly comes to rejoice in the aggregate of merit of all however many sentient beings there are in the world who "seek virtue" for themselves and who desire to benefit other beings. Why is that? It is because whatever virtue bodhisattvas accumulate is for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings. Those irreversible bodhisattvas, by the power of that excellent path, will attain all the qualities of the omniscient victors, and in order to exhaust without remainder the suffering of sentient beings wandering in cyclic existence, they give the gift of dharma in all worlds and establish beings without remainder on the path of awakening. Thus it is said.

heading: **འཇུག་པ་གཟུང་རྟོག**
translation: Conception of an apprehended object concerning engaging. First, to teach the conception of an apprehended object concerning engaging, the meaning of the one verse stated starting with "A bodhisattva..." is: A bodhisattva who, abiding in the pristine wisdom that does not conceptualize truly, completely knows that all thoroughly afflicted and purified phenomena are empty of nature, ultimately without marks, and without the elaborations or wishes of true establishment, does not seek awakening by way of true establishment or grasping at the two extremes through the wisdom realizing the pairs of thorough affliction and purification, apprehended and apprehender, and object to be abandoned and antidote and so forth to be without true existence. That yogi abiding on the path of seeing free from all elaborations of dualistic appearance exerts themselves in the supreme perfection of wisdom that has become the essence of seeing and meditation. Thus it is said.

Peak training of patience. Third, regarding the peak training of patience: It is stated in the Ornament, from "Of the phenomena of the three omnisciences..." up to "...is plainly called stability." Among the three aspects of this—definition, divisions, and boundary—first: The definition of the peak training of patience is the third aid to penetration of the vehicle, which is the wisdom completely conforming to the three omnisciences and the attainment of stability not diverted from the welfare of others. Second, if that is divided, there are three peak trainings of patience: small, middling, and great. The boundary is solely on [the level of] patience. To explain this very stability or peak training of patience, which is the firm attainment of the realization of method and wisdom, one verse starting with "Irreversible awakening" was stated. Although Buddhaśrī applies [the text] from here onwards to the state of mind continually abiding, it is as the Master applied it to stability. Moreover, if someone else rejoices from the depths of their heart at the mind generation of that person—a bodhisattva who, having stably attained the realization of method and wisdom, possesses a stable, intense mind generation (the intention desiring to establish beings in supreme awakening without turning back from the Great Vehicle) and who has thoroughly engaged by means of the application of practicing the perfections and so forth—then, while it is possible to capture the measure by weighing on a scale the kings of mountains, the Mount Merus, present in this great trichiliocosm, that virtue of rejoicing in the bodhisattva's roots of virtue cannot be thus measured, because it is limitless. Gungtang Jamyang stated that this is the hidden meaning, because it teaches that rejoicing illustrates their firm realization of method and wisdom.

To explain the peak training of the state of mind continually abiding, the meaning of the one verse stated starting with "Seeking virtue" is: If one asks what the reason is that rejoicing in the roots of virtue of a bodhisattva in that way has such great benefits: By directly rejoicing solely in that virtue of the bodhisattvas, one indirectly comes to rejoice in the aggregate of merit of all however many sentient beings there are in the world who "seek virtue" for themselves and who desire to benefit other beings. Why is that? It is because whatever virtue bodhisattvas accumulate is for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings. Those irreversible bodhisattvas, by the power of that excellent path, will attain all the qualities of the omniscient victors, and in order to exhaust without remainder the suffering of sentient beings wandering in cyclic existence, they give the gift of dharma in all worlds and establish beings without remainder on the path of awakening. Thus it is said.

heading: **ལྡོག་པ་གཟུང་རྟོག**
translation: Conception of an apprehended object concerning turning back. Second, to teach the conception of an apprehended object concerning turning back, the meaning of the one verse stated starting with "That realm of space..." is: For example, because space is merely the absence of obstruction and contact, there is no entity of that realm of space itself, nor is there anything incompatible that cannot co-exist with that space, nor is there anything obstructing the occurrence of other physical forms. Because the realm of space and what is called space are equally non-entities, their entity is not attained by any physical thing at all. Similar to that example, a bodhisattva who is skilled in practicing the profound wisdom that realizes the nature of the path of seeing—the pairs of things to be adopted and discarded, and objects to be abandoned and antidotes, and so forth—as equality in being empty of true existence, also abides in non-conceptual pristine wisdom like space, possessing the greatness of practicing the complete pacification of all conceptions apprehending true existence, which are what turn one back to the inferior path. Thus it is said.

Peak training of patience. Third, regarding the peak training of patience: It is stated in the Ornament, from "Of the phenomena of the three omnisciences..." up to "...is plainly called stability." Among the three aspects of this—definition, divisions, and boundary—first: The definition of the peak training of patience is the third aid to penetration of the vehicle, which is the wisdom completely conforming to the three omnisciences and the attainment of stability not diverted from the welfare of others. Second, if that is divided, there are three peak trainings of patience: small, middling, and great. The boundary is solely on [the level of] patience. To explain this very stability or peak training of patience, which is the firm attainment of the realization of method and wisdom, one verse starting with "Irreversible awakening" was stated. Although Buddhaśrī applies [the text] from here onwards to the state of mind continually abiding, it is as the Master applied it to stability. Moreover, if someone else rejoices from the depths of their heart at the mind generation of that person—a bodhisattva who, having stably attained the realization of method and wisdom, possesses a stable, intense mind generation (the intention desiring to establish beings in supreme awakening without turning back from the Great Vehicle) and who has thoroughly engaged by means of the application of practicing the perfections and so forth—then, while it is possible to capture the measure by weighing on a scale the kings of mountains, the Mount Merus, present in this great trichiliocosm, that virtue of rejoicing in the bodhisattva's roots of virtue cannot be thus measured, because it is limitless. Gungtang Jamyang stated that this is the hidden meaning, because it teaches that rejoicing illustrates their firm realization of method and wisdom.

Peak training of supreme dharma. Fourth, regarding the peak training of supreme dharma: It is stated in the Ornament, from "Those in four continents, a thousand..." up to "...are proclaimed to be the meditative concentration." To explain the peak training of the state of mind continually abiding, the meaning of the one verse stated starting with "Seeking virtue" is: If one asks what the reason is that rejoicing in the roots of virtue of a bodhisattva in that way has such great benefits: By directly rejoicing solely in that virtue of the bodhisattvas, one indirectly comes to rejoice in the aggregate of merit of all however many sentient beings there are in the world who "seek virtue" for themselves and who desire to benefit other beings. Why is that? It is because whatever virtue bodhisattvas accumulate is for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings. Those irreversible bodhisattvas, by the power of that excellent path, will attain all the qualities of the omniscient victors, and in order to exhaust without remainder the suffering of sentient beings wandering in cyclic existence, they give the gift of dharma in all worlds and establish beings without remainder on the path of awakening. Thus it is said.

heading: **ལྡོག་པ་གཟུང་རྟོག**
translation: Second, to teach the first conception of an apprehender, which has the basis of a person substantially existing, the meaning of the two verses stated starting with "In the midst of people..." is: For example, in the midst of a large crowd of people gathered to watch a spectacle, an illusory person—a person emanated by means of illusory mantras and substances—does not think: "I shall please this large crowd of people with my excellent form and diverse activities," but still performs actions that please and delight the spectators, thoroughly displaying diverse miracles such as going and staying. Even though the crowd of people sees that, the illusory emanation is not established as a human body, it does not have a mind, and even its name is not ultimately established.

Peak training of patience. Third, regarding the peak training of patience: It is stated in the Ornament, from "Of the phenomena of the three omnisciences..." up to "...is plainly called stability." Among the three aspects of this—definition, divisions, and boundary—first: The definition of the peak training of patience is the third aid to penetration of the vehicle, which is the wisdom completely conforming to the three omnisciences and the attainment of stability not diverted from the welfare of others. Second, if that is divided, there are three peak trainings of patience: small, middling, and great. The boundary is solely on [the level of] patience. To explain this very stability or peak training of patience, which is the firm attainment of the realization of method and wisdom, one verse starting with "Irreversible awakening" was stated. Although Buddhaśrī applies [the text] from here onwards to the state of mind continually abiding, it is as the Master applied it to stability. Moreover, if someone else rejoices from the depths of their heart at the mind generation of that person—a bodhisattva who, having stably attained the realization of method and wisdom, possesses a stable, intense mind generation (the intention desiring to establish beings in supreme awakening without turning back from the Great Vehicle) and who has thoroughly engaged by means of the application of practicing the perfections and so forth—then, while it is possible to capture the measure by weighing on a scale the kings of mountains, the Mount Merus, present in this great trichiliocosm, that virtue of rejoicing in the bodhisattva's roots of virtue cannot be thus measured, because it is limitless. Gungtang Jamyang stated that this is the hidden meaning, because it teaches that rejoicing illustrates their firm realization of method and wisdom.

Peak training of supreme dharma. Fourth, regarding the peak training of supreme dharma: It is stated in the Ornament, from "Those in four continents, a thousand..." up to "...are proclaimed to be the meditative concentration." Among the three aspects of this, first: The definition of the peak training of supreme dharma is the fourth aid to penetration of the Great Vehicle, which attains the state of mind continually abiding in meditative concentration passed beyond extremes, from the perspective of having ripened the capacity to generate the path of seeing of the Great Vehicle, which is its fruition. To explain the peak training of the state of mind continually abiding, the meaning of the one verse stated starting with "Seeking virtue" is: If one asks what the reason is that rejoicing in the roots of virtue of a bodhisattva in that way has such great benefits: By directly rejoicing solely in that virtue of the bodhisattvas, one indirectly comes to rejoice in the aggregate of merit of all however many sentient beings there are in the world who "seek virtue" for themselves and who desire to benefit other beings. Why is that? It is because whatever virtue bodhisattvas accumulate is for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings. Those irreversible bodhisattvas, by the power of that excellent path, will attain all the qualities of the omniscient victors, and in order to exhaust without remainder the suffering of sentient beings wandering in cyclic existence, they give the gift of dharma in all worlds and establish beings without remainder on the path of awakening. Thus it is said.

heading: **ལྡོག་པ་གཟུང་རྟོག**
translation: Likewise, bodhisattvas who practice the perfection of wisdom that does not conceptualize the nature of the path of seeing as truly existent never think, "Having ultimately realized great awakening, I will completely liberate beings from cyclic existence." Although they do not think that, for the sake of taming disciples, they demonstrate diverse births as gods, humans, and so forth, and possess many activities that accomplish the benefit and happiness of beings. Although they do not ultimately exist, they conventionally demonstrate them like illusions, and they practice by way of not conceptualizing those things as truly existent. Thus it is said.

First, to teach the conception of an apprehended object concerning engaging, the meaning of the one verse stated starting with "A bodhisattva..." is: A bodhisattva who, abiding in the pristine wisdom that does not conceptualize truly, completely knows that all thoroughly afflicted and purified phenomena are empty of nature, ultimately without marks, and without the elaborations or wishes of true establishment, does not seek awakening by way of true establishment or grasping at the two extremes through the wisdom realizing the pairs of thorough affliction and purification, apprehended and apprehender, and object to be abandoned and antidote and so forth to be without true existence. Conception of an apprehended object concerning turning back. Second, to teach the conception of an apprehended object concerning turning back, the meaning of the one verse stated starting with "That realm of space..." is: For example, because space is merely the absence of obstruction and contact, there is no entity of that realm of space itself, nor is there anything incompatible that cannot co-exist with that space, nor is there anything obstructing the occurrence of other physical forms. Because the realm of space and what is called space are equally non-entities, their entity is not attained by any physical thing at all. Similar to that example, a bodhisattva who is skilled in practicing the profound wisdom that realizes the nature of the path of seeing—the pairs of things to be adopted and discarded, and objects to be abandoned and antidotes, and so forth—as equality in being empty of true existence, also abides in non-conceptual pristine wisdom like space, possessing the greatness of practicing the complete pacification of all conceptions apprehending true existence, which are what turn one back to the inferior path. Second, to teach the first conception of an apprehender, which has the basis of a person substantially existing, the meaning of the two verses stated starting with "In the midst of people..." is: For example, in the midst of a large crowd of people gathered to watch a spectacle, an illusory person—a person emanated by means of illusory mantras and substances—does not think: "I shall please this large crowd of people with my excellent form and diverse activities," but still performs actions that please and delight the spectators, thoroughly displaying diverse miracles such as going and staying. Even though the crowd of people sees that, the illusory emanation is not established as a human body, it does not have a mind, and even its name is not ultimately established.

heading: **ལྡོག་པ་གཟུང་རྟོག**
translation: Second, to teach the second conception of an apprehender, which has the basis of a person existing imputedly, the meaning of the two verses stated starting with "For example, a Buddha..." is: Even though emanations, such as supreme emanation bodies, perform all the activities of a Buddha such as teaching the Dharma, with regard to those emanations performing the activities of a Buddha, pride and arrogance thinking "I am the performer of the Buddha's activities" do not arise even slightly, because they do not have any conceptualization whatsoever. Likewise, a bodhisattva who is skilled in practicing the wisdom that does not conceptualize apprehended and apprehender as truly existing, although realizing all phenomena to be of one taste in being empty of true existence, conventionally performs all activities, such as the three of perfecting, ripening, and purifying, and demonstrates diverse activities, like emanations and illusions.

Conception of an apprehended object concerning engaging. First, to teach the conception of an apprehended object concerning engaging, the meaning of the one verse stated starting with "A bodhisattva..." is: A bodhisattva who, abiding in the pristine wisdom that does not conceptualize truly, completely knows that all thoroughly afflicted and purified phenomena are empty of nature, ultimately without marks, and without the elaborations or wishes of true establishment, does not seek awakening by way of true establishment or grasping at the two extremes through the wisdom realizing the pairs of thorough affliction and purification, apprehended and apprehender, and object to be abandoned and antidote and so forth to be without true existence. That yogi abiding on the path of seeing free from all elaborations of dualistic appearance exerts themselves in the supreme perfection of wisdom that has become the essence of seeing and meditation. Thus it is said.

Conception of an apprehended object concerning turning back. Second, to teach the conception of an apprehended object concerning turning back, the meaning of the one verse stated starting with "That realm of space..." is: For example, because space is merely the absence of obstruction and contact, there is no entity of that realm of space itself, nor is there anything incompatible that cannot co-exist with that space, nor is there anything obstructing the occurrence of other physical forms. Because the realm of space and what is called space are equally non-entities, their entity is not attained by any physical thing at all. Similar to that example, a bodhisattva who is skilled in practicing the profound wisdom that realizes the nature of the path of seeing—the pairs of things to be adopted and discarded, and objects to be abandoned and antidotes, and so forth—as equality in being empty of true existence, also abides in non-conceptual pristine wisdom like space, possessing the greatness of practicing the complete pacification of all conceptions apprehending true existence, which are what turn one back to the inferior path.
