From this point downwards, there is no correlation with the Ornament. Although a system of correlating it has existed from previously, the master Haribhadra refuted it. As for our own system, explaining in accordance with the master's assertion: in order to generate in one's own continuum the eight clear realizations as explained above, one must be preceded by listening to, reflecting on, and meditating on the Mother, the perfection of wisdom. Therefore, having earnestly sought a fully qualified spiritual friend of the Great Vehicle and having pleased them by practicing according to whatever they say, the manner of engaging in earnest practice with great patience, without the mind becoming weary from the suffering of ascetic hardships on the path, through intense and uninterrupted irreversible joyous effort, is as follows: The meaning taught by the four verses beginning with "Whatever bodhisattva..." is this: If a yogi—who, out of affection and great compassion, desires to accomplish the aim of others by remaining in this place of cyclic existence for an immeasurably long time and never giving up acting for the welfare of sentient beings; and who exerts themselves in activities for wandering beings, such as completely maturing sentient beings by remaining in cyclic existence for the sake of others, and in purifying their own Buddha-field, completely fulfilling their aspirations, and so forth—does not generate even an atom of a mind of weariness towards the long duration of time and the suffering of ascetic hardships and so forth, then they are endowed with the three types of the perfection of joyous effort, such as acting for the welfare of sentient beings, and will become undistracted in accomplishing the aims of others.

If one asks, "What fault is there in generating a mind of weariness?" To teach that: If any bodhisattva unskilled in means counts the measure of tens of millions of eons and so forth, thinking, "Having exerted myself for this long, I will attain the awakening of a Buddha," and if they practice for awakening through the perception of such a long time and the perception of suffering in giving away their head, limbs, and so forth, then at that time of accomplishing the pure dharma of unsurpassable awakening for the sake of others, through the power of that very perception, it will become a long, suffering, and difficult task. And because of that erroneous perception, they will degenerate from the perfection of joyous effort and become lazy, experiencing discouragement, self-contempt, and so forth.

If one asks, "Then how does one not generate a mind of weariness?" Wise bodhisattvas must generate courage without looking at the long duration of time and the difficulty of the tasks, like the noble Sadāprarudita. If, beginning from the very first generation of the mind set on supreme awakening until finally attaining the state of a perfectly complete Buddha of unsurpassable great awakening, they mentally consider all those periods of time as being as easy to pass as the measure of a single day and night, and generate a perception of joy, then bodhisattvas skilled in means will have destroyed the darkness of laziness through the luminosity of the wisdom that realizes all phenomena to be empty of true existence and illusion-like; you should know that the manner of exerting joyous effort is like that. Having generated courage and joy, thinking, "Although I have experienced intense and uninterrupted suffering in this place of cyclic existence since beginningless lifetimes, I have had no weariness or aversion, so why should I not bear the suffering of ascetic hardships now in accomplishing the excellent path of the supreme vehicle that will make me attain the great purpose, the state of a Buddha?"—through the power of that, they will overwhelm the long duration of time and all suffering, and their joyous effort will extensively increase.

heading: འབྲས་བུ་ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: Even if one exerts joyous effort in that way, it is important to be without adherence. If one exerts oneself in accomplishing the welfare of others with body, speech, and mind from within a state of perception that apprehends characteristics of self and other, thinking, "Through the wondrous conduct of being skilled in means to tame whoever needs taming, such as teaching the profound and vast dharma, I shall completely mature wandering beings and accomplish the welfare of others, such as placing them on the grounds and paths!"—because one abides in the perception of a personal self, it becomes laziness relative to the supramundane objectless joyous effort. Because one is bound by the apprehension of characteristics, it has become the discordant class of pure joyous effort, and therefore one will become far from omniscience itself, just as, for example, a place and the ground are far apart.

Work: ཡོན་ཏན་རིན་པོ་ཆེ་སྡུད་པ་ཚིགས་སུ་བཅད་པའི་འགྲེལ་པ་ཟབ་མོ་རྟེན་འབྱུང་གི་དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཉིད་གསལ་བར་བྱེད་པའི་ནོར་བུའི་སྒྲོན་མེ་སྐལ་བཟང་རེ་སྐོང་། (Khenrab Jamyang, Commentary on the Verses of the Precious Qualities Collection), author: མཁྱེན་རབ་འཇམ་དབྱངས་བློ་བཟང་འཕྲིན་ལས།. འདི་མན་ཆད་རྒྱན་དང་སྦྱོར་དུ་མེད་ལ། སྦྱོར་བའི་ལུགས་ཤིག་སྔོན་ནས་ཀྱང་ཡོད་འདུག་པ་སློབ་དཔོན་སེངྒེ་བཟང་པོས་བཀག་གོ །རང་ལུགས་ནི་སློབ་དཔོན་གྱི་བཞེད་པ་ལྟར་འཆད་པ་ལ། གོང་དུ་ཇི་སྐད་བཤད་པའི་མངོན་པར་རྟོགས་པ་བརྒྱད་རང་རྒྱུད་ལ་བསྐྱེད་པ་ལ་ཡུམ་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ཐོས་བསམ་བསྒོམ་གསུམ་བྱེད་པ་མངོན་དུ་འགྲོ་དགོས་པས་ཐེག་པ་ཆེན་པོའི་དགེ་བའི་བཤེས་གཉེན་མཚན་ཉིད་དང་ལྡན་པ་ཞིག་འབད་པས་བཙལ་ཏེ་ཅི་གསུངས་བཀའ་བཞིན་བསྒྲུབས་པས་མཉེས་པར་བྱས་ནས་མི་ལྡོག་པའི་བརྩོན་འགྲུས་ཤུག་དྲག་ལ་རྒྱུན་མི་ཆད་པས་ལམ་ལ་བཀའ་སྤྱད་ཀྱི་སྡུག་བསྔལ་གྱིས་ཡིད་སྐྱོ་བ་མེད་པར་བཟོད་པ་ཆེན་པོས་ནན་ཏན་ཉམས་སུ་ལེན་པ་འཇུག་པའི་ཚུལ་ནི། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གང་ཞིག་ཅེས་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་བཞིས་བསྟན་པའི་དོན་ནི། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གང་ཞིག་བརྩེ་བ་སྙིང་རྗེ་ཆེན་པོས་གཞན་དོན་དུ་ཡུན་རིང་པོ་ཚད་མེད་པར་འཁོར་བའི་གནས་འདིར་གནས་ཤིང་སེམས་ཅན་གྱི་དོན་བྱེད་པ་ནམ་ཡང་མི་གཏོང་བ་སྒྲུབ་པར་འདོད་ཅིང་། གཞན་དོན་དུ་འཁོར་བ་གནས་ནས་སེམས་ཅན་ཡོངས་སུ་སྨིན་པར་བྱེད་པ་སོགས་འགྲོ་བའི་བྱེད་པ་དང་རང་གི་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་ཞིང་སྦྱོང་བ་དང་སྨོན་ལམ་ཡོངས་སུ་རྫོགས་པར་བྱེད་པ་སོགས་ལ་བརྩོན་པའི་རྣལ་འབྱོར་པ་དུས་ཡུན་རིང་བ་དང་དཀའ་སྤྱད་ཀྱི་སྡུག་བསྔལ་སོགས་ལ་སྐྱེ་བའི་བློ་ནི་རྡུལ་ཙམ་ཡང་སྐྱེ་བར་མི་འགྱུར་ན་དེ་ནི་སེམསཅན་གྱི་དོན་བྱེད་པ་སོགས་བརྩོན་འགྲུས་རྣམ་པ་གསུམ་གྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་དང་ལྡན་ཏེ་གཞན་དོན་སྒྲུབ་པ་ལ་གཡེལ་བ་མེད་པར་འགྱུར་བ་ཡིན་ནོ། །

From this point downwards, there is no correlation with the Ornament. Although a system of correlating it has existed from previously, the master Haribhadra refuted it. As for our own system, explaining in accordance with the master's assertion: in order to generate in one's own continuum the eight clear realizations as explained above, one must be preceded by listening to, reflecting on, and meditating on the Mother, the perfection of wisdom. Therefore, having earnestly sought a fully qualified spiritual friend of the Great Vehicle and having pleased them by practicing according to whatever they say, the manner of engaging in earnest practice with great patience, without the mind becoming weary from the suffering of ascetic hardships on the path, through intense and uninterrupted irreversible joyous effort, is as follows: The meaning taught by the four verses beginning with "Whatever bodhisattva..." is this: If a yogi—who, out of affection and great compassion, desires to accomplish the aim of others by remaining in this place of cyclic existence for an immeasurably long time and never giving up acting for the welfare of sentient beings; and who exerts themselves in activities for wandering beings, such as completely maturing sentient beings by remaining in cyclic existence for the sake of others, and in purifying their own Buddha-field, completely fulfilling their aspirations, and so forth—does not generate even an atom of a mind of weariness towards the long duration of time and the suffering of ascetic hardships and so forth, then they are endowed with the three types of the perfection of joyous effort, such as acting for the welfare of sentient beings, and will become undistracted in accomplishing the aims of others.

སྐྱོ་བའི་བློ་བསྐྱེད་པ་ལ་ཉེས་པ་ཅི་ཞིག་ཡོད་ཅེ་ན། དེ་བསྟན་པའི་ཕྱིར། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཐབས་ལ་མི་མཁས་པ་གང་ཞིག་སྐལ་པ་བྱེ་བ་སོགས་ཚད་བགྲངས་ཤིང་འདི་ཙམ་ཞིག་གི་བར་དུ་བརྩོན་ནས་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཐོབ་པར་འགྱུར་རོ་སྙམ་དུ་བསམ་ནས། གལ་ཏེ་དེ་འདྲ་བའི་ཡུན་རིང་བར་འདུ་ཤེས་པ་དང་། མགོ་དང་རྐང་ལག་སོགས་གཏོང་བ་ལ་སྡུག་བསྔལ་བའི་འདུ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་སྒོ་ནས་བྱང་ཆུབ་སྒྲུབ་པར་བྱེད་ན། ཡང་དག་པའི་ཆོས་གཞན་དོན་དུ་བླ་མེད་བྱང་ཆུབ་སྒྲུབ་པར་བྱེད་པ་དེ་ཡི་ཚེ་འདུ་ཤེས་དེ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་དབང་གིས་ཡུན་རིང་པོ་་སྡུག་བསྔལ་བ་དང་བྱ་དཀའ་བར་འགྱུར་ཞིང་། འདུས་ཤེས་ཕྱིན་ཅི་ལོག་དེས་ན་བརྩོན་འགྲུས་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལས་ཉམས་པར་འགྱུར་ཞིང་སྒྱིད་ལུགས་པ་དང་བདག་ཉིད་བརྙེས་པ་སོགས་ལེ་ལོ་ཅན་དུ་འགྱུར་རོ། །
[3-309] translation already produced for this document:
If one asks, "What fault is there in generating a mind of weariness?" To teach that: If any bodhisattva unskilled in means counts the measure of tens of millions of eons and so forth, thinking, "Having exerted myself for this long, I will attain the awakening of a Buddha," and if they practice for awakening through the perception of such a long time and the perception of suffering in giving away their head, limbs, and so forth, then at that time of accomplishing the pure dharma of unsurpassable awakening for the sake of others, through the power of that very perception, it will become a long, suffering, and difficult task. And because of that erroneous perception, they will degenerate from the perfection of joyous effort and become lazy, experiencing discouragement, self-contempt, and so forth.

[3-310] source:
འོ་ན་ཇི་ལྟར་སྐྱོ་བའི་བློ་བསྐྱེད་པར་མི་བྱ་ཞེ་ན། བྱང་སེམས་མཁས་རྣམས་དུས་ཡུན་རིང་བ་དང་བྱ་དཀའ་བ་ལ་མི་ལྟ་བར་སྙིང་སྟོབས་བསྐྱེད་པ་འཕགས་པ་རྟགས་ཏུ་ངུ་ལྟ་བུ་དགོས་པ་ཡིན་ཏེ། བྱང་ཆུབ་མཆོག་ཏུ་སེམས་བསྐྱེད་པ་དང་པོ་གང་ཡིན་པ་དེ་ནས་བཟུང་སྟེ། མཐར་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཆེན་པོ་བླ་ན་མེད་པ་ཡང་དག་པར་རྫོགས་པའི་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་གོ་འཕང་ཐོབ་པར་འགྱུར་གྱི་བར་གྱི་དུས་དེ་དག་ཐམས་ཅད་ལ་དཔེར་ན་ཉིན་མཚན་གཅིག་གི་ཚད་ཙམ་དུ་ནི་འདའ་བར་སླ་བར་ཡིད་ལ་སེམས་པར་བྱེད་ཅིང་སྤྲོ་དགའི་འདུ་ཤེས་བསྐྱེད་ན། བྱང་སེམས་ཐབས་ལ་མཁས་པ་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་བདེན་སྟོང་སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟ་བུར་རྟོགས་པའི་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་འོད་གསལ་བས་ལེ་ལོའི་མུན་པ་བཅོམ་ནས་བརྩོན་འགྲུས་བརྩམ་པའི་ཚུལ་དེ་ལྟ་བུ་ཡིན་པར་རིགས་པར་བྱས་སྟེ། ཚེ་རབས་ཐོག་མ་མེད་པ་ནས་འཁོར་བའི་གནས་འདིར་སྡུག་བསྔལ་ཤུགས་དྲག་ལ་རྒྱུན་མི་ཆད་པ་མྱོང་ཡང་སྐྱོ་བ་དང་སུན་པ་མེད་ན་ད་ལྟ་བདག་གིས་དོན་ཆེན་པོ་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་གོ་འཕང་ཐོབ་པར་བྱེད་པའི་ཐེག་པ་མཆོག་གི་ལམ་བཟང་སྒྲུབ་པ་ལ་དཀའ་སྤྱད་ཀྱི་སྡུག་བསྔལ་ཅི་ཕྱིར་མི་བཟོད་སྙམ་དུ་སྙིང་སྟོབས་བསྐྱེད་དེ་སྤྲོ་བར་བྱས་ནས་དེའི་དབང་གིས་དུས་ཡུན་རིང་བ་དང་སྡུག་བསྔལ་མཐའ་དག་ཟིལ་གྱི་མནན་ནས་བརྩོན་འགྲུས་རྒྱ་ཆེར་འཕེལ་བར་འགྱུར་རོ། །

If one asks, "Then how does one not generate a mind of weariness?" Wise bodhisattvas must generate courage without looking at the long duration of time and the difficulty of the tasks, like the noble Sadāprarudita. If, beginning from the very first generation of the mind set on supreme awakening until finally attaining the state of a perfectly complete Buddha of unsurpassable great awakening, they mentally consider all those periods of time as being as easy to pass as the measure of a single day and night, and generate a perception of joy, then bodhisattvas skilled in means will have destroyed the darkness of laziness through the luminosity of the wisdom that realizes all phenomena to be empty of true existence and illusion-like; you should know that the manner of exerting joyous effort is like that. Having generated courage and joy, thinking, "Although I have experienced intense and uninterrupted suffering in this place of cyclic existence since beginningless lifetimes, I have had no weariness or aversion, so why should I not bear the suffering of ascetic hardships now in accomplishing the excellent path of the supreme vehicle that will make me attain the great purpose, the state of a Buddha?"—through the power of that, they will overwhelm the long duration of time and all suffering, and their joyous effort will extensively increase.

heading: འབྲས་བུ་ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: If one asks, "Then in what manner should one exert joyous effort?" When exerting joyous effort, one does not have a perception of the agent exerting it, of one's own body and mind, or of others as sentient beings, and the perception holding the three spheres of joyous effort to be truly existent is completely reversed; practicing the way of phenomena as empty of true existence and illusion-like, without falling into the two extremes of permanence and annihilation—this is the very perfection of joyous effort of bodhisattvas who desire to attain the state of the supreme qualities of abandonment and realization, great awakening, the pacification of all stains of the two obscurations without ever degenerating, so say the Conquerors who act for the benefit of wandering beings.

From this point downwards, there is no correlation with the Ornament. Although a system of correlating it has existed from previously, the master Haribhadra refuted it. As for our own system, explaining in accordance with the master's assertion: in order to generate in one's own continuum the eight clear realizations as explained above, one must be preceded by listening to, reflecting on, and meditating on the Mother, the perfection of wisdom. Therefore, having earnestly sought a fully qualified spiritual friend of the Great Vehicle and having pleased them by practicing according to whatever they say, the manner of engaging in earnest practice with great patience, without the mind becoming weary from the suffering of ascetic hardships on the path, through intense and uninterrupted irreversible joyous effort, is as follows: The meaning taught by the four verses beginning with "Whatever bodhisattva..." is this: If a yogi—who, out of affection and great compassion, desires to accomplish the aim of others by remaining in this place of cyclic existence for an immeasurably long time and never giving up acting for the welfare of sentient beings; and who exerts themselves in activities for wandering beings, such as completely maturing sentient beings by remaining in cyclic existence for the sake of others, and in purifying their own Buddha-field, completely fulfilling their aspirations, and so forth—does not generate even an atom of a mind of weariness towards the long duration of time and the suffering of ascetic hardships and so forth, then they are endowed with the three types of the perfection of joyous effort, such as acting for the welfare of sentient beings, and will become undistracted in accomplishing the aims of others.

If one asks, "What fault is there in generating a mind of weariness?" To teach that: If any bodhisattva unskilled in means counts the measure of tens of millions of eons and so forth, thinking, "Having exerted myself for this long, I will attain the awakening of a Buddha," and if they practice for awakening through the perception of such a long time and the perception of suffering in giving away their head, limbs, and so forth, then at that time of accomplishing the pure dharma of unsurpassable awakening for the sake of others, through the power of that very perception, it will become a long, suffering, and difficult task. If one asks, "Then how does one not generate a mind of weariness?" Wise bodhisattvas must generate courage without looking at the long duration of time and the difficulty of the tasks, like the noble Sadāprarudita. If, beginning from the very first generation of the mind set on supreme awakening until finally attaining the state of a perfectly complete Buddha of unsurpassable great awakening, they mentally consider all those periods of time as being as easy to pass as the measure of a single day and night, and generate a perception of joy, then bodhisattvas skilled in means will have destroyed the darkness of laziness through the luminosity of the wisdom that realizes all phenomena to be empty of true existence and illusion-like; you should know that the manner of exerting joyous effort is like that. Having generated courage and joy, thinking, "Although I have experienced intense and uninterrupted suffering in this place of cyclic existence since beginningless lifetimes, I have had no weariness or aversion, so why should I not bear the suffering of ascetic hardships now in accomplishing the excellent path of the supreme vehicle that will make me attain the great purpose, the state of a Buddha?"—through the power of that, they will overwhelm the long duration of time and all suffering, and their joyous effort will extensively increase.

heading: འབྲས་བུ་ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: The manner of having to train in the perfection of patience by being unconcerned about ascetic hardships and suffering, like the Conqueror's son Sadāprarudita relying on the noble Dharmodgata in order to seek the perfection of wisdom, is as follows: At the time of acting for the welfare of wandering beings, if one hears from other persons many harsh words speaking ill, such as exposing one's faults and deprecating one, the bodhisattva skilled in means will become joyful, thinking, "The practice of patience arises in dependence on the object of patience, and by its power great merit will increase, therefore this is the cause of my happiness." Not only that, having examined and analyzed with pure reasoning, when searching with rational cognition, thinking, "Who is the speaker speaking these harsh words? And who is the object spoken to that hears them? By what cause, such as anger? Expressing what? For what purpose do they speak?"—one does not find even the slightest thing. Because it is not established ultimately, having realized it to be an illusion-like dependent arising, one who is endowed with the supreme perfection of patience is wise or learned, because they are a supremely wise one who realizes that one should not become angry at phenomena that are like a dream and an illusion.

From this point downwards, there is no correlation with the Ornament. Although a system of correlating it has existed from previously, the master Haribhadra refuted it. As for our own system, explaining in accordance with the master's assertion: in order to generate in one's own continuum the eight clear realizations as explained above, one must be preceded by listening to, reflecting on, and meditating on the Mother, the perfection of wisdom. Therefore, having earnestly sought a fully qualified spiritual friend of the Great Vehicle and having pleased them by practicing according to whatever they say, the manner of engaging in earnest practice with great patience, without the mind becoming weary from the suffering of ascetic hardships on the path, through intense and uninterrupted irreversible joyous effort, is as follows: The meaning taught by the four verses beginning with "Whatever bodhisattva..." is this: If a yogi—who, out of affection and great compassion, desires to accomplish the aim of others by remaining in this place of cyclic existence for an immeasurably long time and never giving up acting for the welfare of sentient beings; and who exerts themselves in activities for wandering beings, such as completely maturing sentient beings by remaining in cyclic existence for the sake of others, and in purifying their own Buddha-field, completely fulfilling their aspirations, and so forth—does not generate even an atom of a mind of weariness towards the long duration of time and the suffering of ascetic hardships and so forth, then they are endowed with the three types of the perfection of joyous effort, such as acting for the welfare of sentient beings, and will become undistracted in accomplishing the aims of others.

If one asks, "What fault is there in generating a mind of weariness?" To teach that: If any bodhisattva unskilled in means counts the measure of tens of millions of eons and so forth, thinking, "Having exerted myself for this long, I will attain the awakening of a Buddha," and if they practice for awakening through the perception of such a long time and the perception of suffering in giving away their head, limbs, and so forth, then at that time of accomplishing the pure dharma of unsurpassable awakening for the sake of others, through the power of that very perception, it will become a long, suffering, and difficult task. And because of that erroneous perception, they will degenerate from the perfection of joyous effort and become lazy, experiencing discouragement, self-contempt, and so forth.

If one asks, "Then how does one not generate a mind of weariness?" Wise bodhisattvas must generate courage without looking at the long duration of time and the difficulty of the tasks, like the noble Sadāprarudita. If, beginning from the very first generation of the mind set on supreme awakening until finally attaining the state of a perfectly complete Buddha of unsurpassable great awakening, they mentally consider all those periods of time as being as easy to pass as the measure of a single day and night, and generate a perception of joy, then bodhisattvas skilled in means will have destroyed the darkness of laziness through the luminosity of the wisdom that realizes all phenomena to be empty of true existence and illusion-like; you should know that the manner of exerting joyous effort is like that. Having generated courage and joy, thinking, "Although I have experienced intense and uninterrupted suffering in this place of cyclic existence since beginningless lifetimes, I have had no weariness or aversion, so why should I not bear the suffering of ascetic hardships now in accomplishing the excellent path of the supreme vehicle that will make me attain the great purpose, the state of a Buddha?"—through the power of that, they will overwhelm the long duration of time and all suffering, and their joyous effort will extensively increase.

heading: འབྲས་བུ་ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: If one asks, "What qualities and benefits are there in patience like that?" If any bodhisattva is endowed with the virtuous phenomena of the patience of being unconcerned about harm-doers and the patience of certainty regarding phenomena, having taken a thorough measure, if some person were to fill this great trichiliocosm with various precious things such as gold and silver and offer it to the knowers of the world, the Lord Buddhas, and to the śrāvaka arhats and pratyekabuddhas, that aggregate of generosity would not dare to compete even for a fraction of merit with that one endowed with the supreme practice of the perfection of patience.

If someone else were to say to them these words, "Destroy this Mount Meru, the king of mountains, and after you have destroyed it you will attain supreme awakening," and having heard that, if they were to think, "How can I destroy this Mount Meru which is extremely vast, high, and firm?" and generate a mind of difficulty and weariness, and also generate or think about the measure of time such as eons—at the time of generating such a discouraged mind, that bodhisattva has become lazy, because their joyous mind has degenerated. Whatever bodhisattva thinks, "If unsurpassable awakening is attained with the measure of just this much joyous effort, why is this difficult at all?" and, without holding to a measure of time, generates courage and a joyous mind that is capable of crushing that Mount Meru into dust in a mere instant of time, that bodhisattva of great courage and skilled in means has exerted the supreme joyous effort; without taking a long time, they will attain the supreme awakening of a Lord Buddha, leading wandering beings out of cyclic existence.

Even if one exerts joyous effort in that way, it is important to be without adherence. If one exerts oneself in accomplishing the welfare of others with body, speech, and mind from within a state of perception that apprehends characteristics of self and other, thinking, "Through the wondrous conduct of being skilled in means to tame whoever needs taming, such as teaching the profound and vast dharma, I shall completely mature wandering beings and accomplish the welfare of others, such as placing them on the grounds and paths!"—because one abides in the perception of a personal self, it becomes laziness relative to the supramundane objectless joyous effort. Because one is bound by the apprehension of characteristics, it has become the discordant class of pure joyous effort, and therefore one will become far from omniscience itself, just as, for example, a place and the ground are far apart.

[3-314] translation already produced for this document:
The manner of having to train in the perfection of patience by being unconcerned about ascetic hardships and suffering, like the Conqueror's son Sadāprarudita relying on the noble Dharmodgata in order to seek the perfection of wisdom, is as follows: At the time of acting for the welfare of wandering beings, if one hears from other persons many harsh words speaking ill, such as exposing one's faults and deprecating one, the bodhisattva skilled in means will become joyful, thinking, "The practice of patience arises in dependence on the object of patience, and by its power great merit will increase, therefore this is the cause of my happiness." Not only that, having examined and analyzed with pure reasoning, when searching with rational cognition, thinking, "Who is the speaker speaking these harsh words? And who is the object spoken to that hears them? By what cause, such as anger? Expressing what? For what purpose do they speak?"—one does not find even the slightest thing. Because it is not established ultimately, having realized it to be an illusion-like dependent arising, one who is endowed with the supreme perfection of patience is wise or learned, because they are a supremely wise one who realizes that one should not become angry at phenomena that are like a dream and an illusion.

heading: འབྲས་བུ་ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: The ripened result of abiding in patience is that the body will become completely pure like refined gold, endowed with the thirty-two excellent marks such as the hands and feet being marked with wheels, and endowed with the eighty minor signs such as the strength and power of Nārāyaṇa and nails that are red like the color of copper, and so on limitlessly. The result of personal effort of the patience of certainty regarding phenomena is that one will proclaim the supremely excellent dharma, profound emptiness, to the sentient beings to be tamed; the dominant result is that in this world wandering beings without exception will pay respect to that bodhisattva endowed with patience; and the result of separation is that, being separated from the delusion of unknowing, one will become skilled in the points of what to adopt and what to reject.

If someone else were to say to them these words, "Destroy this Mount Meru, the king of mountains, and after you have destroyed it you will attain supreme awakening," and having heard that, if they were to think, "How can I destroy this Mount Meru which is extremely vast, high, and firm?" and generate a mind of difficulty and weariness, and also generate or think about the measure of time such as eons—at the time of generating such a discouraged mind, that bodhisattva has become lazy, because their joyous mind has degenerated. Whatever bodhisattva thinks, "If unsurpassable awakening is attained with the measure of just this much joyous effort, why is this difficult at all?" and, without holding to a measure of time, generates courage and a joyous mind that is capable of crushing that Mount Meru into dust in a mere instant of time, that bodhisattva of great courage and skilled in means has exerted the supreme joyous effort; without taking a long time, they will attain the supreme awakening of a Lord Buddha, leading wandering beings out of cyclic existence.

Even if one exerts joyous effort in that way, it is important to be without adherence. If one exerts oneself in accomplishing the welfare of others with body, speech, and mind from within a state of perception that apprehends characteristics of self and other, thinking, "Through the wondrous conduct of being skilled in means to tame whoever needs taming, such as teaching the profound and vast dharma, I shall completely mature wandering beings and accomplish the welfare of others, such as placing them on the grounds and paths!"—because one abides in the perception of a personal self, it becomes laziness relative to the supramundane objectless joyous effort. Because one is bound by the apprehension of characteristics, it has become the discordant class of pure joyous effort, and therefore one will become far from omniscience itself, just as, for example, a place and the ground are far apart.

If one asks, "Then in what manner should one exert joyous effort?" When exerting joyous effort, one does not have a perception of the agent exerting it, of one's own body and mind, or of others as sentient beings, and the perception holding the three spheres of joyous effort to be truly existent is completely reversed; practicing the way of phenomena as empty of true existence and illusion-like, without falling into the two extremes of permanence and annihilation—this is the very perfection of joyous effort of bodhisattvas who desire to attain the state of the supreme qualities of abandonment and realization, great awakening, the pacification of all stains of the two obscurations without ever degenerating, so say the Conquerors who act for the benefit of wandering beings.

[3-314] translation already produced for this document:
The manner of having to train in the perfection of patience by being unconcerned about ascetic hardships and suffering, like the Conqueror's son Sadāprarudita relying on the noble Dharmodgata in order to seek the perfection of wisdom, is as follows: At the time of acting for the welfare of wandering beings, if one hears from other persons many harsh words speaking ill, such as exposing one's faults and deprecating one, the bodhisattva skilled in means will become joyful, thinking, "The practice of patience arises in dependence on the object of patience, and by its power great merit will increase, therefore this is the cause of my happiness." Not only that, having examined and analyzed with pure reasoning, when searching with rational cognition, thinking, "Who is the speaker speaking these harsh words? And who is the object spoken to that hears them? By what cause, such as anger? Expressing what? For what purpose do they speak?"—one does not find even the slightest thing. Because it is not established ultimately, having realized it to be an illusion-like dependent arising, one who is endowed with the supreme perfection of patience is wise or learned, because they are a supremely wise one who realizes that one should not become angry at phenomena that are like a dream and an illusion.

heading: འབྲས་བུ་ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: In order to teach the patience of voluntarily accepting suffering and the patience of individually analyzing phenomena, it was said: If some sentient beings, having taken a packet or powder of sandalwood, were to rub and anoint the body of the bodhisattva with a completely respectful mind, and some other beings, with a mind desiring to do harm, were to scatter impure fire-embers on their head—toward both of these, that bodhisattva, through the power of having meditated on phenomena as being selfless and the power of having trained in the awakening mind of equalizing and exchanging self and others, should generate an even and equal mind without attachment and aversion. If the bodhisattva, skilled in the meaning of the abiding nature, having practiced patience in that way, were to completely dedicate that generation of a mind endowed with patience to the supreme unsurpassable awakening for the welfare of others, that bodhisattva, a great hero who is brave in accomplishing awakening for the welfare of others, by meditating on a patience that benefits all sentient beings in the world, will outshine all the meditations on patience by śrāvaka arhats, pratyekabuddhas, and however many wandering beings there are in the realms of other sentient beings, because it is embraced by special skillful means.

If someone else were to say to them these words, "Destroy this Mount Meru, the king of mountains, and after you have destroyed it you will attain supreme awakening," and having heard that, if they were to think, "How can I destroy this Mount Meru which is extremely vast, high, and firm?" and generate a mind of difficulty and weariness, and also generate or think about the measure of time such as eons—at the time of generating such a discouraged mind, that bodhisattva has become lazy, because their joyous mind has degenerated. Whatever bodhisattva thinks, "If unsurpassable awakening is attained with the measure of just this much joyous effort, why is this difficult at all?" and, without holding to a measure of time, generates courage and a joyous mind that is capable of crushing that Mount Meru into dust in a mere instant of time, that bodhisattva of great courage and skilled in means has exerted the supreme joyous effort; without taking a long time, they will attain the supreme awakening of a Lord Buddha, leading wandering beings out of cyclic existence.

[3-312] translation already produced for this document:
Even if one exerts joyous effort in that way, it is important to be without adherence. If one exerts oneself in accomplishing the welfare of others with body, speech, and mind from within a state of perception that apprehends characteristics of self and other, thinking, "Through the wondrous conduct of being skilled in means to tame whoever needs taming, such as teaching the profound and vast dharma, I shall completely mature wandering beings and accomplish the welfare of others, such as placing them on the grounds and paths!"—because one abides in the perception of a personal self, it becomes laziness relative to the supramundane objectless joyous effort. Because one is bound by the apprehension of characteristics, it has become the discordant class of pure joyous effort, and therefore one will become far from omniscience itself, just as, for example, a place and the ground are far apart.

If one asks, "Then in what manner should one exert joyous effort?" When exerting joyous effort, one does not have a perception of the agent exerting it, of one's own body and mind, or of others as sentient beings, and the perception holding the three spheres of joyous effort to be truly existent is completely reversed; practicing the way of phenomena as empty of true existence and illusion-like, without falling into the two extremes of permanence and annihilation—this is the very perfection of joyous effort of bodhisattvas who desire to attain the state of the supreme qualities of abandonment and realization, great awakening, the pacification of all stains of the two obscurations without ever degenerating, so say the Conquerors who act for the benefit of wandering beings.

[3-314] translation already produced for this document:
The manner of having to train in the perfection of patience by being unconcerned about ascetic hardships and suffering, like the Conqueror's son Sadāprarudita relying on the noble Dharmodgata in order to seek the perfection of wisdom, is as follows: At the time of acting for the welfare of wandering beings, if one hears from other persons many harsh words speaking ill, such as exposing one's faults and deprecating one, the bodhisattva skilled in means will become joyful, thinking, "The practice of patience arises in dependence on the object of patience, and by its power great merit will increase, therefore this is the cause of my happiness." Not only that, having examined and analyzed with pure reasoning, when searching with rational cognition, thinking, "Who is the speaker speaking these harsh words? And who is the object spoken to that hears them? By what cause, such as anger? Expressing what? For what purpose do they speak?"—one does not find even the slightest thing. Because it is not established ultimately, having realized it to be an illusion-like dependent arising, one who is endowed with the supreme perfection of patience is wise or learned, because they are a supremely wise one who realizes that one should not become angry at phenomena that are like a dream and an illusion.

heading: འབྲས་བུ་ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: The one who practices patience should also generate their mind thinking this: "In the hells of sentient beings, the animal realm, and the world of Yama, which is the realm of hungry ghosts, there are many kinds of difficult-to-bear sufferings such as heat, cold, hunger, and thirst. All of those arise from the cause of attachment to contaminated sensory qualities, and although one experiences those harms without any freedom, they are experienced entirely meaninglessly, without even the slightest benefit to oneself or others. If this is so, for the sake of obtaining unsurpassable awakening, which brings the twofold welfare of oneself and others to perfection without exception, why should I not patiently endure the suffering of ascetic hardships now?" Having thought thus, thinking, "I will patiently endure and voluntarily accept being struck with iron, beaten with sticks, pierced by weapons such as swords, being deprived of life and killed, being bound with iron fetters, being struck with stones, fists, and so forth, having my head cut off, having my ears, hands, feet, nose, and so forth cut off, and in short, all the harms and however many sufferings there are in the world," that bodhisattva will abide in the perfection of patience just like Sadāprarudita. Thus it is said. From the commentary on the Verses of the Precious Qualities Collection titled "The Jeweled Lamp that Illuminates the Suchness of Profound Dependent Arising, Fulfilling the Hopes of the Fortunate," this is the commentary on the thirtieth chapter, the chapter on Sadāprarudita.

The manner of having to train in the perfection of patience by being unconcerned about ascetic hardships and suffering, like the Conqueror's son Sadāprarudita relying on the noble Dharmodgata in order to seek the perfection of wisdom, is as follows: At the time of acting for the welfare of wandering beings, if one hears from other persons many harsh words speaking ill, such as exposing one's faults and deprecating one, the bodhisattva skilled in means will become joyful, thinking, "The practice of patience arises in dependence on the object of patience, and by its power great merit will increase, therefore this is the cause of my happiness." Not only that, having examined and analyzed with pure reasoning, when searching with rational cognition, thinking, "Who is the speaker speaking these harsh words? And who is the object spoken to that hears them? By what cause, such as anger? Expressing what? For what purpose do they speak?"—one does not find even the slightest thing. Because it is not established ultimately, having realized it to be an illusion-like dependent arising, one who is endowed with the supreme perfection of patience is wise or learned, because they are a supremely wise one who realizes that one should not become angry at phenomena that are like a dream and an illusion.

If any bodhisattva is endowed with the virtuous phenomena of the patience of being unconcerned about harm-doers and the patience of certainty regarding phenomena, having taken a thorough measure, if some person were to fill this great trichiliocosm with various precious things such as gold and silver and offer it to the knowers of the world, the Lord Buddhas, and to the śrāvaka arhats and pratyekabuddhas, that aggregate of generosity would not dare to compete even for a fraction of merit with that one endowed with the supreme practice of the perfection of patience.

The ripened result of abiding in patience is that the body will become completely pure like refined gold, endowed with the thirty-two excellent marks such as the hands and feet being marked with wheels, and endowed with the eighty minor signs such as the strength and power of Nārāyaṇa and nails that are red like the color of copper, and so on limitlessly. In order to teach the patience of voluntarily accepting suffering and the patience of individually analyzing phenomena, it was said: If some sentient beings, having taken a packet or powder of sandalwood, were to rub and anoint the body of the bodhisattva with a completely respectful mind, and some other beings, with a mind desiring to do harm, were to scatter impure fire-embers on their head—toward both of these, that bodhisattva, through the power of having meditated on phenomena as being selfless and the power of having trained in the awakening mind of equalizing and exchanging self and others, should generate an even and equal mind without attachment and aversion. If the bodhisattva, skilled in the meaning of the abiding nature, having practiced patience in that way, were to completely dedicate that generation of a mind endowed with patience to the supreme unsurpassable awakening for the welfare of others, that bodhisattva, a great hero who is brave in accomplishing awakening for the welfare of others, by meditating on a patience that benefits all sentient beings in the world, will outshine all the meditations on patience by śrāvaka arhats, pratyekabuddhas, and however many wandering beings there are in the realms of other sentient beings, because it is embraced by special skillful means.

heading: འབྲས་བུ་ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: Thus, from the virtuous spiritual friend extensively granting profound and vast instructions to the suitable disciple who has properly relied upon and pleased the holy spiritual friend, since it is the foundation of all qualities, the instruction first on the perfection of moral discipline and then on the perfection of generosity and so forth is as follows. The meaning of what is stated in the eighteen verses starting with "By moral discipline": First, teaching the benefits by identifying the essence of moral discipline: "By moral discipline," such as the moral discipline of restraining faulty behavior, those who desire to obtain the state of peaceful nirvāṇa will obtain the exceptionally exalted qualities of the path, because that moral discipline is like a staircase leading to the mansion of liberation. Moreover, especially, the moral discipline of the bodhisattva "abides in the field of experience of the ten powers," which means it is the moral discipline of training in the footsteps of the Buddha, who possesses the ten powers, because it is not stained by the defilement of lower vehicle mental engagement and, since all faults and downfalls have been abandoned, the moral discipline is unimpaired. This teaches the moral discipline of restraining faulty behavior. As for "restraining," which is moral discipline, it follows after all virtuous phenomena, however many there are, such as the six perfections; because one guards against all discordant factors to be abandoned and practices their antidotes, virtuous phenomena, it is also called the moral discipline of gathering virtuous phenomena. Guarding in order to bring about benefit and happiness for all sentient beings, and dedicating that to great awakening, is the moral discipline of working for the welfare of sentient beings. Having briefly taught the essence of moral discipline in this way, just as the bodhisattva Dharmodgata, although occasionally appearing to joyously enjoy and revel in the five sensory qualities, had completely pure moral discipline, the purity or impurity of a bodhisattva's moral discipline must be posited on the basis of whether or not there is mental engagement in one's own welfare: If one guards moral discipline with a mind desiring to touch or obtain the awakening of a pratyekabuddha or śrāvaka arhat, relative to the path of the Great Vehicle, that person's moral discipline is flawed and they are unskilled in means, and likewise their intention and application are inferior, and they have fallen away from the conduct of a Conqueror's child, because they will fall into the inferior path. If, however, that very guarding of moral discipline is completely dedicated to the supreme unsurpassable awakening, the supreme pacification of the two obscurations, for the welfare of others, even if that bodhisattva abides earnestly enjoying the five sensory qualities, they abide in the perfection of moral discipline, because there is no falling away from the path of the Great Vehicle.

In order to teach the patience of voluntarily accepting suffering and the patience of individually analyzing phenomena, it was said: If some sentient beings, having taken a packet or powder of sandalwood, were to rub and anoint the body of the bodhisattva with a completely respectful mind, and some other beings, with a mind desiring to do harm, were to scatter impure fire-embers on their head—toward both of these, that bodhisattva, through the power of having meditated on phenomena as being selfless and the power of having trained in the awakening mind of equalizing and exchanging self and others, should generate an even and equal mind without attachment and aversion. If the bodhisattva, skilled in the meaning of the abiding nature, having practiced patience in that way, were to completely dedicate that generation of a mind endowed with patience to the supreme unsurpassable awakening for the welfare of others, that bodhisattva, a great hero who is brave in accomplishing awakening for the welfare of others, by meditating on a patience that benefits all sentient beings in the world, will outshine all the meditations on patience by śrāvaka arhats, pratyekabuddhas, and however many wandering beings there are in the realms of other sentient beings, because it is embraced by special skillful means.

[3-318] translation already produced for this document:
The one who practices patience should also generate their mind thinking this: "In the hells of sentient beings, the animal realm, and the world of Yama, which is the realm of hungry ghosts, there are many kinds of difficult-to-bear sufferings such as heat, cold, hunger, and thirst. All of those arise from the cause of attachment to contaminated sensory qualities, and although one experiences those harms without any freedom, they are experienced entirely meaninglessly, without even the slightest benefit to oneself or others. If this is so, for the sake of obtaining unsurpassable awakening, which brings the twofold welfare of oneself and others to perfection without exception, why should I not patiently endure the suffering of ascetic hardships now?" Having thought thus, thinking, "I will patiently endure and voluntarily accept being struck with iron, beaten with sticks, pierced by weapons such as swords, being deprived of life and killed, being bound with iron fetters, being struck with stones, fists, and so forth, having my head cut off, having my ears, hands, feet, nose, and so forth cut off, and in short, all the harms and however many sufferings there are in the world," that bodhisattva will abide in the perfection of patience just like Sadāprarudita. Thus it is said. From the commentary on the Verses of the Precious Qualities Collection titled "The Jeweled Lamp that Illuminates the Suchness of Profound Dependent Arising, Fulfilling the Hopes of the Fortunate," this is the commentary on the thirtieth chapter, the chapter on Sadāprarudita.

heading: འབྲས་བུ་ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: Whichever phenomena to be trained in are practiced by the noble bodhisattvas, through which the qualities of the supreme unsurpassable awakening to be obtained will arise, that is stated to be the meaning of the moral discipline of the bodhisattvas, which is endowed with the virtuous phenomena of accomplishing the benefit and happiness of others. Whatever phenomena are tainted by the defilement of lower vehicle mental engagement, by which the minds that accomplish the benefit and happiness of others completely fall away from the result to be obtained, great awakening, this is stated by the Guide to be the flawed moral discipline of a bodhisattva. If any bodhisattva, although appearing from the perspective of worldly beings to joyously enjoy the five sensory qualities, has taken refuge from the depths of their heart in the Buddha, Dharma, and noble Saṅgha, and, thinking "I will accomplish the state of a Buddha for the welfare of other sentient beings," is not separated from mental engagement in omniscience, that bodhisattva, skilled in means, should be known to abide in the perfection of the moral discipline of the bodhisattva vows.

If one asks, "What qualities and benefits are there in patience like that?" If any bodhisattva is endowed with the virtuous phenomena of the patience of being unconcerned about harm-doers and the patience of certainty regarding phenomena, having taken a thorough measure, if some person were to fill this great trichiliocosm with various precious things such as gold and silver and offer it to the knowers of the world, the Lord Buddhas, and to the śrāvaka arhats and pratyekabuddhas, that aggregate of generosity would not dare to compete even for a fraction of merit with that one endowed with the supreme practice of the perfection of patience.

བཟོད་པ་ལ་གནས་པའི་རྣམ་སྨིན་གྱི་འབྲས་བུ། ལུས་ནི་གཙོ་མའི་གསེར་ལྟར་ཡོངས་སུ་དག་པར་འགྱུར་ཏེ་ཕྱག་ཞབས་འཁོར་ལོས་མཚན་པ་ལ་སོགས་པའི་སུམ་ཅུ་རྩ་གཉིས་ཀྱི་གྲངས་དང་ལྡན་པའི་མཚན་བཟང་པོ་དང་། སྲེད་མེད་ཀྱི་བུས་མཐུ་སྟོབས་དང་སེན་མོ་ཟངས་ཀྱི་མདོག་ལྟར་དམར་བ་ལ་སོགས་པའི་དཔེ་བྱེད་བརྒྱད་ཅུ་དང་ལྡན་པར་འགྱུར་བ་སོགས་ཕ་མཐའ་ཡས་སོ། །ཆོས་ལ་ངེས་སེམས་ཀྱི་བཟོད་པའི་སྐྱེས་བུ་བྱེད་འབྲས་གདུལ་བྱའི་སེམས་ཅན་རྣམས་ལ་ཆོས་རབ་ཏུ་ཕུལ་དུ་བྱུང་བ་ཟབ་མོ་སྟོང་པ་ཉིད་སྒྲོགས་པར་བྱེད་པར་འགྱུར་ཞིང་བདག་པོའི་འབྲས་བུ་ནི་འཇིག་རྟེན་འདི་ནི་བཟོད་པ་དང་ལྡན་པའི་བྱང་སེམས་དེ་ལ་འགྲོ་བ་མ་ལུས་པ་འགའ་ཞིག་བཀུར་སྟི་བྱེད་པར་འགྱུར་ལ། བྲལ་པའི་འབྲས་བུ་ནི་མི་ཤེས་པའི་རྨོངས་པ་དང་བྲལ་ནས་བླང་དོར་གྱི་གནས་ལ་མཁས་པར་འགྱུར་རོ། །
[3-316] translation already produced for this document:
The ripened result of abiding in patience is that the body will become completely pure like refined gold, endowed with the thirty-two excellent marks such as the hands and feet being marked with wheels, and endowed with the eighty minor signs such as the strength and power of Nārāyaṇa and nails that are red like the color of copper, and so on limitlessly. The result of personal effort of the patience of certainty regarding phenomena is that one will proclaim the supremely excellent dharma, profound emptiness, to the sentient beings to be tamed; the dominant result is that in this world wandering beings without exception will pay respect to that bodhisattva endowed with patience; and the result of separation is that, being separated from the delusion of unknowing, one will become skilled in the points of what to adopt and what to reject.

[3-317] source:
སྡུག་བསྔལ་དང་ལེན་གྱི་བཟོད་པ་དང༌། ཆོས་ལ་སོ་སོར་རྟོག་པའི་བཟོད་པ་བཅས་བསྟན་པའི་ཕྱིར་གསུངས་པ། གལ་ཏེ་སེམས་ཅན་ལ་ལས་ཙན་དན་གྱི་ཕུར་མའམ་ཕྱེ་མ་བླངས་ནས་རབ་ཏུ་གུས་པའི་ཡིད་ཀྱིས་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཡི་ལུས་ལ་ནི་ཉུག་ཅིང་བྱུག་པར་བྱེད་ལ། སྐྱེ་བོ་གཞན་འགའ་ཞིག་གིས་འཚེ་བར་འདོད་པའི་སེམས་ཀྱི་མེ་མ་དག་དེ་ཡི་མགོ་ལ་འཐོར་བར་བྱེད་པ་དེ་གཉིས་ཀ་ལ། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་དེ་ཡིས་ཆོས་ལ་བདག་མེད་པ་བསྒོམས་པའི་སྟོབས་དང་བདག་གཞན་མཉམ་བརྗེས་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཀྱི་སེམས་འབྱོངས་པའི་སྟོབས་ཀྱིས་ཆགས་པ་དང་སྡང་བ་མེད་པར་མཉམ་ཞིང་སྙོམས་པའི་སེམས་ནི་བསྐྱེད་པར་བྱའོ། །བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གནས་ལུགས་ཀྱི་དོན་ལ་མཁས་པས་དེ་ལྟར་བཟོད་པར་བྱས་ནས། བཟོད་པ་དང་ལྡན་པའི་སེམས་བསྐྱེད་དེ་ནི་གཞན་དོན་དུ་བླ་མེད་བྱང་ཆུབ་མཆོག་ཏུ་ཡོངས་སུ་བསྔོ་བར་བྱས་ན། གཞན་དོན་དུ་བྱང་ཆུབ་སྒྲུབ་པ་ལ་དཔའ་བའི་དཔའ་བོ་ཆེན་པོ་བྱང་སེམས་དེ་ནི་འཇིག་རྟེན་སེམས་ཅན་ཀུན་ལ་ཕན་པའི་བཟོད་པ་བསྒོམ་པས་ཉན་ཐོས་དགྲ་བཅོམ་པ་དང་རང་རྒྱལ་རྣམས་དང་གཞན་སེམས་ཅན་གྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་འགྲོ་བ་མང་པོ་ཇི་སྙེད་མཆིས་པ་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་བཟོད་པ་བསྒོམ་པ་ཐམས་ཅད་ཟིལ་གྱིས་གནོན་པར་འགྱུར་ཏེ་ཐབས་ཁྱད་པར་ཅན་གྱིས་ཟིན་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །
[3-317] translation already produced for this document:
In order to teach the patience of voluntarily accepting suffering and the patience of individually analyzing phenomena, it was said: If some sentient beings, having taken a packet or powder of sandalwood, were to rub and anoint the body of the bodhisattva with a completely respectful mind, and some other beings, with a mind desiring to do harm, were to scatter impure fire-embers on their head—toward both of these, that bodhisattva, through the power of having meditated on phenomena as being selfless and the power of having trained in the awakening mind of equalizing and exchanging self and others, should generate an even and equal mind without attachment and aversion. If the bodhisattva, skilled in the meaning of the abiding nature, having practiced patience in that way, were to completely dedicate that generation of a mind endowed with patience to the supreme unsurpassable awakening for the welfare of others, that bodhisattva, a great hero who is brave in accomplishing awakening for the welfare of others, by meditating on a patience that benefits all sentient beings in the world, will outshine all the meditations on patience by śrāvaka arhats, pratyekabuddhas, and however many wandering beings there are in the realms of other sentient beings, because it is embraced by special skillful means.

[3-318] source:
བཟོད་པ་བྱེད་པ་པོ་དེ་འདི་སྙམ་དུ་ཡང་རང་གི་སེམས་ནི་བསྐྱེད་པར་བྱ་སྟེ། སེམས་ཅན་དམྱལ་བ་རྣམས་དང་དུ་དུད་འགྲོ་དང་གཤིན་རྗེའི་འཇིག་རྟེན་ཏེ་ཡི་དྭགས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ན་ཚ་གྲང་བཀྲེས་སྐོམས་སོགས་སྡུག་བསྔལ་བཟོད་དཀའ་ཞིང་རྣམ་པ་མང་པོ་ཡོད་པ་དེ་དག་ཐམས་ཅད་ཟག་བཅས་ཀྱི་འདོད་པའི་ཡོན་ཏན་ལ་ཆགས་པའི་རྒྱུ་ཡིས་འབྱུང་ཞིང་རང་དབང་མེད་པར་གནོད་པ་དེ་དག་མྱོང་ཡང་རང་གཞན་ལ་ཕན་པ་ཅུང་ཟད་མེད་པར་དོན་མེད་ཁོ་ནར་མྱོང་བ་ཡིན་ན། རང་གཞན་གྱི་དོན་གཉིས་མ་ལུས་པ་མཐར་ཕྱིན་པའི་བླ་མེད་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཐོབ་པའི་ཆེད་དུ་ཅི་ཡི་ཕྱིར་ན་ད་ལྟ་བདག་གིས་དཀའ་སྤྱད་ཀྱི་སྡུག་བསྔལ་བཟོད་པར་མི་བྱ་སྙམ་དུ་བསམ་ནས། ལྕགས་གིས་གཞུར་བ་དང་དབྱུག་པས་བརྡེག་པ་དང་རལ་གྲི་ལ་སོགས་པའི་མཚོན་གྱིས་བསྣུན་པ་དང་སྲོག་བཅད་དེ་བསད་པ་དང་ལྕགས་སྒྲོགས་ཀྱིས་བཅིངས་པ་དང་རྡོ་དང་ཁུ་ཚུལ་སོགས་ཀྱིས་བརྡེག་པ་དང་མགོ་བོ་གཅོད་པ་དང་རྣ་བ་རྐང་ལག་སྣ་ལ་སོགས་པ་གཅོད་པ་དང་། མདོར་ན་འཇིག་རྟེན་ན་གང་དག་ཡོད་པའི་གནོད་པ་དང་སྡུག་བསྔལ་ཇི་སྙེད་པ་ཐམས་ཅད་བདག་གིས་བཟོད་པར་བྱས་ནས་དང་དུ་བླངས་བར་བྱའོ་སྙམ་པ་ཡི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་དེ་ནི་རྟག་ཏུ་ངུ་བཞིན་དུ་བཟོད་པའི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་གནས་པར་འགྱུར་རོ། །ཞེས་པའོ། །ཡོན་ཏན་རིན་པོ་ཆེ་སྡུད་པ་ཚིགས་སུ་བཅད་པའི་འགྲེལ་བ་ཟབ་མོ་རྟེན་འབྱུང་གི་དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཉིད་གསལ་བར་བྱེད་པའི་ནོར་བུའི་སྒྲོན་མེ་སྐལ་བཟང་རེ་སྐོང་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལས། རྟག་ཏུ་ངུའི་ལེའུ་སྟེ་སུམ་བཅུ་པའི་འགྲེལ་བའོ༎   །།
[3-318] translation already produced for this document:
The one who practices patience should also generate their mind thinking this: "In the hells of sentient beings, the animal realm, and the world of Yama, which is the realm of hungry ghosts, there are many kinds of difficult-to-bear sufferings such as heat, cold, hunger, and thirst. All of those arise from the cause of attachment to contaminated sensory qualities, and although one experiences those harms without any freedom, they are experienced entirely meaninglessly, without even the slightest benefit to oneself or others. If this is so, for the sake of obtaining unsurpassable awakening, which brings the twofold welfare of oneself and others to perfection without exception, why should I not patiently endure the suffering of ascetic hardships now?" Having thought thus, thinking, "I will patiently endure and voluntarily accept being struck with iron, beaten with sticks, pierced by weapons such as swords, being deprived of life and killed, being bound with iron fetters, being struck with stones, fists, and so forth, having my head cut off, having my ears, hands, feet, nose, and so forth cut off, and in short, all the harms and however many sufferings there are in the world," that bodhisattva will abide in the perfection of patience just like Sadāprarudita. Thus it is said. From the commentary on the Verses of the Precious Qualities Collection titled "The Jeweled Lamp that Illuminates the Suchness of Profound Dependent Arising, Fulfilling the Hopes of the Fortunate," this is the commentary on the thirtieth chapter, the chapter on Sadāprarudita.

heading: འབྲས་བུ་ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: Alternatively, if one practices the ten virtuous paths of action for hundreds of thousands of ten millions of eons, yet generates a desire to obtain for oneself the level of a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha arhat, then a fault has occurred in the bodhisattva's moral discipline and the moral discipline uncommon to the Great Vehicle is impaired, because having abandoned the welfare of others, generating a mind desiring to obtain the awakening of a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha for one's own welfare is a much heavier fault for that bodhisattva than the occurrence of the four root downfalls of a fully ordained monk, since they will fall away from unsurpassable awakening.

Work: ཡོན་ཏན་རིན་པོ་ཆེ་སྡུད་པ་ཚིགས་སུ་བཅད་པའི་འགྲེལ་པ་ཟབ་མོ་རྟེན་འབྱུང་གི་དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཉིད་གསལ་བར་བྱེད་པའི་ནོར་བུའི་སྒྲོན་མེ་སྐལ་བཟང་རེ་སྐོང་། (Khenrab Jamyang, Commentary on the Verses of the Precious Qualities Collection), author: མཁྱེན་རབ་འཇམ་དབྱངས་བློ་བཟང་འཕྲིན་ལས།. [3-319] source:
དེ་ལྟར་བཤེས་གཉེན་དམ་པ་ཚུལ་བཞིན་དུ་བསྟེན་ཅིང་མཉེས་པར་བྱས་པའི་སྣོད་ལྡན་གྱི་གདུལ་བྱ་ལ་དགེ་བའི་བཤེས་གཉེན་གྱིས་ཟབ་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་གདམས་པ་རྒྱ་ཆེར་སྩལ་བར་འགྱུར་བ་ལས་ཡོན་ཏན་ཐམསཅད་ཀྱི་གཞི་ཡིན་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཐོག་མར་ཚུལ་ཁྲིམསཀྱི་ཕར་ཕྱིན་དང་དེ་ནས་སྦྱིན་པའི་ཕར་ཕྱིན་སོགས་ལ་གདམས་པ་ནི། ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་ཀྱིས་ནི་ཞེས་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་བཅོ་བརྒྱད་གསུངས་པའི་དོན་ནི། ཐོག་མར་ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་ངོ་བོ་ངོས་བཟུང་བའི་སྒོ་ནས་ཕན་ཡོན་བསྟན་པ་ནི། ཉེས་སྤྱོད་སྡོམ་པའི་ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་ལ་སོགས་པའི་ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་ཀྱིས་ནི་ཞི་བ་མྱང་འདས་ཀྱི་གོ་འཕང་ཐོབ་པར་འདོད་པ་རྣམས་ལ་ལམ་གྱི་ཡོན་ཏན་ཁྱད་པར་དུ་འཕགས་པ་ཐོབ་པར་འགྱུར་ཏེ་ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་དེ་ནི་ཐར་པའི་ཁང་བཟང་དུ་བསྒྲོད་པའི་ཐེམ་སྐས་ལྟ་བུ་ཡིན་པའི་ཕྱིར། ཁྱད་པར་དུ་ཡང་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའི་ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་ནི་སྟོབས་བཅུའི་སྤྱོད་ཡུལ་གནས་ཤིང་ཞེས། སྟོབས་བཅུ་མངའ་བ་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་རྗེས་སུ་སློབ་པའི་ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་ཡིན་ཏེ། ཐེག་དམན་ཡིད་བྱེད་ཀྱི་དྲི་མས་མ་གོས་ཤིང་ཉེས་ལྟུང་མཐའ་དག་སྤངས་པས་ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་ཉམས་པ་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །འདིས་ཉེས་སྤྱོད་སྡོམ་པའི་ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་བསྟན་ཏོ། །སྡོམ་བ་བྱ་བ་སྟེ་ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་ནི། ཕར་ཕྱིན་དྲུག་ལ་སོགས་པའི་དགེ་བའི་ཆོས་ཇི་སྙེད་ཡོད་པ་ཀུན་གྱི་རྗེས་སུ་འཇུག་པ་ཡིན་ཏེ། སྤངས་བྱ་མི་མཐུན་ཕྱོགས་མཐའ་དག་ལས་སྲུང་ཞིང་དེའི་གཉེན་པོ་དགེ་བའི་ཆོས་ཉམས་སུ་ལེན་པའི་ཕྱིར་དགེ་བ་ཆོས་སྡུད་ཀྱི་ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་ཞེས་ཀྱང་བྱ་ལ། སེམས་ཅན་ཀུན་ལ་ཕན་པ་དང་བདེ་བ་འབྱུང་བའི་ཕྱིར་སྲུང་བར་བྱེད་ལ་དེ་ཡང་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཆེན་པོར་བསྔོ་བ་ནི་སེམས་ཅན་དོན་བྱེད་ཀྱི་ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་ཡིན་ནོ་ཞེས་ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་ཀྱི་ངོ་བོ་མདོར་བསྟན་ནས་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཆོས་འཕགས་གནས་སྐབས་བདོད་ཡོན་ལྔ་ལ་དགའ་མགུར་སྤྱོད་ཅིང་རོལ་པ་ལྟར་སྣང་ཡང་ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་རྣམ་པར་དག་པ་བཞིན་བྱང་སེམས་ཀྱི་ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་དག་པ་དང་མ་དག་པ་ནི་རང་དོན་ཡིད་བྱེད་ཡོད་མེད་ཀྱི་སྟེང་ནས་འཇོག་དགོསཔ་ནི། གལ་ཏེ་རང་རྒྱལ་དང་ཉན་ཐོས་དགྲ་བཅོམ་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་ལ་རེག་པའམ་ཐོབ་པར་འདོད་པའི་སེམས་ཀྱིས་ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་སྲུང་བར་བྱེད་ན། ཐེག་ཆེན་གྱི་ལམ་ལ་ལྟོས་ཏེ་གང་ཟག་དེ་ནི་ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་འཆལ་ཞིང་ཐབས་ལ་མི་མཁས་པ་ཡིན་ལ་དེ་བཞིན་དུ་བསམ་སྦྱོར་དམན་ཞིང་རྒྱལ་སྲས་ཀྱི་སྤྱོད་པ་ལས་ཉམས་པ་ཡིན་ཏེ་དམན་ལམ་དུ་ལྟུང་བར་འགྱུར་བའི་ཕྱིར། ཇི་སྟེ་ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་སྲུང་བ་དེ་ཉིད་གཞན་དོན་དུ་བླ་ན་མེད་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སྒྲིབ་གཉིས་ཞི་བ་མཆོག་ཏུ་ཡོངས་སུ་བསྔོ་ན། བྱང་སེམས་དེ་འདོད་པའི་ཡོན་ཏན་ལྔ་ལ་ལོངས་སྤྱོད་ཅིང་བརྩོན་པས་གནས་ན་ཡང་ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལ་གནས་པ་ཡིན་ཏེ། ཐེག་པ་ཆེན་པོའི་ལམ་ལས་ཉམས་པ་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །
[3-319] translation already produced for this document:
Thus, from the virtuous spiritual friend extensively granting profound and vast instructions to the suitable disciple who has properly relied upon and pleased the holy spiritual friend, since it is the foundation of all qualities, the instruction first on the perfection of moral discipline and then on the perfection of generosity and so forth is as follows. The meaning of what is stated in the eighteen verses starting with "By moral discipline": First, teaching the benefits by identifying the essence of moral discipline: "By moral discipline," such as the moral discipline of restraining faulty behavior, those who desire to obtain the state of peaceful nirvāṇa will obtain the exceptionally exalted qualities of the path, because that moral discipline is like a staircase leading to the mansion of liberation. Moreover, especially, the moral discipline of the bodhisattva "abides in the field of experience of the ten powers," which means it is the moral discipline of training in the footsteps of the Buddha, who possesses the ten powers, because it is not stained by the defilement of lower vehicle mental engagement and, since all faults and downfalls have been abandoned, the moral discipline is unimpaired. This teaches the moral discipline of restraining faulty behavior. As for "restraining," which is moral discipline, it follows after all virtuous phenomena, however many there are, such as the six perfections; because one guards against all discordant factors to be abandoned and practices their antidotes, virtuous phenomena, it is also called the moral discipline of gathering virtuous phenomena. Guarding in order to bring about benefit and happiness for all sentient beings, and dedicating that to great awakening, is the moral discipline of working for the welfare of sentient beings. Having briefly taught the essence of moral discipline in this way, just as the bodhisattva Dharmodgata, although occasionally appearing to joyously enjoy and revel in the five sensory qualities, had completely pure moral discipline, the purity or impurity of a bodhisattva's moral discipline must be posited on the basis of whether or not there is mental engagement in one's own welfare: If one guards moral discipline with a mind desiring to touch or obtain the awakening of a pratyekabuddha or śrāvaka arhat, relative to the path of the Great Vehicle, that person's moral discipline is flawed and they are unskilled in means, and likewise their intention and application are inferior, and they have fallen away from the conduct of a Conqueror's child, because they will fall into the inferior path. If, however, that very guarding of moral discipline is completely dedicated to the supreme unsurpassable awakening, the supreme pacification of the two obscurations, for the welfare of others, even if that bodhisattva abides earnestly enjoying the five sensory qualities, they abide in the perfection of moral discipline, because there is no falling away from the path of the Great Vehicle.

བསླབ་པར་བྱ་བའི་ཆོས་གང་ཞིག་ཉམས་སུ་བླངས་པའི་དེས་པ་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་རྣམས་ཀྱི་ཐོབ་བྱ་བླ་མེད་བྱང་ཆུབ་མཆོག་གི་ཡོན་ཏན་འབྱུང་བར་འགྱུར་བ་དེ་ནི་གཞན་གྱི་ཕན་བདེ་སྒྲུབ་པའི་ཡོན་ཏན་གྱི་ཆོས་དང་ལྡན་པ་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་རྣམས་ཀྱི་ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་ཀྱི་དོན་ཡིན་པར་གསུངས་ལ། ཐེག་དམན་ཡིད་བྱེད་ཀྱི་དྲི་མས་སྤགས་པའི་ཆོས་གང་ཞིག་གཞན་གྱི་ཕན་བདེ་སྒྲུབ་པར་བྱེད་པའི་སེམས་རྣམས་ཐོབ་བྱའི་འབྲས་བུ་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཆེན་པོ་ལས་ཡོངས་སུ་ཉམས་པ་འདི་ནི་བྱང་སེམས་ཀྱི་ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་འཆལ་བ་ཡིན་ནོ་ཞེས་རྣམ་པར་འདྲེན་པས་གསུངས་སོ། །གལ་ཏེ་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གང་ཞིག་འཇིག་རྟེན་པའི་སྣང་ངོར་འདོད་པའི་ཡོན་ཏན་ལྔ་ལ་དགའ་མགུར་སྤྱོད་པར་གྱུར་ཀྱང་། སངས་རྒྱས་དང་ཆོས་དང་འཕགས་པའི་དགེ་འདུན་རྣམས་སྙིང་ཐག་པ་ནས་སྐྱབས་སུ་སོང་སྟེ་བདག་གིས་གཞན་སེམས་ཅན་གྱི་དོན་དུ་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་གོ་འཕང་འགྲུབ་པར་བྱའོ་སྙམ་དུ་ཀུན་མཁྱེན་ཡིད་བྱེད་དང་མ་བྲལ་ན། བྱང་སེམས་ཐབས་ལ་མཁས་པ་དེ་ནི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའི་སྡོམ་པའི་ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལ་གནས་པར་རིག་པར་བྱའོ། །
[3-320] translation already produced for this document:
Whichever phenomena to be trained in are practiced by the noble bodhisattvas, through which the qualities of the supreme unsurpassable awakening to be obtained will arise, that is stated to be the meaning of the moral discipline of the bodhisattvas, which is endowed with the virtuous phenomena of accomplishing the benefit and happiness of others. Whatever phenomena are tainted by the defilement of lower vehicle mental engagement, by which the minds that accomplish the benefit and happiness of others completely fall away from the result to be obtained, great awakening, this is stated by the Guide to be the flawed moral discipline of a bodhisattva. If any bodhisattva, although appearing from the perspective of worldly beings to joyously enjoy the five sensory qualities, has taken refuge from the depths of their heart in the Buddha, Dharma, and noble Saṅgha, and, thinking "I will accomplish the state of a Buddha for the welfare of other sentient beings," is not separated from mental engagement in omniscience, that bodhisattva, skilled in means, should be known to abide in the perfection of the moral discipline of the bodhisattva vows.

heading: འབྲས་བུ་ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: If one guards moral discipline and completely dedicates it to supreme awakening, has no conceit due to adhering to that moral discipline as truly existent, does not praise oneself and deprecate others on account of having heard much, moral discipline, and so forth, and has completely abandoned the perception of a naturally established 'I' and the perception of a sentient being and so forth, that bodhisattva endowed with special means and wisdom is said to abide in the perfection of moral discipline. That one must not generate true adherence and conceit even regarding such moral discipline: If bodhisattvas practicing the phenomena of the Conqueror's path, the Great Vehicle, think, "These sentient beings are endowed with moral discipline and these have flawed moral discipline," and, having adhered to the objects to be adopted and abandoned as truly existent, engage with a diverse perception, because of being bound by the apprehension of signs they are said to have very flawed moral discipline; by the downfall of dividing self and other into factions and deprecating others and so forth, the bodhisattva's moral discipline is impaired, and that person does not have completely pure moral discipline.

Thus, from the virtuous spiritual friend extensively granting profound and vast instructions to the suitable disciple who has properly relied upon and pleased the holy spiritual friend, since it is the foundation of all qualities, the instruction first on the perfection of moral discipline and then on the perfection of generosity and so forth is as follows. The meaning of what is stated in the eighteen verses starting with "By moral discipline": First, teaching the benefits by identifying the essence of moral discipline: "By moral discipline," such as the moral discipline of restraining faulty behavior, those who desire to obtain the state of peaceful nirvāṇa will obtain the exceptionally exalted qualities of the path, because that moral discipline is like a staircase leading to the mansion of liberation. Moreover, especially, the moral discipline of the bodhisattva "abides in the field of experience of the ten powers," which means it is the moral discipline of training in the footsteps of the Buddha, who possesses the ten powers, because it is not stained by the defilement of lower vehicle mental engagement and, since all faults and downfalls have been abandoned, the moral discipline is unimpaired. This teaches the moral discipline of restraining faulty behavior. As for "restraining," which is moral discipline, it follows after all virtuous phenomena, however many there are, such as the six perfections; because one guards against all discordant factors to be abandoned and practices their antidotes, virtuous phenomena, it is also called the moral discipline of gathering virtuous phenomena. Guarding in order to bring about benefit and happiness for all sentient beings, and dedicating that to great awakening, is the moral discipline of working for the welfare of sentient beings. Having briefly taught the essence of moral discipline in this way, just as the bodhisattva Dharmodgata, although occasionally appearing to joyously enjoy and revel in the five sensory qualities, had completely pure moral discipline, the purity or impurity of a bodhisattva's moral discipline must be posited on the basis of whether or not there is mental engagement in one's own welfare: If one guards moral discipline with a mind desiring to touch or obtain the awakening of a pratyekabuddha or śrāvaka arhat, relative to the path of the Great Vehicle, that person's moral discipline is flawed and they are unskilled in means, and likewise their intention and application are inferior, and they have fallen away from the conduct of a Conqueror's child, because they will fall into the inferior path. If, however, that very guarding of moral discipline is completely dedicated to the supreme unsurpassable awakening, the supreme pacification of the two obscurations, for the welfare of others, even if that bodhisattva abides earnestly enjoying the five sensory qualities, they abide in the perfection of moral discipline, because there is no falling away from the path of the Great Vehicle.

Whichever phenomena to be trained in are practiced by the noble bodhisattvas, through which the qualities of the supreme unsurpassable awakening to be obtained will arise, that is stated to be the meaning of the moral discipline of the bodhisattvas, which is endowed with the virtuous phenomena of accomplishing the benefit and happiness of others. Whatever phenomena are tainted by the defilement of lower vehicle mental engagement, by which the minds that accomplish the benefit and happiness of others completely fall away from the result to be obtained, great awakening, this is stated by the Guide to be the flawed moral discipline of a bodhisattva. If any bodhisattva, although appearing from the perspective of worldly beings to joyously enjoy the five sensory qualities, has taken refuge from the depths of their heart in the Buddha, Dharma, and noble Saṅgha, and, thinking "I will accomplish the state of a Buddha for the welfare of other sentient beings," is not separated from mental engagement in omniscience, that bodhisattva, skilled in means, should be known to abide in the perfection of the moral discipline of the bodhisattva vows.

heading: འབྲས་བུ་ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: Therefore, explaining in order to teach that one must not manifestly adhere to true existence: Because of realizing all phenomena as empty of true existence, like an illusion, and realizing and familiarizing oneself with the selflessness of persons, which lacks the perception of self and the perception of other sentient beings with respect to any object, for that one who is free from the perception of self-apprehension and the attachment arisen by the power of that, how could there be non-vows, that is, flawed moral discipline? Because there is no cause to generate it. For whatever person there is no conceit of apprehending dualistically those endowed with vows and those with non-vows, flawed moral discipline, through knowing all phenomena as having no nature, this is stated by the Guide to be the vows of a bodhisattva's moral discipline. As for "unestablished by nature" or "empty by nature," since it means empty from its own side, it means that except for being merely designated by name and concept, it is not established upon the object or from the object.

ཁྱད་པར་དུ་ཡང་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའི་ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་ནི་སྟོབས་བཅུའི་སྤྱོད་ཡུལ་གནས་ཤིང་ཞེས། སྟོབས་བཅུ་མངའ་བ་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་རྗེས་སུ་སློབ་པའི་ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་ཡིན་ཏེ། ཐེག་དམན་ཡིད་བྱེད་ཀྱི་དྲི་མས་མ་གོས་ཤིང་ཉེས་ལྟུང་མཐའ་དག་སྤངས་པས་ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་ཉམས་པ་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །འདིས་ཉེས་སྤྱོད་སྡོམ་པའི་ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་བསྟན་ཏོ། །སྡོམ་བ་བྱ་བ་སྟེ་ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་ནི། ཕར་ཕྱིན་དྲུག་ལ་སོགས་པའི་དགེ་བའི་ཆོས་ཇི་སྙེད་ཡོད་པ་ཀུན་གྱི་རྗེས་སུ་འཇུག་པ་ཡིན་ཏེ། ཐེག་ཆེན་གྱི་ལམ་ལ་ལྟོས་ཏེ་གང་ཟག་དེ་ནི་ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་འཆལ་ཞིང་ཐབས་ལ་མི་མཁས་པ་ཡིན་ལ་དེ་བཞིན་དུ་བསམ་སྦྱོར་དམན་ཞིང་རྒྱལ་སྲས་ཀྱི་སྤྱོད་པ་ལས་ཉམས་པ་ཡིན་ཏེ་དམན་ལམ་དུ་ལྟུང་བར་འགྱུར་བའི་ཕྱིར། Thus, from the virtuous spiritual friend extensively granting profound and vast instructions to the suitable disciple who has properly relied upon and pleased the holy spiritual friend, since it is the foundation of all qualities, the instruction first on the perfection of moral discipline and then on the perfection of generosity and so forth is as follows. The meaning of what is stated in the eighteen verses starting with "By moral discipline": First, teaching the benefits by identifying the essence of moral discipline: "By moral discipline," such as the moral discipline of restraining faulty behavior, those who desire to obtain the state of peaceful nirvāṇa will obtain the exceptionally exalted qualities of the path, because that moral discipline is like a staircase leading to the mansion of liberation. Moreover, especially, the moral discipline of the bodhisattva "abides in the field of experience of the ten powers," which means it is the moral discipline of training in the footsteps of the Buddha, who possesses the ten powers, because it is not stained by the defilement of lower vehicle mental engagement and, since all faults and downfalls have been abandoned, the moral discipline is unimpaired. This teaches the moral discipline of restraining faulty behavior. As for "restraining," which is moral discipline, it follows after all virtuous phenomena, however many there are, such as the six perfections; because one guards against all discordant factors to be abandoned and practices their antidotes, virtuous phenomena, it is also called the moral discipline of gathering virtuous phenomena. Guarding in order to bring about benefit and happiness for all sentient beings, and dedicating that to great awakening, is the moral discipline of working for the welfare of sentient beings. Having briefly taught the essence of moral discipline in this way, just as the bodhisattva Dharmodgata, although occasionally appearing to joyously enjoy and revel in the five sensory qualities, had completely pure moral discipline, the purity or impurity of a bodhisattva's moral discipline must be posited on the basis of whether or not there is mental engagement in one's own welfare: If one guards moral discipline with a mind desiring to touch or obtain the awakening of a pratyekabuddha or śrāvaka arhat, relative to the path of the Great Vehicle, that person's moral discipline is flawed and they are unskilled in means, and likewise their intention and application are inferior, and they have fallen away from the conduct of a Conqueror's child, because they will fall into the inferior path. If, however, that very guarding of moral discipline is completely dedicated to the supreme unsurpassable awakening, the supreme pacification of the two obscurations, for the welfare of others, even if that bodhisattva abides earnestly enjoying the five sensory qualities, they abide in the perfection of moral discipline, because there is no falling away from the path of the Great Vehicle.

Whichever phenomena to be trained in are practiced by the noble bodhisattvas, through which the qualities of the supreme unsurpassable awakening to be obtained will arise, that is stated to be the meaning of the moral discipline of the bodhisattvas, which is endowed with the virtuous phenomena of accomplishing the benefit and happiness of others. Whatever phenomena are tainted by the defilement of lower vehicle mental engagement, by which the minds that accomplish the benefit and happiness of others completely fall away from the result to be obtained, great awakening, this is stated by the Guide to be the flawed moral discipline of a bodhisattva. If any bodhisattva, although appearing from the perspective of worldly beings to joyously enjoy the five sensory qualities, has taken refuge from the depths of their heart in the Buddha, Dharma, and noble Saṅgha, and, thinking "I will accomplish the state of a Buddha for the welfare of other sentient beings," is not separated from mental engagement in omniscience, that bodhisattva, skilled in means, should be known to abide in the perfection of the moral discipline of the bodhisattva vows.

heading: འབྲས་བུ་ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: Therefore, for one who desires to enter the path of the supreme vehicle, in order to unmistakably generate the Middle Way view free from extremes in their mindstream, having properly relied on a learned spiritual friend, extensively seeking much hearing on the profound Middle Way texts and striving in accumulating merit, purifying obscurations, and so forth should be known as the supreme essence of the instructions. Explaining in order to teach that one endowed with moral discipline is able to also engage in the perfection of generosity: Whichever pure being whose mindstream is completely ripened, free from the perception of self-apprehension and the attachment arisen by the power of that just as explained earlier, and endowed with completely pure moral discipline, lacks the view of manifestly adhering to signs regarding all phenomena, attractive, i.e., agreeable, and unattractive, disagreeable. Therefore, they give even their head, limbs, and so forth to others, and at that time they do not have a mind of attachment or discouragement; by way of discarding oneself and cherishing others, they give whatever belongings or possessions one has to others, and at all times they also have no attachment to them, because, in this way, phenomena such as body, enjoyments, and so forth are natureless and selfless, arisen merely from a collection of causes and conditions; having known them as essenceless mirages, they give even the flesh of their own body to others, and if not even the slightest mind of discouragement arises regarding that, then what need is there to mention being able to give external things such as wealth, possessions, and so forth? If there were miserliness regarding those enjoyments, that is in all ways impossible, i.e., nonexistent and has no opportunity, because attachment and adherence are completely nonexistent. Teaching the drawbacks of miserliness along with the benefits of a bodhisattva's generosity: Despite 'I' or self being unestablished by nature, for fools who, perceiving a naturally established self, and, thinking 'mine' regarding things such as eyes and so forth, by apprehending them as one's own, are attached and adhere, how could they have a mind of giving away body, enjoyments, and so forth without regret? They do not; miserly ones will be born in the realms of hungry ghosts, and even if on a rare occasion they are born as humans by the power of other karma, at that time they will become poor, lacking wealth and enjoyments.

If one guards moral discipline and completely dedicates it to supreme awakening, has no conceit due to adhering to that moral discipline as truly existent, does not praise oneself and deprecate others on account of having heard much, moral discipline, and so forth, and has completely abandoned the perception of a naturally established 'I' and the perception of a sentient being and so forth, that bodhisattva endowed with special means and wisdom is said to abide in the perfection of moral discipline. That one must not generate true adherence and conceit even regarding such moral discipline: If bodhisattvas practicing the phenomena of the Conqueror's path, the Great Vehicle, think, "These sentient beings are endowed with moral discipline and these have flawed moral discipline," and, having adhered to the objects to be adopted and abandoned as truly existent, engage with a diverse perception, because of being bound by the apprehension of signs they are said to have very flawed moral discipline; by the downfall of dividing self and other into factions and deprecating others and so forth, the bodhisattva's moral discipline is impaired, and that person does not have completely pure moral discipline.
